Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Surface combustion, shs, fire safety and smoldering
Task Description: This study, along with the numerical simulation work conducted by the Laboratory for Computational Physics & Fluid Dynamics at the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), focuses on the suppression of small fires in large compartments and enclosures in various gravitational environments, such as the ones experienced by spacecraft in orbit and on the surface of the Moon and Mars. The primary goal of the experimental effort is to provide data, via ground-based, normal-gravity tests, for validating key elements of the numerical model, while providing complementary information on the interactions between the suppressant and the fire. Two classes of experiments are conducted: gaseous-fuel diffusion flames and solid-fuel thermoplastic fires. On both fire scenarios, fine water mist is used as the suppression agent. The experimental validation program provides the close coupling of the experiments to the numerical simulation work performed by the Naval Research Laboratory team (whose numerical results are published in a separate report), while simultaneously providing a realistic fire scenario in which many factors including gravity effects, obstructions, and ventilation, play a part in the response of the fire to the suppressant. In this way, the experimental work provides rapid validation data for the models and a systematic method for approaching realistic water mist fire suppression design problems for applications typically protected by other means, thus enabling a reduction in the amount of full-scale testing needed.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research will also provide additional basic information on fire suppression and thus will enhance our knowledge base for fighting fires on Earth, specially fires on enclosed spaces such as aircraft cabins and cargo bays, ships, machinery and telecommunication rooms, museums, and libraries.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
The work performed to characterize the suppression effectiveness of water mist on gaseous-fuel diffusion flames is conducted on a 1.25-cm diameter methane gas-jet burner where information is gathered on flame heights, fuel flow, and fuel velocity. The first set of experiments consists of flowing methane (99.99%) through the tube at various flow rates varying from 0 to 300 sccm, corresponding to flow velocities of approximately 0-240 cm/min. It is noticed that the flame height grows linearly with flow velocity up to a velocity of approximately 240 cm/min, after which the flames become unstable and tend to flicker. Subsequent tests include an incursion into the unstable flow region to replicate flame conditions encountered in turbulent gas-jet flames, which correspond to typical flames found in most fire scenarios. Video images and temperature measurements are taken from flames with methane fuel flows of 250 to 1000 sccm ejecting into open air in the combustion chamber.
After running the dry runs described above, several tests were conducted to characterize the suppression and extinction behavior of gaseous-fuel diffusion flames. Initially, a water-mist nozzle located 50 cm directly above the burner is selected with a 0.20-mm orifice and with a spray cone angle of 30 degrees. For all tests it is run at 100 psi and a water flow rate of 0.5 ml/s, which is the lowest flow rate possible for this nozzle. It is necessary to go this low in flow rate because the immediate suppression of all flames at higher flows. The Sauter Mean Diameter (D32) of the water mist for this nozzle at this pressure is approximately 35 microns as measured at a 15-cm distance from the tip of the nozzle.
For a methane flow rate of 200 cc/min (with a steady flame), an average extinction time of 0.5 seconds is observed. The flame is very quickly extinguished as soon as it gets in contact with the water mist. The flame appears to broaden and move rapidly from side to side before extinction. Its temperature is quickly lowered by the mist as evidenced from the transition from a bright yellow flame to a dim orange-blue flame before total extinction. For a methane flow rate of 350 cc/min (with an unsteady, flickering flame), an average extinction time of 2.5 seconds is observed. For this higher methane flow rate, the unstable flame resists the flow of water mist for a longer time than the case of the smaller stable flame described above. As in the case of a lower methane flow rate, the flame appears to broaden as soon as it gets in contact with the mist, and moves rapidly from side to side before extinction. Similarly, the flame temperature is quickly lowered by the mist as evidenced from the transition from a bright yellow flame to a dim orange-blue flame before total extinction. In order to prolong the extinction time to observe the behavior of the flame in more detail, it was decided to locate the nozzle off-axis, but closer to the burner. Thus, a nozzle height of 35 cm above the flame and an off-axis distance of 2 cm are selected with a water flow rate of 0.65 ml/s. The extinction times turned out to be quite sensitive to the flow rate, so the flow was slowly increased until the extinction times consisted of a few seconds (to avoid long computer processing time during the simulations). For a methane flow rate of 200 cc/min (with a steady flame), an average extinction time of 5.4 seconds is observed. In the case of a methane flow rate of 350 cc/min (with an unsteady, flickering flame), an extinction time of 8.3 seconds is recorded. These measurements reflect an average result from 10 tests per case. These were the final numbers provided to the NRL team for their incorporation into the numerical model for validation and verification of the gaseous–fuel diffusion flame case.
To complement the gaseous-fuel flame studies discussed above and the experimental results provided to NRL, an investigation on the effectiveness of water mist as a fire suppressant in a more conventional environment is undertaken. The goals of this part of the investigation are twofold: to provide a more realistic fire scenario in which many factors, including gravity effects, obstructions, and ventilation play a part in the response of the fire to the suppressant and to develop a systematic method for approaching realistic water mist fire suppression design problems for applications typically protected by other means, possibly enabling a reduction in the amount of full-scale testing needed. Data produced in this work can be used to calibrate future numerical models that may aid both the scientific community and fire engineers in better understanding water mist fire suppression. The system selected for study is water-mist suppression of real-scale thermoplastic fires in electronics cabinets.
Water mist shouldn’t be expected to behave like a total flooding agent, however it can still be effective as a fire suppressant for electronics cabinets if the system is designed in a manner that allows the mist to penetrate into all flammable areas. The most effective nozzle configuration used in this work was a four-nozzle cluster, which incorporate the benefits of a direct spray, which can quickly lower the local temperature and oxygen levels below their thresholds capable of sustaining combustion, with an indirect spray that prevents the recovery of the local oxygen concentration and lowers the ambient temperature in the cabinet. Compared with tests of a single nozzle, this nozzle configuration confirms that the reduction of the local oxygen concentration is more important for fire extinction than lowering the local temperature. The optimal nozzle configuration (the four-nozzle cluster) for the experiments in this investigation allows relatively small droplets to penetrate to the base of the fire. If the droplets evaporate on or in the near vicinity of the burning surface the fire is extinguished immediately. This result indicates that the droplet momentum and focus of the spray is very important for water mist fire suppression in this application. The droplet size is important because, especially in this application, any excess water is highly undesirable. However, if the droplets cannot reach their most effective location, their performance suffers and the penalty of damaged equipment is high.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Surface combustion, shs, fire safety and smoldering
Task Description:
This investigation is intended to answer fundamental questions about the suppression mechanisms and the suppression effectiveness of carbon dioxide (CO2) and water-mist on gas-jet and liquid-pool fires in different gravitational environments, such as the ones experienced by spacecraft in orbit and on the surface of the Moon and Mars. The objectives of the proposed investigation are to understand and quantify: 1) the relative importance of various postulated suppression mechanisms, and 2) the relative suppression effectiveness of carbon dioxide (CO2) and water-mist on both gas-jet and liquid-pool fires in different gravitational environments. These objectives will be achieved by conducting experiments at the Colorado School of Mines fire suppression facility to validate the results of numerical simulations conducted at the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) for specific conditions at normal-gravity and then using the validated simulation tool to predict the effects of reduced gravity on fire suppression in large (rack-scale) compartments. Conducting space-based testing of fire suppression in large compartments is a daunting task from both the safety and the cost points of view. Simulations using a validated and verified numerical tool will provide valuable information that can complement and reduce the number of tests needed, as well as help design better and safer experiments for testing fire-safety policies and practices. Specifically, a computational tool will be developed to characterize the flow field in space compartments and to investigate the transport of fire-fighting agents and their interaction with the air and fuel surrounding a fire. By understanding and quantifying the relative effectiveness of CO2 and water-mist for fire suppression, a more informed decision can be made on the choice of fire suppressants for future spacecraft.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research will also provide additional basic information on fire suppression and thus will enhance our knowledge base for fighting fires on Earth, specially fires on enclosed spaces such as aircraft cabins and cargo bays, ships, machinery and telecommunication rooms, museums, and libraries.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
The investigation during the 2005 fiscal year focused on finishing the development of the apparatus for the methane gas jet burner suppression experiments and performing the first set of tests to gather information on flame heights, fuel flow, and fuel velocity with gas-jet flames with no suppression agent present. The initial experiments consisted of flowing methane through a 1.25-cm diameter stainless steel tube at various flow rates varying from 0 to 300 sccm, corresponding to flow velocities of approximately 0-240 cm/min. It was noticed that the flame height grows linearly with flow velocity up to an approximate velocity of 240 cm/min, after which the flames become unstable and tend to flicker. Subsequent tests included an incursion into the unstable flow region to replicate flame conditions encountered in turbulent gas-jet flames, which correspond to typical flames found in most fire scenarios. Video images and temperature measurements were taken from flames with methane fuel flows up to 1000 sccm ejecting into open air in the combustion chamber. For the unstable flow tests, the images and temperature data show two buoyancy driven flame fluctuations consisting of a rapid fluctuation at a frequency of approximately 5 Hz, which is at the same time embedded in another flame fluctuation with a smaller frequency of approximately 1 Hz. These preliminary data were provided to the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) modeling team for calibration and verification of their numerical model. Once their numerical validation is complete, we will provide them with data from the suppression experiments which include flame temperature, video images, and water/gas concentration during the flame suppression event with water mist and carbon dioxide, as well as the extinction time and behavior observed.

Task Progress:
For the first six months of the project, the experimental work at the Colorado School of Mines has concentrated on selecting the components for the first group of experiments, which include a gas-jet fuel burner, a mass-flow controller, and a set of low-pressure water nozzles with a small droplet-size distribution. We have started making several modifications to the existing combustion facility to accommodate gaseous and liquid fire scenarios. For the next six months of the first year of the project, we anticipate to assign a graduate student to conduct all the experimental work. We will also start discussions with NRL on the details of the experimental facility including key dimensions plus the locations and sizes of the air inflow, gas-jet fuel inflow, and water-mist injection ports. Finally, by the end of the first year of the grant, we expect to have preliminary experimental results that can be transferred to the modeling team to initiate the validation of the numerical code.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:
NOTE: Received NCE to 9/30/2007, per N. Hall (9/06)
Task Description: This investigation provides an integrated suite of tasks that involve both experimental studies and detailed modeling of fine water mist in fire suppression scenarios relevant to spaceflight needs. The overall goal of this fundamental study and the resulting numerical code, validated with experiments, is to evaluate the role of water mist in the next generation of fire safety systems on spacecraft and habitation modules on the surface of other planets. Ultra-fine water mist driven by air or by nitrogen is compared to carbon dioxide and nitrogen to evaluate their performance to suppress and extinguish both direct and highly obstructed fires involving energized wires, electrical components on circuit boards, and cloth. Extinction time and suppressant amount are used as a measure of agent effectiveness. The numerical-experimental study is based on a hierarchical model. First, a study of simplified scenarios is performed at a detailed level. Second, the critical elements of the detailed model are extracted and then encapsulated in a reduced-order manner for inclusion in the next higher-level scenario. The process is continued until a robust understanding of fire suppression at the level of a Space Shuttle Mid-Deck Locker is obtained. The experiments are performed in normal gravity for an accurate validation of the numerical model and to provide observations of fire suppression behavior under realistic spacecraft fire scenarios.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The results on the effectiveness of the various suppressant agents used in this project serve to determine an optimum fire-fighting technique for space and for Earth applications. While the main emphasis is on fighting fires on spacecraft, the results are generalized for all gravity conditions, including Earth's gravity. The software code developed serves as a tool for designing fire suppression systems for aircraft, ships, museums, libraries, and a variety of enclosed spaces.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
An experimental investigation on the effectiveness of various suppressant agents in spacecraft fires under normal-gravity conditions has been conducted. Ultra-fine water mist clouds (mean diameter of 8 microns) driven by air or by nitrogen (N2) are compared to single-fluid agents such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and pure N2 to evaluate their performance to suppress and extinguish typical fires that may be encountered in spacecraft such as energized wires, electrical components on circuit boards, and cloth. The suppressants are injected into a chamber with similar dimensions to the Space Shuttle Mid-deck Locker at low (0.2 g/s), medium (1.0 g/s) and high (2.0 g/s) mass-flow rates. A highly obstructed path to the fire is provided by a large baffle located perpendicular to the agent stream, between the nozzle and the fire. Extinction time and amount of suppressant agent needed to put out the flames are measured and used in the comparative study, along with other performance variables related to practical aspects of fighting fires under spacecraft conditions.
a) Fire Scenario 1: Overheated Wire.
As expected for agents with similar heat capacities per unit mass, the extinction time for CO2 and N2 is quite comparable. Interestingly, ultra-fine mist driven by air is not as effective as the gaseous agents for this fire scenario, taking considerably longer to extinguish the fire. This apparent weakness is in sharp contrast to the advantages of using water mist in the burning-element and burning-cloth cases. This discrepancy may be explained by a combination of two factors: a) the overwhelming heat generated by the electrical power applied to the wire (35 W), approximately half of the fire power, and b) the “small-fire syndrome,” a phenomenon frequently observed in weekly burning fires suppressed with water, where the small fire is able to survive with barely adequate levels of oxygen by reducing the water evaporation rate below a critical value. It is believed that these two reasons may explain why the water droplets are not being efficiently used to put out the fire. During the experiments, it is observed that the mist quickly reaches the fire after less than 5 seconds from injection and immediately suppresses it by significantly diminishing its size and its spread rate. Nevertheless, after that rapid initial suppression, some amount of water mist appears to be spent cooling the hot copper wire by evaporating around it, another group of droplets just re-circulates inside the test chamber, while the rest of the droplets concentrates near the small fire. To verify this hypothesis, the ultra-fine mist is introduced at the slow mass-flow rate of 0.2 g/s, resulting in 65% less water needed to put out the fire even though it takes much longer to extinguish it, indicating that at higher mass-flow rates, the water is not effectively used to control the fire (on a mass basis). If extinction time is the main design parameter, it is interesting to note that although it takes more than three times longer to extinguish the fire, the final position of the flame at the low mass-flow rate case is just a few millimeters past the spot where the flame extinguishes under the medium mass-flow rate case. Obviously, ultra-fine mist acts as an extremely efficient suppressant, but it has a more difficult time to completely extinguish the small remaining flame, as compared to the gaseous agents.
To verify the “small-fire syndrome” hypothesis, 0.5 g/s of ultra-fine mist are introduced in the chamber driven by 0.5 g/s of N2. This combination effectively cools down the wire, rapidly suppresses the spread rate of the flame, and quickly puts out the remaining small fire. For the water-mist/N2 combination, both the extinction time and the total amount of suppressant used to extinguish the flame are comparable to the values obtained for the gaseous agents. It is important to point out that neither CO2 nor N2 are capable of suppressing the fire at mass-flow rates lower than 1 g/s. Under these conditions, most of the time the wire breaks before the flame is extinguished, and on other occasions the insulation completely melts down and falls to the bottom of the chamber, making it impossible to quantify the effectiveness of the agent. For this particular case, the unique suppression properties of water mist in conjunction with the oxygen-depletion attributes of N2 result in a superior combination with excellent performance.
b) Fire Scenario 2: Burning Element on a Circuit Board.
In the simulated case of a burning element on a circuit board case, only 25 W are applied to the heater cartridge to preheat the PMMA rod, allowing the water droplets to concentrate on putting out the fire instead of cooling the heated element. Consequently, ultra-fine mist gives the best results based on time and suppressant amount, followed closely by the two other gaseous agents. As with the overheated wire case, the ultra-fine mist is also introduced at the slow mass-flow rate of 0.2 g/s, resulting in less water needed to put out the fire even though it takes much longer to extinguish it. In addition, although it takes more than four times as long to extinguish the fire, the final position of the flame at the low mass-flow rate case is just a few millimeters past the spot where the flame extinguishes with the medium mass-flow rate. This is another case where fire suppression is effectively and quickly accomplished by the ultra-fine mist with the rest of the time spent to completely extinguish the small remaining flame. The gaseous agents are again incapable of putting the fire out at the low mass-flow rate with the flame completely consuming all the PMMA material.
c) Fire Scenario 3: Burning Cloth.
For the burning cloth case, a representative example of a fire burning completely unaided by any external heating, ultra-fine mist clearly is the most effective suppressant as compared to the CO2 and N2 gases. On a mass basis, its effectiveness its further enhanced when ultra-fine mist is introduced at the low mass-flow rate of 0.2 g/s, while the gaseous agents are incapable of putting the fire out at this lower rate. For the high mass-flow rate case, CO2 and N2 not only introduce convective currents that would enhance the flame strength under low-gravity conditions, but they also blow away the smoldering embers that remain in the post-flame zone on top of the burning rag. An added benefit of using water droplets in this particular case is the ability of the water to extinguish the smoldering embers considerably faster than the other two agents. This is due to the moisture absorbed by the cloth that forms an obstructive barrier for further flame propagation.
Thus, on a mass-basis comparison, ultra-fine mist is found to be more effective than CO2 and N2, with the exception of the burning-wire scenario with a high preheating power. In this case, ultra-fine mist is used to not only extinguish the fire, but also to cool the hot copper wire. This fact, in conjunction with the “small-fire syndrome” characteristic of water-mist suppressed fires, results in longer extinction times for ultra-fine mist, as compared to gaseous agents. Although at first the longer extinction times and additional mass of agent may appear as a disadvantage of water mist against CO2 or N2, the cooling effect of the water mist has the advantage of preventing the rupture of the wire, as it occurs when CO2 and N2 are applied at low mass-flow rates. This cooling effect may be essential to avoid disrupting the operation of critical equipment onboard the spacecraft while the fire is being suppressed. If shorter extinction times are desired, ultra-fine mist driven by N2 can be used to combine the unique suppression properties of water mist in conjunction with the oxygen-depletion attributes of N2. It is observed that the use of this mixed-agent suppressant results in a superior combination with excellent performance. These observations are supported and explained by the numerical model results which compare favorably to the observed experimental data and emphasize the advantage of using a combined water-mist/nitrogen system to effectively cool, suppress, and extinguish this type of small fires. On a parallel study of the behavior of ultra fine mist as it approaches the fire, the numerical analysis of the idealized behavior of a mist parcel with droplet sizes on the order of a few microns shows that collisions have negligible influence on the droplet size distribution evolution over time scales commensurate with the flow residence time. In addition, it is found that drag, heat transfer, and evaporation occur on time scales that are significantly shorter than that of the flow field, indicating that droplets will trace the flow of the continuous phase, and quickly reach thermodynamic equilibrium with it.
Ultra-fine mist is also effective on reducing smoldering extinction times with cloth fires by adding moisture to the burning rag and preventing the blowing of hot smoldering embers that can cause ignition of neighboring material in a tightly packed spacecraft under low-gravity conditions. In addition, the low-momentum injection of water mist may prevent the strengthening of the weak-burning low-gravity fires by reducing the convective currents, which are observed with the gaseous agents injected at high flow rates. Finally, the low momentum and pseudo-gas properties of ultra-fine mist with lower-than-10-micron droplets are also more effective than the high-momentum and larger droplet sizes generated by high-pressure water-mist sprays, which make water droplets incapable of moving around obstacles and reaching the fire.
These results point to ultra-fine water mist (or a combination of water mist driven by N2) as a promising candidate to be used as agent in the next-generation spacecraft fire suppression system. The final selection of the optimum suppressant agent will depend on a detailed assessment of all the relevant design parameters and their relative importance for this unique application.

Task Description:
This investigation is intended to provide an integrated suite of tasks that involve both experimental studies and detailed modeling of fine water mist in fire suppression scenarios relevant to spaceflight needs. All research on water mist will be done in comparison to a baseline of CO2, the suppression agent of choice onboard the ISS and the most abundant component in the Martian atmosphere. The research plan is based on a hierarchical model. First, a study of simplified scenarios is performed at a detailed level. Second, the critical elements of the detailed model are extracted and then encapsulated in a reduced-order manner for inclusion in the next higher-level scenario. The process is continued until a robust understanding of fire suppression at the level of an ISS rack is obtained. The experiments will be performed in both normal and reduced gravity for an accurate validation of the numerical model and to provide observations of fire suppression behavior under extraterrestrial conditions. The overall goal of this fundamental study and the resulting numerical code, validated with experiments, is to evaluate the role of water mist in the next generation of fire safety systems on spacecraft and habitation modules on the surface of other planets. This project will simultaneously satisfy two needs – scientific and NASA programmatic. At the scientific level, the combined experiment/modeling program will lead to a basic understanding of water mist and CO2 fire suppression in realistic fire scenarios (e.g., wire bundles, burning cloth, etc). A determination will be made of the interaction of reduced oxygen concentration and lowered temperature with smoldering rates and smoke generation. This basic understanding will advance the field of fire suppression for both spacecraft and terrestrial applications. At the NASA programmatic level, a series of sub-models (fire source, suppression agent generation and distribution, and radiation models) will be developed resulting on an integrated model that can be employed by NASA as design aids for spaceflight hardware. Deliverables will also fall into scientific and programmatic categories. In the scientific category there will be studies in the form of peer-reviewed journal articles on the basic understanding gained in the sub-models and the issues resolved in model integration. In the programmatic category there will be software modules at the sub-model and integrated model level, and data that will be available to investigators of reduced gravity flame spread, and fire growth and suppression.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The results on the effectiveness of the various suppressant agents used in this project will serve to determine an optimum fire-fighting technique for space and for Earth applications. While the main emphasis is on fighting fires on spacecraft, the results will be generalized for all gravity conditions, including Earth's gravity. The software code developed will serve as a tool for designing fire suppression systems for aircraft, ships, museums, libraries, and a variety of enclosed spaces.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
During FY2005, the investigation focused on the study of water mist as a suppressant agent in electrical fires under normal-gravity conditions. The experimental work concentrated on evaluating the suppression effects of various droplet size distributions and the behavior of water mist in a constrained geometry. In a parallel effort, the numerical work focused on the simulation of the generation, evaporation, and distribution of the mist as it moves through the container and as it interacts with the fire source.
Direct and indirect water-mist injection with a high-momentum jet are used with various droplet-size distributions and flow rates to extinguish a burning wire inside a container similar to the Space Shuttle mid-deck locker. The wire is located 40 cm from the water mist injector and for the indirect-injection tests a 13-cm wide, 25-cm high baffle is placed at 26 cm from the nozzle, in front of the burning wire. This last configuration is used to provide an extremely difficult path for the water mist to reach the burning wire. Interestingly, varying the width of the baffle from 5 to 13 cm had only a minor effect on the suppression efficacy of the high-momentum jet. Different droplet-size distributions and flow rates are possible by varying the water pressure on a water-mist injector with a 0.2-mm diameter orifice. Droplet size distributions with a Sauter mean diameter (SMD) of 40 to 27 microns are achieved with pressures varying from 100 to 1000 psi, respectively. Water mist quickly extinguishes a fire that is directly impacted by the droplets. However, much longer spraying times and larger amounts of water are required to suppress fires burning behind a baffle. Extinction times and water amounts are reduced as the droplet size distribution is lowered. A numerical model simulating the generation, evaporation, and distribution of a polydispersed spray accurately captures the phenomena observed experimentally. The predicted behavior of the water mist blocked by the baffle shows no direct interaction between the mist and the burning wire. The droplets do not have significant inertia to move around the obstacle and instead a large recirculation region is generated, where the mist will eventually impinge on the chamber walls. In the case where the water mist is accompanied by a 5 m/s coflow, the droplets get diverted and move around the obstacle, but even under these conditions, the reattachment length for the spray occurs past the chamber wall, making it impossible to have direct interaction with the wire. The experimental results show that the wire will interact with only about 1.5% of the mist by mass. The discretization process associated with the numerical model is not accurate to that low percentage level. Increasing the number of representative droplets would increase the model accuracy and might allow the description of this interaction. In the current scenarios, the lack of interaction would suggest, as confirmed by experiments, that fire suppression effects would be minimal, and they would mainly be due to mechanisms other than enthalpy extraction. This experimental-numerical comparison has provided valuable information in the on-going validation of the mist dispersion sub-model, which is part of a three sub-model suite (along with the fire and radiation sub-models) required for the final development of a reduced order model to describe the complete fire suppression process.
As a result of the ineffectiveness of high-momentum, large-droplet-size spray jets to maneuver around obstacles and extinguish obstructed fires, the research effort is now shifting to the study of low-momentum, ultra-fine mist as a technique to produce total flooding of the confined space and effective suppression even in complicated geometries with fires hidden by multiple obstacles. For these tests, the high-pressure nozzles are replaced by an ultrasonic mist generator, which generates a droplet size distribution with a SMD lower than 10 microns at flow speeds in the vicinity of 0.5 m/s. From the few cases run to date, it is clear to see that ultra-fine mist can easily go around the baffle and rapidly flood the entire container in a gas-like manner. For the same experimental conditions described for the indirect-injection case with a baffle, the flame propagating down the insulated wire was extinguished by the ultra-fine mist with an average of 4 ml of water in approximately 10 seconds, an order of magnitude lower, in both extinction time and water amount, than the high-momentum, large-droplet-size spray jet.
These promising results have prompted an evaluation of ultra-fine water mist as a potential agent for the suppression of the fire types most likely to be encountered in spacecraft applications. An experimental and numerical feasibility study of the fire suppression properties of ultra-fine water mist will be an important part of the next phase of the project.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The experimental study of water mist dispersion and the various fire scenarios and fire suppression methods will be carried out in a test apparatus that is modeled after the Space Shuttle Middeck Locker (SSML). To replicate a fire suppression scenario under these conditions, we have started the construction of the Middeck Locker Fire Testing Apparatus (MLFTA), which is built of aluminum and tempered glass and has approximate dimensions of 17.3” x 10.0” x 20.3”. The top panel of the apparatus is transparent to allow video data collection and an adjustable ventilation system provides airflow and purging of combustion gases. In this pseudo-locker we will test a variety of suppression methods, such as water-mist, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen with single and multiple injection points. These injection methods cover the current ISS fire suppression method of a portable hand-held fire extinguisher spraying through a port in a rack and also possible next-generation spacecraft components that may have a multi-point suppression delivery system built into the design. We will also test hybrid suppression methods such as water mist with a CO2 or N2 atomizing fluid. At first, experiments will be done in our laboratory in normal gravity where we have the greatest access to instrumentation (e.g., gas chromatography) and the experiments can be carried out with greater repetition rates. The normal gravity experiments will provide preliminary heat release rate input for the fire source numerical sub-model and will also be used to identify worst-case burning materials and fire configurations. In the past few months, we have conducted the first experiments with polyethylene-insulated cable to measure ignition energies and times, burning behavior, flame spread rates, and heat-release rates under upward, downward, and horizontal configurations. We plan to continue this type of testing to collect information on all the different materials that will be burned and suppressed in this investigation. In anticipation of the experiments that will be conducted in reduced gravity, we met with members of the Reduced Gravity Office at NASA GRC to discuss the requirements for rig construction, safety practices, documentation, and possible flight dates for this experiment. The long-term modeling effort of this project consists of developing detailed sub-models of the fire source, the suppression agent generation and distribution, and the radiative shielding of the suppression agent. These sub-models will then be integrated into a high-fidelity, fire-suppression model. Finally, a reduced order model will be developed to minimize the computational requirements, yet retain the simulation capabilities of the original formulation. To date, we have obtained preliminary results in the development of the polydispersed mist model, where water mist injection characteristics include the number of injectors and their position in the domain considered, the mass flow rate injected (which may be time-dependent), the injection orifice size, the droplet size and velocity distribution, and the spray cone-angle. These preliminary numerical results provide interesting insight regarding the mist evaporation dynamics that is directly relevant to the issue of droplet penetration in the presence of obstacles.

Task Description: Microgravity and Ground-based experimental studies of premixed-flame propagation in low-intensity turbulent flow under microgravity conditions are to be undertaken The focus of the research is on the hydrodynamic coupling between flame and flow-field dynamics at low turbulence intensities, which may lead to flame-generated turbulence, flame acceleration and enhancement of burning rates. As a result of hydrodynamic coupling the transition from initially planar or wrinkled laminar flames to fast turbulent flames or detonations is possible, even when diffusive-thermal effects associated with non-unity reactant Lewis numbers are not destabilizing. Therefore, the proposed work is relevant to microgravity fire safety.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress: During the past year, we have completed construction of a new non-rotating burner to be used for ground-based and microgravity studies of the Darrieus-Landau hydrodynamic instability on annular-flame propagation. We have also developed and tested new optical tools to enable measurements of turbulence properties in a second, rotating burner to be under construction soon. Preliminary ground-based studies will be carried out at UC Davis over the next few months, after-which microgravity experiments at the NASA Glenn Research Center will be conducted.

Task Description:
The overall task was divided into experimental and computational parts. The experimental effort consisted of using a porous spherical burner to issue C2H4 fuel and mixtures (with CO2 & N2) into a controlled oxidizing environment (with various concentrations of O2, CO2, and N2). These experiments provided data for understanding flame chemistry and flame radiation interactions. Computational models with detailed chemistry and radiation were developed to better understand these interactions. Only the 2.2s drop tower experiments were completed. The proposed experiments for longer microgravity duration in the 5s drop tower were not completed due to shortened time. The supporting numerical calculations with detailed chemistry have also been completed.
Task Objective:
The objective of this research was to experimentally and computationally investigate the conditions that will lead to extinction of gaseous diffusion flames in µg and understand the role played by gas and soot radiation in flame extinction. The scientific goal was to develop a fundamental understanding of the interaction between radiation and flame chemistry that is responsible for extinction of diffusion flames. The practical goal was to help develop fire suppression and detection technology for space applications.
Task Significance:
This research is intended develop a fundamental understanding of the interaction between flame radiation and flame chemistry that is responsible for extinction of diffusion flames. The practical goal is to help develop fire suppression and detection technology for space applications. The results of work are also applicable to practical combustion systems where exhaust gas recirculation is used as a method of pollutant control in engines and furnaces.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research will help develop fire suppression and detection technology for space applications. The results of work and the science developed are applicable to practical combustion systems where exhaust gas recirculation is used as a method of pollutant control in engines and furnaces. Invovative Technologies Developed: 1. Method of transient measurements of spectral radiation emitted from the flame ; 2. Method of determining the spatial soot profile by soot scattering imaging.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
This project was divided into two parts:
(i) An experimental component conducted at the NASA-Glenn drop tower facility, and
(ii) A computational component conducted at the University of Michigan. Progress made in these components is summarized below:
Experimental: The Ph.D. students successfully completed their degree. Dr. Melissa Chernovsky worked on the experimental part of the project and Dr. Songtao Tang worked on the computational part of the project. We have also written several Journal publications and presented conference papers based on their work. These are summarized below. Melissa collected a large amount of data which will be the basis of several future publications.
A brief summary of the work is presented below:
Experimental work: Melissa’s Ph.D. thesis presents experimental research conducted to improve our understanding of flames in microgravity conditions. Of particular interest is to understand the effects of radiation heat loss and reabsorption because of their importance in flame extinction and implications for fire safety in low gravitational environments. Spherical diffusion flames were chosen for this study because they amplify the effect of radiation heat loss. Flames in microgravity naturally develop a spherical character due to diffusional symmetry, and consequently their one-dimensionality enables detailed models with chemistry and radiation. The focus of this microgravity diffusion flame study is to examine the effects of various diluents introduced on the fuel and oxidizer sides of a spherical diffusion flame. Characterization of the flame consisted of flame growth rate, temperature field, and spectral radiation emission measurements.
Transient measurements were conducted at atmospheric pressure using a porous spherical burner aerodynamically supporting an ethylene diffusion flame in an oxidizing atmosphere. The effect of diluent on the fuel side of the reaction zone was investigated by comparing non-radiative N2 with a radiative diluent mixture including CO2 and He, while maintaining equivalent adiabatic flame temperatures. The influence of CO2 on the fuel side of the reaction zone reduced flame temperatures and inhibited soot formation. CO2 enhanced the heat release rate of the flames without contributing significantly to radiation reabsorption. The effect of diluent on the oxidizer side of the reaction zone was similarly investigated by replacing N2 in the oxidizer with CO2 and/or He. The influence of He on the oxidizer side initially increased heat release of the flame and decreased the flame temperature due to the enhanced thermal conductivity dominating the decreased thermal capacity of the mixture. The influence of CO2 on the oxidizer side also reduced flame temperatures and inhibited soot formation. However, the mechanisms by which CO2 affected the oxidizer were different from that of the fuel side. While CO2 in the oxidizer similarly enhanced heat release from the flame, spectral radiation emission measurements showed significant radiation reabsorption effects. This study provides important implications for extinguishment mechanisms of flames in low gravitational environments.
Computational Work: The goal of the computational work was to assess the effects of gas radiation as a means to promote flame extinction. To investigate these phenomena, a one-dimensional computational model was developed to simulate the evolution of a spherical diffusion flame with consideration of detailed chemistry and transport properties. Various levels of radiation models were implemented and the results were compared with experimental measurements of flame radius and temperature profiles. It was shown that the statistical narrow band (SNB) combined with the discrete ordinate method (DOM) reproduced the experimental results with highest accuracy, and this combination of the radiation models were adopted in the subsequent parametric studies.
The parametric studies explored the relative effectiveness of fuel- and oxidizer-side dilution on the flame radius and temperature behavior, with nitrogen, CO2, and helium as diluents. In the spherical configuration considered in this study, the oxidizer-side dilution has a stronger effect on flame transient behavior than the fuel-side dilution, thereby suggesting a more effective means to induce flame extinction by dilution.
Study on various oxidizer-side dilution cases shows that CO2 has a larger suppression effect than helium or nitrogen with the same dilution level. CO2 dilution has multiple effects on flame behavior including radiation, thermodynamic, diffusion, and chemical effects. Quantitative analysis shows that the radiation effect is the primary factor accounting for flame temperature drop by approximately 60%, as compared to the thermal/diffusion (30%), and chemical effect (10%).
Considering the dominance of the radiative heat loss on flame extinction, a unified extinction criterion that applies to a wide range of parametric conditions was sought. The compiled computational results indicated that a critical flame temperature of 1130 K at extinction appears to be valid for most of the conditions under study. Therefore, it is concluded that extinction of spherical diffusion flame is primarily dictated by the local condition in the flame zone rather than by the volumetric radiative heat transfer in the surrounding gases.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
This project is divided into two parts: (i) An experimental component conducted at the NASA-Glenn drop tower facility, and (ii) A computational component conducted at the University of Michigan.
Progress made in these components is summarized below:
Experimental: Last year, final adjustments to measurement calibration and experimental control were made to the newly reconstructed experimental drop rig and safety approval was obtained. Several microgravity experiments were conducted in the 2.2 second drop tower facility using ethylene, a well documented sooty fuel, with total flow rate of 5cm3/s into air (21%O2, 79%N2) at 14.7psia. Studies of interest included investigating the role of fuel diluents CO2 and helium on radiative and chemical properties of the spherical diffusion flames. Fuel mixtures using ethylene (C2H4), and diluents CO2, He, and N2 were selected to maintain the temperature dependent energy storage term rho CP(T) approaches constant. Consideration was also made to balance CP while maintaining a constant fuel flow rate. This condition is important because the flame temperatures in both cases are nearly equal at the onset of the established flame. Temporal and spatial distributions of temperature, spectral radiation, and soot were measured with calibrated detectors. These experiments established the repeatability and accuracy of measurements and provided data for the effect of dilution on radiative and chemical flame properties. Considerable effort was spent on developing data processing techniques, programs and analysis tools. A new set of experiments are currently underway. In these experiments the atmosphere is modified by oxidizer side diluents. A new safety permit was obtained and safety protocols were satisfied. Currently experiments are being done with 18-50%O2 / 0-72%N2 / 0-40%CO2 / 0-52%He with ethylene as the fuel.
Results of the fuel side dilution experiments enable us to understand of the effect of radiation absorption on micro-g flames. Visible flame images, flame growth rate, temperature field, spectral radiation measurements, and soot distribution measurements demonstrate the effect of CO2 as a diluent on the fuel side of the reaction zone. CO2 addition was found to decrease flame growth rate and reduce flame temperature for similar dilution despite efforts to balance the amount of fuel and temperature dependent properties, specifically CP, between test and control cases. Temperature data for enhanced CO2 on the fuel side indicates increased flame interior temperature which could be attributed to radiation reabsorption.
Computational: First, the transient expansion of µg spherical diffusion flames was computationally simulated without including soot and flame radiation. Next, a one-dimensional spherical model was set up to study the transient ignition, combustion, and extinction process for highly radiating diffusion flames. Detailed chemical kinetic rates and transport properties were incorporated through the CHEMKIN and TRANSPORT packages and Newton iteration scheme via the TWOPNT module. A stiff differential-algebraic equations solver, DASPK, is also employed to find the transient flame dynamics.
This model with detailed chemistry & radiation and the measurements will enable accomplishing the scientific goal of developing a fundamental understanding of the interaction between radiation and flame chemistry that will help fire suppression in space and pollutant-fee combustion on ground.

Task Description:
The overall task was divided into experimental and theoretical/computational components. The experimental effort consisted of using a porous spherical burner to issue various fuels (CH4, C2H4 & C2H2) and their mixtures (with CO2 & N2) into a controlled oxidizing environment (with various concentrations of O2, CO2, H2O and N2). These experiments provided data for understanding the flame chemistry at extinction via computations with detailed chemistry. The experiments are conducted in the 2.2s (and 5s) drop towers at the GRC. The supporting numerical calculations with detailed chemistry, soot and radiation are conducted at Michigan.

Task Description:
The broad-based objective of this project is to improve the performance of liquid fuel combustion. The perspective of spherical droplet flames promoted in a microgravity environment is used as the benchmark configuration from which to gain insights on mechanisms and processes for generalization. The project has focussed on three key parameters: ambient pressure, fuel composition and initial droplet diameter on burning. The results have shown the importance of new influences of soot formation that were previously unknown. And results have highlighted the importance of considering detailed flame chemistry and radiation in modeling the measurements.
In the current grant year, we performed a number of systematic experiments to examine burning of nonane droplets at high pressure, determined a new scaling that consolidates the burning rates at different initial droplet diameters of nonane, shown the influence of thermal stability additives on combustion of JP8 fuel droplets, and documented the development of soot dynamics at high pressures, up to 15atm, for nonane. The ambient gas is room temperature for all of the experiments. Experiments were performed in both air and in an oxydizing atmosphere consisting of oxygen and helium to compare with a condition where soot formation is minimal.
Measurements were made of the droplet, outer luminous zone, and the soot shell diameters using photographic documentation based on color, and black and white, 16mm high speed movie images. The images were digitized and analyzed using commercial software. The broad objective is to develop a detailed understanding of liquid fuel combustion from the perspective of processes at the droplet level with application to environmental air quality and combustion efficiency. Over the past year we carried out several tasks designed to address certain specific questions and processes. These included 1) studying the flame structure and soot dynamics of nonane droplets at elevated pressure; 2) determination of the mechanism responsible for an initial droplet diameter influence on droplet burning, development of a universal correlation for nonane for the droplet diameter range examined, and identification of the possible role of soot formation; and 3) showing how a thermal stability additive blended with JP8 in trace quantities influences the droplet burning dynamics and soot formation. Summaries of these tasks are given in subsequent sections. Many industrial combustion processes are carried out at high pressures, over a wide range of initial droplet diameters representative of spray flames, and for fuels that can be multicomponent, yet little is known about the spherical droplet burning behavior at high pressure and the influence of initial droplet diameter. The challenges are many: creation of spherical droplet flames and soot cloud structures at elevated pressures (greater than 5 atm, for example) is experimentally difficult; development of correlations for droplet burning which can be applied across a range of initial droplet diameters would have great practical value for spray codes that rely on droplet sub-models for the droplet burning rate as a correction to the spherically symmetric value; and determination of the role of thermal stability additives that were developed for processes unrelated to combustion yet which are routinely blended with JP8 and burned as a blend could significantly enhance the development and utilization of such blends if they can be shown to mitigate soot formation. These questions are also very relevant to a terrestrial environment yet we study them from the perspective of spherical droplet flames in microgravity because of the basic and simplified combustion dynamic it promotes, with the droplet and flame being spherical and concentric. This situation corresponds to a one-dimensional transport situation which makes droplet burning modellable and hence valuable for developing the needed understanding for generalization.
Spherical droplet flames promoted by microgravity are ideal for examining droplet burning and developing correlations because of the one-dimensional gas phase transport process it promotes which simplifies mechanisms and facilitates understanding. At the same time, results from the spherically symmetric configuration are the limit to which the influences of convection revert as convection is reduced. The dependence of droplet burning rate with droplet diameter and time are among the unique contributions that experimentation in microgravity have revealed. With the current generation of hardware for microgravity experimentation, idealized (surrogate) fuels which are often used as models for multicomponent blends (e.g., the nonane/hexanol mixtures of this study) can give way to practical fuel systems. Doing so further bridges the divide between microgravity and terrestrial applications.

Task Description:
One of the most important challenges of our time is to mitigate the harmful impacts of particulate emissions (soot) from combustion engines on global climate change, and to reduce the consumption of liquid petroleum fuels that power transportation systems. A promising concept is to mix petroleum fuels with bio-derived fuels. An evaluation of the performance benefits rests on diagnostics to unravel the complex relationships between soot formation and fuel properties. Under some conditions the presence of soot itself in the combustion field can intrude on this effort. Measurements that rely on digital video imaging of the fuel burning process, such as employed in the FLame Extinguishment eXperiment (FLEX), are vulnerable to this concern.
FLEX was developed to understand mechanisms that control flame extinction as it relates to cabin fire safety aboard manned spaceflight, though the broad methodologies are more widely applicable to combustion of fuel systems in combustion engines. The configuration of isolated droplets burning with near spherical symmetry was employed to elucidate the mechanisms involved. The main diagnostic was digital video imaging. From this information, quantitative measurements of the droplet and flame boundaries were made using suitable computer-based data extraction algorithms that revealed the influence of ambient gas conditions and liquid fuel properties on flame extinction. For some of the fuels employed in FLEX, soot formation was evident (i.e., n-heptane droplets burning in air), which obscured part of the droplet and flame boundary that can compromise data accuracy.
The success of the FLEX program assumes the existence of efficient and accurate computer-based algorithms that can overcome the obscuration influence of soot on droplets, are able to track droplets if they move, and can account for deviations from sphericity due to ignition disturbances. However, this is not the case. Commercial image analysis packages are limited in their ability to deal with the presence of soot in the imaging field without significant user input. Failure to address this problem impacts not only deriving full benefit from the FLEX experiments already carried out, but also follow-on studies which would utilize digital video imaging to study droplet combustion dynamics of sooting fuels used in commercial transportation systems. In this proposal we address this problem be developing a diameter estimation refinement algorithm that employs concepts that automate droplet and flame diameter measurements from video images in the presence of soot. The algorithm will be used to re-analyze certain FLEX data on the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system -- results from a proof-of-concept program are included in the proposal for illustration -- and to extract quantitative data from new proposed experiments to study the influence of mixture fraction on blends of bio-derived fuels with an aviation fuel: hydroprocessed renewable jet fuel derived from algae with Jet-A (algal feedstocks have potential for larger yields compared to outer sources) for which soot formation is expected. The outcome will be a robust capability to process digital video images that efficiently and precisely extracts measurements from digital images even in the presence of soot aggregates. The results -- data and software -- will be freely available on various outlets as discussed in the proposal.
The project includes a team with expertise in developing algorithms for image analysis (Prof. Anthony Reeves of Cornell's Electrical and Computer Engineering Department) and experience in droplet combustion experimentation (Prof. C. Thomas Avedisian of Cornell's Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering (MAE) Department). The project team has supplies of the algae-derived and jet fuel systems that will be studied (Terravia, Inc; and the Air Force).

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
This brief report summarizes research carried out under NASA Grant #80NSSC18K0480. The development of a new image analysis algorithm was accomplished for measuring droplet diameter in the presence of soot formed during the burning process. The algorithm was applied to digital video images from experiments carried out as part of the Flame Extinguishment Experiment-2 (FLEX2) on the International Space Station (ISS). Some of the FLEX2 fuel systems had a strong propensity to produce soot. The presence of soot aggregates significantly impacted the ability to obtain quantitative data from video images of the droplet burning process. We developed an image analysis algorithm in response to this challenge. The FLEX2 fuel systems investigated were 'surrogates' for petroleum-based fuels used in terrestrial propulsion systems (fuels for automotive and jet engines). These were principally binary mixtures of hydrocarbons as noted in the report and all had a propensity to produce soot in various degrees.
Soot formation can be a prime concern in the measurement of droplet diameter from video images because many practical hydrocarbon fuels have a high sooting propensity. The algorithm developed as part of the project is able to reconstruct sections of a droplet boundary that are obscured by soot. With data resulting from such an ability that extends current capabilities of image analysis where no data could be obtained, a more complete understanding of droplet burning is enabled.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
In the first phase of this research we developed a general tracking and measuring system for any image sequence of a moving circle. This involved a tracking stage that identified the location of the circle in each image and a precision diameter measuring stage. The tracking system could address very large motions of the droplet between images. For measurement the system employs an iterative ray casting method that measures each radial ray to subpixel accuracy in a directed gradient image. In the second phase, we focused on the soot problem with backlight droplet image videos. For this task, changes between images were small and the tracking stage was not required. However, there were a number of different soot types that required different algorithm modifications. The different soot types are powder soot, in which particles smaller than a pixel darken the background, granular soot in which particles may be several pixels in size and cause a positive bias to the diameter measurement, and occluding soot that is large opaque consolidated masses of soot that, in extreme cases, can completely cover the droplet and make measurement impossible.
For the powdered soot no explicit modifications to the algorithm are needed since measurement is performed a sub-pixel accuracy on a directed gradient image. This approach has shown to give very good results when traditional image-intensity based semiautomated methods fail. For the granular soot there is a measurement bias associated with the radial measurements going to the boundary of soot granules that connect to the the boundary of the droplet. We are exploring two methods to correct these errors--first a set of outlier radial measures are discounted since they have lower reliability; second a modification is made to the loss function of the Mean Squared Error (MSE) optimization algorithm used to refine the diameter measurement. For the occlusion there are situations that we have recently found where the whole droplet is occluded and no measurement is possible. To deal with situation we have developed a linear predictive tracking algorithm that carefully reviews a large location and size search region following the detection of a full occlusion event. In this way the algorithm recaptures the droplet when it eventfully comes out from behind the occluding soot cloud. No measurements are recorded in a region where there is full occlusion.
For each image measurement, 7 different image quality measurements are made in order to estimate measurement error; these include standard deviation of the radial boundary measurements, mean signal of the boundary, and the number of discarded radii due to there being no gradient peak or being a significant outlier. In the next phase of this research we will use the image quality measures to for a model for predicting measurement error by the use of Monte Carlo simulations.
To date we have evaluated this algorithm on 125 video image sequences for all the FLEX2 involving the following fuel mixtures: Propylbenzene100, Decane25 Propylbenzene75, Decane50 Propylbenzene50, Decane75 Propylbenzene25, and Heptane50 Toluene50. Using our phase 1 method we successfully measured 57% of these sequences. By using the advanced measurement methods to manage soot we have increased this to 88% success. With revisions to our prediction method we plan to be able to successfully measure all the image sequences.
In a second study based on a local drop tower for data, we report the results of a fundamental study of hydroprocessed renewable jet fuel derived from heterotrophic algae (AHRJ) burning under conditions that promote one-dimensional transport dynamics and near spherically symmetric burning conditions. The results are compared to Jet-A and three AHRJ/Jet-A blends containing 25%, 50%, and 75% AHRJ by volume. The results show that AHRJ droplets burn slightly faster than Jet-A while adding AHRJ to Jet-A reduces the sooting propensity. These trends suggest the viability of blending Jet-A with AHRJ to fuel combustion engines.

COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Combustion science
Task Description:
One of the most important challenges of our time is to mitigate the harmful impacts of particulate emissions (soot) from combustion engines on global climate change, and to reduce the consumption of liquid petroleum fuels that power transportation systems. A promising concept is to mix petroleum fuels with bio-derived fuels. An evaluation of the performance benefits rests on diagnostics to unravel the complex relationships between soot formation and fuel properties. Under some conditions the presence of soot itself in the combustion field can intrude on this effort. Measurements that rely on digital video imaging of the fuel burning process, such as employed in the FLame Extinguishment eXperiment (FLEX), are vulnerable to this concern.
FLEX was developed to understand mechanisms that control flame extinction as it relates to cabin fire safety aboard manned spaceflight, though the broad methodologies are more widely applicable to combustion of fuel systems in combustion engines. The configuration of isolated droplets burning with near spherical symmetry was employed to elucidate the mechanisms involved. The main diagnostic was digital video imaging. From this information, quantitative measurements of the droplet and flame boundaries were made using suitable computer-based data extraction algorithms that revealed the influence of ambient gas conditions and liquid fuel properties on flame extinction. For some of the fuels employed in FLEX, soot formation was evident (i.e., n-heptane droplets burning in air), which obscured part of the droplet and flame boundary that can compromise data accuracy. The success of the FLEX program assumes the existence of efficient and accurate computer-based algorithms that can overcome the obscuration influence of soot on droplets, are able to track droplets if they move, and can account for deviations from sphericity due to ignition disturbances. However, this is not the case. Commercial image analysis packages are limited in their ability to deal with the presence of soot in the imaging field without significant user input. Failure to address this problem impacts not only deriving full benefit from the FLEX experiments already carried out, but also follow-on studies which would utilize digital video imaging to study droplet combustion dynamics of sooting fuels used in commercial transportation systems. In this proposal we address this problem be developing a diameter estimation refinement algorithm that employs concepts that automate droplet and flame diameter measurements from video images in the presence of soot. The algorithm will be used to re-analyze certain FLEX data on the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system -- results from a proof-of-concept program are included in the proposal for illustration -- and to extract quantitative data from new proposed experiments to study the influence of mixture fraction on blends of bio-derived fuels with an aviation fuel: hydroprocessed renewable jet fuel derived from algae with Jet-A (algal feedstocks have potential for larger yields compared to outer sources) for which soot formation is expected. The outcome will be a robust capability to process digital video images that efficiently and precisely extracts measurements from digital images even in the presence of soot aggregates. The results -- data and software -- will be freely available on various outlets as discussed in the proposal.
The project includes a team with expertise in developing algorithms for image analysis (Prof. Anthony Reeves of Cornell's Electrical and Computer Engineering Department) and experience in droplet combustion experimentation (Prof. C. Thomas Avedisian of Cornell's Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering (MAE) Department). The project team has supplies of the algae-derived and jet fuel systems that will be studied (Terravia, Inc; and the Air Force).

Task Description:
NOTE Update August 2020: New grant issued for Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames, with grant number 80NSSC20M0072, which continues to 4/30/2022. NOTE (September 2015): Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A).
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2026
Task Progress: We completed Round 1 (normal flames) and Round 2 (inverse flames) of Flame Design testing aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and processed and analyzed the data. We performed extensive analyses of the data and conducted numerical modeling, primarily with Sphdif. We also conducted many experiments of laminar flames in normal gravity. Thirty-four journal papers and 67 conference papers were published. [Ed. Note: See Cumulative Bibliography.] This body of work was recognized with five awards. This project resulted in 16 theses and dissertations. Most of the associated students are now employed in academia, government or industry, and many are conducting research.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2024
Task Progress:
We have completed Round 1 (normal flames) and Round 2 (inverse flames) of Flame Design testing and are processing and analyzing the data. We are running Sphdif simulations and publishing the findings.
Three journal papers were published this year and one other was submitted. One conference paper was published and presented. Kendyl Waddell defended and published his Ph.D. dissertation.
Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. February 2024 Update per PI. See Bibliography for additional information. (Ed., 2/15/24)
Despite a range of conditions, all flames extinguish at a critical temperature of 1130 K, a fuel-based mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames. With this information, we have developed a simple equation to estimate the flame size (i.e., location of peak temperature) at extinction for any atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given only the reactant mass flow rate. Flame growth, which ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development of the diffusion limited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the flame temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth).
Reference: Irace PH, Waddell KA, Constales D, Sunderland PB, Axelbaum RL. "Critical temperature and reactant mass flux for radiative extinction of ethylene microgravity spherical diffusion flames at 1 bar." Proc. Combust. Inst. 2023 Jan 1;39(2):1905-13. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2022.07.043
Despite a narrow range of attainable conditions, flames that exhibit steady-state behavior are observed aboard the International Space Station (ISS) for up to 870 seconds, even with the constraint of a finite boundary. Steady-state flames are simulated using the numerical model for over 100,000 seconds.
Reference: Irace PH, Waddell KA, Constales D, Kim M, Yablonsky G, Sunderland PB, Axelbaum RL. "On the existence of steady-state gaseous microgravity spherical diffusion flames in the presence of radiation heat loss." Proc. Combust. Inst. 2023 Jan 1;39(2):1721-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2022.07.049

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
We have completed Round 1 (normal flames) and Round 2 (inverse flames) of Flame Design testing and are processing the data. This includes making videos from HiBMs still images, converting video from the ops camera from ts to mp4 format, plotting the digital data for all tests, and measuring flame diameters.

We continue to plot and analyze the thermocouple data.
We continue to process the HiBMs data to obtain soot volume fraction and are using the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) images to obtain soot temperature. Fiber temperature is being used to measure flame temperature at the sooting limit. We have compiled all of our radiative extinction data, excluding extinction temperature.
An analytical model of steady-state diameters of gas-fed spherical diffusion flames was improved and included in several journal paper submissions.
Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. We simulated ethylene flames to perform parametric studies in an attempt to find conditions that are favorable to steady state flames.
