Task Description:
NOTE Update August 2020: New grant issued for Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames, with grant number 80NSSC20M0072, which continues to 4/30/2022. NOTE (September 2015): Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A).
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI (Principal Investigator), the Co-Is (Co-Investigators), and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, and Peter Sunderland directing experiments and numerical simulations at University of Maryland.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
We have completed Round 1 of Flame Design testing and are processing the data. This includes making videos from HiBMs still images, converting video from the ops camera from ts to mp4 format, plotting the digital data for all tests, and measuring flame diameters. We have finalized the test matrix for Round 2.
We are organizing the results of Flame Design Round 1 (flame diameter, fiber temperature, PMTs, radiometers, etc.). Particular focus has been placed on using two-color ratio and ratio intensity pyrometry to obtain fiber temperature. We continued to plot and analyze the thermocouple data.
We are processing HiBMs data to obtain soot volume fraction and are using the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) images to obtain soot temperature. Fiber temperature is being used to measure flame temperature at the sooting limit. We have compiled all of our radiative extinction data, excluding extinction temperature.
We have performed thin-filament pyrometry for several International Space Station (ISS) flames based on color ratios and based on grayscale intensity.
We have completed soot temperature measurements of ethylene and methane tri-axial flames using two-color pyrometry. We performed narrow-angle radiometer measurements of radiant emissions in ethylene tri-axial flames. Soot volume fraction measurements using color pyrometry and an absolute intensity calibration have been performed. In our research on double luminous zones, we have made our chemiluminescence images quantitative and have chosen some of them to be displayed as color contour plots of intensity at specific wavelengths. Thermocouple probing of the double luminous zones was performed. Work continued on the imaging of excited species.
An analytical model of steady-state diameters of gas-fed spherical diffusion flames was created.
Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. Because burner heating can significantly affect the flame diameter and lifetime, we have started to implement a heat balance at the burner surface to solve for burner temperature and better conserve enthalpy. We simulated ethylene flames to perform parametric studies in an attempt to find conditions that are favorable to steady state flames. We compared the simulation results with experimental results. Work is underway to update the globally implicit solver to the time-splitting method. We modified the SphDiff code to plot the radius of stoichiometric mixture fraction as a function of time, both for non-reacting and reacting flows. We added 2nd order upwind scheme. We modified the transient term in the conservation of mass equation so that it captures the density change due to temperature and concentration changes. We added an automatic temperature initialization scheme from an analytical droplet combustion model.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
Many laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) tests were performed. The system was optimized and the signal/data processing methodology was improved. We obtained calibration data of the relation between atomic ratio and intensity ratio of major elements (C,H,O,N) from a McKenna flat-flame burner. We reduced the burden on the transition stage by cutting down the distance from the measured point to the transition stage (for ethylene-air counter-flow burner). We measured the C/O, H/O, C/H atomic ratios along the center line of ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame. We used the acoustic system (LIBT) to measure the temperature profile on the center line of an ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame. All the results have been compared to the OPPDIF simulation and Wengdong's previous data, and we have verified that the LIBS measurement is reliable and repeatable.
At Washington University in the last two months, we have performed experiments to show the PM emissions from the pure ethylene flame and comparing PM (particulate matter) data of newly bought low pressure impactor [Electrical Low-Pressure Impactor (ELPI), model ELPI+, Dekati] and Scanning Mobility Particle Spectrometry (SMPS, model 3080, TSI Inc.). A rich ethylene flame was chosen as it produces soot at a uniform rate. A co-flow diffusion flame burner was used, which comprised of two coaxial channels for the flow of fuel and air, respectively. Particle sampling is achieved with an N2-diluted sampling probe. The flow of dilution N2 through the annulus gap provides the negative pressure needed to sample the flue gas as well as cool down and dilute the particle-laden flow. The dilution ratio (DR) is controlled by N2 flow rate and the physical dimension of the annulus gap, and CO2 is chosen as the tracer gas for dilution ratio measurement. A high flow rate of dilution N2 (~45 SLPM) is applied and the dilution ratio is controlled to a range of 30 – 200. The probe samples the whole particle stream while maintaining quasi-isokinetic sampling, and is expected to cause little bias for particle measurements. The ELPI and SMPS (scanning mobility particle spectrometer) data show similar trends. The experiments were also conducted to know the efficiency of ELPI with respect to time to get the correct PSD (particle size distribution) data. It was found that after 2 minutes of measurements, ELPI have to be cleaned as it creates a virtual mode owing to the partly over filing of ELPI stages. In the future, a new dilution system will be used and PM data will be compared between SMPS and ELPI at dilution ratio of the order of 10000 using rich ethylene flames.
At University of Maryland (UMD), the possible appearance of double luminous zones in normal diffusion flames was investigated in the literature and in the laboratory. Additional published flame lengths were added to our draft paper on flame lengths. Oxygen concentrations were measured in the chimney for inverse diffusion flames. A presentation on double luminous zones was made at ASGSR (American Society for Gravitational & Space Research) in Seattle.
At UMD we tested IDFs (inverse diffusion flames) with CO2 as diluent in both fuel side and oxidizer side. These did not have double luminous zones. We also tested IDFs with Ar and He as diluent. These had the most remarkable double luminous zones we have seen to date.
At UMD, work continues on improved imaging of species in normal and inverse diffusion flames. Interference filters have been acquired to allow the imaging of OH*, CH*, C2*, and CO2*. A Matlab script for Abel deconvolution has been modified for the resulting images. We have imaged our normal and inverse diffusion flames with various optical filters to identify the source of the blue emissions observed. We also have applied deconvolution to these images.
Work has progressed on identifying the species responsible for double blue zones in normal and inverse gas jet diffusion flames. Bandpass filters allow imaging of C2* (515 nm), CO2* (455 nm), CH* (430 nm), and OH* (310 nm). The images are deconvolved, and corrections for CO2* emissions are made in the images of C2* and CH* emissions.
WashU and UMD have been working together to begin welding B-type thermocouples (0.0015 in, 38 micron). These will initially be used to measure temperatures of co-flow diffusion flames at various stoichiometric mixture fraction.
The injection port of the single droplet generator has been modified to allow for continuous operation with a Hencken flat flame. Droplet generation in the previous design was unstable when run with a flame. The single droplet generator will allow for the study of preferential vaporization in nonpremixed flames. We modified the design of the droplet generator to be able to maintain a steady droplet stream with flame. Drawings were sent to machine shop and parts have been modified.
A new student has started at Wash U and he has been learning high-speed videography, PDPA, and manufacturing of fine-wire thermocouples. We are also developing a new method of making temperature measurements with high-speed videography.
The spherical flame code has been demonstrated for the first time by the new team of Ph.D. students. Work at UMD has emphasized the numerical model. The current graduate students are now able to simulate spherical normal and inverse diffusion flames. They have implemented an improved method of choosing the initial temperature profile.
The numerical modeling of spherical diffusion flames has progressed. This indicates that some normal flames of ethylene burning in air may be able to reach steady state. Furthermore, flames that continue burning with peak temperatures as low as 1000 K are observed. Previously no flames were predicted with these temperatures below 1100 K.
We completed the final review of “Science Protocol on Intent to Conduct an International Collaborative Research Effort Entitled Flame Design,” to support collaborative research with Russian Scientists.
Employing the principles developed by Long to support ACME (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments) research projects, WashU is developing capabilities to measure particle temperatures through direct photography.
Based on recent findings, the new graduate student at Washington University is beginning to construct a tri-coflow burner to test a theory of applying Flame Design concepts to control heat flux. We have modified an existing burner to create a triaxial coflow flame. The inner nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air, the middle nozzle supplies fuel (methane) or nitrogen diluted fuel, and the outer nozzle supplies air or oxygen enriched air. The inner oxidizer creates an inner flame sheet, resulting in two distinct flame zones. The goal of this project is to maximize radiation heat transfer in methane combustion by using flame design concepts to create a soot favorable environment at the inner flame sheet and then oxidize soot particles before they are released to the ambient environment. We have been taking high speed videos of the flame sheet interactions and are preparing to take radiation measurements.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
The laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) measurement method has been improved at Washington University in St. Louis. This includes a new oscilloscope setup and preparation for better acoustic monitoring. We have synchronized the new oscilloscope with the LIBS system. We completed work on noise filtering of the acoustic measurements. We performed Matlab programming on automated acoustic aided LIBS measurements. We performed high temperature LIBS tests in a Hencken burner, LIBS tests in a McKenna burner under same equivalence ratio and different temperature, and acoustic aided LIBS measurements in a McKenna burner with varying equivalence ratio. We adapted a maximum likelihood estimation method instead of average in LIBS data processing; compared and correlated the baseline for different element emission lines; and worked on the scalar measurement. We investigated the compositional effects in laser-induced backward transfer (LIBT) measurement and investigated the screening methods of LIBT measurement by looking into the statistics. We investigated the simultaneous composition and temperature measurement using laser induced plasma. We explored the water-gas-shift equilibrium in higher hydrocarbon flames and investigated the potential of inferring molecular profiles from LIBS measured elemental compositions. We investigated the water-gas-shift equilibrium in higher hydrocarbons using detailed mechanisms for heptane and toluene. We developed a plasma model to simulate the sound wave generation as a function of laser energy input and local gas properties and to optimize the measurements using a CCD based spectrometer.
Wendong Wu successfully defended his Ph.D. in May, 2017, at Washington University in St. Louis. The collaboration between Washington University and Shanghai Jiaotong University will continue in the field of laser plasma diagnostics. Graduate student Pan Du has joined the Flame Design team.
At the University of Maryland, we continue to examine the effects of dilution on lengths of normal and inverse gas jet diffusion flames. The method of measuring flame lengths was refined to examine only the blue intensities in the recorded images. Both normal and inverse flames now correlate together according to the theory of Roper. We have also characterized the double flame structure visible in some inverse diffusion flames. We imaged the double flames at 310 and 430 nm. We are measuring oxygen concentrations and temperatures in and above the double flames. This will help to determine if oxygen in this region contributes to the formation of the double luminous zones. A paramagnetic oxygen analyzer is being used, which has a mole fraction range of 0-1 and an accuracy of 0.001%.
At the University of Hawaii Manoa, Beei-Huan Chao has retired and resigned from his role as Flame Design Co-Investigator. His invaluable contributions to Flame Design are greatly appreciated and will be missed going forward. Prior to his retirement, progress was made on analytical studies of C/O ratio in diffusion flames. We examined extinction of spherical diffusion flames attached to a burner and revisited reactant leakage of diffusion flames. We revisited Linan's 1974 paper following the “total enthalpy” concept.
The research team published two journal papers, four conference papers and abstracts, and one Ph.D. dissertation.
The flight experiment was supported in various ways. For example, the research team responded to issues raised by NASA engineers in refining the test matrix and ACME requirements document. The research team also aided staff at NASA Glenn with burner characterization drop testing in the 2 s drop facility.

NOTE: Continuation of Flame Design - A Novel Approach to Clean Efficient Diffusion Flames (NNX09AO53A).
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This effort is a collaborative effort between the Principal Investigator, the three Co-Investigators, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor has Richard Axelbaum directing normal gravity experiments and computations at Washington University, David Urban providing guidance for the flight experiments, Peter Sunderland directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland (UMD), and Beei-Huan Chao directing analytical work and computations at University of Hawaii.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
Summary of Accomplishments
• The research team published 6 conference papers and abstracts during this period.
• Work at Univ. of Maryland has started a new experimental study on the effects of dilution on the stoichiometric lengths of normal and inverse gas jet diffusion flames Two new graduate students were added to this project at UMD: Zhengyang Wang (Ph.D.) and Mohamed El Makawy (M.S.). They have generated predictions of these effects from the model of Roper (1977). Stoichiometric lengths of over 250 flames have been measured. Physical constants in the model of Roper have been adjusted such that it predicts these reasonably well.
• Work at Washington University continued to pursue normal gravity experiments of soot formation in diffusion flames, numerical modeling, chemical kinetics, water-gas shift reaction rates, and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS). The LIBS measurement method has been improved. We now use a gated spectrometer to utilize C, H, N, O atomic lines instead of ionic lines in atomic ratio measurement. We improved accuracy with acoustic aid and automated baseline correction. Shot-to-shot variation is analyzed with relative standard deviation.
• Work at Univ. of Hawaii continued to pursue analytical and computational studies of soot formation, radiation, and extinction in diffusion flames. Also being investigated are ignition behavior and effects of C/O ratio in diffusion flames.
• The flight experiment was supported in various ways. For example, the research team responded to issues raised by NASA engineers in refining the test matrix and ACME requirements document. The research team also aided staff at NASA Glenn with burner characterization drop testing in the 2 s drop facility.
Scientific Context, Hypothesis, and Research Objectives
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. Additional Accomplishments
W. Wu, G. Yablonsky, R.L. Axelbaum, Observation of Water-Gas Shift Equilibrium in Diffusion Flames, Combustion and Flame, accepted. The kinetic behavior of the water-gas-shift (WGS) sub-system has been studied computationally for hydrocarbon diffusion flames in the counterflow geometry. Of specific interest was the spatial domain in which the reactions in the WGS-complex exhibit characteristics that lead to species concentrations approaching those expected from equilibrium. Two scenarios were observed for WGS equilibrium:
(1) Full equilibrium in which every step of the WGS-mechanism is nearly in equilibrium;
(2) “Apparent” equilibrium, which is achieved via opposing but coherent shifts away from equilibrium for the two key elementary reactions that constitute the WGS reaction. This interesting phenomenon is caused by the supply of the H radical, which participates in the forward reaction of one step and the reverse reaction of the other. This new form of apparent equilibrium differs from well-known “quasi” equilibrium, which is typically caused by the combination of a fast reversible step and slow irreversible step.
Parametric domains where found in which these two scenarios are observed. For a given fuel type it was shown that the two scenarios can be separated by the location of stoichiometry. On the oxidizer side, full equilibrium of the overall WGS reaction is achieved, while on the fuel side, apparent equilibrium can occur.
Z. Wang, M. El Makawy, P.B. Sunderland, B. Chao, R.L. Axelbaum, The Effects of Reactant Dilution on Lengths of Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames, Abstract, ASGSR, Cleveland OH (2016). Many past studies have examined the stoichiometric lengths of laminar gas jet diffusion flames. These are found to be independent of pressure and burner diameter for fixed fuel mass flow rate. However, some studies report flame lengths increase when inert is added to the fuel stream, whereas others report no change. Furthermore, measurements of effects of inert in the ambient gas are sparse, as are measurements for inverse flames. The analytical model of Roper (CNF 29:219, 1977) accounts for the full range of reactant dilution and inverse flames, but has only been tested for fuel-air systems.
This work examines the stoichiometric lengths of normal and inverse steady methane/oxygen/nitrogen jet flames burning on a 3.0 mm coflowing burner inside a glass chimney. Nitrogen dilution is such that methane mole fractions vary from 0.15 – 1 and oxygen mole fractions vary from 0.18 – 1. The measured flame lengths vary from 3 – 53 mm. Stoichiometric lengths are measured from visible emissions of the blue flame sheets. Reactant flow rates are measured with calibrated rotameters.
The predictions of the Roper model are compared with the measured flame lengths. For normal flames the agreement is best for a mass diffusivity at 25 C of 17 mm2/s and a temperature of 0.94 times the adiabatic flame temperature. This contrasts to values used by Roper for methane/air flames of 20 mm2/s and 1500 K, respectively. For the present conditions the predictions match the measurements with a R2 coefficient of determination of 0.91.
For fixed fuel flow rate, inert addition to the fuel stream is found to increase flame length, but this effect is negligible for fuel mole fractions above 0.5.
A simplified approximation of the Roper model has been obtained for normal methane/nitrogen/oxygen diffusion flames. This removes the requirement to specify adiabatic flame temperature and stoichiometric mixture fraction. The simplified model predicts flame length from the methane flow rate and mole fraction and the oxygen mole fraction.
W. Wu, R.L. Axelbaum, Interpreting Flame Structure by Mixture Fraction Measurement Using Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy, Abstract, ASGSR, Cleveland OH (2016). Measuring mixture fractions in a broad range of combustion systems with a suitable spatial and temporal resolution is critical not only for understanding the flame behavior, but also for the validation of rapidly developing numerical models. Instead of deriving the mixture fraction from measured molecular profile, a new approach of obtaining such quantities from atomic ratios measured by laser induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) is introduced in this study. The atomic ratios for C, N, H, and O (e.g., C/O, H/O, and N/O) for the LIBS system were first calibrated in an ethylene-air premixed flat flame, where the equivalence ratio of the pre-mixture was varied from 0.60 to 1.80. Then the atomic ratio distributions along the centerline of an ethylene-air counter-flow diffusion flame were measured to demonstrate the capability of LIBS to measure atomic ratios between different elements throughout the entire flame. The elemental mass fractions for C, H, N, O can be thus obtained from atomic ratio profiles. The mixture fraction distribution was calculated from elemental mass fractions. Numerical results were compared to the experimental results and showed excellent agreement. The results of this work demonstrate that the LIBS technique holds promise as a simple tool for measuring atomic ratios and mixture fraction in diffusion flames.
Practical Applications. This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.

We plan to perform additional simulations at Washington Univ., Univ. of Hawaii, and Univ. of Maryland. We plan to continue efforts to advance to flight tests and spherical burner development.

Additional Accomplishments
W. Wu, P.B. Sunderland, B.-H. Chao, D.L. Urban, R.L. Axelbaum, Recent Advances in Flame Design, A Spaceflight Combustion Experiment, Abstract, ASGSR, Alexandria, VA, 2015.
Flame Design is a spaceflight combustion experiment that will examine several unusual aspects of spherical diffusion flames fueled by gases. Its emphasis is on soot formation and flame extinction. This experiment, and associated ground-based work, attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This presentation will introduce the overall concepts of Flame Design. It will summarize observations in the NASA Glenn 2.2 s and 5 s drop facilities, which have yielded important insights into soot formation and flame extinction behavior. Detailed numerical modeling of spherical diffusion flames have aided the understanding of the observations. Recent advances in Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) will be discussed. LIBS allows the C/O atom ratio to be measured in flames. This diagnostic is well suited to use in spaceflight experiments.

Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
As the goal of this program is to develop an understanding of combustion with the aim of reducing pollutants and increasing combustion efficiency, the results are directly applicable to terrestial power generation. In particular, with the present interest in carbon sequestration via oxygen-enriched combustion the present work is of particular importance as it identifies methods of controlling a number of pollutants through oxygen-enriched combustion.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Below is a summary of the progress on this project for the year ending January 1, 2006:
Flame Design benefited from several analytical and computational advances in 2005. These have yielded important insight into many experimental observations by this project. This has laid the groundwork for two journal publications, one which was submitted and one which is nearing submission.
Work on the general behavior of spherical diffusion flames has demonstrated that a detailed transient numerical model (with detailed chemistry, transport, and radiation) can predict flame size and flame temperature for microgravity spherical diffusion flames. A simplified model indicates that Lewis number can have a large effect on flame temperature for microgravity diffusion flames. This work has been submitted to the Combustion Symposium.
Work on radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames has demonstrated that the detailed transient model can predict extinction times for microgravity spherical diffusion flames. The work identified several scaling relationship for extinguishing diffusion flames. This work is being finalized for an upcoming journal submission.
A Nikon D100 color digital still camera has been configured for use in the 2.2 second drop tower. This provides four images per drop. The images have 6 megapixels and 12 x 3 bit depth and are among the highest-fidelity images ever recorded in the drop tower.
This camera has been used to record images of 15 micron SiC fibers in flames in the 2.2 second drop tower. This has yielded qualitative thin-filament pyrometry results for extinguishing spherical diffusion flames. Eighteen successful drop tests were performed in the 2.2 second drop tower.

Task Description:
The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed 'Flame Design' as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Recognizing the unique benefits of spherical diffusion flames, employ such flames to:
1. Obtain soot-inception limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction (direction across the flame front, i.e., towards the fuel or towards the oxidizer), amount of inert (nitrogen) and pressure for ethylene and methane flames. Identify the corresponding soot-inception temperature;
2. Determine effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on the phenomenon of permanently blue flames and, to this end, determine the effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on flame temperature, size, color and soot volume fraction;

The division of labor is roughly broken up with DLU and PBS performing microgravity experiments at the NASA Glenn Research Center, PBS directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland, BHC performing analytical work at University of Hawaii, and RLA performing normal gravity experiments at Washington University. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2009
Task Progress:
The following is a summary of the research activities during the period Oct. 2006 - Sept. 2009.
1) Numerical and Experimental Observations of Spherical Diffusion Flames. Spherical diffusion flames supported on a porous sphere were studied numerically and experimentally. Experiments were performed in 2.2 s and 5.2 s microgravity facilities. Numerical results were obtained from a Chemkin-based program. The program simulates flow from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment, yields both steady state and transient results and accounts for optically thick gas-phase radiation. The low flow velocities and long residence times in these diffusion flames lead to enhanced radiative and diffusive effects. Despite similar adiabatic flame temperatures, the measured and predicted temperatures varied by as much as 700 K. The temperature reduction correlates with flame size but characteristic flow times and Lewis number also influence temperature. The numerical results show that the ambient gas Lewis number would have a strong effect on flame temperature if the flames were steady and nonradiating. For example, a 10% decrease in Lewis number would increase the steady state flame temperature by 200 K. However, for these transient, radiating flames the effect of Lewis number is small. It was also observed that when hydrocarbon fuel is supplied from the ambient the large diffusion distances associated with these flames can lead to unusual steady state compositions near the outer boundary because decomposition products can diffuse to the outer boundary. This results in a loss of chemical enthalpy from the system but the effect on flame temperature is small. Transient predictions of flame sizes are larger than those observed in microgravity experiments. Close agreement could not be obtained without either increasing the model’s thermal and mass diffusion properties by 30% or reducing mass flowrate by 25%.
2) Radiative Extinction of Gaseous Spherical Diffusion Flames in Microgravity. Radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames was investigated experimentally and numerically. The experiments involved microgravity spherical diffusion flames burning ethylene and propane at 0.98 bar. Both normal (fuel flowing into oxidizer) and inverse (oxidizer flowing into fuel) flames were studied, with nitrogen supplied to either the fuel or the oxygen. Flame conditions were chosen to ensure that the flames extinguished within the 2.2 s of available test time; thus extinction occurred during unsteady flame conditions. Diagnostics included color video and thin-filament pyrometry. The computations, which simulated flow from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment, included detailed chemistry, transport, and radiation and yielded transient results. Radiative extinction was observed experimentally and simulated numerically. Extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction were found to be independent of flow rate except at very low flow rates. Radiative heat loss was dominated by the combustion products downstream of the flame and was found to scale with flame surface area, not volume. For large transient flames the heat release rate also scaled with surface area and thus the radiative loss fraction was largely independent of flow rate. Peak temperatures at extinction onset were about 1100 K, which is significantly lower than for kinetic extinction. An important observation of this work is that while radiative heat losses can drive transient extinction, this is not only because radiative losses are increasing with time but also because the heat release rate is falling off as the flame expands away from the burner and the reactant supply to the flame decreases.
3) Soot Inception Limits in Laminar Diffusion Flames with Application to Oxy–Fuel Combustion. For diffusion flames, the combination of oxygen enrichment and fuel dilution results in an increase in the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, and alters the flame structure, i.e., the relationship between the local temperature and the local gas composition. Increasing Zst has been shown to result in the reduction or even elimination of soot. In the present work, the effects of variable Zst on soot inception are investigated in normal and inverse coflow flames, using ethylene as the fuel. Use of the inverse coflow flame underscores the validity of these concepts, since the convective field in the inverse flame directs particles into the fuel-rich region. Sooting limits based on particle luminosity are measured as a function of Zst. The sooting limit is obtained by varying the amount of inert gas until soot appears above a predefined height. For each limit flame, the adiabatic flame temperature is calculated and the flame temperature at the half-height is measured. The flame temperature at the sooting limit is found to increase with Zst for both normal and inverse flames. The effects of residence time are also investigated, and the sooting limit inception temperature is found to be dependent on fuel stream velocity for both the normal and inverse configurations. A simple model applicable to oxy–fuel combustion is presented which describes how increasing Zst results in the reduction and ultimately elimination of soot. This model assumes that soot inception can only occur in a region where critical values for species, temperature, and residence time are met. The soot inception region is shown to be bounded by two isotherms: a low-temperature boundary that is a function of residence time, and a high-temperature boundary that corresponds to the location of a critical local carbon-to-oxygen ratio. The effect of increasing Zst is to move the boundaries of the soot inception zone towards each other, until the zone is infinitely thin and thus the sooting limit is reached. By comparing the model to experimental data, a critical local C/O ratio of 0.53 and a sooting limit inception temperature of 1640 K (for a characteristic residence time of 22 ms) were determined for ethylene.
4) Characteristics of Non-Premixed Oxygen-Enhanced Combustion: I. The Presence of Appreciable Oxygen at the Location of Maximum Temperature. The presence of appreciable molecular oxygen at the location of maximum temperature has been observed in non-premixed oxygen-enhanced combustion (OEC) processes, specifically in flames having a high stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst) produced with diluted fuel and oxygen-enrichment. For conventional fuel–air flames, key features of the flame are consistent with the flame sheet approximation (FSA). In particular, the depletion of O2 at the location of maximum temperature predicted by the FSA correlates well with the near-zero O2 concentration measured at this location for conventional fuel–air flames. In contradistinction, computational analysis with detailed kinetics demonstrates that for OEC flames at high Zst: (1) there is an appreciable concentration of O2 at the location of maximum temperature and (2) the maximum temperature is not coincident with the location of global stoichiometry, O2 depletion, or maximum heat release. We investigate these phenomena computationally in three non-premixed ethylene flames at low, moderate, and high Zst, but with equivalent adiabatic flame temperatures. Results demonstrate that the location of O2 depletion occurs in the vicinity of global stoichiometry for flames of any Zst and that the presence of appreciable O2 at the location of maximum temperature for high Zst flames is caused by a shift in the location of maximum temperature relative to the location of O2 depletion. This shifting is attributed to: (1) finite-rate multi-step chemistry resulting in exothermic heat release that is displaced from the location of O2 depletion and (2) the relative location of the heat release region with respect to the fuel and oxidizer boundaries in mixture fraction space. A method of superposition involving a variation of the flame sheet approximation with two heat sources is shown to be sufficient in explaining this phenomenon.

Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
The following is a summary of the research activities during this period.
1) Work has continued on radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames, which are being investigated experimentally and numerically. The experiments involved microgravity spherical diffusion flames burning ethylene and propane at 0.98 bar. Both normal (fuel flowing into oxidizer) and inverse (oxidizer flowing into fuel) flames are studied, with nitrogen supplied to either the fuel or the oxygen. Flame conditions were chosen to ensure that the flames extinguished within the 2.2 s of available test time; thus extinction occurred during unsteady flame conditions. Diagnostics included color video and thin-filament pyrometry. The computations, which simulated flow from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment, include detailed transport properties, detailed chemistry and an optically thick radiative heat loss model to study the transient radiative extinction of spherical diffusion flames supported by a porous spherical burner. A flow of a reactant (fuel or oxidizer) issued from a porous sphere into a quiescent environment of the other reactant was considered in the simulation. Radiative extinction was observed experimentally and simulated numerically. Extinction time, peak temperature, and radiative loss fraction (ratio of the radiative heat loss rate to the heat generation rate) were found to be independent of flow rate except at very low flow rates. Radiative heat loss was dominated by the combustion products downstream of the flame and was found to scale with flame surface area, not volume. For large transient flames the heat release rate also scaled with surface area and thus the radiative loss fraction was largely independent of flow rate. Peak temperatures at extinction onset were about 1100 K, which is significantly lower than for kinetic extinction. One observation is that while radiative heat losses can drive transient extinction, this is not because radiative losses are increasing with time (flame size) but rather because the heat release rate is falling off as the temperature drops.
2) A new numerical study of limiting conditions for soot particle inception in spherical diffusion flames has been initiated. The flames were modeled using a one-dimensional, time accurate diffusion flame code with detailed chemistry and transport and an optically thick radiation model. Seventeen normal and inverse flames were considered, covering a wide range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic flame temperature, and residence time. These flames were previously observed to reach their sooting limits after 2 s of microgravity. Sooting-limit diffusion flames with residence times longer than 200 ms were found to have temperatures near 1190 K where C/O = 0.6, whereas flames with shorter residence times required increased temperatures. Acetylene was found to be a reasonable surrogate for soot precursor species in these flames, having peak mole fractions of about 0.01.
3) Our previous studies have shown a linear relationship between the limit flame temperature and stoichiometric mixture fraction for coflow flames at their sooting limit. The sooting limit in coflow flames is obtained by varying the amount of inert gas until soot appears above a predefined height. In this work sooting limits based on particle luminosity were measured as a function of Zst. For each limit flame, the flame temperature was measured and defined as the limit flame temperature. The limit flame temperature increases linearly with Zst, for both normal and inverse flames. The effects of residence time have also been investigated, and the soot inception temperature was found to be dependent on fuel stream velocity for both the normal and inverse configuration. Earlier experimental results and modeling indicated that a critical carbon to oxygen (C/O) ratio exists in the fuel rich region of the flame where soot inception is no longer favorable due to the presence of oxygen containing species. We extended this model to include the effects of finite rate chemistry and thus residence time on the sooting limit. This involved considering two boundaries for the soot inception zone, one dictated by the C/O ratio and the other by the finite rate chemistry of fuel pyrolysis and soot inception. By combining these two boundaries, a simple model was developed that describes how a sooting limit is attained. By utilizing measured limit temperature data with the model we found the limit inception temperature for soot formation to be 1640 K and the critical carbon to oxygen ratio to be 0.53.
4) Performed analytical analysis of the kinetic and radiative extinction limits of a steady spherical diffusion flame supported by a porous burner. A single step, overall and irreversible reaction that follows high activation energy Arrhenius kinetics was adopted to describe the reaction rate. An optically thin radiation model was used to describe the radiative heat loss. The kinetic and radiative extinction limits were observed from the analysis. Results show that the flame is easier to extinguish when the radiation intensity is higher, as expected, and there exists a maximum radiation intensity above which steady burning is not possible.

V.R. Lecoustre, P.B. Sunderland, B.H. Chao, R.L. Axelbaum, Modeled Quenching Limits of Spherical Hydrogen Diffusion Flames, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute 34 (2013) 887-894. Hydrogen-air diffusion flames were modeled with an emphasis on kinetic extinction. The flames were one-dimensional spherical laminar diffusion flames supported by adiabatic porous burners of various diameters. Behavior of normal (H2 flowing into quiescent air) and inverse (air flowing into quiescent H2) configurations were considered using detailed H2/O2 chemistry and transport properties with updated light component diffusivities. For the same heat release rate, inverse flames were found to be smaller and 290 K hotter than normal flames. The weakest normal flame that could be achieved before quenching has an overall heat release rate of 0.25 W, compared to 1.4 W for the weakest inverse flame. There is extensive leakage of the ambient reactant for both normal and inverse flames near extinction, which results in a premixed flame regime for diffusion flames except for the smallest burners with radii on the order of 1 micron. At high flow rates H+OH(+M)?H2O(+M) contributes over 40% of the net heat release. However at flow rates approaching quenching limits, H+O2(+M)?HO2(+M) is the elementary reaction with the largest heat release rate. The corresponding author for this paper was P.B. Sunderland.
F. Xia, R.L. Axelbaum, Simplifying the complexity of diffusion flames through interpretation in C/O ratio space, Computers and Mathematics with Applications, 65 (2013) 1625-1632. Understanding the structure of diffusion flames is often complicated by the dependence of flame structure on the boundary conditions, e.g. composition, temperature and flow field (e.g., strain rate in a counterflow flame.) In this paper, the local carbon-to-oxygen atom ratio (C/O ratio) is applied as a variable to interpret the flame and soot zone structures of counterflow diffusion flames from numerical results with detailed chemical kinetics and transport. Radical pool and soot precursor zones are shown to be clearly delineated in C/O ratio space. The boundary of these two zones, as well as the flame location, are shown to be independent of both stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst) and strain rate when interpreted in C/O space. The kinetic ratio is used to study the characteristics of key chemical reactions and to identify regions of equilibrium for these reactions. The results of this paper indicate that the C/O ratio is a valuable variable for interpreting flame structure and soot precursor chemistry for diffusion flames. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.
F. Xia, G.S. Yablonsky, R.L. Axelbaum, Numerical Study of Flame Structure and Soot Inception Interpreted in Carbon-to-Oxygen Atom Ratio Space, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 34 (2013) 1085-1091. The utility of interpreting flame results in carbon-to-oxygen atom ratio (C/O ratio) space, as opposed to physical space or mixture fraction space, is evaluated. Flame and soot zone structures of counterflow diffusion flames have been studied for C2H4 and C3H8 and interpreted in C/O ratio space as a function of stoichiometric mixture fraction (Zst). The Burke-Schumann results expressed in C/O ratio space demonstrate how a clear and direct understanding of how structure is affected by Zst can be realized in C/O ratio space because, unlike physical or mixture fraction space, the flame location is independent of stoichiometric mixture fraction. Numerical results with detailed chemical kinetics also indicate that C/O ratio space is a fundamental variable in the sense that, for a given fuel, the location of the flame zones and critical reactions is invariant with Zst and strain rate. Two zones are clearly observed, namely the radical pool and the soot precursor zone located on the fuel side of the flame. The onset threshold of soot precursors (C6H5 and C6H6) for the high temperature side of the soot precursor zone is characterized by the depletion of radicals. The role of the hydrogen radical in flame structure and soot inception is demonstrated by studying its production and consumption channels in C/O ratio space. Finally, a modified (C/O)* is given to interpret the physical meaning of C/O ratio. The numerical results in this work indicate and explain the advantages of applying C/O ratio space in the analysis of flame structure and soot precursor chemistry. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.
F. Yi, R.L. Axelbaum, Stability of Spray Combustion for Water/Alcohols Mixtures in Oxygen-Enriched Air, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 34 (2013) 1697-1704. The feasibility of burning fuels that are heavily diluted with water was evaluated. This concept could potentially be utilized to directly generate steam for a variety of applications, including power generation and enhanced oil recovery. Two water-soluble fuels, ethanol and 1-propanol, were heavily diluted with water and sprayed into a swirl-stabilized burner and the blow-off limits were obtained to identify the flame stability. The blow-off limit was experimentally determined as the lowest O2 concentration where a flame could exist under a given oxidizer flow rate. For the present experimental system, stability maps were determined as a function of fuel concentration and oxidizer flow rate for different types of nozzles and both alcohols. Contours of temperature and overall fuel mass fraction in the droplets were obtained for a flame burning 15 wt% ethanol in an oxidizer of 50% O2 and 50% N2. The results revealed that preferential vaporization of ethanol over water plays an important role in enhancing flame stability. To further understand this, a model of bi-component droplet vaporization was employed for both the diffusion limit and distillation limit modes of liquid mass transfer. The results confirmed the preferential vaporization of ethanol and demonstrated that it is necessary to account for the non-ideal solution behavior of the alcohol-water mixture to appropriately model the vaporization process. The model also demonstrated that for this experimental system, droplet vaporization was better characterized by the distillation limit mode with enhanced mass transfer by convection. The corresponding author for this paper was R.L. Axelbaum.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Task Description:
This effort is a collaborative effort between the PI, the three Co-Is, and staff at NASA Glenn Research Center. The division of labor is roughly broken up with DLU and PBS performing microgravity experiments at the NASA Glenn Research Center, PBS directing numerical simulations at University of Maryland, BHC performing analytical work at University of Hawaii, and RLA performing normal gravity experiments at Washington University. The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project has the potential for improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in terrestrial combustors. For example, it is contributing to novel designs of future coal power plants.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Task Description:
This investigation examines the interaction between magnetic fields and combustion processes. Using both experimental and mathematical models, the impact of magnetic fields on laminar diffusion flames will be quantified. Initially, terrestrial based experiments will be conducted to gain insight into the magnetocombustion interaction. This data will also be used to gauge the effectiveness of mathematical magnetocombustion models. The mathematical models will then be used to guide the development of a series of reduced gravity experiments. Unfortunately, due to the fact that both magnetic and gravitational forces are body forces, it is impossible to isolate magnetic field effects in a terrestrial environment. The experimental component of the study will examine the impact of non-uniform magnetic fields on laminar diffusion flames in a reduced gravity environment where the impact of gravitational acceleration is greatly reduced. The goal of the study is to explore the interaction between magnetic fields and combustion processes. The three principal objectives of the research are:
1. To experimentally observe, in an environment where buoyant forces are negligible, the effect of non-uniform magnetic fields on diffusion flame characteristics and on the associated temperature fields;
2. To better understand the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in non-uniform magnetic fields and the impact that paramagnetism and diamagnetism have with regard to transport phenomena in the vicinity of such flames; and
3. To formulate mathematical models that can accurately predict experimentally observed magnetocombustion behavior. Magnetic fields affect diffusion flame behavior as a result of the paramagnetic and diamagnetic characteristics of the constituent gases. By developing a fundamental understanding of this interaction, it will be possible to intelligently control the transport characteristics in the vicinity of the flame. This study seeks to quantify magnetocombustion interactions by examining such behavior in an environment where magnetic fields effects can be isolated from buoyancy effects.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
By examining the impact of magnetic fields on laminar diffusion flames, a better fundamental understanding of how magnetic fields can be used to intelligently control the behavior of flame is being developed. This understanding could potentially be used to develop technology which can improve combustion efficiency and reduce harmful emissions from combustion related processes.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
The past year has primarily focused on the design and fabrication of an experimental test cell for the MACE project. A first draft of the TEDP was received by NASA and significant revisions to document and to the design of the test cell were required. This has resulted in the inclusion of a much expanded structural analysis in the TEDP. While the initial design of the experimental frame met or exceeded NASA requirements, complete documentation of the calculations used to show that these requirements were met have now been included in the TEDP. As per other comments made regarding the first version of the TEDP, the overall design and arrangement of the experimental components have been modified. This redesign and refabrication took considerable time as it required a dismantling of the original test cell which had flown previously during two NASA Reduced Gravity Student Flight Opportunities Program campaigns.
In parallel to the experimental effort, the effort related to the theoretical modeling of magnetocombustion behavior continued. A complete investigation as to the impact of non-uniform magnetic fields on laminar diffusion flames was conducted using the magnetocombustion flame height model previously developed. In addition, the flame height model is being modified to predict flame shape. Data from the theoretical model have not only yielded insight into the fundamental nature of the interaction between magnetic fields and diffusion flames but have also been useful in the redesign of the experimental test cell.
The second draft of the TEDP was recently submitted to NASA and comments/suggestions regarding the second TEDP have been received from NASA.

Task Description:
Funding is for Dr. Beeson's role as U.S. Co-Investigator for the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)-sponsored project, “Flammability Limits At Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE)." JAXA International Announcement of Opportunity (AO) to fund experiments to be conducted aboard the Japanese Experiment Module, Kibo, 2012.
NASA’s fire safety standards have not confirmed scientifically that they are always conservative for fire safety in space because the test is based on the flammability in the normal gravity. It is already known that a solid material’s flammability in microgravity may be greater than in normal gravity for some conditions. Therefore, whether the NASA's standards will be applied for future space missions by individual countries, or if better general standards for fire safety (e.g., oxygen index method) would be better for fire safety in space should be studied. This work aims to determine what standards are adequate for the evaluation of fire safety and material flammability in space.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Studying materials flammability in space allows us to accurately control the flow field and thus elucidate the importance of a critical Damkohler number (flow time /reaction time) on flame extinction. The anticipated improved methodology should reduce time and cost for the spacecraft material screening. Investigation and results have Earth benefits for terrestrial fire safety.

Task Description:
Despite intensive research on microgravity flame spread in the last decade, inspired primarily from fire safety concerns in manned space travel, a number of aspects of the flame spread problem has been identified that still remain unexplored or unresolved. Primary among those is to establish experimentally whether a spreading flame self-extinguishes in a quiescent microgravity environment, and if so, under what circumstances. Although there is some experimental evidence that for thick fuels steady spread does not occur, the phenomenon of self-extinguishment, with its importance fire-safety related consequences, deserves to be scrutinized further. Moreover, the mechanism of extinguishment remains to be addressed. For instance, we would like to answer if extinction occurs at a particular critical fuel thickness, how that thickness depends on the ambient and fuel parameters, how long does it take for a flame to extinguish, etc.
To settle this important issue and address a number of related outstanding problems of flame spread, we propose four space-based experiments on flame spread over thin sheets of PMMA placed in the center of a wind tunnel in which a fully developed flow of oxygen/nitrogen mixture with prescribed average velocities can be created. The experiments are made compact by moving the fuel, spooled on two rollers, opposite to the direction of the spread to make the flame stationary. As a result, experimental parameters, especially flow velocity and fuel thickness, can be varied in a single experiment without intervention from an operator. By simply changing the location of the igniter the experiment can be re-configured for concurrent-flow spread.
The project is directly related to basic understanding of flame spread important for materials selection leading to minimization of risk of ignition and fire hazard in space stations and space voyages. Besides the outstanding issues, microgravity offers a unique opportunity to link the two paradigms of flame spread - wind-aided and wind opposed configurations - by gradually reversing the direction of flow velocity in the same experiment. Moreover, the rich data set produced by the proposed experiments will help verify existing spread rate formulas and fuel development of new formulas that bring together the two regimes of concurrent-flow and opposed-flow flame spread. Currently such data is available only for flow velocities greater than the velocity induced by buoyancy driven flow. As a result flame spread formulas are unavailable or untested at the low velocity range most relevant to microgravity environment. The proposed imaging diagnostics, builds upon earlier development of emission pyrometry by the first PI, and is expected to produce improved non-obtrusive measurement of line-of-sight-averaged temperature and concentration field. The orginal goal of the proposed effort is to conduct a simple yet definitive set of experiments that, coupled with computational modeling and theoretical effort, can resolve the ten outstanding issues of flame spread. Although many of these issues involve refinement of existing models to unify different sub-regimes of flame spread, issue 3, that defines appropriate gravity level in an experiment, issues 7 and 8, that experimentally resolve the mechanism of flame extinction at quiescent environment, and issue 9, that links concurrent-flow flame spread with opposed-flow spread, are the core issues of this proposal. The simplicity of the experiment allowing a huge volume of data without any additional cost offers a unique opportunity to address the rest of the issues. The importance of fire safety in manned space travel cannot be overstated. The proposed research hopes to establish criteria under which flames, previously thought to be self propagating, extinguishes by itself. If a critical fuel thickness can be reliably predicted above which steady flames cannot be sustained over a combustible material, it will have a direct impact on how combustible materials are made fire safe in the Internal Space Station.
The study of transition between wind-aided spread rate to wind-opposed spread rate will allow us to leverage the microgravity experiments to link earth bound flames, which are mostly wind-aided, to wind-opposed flames, which are theoretically better understood.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
1. We have theoretically shown that all fuels behave as thermally thin fuel in a perfectly quiescent environment. More interestingly, we have developed an expression that predicts a critical fuel thickness, above which steady flame cannot be sustained in such an environment irrespective of the ambient conditions. Our drop tower data and previously published flammability data are consistent with these conclusions.
2. We have developed flame spread rate expressions both for thin and thick fuels in a low velocity opposed-flow environment that microgravity typically offers. These expressions, similar to de Ris spread rate formulas, are first of its kind that clearly decouples the radiative effects. We have posted a Java applet in the web site of this project, flame.sdsu.edu, which calculates spread rate in opposed-flow configuration for a variety of fuel and ambient conditions.
3. Using the microgravity flame spread rate expressions, flammability maps are derived for both PMMA and cellulosic fuels, which compare quite well with the available experimental data. It is shown that the radiative effects alone dominate the microgravity flame extinction.
4. A comprehensive computational model that includes gas and surface radiation is used to predict the spread rates for which experimental results were obtained earlier in the MGLab of Japan. Computational and experimental spread rates are compared with the theoretical predictions for various fuel thickness, opposing flow velocity, and oxygen level. The results show reasonably good agreement, the first of its kind in published literature.
5. The comprehensive computational model is used to produce correlations for flame length and stand-off distance with known parameters.
5. The computational model is extended to study transition between wind-opposed and wind-aided flame spread. Compuational results are compared with experiments performed in the MGLab of Japan.
4. The educational outreach site we developed ( http://thermo.sdsu.edu) continues to be used by educators, professionals, and students. There are more than 6700 registered users of this site.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The space based experiment that was originally proposed could not materialize after we were instructed to conduct only ground-based research. The ground based data we acquired in the MGLAB of Japan and parabolic flights in Nagoya were analyzed. The data agreed reasonably well with our proposed theory of microgravity flame spread rate. Our achievements can be summarized as follows.
1. We have theoretically shown that all fuels behave as thermally thin fuel in a perfectly quiescent environment. More interestingly, we have developed an expression that predicts a critical fuel thickness, above which steady flame cannot be sustained in such an environment irrespective of the ambient conditions. Our drop tower data and previously published flammability data are consistent with these conclusions.
2.We have developed flame spread rate expressions both for thin and thick fuels in a low velocity opposed-flow environment that microgravity typically offers. These expressions, similar to de Ris spread rate formulas, are first of its kind that clearly decouples the radiative effects. We have posted a Java applet in the web site of this project, flame.sdsu.edu, which calculates spread rate in opposed-flow configuration for a variety of fuel and ambient conditions.
3. Using the microgravity flame spread rate expressions, flammability maps are derived for both PMMA and cellulosic fuels, which compare quite well with the available experimental data. It is shown that the radiative effects alone dominate the microgravity flame extinction.
4. The educational outreach site we developed ( http://thermo.sdsu.edu) continues to receive great comments from users, students, educators and professionals, around the world. To date more than 2300 educators have registered to use this site.
The flame tracker hardware we built at SDSU has demonstrated the feasibility of our proposed experiment in space in which a flame is made stationary by moving the fuel. We have completed the construction of the vertical tower flame spread facility. Some of the preliminary results in which the flow velocity is changed from +60 cm/s to -60 cm/s (wind opposed and wind-aided configurations) are reported here for the first time. The development of the object-oriented three dimensional computational code is also proceeding well. We have requested a no-cost extension of the grant. Hopefully, by the next reporting period we will have some new computational results to present.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
We have completed the development of microgravity flame spread theory and published the results in the 30th symposium of combustion.
We have also completed the construction of the SDSU Flame Tower in which a sample can be moved upward or downward at any desired velocity. Our preliminary data indicate that the flow configuraiton can be effectively controlled from wind-opposed to wind-aided spread.

Abstracts for Journals and Proceedings
S. Bhattacharjee "A Time-Scale Analysis of Opposed-Flow Flame Spread" Opposed-flow flame spread over solid fuels has been extensively studied over the last three decades1-5. While most of the work have been concentrated into separate studies of the sub-categories such as the thermal regime, thick fuels, thin fuels, super-thin fuels, downward spread, kinetic regime, radiative regime, and, recently, microgravity regime, efforts to bring them together through a single analysis have been relatively few5. Although scaling arguments5,6 have been used in the past to understand the mechanism of flame spread and the complicated energy balance on the fuel surface, in this work we offer a novel time scale analysis encompassing all sub-regimes for the first time following the scale-analysis conventions established by Bejan7. Existing analytical solutions, comprehensive computational model and available experimental data will be used to validate the results and, whenever possible, determine critical values of the non-dimensional numbers arising out of scaling arguments that delineate the sub-regimes of opposed-flow flame spread. 4th Int. Symp. On Scale Modeling (ISSM-IV), Cleveland, Sept. 17-19, 2003 , Sep-2003
Abstracts for Journals and Proceedings
Paolini, C., Yeo, K.H., and Bhattacharjee, S. "An Object Oriented Formulation for the Finite Volume SIMPLER" Object oriented programming (OOP) offer several advantages over traditional structural languages. Most of the codes to implement finite-volume formulation, however, are legacy codes that are written primarily in Fortran. If a finite volume cell can be treated as an object, it can be imparted the decision making power to update its field. A cell where nothing is happening will simply turn itself off, thereby, saving unnecessary computations. Parallelization can be a natural extension of such computing approach. In this paper an object-oriented design of the SIMPLE algorithm is presented. Using Java a three-dimensional energy equation solver has been implemented. The ultimate goal of this project is to develop an object-oriented code that can be easily adopted to simulate opposed and concurrent-flow flame spread. Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of "Residence Time Driven Flame Spread Over Solid Fuels," grant # NNX10AE03G, with the same Principal Investigator (PI) Subrata Bhattacharjee, PhD.
Flame spread over solid fuels in an opposed-flow environment has been investigated for over four decades for understanding the fundamental nature of hazardous fire spread. The appeal for this configuration stems from the fact that flame spread rate remains steady, even if the flame itself may grow in size. For practical fire safety issues, however, wind-assisted flame spread is more relevant.
However, these two regimes have always been studied in isolation without much effort to establish a connection, even though the underlying mechanism of flame spread is the same in all regimes. Sitting between the two regimes are high-residence time flames, as found in a low-velocity or quiescent microgravity environment. Residence time is the time spent by an oxidizer in the combustion zone. Such flames, which are of interest on their own merit due to fire safety issues in spacecraft, offer some unique characteristics because of the high residence time. Radiation becomes dominant and, based on previous space experiments and analysis, we contend that a vigorously spreading flame on Earth becomes self-extinguishing in a microgravity environment under certain conditions such as the fuel thickness being greater than a critical value.
The goal of the RTDFS (Residence Time Driven Flame Spread) experiments as part of the SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction) program is to experimentally test the hypothesis that radiative quenching of a flame in a low gravity environment is caused by the asymmetry between how the species field and temperature field evolve. While the radiation loss, enhanced due to higher residence time, restricts the size of the reaction zone, the combustion products field keeps expanding around the flame, displacing the oxidizer, in effect choking the flame.
Using results from BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids) experiments, part of our hypothesis that under a critical flow velocity flames will extinguish in a microgravity environment has already been tested successfully, resulting in a number of publications. The RTDFS experiments will provide us with much more comprehensive measurements on the species and temperature distribution around the flame, leading to a better understanding of the mechanism of flame quenching. Moreover, flame spread experiments over samples covering a range of thicknesses will help us experimentally establish the critical fuel thickness above which flames become self extinguishing, a phenomenon predicted by theoretical and computational analysis.
One of the significant works we have carried out this year is to explore the similarities between flame spread in a microgravity environment with that in a low-pressure terrestrial environment. We have identified the non-dimensional numbers that capture the radiative and chemical kinetics effects, which are both affected by gravity and pressure. The work, published in the 38th Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, shows that while the a reduction in pressure or gravity affects the radiation number in a similar manner, their effect on the kinetics number (Damkohler number) is just the opposite. Therefore, a low-pressure experiment cannot be a substitute for a low-gravity experiment.
Another key work involved a comprehensive comparison of different radiation sub-models to evaluate the importance of (i) surface radiation loss, (ii) gas radiation loss; and (iii) radiation feedback on flame spread rate and flame structure in different regimes of opposed-flow flame spread.
In preparation to the RTDFS experiments we will focus our work on: (i) Comprehensive numerical modeling of the entire experimental matrix; (ii) Improving the pyrolysis kinetics model; (iii) Investigating effect of solid conductivity on radiative quenching of flames; (iv) Predicting of flame length; (v) Expanding our work to cylindrical geometry.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research has four components. (a) We have built three experimental setups at San Diego State University (SDSU) : Flame Tower where a test sample can be traversed up or down at any desired velocity; Flame Stabilizer where the motion of the flame can be arrested by moving the sample exactly at the speed of the flame spread in the opposite direction; and a rotating Flame Tunnel where a combustion tunnel can be oriented at any desired angle to study the interaction of buoyancy and forced flow; (b) Theoretical and computational work that explores the similarity and differences between the mechanisms flame spread in a zero gravity space environment and on Earth; (c) Support the space based experiment (in the SoFIE project) to establish extinction mechanism of flames; (d) Develop software tools for data analysis and share those with the research community.
The data that we are acquiring in the experiments provide the research community with a comprehensive set of results for testing different theories of flame spread in a normal gravity environment. Moreover, by controlling the residence time, various regimes of flame spread, including the microgravity regime, can be explored in the Flame Tower. Our theoretical work predicts a fuel thickness beyond which steady flame spread is unsustainable in a gravity free environment. If we are successful in establishing a critical thickness, this will have a powerful impact on making fire resistant environment for humans in space.
As part of this project, we are developing thermodynamic calculators for combustion and equilibrium calculations, which has a significant educational component. These are available to the community through http://www.thermofluids.net . We have also developed a MATLAB based image processing tool named FIAT (Flame Image Analysis Tool), which is now available to the community from http://flame.sdsu.edu .
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
With the difficulties accessing SDSU laboratories due to COVID related restrictions, our research focus for this period has been mostly theoretical. To understand the mechanism of opposed-flow flame spread and to develop predictive abilities, the flame was divided into three zones: preheat zone, pyrolysis zone, and the plume region. Our work on the pyrolysis zone led to an ASGSR presentation and submission of two manuscripts, one to the 39th International Symposium on Combustion and another to the ICES 2022 conference. Another theoretical work we undertook – developing flame spread rate expressions for cylindrical sample – led to two conference presentations and submission of a manuscript to the 39th International Symposium on Combustion.
We also continued our collaborative research work with our Japanese colleagues, which led to a third manuscript for the 39th International Symposium on Combustion.
Now that the pandemic related restrictions are easing, we have restarted our experimental effort, recruited new students, and looking forward to a productive research year ahead. [Ed. Task Description:
