Radiation becomes dominant and, based on previous space experiments and analysis, we contend that a vigorously spreading flame on Earth becomes self-extinguishing in a microgravity environment under certain conditions such as the fuel thickness being greater than a critical value.
The proposed research uses a comprehensive approach-- a novel experimental set up and a theoretical framework based on scaling and numerical modeling-- to investigate flame spread driven by varying residence time, from blow-off extinction in an opposed-flow configuration through high residence time flame to blow-off extinction in a concurrent-flow configuration. At the heart of this proposal is a novel but simple experiment where the residence time of the oxidizer can be controlled and high residence time flames can be established for a long duration (compared to drop towers). As a proof of concept, we have constructed a flame tower at San Diego State University (SDSU) in which, after a sample is ignited, the sample holder, placed in an open moveable cart, can be traversed at any desired speed upward or downward, creating an external flow that can augment or mitigate the buoyancy-induced flow. Preliminary results show that we can control the residence time and create flames in different regimes, including a transition between a wind-aided and wind-opposed configuration. At Gifu University in Japan, we have been developing an interferometry based imaging system which we intend to enhance to capture the thermal footprint of a flame's leading edge. The leading edge is central to our understanding of mechanism of flame extinction. Further development of this technology will enable us to integrate diagnostics in future space based experiments and provide validation data to a comprehensive numerical model. The comprehensive model, to be built upon our existing two-dimensional model, will solve an unsteady, three-dimensional, Navier stokes equation with finite rate kinetics in the gas and solid phases and radiation in the gas phase. The software implementation will be object-oriented and utilize a new technology called Web Services that will decouple various sub-models and enhance parallel execution.
The radiation model will also be refined by including the equilibrium composition of species for finding radiative properties in high residence-time flames. The comprehensive model, tested against available theory, data in literature, and data generated at SDSU and Gifu, was applied to test the three hypotheses presented in the preceding grant regarding flame extinguishment in a microgravity environment. A successful outcome of that project is leading to a well thought out space-based experiment on the mechanism of flame extinction in a gravity free environment. We have received authority to proceed to Preliminary Design Review.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
We have completed a very productive year with vigorous experimental, theoretical, and numerical research in support of the Residence Time Driven Flame Spread (RTDFS) module of the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. The major achievements of this period include publication of archival journal papers, several conference papers, further development of the radiation model, ground based experiments at San Diego State, and preparations for analysis of the expected data from the SoFIE experiments.
Luca Carmignani has defended his Ph.D. dissertation and joined the Fernandez-Pello research group at University of California (UC) Berkeley in January, 2020. Several Masters students, undergraduate students, and visiting research students from Germany have contributed to our research effort during this reporting period.

Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of "Residence Time Driven Flame Spread Over Solid Fuels," grant # NNX10AE03G, Principal Investigator Subrata Bhattacharjee, PhD.
Flame spread over solid fuels in an opposed-flow environment has been investigated for over four decades for understanding the fundamental nature of hazardous fire spread. The appeal for this configuration stems from the fact that flame spread rate remains steady, even if the flame itself may grow in size. For practical fire safety issues, however, wind-assisted flame spread is more relevant.
However, these two regimes have always been studied in isolation without much effort to establish a connection, even though the underlying mechanism of flame spread is the same in all regimes. Sitting between the two regimes are high-residence time flames, as found in a low-velocity or quiescent microgravity environment. Residence time is the time spent by an oxidizer in the combustion zone. Such flames, which are of interest on their own merit due to fire safety issues in spacecraft, offer some unique characteristics because of the high residence time. Radiation becomes dominant and, based on previous space experiments and analysis, we contend that a vigorously spreading flame on Earth becomes self-extinguishing in a microgravity environment under certain conditions such as the fuel thickness being greater than a critical value.
The proposed research uses a comprehensive approach-- a novel experimental set up and a theoretical framework based on scaling and numerical modeling-- to investigate flame spread driven by varying residence time, from blow-off extinction in an opposed-flow configuration through high residence time flame to blow-off extinction in a concurrent-flow configuration. At the heart of this proposal is a novel but simple experiment where the residence time of the oxidizer can be controlled and high residence time flames can be established for a long duration (compared to drop towers). As a proof of concept, we have constructed a flame tower at San Diego State University (SDSU) in which, after a sample is ignited, the sample holder, placed in an open moveable cart, can be traversed at any desired speed upward or downward, creating an external flow that can augment or mitigate the buoyancy-induced flow. Preliminary results show that we can control the residence time and create flames in different regimes, including a transition between a wind-aided and wind-opposed configuration. At Gifu University in Japan, we have been developing an interferometry based imaging system which we intend to enhance to capture the thermal footprint of a flame's leading edge. The leading edge is central to our understanding of mechanism of flame extinction. Further development of this technology will enable us to integrate diagnostics in future space based experiments and provide validation data to a comprehensive numerical model. The comprehensive model, to be built upon our existing two-dimensional model, will solve an unsteady, three-dimensional, Navier stokes equation with finite rate kinetics in the gas and solid phases and radiation in the gas phase. The software implementation will be object-oriented and utilize a new technology called Web Services that will decouple various sub-models and enhance parallel execution.
The radiation model will also be refined by including the equilibrium composition of species for finding radiative properties in high residence-time flames. The comprehensive model, tested against available theory, data in literature, and data generated at SDSU and Gifu, was applied to test the three hypotheses presented in the preceding grant regarding flame extinguishment in a microgravity environment. A successful outcome of that project is leading to a well thought out space-based experiment on the mechanism of flame extinction in a gravity free environment. We have received authority to proceed to Preliminary Design Review.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research has four components. (a) We have built three experimental setups at SDSU: Flame Tower where a test sample can be traversed up or down at any desired velocity; Flame Stabilizer where the motion of the flame can be arrested by moving the sample exactly at the speed of the flame spread in the opposite direction; and a rotating Flame Tunnel where a combustion tunnel can be oriented at any desired angle to study the interaction of buoyancy and forced flow; (b) Theoretical and computational work that explores the similarity and differences between the mechanisms flame spread in a zero gravity space environment and on Earth; (c) Support the space based experiment (in the SoFIE project) to establish extinction mechanism of flames; (d) Develop software tools for data analysis and share those with the research community.
The data that we are acquiring in the experiments provide the research community with a comprehensive set of results for testing different theories of flame spread in a normal gravity environment. Moreover, by controlling the residence time, various regimes of flame spread, including the microgravity regime, can be explored in the Flame Tower. Our theoretical work predicts a fuel thickness beyond which steady flame spread is unsustainable in a gravity free environment. If we are successful in establishing a critical thickness, this will have a powerful impact on making fire resistant environment for humans in space.
As part of this project, we are developing thermodynamic calculators for combustion and equilibrium calculations, which has a significant educational component. These are available to the community through http://www.thermofluids.net/ . We have also developed a MATLAB based image processing tool named FIAT (Flame Image Analysis Tool), which is now available to the community from http://flame.sdsu.edu .
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
The tasks we have performed to date can be separated into four different categories. Below, we list the progress we are making in each.
A. Ground-Based Experimental Work: The goal of this work is to establish the role of residence time, time spent by an oxidizer in a flame leading edge, on the mechanism and control of flame spread. Towards this goal, we have been building a number of ground-based experiments involving flame spread over thin solid fuels in an opposed flow environment.
A.1: SDSU Flame Tower: The flame tower is the centerpiece of our ground-based activities. We have finished the construction of a 10 m tall steel chamber (details on year-1 report--FY2011 report for predecessor grant NNX10AE03G) inside which a fuel sample mounted on a cart can be traversed up or down a vertical rail with a prescribed velocity. We have been successful in developing a completely remote controlled system to move a cart at any desired speed (from -3 m/s to + 3 m/s: details in year-2 report, FY2012 report for predecessor grant NNX10AE03G). We have conducted detailed velocity measurement to establish that the flow seen by the flame is uniform upstream over a 40 mm by 40 mm area upstream of the fuel sample (which is 20 mm wide).
The design and operation of the micro flame tracker, which is housed inside the moving cart, has been described in the year-2 report (FY2012 report for predecessor grant NNX10AE03G). Once the flame is ignited, a gas phase thermocouple, attached to a linear motion system on the cart, tracks its motion of the leading edge of the flame, providing the instantaneous flame spread rate. The flame spread is also obtained by analyzing the side-view digital video of the flame, allowing us to verify the data from the automated tracking system.
Data on flame spread rate and flame shape were obtained for flame spread over ashless filter paper with the relative flow velocity varying from positive (opposed flow configuration) to negative (concurrent flow configuration). The spread rate behavior was consistent with theoretical prediction for the opposed flow configuration. When the cart was moved upward (in the same direction of the buoyancy driven flow), the flame spread rate remained fairly constant (or slightly increasing) until about a flow speed of -40 cm/s, when the flame converted itself into its concurrent-flow configuration (wind assisted flame spread). We are still analyzing the wealth of data produced by these experiments.
The flow velocity at which blow-off extinction occurs was found to be sensitive to the development length of the boundary layer. Using an air flow sensor, we characterized the velocity field seen by our moving sample. A detailed study using Fluent was used to relate that cart velocity with the velocity seen by the flame (see previous reporting).
The effect of the flow velocity and the boundary development lengths were experimentally studied using ashless filter paper and the results strongly support an effective velocity correlation that we developed from scale analysis (see details in phase-I, year-4 report).
We have begun new experiments with PMMA (polymethyl-methacrylate) samples. Results of these experiments will be reported in the next year’s progress report.
A.2: Flame Stabilizer: One of the challenges in the experimental study of flame spread is that even if the flame spreads at a steady rate, the propagating flame creates an unsteady phenomenon with respect to the laboratory frame of reference. As a result, it is difficult to obtain detailed data, necessary for validating models, in a spreading flame. To remedy this situation, we have built a novel flame spread apparatus that moves the fuel in the opposite direction of the flame spread to keep the leading edge of the flame stationary with respect to the laboratory. A thermocouple, fixed to the laboratory frame of reference, in front of the leading edge of the flame senses the presence of the flame and a proportional–integral–derivative controller (PID controller) keeps its temperature constant by moving the sample holder, driven by a stepper motor, in the opposite direction at the velocity of the spread. Instantaneous flame spread rate and the visible flame structure are compared for a downward spreading flame over ashless filter paper with the corresponding stationary flame. The results indicate that the difference between the two configurations are within experimental uncertainties and the stabilized flame can represent a spreading flame adequately, including variability of flame spread rate and the flame geometry, for further observation.
We have presented this work in the 34th International Symposium on Combustion. With a spreading flame stabilized by this apparatus, we are in a position to measure gas phase temperature, including in the plume region, where fluctuations due to turbulence makes it very difficult to map out the thermal field of a spreading flame.
Using a K type thermocouple we mapped the gas phase temperature field of a stabilized flame. An infrared CO2 sensor was used to map out the CO2 concentrations.
When the temperature and CO2 concentrations are normalized by their equilibrium values (0 for ambient conditions and 1 for chemical equilibrium values), the similarity between the temperature and CO2 is remarkable (see FY2014 report for predecessor grant NNX10AE03G). Using the fluctuations in the signal, the pseudo-turbulence intensity was calculated for both the temperature and CO2 concentrations showing strong similarity. Turbulence is most intense at the far downstream of the flame and in the outer zone of entrainment.
In the subsequent years we have improved the flame stabilizer by replacing the thermocouple with a radiometer to sense the advancing flame. The data acquisition capabilities now include measurement of thermal radiation and gas phase temperature using S-type thermocouple.
A.3 The Flame Tunnel: We have designed and fabricated a wind tunnel for combustion experiments where we can create a prescribed flow of air over different types of fuel samples (flat or cylindrical). The unique design also allows us to change the orientation of the tunnel making it possible to create downward, opposed-flow, horizontal, and concurrent-flow flame spread. In addition, the angle of the tunnel with the vertical axis can be changed to study effect of inclination on flame spread.
A.4 The Ignition Delay Apparatus: The Burning and Suppression of Solids –II (BASS-II) experiments have generated a wealth of information on ignition time of solid fuels. Yet, almost none of these data have been analyzed. We have built a simple apparatus with the goal of accurately measuring ignition delay time of solid fuels. Two horizontal parallel cylindrical wires (Kanthal) are electrically heated in a symmetric fashion. Once they reach steady state, a sample is suddenly inserted in between the two ignition wires. An infra-red camera monitors the rise in temperature of the fuel and an inflexion point in the rise in temperature, which is followed by ignition, is used to identify the ignition time.
B. Preparation for Space-Based Experimental Work:
We have proposed an experimental matrix in the BASS-II project to that will help us (a) determine a suitable ignition method; (b) select an oxygen level suitable for flame spread over PMMA ; (c) estimate extinction time at lower oxygen level; and (d) evaluate the width effect to supplement our original experimental matrix in the SoFIE project.
Results from BASS-II experiments have been used in several archival journal publications. The results have reinforced our theoretical prediction that below a certain critical velocity, flame extinguishes due to radiative cooling.
C. Theoretical/Modeling Work: We are continuing to make progress in modeling flame spread over solid fuels under different conditions. Our modeling/theoretical effort can be summarized as follows:
1. We have been developing Web based tools for calculating equilibrium temperature of PMMA and Cellulose combustion. This calculation tool, which can be used by the community, helps us determine exactly how much sample burn is possible (under different conditions) in a closed chamber without significantly altering the oxygen level. It also predicts the equilibrium composition providing us with the thermodynamic limits of CO2 level and temperature in the gas phase to be expected.
2. We are using a two dimensional model with finite-rate one-step kinetics, and radiation to simulate opposed flow flame spread. The model has been used to compare downward flame spread results with experiments conducted in the lab. The spread rate from the model for three different fuel thicknesses agreed quite well with the experimental results for downward spread over PMMA sheets under the ambient conditions.
3. The model was used to compare pure downward flame spread with the stabilized flame produced by our stabilizer device. The comparison of the numerical results as well as experimental data established the flame stabilizer does reproduce all the characteristics of a downward spreading flame, only the flame is now frozen in the laboratory coordinate ready for prolonged examination. This study established the flame stabilizer as a new viable platform for experimental studies of flame spread.
4. The data from the flame tower showed that the blow off velocity (of the opposing flow) was related to the boundary layer development length. The computational model, along with scale analysis, was used to quantify the effect of the development length in terms of an effective velocity. An effective velocity for a flame, embedded in a boundary layer, is defined as an equivalent velocity seen by the flame. The effective velocity is then correlated with free stream velocity, development length of the boundary layer, and fluid and fuel properties. The resulting correlations were remarkably accurate in explaining the blow off extinction velocity over a wide range of parametric conditions.
5. We have done detailed radiation calculations to establish the importance of radiation loss versus radiation feedback. Also, the radiation loss correction of thermocouple measurement has been computed taking into account both radiative loss and gain by the thermocouple bead.
6. We have developed a MATLAB based image analysis tool (FIAT (Flame Image Analysis Tool)) that can be used to analyze videos of any flame spread experiment.
D. Space Based Experiments (BASS-II): We have conducted three sets of experiments as part of the BASS-II project, burning twenty samples of PMMA. Computational and theoretical work in support of these experimental results have been published in several archival journal papers. The experimental matrix for the SoFIE experiments has been finalized.
E. Dissemination of Results: We have published a significant number of journal and conference papers, one textbook, and updated our research and outreach websites ( http://www.thermofluids.net/ , http://flame.sdsu.edu ). The MATLAB based application FIAT (Flame Image Analysis Tool) is available for download from our website flame.sdsu.edu .

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
We have completed another productive year with vigorous experimental, theoretical, and numerical research in support of the Residence Time Driven Flame Spread (RTDFS) module of the SoFIE project. The major achievements of this period include further analysis of Burning and Suppression of Solids –II (BASS-II) experimental results (obtained from experiments aboard International Space Station-ISS), experiments with fuel of different geometry, publication of three archival journal articles based on these results, and several conference papers.
Luca Carmignani, the Ph.D. student in the Joint Doctoral Program between SDSU and UCSD (University of California-San Diego), is performing a lead role, advising several Masters and undergraduate students while continuing his own research of flame spread. Blake Road and Thomas Delzeit completed their Masters theses. Several Masters students, Ken Kievens, Ryan Chan, Yonatan Dawit, Robert Clay, and Ally Ferrel are at various stages of their research towards their theses. Several undergraduate students are doing their senior design project in our laboratory.

Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of "Residence Time Driven Flame Spread Over Solid Fuels," grant # NNX10AE03G.
Flame spread over solid fuels in an opposed-flow environment has been investigated for over four decades for understanding the fundamental nature of hazardous fire spread. The appeal for this configuration stems from the fact that flame spread rate remains steady, even if the flame itself may grow in size. For practical fire safety issues, however, wind-assisted flame spread is more relevant.
However, these two regimes have always been studied in isolation without much effort to establish a connection, even though the underlying mechanism of flame spread is the same in all regimes. Sitting between the two regimes are high-residence time flames, as found in a low-velocity or quiescent microgravity environment. Residence time is the time spent by an oxidizer in the combustion zone. Such flames, which are of interest on their own merit due to fire safety issues in spacecraft, offer some unique characteristics because of the high residence time. Radiation becomes dominant and, based on previous space experiments and analysis, we contend that a vigorously spreading flame on Earth becomes self-extinguishing in a microgravity environment under certain conditions such as the fuel thickness being greater than a critical value.
The proposed research uses a comprehensive approach-- a novel experimental set up and a theoretical framework based on scaling and numerical modeling-- to investigate flame spread driven by varying residence time, from blow-off extinction in an opposed-flow configuration through high residence time flame to blow-off extinction in a concurrent-flow configuration. At the heart of this proposal is a novel but simple experiment where the residence time of the oxidizer can be controlled and high residence time flames can be established for a long duration (compared to drop towers). As a proof of concept, we have constructed a flame tower at San Diego State University (SDSU) in which, after a sample is ignited, the sample holder, placed in an open moveable cart, can be traversed at any desired speed upward or downward, creating an external flow that can augment or mitigate the buoyancy-induced flow. Preliminary results show that we can control the residence time and create flames in different regimes, including a transition between a wind-aided and wind-opposed configuration. At Gifu University in Japan, we have been developing an interferometry based imaging system which we intend to enhance to capture the thermal footprint of a flame's leading edge. The leading edge is central to our understanding of mechanism of flame extinction. Further development of this technology will enable us to integrate diagnostics in future space based experiments and provide validation data to a comprehensive numerical model. The comprehensive model, to be built upon our existing two-dimensional model, will solve an unsteady, three-dimensional, Navier stokes equation with finite rate kinetics in the gas and solid phases and radiation in the gas phase. The software implementation will be object-oriented and utilize a new technology called Web Services that will decouple various sub-models and enhance parallel execution.
The radiation model will also be refined by including the equilibrium composition of species for finding radiative properties in high residence-time flames. The comprehensive model, tested against available theory, data in literature, and data generated at SDSU and Gifu, was applied to test the three hypotheses presented in the preceding grant regarding flame extinguishment in a microgravity environment. A successful outcome of that project is leading to a well thought out space-based experiment on the mechanism of flame extinction in a gravity free environment. We have received authority to proceed to Preliminary Design Review.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research has four components. (a) We have built three experimental setups at SDSU: Flame Tower where a test sample can be traversed up or down at any desired velocity; Flame Stabilizer where the motion of the flame can be arrested by moving the sample exactly at the speed of the flame spread in the opposite direction; and a rotating Flame Tunnel where a combustion tunnel can be oriented at any desired angle to study the interaction of buoyancy and forced flow; (b) Theoretical and computational work that explores the similarity and differences between the mechanisms flame spread in a zero gravity space environment and on Earth; (c) Support the space based experiment (in the SoFIE project) to establish extinction mechanism of flames.; (d) Develop software tools for data analysis and share those with the research community.
The data that we are acquiring in the experiments provide the research community with a comprehensive set of results for testing different theories of flame spread in a normal gravity environment. Moreover, by controlling the residence time, various regimes of flame spread, including the microgravity regime, can be explored in the Flame Tower. Our theoretical work predicts a fuel thickness beyond which steady flame spread is unsustainable in a gravity free environment. If we are successful in establishing a critical thickness, this will have a powerful impact on making fire resistant environment for humans in space.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
Significant progress has been made during this period of the project. The major highlight of this period is further analysis of BASS-II experimental results (obtained from experiments aboard International Space Station-ISS) and publication of two archival journal articles based on these results. We also presented several conference papers. In this period we have significantly expanded the capabilities of our Flame Stabilizer apparatus for automated data acquisition. One of our major accomplishment is the publication in the 36th International Symposium on Combustion, the abstract of which is highlighted below (see also Bibliography section):
The three regimes of opposed-flow flame spread – radiative, thermal, and kinetic regimes – are well known. For thermally thin fuels, the spread rate is independent of opposing flow velocity in the thermal regime. It decreases with an increase in the flow velocity in the kinetic regime, leading to blow off extinction. In the radiative regime which occurs mostly in a buoyancy-free environment of microgravity, the spread rate decreases with a decrease in flow velocity leading to radiative extinction unless the oxygen level is very high. In a recent experiment aboard the International Space Station, thin sheets of (Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) were ignited in a flow tunnel with the opposing flow varying over a wide range. All three regimes of flame spread were captured in a single set of experiments for the first time. Instantaneous spread rates were obtained from digital video processing and compared with a computational model in all three regimes along with the evolution of flame shapes. Spread rates in the radiative and thermal regimes are also compared with existing theories of flame spread in the thermal and the radiative regime producing remarkable qualitative agreement.

Task Progress:

A. Ground-Based Experimental Work: The goal of this work is to establish the role of residence time, time spent by an oxidizer in a flame leading edge, on the mechanism and control of flame spread. A.1: SDSU Flame Tower: The flame tower is the centerpiece of our ground-based activities. We have finished the construction of a 10 m tall steel chamber (details on year-1 report) inside which a fuel sample mounted on a cart can be traversed up or down a vertical rail with a prescribed velocity. We have been successful in developing a completely remote controlled system to move a cart at any desired speed (from -3 m/s to + 3 m/s: details in year-2 report). We have conducted detailed velocity measurement to establish that the flow seen by the flame is uniform upstream over a 40 mm by 40 mm area upstream of the fuel sample (which is 20 mm wide).

Once the flame is ignited, a gas phase thermocouple, attached to a linear motion system on the cart, tracks its motion of the leading edge of the flame, providing the instantaneous flame spread rate. The flame spread is also obtained by analyzing the side-view digital video of the flame, allowing us to verify the data from the automated tracking system.
Data on flame spread rate and flame shape were obtained for flame spread over ashless filter paper with the relative flow velocity varying from positive (opposed flow configuration) to negative (concurrent flow configuration). The spread rate behavior was consistent with theoretical prediction for the opposed flow configuration. When the cart was moved upward (in the same direction of the buoyancy driven flow), the flame spread rate remained fairly constant (or slightly increasing) until about a flow speed of -40 cm/s, when the flame converted itself into its concurrent-flow configuration (wind assisted flame spread). We are still analyzing the wealth of data produced by these experiments.
The flow velocity at which blow-off extinction occurs was found to be sensitive to the development length of the boundary layer. Using an air flow sensor, we characterized the velocity field seen by our moving sample. A detailed study using Fluent was used to relate that cart velocity with the velocity seen by the flame (see year-4 report).
The effect of the flow velocity and the boundary development lengths were experimentally studied using ashless filter paper and the results strongly support an effective velocity correlation that we developed from scale analysis (see details in year-4 report).
A.2: Flame Stabilizer: One of the challenges in the experimental study of flame spread is that, even if the flame spreads at a steady rate, the propagating flame creates an unsteady phenomenon with respect to the laboratory frame of reference. As a result, it is difficult to obtain detailed data, necessary for validating models, in a spreading flame. To remedy this situation, we have built a novel flame spread apparatus that moves the fuel in the opposite direction of the flame spread to keep the leading edge of the flame stationary with respect to the laboratory. The results indicate that the difference between the two configurations are within experimental uncertainties and the stabilized flame can represent a spreading flame adequately, including variability of flame spread rate and the flame geometry, for further observation. When the temperature and CO2 concentrations are normalized by their equilibrium values (0 for ambient conditions and 1 for chemical equilibrium values), the similarity between the temperature and CO2 is remarkable. Using the fluctuations in the signal, the pseudo-turbulence intensity was calculated for both the temperature and CO2 concentrations showing strong similarity. Turbulence is most intense at the far downstream of the flame and in the outer zone of entrainment.

Establish that steady flame spread over solid fuel in a quiescent microgravity environment is possible only if the fuel thickness is less than a critical value. b. Task Description:
Flame spread over solid fuels in an opposed-flow environment has been investigated for over four decades for understanding the fundamental nature of hazardous fire spread. The appeal for this configuration stems from the fact that flame spread rate remains steady, even if the flame itself may grow in size. For practical fire safety issues, however, wind-assisted flame spread is more relevant.
However, these two regimes have always been studied in isolation without much effort to establish a connection, even though the underlying mechanism of flame spread is the same in all regimes. Sitting between the two regimes are high-residence time flames, as found in a low-velocity or quiescent microgravity environment. Residence time is the time spent by an oxidizer in the combustion zone. Such flames, which are of interest on their own merit due to fire safety issues in spacecrafts, offer some unique characteristics because of the high residence time. Radiation becomes dominant and, based on previous space experiments and analysis, we contend that a vigorously spreading flame on Earth becomes self-extinguishing in a microgravity environment under certain conditions such as the fuel thickness being greater than a critical value.
The proposed research uses a comprehensive approach-- a novel experimental set up and a theoretical framework based on scaling and numerical modeling-- to investigate flame spread driven by varying residence time, from blow-off extinction in an opposed-flow configuration through high residence time flame to blow-off extinction in a concurrent-flow configuration. At the heart of this proposal is a novel but simple experiment where the residence time of the oxidizer can be controlled and high residence time flames can be established for a long duration (compared to drop towers). As a proof of concept, we have constructed a flame tower at SDSU in which, after a sample is ignited, the sample holder, placed in an open moveable cart, can be traversed at any desired speed upward or downward, creating an external flow that can augment or mitigate the buoyancy-induced flow. Preliminary results show that we can control the residence time and create flames in different regimes, including a transition between a wind-aided and wind-opposed configuration. At Gifu University in Japan, we have been developing an interferometry based imaging system which we intend to enhance to capture the thermal footprint of a flame's leading edge. Task Description:
Flame spread over solid fuels in an opposed-flow environment has been investigated for over four decades for understanding the fundamental nature of hazardous fire spread. The appeal for this configuration stems from the fact that flame spread rate remains steady, even if the flame itself may grow in size. For practical fire safety issues, however, wind-assisted flame spread is more relevant.
However, these two regimes have always been studied in isolation without much effort to establish a connection, even though the underlying mechanism of flame spread is the same in all regimes. Sitting between the two regimes are high-residence time flames, as found in a low-velocity or quiescent microgravity environment. Residence time is the time spent by an oxidizer in the combustion zone. Such flames, which are of interest on their own merit due to fire safety issues in spacecrafts, offer some unique characteristics because of the high residence time. Radiation becomes dominant and, based on previous space experiments and analysis, we contend that a vigorously spreading flame on Earth becomes self-extinguishing in a microgravity environment under certain conditions such as the fuel thickness being greater than a critical value.
The proposed research uses a comprehensive approach-- a novel experimental set up and a theoretical framework based on scaling and numerical modeling-- to investigate flame spread driven by varying residence time, from blow-off extinction in an opposed-flow configuration through high residence time flame to blow-off extinction in a concurrent-flow configuration. At the heart of this proposal is a novel but simple experiment where the residence time of the oxidizer can be controlled and high residence time flames can be established for a long duration (compared to drop towers). As a proof of concept, we have constructed a flame tower at SDSU in which, after a sample is ignited, the sample holder, placed in an open moveable cart, can be traversed at any desired speed upward or downward, creating an external flow that can augment or mitigate the buoyancy-induced flow. Preliminary results show that we can control the residence time and create flames in different regimes, including a transition between a wind-aided and wind-opposed configuration. At Gifu University in Japan, we have been developing an interferometry based imaging system which we intend to enhance to capture the thermal footprint of a flame's leading edge. The leading edge is central to our understanding of mechanism of flame extinction. Further development of this technology will enable us to integrate diagnostics in future space based experiments and provide validation data to a comprehensive numerical model. The comprehensive model, to be built upon our existing two-dimensional model, will solve an unsteady, three-dimensional, Navier stokes equation with finite rate kinetics in the gas and solid phases and radiation in the gas phase. The software implementation will be object-oriented and utilize a new technology called Web Services that will decouple various sub-models and enhance parallel execution.
The radiation model will also be refined by including the equilibrium composition of species for finding radiative properties in high residence-time flames. The new data generated by our proposed ground-based experiment will be the first of its kind to encompass flame spread across different regimes and will stimulate fundamental theoretical research to unify different regimes of flame spread. The comprehensive model, tested against available theory, data in literature, and data generated at SDSU and Gifu, will be applied to test the three hypotheses presented in this proposal regarding flame extinguishment in a microgravity environment. A successful outcome of this project will lead to a well thought out space-based experiment on the mechanism of flame extinction in a gravity free environment.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research has three components: We have built a novel experimental facility called Flame Tower at SDSU, where ground based experiments on flame spread are being conducted; Theoretical and computational work that explore the similarity and differences between the mechanisms flame spread in a zero gravity space environment and on Earth; Design and propose a space based experiment to establish extinction mechanism of flames.
The data that we are acquiring in the Flame Tower will provide the research community with a comprehensive set of results for testing different theories of flame spread in a normal gravity environment. Moreover, by controlling the residence time, various regimes of flame spread, including the microgravity regime, can be explored in the Flame Tower. Our theoretical work predicts a fuel thickness beyond which steady flame spread is unsustainable in a gravity free environment. If we are successful in establishing a critical thickness, this will have a powerful impact on making fire resistant environment for humans in space.

1. Abstract
This has been the most productive period for this project. 3. Ground based Experimental Approach
3.1: SDSU Flame Tower: The flame tower is the centerpiece of our ground-based activities. We have finished the construction of a 10m tall steel chamber (details on year-1 report) inside which a fuel sample mounted on a cart can be traversed up or down a vertical rail with a prescribed velocity. We have been successful in developing a completely remote controlled system to move a cart at any desired speed (from -2 m/s to + 2 m/s: details in year-2 report). We have conducted detailed velocity measurement to establish that the flow seen by the flame is uniform upstream over a 40 mm by 40 mm area upstream of the fuel sample (which is 20 mm wide).
The design and operation of the micro flame tracker, which is housed inside the moving cart, has been described in the year-2 report. Once the flame is ignited, a gas phase thermocouple, attached to a linear motion system on the cart, tracks the motion of the leading edge of the flame, providing the instantaneous flame spread rate. The flame spread is also obtained by analyzing the side-view digital video of the flame, allowing us to verify the data from the automated tracking system.
Data on flame spread rate and flame shape were obtained for flame spread over ash less filter paper with the relative flow velocity varying from positive (opposed flow configuration) to negative (concurrent flow configuration). The spread rate behavior was consistent with theoretical prediction for the opposed flow configuration. When the cart was moved upward (in the same direction of the buoyancy driven flow), the flame spread rate remained fairly constant (or slightly increasing) until about a flow speed of -40 cm/s, when the flame converted itself into its concurrent-flow configuration (wind assisted flame spread). We are still analyzing the wealth of data produced by these experiments. The flow velocity at which blow-off extinction occurs was found to be sensitive to the development length of the boundary layer. In order to minimize the effect of the sample holder, we are redesigning the micro flame tracker so that the sample sees nothing but the flow of oxidizer. We also are in the process of acquiring data with thin films of PMMA.
3.2: Flame Stabilizer: One of the challenges in the experimental study of flame spread is that, even if the flame spreads at a steady rate, the propagating flame creates an unsteady phenomenon with respect to the laboratory frame of reference. As a result, it is difficult to obtain detailed data, necessary for validating models, in a spreading flame. To remedy this situation, we have built a novel flame spread apparatus that moves the fuel in the opposite direction of the flame spread to keep the leading edge of the flame stationary with respect to the laboratory. A thermocouple, fixed to the laboratory frame of reference, in front of the leading edge of the flame senses the presence of the flame and a PID controller keeps its temperature constant by moving the sample holder, driven by a stepper motor, in the opposite direction at the velocity of the spread. Instantaneous flame spread rate and the visible flame structure are compared for a downward spreading flame over ashless filter paper with the corresponding stationary flame. The results indicate that the difference between the two configurations are within experimental uncertainties and the stabilized flame can represent a spreading flame adequately, including variability of flame spread rate and the flame geometry, for further observation. We have presented this work in the 34th International Symposium on Combustion. With a spreading flame stabilized by this apparatus, we are in a position to measure gas phase temperature, including in the plume region, where fluctuations due to turbulence makes it very difficult to map out the thermal field of a spreading flame. We are also making CO2 field measurements and comparing the gas phase fields with our computational results.
4. Space based Experimental Approach
We have refined the objectives of our space-based experiments and produced a concept design for the proposed experiment. The objectives for the space-based experiments are the following: a. Establish that steady flame spread over solid fuel in a quiescent microgravity environment is possible only if the fuel thickness is less than a critical value. b. Investigate the propagation of the products and temperature fields to uncover the mechanism of flame extinguishment. c. Determine how the ambient pressure and presence of a mild opposing flow affect the flame spread rate and extinction behavior.
The basic concept of the proposed experiment is as follows: A carousal driven by a stepper motor holds several sample holders, each of which are placed in the test zone by rotating the carousal. Samples of different thicknesses are held in each sample holder, which carries its own igniter. When a sample is rotated into the test zone, the igniter snaps into the ignition circuit. As the flame spreads over the sample, gas phase thermocouples and CO2 sensors monitor the propagation of the thermal diffusion fronts. Once the propagating flame reaches the end of the sample or extinguishes, the recording of the temperature and species field will continue to provide valuable data on transient cooling of the gas phase and the diffusion of species. After a preset interval, the next sample is rotated into position and the experiment is repeated for a new fuel thickness. The carousel will then be replaced with a second carousel and the ambient pressure will be reduced, which is predicted to be a significant parameter just like the fuel thickness in determining the critical fuel thickness.
We are using the flame stabilizer to probe a standing flame with CO2 probe and thermocouples to see their impact on the flame. The purpose is to ascertain that the diagnostics of the proposed experiment do not distort the flame being observed.
5. Theoretical/Modeling Work
We have made considerable progress in modeling flame spread over solid fuels under different conditions. Our modeling/theoretical effort can be summarized as follows:
5.1. We have been developing Web based tools for calculating equilibrium temperature of PMMA and Cellulose combustion. This calculation tools, which can be used by the community, helps us determine exactly how much sample burn is possible (under different conditions) in a closed chamber without significantly altering the oxygen level. It also predicts the equilibrium composition providing us with the thermodynamic limits of CO2 level and temperature in the gas phase to be expected.
5.2. We are using a two dimensional model with finite-rate one-step kinetics, and radiation to simulate opposed flow flame spread. The model has been used to compare downward flame spread results with experiments conducted in the lab. The spread rate from the model for three different fuel thicknesses agreed quite well with the experimental results for downward spread over PMMA sheets under the ambient conditions.
5.3. The model was used to compare pure downward flame spread with the stabilized flame produced by our stabilizer device. The comparison of the numerical results as well as experimental data established the flame stabilizer does reproduce all the characteristics of a downward spreading flame, only the flame is now frozen in the laboratory coordinate ready for prolonged examination. This study established the flame stabilizer as a new viable platform for experimental studies of flame spread.
5.4. The data from the flame tower showed that the blow off velocity (of the opposing flow) was related to the boundary layer development length. The computational model, along with scale analysis, was used to quantify the effect of the development length in terms of an effective velocity. An effective velocity for a flame, embedded in a boundary layer, is defined as an equivalent velocity seen by the flame. The effective velocity is then correlated with free stream velocity, development length of the boundary layer, and fluid and fuel properties. The resulting correlations were remarkably accurate in explaining the blow off extinction velocity over a wide range of parametric conditions.
5.5 Work is underway to obtain the detailed radiation field inside the flame so that thermocouple measurements can be corrected for radiation loss or gain for a spreading flame.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2012
Task Progress:
The tasks we have performed to date can be separated into four different categories. Below, we list the progress we are making in each.
A. Ground-Based Experimental Work: The goal of this work is to establish the role of residence time, time spent by an oxidizer in a flame leading edge, on the mechanism and control of flame spread. Towards this goal, we have been building a number of ground-based experiments involving flame spread over thin solid fuels in an opposed flow environment.
A.1: SDSU Flame Tower: The flame tower is the centerpiece of our ground-based activities. We have finished the construction of a 10m tall steel chamber (details on year-1 report) inside which a fuel sample mounted on a cart can be traversed up or down a vertical rail with a prescribed velocity. We have been successful in developing a completely remote controlled system to move a cart at any command speed (from -3 m/s to + 3 m/s). Analysis of video images and data from velocity probes (details on year-2 report) confirm the success of our approach in creating a relative velocity with precision.
A.2: MicroFlameTracker: The cart carrying the fuel sample must be self sufficient to ignite the sample, record flame spread rate in real time, acquire temperature and flow velocity data, take video of the flame from different angles - all these while being operated remotely from outside the chamber. This complex piece of equipment has been developed and successfully tested. An onboard microcontroller coupled with an onboard laptop (all operated by onboard battery) communicates with an outside command computer through a wireless network. The command computer also communicates wirelessly with the motion system that creates the desired cart velocity. Instead of describing the details of our design and fabrication, let us describe how the system is supposed to accomplish our goal.
To begin an experiment, a hatch door is opened, and a new sample is mounted on the MicroFlameTracker. After the hatch is closed, the MicroFlameTracker is sent to one end of the tower, say, to the top for a downward run. Using Windows Remote Desktop, the command computer gains access of the onboard laptop. A Webcam (coupled with a LED light -the sealed tower is completely dark) focuses on a measuring tape attached to the tower guide rail, which ascertains the current location of the cart. Through a graphical command application developed by us, we can access the data recording system, ignition system, the flame tracking mechanism, and the video camera. We first turn on the data acquisition system, controlled by the onboard microcontroller, which also turns on a digital stopwatch. The video recorder, a high-resolution CCD camera, is then turned on which records the clock in the background as it captures the propagation of the flame from ignition to extinction. This allows us to synchronize the video data with all other data. The ignition command is sent and a Kanthal (iron-chromium-aluminum, FeCrAl) alloy igniter attached to the sample holder is heated by a circuit controlled by the microcontroller. The ignition wire is in contact with one end of the fuel sample which is secured in a magnetized frame with a rectangular cut out. Once ignition is visually confirmed from the Webcam window, the igniter is turned off. The tracking system consists of a thermocouple riding on a linear motion system parallel to the fuel sample. A PID control algorithm ensures that the thermocouple temperature remains unchanged by moving it in the direction of spread. As the thermocouple tracks the thermal front of the flame, the motion of the cart at a desired velocity is activated. For a velocity of, say, 20 cm/s, the cart takes about 35 seconds to traverse the effective length of the rail. As soon as the run is over, instantaneous spread rate (from the motion 0f the thermocouple) data is available. We have just finished our first set of preliminary experiments and by the next reporting period we expect to acquire a large set of data on flame spread rate vs. the flow velocity (both positive and negative).
A.3: Flame Stabilizer: One of the challenges in the experimental study of flame spread is that, even if the flame spreads at a steady rate, the propagating flame creates an unsteady phenomenon with respect to the laboratory frame of reference. As a result, it is difficult to obtain detailed data, necessary for validating models, in a spreading flame. To remedy this situation, we have built a novel flame spread apparatus that moves the fuel in the opposite direction of the flame spread to keep the leading edge of the flame stationary with respect to the laboratory. Instantaneous flame spread rate and the visible flame structure are compared for a downward spreading flame over ashless filter paper with the corresponding stationary flame. The results indicate that the difference between the two configurations are within experimental uncertainties and the stabilized flame can represent a spreading flame adequately, including variability of flame spread rate and the flame geometry, for further observation.
B. Preparation for Space-Based Experimental Work: We have refined the objectives of our space-based experiments and produced a concept design for the proposed experiment. The hypothesis to be tested in the space-based experiments are the following: a. Flame spread rate over a thin fuel sample can be predicted by the closed form expression developed by our theoretical work in the past, including the effect of fuel thickness, pressure, and flow velocity. b. Under certain conditions (high fuel thickness, low ambient pressure, and low flow velocity) a steady flame spread cannot be sustained even at high oxygen level. c. The separation between the thermal and species fields is responsible for flame extinguishment and may provide clues to the time of extinction for unsteady flames.
To achieve these goals we propose an experiment; the basic concept is as follows: A carousal driven by a stepper motor holds several sample holders, each of which are placed in the test zone by rotating the carousal. Samples of different thicknesses are held in each sample holder, which carries its own igniter. As a sample is rotated into the test zone, the igniter snaps into the ignition circuit. As the flame spreads over the sample, gas phase thermocouples and CO2 sensors monitor the propagation of the thermal diffusion fronts. Also, instantaneous propagation speed of the thermal front is recorded by a flame tracker mechanism like the one discussed in Sec. A.2. Once the propagating flame reaches the end of the sample or extinguishes, the recording of the temperature and species field will continue to provide valuable data on transient cooling of the gas phase and the diffusion of species. After a preset interval, the next sample is rotated into position and the experiment is repeated for a new fuel thickness. The carousel will then be replaced with a second carousel and this time a jet flow facility used by other researchers in their experiments will be utilized to created prescribed flow velocities.
C. Theoretical/Modeling Work: We have made considerable progress in modeling flame spread over solid fuels under different conditions. Our modeling/theoretical effort can be summarized as follows: 1. We have been developing Web based tools for calculating equilibrium temperature of PMMA and Cellulose combustion. This calculation tools, which can be used by the community, helps us determine exactly how much sample burn is possible (under different conditions) in a closed chamber without significantly altering the oxygen level. 2. We are using a two dimensional model with finite-rate one-step kinetics, and radiation to simulate opposed flow flame spread. The model clearly shows the separation between the thermal and species field for flame close to extinction. It also supports the theoretical prediction about the existence of a critical fuel thickness beyond which steady spread is not sustainable. 3. By comparing narrow band calculations with total calculations, we have established that total radiation calculation is sufficient for accurate radiation modeling. Radiation signature, as measured by the percentage of heat generated that is lost by radiation, has been calculated showing the importance of radiation in the microgravity regime. 4. We are modeling downward flame spread in preparation for a comparison with the data acquired from the stabilizer apparatus as well as the flame tower.

Task Description:
Flame spread over solid fuels in an opposed-flow environment has been investigated for over four decades for understanding the fundamental nature of hazardous fire spread. The appeal for this configuration stems from the fact that flame spread rate remains steady, even if the flame itself may grow in size. For practical fire safety issues, however, wind-assisted flame spread is more relevant.
However, these two regimes have always been studied in isolation without much effort to establish a connection, even though the underlying mechanism of flame spread is the same in all regimes. Sitting between the two regimes are high-residence time flames, as found in a low-velocity or quiescent microgravity environment. Residence time is the time spent by an oxidizer in the combustion zone. Such flames, which are of interest on their own merit due to fire safety issues in spacecrafts, offer some unique characteristics because of the high residence time. Radiation becomes dominant and, based on previous space experiments and analysis, we contend that a vigorously spreading flame on Earth becomes self-extinguishing in a microgravity environment under certain conditions such as the fuel thickness being greater than a critical value.
The proposed research uses a comprehensive approach-- a novel experimental set up and a theoretical framework based on scaling and numerical modeling-- to investigate flame spread driven by varying residence time, from blow-off extinction in an opposed-flow configuration through high residence time flame to blow-off extinction in a concurrent-flow configuration. At the heart of this proposal is a novel but simple experiment where the residence time of the oxidizer can be controlled and high residence time flames can be established for a long duration (compared to drop towers). As a proof of concept, we have constructed a flame tower at SDSU in which, after a sample is ignited, the sample holder, placed in an open moveable cart, can be traversed at any desired speed upward or downward, creating an external flow that can augment or mitigate the buoyancy-induced flow. Preliminary results show that we can control the residence time and create flames in different regimes, including a transition between a wind-aided and wind-opposed configuration. At Gifu University in Japan, we have been developing an interferometry based imaging system which we intend to enhance to capture the thermal footprint of a flame's leading edge. The leading edge is central to our understanding of mechanism of flame extinction. Further development of this technology will enable us to integrate diagnostics in future space based experiments and provide validation data to a comprehensive numerical model. The comprehensive model, to be built upon our existing two-dimensional model, will solve an unsteady, three-dimensional, Navier stokes equation with finite rate kinetics in the gas and solid phases and radiation in the gas phase. The software implementation will be object-oriented and utilize a new technology called Web Services that will decouple various sub-models and enhance parallel execution.
The radiation model will also be refined by including the equilibrium composition of species for finding radiative properties in high residence-time flames. The new data generated by our proposed ground-based experiment will be the first of its kind to encompass flame spread across different regimes and will stimulate fundamental theoretical research to unify different regimes of flame spread. The comprehensive model, tested against available theory, data in literature, and data generated at SDSU and Gifu, will be applied to test the three hypotheses presented in this proposal regarding flame extinguishment in a microgravity environment. A successful outcome of this project will lead to a well thought out space-based experiment on the mechanism of flame extinction in a gravity free environment.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research have three components: We are building a novel experimental facility called Flame Tower at SDSU, where ground based experiments on flame spread will be conducted; Theoretical and computational work that explores the similarity and differences between the mechanisms flame spread in a zero gravity space environment and on Earth; Design and propose a space based experiment to establish extinction mechanism of flames.
The data that we plan to acquire in the Flame Tower will provide the research community with a comprehensive set of results for testing different theories of flame spread in a normal gravity environment. Moreover, by controlling the residence time, various regimes of flame spread, including the microgravity regime, can be explored in the Flame Tower. Our theoretical work predicts a fuel thickness beyond which steady flame spread is unsustainable in a gravity free environment. If we are successful in establishing a critical thickness, this will have a powerful impact on making fire resistant environment for humans in space.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2011
Task Progress:
1. Progress in building the Flame Tower: The proposed flame tower is the center piece of our ground based activities. When completed, it will provide a regulated environment in terms of ambient pressure and oxygen concentration in a 8 m tall closed chamber. The sample holder assembly, mounted on a vertical rail, can be moved up or down at any desired velocity, thus, creating a known free-stream flow (concurrent or opposed) relative to the fuel sample.
In this period, we have considered different design ideas and finally converged on a ladder like structure, which had several advantages over other ideas. Most importantly, it was very simple consisting of only three different pieces: vertical columns, horizontal braces, and skin sheets. Steel was selected as the working substance and a finite element analysis was carried out to ensure that the structure can withstand low internal pressure. The structure was fabricated at SDSU spanning two floors in the engineering building. We hope to construct the motion system for the sample holder and an automated sample carriage in the near future. Our goal is be able to acquire data under atmospheric condition by the next reporting period.
2. Progress in Building the Flame Tracker: This apparatus will allow us to measure instantaneous flame spread rate and monitor changes in flame shape or size in real time by moving the sample in opposite direction of flame spread so that the flame leading edge remains stationary.
We have already built this apparatus in the laboratory and demonstrated that a spreading flame can be converted into a stationary flame. We are now working on miniaturizing the system so that it can be mounted in the flame tower and moved up and down at any desired velocity.
3. Scale Analysis: We have continued further development of scale analysis of the flame to produce formulas for flame shape and flame size for opposed-flow flame spread in the thermal regime. A paper was presented in the 33rd Symposium on Combustion on this work.
4. Computational Tools: We have developed a rich internet application to calculate equilibrium flame temperature for different kinds of fuels. We plan to use these web service based tool to develop a flame spread rate calculator.
5. Computational Simulation: We have been using the existing numerical model to explore thickness effect on flame spread rate. We plan to expand this study to map the entire radiative extinction regime.
6. Space Experiment Concepts: We are working on a simplified space experiment that can establish the central thrust of our proposal - to establish that the separation between thermal and species field is responsible for flame extinction in the radiative microgravity regime. Two preliminary concepts are under development at this stage. In the next couple of months, we plan to have these concepts fleshed out and ready to be integrated with experiments from other PIs.

Task Description:
Experimental work is combined with numerical modeling. The project tasks are: 1. to stabilize methane and ethene inverse flames in the 2.2-second drop tower, 2. to collect and measure the amounts of carbone monoxide (CO) and soot produced by these flames, 3. to analyze the collected soot for size, shape, hydrogen/carbon content, and organic/graphitic makeup, 4. to develop a fiber-optic-coupled CO sensor for monitoring flames during drops, and 5. to use numerical modeling to predict the pathways followed by CO and soot in these flames. Measured CO and soot information will be combined with local computed flow pathways to illuminate the ways that CO and soot are formed during underventilated combustion.
The objective of this project is to study CO and soot formation during the dangerous underventilated burning period characteristic of certain fires. Under-ventilated burning is obtained in the present study using an inverse diffusion flame established at the interface of a round air jet and an annular fuel stream. Microgravity is used to ensure that a wide range of stable, laminar, inverse-flame operating conditions can be achieved.
The project will provide fundamental knowledge aimed to improve the CO and soot predictive capabilities of existing fire-behavior computer models. In addition, an understanding of noxious gas formation and flame soot signatures during underventilated fires in spacecraft will be obtained. Finally, the existing knowledge of pollutant formation in practical, staged combustors will be improved.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:
NOTE: Received NCE to 11/17/2007 per PI (4/07)
Task Description:
The investigation of the high pressure combustion chemistry of carbon monoxide was proposed for application to the rocket engine propulsion of a Mars surface vehicle. The rocket engine will be fueled with carbon monoxide and oxygen produced in-situ from the electrolysis of Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide. In-situ production has the advantage of eliminating the need to transport fuel and oxidizer from Earth but has, in the case of a carbon monoxide/oxygen rocket engine, the disadvantage of generating a fuel with relatively low performance in the rocket engine. Consequently, the maximum performance possible from a carbon monoxide engine is necessary and optimal engine design is required to achieve it. Part of the engine design involves an evaluation of the effect of finite rate oxidation chemistry of carbon monoxide on performance. The evaluation of the chemistry necessitates a detailed chemical kinetic model that for the best engine design needs to capture very accurately all the chemical steps that influence the combustion of carbon monoxide. There are detailed chemical kinetic models available that do include the most current understanding of carbon monoxide oxidation but they have never been validated by experiments conducted at the operating pressures of the proposed Martian vehicle rocket engines: 200-300 psi (13.7-20.4 atm) for pressure fed engines, 2000-3000 psi (136-204 atm) for turbopump fed engines. These high pressures are rarely achievable in laboratory experiments that investigate chemical kinetics but are routinely accessed in the very high pressure single pulse shock tube operating at the University of Illinois at Chicago. This shock tube can create pressure ranges from 5-1000 atm, temperatures currently from 950-1450 K but extendable to 1900K and reaction times from 0.5-2.5 msec. These are the ranges of conditions that will used to experimentally examine the bone dry and hydrogen containing oxidation of carbon monoxide. Gas chromatography/mass spectrometry/thermal conductivity measurements of the carbon monoxide, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water species concentrations as a function of pressure, temperature, hydrogen content or water content, and stoichiometry can be compared with the predictions from existing models. Prior work examining the comparison between predictions of existing models for hydrocarbon oxidation and high pressure results obtained from the shock tube have shown that hydrocarbon models developed and validated against lower pressure experiments require modification in order to predict high pressure results. Therefore the hypothesis underlying the experimental examination of the oxidation of carbon monoxide is that current chemical kinetic models for this reactant system need to be modified to account for high pressure effects. The modifications of these models will lead to a more accurate, comprehensive detailed chemical kinetic model that when coupled with computer design codes currently used by NASA will lead to the highest performance possible in the Mars vehicle rocket engine.
The task objective has been to use the unique single pulse shock tube at UIC to examine the oxidation of carbon monoxide with and without a hydrogen source over an extreme range of pressures and temperatures that encompass the design range of the Mars vehicle rocket engine so that recent models for carbon monoxide oxidation can be validated and made more comprehensive for application to the design of the high pressure rocket engine.
To achieve the maximum performance from the Mars exploration vehicle rocket engine, which would be either pressure fed at 200-300 psi or pump fed at 2000-3000 psi, predictions or measurements of critical performance characteristics resulting from the use of carbon monoxide as the fuel are necessary. Among the critical characteristics are ignition of the combustible mixture, flame front heat release, and the effects of finite rate chemistry on specific impulse. These characteristics can be better predicted through an improved knowledge of the high pressure oxidation kinetics of carbon monoxide, as will be obtained in this task, and the better predictions necessary to achieve improved Mars rocket engine performance constitute the significance of the work.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Carbon monoxide oxidation kinetics are an essential part of the modeling of the combustion of earth based hydrocarbon fuels such as gasoline, kerosene and jet propulsion fuels. Cleaner and more efficient combustion of these earth based fuels will come from better designs of combustion devices which have incorporated accurate models of hydrocarbon combustion into the design process. Therefore, an improved high pressure carbon monoxide oxidation model, that has come from this task work, could aid in the modeling and design of earth based combustion devices especially those operating at high pressures.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
CO oxidation experiments were performed over a wide temperature range (1000-1500 K) for stoichiometric (phi=1) and fuel lean (phi=0.5) mixtures. Seven sets of data were obtained with abundant amount of H2 in the reactant mixture, four data sets at nominal pressures of 24, 43, 256 and 450 atm for stoichiometric oxidation, three data sets at nominal pressures of 24, 43 and 256 atm for fuel lean oxidation, comprising more than 150 experiments. For all the experiments, profiles for CO, CO2 and O2 were obtained.
No significant difference has been observed in the species profiles from the stoichiometric to the fuel lean mixtures for the 24, 43, and 256 atm data sets. On the other hand, the system shows pressure dependence as the pressure is raised from 24 to 256 atm and a slower decay for CO is observed. No significant difference has been observed in the species profiles as the pressure is further raised from 256 to 450 atm, indicating that reactions have reached the high pressure limit at 256 atm.
The experimental data have been simulated using the most recent model for H2/CO combustion developed by Davis and co-workers, and GRI-Mech 3.0. While GRI-Mech is not able to predict correctly the species behavior, trends for CO, O2 and CO2 are well described by the Davis et al. model. However especially for the higher pressure data sets the model does not do a good job, and further work was required to improve the model. In particular sensitivity analysis and reaction pathway analysis showed the importance of the reactions H+O2=O+OH, H+O2+M=HO2+M, and CO+OH=CO2+H under all pressure conditions. The rate coefficients of these reactions have been extensively studied. However within their remaining uncertainties there was no possibility to significantly improve the accuracy of the simulation results over the entire pressure range.
Because of the elevated pressures in the present study, reactions involving the HO2 radical start to become the next most influential reactions. Among these reactions, the reaction HO2+OH=O2+H2O has been extensively studied. In particular a new rate coefficient expression has been employed to take into account the very strong and peculiar temperature dependence of this reaction. With this single rate revision, the revised Davis et al. model can accurately simulate the shock tube data for the entire pressure range of 24-450 atm. The revision does not affect the accuracy of the model against the data sets presented in previous publications.
An additional data set was obtained by decreasing the amount of H2 in the reactant mixture. The mixture used for the experiments was a fuel lean mixture composed of 235 ppm of CO, 48 ppm of H2 and 273 ppm of O2 in Argon. The ratio between the amount of H2 and CO (~ 0.21) is much smaller than the ratios of the mixtures previously studied (~ 0.36-0.40). The pressure at which the new data set was obtained was 256 atm, while the temperature varied from 1100 to 1550 K.
The experimental procedure was slightly modified, as the analyses of the reactant and product species were conducted using an additional detector, the PDD detector. This detector is able to measure the mole fraction of H2 present in a mixture down to ppb levels. Such measurement is very important in order to test the accuracy of the revised Davis et al. model with respect to the amount of H2 present in the mixture.
The experimental results for CO and H2, have been compared with the simulations obtained using the revised Davis et al. model. The model does an excellent job in simulating both the CO and the H2 species profiles.
For a simple system as the one studied, the accuracy in simulating CO, CO2, O2, and H2 profiles implies accuracy also in predicting the amounts of all the other species present in the mixture, i.e. H2O. This feature makes the revised Davis et al. model an excellent tool for simulations and predictions over a wide range of pressures (up to 450 atm), temperatures (up to 1550 K) and initial mixture composition.
The model has been subsequently used for some complementary modeling studies. The goal of these studies is to understand how the kinetics of the carbon monoxide oxidation is influenced by the amount of hydrogen source present in the initial mixture.
CO profiles have been obtained for fuel lean (phi=0.5) mixtures at 2 different pressures (48 atm and 338 atm) and over a wide range of temperature (1150 K to 1600 K). The initial CO mole fraction is 225 ppm, while the amount of H2 is varied (25 ppm, 5 ppm, and 1 ppm). Thus the ratio between the mole fractions of H2 and CO is respectively 0.11, 0.02, and 0.004. These ratios are much smaller than the ones of the experimental mixtures; the reduction in the relative amount of H2 leads to a shift of the profiles toward higher temperatures. This shift affects the pressure dependence of the global reaction system; at low H2 mole fractions an increase in pressure leads to higher conversion of CO, in contrast to prior experimental results. This difference can be explained by investigating the relative importance of the single reactions at different temperature and pressure conditions. At all the conditions, the dominant reaction for CO consumption is CO+OH=CO2+O. Thus the rate of CO decay depends on the concentration of OH; the latter species is mainly formed through the reaction H+O2=OH+O. This is not the only possible channel for the recombination of H and O2 as in presence of a third body the two species can recombine forming HO2, i.e. H+O2+M=HO2+M. This termolecular reaction depends on both temperature and pressure; at relatively low temperatures, HO2 production increases with pressure and the amount of OH available in the system decreases. As a consequence, the CO conversion decreases, as observed previously. But as the system reaches higher temperatures, the backward rate of the reaction H+O2+M=HO2+M becomes predominant in comparison with the forward rate. The HO2 converts back to H and O2, forcing the production of OH through the reaction H+O2=OH+O. As a consequence, the CO conversion increases with pressure.
Similar trends are shown for mixtures containing H2O as hydrogen source. The type of hydrogen source, i.e. H2 or H2O, does not affect the dependence of the system on the pressure, but H2O has been found to be less effective than H2 in decreasing the overall activation energy.
Reference: S. G. Davis, A. V. Joshi, H. Wang, F. Egolfopoulos, Proc. Combust. Inst. 30 (2004) 1283-1292.
