Task Description:
The investigation of the high pressure combustion chemistry of carbon monoxide is proposed for application to the rocket engine propulsion of a Mars surface vehicle. The rocket engine will be fueled with carbon monoxide and oxygen produced in-situ from the electrolysis of Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide. In-situ production has the advantage of eliminating the need to transport fuel and oxidizer from Earth but has, in the case of a carbon monoxide/oxygen rocket engine, the disadvantage of generating a fuel with relatively low performance in the rocket engine. Consequently, the maximum performance possible from a carbon monoxide engine is necessary and optimal engine design is required to achieve it. Part of the engine design involves an evaluation of the effect of finite rate oxidation chemistry of carbon monoxide on performance. The evaluation of the chemistry necessitates a detailed chemical kinetic model that for the best engine design needs to capture very accurately all the chemical steps that influence the combustion of carbon monoxide. There are detailed chemical kinetic models available that do include the most current understanding of carbon monoxide oxidation but they have never been validated by experiments conducted at the operating pressures of the proposed Martian vehicle rocket engines: 200-300 psi (13.7-20.4 atm) for pressure fed engines, 2000-3000 psi (136-204 atm) for turbopump fed engines. These high pressures are rarely achievable in laboratory experiments that investigate chemical kinetics but are routinely accessed in the very high pressure single pulse shock tube operating at the University of Illinois at Chicago. This shock tube can create pressure ranges from 5-1000 atm, temperatures currently from 950-1450 K but extendable to 1900K and reaction times from 0.5-2.5 msec. These are the ranges of conditions that will used to experimentally examine the bone dry and hydrogen containing oxidation of carbon monoxide. Gas chromatography/mass spectrometry/thermal conductivity measurements of the carbon monoxide, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water species concentrations as a function of pressure, temperature, hydrogen content or water content, and stoichiometry can be compared with the predictions from existing models. Prior work examining the comparison between predictions of existing models for hydrocarbon oxidation and high pressure results obtained from the shock tube have shown that hydrocarbon models developed and validated against lower pressure experiments require modification in order to predict high pressure results. Therefore the hypothesis underlying the proposed experimental examination of the oxidation of carbon monoxide is that current chemical kinetic models for this reactant system will have to be modified to account for high pressure effects. The modifications of these models will lead to a more accurate, comprehensive detailed chemical kinetic model that when coupled with computer design codes currently used by NASA will lead to the highest performance possible in the Mars vehicle rocket engine.
The task objective is to use the unique single pulse shock tube at UIC to examine the oxidation of carbon monoxide with and without a hydrogen source over an extreme range of pressures and temperatures that encompass the design range of the Mars vehicle rocket engine so that recent models for carbon monoxide oxidation can be validated and made more comprehensive for application to the design of the high pressure rocket engine.
To achieve the maximum performance from the Mars exploration vehicle rocket engine, which would be either pressure fed at 200-300 psi or pump fed at 2000-3000 psi, predictions or measurements of critical performance characteristics resulting from the use of carbon monoxide as the fuel are necessary. Among the critical characteristics are ignition of the combustible mixture, flame front heat release, and the effects of finite rate chemistry on specific impulse. These characteristics can be better predicted through an improved knowledge of the high pressure oxidation kinetics of carbon monoxide, as will be obtained in this task, and the better predictions necessary to achieve improved Mars rocket engine performance constitute the significance of the work.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Carbon monoxide oxidation kinetics are an essential part of the modeling of the combustion of earth based hydrocarbon fuels such as gasoline, kerosene and jet propulsion fuels. Cleaner and more efficient combustion of these earth based fuels will come from better designs of combustion devices which have incorporated accurate models of hydrocarbon combustion into the design process. Therefore, an improved high pressure carbon monoxide oxidation model, as will come from this task work, will aid in the modeling and design of earth based combustion devices especially those operating at high pressures.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Significant progress was made towards achieving the goals of the proposed study that involves:
A: An Experimental and Modeling study of the High Pressure Oxidation of Carbon Monoxide.
B: Obtaining a measurement of the “real” temperature in the shock tube.
A: The Mars In-Situ Propellants Rocket (MIPR) is a small vehicle proposed to fly autonomously on Mars, using in-situ propellant production with the propulsion system being fueled by carbon monoxide and oxygen. There are detailed models available for carbon monoxide oxidation, but they have never been validated by experiments conducted at the operating pressures of the proposed Martian vehicle rocket engine, 200-300 psi (13,7-20.4 atm) for pressure fed engines, 2000-3000 psi (137-204 atm) for turbopump fed engines. Consequently the high pressure shock tube has been used in this work to study the combustion of CO/H2 mixtures over a wide range of pressures and temperatures relevant to the operating conditions of the proposed engine in order to develop a validated model that can determine the optimum design parameters for the proposed MIPR.
Eight experimental data sets with more than 150 experiments spanning pressures from 25-550 bars over the temperature range 1000-1500 K with nominal reaction times of 1.2-1.8 ms were obtained. Five sets of experiments were performed for stoichiometric CO oxidation (F=1) spanning pressures from 25 to 550 bars and three sets of experiments at 25, 50 and 300 bars were performed using fuel lean (F=0.5) mixtures. The mixtures were doped with 160-225 ppm of H2. Standard GC/TCD-FID and GC/MS techniques were used to analyze the stable species (CO, CO2 and O2) from the shock samples. The experimental data was simulated using the recent Davis et al. model (An optimized model for CO/H2 combustion). Preliminary simulations indicate that the Davis et al. model is able to capture the trends for the lower pressure data sets (25 and 50 bars) but under predicts CO and O2 conversion and CO2 formation at high pressures. The modeling work is in progress and preliminary results suggest a modification in the fall-off parameters is warranted for the pressure dependent reaction H+O2+(Ar)=HO2(+Ar) in order to match the trends observed in the experiments.
B: A fast response thermocouple (Type C) from NANMAC Corporation was found to be the best choice for obtaining the actual temperature within the shock tube. High frequency noise of amplitude of several orders of magnitude greater than the expected signal from the thermocouple was recorded by the data acquisition card during our preliminary tests and this resulted in the raw signals being masked noise. A detailed analysis of the source of the noise and methods to avoid the high frequency noise to be picked up by the data acquisition card was performed. The problems with the background noise have been resolved by the use of a differential amplifier as well as special electrical insulation (Kapton Tape) that was wrapped around all exposed parts of the thermocouple as well as the amplifier and currently experiments are in progress to obtain raw temperature measurements from the thermocouple.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The task is well underway. Details of the progress are given in our annual report. For now, it suffices to say, that an excellent graduate student is working on this project. In the last year he has not only examined the theoretical aspects of this project but designed and had implemented many of the experimental aspects. Here is a very brief summary: During the first few months of the project all the literature regarding the Mars rocket engines, the shock tube, and carbon monoxide oxidation was carefully examined and studied by the new graduate student. Furthermore, the experimental apparatus present in laboratory was examined through available documentation and articles. The devices necessary to start the research were selected after an accurate examination of all the possible solutions provided by different companies. The new end-cap of the shock tube was designed to allow a new fast thermocouple to be introduced inside the shock tube. The fast thermocouple has been connected to the data collection card. The data acquisition software was modified to allow the information from the new thermocouple to be read, displayed, and saved. Please see our annual report for more details

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous flames - premixed
Task Description: This joint program aims to gain fundamental understanding of the structure and dynamics of sooting premixed flames in simple, well-defined, one-dimensional, burner-supported, cylindrical and spherical flow fields. The proposed program consists of the following four major components: (1) experimental determination of the fundamental sooting limits in the absence of conductive heat loss to the burner; (2) experimental determination of the fundamental laminar flame speed of soot-forming flames; (3) experimental mapping of sooting structure; and (4) detailed modeling of sooting flame propagation and soot formation. The work in components 1 and 2 will demonstrate a novel experimental approach under microgravity and generate fundamental flame and soot data that are suitable for rigorous comparison with detailed numerical simulation. This experimental approach eliminates the ambiguities associated with the boundary conditions in previous soot laminar premixed flame experiments and simulation. Combined with components 3 and 4 of the proposed work, we shall develop a soot research platform which is unique and complementary to the existing soot research tools and facilities. To study rich, freely-propagating, sooting premix flames by microgravity experiments and numerical simulation. This experiment is the first time that sooting flames are studied without the added complications of flame stretch or heat loss to the burner. The results of the study will yield fundemental insight into minimizing particulate pollutant emission from combustion.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Flame soot is a carcinogen and also contributes to global warming. Current work aims to further our anderstanding of sooting premixed flames, and improve current sooting models. This will allow better predictions of soot formation in practical combustion systems.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Surface combustion, shs, fire safety and smoldering
Task Description:
The current flammability requirements for all materials to be used in space vehicles (NASA specifications) are given by the 'Flammability, Odor, Offgassing, and Compatibility Requirements and Test Procedures for Materials in Environments that Support Combustion' document. This document specifies two tests that need to be performed before a material is qualified to be used in a space vehicle, the 'Upward Flame Propagation Test' (Test 1) and the 'Heat and Visible Smoke Release Rates Test' (Test 2). These two tests are expected to properly assess the flammability of a material in micro-gravity conditions. These methods attempt to provide a worst case scenario (Test 1) and a measure of the heat release (Test 2), and consequently, the 'damage potential' of a fire. A detailed description of these test methods is provided in NASA-NHB 8060.1 and an extensive list of the materials that have been tested is provided in the 'Materials Selection List for Space Hardware Systems.'
Recent work, as reported in the proposal for this project and the publications from this research, suggest that current methods of assessing material flamability may be improved. In essence, no single test current test method is capable of providing enough information to fully describe fire growth. Analytical and model-based solutions are sought to support the wealth of earth-gravity flame spread data that is available, to provide a bridge between current fundamental studies and critical fire safety needs. Experiments with advanced diagnostics are performed with PMMA, a well-characterized material that can be readily compared with theory. The goal of this work is thus to provide an improved methodology for assessment of material fire safety in micro-gravity. The objective this work is to provide an improved analytical framework for assessment of material fire safety in micro-gravity environments, based on current fundamental understanding of flame spread. Such a framework would allow the extrapolation of a wealth of earth-gravity flammability data to micro-gravity and allow connection between fundamental knowledge and vital practical safety requirements. Current and planned human space missions are of such duration that the risk of fire could be significant, and the impact of a potential fire could be catastrophic. Improved understanding of material flammability is crucial to minimizing the fire risk. This project will contribute an analytical and model-based framework to better understand and predict material flammability at normal and micro-gravity.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Task Description: The study of edge-flames in contexts relevant to the microgravity experimental program, with particular efforts to describe edge-flames in smolder combustion, an issue of great importance in space safety. To provide, for the first time, a description of edge-waves in smolder combustion, paradigms for 2-dimensional smolder waves with edges. Most of our knowledge of smolder is either 1-dimensional, or 2-dimensional in a boundary-layer like context. Our understanding of smolder spread in a two-dimensional context outside of the aforementioned contexts is inadequate, and so our knowledge of how smolder can spread or transition to flaming combustion is incomplete, dangersously so.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Recently we have examined flames in narrow tubes, and have submitted the following to the 2006 Combustion Institute Proceedings:
‘Flames in Narrow Circular Tubes’ T.L.Jackson, J.Buckmaster, Z.Lu, D.C.Kyritsis, L.Massa
We examine an axi-symmetric deflagration located in a tube with thermally active walls. It is noted that the flame-in-tube configuration defines a classical edge-flame, a flame in a shear flow for which there is a water-shed solution for a critical value of the Damkohler number, ignition front solutions for larger values of the Damkohler, and failure wave solutions for smaller values. We examine semi-infinite tubes with a heat flux imposed at the tube wall ends, to simulate experiments reported in the 30th Symposium. We identify parameters for which stable solutions are obtained at certain flow rates, but unstable solutions are generated at higher flow rates, followed by stable solutions at still higher flow rates. These solutions are consistent with the experimental record. Instability leads either to regular oscillations or to a violent process characterized by quenching and re-ignition.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Droplets, sprays, particles, dust clouds, nanoparticles
Task Description:
Heterogeneous combustion of solid fuels provides a substantial fraction of our energy needs here on earth, as well as in space propulsion applications. An effective and common method of solid fuel combustion is in its particulate form, however, the current theoretical/numerical models available to describe the heterogeneous combustion of such solid particles lack the complex coupling of physical-chemical processes involved. Furthermore, well designed and reliable experimental data are lacking to validate any model development effort. This is certainly true for (a) porous char/graphite particle combustion, which is relevant to efficient and clean combustion of char and (b) magnesium (Mg) particle combustion in CO2/CO environment, applicable for propulsion and energy utilization in Martian atmosphere. The goal of the proposed work is to establish a comprehensive theoretical and experimental approach utilizing NASA Microgravity facilities to develop and validate heterogeneous combustion submodels.
The proposed effort will significantly enhance our understanding of the condensed fuel utilization processes, develop accurate modelling approaches for a wide range of fuels, facilitate future exploration of the Martian atmosphere, and educate young scientist about fundamental concepts of combustion.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Enhance our understanding of the condensed fuel utilization processes, develop accurate modelling approaches for a wide range of fuels, facilitate future exploration of the Martian atmosphere, and educate young scientist about fundamental concepts of combustion.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:
Note: Original end date of 9/30/2007 changed.
Task Description:
Heterogeneous combustion of solid fuels provides a substantial fraction of our energy needs here on earth, as well as in space propulsion applications. An effective and common method of solid fuel combustion is in its particulate form, however, the current theoretical/numerical models available to describe the heterogeneous combustion of such solid particles lack the complex coupling of physical-chemical processes involved. Furthermore, well designed and reliable experimental data are lacking to validate any model development effort. This is certainly true for (a) porous char/graphite particle combustion, which is relevant to efficient and clean combustion of char and (b) magnesium (Mg) particle combustion in CO2/CO environment, applicable for propulsion and energy utilization in Martian atmosphere. The goal of the proposed work is to establish a comprehensive theoretical and experimental approach utilizing NASA Microgravity facilities to develop and validate heterogeneous combustion submodels.
The proposed effort will significantly enhance our understanding of the condensed fuel utilization processes, develop accurate modelling approaches for a wide range of fuels, facilitate future exploration of the Martian atmosphere, and educate young scientist about fundamental concepts of combustion.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Enhance our understanding of the condensed fuel utilization processes, develop accurate modelling approaches for a wide range of fuels, facilitate future exploration of the Martian atmosphere, and educate young scientist about fundamental concepts of combustion.

Task Description:
The overall objective of the program is to study the burner stability of enclosed laminar flames in microgravity environments. The specific objectives are (a) to evaluate the effects of fuel Schmidt number on the transition from lifted flames to blow-out conditions, (b) to study the hysteresis effects observed in the reattachment of lifted flames, (c) to gain physical insight into the transition from lifted to blow-out conditions, and (d) to validate numerical simulation. The current project studies the flame stabilization in coflow environments. The findings will contribute to the fundamentals of combustion theory. The current invetsigation is also of practical significance as practical combustors often have jet flames in flow environments, for example, co-flow inside gas turbine engine combustors and in industrial furnaces. Understanding of the flame stabilization at the fundamental level is key to safety considerations in the design of new combustors. The verified numerical model for the prediction of the flame stabilization can be applied as a design tool for complex engineering systems.

This invetsigation provides additional insight of the structure of the edge flame from stabilized to (near) blowout conditions. Specifically, the ratio of length scales versus the ratio of time scales was extracted from the numerical results, and the ratio of length scales versus Damkohler number was used to characherize the flame regimes. The adpative mesh refinement flame code will also be used to study the deNOx process in catalytic converters.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
An investigation of buoyancy effects on the structure and stability of Burke-Schumann diffusion flames (BSDF) is conducted. The specific objectives are to (1) investigate the importance of the buoyancy-dependent flow-field as affected by oxidizer flow on flame stabilization and (2) examine the state relationships (i.e., flame structure.) of co-flow diffusion flames under the influence of buoyancy conditions. The goal of the research is to improve our understanding of the influence of buoyancy on the stability and structure of Burke-Schumann type diffusion flames.
The publications including student theses that result from this project are summarized in the report. A new numerical method, Lattice Boltzmann Method, was successfully used for simulation of non-premixed flames as documented in the article by Lee et al. (2006) cited in Bibliography.

Task Description:
A joint experimental and computational approach is adopted. Data obtained from ELF Glovebox Investigation were used to evaluate the effects of fuel Schmidt number on the transition from the lifted flame to the blow-out condition. Comparison tests were conducted in normal gravity to allow isolation and identification of the influence of buoyancy. The results were used to map the liftoff and blowout stability limits as a function of the fuel and air velocities for the two buoyancy conditions. A methane and nitrogen mixture (50% on volume basis) was used as the fuel. The experimental results verified the hypothesis that substantially greater velocities are required to destabilize the flame in microgravity. The increase in air velocity required to induce liftoff in microgravity (compared to normal gravity) was roughly equal to the increase required to induce blowout in microgravity. Furthermore, the air velocity increase was relatively independent of the fuel flow, except at low fuel flows. At high fuel flows, the microgravity flames tend to immediately blow out after lift off, in agreement with the free-jet theory in the literature for fuels with a Schmidt number less than 0.7. However, stable lifted flames were achieved within a coflow duct in microgravity at low fuel flows, and in normal gravity. A numerical code with adaptive mesh refinement was developed and used to solve the transport equations, including the finite rate chemistry based on a four-step reduced mechanism. The calculated blowout conditions were in quantitative agreement with ELF results for fuel jet velocity below 0.2 m/s, but only in qualitative agreement for higher fuel jet velocities.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
A numerical code with adaptive mesh refinement was developed and used to solve the transport equations, including the finite rate chemistry based on a four-step reduced mechanism. The calculation based on a four-step reduced mechanism was be able to predict the blowout conditions, and in quantitative agreement with ELF results in microgravity at low fuel jet velocities, e.g., 0.2 m/s, but in qualitative agreement for higher fuel jet velocities. The numerical calculation also shows that the blowout condition is most sensitive to the heat loss level and oxygen content in ambient air. The calculated blowout velocity based on the four-step reduced mechanism is in agreement with that based on the full starting mechanism for the conditions examined. The calculated reaction zone structures are qualitatively similar, but with noted differences... The flame leading edge exhibits significantly different structure, whereas similar structures of the trailing diffusion flames are calculated. Error of the radical diffusive fluxes at the flame leading edge calculated based on the reduced mechanism was responsible for the differences at the leading edge. The four-step reduced mechanism also calculates a different evolution of the flame from a stabilized condition to the blowout although it was able to calculate the blowout air velocity with sufficient accuracy. Comparison of the results shows that the four-step reduced mechanism can properly calculate the major species mass fraction, temperature, velocity, and reaction rates as compared to the results based on the full starting mechanism. It is noted that the computational time requirement of the full starting mechanism is about 3 to 4 times of that based on the four-step reduced mechanism, which is of the order of month for calculation of a single blowout condition. The excessive computational effort required by the full starting mechanism is due to the fact that the number of transport equations is increased, and that a much smaller time step is required. The four-step reduced mechanism seems can be used to calculate the blowout conditions of methane fueled laminar diffusion flames if the blowout out velocity is information of primary interest.

Task Description:
This task is focused on experimental reserach to quantiry the effects of buoyancy on the mean flowfield and its impact on local and overall flame/turbulence interaction processes. The approach is to obtain detailed measurement and analysis of the velocity and scalar fields of premixed turbulent flames in microgravity and in normal, partial and enhanced gravity.
The objective of this research is to proof that buoyancy is a system parameter of laboratory and practical premixed turbulent flames. Buoyancy provides an upstream feedback mechanism that dictates the overall flame flowfield as well as local flame turbulence interaction processes. Consequently the flame structures, stabilization limits, turbulent reaction rates are directly or indirectly coupled with buoyancy.
The subject of our research, lean premixed turbulent flames, is an emerging environmental energy technology because these flames can be exploited to reduce the emission of oxides of nitrogen. Therefore, results of this research will benefit both combustion science and technology. Combustion engineer will have scaling information to eliminate buoyancy influences on practical systems. Experimentalists will gain new knowledge to identify and interpret buoyancy contributions to laboratory flames. Theoretical research will benefit by having a set of reference data to improve the fidelity of turbulent combustion models and to develop methods to address elliptical problems.
Specifically, this research effort will generate the insight to determine significant processes through which gravity affects flame properties such as flame speed and flame structures. The results can be applied to investigate the gravity-influenced limit for premixed turbulent flames. The backward coupling effects of buoyancy (i.e., downstream effects felt upstream) is of particular importance to combustion theory because it relates to the elliptical problem that requires full time dependent treatment of upstream, wall and downstream boundary conditions. Knowledge on the back-coupling buoyancy affected processes is valuable for guiding the development of turbulent combustion models to include these effects. This study will contribute to resolving the inconsistencies that exist between experiments and theories.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Terrestrial laboratory study is an important aspect of our research that provides background information necessary to interpret data from the microgravity experiments. Due to the cancellation of the flight experiments, we re-directed our effort to design an experiment that allows us to investigate buoyancy flame coupling to support the development of models and numerical simulations. The specific goal of our FY06 activities is to collaborate with Ian Shepherd on his NASA project on “Numerical Investigation of Buoyancy and Pressure Affects in Premixed Flames.” The objective of the numerical work is to develop a methodology to address and simulate the large difference between the small length scales that characterize combustion and the large length scales that characterize the buoyant interactions.
For our first problem, we considered the unstable plume of +1g and -1g ring-stabilized Bunsen type conical flames reported in our earlier experimental studies. The experiments have showed that the well-known flame tip flickering phenomenon is a direct consequence of buoyancy induced instability. As the numerical simulation of the flickering flame produces time-dependent scalar and velocity information throughout the flame flowfield, their validation requires similar types of experimental results. The regular flame flickering frequency means that the flickering cycle can provide a time base for phase-locked experimental measurements so that phased averaged velocity can be obtained for direct comparison with the numerical results. Although our ultimate goal is to investigate buoyancy effects on turbulent flames, the unstable laminar flickering flame is presently a more tractable problem to start. The flickering laminar flame experiments were performed in a 25 mm diameter burner developed for our drop-tower and parabolic flight experiments. Two-dimensional, radial, U, and axial, W, velocity data was measured by Particle Imaging Velocimetry (PIV) and phase-locked flowfield information was obtained by triggered the PIV using a schlieren-based flame motion sensor. For each flame, mean velocity vectors were obtained at four or eight phase angles during the cycle.
Examination of the phase-locked and time averaged velocity results from four flames clearly demonstrates the vortex ‘pumping’ mechanism that generates the flame flicker. The effect of this process is also discernible from a comparison of the experimental and numerical phase-averaged axial centerline velocity profiles. This study has shown that the phase-locked PIV technique provides valuable insights to support numerical simulation of the buoyancy induced large scale unstable flow phenomenon. More importantly, the vortex-pairing process shown by the simulation helps to explain some of the ambiguities found in the phased-averaged PIV data. This shows that a synergistic experimental and simulation approach is very beneficial to furthering the understanding of field effects of gravity to combustion. We plan to continue with further analyses of the experimental and numerical data obtained for the laminar pulsating flames. In addition, phase-locked PIV measurements will be made to investigate vortex-pairing and also in turbulent flames to investigate the effect of turbulence in plume vortex formation.

The approach is to obtain detailed measurement and analysis of the velocity and scalar fields of premixed turbulent flames in microgravity and in normal, partial and enhanced gravity.
The objective of this research is to proof that buoyancy is a system parameter of laboratory and practical premixed turbulent flames. Buoyancy provides an upstream feedback mechanis that dictates the overall flame flowfield as well as locak flame turbulence interaction processes. Consequently the flame structures, stabilization limits, turbulent reaction rates are directly or indirectly coupled with buoyancy.
The subject of our reserach, lean premixed turbulent flames, is an emerging environmental energy technology because these flames can be exploited to reduce the emission of oxides of nitrogen. Therefore, tesults of this research will benefit both combustion science and technology. Combustion engineer will have scaling information to eliminate buoyancy influences on practical systems. Experimentalists will gain new knowledge to identify and interpret buoyancy contributions to laboratory flames. Theoretical research will benefit by having a set of reference data to improve the fidelity of turbulent combustion models and to develop methods to address elliptical problems.
Specifically, this research effort will generate the insight to determine significant processes through which gravity affects flame properties such as flame speed and flame structures. The results can be applied to investigate the gravity-influenced limit for premixed turbulent flames. The backward coupling effects of buoyancy (i.e. downstream effects felt upstream) is of particular importance to combustion theory because it relates to the elliptical problem that requires full time dependent treatment of upstream, wall and downstream boundary conditions. Knowledge on the back-coupling buoyancy affected processes is valuable for guiding the development of turbulent combustion models to include these effects. This study will contribute to resolving the inconsistencies that exist between experiments and theories.

Task Progress:
Laboratory study of CLEAN flame is an important aspect of our research that provides background information necessary to interpret data from the flight experiments. We have completed Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) measurements of three laminar and three turbulent CH4/air flames in +1g and -1g under the same initial conditions as those in our flight matrix. The experiments were performed at equivalence ratios, = 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9 with the mean flow velocity U at 3 m/s. For the turbulent flames, a perforated plate was used and it produced a slightly anisotropic turbulence with the axial rms velocity u’ = 0.44 m/s and radial rms velocity v’ = 0.3 m/s. For each flame, the PIV data have been analyzed to obtained the axial and transverse man and rms velocities. Comparing the profiles of +1g and -1g flames provided additional insights into the flowfield characteristics of the CLEAN flame burner and show that the effects of buoyancy occur not only in the flame flowfield but also in the wake region of the flame stabilizer. This is a clear demonstration of the upstream coupling due to field effects of gravity. However, the limited studies available in the open literature on the characteristics of the wake regions downstream of flame stabilizer are not sufficient to help gain better understanding of the processes that cause such significant differences.
We also co-ordinate our work with those of Ian Shepherd’s NASA project on “Numerical Investigation of Buoyancy and Pressure Affects in Premixed Flames.” The objective of his work is to develop a numerical methodology to address and to be able to simulate the large difference between the length scales that characterize the combustion and those that characterize the buoyant interactions. For their first problem, Shepherd and Day simulated in 2D the unstable plume of +1g and -1g conical flames reported in one of our earlier studies. During FY04, they adapted the AMR method to simulate again in 2D a buoyancy stabilized laminar flames reported in another of our publications. Their current plan is to extend the scope of their investigation to simulate additional conical flames to evaluate and refine their simulation methods. Our goal is to facilitate the merging of experiments and simulation through a synergistic effort so that the computational method can be advanced the capability of the AMR methods to simulate in 3D time dependent processes of buoyant and microgravity CLEAN flames.
We have also collaborated on the microgravity combustion project of Prof. Toshihisa Ueda of Keio University. Professor Ueda’s research is to study the relative effects of buoyancy and solid body rotation on the instability of Bunsen type conical flames. The foundation of his project was our previous work on measuring and correlating pulsation frequency of buoyant conical flames. The objective is to extend the investigation to include the study of centrifugal forces on buoyancy effects. Our collaboration has produced two publications.

Task Progress:
Since the Scientific Concept Review in FY02 the focus of our work has been on developing a Phase B plan for Requirements Definition Review (RDR) with our Projects Scientist (PS) and our Engineering Team Leader of NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC).
In our Phase B Plan, we identified 12 open items and described the approaches to resolve them. For the scientific aspects of the flight experiments, the main items are concerned with the hardware, software, and control requirements for the laser diagnostic methods that will enable us to measure conditional velocity statistics and spatial statistical structures of the turbulent flames. We identified that a particle image velocimetry (PIV) is best suited to fulfill these requirement. PIV is a proven method for measuring velocities in a relatively large flowfield domain of 10 cm by 10 cm. From the PIV images, the wrinkled turbulent flame front boundaries are discernible. The flame boundaries can be used as a discriminator for the investigation of conditional statistics. We have developed and tested the software to trace the flame boundaries automatically and to separate and generate the conditional PIV image set. The analysis of the conditioned velocities from the split PIV images, however, is not trivial and requires some software development. We are developing and testing new algorithms for incorporation into the PIV data analysis software.
For measuring scalar statistics, our plan is to use a technique called planar imaging of flame fronts (PIFF) based on Mie scattering from an oil aerosol that burns and evaporates at the flame. The main attribute of this PIFF method is its leniency on laser and optical requirements so that it can be implemented by using our PIV laser, optics and camera. To demonstrate, we used our PIV systems to make PIFF measurements in a laboratory v-flame. The data showed this method to produce very clear and detailed outlines of the flame front boundaries that can be extracted and analyzed by the software we have developed previously for the analysis of the flame front measured by a more elaborate diagnostics such as the Planar Laser Induced Fluorescence of OH radicals.
Laboratory study of CLEAN flame also is an important aspect of our work to provide background information necessary to interpret data from the flame experiments. Thus far we have used our PIV system to investigate +1g and -1g flames with initial conditions same as those of our flight matrix. The experiments consist of three laminar and three turbulent CH4/air flames with equivalence ratios = 0.7, 0.8, and 0.9 with the mean flow velocity U at 3 m/s. For the turbulent flames, turbulence produced by the grid is slightly anisotropic with u’ = 0.44 m/s and v’ = 0.3 m/s.
We are also collaborating on the microgravity combustion project of Prof. Toshihisa Ueda of Keio University in Yokohama Japan. Professor Ueda’s research is to study the relative effects of buoyancy and solid body rotation on the instability of Bunsen type conical flames. The foundation of his project was our previous work on measuring and correlating pulsation frequency of buoyant conical flames. The objective is to extend the investigation to include the study of centrifugal forces on buoyancy effects. Our collaboration has produced two publications.

Task Description:
The ultimate objective of this project is to comprehensively simulate the behavior of a small diffusion flame under the influence of an externally applied electric field in zero-gravity and to use PSI data to confirm the accuracy of that modeling. A detailed model will be used that includes the chemistry of charged ions and chemiluminescent flame intermediates to capture any feedback between ion-driven convection and combustion behavior, and to allow quantitative comparisons with experimental measurements. To date, the capability of accurately simulating electric field flames has eluded researchers because the system exhibits dramatic ranges of coupled temporal and spatial scales. Moreover, in Earth's gravity, the hot combustion products are subject to buoyancy effects that are difficult to isolate from those generated by the electric field. We propose implementations to an existing powerful simulation framework (PeleLM) for this problem, and to use the PSI data set from E-FIELD Flames for validation of the model and investigation of the complex coupled system.
PeleLM is a state-of-the-art reacting flow code tailored with a unique integration scheme that efficiently couples high-speed processes with the slower evolution of the flow structures using the adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) strategy. This project is to improve the ion chemistry (particularly employing reduced chemical mechanisms available in the published literature) to generalize the electric field configurations in PeleLM, and to then simulate zero-g coflow flames in the E-FIELD Flames dataset. Comparisons include V-I (voltage-ion current) curves and flame shapes (deduced from CH* images), varying with fuel types, compositions and flow rates. The data includes step function changes in voltage that can be used to evaluate the time response of the flame. It is important to also consider the impact of image and ion current collection timescales, which will be critical for model validation.
The work takes advantage of the unique E-FIELD Flames data, measured in microgravity, to validate the proposed PeleLM model augmentations, to permit a detailed investigation of the ion dynamics under the influence of electric fields, and to evaluate the subsequent interactions with non-charged species, as well as to assess the potential of electric field forcing to affect thermal transport and sooting in diffusion flames. Once the simulation is validated against the zero-g data, it will be possible to further extend the simulations to flames in Earth's gravity, where potential applications for improved heat release and emission reduction can be explored. This utilization of zero gravity data from the E-FIELD Flames experiment for beneficial purposes on Earth and for a better understanding of combustion control is compatible with the NASA objectives.
The E-FIELD Flames experiment was conceived and directed to create a data set that would permit the detailed assessment of the effects of ion-driven winds and charged species chemistry on non-premixed flames. A microgravity environment is required because the forces of ion driven winds and of gravity driven buoyancy winds are too close in magnitude to effectively separate their effects with any earth-gravity experiments where natural convection is a significant contributor to the combustion process. This rationale has been proven out by the E-FIELD flame experimental data now available as part of the PSI website. The Electric Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was completed in 2018, and with nearly 150 hours of operations over six months and the ignition of 250 electric field flames on the ISS, it was a very successful measurement campaign. The experiment aspect of this project is to extract and assemble a data portfolio that is ideally suited for validating numerical simulations. The simulation aspect of the project employs the PeleLM framework at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), which was previously developed in the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL). This open-source code is for evolving chemically reacting flows at low Mach number with block-structured adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) using the AMReX library. It is the extension of this code that we exploit for comparison with E-FIELD Flames data, with the ultimate goal of understanding and then controlling hydrocarbon flames under the influence of electric fields. PeleLMeX is the non-subcycling version of PeleLM, and this project will use the non-subcycling strategy at the same time understanding other aspects using the PeleLM.
Control of combustion using electric fields has for decades been proposed for extending flammability limits, reducing emissions, and preventing instability and blowoff, as well as modifying soot production. Implementation of the concept has been difficult, however, because of the complex coupling between buoyant driven flows, ion production in the flame, ion acceleration by the electric field, and the resulting forces on the neutral gas. With an efficient and accurate simulation capability, it will be possible to explore temporal and geometric variations of the electric field to manipulate flames in a wide range of beneficial ways.
With the implementation of a super reduced GRI-Mech 3.0-based mechanism and without excited species and with a few ions, the simulation results did not capture a clear difference between microgravity and Earth gravity conditions. This fiscal year is to continue the previous efforts in implementing the San Deigo-based reduced mechanism, as well as testing the new PeleLMeX code specifically for electric field flames research. The specific aims of this project task include:
(1) Understanding the strategy by working with the detailed electric field flames in the PeleLMeX code and its function, including initiating and implementing the code to rapidly perform vast numbers of calculations by graphics processing unit (GPU) (2) Then implementing PeleLMeX CFD with a (newer) reduced chemical mechanism that includes positive ions, negative ions and excited species with 1g condition (3) Verify the fidelity of the PeleLMeX simulation of flames under the influence of electric fields by direct comparison using the previously validated reduced mechanism without electric field in comparison to the schlieren imaging under 1g conditions (4) Demonstrate validated PeleLM simulations of microgravity flames in steady conditions and during unsteady transitions in response to changes in the external electric field

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2026
Task Progress:
As in the above objectives listing, this year has major aspects of working in the PeleLMeX computing by establishing the appropriate electric field flames code, with the more complicated San Diego-based mechanism conducting with the International Space Station (ISS) conditions. The current year’s effort includes continuing to modify the mechanism (with charged and excited species) and addressing/fixing the details in the PeleLMeX CFD code for simulating flames under the influence of an electric field. This year, progress has been made on all the items with emphasis on 1-3 for the new mechanism. Specifically, the progress includes:
Computational Modeling Implementation Employed with a Set of Species
To predict ion concentrations in flames and the effects of ion driven winds in coflow and jet flames, a complete set of charged species and excited species to include in the computation is essential and the most challenging. This task is to find the best scientific method to include more charged species and excited species implementation into the CFD simulation with appropriate reduced chemistry to ensure robust simulation capability.
The previous PeleLM simulation computation capability validation using pressurized conditions also continues. Further details of the project progress through the fourth year are described in the following.
• PeleLMeX Computation
The progress in the PeleLM computational aspects of the project are described in a series of conference papers provided in the publication section of this report and in recent American Society for Gravitational and Space Research (ASGSR) presentations (Grabon et al., 2024, Deu Morel et al., 2023). Much of the work has so far concentrated on the cases without an electric field in order to assess the complications of the code implementation, its conversion to cylindrically symmetric geometry, to identify the choice of reduced models, and to ensure that the boundary conditions are appropriate to simulate an extruded fuel tube.
• Implementation with more species in PeleLMeX – Preliminary Outcome
The PeleLMeX computation of this research is implemented on the UCI High Performance Community Computing Cluster (HPC3) running on Linux 8.6. Its aim is to boost the effectiveness of simulations by utilizing a considerable number of cores. To handle user admission and resource allocation, the cluster employs entities like login nodes and the Slurm scheduler.
As this is the second set of the reduced mechanism for the new PeleLM - PeleLMeX code, the goal of this part of the project is to use the reduced mechanism tested for microgravity conditions. This work initiated with reproducing the behavior of the coflow burner used in the ISS. The primary distinction between the numerical and experimental setups lies in the extruded fuel pipe. As the PeleLMeX code has not integrated the extruded geometry, it is unable to replicate the impact of the fuel pipe on the inflow velocities or temperature. The effect of the extruded tube is simulated using a customized inlet velocity profile. The primary assumption is that the Low Mach number regime is in effect. It is acknowledged that the velocities will remain within this regime. This is a widely accepted hypothesis in the study of combustion and was validated at the conclusion of the simulations.
The simulation was initiated with 19 (and 15) cm/s fuel flow velocity with 3.1 cm/s coflow air with 300K initial temperature with CFL 0.1. This case without the electric field can help explain the operation of PeleLMeX. Moreover, the cases without electric field are distinctive for its shorter compilation time due to the reduced number of equations/species to be solved resulting from the deactivation of the electric field. To bridge the gap between simulation outcomes and empirical data, this part of the work is to evaluate potential mechanism of 45 species and 216 reactions using San Diego reduced mechanism, by López-Cámara et al. This task is to implement the recently published reduced San Diego mechanism in microgravity and with an electric field. These mechanisms are chosen for their comprehensive coverage of ionic and exited species within the flame compared to the mechanism currently used by Di Renzo et al. which is not able to capture the ion current behavior in microgravity condition.
The main difference lies in the reduced San Diego mechanism chemical model, which includes 11 charged species, including H3O+, HCO+, C2H3O+, CH5O+, O2−, OH−, e−, CO3−, CHO2−, O−, and CHO3− (in comparison to the previous used H3O+, HCO+, O2− and e−) and included excited species CH and OH. This mechanism includes many species, and as the electric field is introduced the calculation became extensive and the computation time increased substantially.
With the numerous attempts in the PeleLMeX, the heat released from the calculation is massive in the prior year; this year we have initiated the computation from a GPU desktop and also the HPC supercomputing on campus. The GPU desktop is useful for locally operating the PeleLMeX simulation, and then further allowing the migration to a more complicated environment in the HPC system. This fiscal year, with the PeleLMeX code initiator (Dr. Day’s help) in fixing the San Diego-based PeleLMeX, the code was successfully ignited with a flame at 70% methane concentration at 15 cm/s under 1g conditions. The flame reaches the steady state after several days of running via UCI’s HPC and with the GPU code embedded into the PeleLMeX code.
All testpoints are ignited with a blob with a radius of 1 mm and a temperature of 1,900 K (based on previous work), which ensures an ignition in all cases. The beginning of the ignition being the most unstable part, the simulation was run with a low CFL number of 0.05 in order to have the most stable run, which also meant computation time was quite high. However, even with this setting, stability issues arose: simulation failed around 0.2 ms as the solver was unable to compute the ignition due to initial conditions. To fix this issue, the simulation was set to cap the time-step at 10 - 7 at the beginning of the ignition. In this configuration, the simulation can run with CFL=0.08, while remaining stable. After a run of 0.03 s, the time-step limit was switched off and simulation could run with a time-step of 10 - 5 until reaching steady state. During those first 0.03 s, a set of species at the initial state was used to prevent computation error without the essential species. The current project continues with four testpoints selected before and after the acme point, and they are -3.7, -4.4, -5.5, and -7.4kV.
Conclusions
The newer version of PeleLM (PeleLMeX), using the recently published reduced mechanism, is progressing. Specifically, the non-subcycling version of PeleLM has been debugged and implemented with a GPU. The code is running with the flame ignited. These tests demonstrated that the code will take longer on a weekly basis to run for milliseconds. The code also needs to be continued to be exercised under different coflow flame conditions with different levels of fuel dilution, with carbon dioxide and different pressures, to demonstrate the validity of the previous work with water addition to the boundary condition implementation. Challenges remain for how this relatively large San Diego-based mechanism will be able to accomplish all of the testpoint tests, including more ions and charged species into the newer version of PeleLMeX; and further, whether it will capture the ion current curve measured from the ISS. Continuing work on this project focuses more heavily on the computations, with a detailed assessment of the ion current prediction and the role the chemical mechanism plays in that prediction.

The Electric Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was completed in 2018, and with nearly 150 hours of operations over six months and the ignition of 250 electric field flames on the ISS, it was a very successful measurement campaign. The experiment aspect of this project is to extract and assemble a data portfolio that is ideally suited for validating numerical simulations. The simulation aspect of the project employs the PeleLM framework at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), which was previously developed in the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL). This open-source code is for evolving chemically reacting flows at low Mach number with block-structured adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) using the AMReX library. It is the extension of this code that we exploit for comparison with E-FIELD Flames data, with the ultimate goal of understanding and then controlling hydrocarbon flames under the influence of electric fields. PeleLMeX is the non-subcycling version of PeleLM, and this project will use the non-subcycling strategy at the same time understanding other aspects using the PeleLM.
Control of combustion using electric fields has for decades been proposed for extending flammability limits, reducing emissions, and preventing instability and blowoff, as well as modifying soot production. Implementation of the concept has been difficult, however, because of the complex coupling between buoyant driven flows, ion production in the flame, ion acceleration by the electric field, and the resulting forces on the neutral gas. With an efficient and accurate simulation capability, it will be possible to explore temporal and geometric variations of the electric field to manipulate flames in a wide range of beneficial ways.
As the GRI-Mech 3.0-based super reduced mechanism was implemented but without excited species and with a few ions, in the prior fiscal year, the main focus of this cycle was to implement a more complicated San Diego-based reduced mechanism with positive ions, negative ions, and excited species. The specific aims and objective of this project in this year include:
(1) Establishing flame images for fuel dilution cases, particularly for the 70% and 40% methane dilution in 1-g laboratory electric field flames (2) Understanding transient flame response, particularly the influence of the ion-driven wind in the 1-g in-laboratory electric field flames with the experimental flow conditions and mesh distance matching the microgravity E-FIELD Flames ISS experiments (3) Verify the strategy with understanding the detailed electric field with respect to the PeleLMeX function, and then implementing PeleLMeX CFD with a (newer) reduced chemical mechanism that includes more varieties of charged and excited species (4) Verify the fidelity of the PeleLMeX simulation of flames under the influence of electric fields by direct comparison using the previously validated reduced mechanism without electric fields in comparison to schlieren images of the flame under 1g conditions (5) Demonstrate validated PeleLM simulations of microgravity flames in steady conditions and during unsteady transitions in response to changes in the external electric field
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Once the simulation is validated against the zero-g data, it will be possible to further extend the simulations to flames in Earth gravity, where potential applications for improved heat release and emission reduction can be explored. This utilization of zero gravity data from the E-FIELD Flames experiment for beneficial purposes on Earth and for a better understanding combustion control is compatible with the NASA objectives.

PeleLMeX Computational Results and Discussion
The progress in the PeleLM computational aspects of the project are described in a series of conference papers provided in the publication section of this report and in recent American Society for Gravitational and Space Research (ASGSR) presentations (Grabon et al., 2024, Deu Morel et al., 2023). Much of the work has so far concentrated on the cases without an electric field in order to assess the complications of the code implementation, its conversion to cylindrically symmetric geometry, to identify the choice of reduced models, and to ensure that the boundary conditions are appropriate to simulate an extruded fuel tube.
Using PeleLM with Various Pressures and Fuel Dilution with Different Species – no electric field
This part of the progress continues to investigate high pressure methane diffusion flames with water addition in comparison to CO2 addition using PeleLM simulation (Esquivias et al., 2024). The study used the same geometry coflow burner as for E-FIELD Flames and examined its behavior under the pressure conditions of previous tests of water addition simulation. By examining a similar flame geometry, but under different conditions, the study continues to evaluate the potential for PeleLM simulation to capture the chemico-physical details of small diffusion flames. This work is to study the behavior of a methane diffusion flame with various amounts of water vapor and CO2 added to the fuel and compares the flame behavior with various percentages of water vapor and CO2 content (0% to 65%). It provides the detailed temperature, CO, and CO2 and other species concentration distribution using the PeleLM adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) code. This work computes the combustion behavior of a coflow burner flame jet using PeleLM. The flame was simulated to pressures of 1.0, 1.4, 5.7, and 11.1 atm. The results extracted and analyzed include temperature profiles and various species mole fractions compared with their equilibrium state. The fundamentals between water and CO2 addition on the flame behaviors, peak temperature, as well as maximum mole concentration of CO2 and CO, was studied. The details of how the peak values of species vary for water and CO2 addition as compared to their equilibrium values are investigated.
The peak concentration for species CO, CO2, OH, and H2O were plotted and compared between water addition and CO2 at two pressure conditions, 11.1 and 1 atm. In 1 atm, CO2 addition has less CO and H2O production in comparison to water addition, while the peak value of OH is generally higher in all of the CO2 addition cases. At 11.1 atm, OH is very similar with both diluents added, this is due to the compact nature of the flame under the high pressure that does not allow enough room for the thermo-chemical reaction to reveal itself. Because of the addition of CO2, there is a distinct reduction in the production of CO, meaning that water addition participated in the reaction as both chemical and physical effect, but again, these are the peak value comparison only at atmospheric and high pressure conditions. Detailed reaction evaluations still are needed, as well as a sensitivity analysis. In general, the effect of pressure can be seen in the increase of species of CO, OH, and H2O.
The species of O, H, and OH of water and CO2 addition were compared to equilibrium conditions. The ratio between the OH, O, and H mole fraction species and the mole fraction at equilibrium are plotted against with the increase of the addition concentration. The mole fraction at equilibrium is computed using the Colorado State University online calculator, which is based on the original Stanjan Equilibrium Code (Dandy, 2019). The comparison conditions are 0%, 30% and 65% water addition and CO2 addition to a stoichiometric fuel/air mixture. The ratio of, for example, Hthis sstudy/ Heq., presents the ratio between the equilibrium prediction and the kinetics result for these atoms at all pressure conditions. The results show that H and O are consistently more than two times their equilibrium expectation for all water content at lower pressure, while OH stays near the equilibrium value throughout all the conditions in this study.
There is also relatively limited effect of diluent composition, as the thermal images of flames diluted with water and carbon dioxide are very similar under similar pressure and dilution conditions. The addition of water and carbon dioxide has similar results on the flame behavior. Future work will include an analysis of existing high-pressure experiment results and the superequilibrium prediction for the species (H and O) at different pressures.
These details show that the PeleLM framework is able to capture the proper boundary conditions, even though the absolute geometry is slightly different, because the experiment has a slightly extruded fuel tube and the simulation has a flat inlet. The flow inlet is varied to approximate the conditions expected for the extruded case. Further results appear in all of the conference presentations and publications listed in the publications section of this report.
Preliminary Results 1g Electric Fields Using ISS Conditions – PeleLMeX
The PeleLMeX computation of this research is implemented on the UCI High Performance Community Computing Cluster (HPC3) running on Linux 8.6. Its aim is to boost the effectiveness of simulations by utilizing a considerable number of cores. To handle user admission and resource allocation, the cluster employs entities like login nodes and the Slurm scheduler.
The goal of this project is to use the reduced mechanism Deu Morel et al. (2023, see reference) tested for microgravity condition with a newer version of the PeleLMeX as well as newer HPC3 hardware. This work initiated with reproducing the behavior of the coflow burner used in the ISS. The primary distinction between the numerical and experimental setups lies in the extruded fuel pipe. As the PeleLMeX code has not integrated the extruded geometry, it is unable to replicate the impact of the fuel pipe on the inflow velocities or temperature. The effect of the extruded tube is simulated using a customized inlet velocity profile. The primary assumption is that the Low Mach number regime is in effect. It is acknowledged that the velocities will remain within this regime. This is a widely accepted hypothesis in the study of combustion and was validated at the conclusion of the simulations.
The simulation was initiated with 19 (and 15) cm/s fuel flow velocity with 3.1 cm/s coflow air with 300K initial temperature with CFL 0.1. This case without the electric field can help explain the operation of PeleLMeX. Moreover, the cases without electric field are distinctive for shorter compilation time, due to the reduced number of equations/species to be solved resulting from the deactivation of the electric field. The reduced mechanism (by Di Renzo et al., 2022), comprising 26 species and 134 reactions with only two positive ions, H3O+ and HCO+, and one negative ion, O2- and electrons, was tested in microgravity and gravity conditions. This mechanism is currently used for simulating under 1g condition in comparison to the laboratory results to validate or invalidate the transient flame dynamic response to the ion wind in describing the E-FIELD Flames experiment.
As described in prior reports, for these simulations, the electric field implementation is in operation, requiring the use of HPC3, a supercomputer, due to its substantially longer computational time. Multiple convergence difficulties emerged during these simulations. After resolving these matters, we determined the necessary computation time to achieve a stable state. With the use of the electric field method, it takes 1 hour and 10 minutes to reach 1000 steps, in contrast to 3 minutes without it. Additionally, a stable state is achieved in the simulation within 60 milliseconds in simulation time. With the electric field, 1,000 steps correspond to a maximum of 10E-4 seconds. This requires over 30 days of consecutive simulations on the supercomputer to attain a steady state.
1g In-Laboratory Experiments
The 1g in-laboratory experiments include a coflow burner, rotameters for fuel and air, and a high voltage power supply (Trek 609A) with shunt current resistance for measuring ion current. The details of the experiment setups are described in Chien et al. (2018) Energies 11(5), 1235 and Chien et al. (2019) Combust. Flame 204(250-259). Both the High Voltage Power Supply (HVPS) output and ion current are monitored and controlled all along the running tests using data acquisition system NI 6341. The acquisition signals are sampled at a rate of 1000 samples per second and recorded with a LABVIEW code. The electrode potential is programmed before every recording allowing precise voltage sweeps. For safety, a High Voltage and Reverse Protection Circuit is used in addition to the HVPS. This specialized electronic arrangement is designed to protect electronic devices from potential damage caused by high voltage and reverse current. The High Voltage Protection circuit is composed of Zener diodes, which will open the circuit if the voltage reaches its threshold. This particular device safeguards the sensitive part of the circuit from being harmed by preventing electric arc formation, for instance. The Reverse Current Protection circuit is used to protect electronic components from being damaged by reverse polarity. If the circuit is incorrectly connected with the power supply by the user, diodes will block the current and avoid component destruction.
In this research, the mesh is set at 27 mm height above the burner due to the height limitation of the current experimental setup. The data collected includes ion current to applied voltages, natural flame images using a Nikon D90 camera, and also Shlieren imaging.
The measurements are made with two fuel flow speeds, 19 cm/s and 15 cm/s with airflow of 3.1 cm/s at 100% methane fuel concentration. The flame images were taken at ISO 200, aperture f/4.5, and a shutter speed of 1/10s, and the pictures were taken in the dark with a black fabric piece placed on the back to avoid reﬂections from the glass casing.
The ion current measurement is performed using a shunt resistor circuit. It consists of a 1 𝑀Ω resistor connected in parallel with two Zener diodes. This circuit is symmetrical, which means the polarity isn’t a concern here. The ion current results for positive electric fields are measured and recorded as a confirmation. The results indicate that a positive E-FIELD leads to the appearance of three regions. In the sub-saturation region, ion current increases with applied voltage until it reaches a plateau, known as the saturation region, which is reached at around 1.65 kV/cm for each flame speed. Finally, there is a final increase in ion current in the supersaturation region. The limits between the saturation regions are not the same depending on the ﬂame velocity due to the total amount of carbon content input. Therefore, the saturation plateau appears at a lower electric ﬁeld strength for lower velocity ﬂames.
To understand how the ion-driven wind and the process of electric fields affect the flame dynamics, the Shlieren imaging optics diagnostic technique is performed. The Schlieren imaging is an optical setup composed of two parabolic convergent mirrors (f=48’’), a punctual light source, a razor blade and the Nikon D90 camera as the focal plane. The Z-type optical setup is used due to space limitations. The principle of Schlieren imaging is that the light rays reﬂected by the ﬁrst mirror can be considered parallel because the light source is placed at its focal distance. If nothing is placed between the mirror, the light continues its path through the system and the image projected on the camera sensor is blank. However, if a change in density, which implies a change of refraction index, occurs between the two mirrors, then the ray light will not arrive parallel in the second mirror. These rays will then either be blocked by the razor blade and appear darker or pass above the razor blade and appear brighter.
Schlieren imaging is efﬁcient when it comes to observing density changes and will be employed to validate the simulation. The changes in the ﬂame shape are more remarkable on the 19 𝑐𝑚/𝑠 ﬂame in comparison to the lower flow rate. The Schlieren imaging also shows that the thermal plume is wider for the higher flow rate. As the electric field strength increases for the positive field, the ﬂame is concentrated and pulled upward to the mesh and the thermal plume is narrower. For the negative field configuration, the flame is pushed toward the burner and becomes wider; the thermal plume would be widened instead. When the saturation plateau is reached at around 1. 6 𝑘𝑉/𝑐𝑚, the ﬂame shape doesn’t change signiﬁcantly, nor does the thermal plume as the electric field strength increases. The electric ﬁeld can affect the soot production (orange region of the ﬂame), which can be a great potential for application as soot production can indicate a more efﬁcient combustion.
[Ed. Note: Per the Principal Investigator (PI), the investigation gathered images of negative field and positive field with fuel dilution at 70% and 40%. These images resemble the fuel dilution conditions from the 0g experiments, and further analysis is underway.]
Comparison Between Simulation and Experiments
An initial comparison of the Schlieren imaging and the density profile from the PeleLMeX computation, specifically for flame widths for both flame velocities, are conducted. The result is computed from the reduced mechanism (Di Renzo 2022) under gravitational conditions, which was tested in microgravity. We understand that the comparison is qualitative as each image is normalized relative to its maximum intensity. A detailed Schlieren imaging is needed as well as a higher acquisition rate, for capturing the images between electric field charges can help further understand flame temperature and fully authenticate the chemical mechanism including more positive, negative ions and excited species from the PeleLMeX. The work is currently being carried out on a local high performance computing cluster, but there are limited hours available for that system so additional computational resources will be explored. Further results appear in the publications identified in that section of this report.
Preliminary Outcome for 0g Implementation with More Species – PeleLMeX
To bridge the gap between simulation outcomes and empirical data, this part of the work is to evaluate potential mechanism candidates: (A) 30 species and 86 reaction using Coffee mechanism as foundation (1993) by Pederson and C. Brown; (B) 26 species and 134 reactions but only 4 ionic species using GRI Mech 3.0 by Renzo et al.; and (C) the recently published 45 species and 216 reactions using San Diego reduced mechanism, by López-Cámara et al. This task is to implement the recently published reduced San Diego mechanism in microgravity. These mechanisms are chosen for their comprehensive coverage of ionic and exited species within the flame, compared to the mechanism currently used by Di Renzo et al. which is not able to capture the ion current behavior in microgravity condition as part of work from the previous fiscal year.
The main difference lies in the (C) reduced San Diego mechanism chemical model, which includes 11 charged species, including H3O+, HCO+, C2H3O+, CH5O+, O2−, OH−, e−, CO3−, CHO2−, O−, and CHO3− (in comparison to the previous used (B) H3O+, HCO+, O2− and e−) and included excited species CH and OH. This mechanism includes many species, and as the electric field is introduced, the calculation became extensive and the computation time increased substantially. With various tests and approaches for launching the mechanism at various stages, the simulation remains computing with extended calculation time, unresolved and/or unstable with inconsistent results. The heat release from the calculation can be massive at a single cell and that can lead to a relatively large local flow, and/or the chemical solver may fail to sort through the reaction and lead to confusion. Further tests on the mechanism, particularly on sorting through how the solver processes each step in the calculation, as well as how the mechanism works with a relatively newer version of the simulation, are needed.
Conclusions
The modeling work is progressing with the newer version of PeleLMeX using the reduced mechanism (with four ions, electron, and no excited species) in gravitational environment. The experiments with diluents are completed, and the ion current data and the Schlieren imaging are verified using ISS conditions. Locally with PeleLM non-subcycling version, the code has also continued to be exercised under different coflow flame conditions with different levels of fuel dilution with carbon dioxide and different pressures to demonstrate the validity from the previous work with water addition of the boundary condition implementation. Challenges remain for how to implement a relatively large San Diego based mechanism including more ions and charged species into the newer version of PeleLMeX. Continuing work on this project focuses more heavily on the computations with detailed assessment of the ion current prediction and the role the chemical mechanism plays in that prediction.
