Task Description:
In order to achieve the project objectives, there are two principal thrusts to the research. One focuses on the electrically controlled flame system, where experiments are conducted in an Earth based laboratory enabling a wide range of non-intrusive diagnostics on flames in various g-loading conditions including that equivalent to microgravity. Diagnostics such as schlieren, shadowgraph, deflection imaging, are applied to visualize a burning methane-air flame under the influence of electrically induced microbuoyancy. Numerical simulations predict the forces involved and allow new designs for enhanced flame control.
For the ion wind driven burner and extinguisher systems, it is necessary to understand the limitations of ion winds. For example, it is to be determined whether or not the airflow can be accelerated with the addition of a nozzle and/or if the blowers are staged. From the results, an ionic air swirler is to be designed where a vortex is formed within a tube containing air at STP with adequate strength to hold a flame. The vortical flow can also be applied to a fan-less electrostatic precipitator capable of enhanced particle removal efficiency by combining electrostatic and centrifugal forces on the particles entrained into the system. This project explores the use of electric fields for a wide variety of space exploration applications, primarily those involving combustion. The specific objectives of the study include: 1) Experimentally determine the extent to which electric fields can simulate a variable gravity condition (e.g., Mars gravity, moon gravity, zero gravity) for flames in an Earth-based laboratory so as to study phenomena that will be important in these space and planetary environments. 2) Examine the fundamentals of ion wind interactions with flames and their effects on flame behavior in order to understand the practicality of controlling flames electrically. 3) Determine active control methods to attain and maintain effective g-loadings on flames by ion wind actuation and quantify the extent of this action; such a method can be demonstrated by removing g-jitter from combustion experiments in parabolic flights. 4) Construct a dual-electrostatic burner (i.e., no moving parts) in which a flame is sustained and oxygenated by an air swirl generated from an ion wind and liquid fuel is delivered via wick or electrostatic atomization. 5) Optimize ion wind generation for space-based combustion applications and investigate concepts for maximizing flow. 6) Use ion winds to enhance the performance of electrostatic precipitators. 7) Evaluate the potential for hand-held electrosprays to extinguish fires in a variety of gravity-levels. Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, a technology that not has application in advanced propulsion and power systems, but also toward fire safety in space and on other planets. Appropriately applied fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our facility provides a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of temperature, species concentration, flow patterns, and ion currents.
One goal central to NASA’s mission is to improve spacecraft and remote habitat fire safety for travel and off-world activities. The ion wind and electrospray work is expected to reveal new and improved ways to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires. In addition, advances in small-scale combustion systems capable of providing compact power can be developed without moving parts.

Task Progress:
Taking the specific objectives in turn, the following progress has been achieved over the first year of the project --
• Experimentally determine the extent to which electric fields can simulate a variable gravity condition – A new experimental apparatus was constructed that isolates a small capillary flame from random air currents in the laboratory. The experiment allows full optical access to allow schlieren, chemiluminescence, and other spectroscopic measurements. Using methane fuel, one important finding was the natural instability of the balance condition (the situation where the flame buoyancy and the downward ion wind force cancels). The instability is intermittent and does not appear in the temperature profiles, but is clearly visible in schlieren movies. The instability does not occur for even modest effective gravity conditions. In addition, ion current measurements show that for the simple capillary configuration, the point of force balance occurs at a point when the flame’s ion production is saturated. This coincidence is independent of the spacing between the capillary and the ground pland and is independent of the flow rate of methane (in the low flow rate range examined). This result is interesting, because it must represent a feature of the specific geometry we are using. A flat flame would not behave in this manner. In addition to the methane results, the behavior of several different fuels was examined. The response of the flame followed expectations in that the higher the number of carbons in the fuel, the larger the ion wind force (for a given field). This result is consistent with past findings. In addition, however, we found that the electric field had a profound influence of soot formation, particularly for acetylene flames. It was possible in some circumstances to create a spherical shell of soot within the acetylene flame near the balance condition. Further examination of this phenomenon is underway.
• Examine the fundamentals of ion wind interactions with flames – We have begun constructing a comprehensive CFD model of the capillary flame in an electric field using FEMLAB. So far, we have simulated the flame as a constant potential surface that is also a source of ions. We then can predict the path of the ions. The simulations show that there is a limited region over which the ions can extend before they are dragged to the ground electrode. This region coincides very closely to the region we have found through experiment to be the location of a shear layer separating an outer buoyant plume and the fairly stagnant inner balance region. Eventually, we expect a dynamic model that will allow us to simulate the instantaneous response of the flow field to a step change in potential. This will then help identify the sources of the system characteristic times.
• Determine active control methods – No specific progress on this objective yet, though we have the equipment ready to implement any control scheme developed.
• Construct a dual-electrostatic burner – We have examined the performance of wicks, liquid flow dispersion on rough surfaces, and we have separately examined the generation of ion winds (discussed further below).
• Optimize ion wind generation – A substantial effort has been made in determining the dominant features of an ion wind generator based on a corona ion source. The basic configuration is a needle to a ring electric field. The highly charged needle produces ions that are swept toward the ring by the electric field. These ions then produce a wind by dragging along the neutral air molecules. We have found several geometrical sensitivities in this system, including the distance of the needle to the ring, the width of the ring, the accuracy with which the needle is centered, and the overall obstructions to the flow. We have also discovered that staging needle-tube ion wind generators (i.e., stacking them in series) does not produce ever-higher flow rates. There is a limiting flowrate, which indicates that the ion wind process creates an aerodynamic loss, much as does a pipe corner or valve. We are in the process of measuring this loss coefficient and confirming that it follows a typical minor-loss fluid model. We have further found that it is possible to increase the flow velocity of the ion wind by stacking generators in series and then putting a nozzle at the exit. This then creates sufficient pressure to drive the acceleration through the nozzle but keeps the flow through the ion wind stages low enough that the losses do not remove the advantages. We have studied from 1-10 stages and will be publishing results of these studies very soon.
• Use ion winds to enhance the performance of electrostatic precipitators – We have studied the use of a swirling flow generated by ion winds for improving the performance of electrostatic precipitation, particularly in the size range that would fall between straight electrostatic precipitators and straight cyclone separators. That is, submicron particles are relatively easy to remove electrostatically, and particles larger than 10 microns are relatively easy to separate inertially. Between these limits, removal of particles is difficult and so we examine a combined electrostatic/cyclonic system based on ion winds. The main wind through the precipitator is created by a needle ring ion wind generator. The ions both create the wind and attach to particles. The second, or swirling stage, of the precipitator consists of a cylindrical core electrode with a series of needles jutting out. These needles also produce ions that attach to particles and create a swirling ion wind (the centrifugal component). Talc powder, a controllable and safe source of fine particles (5-100µm), was used to replicate particles found in dusty rooms. It was entrained into the air stream of the precipitator by placing powder onto a vibrating tray placed just below the entrance of the precipitator. The precipitator was run until talc powder accumulated onto the clear acetate walls of the device and the pattern of accumulation was then analyzed qualitatively. The areas very near to the earth rods are lacking in medium to small particles when compared to the areas away from the rods. Otherwise, the distribution of medium and small particles is fairly even over the acetate sheet. There is a slight gradation when moving towards the top of the precipitator, where fewer small to medium particles are found. However, this gradation is more exaggerated for the large particles, so it is difficult to spot large particles higher up the precipitator. It was possible to run the precipitator so that no visible particles escaped the device. As expected, it was necessary to raise the electric field in both stages together to prevent particles from escaping. This is because the higher the linear wind flow through the system (i.e., the shorter the residence time), the stronger the centrifugal component needs to be. The amount of talc lost from the powder tray was compared to the amount collected by the precipitator. The efficiency of the precipitator was effectively 100%. It remains to be determined if this performance is more effective than standard blower designs, but the fact that it has no moving parts and that it is all electric, makes it an attractive possibility for space application.
• Evaluate the potential for hand-held electrosprays to extinguish fires – We have not yet examined this feature of the project. We are, however, looking at electrosprays of biologically active materials to see if they remain viable after processing. This is a cross-over application the application of thin films for topical medical purposes can be accomplished.

Task Description:
Our joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving the performance of energy conversion systems. The utility of electric fields on flames can be divided in two discrete categories: sensing and actuating. As an actuator, relatively high electric fields have been shown to affect flame stability and soot formation; while as a sensing device, the electrical response, even at small electric fields, can detect the presence of a flame as well as provide characteristic information about the combustion process. In the past year, we have continued electric field testing experimentally, with special focus on a coflowing burner, both, in zero and 1g, and numerically, modeling flame structure and the influence of an electric field. These studies directly support the tests proposed for the ISS experiment. In addition, fundamental studies involving partially-admixed and quenched jet flames are directed toward understanding air quality issues involving domestic boilers and stoves. Specific activities over the year included:
1.) Irvine/NASA Glenn testing - Measuring the flame’s electrical response and voltage-current characteristic under various conditions, and reduced gravity testing at the NASA Glenn 2.2-s Drop Tower.
2.) Working to develop a new sensor concept aimed at detecting the onset of quenching and pollutant release in domestic boilers by measuring the contours of first detectable ion current, which when interrupted can warn of incomplete combustion.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Several of the applications we explore have potential uses in earth gravity. Understanding fundamental electrical properties of flames have contributions to earth-based combustion, particularly as regards soot formation and control. Ion current is also a very useful diagnostic tool and sensor for combustion, capable of reflecting flame character and behavior for next generation power generation systems such as homogeneous charge compression ignition engines. There is also the potential to electrically sense and correct off-design combustion that releases toxic carbon monoxide during quenching. Finally, there are important potential applications in combustion synthesis of nanoparticles where ion formation pathways are important.

Task Progress:
Experimental Testing/Development:
UCI Coflow Burner Setup
Experimental work was completed using a coflow burner. The burner consists of two stainless steel plenums threaded together. Fuel is mixed, if desired, with nitrogen in the bottom plenum and passed through a stainless steel tube (2.13 mm ID). The flow at the exit is fully developed. Air is introduced in the top chamber, passing through beads and a honeycomb mesh to create a uniform flow at the exit. A variable high potential supply creates an electric field between the burner and a mesh electrode downstream. Field strength between the electrodes is not linear due to the flame’s space charge; however, the applied field strength can be defined approximately as E = V/d, where V is the applied potential and d is the distance between electrodes. This approximation is used in describing the experiments to provide a consistent reference to field strength. Ion current is computed using Ohm’s law and the measured potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground. The experimental apparatus is housed in an acrylic chamber, which shields the flame from room currents.
NASA Glenn Coflow Burner Setup
At the NASA Glenn Research Center, the burner apparatus includes a cylindrical test chamber, flow system, and data acquisition/control system built into a NASA 2.2 sec. Drop Tower rig. The coflowing burner is placed coaxially inside the test chamber and the stainless-steel fuel tube is coaxially positioned inside a converging nozzle through which air flows. Metering the upstream pressure of a critical flow orifice controls the jet flow rate. A hot-wire ignites the fuel immediately after the drop is initiated. A rotary solenoid briefly positions the igniter near the burner during ignition and away from it otherwise. To provide a uniform flow, two layers of honeycomb, two stainless steel mesh screens atop the honeycomb, and two additional honeycomb layers are placed at the base of the nozzle.
UCI Irvine Coflow Burner Results
The ion current response of a flame to an electric field shows three distinct regions: subsaturation – where the ion current response is parabolic with applied voltage, a saturation region – where the ion current plateaus and remains constant with increasing electric field, and an enhanced ionization regime – where the ion current increases beyond values predicted from a diffusion flame. As a diagnostic tool, the saturation ion current has been directly related to the carbon flux in non-premixed flames (Boothman et al., 1969). When the flame is at the saturation point, ion recombination is effectively halted, and the saturation ion current can be related to the ion production rate in the flame. In addition to the ion motion that results from an electric field, there is also a neutral ion-driven wind. The wind is the phenomenon where chemi-ions accelerated by an external electric field successively collide with the closely packed neutral gas molecules, thereby transferring their acquired kinetic energy to the bulk. The process is much like dragging a screen mesh through a stationary gas, with the gas behind the screen acquiring a velocity that is lower than that of the screen. This neutral wind can modify the local flame structure and influence ion production, which have been able to explain electric field effects identified in the literature.
Recently, we have started using CH* chemiluminescence to measure changes in flame structure. This is an important measurement to consider in the context of electrical properties of flames because the primary radical-radical reactions that give rise to chemi-ions involve CH:
CH + O --> CHO(+) + e-
CH* + O --> CHO(+) + e-
The change in CH* luminosity with applied field illustrates a bi-directional coupling between these two quantities: where the electrical body force can modify the flame structure, and this change in flame structure affects ion production, which determines the strength of the body force. Exhibited clearly in µg, this relationship makes it difficult to measure ion concentrations in a diffusion flame without the influence of an electric field. By increasing the electric field, both the ion current and CH* luminosity show a gradual increase and eventual plateau in their values. When considering the similarity between the two curves and the initial chemi-ionization reactions, which involve excited state CH radicals, it is plausible that a relationship exists between both values. This relationship, between CH* luminosity and ion current, occurs at the saturation condition and is consistent over a number of conditions. The saturation condition is a characteristic of premixed flames, much like the laminar burning velocity. It is important to recognize that it is only the saturation ion current that can be considered representative of a mixture, which is consistent with the luminosity finding. After calibrating the PMT, it should be possible to determine the ratio of CH* radicals that eventually produce H3O+ ions, as well as identifying what factors influence the ratio. A calibration of the CH* emission was accomplished by Walsh et al., 2005, in determining the absolute CH* concentration (as compared to that of unexcited CH). That work discussed the calibration method but did not include any ion current measurements. Additional tests would help determine whether CH* emission, not complicated by soot radiation, can indicate ion concentration without an applied field and may help design electrodes that directly act on these regions.
Enhanced Ionization: Positive Field
Regardless of polarity, the ion current response exhibits an enhanced ionization regime during which the ion current continues to increase beyond saturation levels. Initial measured suggested that a positive electric field accelerated the main flow, which entrained additional air through the quench zone, partially premixing the flame. Numerical simulations by Yamashita et al. [2009] that show the additional increase in ion current corresponding with an increase in the local oxygen concentration near the flame sheet support this assumption. This prediction is also consistent with work published by Weinberg and Carleton [2009], which showed that the saturation ion current of diffusion flames is fairly insensitive to aeration until reaching the rich flammability limit where the ion current shows a sharp increase.
This numerical observation was explored experimentally by raising the fuel jet above the honeycomb mesh and measuring the laser-induced fluorescence from acetone vapor seeded in the coflowing air stream using a nitrogen carrier gas. Although the amount of acetone evaporated into each bubble would have exceeded the rich flammability limit for burning in air, nitrogen was used as a precaution. The additional nitrogen had a negligible influence on the coflowing gas composition (
Acetone’s relatively low thermal decomposition temperature made it difficult to visualize near the flame sheet. Because of this, and with the exception of highly lifted flames that rested on a pocket of air, measurements did not show air leakage through the quench zone of the flame sheet. Despite the inability to directly observe leakage, the images did show the influence of an accelerating ion plume and the subsequent entrainment downstream of the flame sheet. The non-monotonic response of the coflowing jet is particularly fascinating. By gradually increasing the field strength, hot products accelerating toward the downstream electrode entrain additional gas. This can be observed as the gradual decrease in fluorescence thickness with increasing height above the burner surface. However, at 5.7 kV, the PLIF response of the coflowing gas begins to widen near the base. This same voltage also corresponds to the start of the enhanced ionization regime in ion current measurements. The coincidence between the start of the enhanced ionization regime and a change in the local flow field hints to an effect at the burner base that contributes to ion production yet counteracts the effects of the ion wind.
To isolate the source of this anomalous effect, it is necessary to study ion formation mechanisms outside of hydrocarbon combustion. Additional mechanisms that are relevant to this experiment included the burner geometry and material, the applied field strength, and local temperatures. Without a flame, a flush jet and a raised jet configuration show negligible changes in ion current with electric field. Although the system appears insensitive to geometry, it must also be considered in combination with temperature. By substituting methane with hydrogen in the same two burner geometries, and because hydrogen is non-ionizing, the effect of a heat source at the same location can be tested without the contribution of combustion ions. The Voltage-Current Characteristic (VCC) curves for a CH4/air mixture in the 1g coflow burner for a number of electrode separations, the separation between the electrodes can modify the slope and onset of this enhanced ionization region when the field is directed toward the burner. Methane flame studies at NASA Glenn
In a 1g environment, the plume of hot gases from a flame naturally induces, through mass continuity, a convective flow to the neighboring cooler environment. This natural convection gives rise to a flame’s egg-like shape in Earth gravity. In microgravity environments, buoyant convection, which is mainly responsible for the transport of fresh oxidizer to a flame, is removed and the flame is mainly driven by molecular diffusion and forced convection [Ross, 2001]. A number of experiments have studied the influence of an electric field in microgravity environments to measure ion mobility [Yuan and Hegde, 2003], burning rate [Yamashita et al., 2008], and the feasibility of inducing convection in the absence of gravity [Carleton and Weinberg, 1987]. This section describes new experiments involving a jet flame under the influence of an electric field in 1g and µg using the NASA 2.2-s Drop Tower to identify the role buoyancy-driven convection and ion wind-driven convection play in controlling flame shape.
By aligning an applied electric field with the main flow of the jet in a µg environment, the resulting ion wind drives away combustion products, much like buoyancy, while entraining additional air to the reaction zone. Images extracted from videos show steady flames taken under different gravity and voltage conditions, with the exception of the µg flame without an applied field. Without an electric field or forced convection, a µg flame requires a longer settling time than is available on the drop tower and the flame continues to expand over the drop duration. Without external influences, a low initial momentum µg flame takes on a near spherical shape owing to the lack of a preferential transport direction of products. This is in sharp contrast to a 1g environment where buoyancy is a dominating force and can overwhelm the electric field influence.
The relative contribution of gravity, forced convection, and electric field to flame area and location were compared. The flame was idealized as an oblate spheroid to calculate area and was compared to a 1g flame without an electric field or coflow as a reference. Images were taken from drop videos when the flame appeared stable. Images show a small impact of an electric field on flame area and location in 1g, while in microgravity there is a clear similarity between the impact of the electric field and forced convection on a flame’s shape and area. Results show that a flame in µg with a 0.6 kV/cm average applied electric field or a coflow velocity of 24 cm/s will produce a flame with a similar area and flame base location as an unforced 1g flame. In addition to area calculations, similarity was also measured by taking the absolute difference between a microgravity image and a 1g reference flame and computing the RMS of the entire differenced image. When used for image comparison, the RMS metric is a quadratic mean that assumes that a reference image is known, which in this case is the 1g flame, while the µg flame is a distorted version of this reference. A low computed RMS value corresponds to strong similarity between images. Both the images and computed RMS values show the closest match to be between the microgravity flame with -5 kV (1 kV/cm) applied and a 1g flame without an applied field. Carleton et al. [1998] observed in their research that similar field strengths were necessary to simulate microgravity in an Earth based laboratory environment. Differences in soot luminosity were not evaluated because of pixel saturation; however, future work will include the use of a filter to normalize the color channels, improving comparisons. Understanding the differences between the two comparison techniques as well as the potential to infer similarity from Schlieren images will continue to be explored.
Quenching studies
The research underway at Imperial College examines the effects of quenching on flame structure and understanding the hazardous conditions created by poorly tuned industrial boilers. In our studies, appreciable concentrations of carbon monoxide appear within the flame cone, particularly for burners with a spatial scale of the order of a diffusion flame thickness, which raised concerns regarding the potential hazard that if by partially quenching the flame, dangerous levels of CO were released into the ambient atmosphere.
Initially the burner was a copper tube, with a 4 mm internal and 6 mm external diameter (since gas heaters in boilers often consist just of multiple apertures in metal tubes, thick – walled, small diameter burners were quite appropriate for the planned quenching measurements). Previous experimental results, as well as those obtained by numerical simulation, imply that, while no CO would emerge into the atmosphere if the flame reaction proceeded to completion normally, CO escape might pose a serious hazard if quenched before completion - particularly if that occurred close to the peak of CO concentration arrested the reaction. During 1999-2004, CO poisoning caused 16,447 deaths in the United States; the principal cause being incomplete combustion in malfunctioning heaters/boilers.
Current measurements were plotted against electrode separation for a flame burning 82.75 ml/min natural gas on a sharp-edged burner with a 4 mm inner diameter. The burner is one electrode, and gauzes previously used for quenching measurements are the other. The two metals, stainless steel and aluminium, were chosen for their different equilibrium temperatures and quenching characteristics (see previous work; also Weinberg et al., Combustion and Flame 158 (2011) 273). The voltage of 38.7 V is delivered by four nominally "9 V" batteries in series. The graphs show the effect, for both polarities, of lowering the gauzes, starting from the product gases at a height well above both, the luminosity of the flame and any CO release by quenching.
While the apparatus is very simple, the electrical structure is quite complex. The reaction zone is the source of all electrical charges. The field strength, and hence the current, increases as the distance between the electrodes decreases. The local current density is j = K± E e n±
where K is the charge carrier mobility and E, e, n, represent electric field vector, fundamental charge, and number density respectively. The sign in the suffix denotes the polarities over which j is summed – (see e. g. Lawton and Weinberg (1969) "Electrical Aspects of Combustion," Clarendon Press, Oxford)
In the absence of soot particles (which we tried to avoid because of their very low mobilities) there are two types of charge carriers: electrons and ions. Electrons have a mobility at least two orders of magnitude greater than ions and hence carry most of the current. All positive charges are ions; negative charges are electrons initially, though they can attach to form negative ions, particularly if they travel through cold gas for more than a very few millimetres.
The other regions are the hot inert product gases above the reaction zone in which no charge is generated and the two narrow regions which are cooled by the burner rim and the quenching gauze. Neither of the two grids appear to emit electrons thermionically.
Starting with the gauzes at over 30 mm above the burner and lowering them to the top of the reaction zone at around 17 mm above the burner, with the burner negative, electrons traversing the hot products from the reaction zone encounter little resistance and the current rises. With the burner positive, however, the resistance to positive ions is too great for the current to flow and the system acts as a rectifier. This ceases to be the case once the gauze contacts the reaction zone. Below this position the current rises steeply and continuously.
For our first objective above, it is sufficient to note that the electrical detection of proximity to the flame of a quenching surface should be based on a positively charged burner to utilize the further electron penetration. The results show that as a ''quench detector" with the burner +ve, the current signals the approach to a quenching surface at a height which is more than about 2 mm in excess of that at which any quenching is ever recorded.
In practice, of course, quenching may occur by surfaces not directly above the flame. To explore the loci of electrical quenching detection, a rod with a rounded end was used as the negative electrode. It was clamped in the x-y-z positioner and approached the flame orthogonally at locations around its periphery. The contours of the first detection of a current for two potentials (37.6 V and 60 V) lie well outside the regions in which quenching had previously been measured. These results show clearly that detecting electrically the proximity to the flame of quenching surfaces, to give a warning before any carbon monoxide is released, is feasible. It can be achieved using only small batteries and could readily be developed into a system which would give warning of hazardous conditions arising from, for example, an unexpected elongation of the flame due to an obstruction in the feed.
Numerical Simulations
Recently, we have started exploring the effect of electric fields on combustion using OpenFOAM, an open source software package. The strong coupling between the chemistry, flow field, and electric field, combined with the difficulty in directly probing the flame due to field interference makes numerical simulations a potentially valuable resource to consider. OpenFOAM (Open Field Operation and Manipulation) is a collection of partial differential solver libraries, written in C++ that can be easily adapted to a number of interesting problems, including combustion. Our model implements the use of reactingFoam, which is an explicit turbulent reacting flow solver that we have adopted for laminar simulations and have included electric fields interactions in the fluid flow. To solve this deeply coupled problem, Poisson's equation must be solved for the electric potential distribution with the influence of space charge, the Navier-Stokes equation includes an additional term to account for the electric body force on the neutral gas by the colliding ions, and the species transport equation includes the effects of ion drift velocity on the distribution of charged species. The problem is solved with a 2D axisymmetric domain modeled in a coflowing geometry with a 2.1 mm inner jet and a 25.4 mm outer jet (matching the geometry of the experimental apparatus). The downstream boundary, which also serves as the mesh electrode, is 5 cm from the base of the burner. No radiation model is implemented. Numerical simulations were performed using GRI-Mech Version 3.0 with nitrogen species neglected for the neutral mechanism and additional chemistry by Prager, et al. (2007) and Walsh, et al. (1998), which include charged species and CH* radical chemistry. Species diffusion is computed using a mixture averaged relationship proposed by Mitchell (1979). The simulation assumes a unity Schmidt number and a 0.7 Prandtl number, which is a sufficient assumption for initial simulation. Future work will include the effects of mixture-averaged transport properties. Predicted temperatures are higher than expected, which can be attributed to the lack of a radiation heat loss model. Flame heights are larger than experimentally observed heights and predictions by Roper. Nevertheless, the results predict a peak in ion formation at a reaction kernel located at the base of the flame. This location coincides with peak heat release and CH concentration, which are consistent predictors of ion production. Identifying that ion production can be localized to specific regions, sheds light on the ionization process and will aid in creating simplified models to describe ion/flame interactions. This result also lends insight in understanding why the majority of the observed effects (e.g. flame stabilization and oscillations), with the exception of highly sooting flames where flame tip deformation is observed, are localized at the flame base.

Task Description:
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving the performance of energy conversion systems. Electric fields have been shown to affect flame stability and soot formation; while as a sensing device, the flames electrical response can describe flame characteristics. In the past year, we have continued electric field testing on a coflow burner and jet diffusion burner for both methane and ethylene, which are proposed for the ISS experiment along with fundamental studies involving partially-admixed air/fuel jet flames. Specific activities over the year included:
1) Participating in the Requirements Definition Review to finalize requirements for our experiment and assure they are within CIR capabilities.
2) Irvine/NASA Glenn testing included, measuring the flame’s electrical response and voltage-current characteristic under various conditions, and reduced gravity testing at the NASA Glenn 2.2-s Drop Tower.
3) Experiments and numerical simulations of CO, H2, and ion formation in flames with varying levels of aeration.
4) Experiments designed to measure the ion current of a flame as it is progressively quenched.
5) Blackbody calibration of cameras for ground-based studies and development of algorithms to process color-filtered images from hardware expected for the ISS experiment for soot pyrometry.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Several of the applications we explore have potential uses in earth gravity. Understanding fundamental electrical properties of flames have contributions to earth-based combustion, particularly as regards soot formation and control. Ion current is also a very useful diagnostic tool and sensor for combustion, capable of reflecting flame character and behavior for next generation power generation systems such as homogeneous charge compression ignition engines. Finally, there are important potential applications in combustion synthesis of nanoparticles where ion formation pathways are important.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2011
Task Progress:
UCI Coflow Burner -- Experimental work was completed using a coflow burner. The burner consists of two stainless steel plenums threaded together. Fuel is mixed, if desired, with nitrogen in the bottom plenum and passed through a stainless steel tube (2.13 mm ID). The flow at the exit is fully developed. Air is introduced in the top chamber, passing through beads, and a honeycomb mesh to create a uniform flow at the exit. A variable high potential supply creates an electric field between the burner and mesh electrode. Field strength between the electrodes is not linear due to the flame’s space charge; however, the field can be approximated as E = V/d, where V is the applied potential and d is the distance between electrodes. This approximation is used in describing the experiments. Ion current is computed using Ohm’s law and the measured potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground. An acrylic chamber protects the burner from room currents. The measurement circuitry includes provisions to protect the data acquisition hardware from accidental discharges: damping resistors, diodes, and an isolation amplifier.
NASA Glenn Coflow Burner -- At the NASA Glenn Research Center, the burner apparatus includes a cylindrical test chamber, flow system, and data acquisition/control system built into a NASA 2.2 sec. Drop Tower rig. The coflowing burner is placed coaxially inside the test chamber. A stainless-steel fuel tube is coaxially positioned inside a Pyrex converging nozzle, through which air flows. Gas flow rates were measured by mass flow meters. To dampen out spurious fluctuations, present only in microgravity environments, a flow orifice was placed downstream of the mass flow meters. Recently, the mass flow meters were found responsible for the fluctuations and subsequently replaced with a critical flow orifice as the rig’s sole monitoring device. A hot-wire igniter is used to ignite the fuel. To provide a uniform flow, two layers of honeycomb plates, two stainless steel mesh screens atop the honeycomb, and two additional honeycomb plates are placed in the base of the nozzle. The burner does not have a honeycomb mesh in contact with the fuel tube at the jet exit, creating a deformed field converging toward the jet tube in contrast to the quasi-parallel electric field lines around the base of the jet when a honeycomb is present. This, however, is a minor issue when considering the electrical nature of the flame, which deforms the electric field lines due to the flame’s space charge.
Methane flame studies at NASA Glenn -- Experiments at the NASA 2.2 Second Drop Tower are aimed at removing gravity’s influence on a flame under the influence of an electric field. The similar influence of buoyant convection and the ion-driven wind make it difficult to decouple the effects in a 1g environment. The results will help isolate the relevant physics of a buoyant free, electrically manipulated flame and facilitate tailoring the test matrix for the ISS mission. By removing the influence of large coflow velocities and buoyancy, videos and ion current measurements can show the complex interaction between ionization, flame shape, and ion-driven wind. In a µg environment, flames take on a spherical shape owing to the lack of a preferential transport direction of hot products (buoyancy). When a field is applied, the resulting ion wind drives away combustion products, much like buoyancy, and entrains air to the reaction zone. Under field between -0.6 and -1kV/cm, the flame will mimic the structure of a 1g flame. Along with images of the flame, ion current measurements were taken both in 1g and µg environments. Regardless of gravity level both V-I curves have similar features. The ion current exhibits minor differences when changing gravity levels with an upward directed field (negative applied potential); however, by changing polarity in µg, the flame is quenched on the burner jet, weakening the flame and the ion current. Once an electric field is applied to a flame, the flame’s settling time, is dependent on the apparent gravity field acting on the flame. In a 1g environment, the flame takes on an egg shape, resulting from the buoyant acceleration of hot products from the reaction zone. Any additional velocity resulting from the ion wind creates a small change in the flame promptly (~10ms). In a µg environment, buoyancy is not a factor leaving the ion wind as the flame’s only external influence. The experimental results show the transition between two applied voltages (-1kV to -2kV). With a net upward wind, fresh oxidizer is brought to the reaction zone, increasing the reaction rate and the ion current, further increasing the ion wind strength. The ion current reaches a maximum at 600ms, after which the ion current begins to decrease as a result of the increase in soot. Soot is an electron emitter and has been shown to interfere with ion current measurements. Recently, efforts have included a study to remove the contribution of soot radiation in chemiluminescent CH* measurements, a precursor species to ion formation.
Partial aeration studies -- Our Imperial College collaborative activity is examining the effects of partial aeration on the structure of flames and its relation to saturation ion current, CO and H2 formation, and understanding the hazardous conditions created by poorly tuned industrial boilers. Results in the literature showed that saturation ion current would scale with the amount of carbon present in a diffusion flame; however, when flames are fully premixed, saturation ion current is a function of temperature. Between these established regimes, there exists a region largely unexplored, where air is premixed in concentrations below the rich flammability limit. In our studies, appreciable concentrations of carbon monoxide appear within the flame cone, particularly for burners with a spatial scale of the order of a diffusion flame thickness, which raised concerns regarding the potential hazard that if by partially quenching the flame, dangerous levels of CO were released into the ambient atmosphere. Hence, the object of the current study was to investigate, both experimentally and by numerical simulation, the formation and spatial distribution of CO and H2 under the aerated small flame conditions relevant to burners in domestic boiler systems and then to determine the effect of various quenching surfaces on CO escape into the surroundings.
The burner system is a simple fuel jet. The fuel flow rate was fixed for each series and a progressively increasing proportion of air was admixed. The appearance and shape of the flames does not vary appreciably, in spite of the substantial increase in total flow velocity. This is in accord with classical diffusion flame theory, which predicts that these quantities depend on the volumetric flow rate of fuel alone, even in the presence of other gases. This applies until the mixture becomes flammable. Once the air admixture crosses the 85% boundary (all concentrations are expressed as % by volume), an inner cone forms, gradually detaches and shrinks, reaching a minimum around the stoichiometric composition and then grows again.
Sampling was carried out at a grid of points across an axial plane by means of a quartz microprobe. Since visual observation and flame photographs showed the flame base to overhang the burner by several millimetres, sampling was extended to the edge of flame luminosity. The aspirated gas was analysed for its CO and H2 content by carbon monoxide and hydrogen detectors, respectively. A traverse across the burner diameter using a chromel-alumel (K-type) thermocouple with a 30 mm diameter wire was carried out at a height of 2 mm above the burner rim, as a function of air admixture (and hence flow velocity).
Quenching -- The main sequence of measurements was obtained using an apparatus comprised of a flame trap matrix above the burner mouth. The flame trap matrix was wound, using alternately plane and corrugated stainless steel strips, into a cylindrical plug. To vary the quenching surface, grids of different metals could be placed immediately upstream of the plug. Using this system, the average CO emitted by an uncooled burner is around 2.6ml/min. When other quenching surfaces were interposed ahead of the matrix, the expanded aluminium laminate led to the largest CO emissions once again. Results included values in excess of 3 ml/min, even for a flame with no air addition. At 75% air this rises to 4 ml/min. The highest CO emission rate measured was about 4ml/min. This is close to 10% of the CH4 fed into the burner and clearly poses a potentially serious hazard. Expressing this in terms of the maximum carbon monoxide release for a practical boiler yields about 0.177 L/min/kW. For the 30kW recommended for a 1 bedroom flat this would exceed 5 litres per minute.
Numerical simulation -- Numerical simulations were performed using GRI-Mech Version 3.0 and the chemical kinetics program, CRESLAF, included in the CHEMKIN package, to predict gas-phase temperatures, velocities and concentrations. The model reduces the Navier-Stokes equations by making a boundary-layer assumption that a principal flow direction exists, where convection is the primary transport mechanism and diffusion is neglected axially (radial diffusion is retained). After discretizing the relevant equations, the solver, DASSL, marches axially by minimizing the formulated residual at every grid point at a given height, before moving downstream.
Although there have been many significant numerical simulation studies of small coflow diffusion flames, having to provide insight for the specific geometry, air admixing conditions, and quenching experiments of our study demanded that we develop customized simulations to match our experimental conditions. Using the same inlet velocities as in the experiment, we produced concentration profiles analogous to experimentally measured values. Results show that although regions of maximum CO concentrations are near the flame centerline; the maxima in CO flux are shifted towards regions of larger radius, as shown clearly in the figure. We were unable to simulate the quenching effects of the flame trap matrix; however, summing the differential volume flux at a given height above the burner would represent the amount of CO released, were the downstream kinetics frozen. Scaling the volume flow rate to 300K shows trends comparable to our experimental results, with the maximum CO flux occurring at 4mm.
The numerical simulations resemble the experimental results. The CO concentration for 75% air again exceeds that for pure fuel, though the difference is greater in the simulation than in the experiment; also the peak in the core of a vortex around the axis in the former case is not reproduced. The contour appears more mushroom shaped - though a single point could transform it from one to the other geometry. We attribute the difference to the assumption of a parabolic flow profile in the simulation, as against the flow pattern above the thick - walled burner port. Preliminary experimental studies using the cork borer burner at higher flow velocities show a highly arched biconvex contour, rather than a closed vortex.
Electrical Properties of Quenched Flames -- In addition to our efforts at Imperial College, parallel studies are underway at UC Irvine, studying the electrical properties of partially quenched flames. Our work at Imperial College has illuminated the potential dangers of improperly turned boilers and the high concentration of carbon monoxide and hydrogen potentially emitted when quenched. This portion of our research is aimed at understanding the electrical behavior of a plate incrementally lowered toward a flame and measuring the corresponding ion current. The study is a proof of concept to explore the potential of detecting flame impingement electrically without visual inspection. Preliminary studies involve plates of varying metals placed above an axisymmetric jet flame with a small potential difference between the two surfaces (~3V). Ion current is measured after a few minutes to ensure thermal equilibrium. Significant amplification is necessary due to the small voltages applied. As the plate is lowered toward the flame there is a gradual increase in ion current, an increase is attributed to the increase in electric field strength. Ion current sharply increases at distances below 3 cm, finally saturating the A/D module of the data acquisition hardware at 1cm above the jet exit, at which point, the flame sheet is interrupted by the quenching plate. From this point the burner acts as a low resistance pathway between both electrodes allowing current to flow freely. Further lowering the plate toward the jet exit, the ion current decreases as the flame temperature and ion production falls. The next phase of this work will involve actively cooling the plate and emissions sampling.

Task Description:
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London, with support from researchers at NASA Glenn Research Center, explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving performance of combustion-based energy conversion systems. Electric fields have been shown to affect flame stability and soot formation; using the flames electrical response as a sensor, it is also possible to describe flame character. Recently, the project has focused on continued electric field testing on a coflow burner for both methane and ethylene, which is proposed as a potential ACME spaceflight experimental platform, and fundamental studies involving partially premixing air in the fuel stream of a jet flame. Current studies include:
1) High resolution voltage-current characteristics under steady DC-fields and the dynamic response of flames to such fields. Testing includes, measuring the flame’s electrical response and voltage-current characteristic under various fuel and air co-flow conditions, including testing at reduced gravity using NASA Glenn 2.2-s Drop Tower.
2) Experiments and numerical studies of CO and H2 concentrations in flames with varying levels of aeration.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Several of the applications we explore have potential uses in earth gravity. Understanding fundamental electrical properties of flames have contributions to earth-based combustion, particularly as regards soot formation and control. Ion current is also a very useful diagnostic tool and sensor for combustion, capable of reflecting flame character and behavior for next generation power generation systems such as homogeneous charge compression ignition engines. Finally, there are important potential applications in combustion synthesis of nanoparticles where ion formation pathways are important.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2010
Task Progress:
Experimental work was accomplished using a coflow burner. The burner consists of two stainless steel plenums threaded together. Fuel is mixed, if desired, with nitrogen in the bottom plenum and passed through a stainless steel tube (2.13 mm ID). The flow at the exit is fully developed. Air is introduced in the top chamber, passing through beads, and a honeycomb mesh to create a uniform flow at the exit. A variable high potential supply creates an electric field between the burner and mesh electrode. Field strength between the electrodes is not linear due to the flame’s space charge; however, the field can be approximated as E = V/d, where V is the applied potential and d is the distance between electrodes. The above approximation is used in describing the relative field strength used for different experiments. Ion current is determined using Ohm’s law and the potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground.
An interesting and new finding this year was that some voltages lead to an oscillating flame. The term “oscillation” is used as opposed to flicker because of the wide behavioral range of motion. Tip and bulk flickering, are described as the flame top oscillating or elongating periodically; and the flame separating from the top of the main body, respectively. Depending on conditions, ion current oscillations due to a static field can involve the movement of the entire flame body or no movement at all. As an example, the transient ion current for a CH4 flame (23.2 mg/min) in a coflow, at an applied field of -2.15 kV/cm, shows a ~43Hz oscillation. The ion current fluctuation is not obvious in the flame luminosity, shape or position. Initial PMT measurements are able to capture the fluctuations, which match in frequency the ion current fluctuation, albeit with a small phase lag (~5ms). The period of the peak oscillation is ˜23ms. The response time of the flame is ~100ms, assuming a 1cm reaction zone and a burned gas density that is 15% of ambient. The time scale suggests that ion current oscillations are too fast to cause a noticeable movement or disruption of the flame.
Ethylene studies -- Soot is known to be charged and will influence ion current measurements. Ethylene is used because of its simple structure and high sooting propensity. A unique ion current response is observed with ethylene as the fuel source. Luminous soot in the flame is strongly affected by the applied field. At a flow rate of 35.4 cc/min C2H4, electric fields destabilize the flame with the oscillation of luminous soot dominating the flame’s movement. Near saturation, the flame begins to oscillate at ~23Hz. Higher applied fields distort the flame shape, although not affecting the frequency, resulting in heavy soot deposits on the honeycomb annulus. Nitrogen dilution of the fuel muted the flame distortion. Images show a gradual reduction of luminous soot with applied field. The most interesting finding is in the absolute ion current measurements for an ethylene flame with varies levels of nitrogen dilution. The measured ion current per unit carbon increases with nitrogen dilution. Premixing ethylene with nitrogen reduces combustion temperatures and the amount of luminous soot. The high thermal ionization potential of soot, due to its low work function, complicate ion current measurements by introducing additional electron emitters. The role of ions in soot formation is an unresolved question; however, soot extinction measurements would aid the in the understanding of how an electric field affects soot luminosity.
Partially premixed studies – Professor Felix Weinberg at Imperial College is currently studying the effects of partial aeration on the structure of flames. Previous work involved CO and H2 sampling by means of a quartz microprobe mounted on an x-y-z translation stage for regions bounded by the I. D. of the burner mouth. The data showed large concentrations of CO and H2 inside the flame boundary. As the flame base overhangs that diameter to a substantial extent, sampling was extended to larger radii. CO concentrations for 75% air admixture as contour lines at 0.5% intervals were measured. The maximum at the core of the torus is 5.5 volume %. Similar structures are seen in CHEMKIN simulations.
A surprising result was the appearance of CO in flames in the absence of air admixture. Moreover, some of it appeared well within the burner mouth. The implication is that we never have a pure diffusion flame and we suspected air entrainment, possibly due to convection currents occasioned by the elevated burner temperature (> 300oC) to be the cause. To ascertain the extent of penetration below the plane of the burner mouth, it was necessary to replace the normally horizontal sampling capillary by a vertical probe. Comparing CO and H2 percentages measured on the burner axis with different probes orientations show measurable concentrations of CO and H2 occur at least 1mm and 3mm, respectively, below the plane of the burner mouth. This is for the extreme case of no aeration. The penetration decreases with increasing air addition – and hence flow velocity - until at 75% air there is no CO below the rim and H2 at 1mm below is reduced to one tenth of the value compared to the pure fuel case. Whilst the results close to the burner mouth and well above it are very similar for the two orientations, the maxima are somewhat greater and displaced upward in the case of the vertical probe.
CO contour maps suggest that no CO would emerge into the atmosphere if the flame reaction proceeded to completion normally. However, if the reaction was arrested by quenching before completion, (particularly, if occurring close to the peak of CO concentration) the consequent CO escape might pose a serious hazard. In order to examine this possibility, we compared CO volumetric flow rates of a cooled and uncooled burner for 75% air addition; they show similar results, albeit somewhat displaced with respect to each other. The average CO emitted is around 2.6ml/min. That appears close to the maximum attainable, in that the curves suggest a fall in CO, had it been possible to lower the quenching surface further without extinguishing the flame. The highest CO emission rate measured is about 4ml/min. This is close to 10% of the CH4 fed into the burner and clearly poses a potentially serious hazard, as will be apparent if the CH4 feed is expressed in terms kilowatts for a practical boiler.
We continue to evaluate the potential CO emission and how electric fields can be used to mitigate these releases.

Task Description:
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving performance of energy conversion systems. The project this year focused mainly on preparation for a scheduled spaceflight experiment as well as a requirements review later on this year. Current studies included:
1) Design of a new experimental configuration based on the recommendations of the Science Concept Review (SCR) panel. A substantial portion of development time focused on developing an automated data acquisition scheme so that potential obstacles in automated data acquisition in space could be anticipated.
2) Continued numerical simulations of flame dynamics under the influence of electric fields. The modelling has been expanded to include combustion kinetics.
3) Additional developments in how flame saturation current changes as a function of air dilution into the fuel stream and whether this change can be used to characterize combustion performance.
