Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
Taking the three specific objective topics in turn, the following progress has been achieved over the past year of the project.
Developing a new experimental platform - Along with improving the experimental setup (e.g., we transitioned from using Real Time Windows Workshop, The Mathworks Inc. to the Data Acquisition toolbox package in Matlab), characterization studies proposed for the spaceflight were performed to create a quantitative database of testing conditions. Along with fundamental characterization studies (e.g. VCC curves, step response), we have begun exploring the effect of electric fields on promoting stability of near limit and lifted flames (Science Data End Product D). Calculations on the flow rate required to achieve a lifted flame with the jet diffusion burner showed that an alternative combustion platform was necessary. The CLD Flames group from Yale University (also part of the ACME project) has developed an over-ventilated laminar diffusion flame, which under flow conditions comparable to those planned for the jet diffusion flame are capable of creating a lifted flame. This additional burner configuration allows us to understand the behavior of electric fields over a greater set of flow/flame conditions while taking advantage of the experimental and modeling database available for the coflow burner. We obtained plans for the burner from the CLD Flames group, had the burner constructed, and have begun testing. From the Science Concept Review in March, it was recommended that focus for the spaceflight experiment include this coflow burner. The burner and relevant circuitry for the experiment have been designed, fabricated, and tested.
Baseline testing has revealed interesting and substantial differences between the Voltage-Current Characteristic (VCC) curves of the coflow and the inverted jet flames. With an electric field directed downstream, the behavior of both the jet diffusion and the laminar co-flowing flames initially show similar characteristics. Both burners display a sub-saturation region, where the measured current increases parabolically with electric potential. At a given field strength, which is a function of flow conditions, a saturation region is observed where the rate of ion formation is equal to the current collected. At greater field strengths, the behaviors of the two burner types diverge. The measured saturation current of the co-flow flame is constant while the gas jet flame exhibits a region of enhanced ion formation. The measured saturation current for the co-flowing flame without co-flowing air at 100% CH¬4 is 70% the saturation current of the jet diffusion flame at the same flow rate but is only slightly larger than a co-flowing flame with 50% CH4. These results show that the change in geometry causes a reduction in the collected current and removes the super-saturation region. The increased saturation current for the 50% CH4 case with co-flowing air may be the result of the triple flame structure of the co-flowing flame, where a portion of the flame is a lean premixed flame. VCC curves of both burners with various levels of nitrogen dilution can be compared. The jet-diffusion flame has a consistent sub-saturation region regardless of dilution levels; the only difference in the curves is when saturation is achieved. Under the same conditions with a co-flow annulus, the VCC curves of the over-ventilated burner have different slopes but, for the conditions tested, the flames reach saturation at the roughly the same applied potential (~3.6kV), independent of liftoff height. These results present interesting questions regarding the potential effects of geometry. Due to the capillary exit placed flush with the honeycomb annulus, flame instability prevented testing at more than one condition without co-flowing air, making it not possible to isolate the effects of geometry. As a rough confirmation to determine if the capillary flush with the flow straightening honeycomb prevented blowoff, additional tests show that with the capillary raised approximately 25 mm above the flow straightening mesh, the flame could be extinguished by the ion-driven wind. A pure methane flame under increased field strength shows that at -8 kV the flame is oscillating violently, and further increases in field result in flame extinguishment. It is also worth noting that with an increased applied potential; there is a notable reduction in luminous soot
The literature has reported that ion wind effects of a flame when under the influence of applied DC potential are negligible and do not contribute significantly to flame reattachment. However, the conclusions presented in the papers do not include critical measurements of the ion current to understand the contribution, if any, of an ion-driven wind. Experiments on a lifted flame under a DC potential in our laboratory showed a significant reduction in liftoff height. In addition to a study of DC effects on flame liftoff, measurements have also been taken on a lifted flame under an oscillating field.
A significant amount of hysteresis can be observed when a flame is placed under an oscillating field. The maximum ion current observed is also dependent on the forcing frequency. A plot of voltage and the resulting ion current vs. time. The measured current leads the applied voltage, a behavior expected in a capacitor. This behavior, which comes from the capacitance in the electrode mesh not the flame, has been reported in previous work and its presence was compensated for in a closed loop control algorithm created for the jet diffusion burner (F. Borgatelli and D. Dunn-Rankin). Schlieren images of the co-flowing flame with oscillating potentials show that a possible reason for the observed improvement in reattachment is the enhanced mixing caused by the oscillating field creating a fluctuating ion wind.
Numerical Simulation of Small Flames in Electric Fields – Previous numerical simulations have simplified the problem to include static flame shapes with constant properties (e.g. ion number density and flame temperature). These simulations accurately captured experimental measurements of temperature gradients and ion profiles at the grounded mesh for a neutrally buoyant flame. Additional simulations included non-spherical flame shapes to understand the effect of flame shape on the ion flux profile while keeping properties constant (there was little sensitivity to flame shape since the ion field is dominated near the flame by space charge repulsion). Recent developments have been directed toward understanding the mechanism behind the ion current saturation and super-saturation observed in experimental measurements. To further elucidate the complex behavior observed in the flame, a model has been developed by a visiting post-doctoral scholar allowing us to couple combustion kinetics with CFD calculations using PHOENICS/CHEMKIN to simulate the geometry of the jet diffusion flame. Understanding the combustion of methane in the presence of electric fields provides a greater understanding of how ion production is affected by various burner geometries and flow conditions. Focus has been placed initially on the inverted jet diffusion flame due to its broad experimental base with electrical fields, which will allow easy verification of the models performance with our prior measurements.
Simulations on a 2D axisymmetric model of the flame in a downward configuration were run. The flame is created by introducing into an inverted capillary 40 mg/min of methane without dilution. A hot spot of 2000K is placed in the path of the traveling fuel in order to begin the reaction. Using a previously published kinetic mechanism (J. Hu, B. Rivin, and E. Sher, Experimental Thermal and Fluid Science, 21:124–133, 2000), which assumes oxonium (previously called hydronium) ion to be the dominant charged species, simulations were run looking at spatial variations of combustion products under an electric field.
Example results from these calculations include the methane concentration, the ion concentration, the temperature profile of the inverted methane jet for different field conditions, and the flow field for the zero field condition. The temperature surface profiles show that heat is drawn downward as field strength increases as expected from laboratory-based experiments. These results show that although charged species make up a small portion of the total fluid number density, the energy imparted by the electric field, the ion wind effect is an important fluid flow mechanism opposing buoyancy driven natural convection. The most significant results to date from the model are that the simulation can capture the ion current increase with voltage seen in the experiments remarkably well. The absolute value of ion current is in excess by a factor of 2, but the behavior is identical, with the onset of saturation predicted very closely and the super-saturation condition is also seen. We have not yet identified from the model the reason for super-saturation, but it is not due to an absolute increase in ion concentration. Rather, it appears that the ion concentration remains constant while the voltage increases, producing a higher ion flux and higher ion currents. The ability of the flame to continue to source ions at higher field conditions is the reason for super-saturation, and we suspect that this is due to a partial premixing behind the flame sheet by the downward ion wind. The same cannot occur in the co-flow flame because the mesh prevents outside air from breaking into the fuel side of the flame. Naturally, much more work is needed to confirm this mixing hypothesis.
Characterizing Flames by their Saturation Currents – An important conclusion of the earlier phase was that it was certainly possible to distinguish between diffusion and premixed flames by their saturation current - so long as premixed flames were defined in terms of compositions lying between the flammability limits. In fact, one of the mysteries revealed by that work was that, for admixtures of less than 70%, air appears to act as an inert diluent. All the experiments were carried out using a 4mm capillary jet burner, this being the only diameter that could bridge the diffusion and premixed flame regimes. The chief objectives of the current experiments reported here were: 1) the measurement of chemiluminescence; especially CH* emission and 2) relating the total saturation currents, Js, to saturation current densities, js, in the premixed domain and, more generally, to determine fluxes (i.e. variables/time/area) of other relevant parameters. This requires knowledge of the flame area in addition to the flow rate. In the premixed domain, the flame area, A, can be related to the volume flow rate, Q, directly through the burning velocity, Su.
Three optical filters were used for the chemiluminescence measurements, transmitting at 405 nm, 430 nm, and 515 nm. Initially we attempted to photograph the flame through the CH* (430 nm) filter but there was barely enough luminosity even for the brightest of flames. We might revisit this with a better camera but, as far as we could tell, the geometry of our images did not differ substantially from the corresponding unfiltered luminous shapes. We found that collecting total CH* emission within a constant solid angle is equivalent to measuring total saturation current. In contradistinction to the case of saturation currents, there is no peak in the chemiluminiscence curves corresponding to the premixed regime (just possibly a very small one for C2). However, in interpreting the steady decrease in that region, it should be borne in mind that the flame area rapidly decreases there. Since, at constant volumetric flow rate, the flame area shrinks in inverse proportion to the burning velocity, which reaches a maximum just rich stoichiometric, the CH* emission per unit flame area may, in fact, increase.
For a given reactant composition, temperature and pressure, each premixed flame is characterized by an approximately constant structure orthogonally to its entire area. This is not true of diffusion flames since there is increasing dilution by products in ascending the flame. It could be said that fluxes such as saturation current densities, js, are meaningful only for premixed flames and, conversely, that diffusion flames can be characterized only by the total saturation currents, Js, for a given volumetric flow rate. Therefore, the intermediate region of particular current interest - that rich of stoichiometric composition - presents something of a problem. In the previous report, it was said of this region that, while there is an inner cone visible in photographs at near stoichiometric compositions, there is no conspicuous difference in its appearance from that beyond this limit on the fuel-rich side. This statement had to be reviewed in attempting to measure flame areas. To avoid the tedium of numerical integration, a program that yields surface areas of rotation around a central axis from a contour line “SolidWorks”, a PC based program, was employed. In the case of diffusion flames, the reaction zone was deemed to coincide with the most luminous zone. For premixed flames, the relevant area may depend on the particular parameter investigated.
Burning velocities for premixed methane/air flames are well documented and provide a good starting point. The concept is without significance for diffusion flames, since these do not propagate; it is merely the volumetric flux of reactants. The relevant area for premixed flames is clearly the innermost contour, since the definition of burning velocity, Su, relates to cold unburned reactants. Thus, even the contour of the first onset of luminosity will yield too large an area - i.e. too low an Su value. There is obviously also a margin of uncertainty due to individual judgment as to where to draw the contour. This also applies to the judgment of where the regime changes from diffusion to premixed; i.e. where the transition from maximum luminosity to its first onset is deemed to occur. The other problem lies in the narrowness of the region of the premixed regime within which the burning velocity varies by a factor of about 20. There is virtually a discontinuity in gradient at the peak, so that the maximum value can only be guessed at. Literature values of maximum burning velocities of methane/air mixtures are of the order 35 cm/s (50% higher than our measured values) in the absence of stretch. However, our flames are small (so that average burning velocities will be disproportionately biased by burner rim quenching) and subject to stretch. The peak in ion concentration for an unperturbed flame (one in the absence of applied fields; i. e. in ionization - recombination equilibrium) has been located by probe measurements in premixed flames. It occurs in the main reaction zone. That may not, however, correspond to where the ions are generated. We have used same areas as in the burning velocity measurements, i.e. the centre of the luminous zone for diffusion flames and the first onset of luminosity for premixed flames. This was done partly for convenience but mainly because the resulting maximum saturation current densities still fell below the accurate measurements on flat premixed flames by Lawton and Weinberg. The fractional shortfall was similar to that for burning velocities and analogous arguments apply. The calculation involved tedious interpolations of the original Js curves (see last report), since individual measurements were carried out at different air percentages. Some error may have been incurred in this process, especially around the (somewhat indeterminate) maxima. For diffusion flames, as expected, Js is small and virtually constant at constant fuel flow rate; there may, in fact, be a slight dip as the percentage of air approaches the upper flammability limit. Beyond this point, there is a steep rise in the curve, the values around stoichiometric composition rising by an order of magnitude above those of the diffusion flames.
In determining the CH* per unit flame area, there is again the problematic choice of flame contour defining the area. According to Gaydon, the main reaction giving rise to CH is C2 + OH = CO + CH*. This is consistent with observations from the literature that, for premixed flames, the sequence of the spatial location of the peak intensities tends to be OH*, followed by C2* and then CH* from the unburnt-gas side and this observation is consistent over a range of equivalence ratios. For an ethylene/oxygen diffusion flame, Gaydon finds the same sequence on the fuel side followed by a much larger OH* peak near the maximum temperature. At 1 cm above the base of the Wolfhard - Parker burner, the CH peak is about 1 cm on the fuel side of the maximum temperature. Comparison with ion current measurements suggests that the decrease observed there is largely due to a decrease in flame area. However, the proportional increase in going from diffusion to premixed flames is nowhere near as large as for js and Su. It would be interesting to repeat the calculation for an area close to the contour of maximum luminosity.
Closer examination of the flame photographs suggests that a ring of brighter luminosity occurs within the flame contour. This starts above the burner rim and grows towards the flame apex as the percentage of air increases. Eventually it converges to a point on the axis. After the upper limit of flammability is crossed, this luminous zone detaches from the flame contour and forms an inner cone. If this progression represents the formation of a premixed flame from a pre-reaction zone, which is only stable due to heat and radical transport from the diffusion flame, it may explain why Js does not increase before the upper limit is reached. Pyrolysis due to the adjacent diffusion flame may produce syngas and neither the burning of carbon-monoxide nor that of hydrogen leads to appreciable chemi-ionization. We propose to try shadowgraphy and, if necessary, possibly other optical methods, to establish whether the existence of a premixed pre-reaction zone adjacent to the diffusion flame can be visualized. We plan to pursue parallel numerical simulation of this situation as well. We also propose to measure CH* (and perhaps C2*) emission across the entire range of fuel flow rates and various burner diameters to establish whether the unique dependence of ionization rates on the flux of carbon atoms is paralleled by chemiluminescence at these wavelengths.

Task Description:
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving performance of energy conversion systems. The project this year focused on electrical effects that can be explored effectively in extended microgravity conditions and on the effects on flame saturation current of oxidizer dilution in the fuel stream. The studies included: 1) Continued numerical simulation of ion pathlines and ion-driven winds from small diffusion flames now extended to non-spherical flame shapes 2) Design of a new experimental configuration and procedures consistent with experiments that can be conducted in an extended zero gravity environment 3) Evaluation of how the flame saturation current changes as a function of air dilution into the fuel stream and whether this change can be used to characterize combustion performance
Task Description: The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy. The actuation of the flame can be used as part of a feedback control loop to maintain flame performance despite external fluctuations.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
In order to examine the above listed opportunities, we focused this year on two principal thrusts of the research. One focus was on the electrically controlled flame system, where experiments are conducted on a small diffusion flame sandwiched between two electrodes. With preparations for a flight experiment, we adjusted the laboratory experiment to mimic the constraints expected and we enhanced the numerical simulation to include flame shapes we expect in the microgravity environment. The second focus was on how to use the electrical properties of a flame to identify to identify its combustion behavior.
Task Significance: Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Several of the applications we explore have potential uses in earth gravity as well as microgravity. For example, the application of ion winds for transport in miniature thermal systems can be valuable for heat transfer in small spaces. Understanding fundamental electrical properties of flames will also have contributions to earth-based combustion, particularly as regards soot formation and control, though the forces from electric fields will be less dramatic in the presence of natural convection.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
Taking the three specific objective topics in turn, the following progress has been achieved over the past reporting period of the project –
Numerical Simulation of Small Flames in Electric Fields – Previous simulations focused on a spherical flame shape, characteristic of a neutrally buoyant flame. This flame shape is representative of ground-based experiments when the applied potential is large enough to partially balance buoyant natural convection. In microgravity, this flame shape is the base from where additional conditions will be explored. Recent simulations reflect the expected experimental setup on the ISS. In the interest of creating a data set that is representative of the relevant boundary conditions of the system, an important parameter to quantify would be the temperature near the burner tip.
Simulations on a 2D axisymmetric model of the flame in a downward driven configuration were run. The flame is assumed to have constant 1400 K temperature, with a flame height/width ratio of 3:1. The upper mesh has been removed to match our current experimental embodiment and we have assumed that the ion concentration is independent of flame shape. Our experiment has been altered so that polarity is set relative to a grounded capillary (active mesh configuration) as opposed to a grounded mesh. Simulations have shown that by applying a large negative potential at the lower mesh relative to the capillary, the potential distribution local to the capillary and the resulting path lines are equivalent to our original configuration. The potential distribution is slightly altered in the far field due to the experimental enclosure being essentially at ground. This change would potentially aid in ion collection at the lower plane by effectively limiting the number of surfaces which the ions would be drawn to.
The results show that the outermost ion path lines for a downward driven flame are within a 3 cm radius about the capillary. The surface profile shows that heat is drawn downward as expected from our laboratory-based experiments. The ion wind effect is the dominant fluid flow mechanism as opposed to buoyancy driven natural convection. This is shown by the direction of the arrows. To quantify the collected ion current, total ion flux at the charged mesh is determined as a function of radial distance from the axis of symmetry. Taking the surface integral and scaling according to ion concentration and charge, results in a current of 0.28 microA, which is on the order of our experimental values. The ion current is approximately two-thirds that found in the spherical flame simulations. Future work planned for this aspect of the project includes taking schlieren images of the downward driven flame and recreating the dimensions in our model to further validate the simulation.
Conceptual Design of Flight Compatible Experiment – Design of the extended microgravity spaceflight experiment (now called E-FIELD — Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames) is a coordinated effort among NASA engineers and the research group at the University of California, Irvine. The experiment is currently in a preliminary design state, and is expecting a critical review early in 2008. The design aspects completed thus far include burner selection, conceptual drawings for an experimental configuration within the test chamber, electrical schematics for electric field generation and ion current measurement, an initial test matrix, and experimental requirements. The following is a brief discussion of each of these design aspects and the laboratory-based experiments performed to support some of the design decisions. The first E-FIELD burner proposed was a spherical, porous steel burner in order to limit the amount of time that ISS mission specialists would have to spend reconfiguring the experiment on-orbit. Several laboratory experiments were conducted to determine if the spherical burner was compatible with our spaceflight experimental objectives. These experiments showed that the ion-driven wind was not effective in substantially modifying combustion in this burner. Since observing flame shape changes in the high-voltage electric field was an important experimental objective, the proposed spaceflight experiment will employ the small gas jet flame used in the prior laboratory experiments.
Although the spherical burner will not be used in the E-FIELD experiment, the laboratory experiments were indirectly responsible for the development of the high-voltage protection circuit now implemented in the E-FIELD design. During one experiment, a high-voltage arc formed between the burner and the mesh due to breakdown in the air and the electrical pathway created by the mobile ions. This arc created a short circuit current that destroyed the data acquisition hardware used to measure the ion current. To prevent this from happening in the laboratory and spaceflight experiments, a Zener diode was placed in parallel with the sense resistor. This protection circuit tested successfully in all experimental configurations. In addition, it was determined that the Zener diode does not interfere with the ion current measurements so long as the cathode direction is flipped when altering the polarity of the high-voltage mesh.
The test matrix for the experiment design requires disclosure of fuel types, flow rates, instruments required, and the operational sequence for those instruments. One important experimental sequence for E-FIELD is capturing the voltage-current characteristic (VCC) curve for various fuels and mixtures. Several experiments were conducted to determine the requirements for sampling rate, sampling period, and number of voltage steps required to obtain the VCC curves. It was observed that longer sampling periods resulted in a higher current/volt ratio in the super-saturated region of the VCC curve. This is because the overall settling time for the flame exceeds the initial electrical response predicted in simulations and observed in previous step-response experiments (approximately 0.25 seconds or less). After the initial step-response settling, the ion current increases until it reaches a steady-state value. This slow timescale may be due to thermal interactions with the burner tip, which is allowed to cool when the flame is pulled away from the burner tip by the ion wind force at mesh potentials greater than 5 kV in the positive mesh polarity configuration, and 2 kV in the negative mesh polarity configuration. In order to capture the fully settled ion current value, the sampling rate must be longer than the flame settling time. The conclusion from the experiments was that the maximum ion current is obtained at 5-second sampling periods. Sampling periods greater than 5 seconds result in the same curve, and sampling periods below 5 seconds result in a smaller current/volt ratio in the super-saturated region. We expect less thermal interaction at zero gravity since the flame will not ever burn around the gas jet, but in order to conserve fuel on the spaceflight experiment, the number of data points must be taken at a resolution that still enables the saturation point to be identified.
Characterizing Flames by their Saturation Currents – Saturation current densities (js) for premixed flames of numerous hydrocarbons with air have been documented as functions of fuel-air ratio and the initial mixture temperature, as long ago as 1964 (J. Lawton and F.J. Weinberg, Proc. Roy. Soc. A.277, 468, 1964; see also "Electrical aspects of combustion" Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1969). However, the mixture compositions did not extend much beyond stoichiometric into the fuel-rich region because the accuracy of the flat-flame method used would have been compromised by sooting and by the formation of a secondary diffusion flame due to the burning of excess fuel. In these prior studies, the dependence on flame temperature could be represented by an activation energy - such that an increase of 100K in flame temperature would result in a 2 - 4 fold (depending on the hydrocarbon) increase in ionisation rate. At the other extreme, total saturation currents, Js, measured for pure diffusion of flames of hydrocarbons and including inert diluents are also available in the literature (e.g., D. Boothman, J. Lawton, S.J. Melinek and F.J. Weinberg, Proc. of The Combustion Institute, vol. 12, p. 969, 1969). These total saturation currents indicate an approximately constant yield of ions per carbon atom and, by contrast with premixed flames, are largely independent of temperature and diluents. “Diluents” here include hydrogen which, although it is a fuel, does not contribute to any ionisation. This relationship between carbon atom flux and ion current has been used as the basis for quantitative detectors, e.g., in gas flame ionization detectors (FID) for hydrocarbon analysis in combustion exhaust. In between the compositions described above there is an extensive unexplored range of fuel-rich mixtures extending from small additions of air to a fuel jet all the way to beyond the upper limit of flammability at about 85% of air.
In the experimental system, volumetric flow rates of fuel (Qf), which was natural gas throughout this study, and air (Qa) were metered by rotameters calibrated against bubble meters. The diameter of the outer tube is 25mm. The polarity of the burners was always negative with respect to ring electrode, to minimize wind effects by causing the low-mobility positive ions to travel the shorter path to the burner. Even though some of the electrons are likely to attach during their longer travel and become negative ions, the predominant ion wind was directed downwards (see below). Different burner diameters were used because each was restricted to a limited operability range in terms of flow rate and fuel/air ratio. In the time available, 1, 3 and 4 mm diameters were explored. The operability limits were due to: 1) sooting in the case of diffusion flames, at high flow-rates. The limit was set arbitrarily at luminous lengths of less than 10% of the total flame length; 2) blow off; 3) flashback for premixed flames; 4) excessive flame distortion by applied fields. An extreme case occurred for very fuel rich flames in large fields. Positively charged soot particles can be seen looping back to deposit on the burner and inducing a toroidal vortex in the flow; and 5) the absence of a saturation plateau at high flow rates when the rate of ion generation always exceeds the rate of the removal by the field.
A summary of these limitations are mapped; we find that for premixed flames - in particular compositions lean of stoichiometric - are attainable only for the larger burner diameters. The effect of preheating was also briefly investigated for the 1 mm diameter burner with a heating coil wound around its mouth.
The experimental results showed that there was no contribution to the current at any voltage (V) from “clean” burners. For soot-coated burners and for electrically heated burners, some field emission set in at high potentials - well beyond values at which saturation current measurements were completed. In many cases there was a very gradual increase in current beyond the initial plateau in the current/voltage relationship. Since this must be due to some modification of the flame by the field, no matter how small, the value of the saturation current was always taken at the onset of the plateaux. In the above-mentioned case of large currents - for premixed flames at large flow rates, dJ/dV never tended to zero and they were considered to be outside the tractable regime. The limits to this regime can be plotted on a fuel-flow vs. air-flow diagram so that loci of constant compositions are straight lines radiating from the origin, while total flow rate loci linearly join the corresponding values on each axis. We find that the locus of stoichiometric compositions is, to a good approximation, the line bisecting the angle between the two limits of flammability. Only flames stabilizable on the 4mm diameter burner penetrate into the fuel-lean domain. With the exception of the preheat case, all the results can be shown as saturation current plotted against total flow (Q) to emphasize the different ranges of the three burners. In this kind of mapping, however, the fuel air ratio, of course also varies; this is discussed in the next section. The peaks correspond to stoichiometric conditions. It was not feasible to plot a three-dimensional graph because of the large variations involved.
From previous work, outlined earlier, plotting (Js/Qf) (i.e., effectively the number of ion pairs per carbon atom) against the proportion of air added, should at least start as a horizontal line. According to prior studies in the literature the magnitude should be approximately 0.035 microA for methane, though some variations were seen in the experimental value, depending on the type of diffusion flame. This relationship would not be expected to extend into the premixed regime, in any case. For premixed conditions we can roughly estimate what would be expected from the previously mentioned accurate measurements of saturation current density, js, for flat un-stretched flames, since Js should equal A* js, where A is the area of the premixed flame. Since, according to the simple theory of premixed flames, the total volumetric flow rate, Q = A*Su , where Su is the normal burning velocity, we predict that Js =Q*js/Su. When all the total flow rate results are replotted in this format, it is immediately apparent that this is a rational basis for correlating the wide range of results. The larger burners give close to the predicted results at the few points where comparisons are possible. The 1mm burners tend to high values at the diffusion flame end, though it should be pointed out that a change in flow metering equipment was necessitated by the almost 10 fold change in the flow rate ranges. What seems surprising is that admixture of air to a pure fuel gas, even in amounts of up to 70%, appears to be no different in its effect on ionisation than dilution by an inert. It is not until the air content reaches the upper (fuel-rich) limit of flammability that there is a remarkable rise in charge per carbon atom. There is an inner cone visible at this composition, but there is no conspicuous difference in its appearance from that beyond this limit on the fuel-rich side. For the one set of results approaching the lower limit of flammability, the saturation current also falls below its diffusion flame value; the value is close to the prediction from our Js =Q*js/Su calculation. Another intriguing feature, which should provide a challenge for numerical simulation, is that all those burners capable of stabilising premixed flames appear to show a dip in Js/Qf near the rich limit of flammability, just before the rise.
Finally, there was time for just one set of measurements on the effect of raising the initial temperature to about 320C for the 1 mm burner. The result is exactly in accordance with the aforementioned principles: there is no discernible effect on the diffusion flame region of the graph which again extends to about 70% air admixture. Beyond that, however, it is now possible for the first time to reach into the premixed regime with a 1mm burner, with the concomitant rise in in Js/Qf.

Task Description:
NOTE this is a successor agreement to "Applications of Electric Fields in Microgravity Combustion Science (NNX07AB55A)," per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
This project at the University of California, Irvine explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving the performance of energy conversion systems. As an actuator, electric fields can affect flame stability and soot formation, while, as a sensing device, the electrical response at saturation is an inherent flame characteristic. In addition to preparing for the proposed ACME E-FIELD experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS), we have performed an evaluation of an experimental method of measuring ion number density in a flame using a Langmuir probe, studied the dynamic interaction between the flame and chemi-ions, analyzed the source of increased saturation ion currents found in I-V curves, used electric fields to control flames impinging on a surface, and begun to develop computational models to predict chemi-ion concentrations in flames. This report summarizes recent findings. Specific activities include:
1.) A study on the dynamic interaction between the flame and the electrical body force created by a flux of chem-ions. This was done in several ways, by analyzing the dynamic response of the gaseous flow field in response to a sudden application of an electric field, by comparing transient flame behavior using a high speed camera and the transient ion current collected when an electric field is turned on.
2.) A study of the interaction between the flame and the DC electric fields. This was done by studying the flame geometry to varies steady electric field strengths and analyzing I-V curves for different burner geometries.
3.) A study to construct a framework and approach for building computational models to predict ion concentrations in the flame, including the effects of ion driven winds. Different burner geometries were tested. Different ion chemistry models were used to test the current level of understanding of how ions are produced in the flames.
Summaries of these findings appear in this report with the details of all the work appearing in the publications and conference proceedings identified at the end of this document. Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The control of combustion has the potential to improve efficiency and reduce emissions from burning fuels. Since high power density often requires combustion, these improvements will be important no matter what the fuel source. Electric fields acting on flames have the potential to aid in combustion control. In addition, electrical properties of flames can identify poor performing boiler flames that release poisonous carbon monoxide. Our studies show that a flame's electric signature can capture incipient quenching before dangerous emissions result. Understanding the links between electrical character and flame behavior may allow improved sensing of poor performing combustion systems.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
Experimental Activities: All ground-based experiments described were performed using a coflow burner that is dimensionally similar to the proposed ISS coflow burner but with a fuel jet matching the dimension of the ISS jet burner. In many experiments, the center fuel jet was slighting extruded above the top surface of the coflow burner to more closely approximate a jet burner.
A variable high-tension power supply connected between the burner and downstream mesh electrode produces an applied electric field. Although the electric field distribution is deformed locally by the flame’s space charge, defining an applied field strength, E = V/H is a useful approximation when describing experimental results. Ion current is calculated using Ohm’s law and the measured potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground. An acrylic chamber shields the flame from room air currents.
External electric fields have long been known to modify the geometry of the flame. It has been demonstrated since the midpoint of the 20th century that flames may deflect in the direction of an electrode with a negative electrical bias. This study seeks to understand the flame geometry behavior of a non-premixed, conical shaped flame that is stabilized on a coflow burner. The central tube is extruded 3 mm above the coflow surface.
The electric field was initiated and the flame was given sufficient time to stabilize. Images were taken of the flame after the flame had reached its new electrically modified state. Flame images were taken under various electric field strengths. Abel inverted flames calculated from the images show the true contour of the chemiluminescence. Abel inverted flame contours were experimentally found under the influence of several electric field strengths. The general trend that was observed was that the flame height slightly decreases with an increasing applied field and the flame contour's radius also decreases with increasing field. It can also be seen that the general trend of brightness of the flame contour increases with increasing field strength.
The normalized maximum light intensity in the brightest portion of the flame was found as a function of field strength. It was noticed that an initial peak is found at 1 kV/cm. Following this peak, a decrease was found up till 2 kV/cm followed by a large increase. This trend has also been seen in the ion current measurement. Finally, it was also observed that the high electric fields produced lifted flames which likely create a tribrachial flame region near the base of the flame. What effect this may be having on the light emission of the flame and ion current measurements (or vice versa) is yet to be determined.
Current voltage curves (I-V curves) are used to characterize the strength of the electrical body force as a function of field strength. I-V curves can be used to determine what parameters create and control the electric field driven instabilities and secondary ionization mechanisms. This study also emphasizes the importance of taking ion current measurements when performing electric field combustion experiments. The purpose of this study is to determine a means of measuring the electrical body force through experimental parameters. Since the electrical body force is a result of not only an electric field but also a flux of flame ions, I-V curves may serve as a global indicator of the strength of the electric forcing. Typical I-V curves show that as the electric potential increases (from left to right) the ion current increases until a saturation point is reached. At saturation the ion current is balanced by the rate of ion production in the flame, therefore, no more ions can be extracted. Three burner configurations that were tested were a coflow burner, a coflow burner with the central fuel tube extruded 3 mm above the top of the coflow section, and a circular jet nozzle. The I-V curves were obtained by gradually increasing the electrode potential and holding each voltage for 2 seconds. In the coflow burner with an extruded fuel tube, the saturation current began to increase close to 1.5-2 kV/cm. For the jet nozzle, the saturation current appeared constant after saturation, however, large error bars appeared which indicated large deviations of the measured values from averaged values. This occurred because the jet flow/flame became unstable soon after the saturation.
The increase beyond saturation ion currents has been measured before but not well explained. Two hypotheses may explain the increase: (1) secondary ionization may be more prevalent due to large field strengths; electrical breakdown of the gas is unlikely due to the relatively low field strengths used in these experiments. However, local breakdown due to corona discharge may provide a source of secondary ionization. Another source of secondary ionization could come from thermi-ionization from the hot surfaces. (2) flame dynamics may also provide an explanation to the increase in saturation ion current; that is, a strong ion wind may provide the flame with an environment in favor of enhanced chemi-ionization reaction rates. The hydrogen flame test presents the case of no chemi-ionization reaction but with a hot burner/electrode. The results of this test were compared to the methane tests. With a hydrogen flame stabilized on a flat coflow burner, increases to the ion current measurements were not observed. This suggests that secondary ionization is not a factor in these experiments. However, an ion current is measured with the hydrogen flame stabilized on the coflow burner with an extruded central fuel tube above 3.5-4 kV/cm. However, It should be noted that the methane equivalent tests show an increase in saturation ion current much before these field strengths, and thus, it may be concluded that the increase in saturation ion currents are not initially affected by secondary ionization.
The deviation from the averaged methane ion current values shows an interesting correlation when compared to the hydrogen ion current measurements. In nearly all the data points the error bars are negligible because the ion current measurements were very stable under a steady DC electric field. However, above 3 kV/cm slight deviations from the averaged values were measured indicating a small instability in the ion current measurements. It was also observed that the methane flame became highly unstable and eventually became extinguished at 4 kV/cm. It was also observed that the ion current measurements from the hydrogen flame are occurring at these very high field strengths. The same observation, however more dramatic, was made in the jet burner I-V curves. These observations must suggest that the effects of ionization are not the source of increasing saturation ion current measurements but are the source in the flame/ion current instability. In order to understand more clearly these interactions, further experimentation is needed. However, the current hypothesis focuses around an ion wind affecting the flame/burner interaction. That is, the large ion winds that were seen to be lifting the flame in the last section could be reducing the heat transfer to the burner, thus allowing for higher chemi-ionization reactions to occur. Also, lifted flames are known to produce partially premixed edge flames near the flame base. Premixed flames have been known from the literature to produce higher ion concentrations than non-premixed flames. More studies will be performed in the future to better understand these results.
A schlieren system was built in the lab to study the dynamic flow effect of instantaneously switching on an electric field. At t=0, a negatively biased electric potential is applied to the downstream mesh electrode. The potential is reached within 1 ms after being triggered. When the high voltage electric potential is triggered and applied to the mesh electrode, a pinching like effect is observed in the schlieren column close to the fuel tube exit. The pinching effect propagates along the length of the schlieren column in a wave-like motion. The initial wave is followed by 1-2 more secondary waves that follow until the entire schlieren column re-stabilizes into a thinner column than prior to the external field. The entire process lasts approximately 100 ms for re-stabilization to be achieved.
This analysis was used to determine where the wave was in time. The same process was used but this time using more heights. This was done for multiple field strengths for a 3.5 cm electrode spacing and 27 sccm fuel flow rate. It should also be noted that no modification to the schlieren image or flame behavior could be observed with field strengths less that 0.6 kV/cm. This would imply that the ion flux is too small to produce a significant body force in the gas. A first order polynomial fit was used to determine the wave velocity. The velocities were plotted as a function of velocity. Because the velocity of this thermal wave is related closely to the convection of the gas, it is implied that the velocity of the gas downstream of the flame could be accelerated by an order of magnitude by high external fields. It was also seen from that comparing a 1.1 kV/cm to a 2.7 kV/cm field strength an ion current increased from 1.7 to 2 µA and subsequently produced an increase in thermal wave velocity from 373 to 700 cm/s. That is, a 17\% increase above the saturation ion current produced a 90% in the thermal wave velocity. One thing that could explain this is the increase in field strength. Future studies will take a closer look at local current densities within the electrode gap to understand better the distribution of migrating charges at various field strengths.
Numerical Simulation Activities: The aim of this study is to better understand, through numerical simulations, the effects of chemi-ionization and electric fields on a non-premixed coflow flame that impinges on a metallic plate; this configuration is very useful in order to investigate both how electric fields can be used to reduce carbon monoxide emissions and how they affect the heat flux on a solid surface. In order to analyze how chemi-ionization and electric fields influence the fluid dynamics and the chemistry of a flame in this configuration, numerical simulations have been performed using OpenFOAM. The validation of the numerical model has been performed by comparing numerical results to experimental results; these comparisons show that, taking into account some simplifying assumptions (e.g., axialsymmetric geometry, absence of radiation heat losses, unitary Lewis and Schmidt number) introduced in the model, results agree well with literature findings.
Study Case 1-- The reduced ions mechanism used in the study of the non-premixed coflow flame that impinges on a metallic plate was developed using the simplest reduction concept of combining what looked to be the most important ion reactions with the most important related neutral molecule reactions in combustion. It is a mechanism that has not been validated in other systems so it represents more of an exploration of the level of computation that might be feasible for the entire electrically activated flame system. The plate itself acts as the negative electrode, while the burner is the positive electrode. A negative potential and a zero potential will be assigned to the plate and to the exit area of the burner respectively. The effects of the self-induced electric field can be summarized in this way: (a) the peak temperature leads to a 5% overestimation of the experimental results; (b) the electric potential (and subsequently the electric field) is established only in the flame zone, because it is only here that charges are created; (c) the bulk velocity is slightly increased (with respect to the case when the Poisson’s equation is not modeled in the solver) by the inclusion of the charged species in creating an electric field; (d) the mass fraction of CH3 increases, and this reflects in an increase of the mass fraction of CH; this enhances the chemi-ionization process, subsequently the mass fraction of key ions also increase. This happens because now the solver takes into account the charge accumulation in the flame zone; this means that the weak self-induced electric field facilitates the charge generation in the flames zone. And the charges created here tend to move away from each other only because of self-repulsion, since no electric field has been applied on the plate.
The preliminary simulations performed in the current study showed to have good comparison with experiments and very good predictions of the behavior of impinging flames in general. The results also show good agreement with peak temperatures (error estimation under 10%), and the temperature profiles are very similar to those obtained with the schlieren technique. In addition, the mass fraction of important species like CO and OH match qualitatively and quantitatively; and the mass fractions of charged species also match either with those expected from literature and with those obtained from other numerical simulations.
Study Case 2 -- In a second case, chemiluminescence of the flame is also taken into account. Excited species are important as an indicator for many flame properties including reaction zone position. It would be valuable, therefore, to add reactions involved with important excited species, such as excited hydroxyl, OH*, and methylidyne, CH*. At the moment, there is no published model for non-premixed co-flow methane/air flames that contains both chemi-ions and excited species. For this case, a new mechanism that combines the mechanisms from two known chemical mechanisms from the literature (1 methane-air neutral chemical mechanism and the other a Chemilumenscence mechanism) and a selection of reactions from GRI-Mech 3.0 that were important for the formation and consumption of ions and excited species is used in OpenFoam simulations without the metallic plate placed above the burner. Excited species were taken into account due to chemiluminescence of OH* and CH* excited radicals.
Hence, a new compact chemical kinetic mechanism of 73 reactions and 33 species (neutral molecules, chemi-ions, electrons, and excited species) is used for the study of the non-premixed burner configuration without metallic plate placed above the burner. In the simulation for the burner configuration without a metallic plate placed above the burner, the same user-defined solver used for the Study Case 1 was used; as for the Study Case 1, a zero potential has been set on the plate and the burner walls. A summary of the conclusions are described below: (a) it has been demonstrated that the zones with high concentration of OH (> 0.0017) coincide with the zones where OH* appears; (b) Results for CH and CH* tend to do the same but in this case, in some regions such as the top of the flame where there is less concentration of CH, there is still a considerable amount of CH*. Further research has to be done to predict better results for CH and CH* to match with the experimental ones; (c) zones with high concentration of HCO+ in the flame have low concentration of CH. Because there is a strong link between CH and CH*, also a high concentration of HCO+ would mean a low concentration of CH*, and vice versa. On the other hand, some other variable is needed to explain the relation between CH* and HCO+. That variable may be the oxygen concentration, which is also important for the chemo-ionization reaction; (d) generally, the highest concentration of H3O+ will be in the regions where the concentration of HCO+ is lower. However, because the reaction of production of H3O+ requires 4 times more energy of activation than the reaction for the production of HCO+, we might expect some regions with high concentration of HCO+ and also high concentration of H3O+; (e) H3O+ is transported far away. HCO+ is produced but is very short lived and reacts very quickly into H3O+. H3O+ has a much longer life time which explains how it is able to travel further outside the flame and have much higher concentrations than other ions.
Study Case 3 -- In order to delve deeper into the chemical reactions that could be giving rise to the results found in the CFD simulation of the small diffusion flame, and in order to separate effects that could be due to transport and mixing, the 1-D counter-flow configuration in CHEMKIN® was employed.
Two reaction mechanisms, GRI-Mech 3.0 v.2 and GRI-Mech 3.0 v.3., are compared. Both are based on the GRI-Mech 3.0 for the neutral species, including the reactions for the excited species. However, the GRI-Mech 3.0 v.3. also includes a well-known ion model from the literature. These were compared to the new mechanism (NC Model) described in Study Case 2.
For the main neutral species and temperature profiles, the results between the three versions of the GRI-Mech 3.0 produced no variation. Hence, the results for neutral species and temperature profile for the GRI-Mech 3.0 are compared with the results for the NC Model.
The temperature profiles reveal a maximum difference of less than 3%. Also, the peak of temperature (2000K and 2040K for GRI-Mech 3.0 and NC Model, respectively) is located at the same axial distance (0.755 m and 0.769 m for GRI-Mech 3.0 and NC Model, respectively), again with less than 3% difference. The neutral species profiles shapes are similar in both cases.
The temperature profiles for all models are similar and the location of the peak of maximum concentration of CH the same for all models studied. However, the NC Model shows concentrations of CH that are 4 orders of magnitude below the ones predicted by the GRI-Mech 3.0 models, and the NC Model shows an increase of the concentration of CH radical as soon as the temperature rises, while the increment of CH concentration begins 0.2 mm before the peak of maximum temperature.
Similar to the CH, the peak of maximum concentration of CH* is located at the same axial location for all reaction models studied. However, the width of the peak is slightly different. For the NC Model, the CH* mole fraction rises around 6.4 mm of axial distance while for the GRI-Mech 3.0 based models it is at 6.6 mm.
For the main ionic species, H3O+ and HCO+, a comparison was also made. In this case, the only mechanism based on the GRI-Mech 3.0 that contains ionic species is the v.3. of the model. The hydronium ion profiles present significant differences depending on the reaction model used. Concentrations of hydronium ion using the NC Model are two orders of magnitude below the ones obtained using GRI-Mech 3.0 v3. Even though the peak of maximum hydronium concentration for both cases is around 6.65 mm (axial distance), the concentration of H3O+ increases sharply for the GRI-Mech 3.0 v3 around 6.65 mm while it increases gradually for the NC Model since at axial distance of 4.25 mm.
The formyl cation profiles show fewer differences between mechanisms. The concentration of this ion for the NC Model presents a larger width than the one for the GRI-Mech 3.0. v.3. However, the peak of maximum concentration is located at the same axial distance for both mechanisms.
In all cases, the species profiles have larger widths for the NC model compared to the GRI-Mech 3.0. v.3. It is readily shown that that the difference between widths increases along the chemical pathway from CH to HCO+ to H3O+ . This is most likely due to errors that are generated during the prediction of CH that propagate down this chemical pathway into the prediction of chemi-ions. Further work is needed to determine the source of these errors. However, it seems that the C2H and O species are closely related with these differences due to the fact that they are the precursors of CH.
Study Case 4 -- The experience described above suggests that it will be difficult to couple the small concentration ions with the overall flow field in a numerical simulation. To have a better chance at accomplishing this coupling, we are exploring a highly adaptive mesh refinement approach pioneered at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL). The code under development at LBNL uses BoxLib, a software library containing the functionalities (written either in C++ and Fortran90) required to perform adaptive mesh refinement (AMR); the basic idea of this technique is that the governing equations can be solved, at each time step, on a multilevel grid: at each level, the mesh is refined only where it is needed (typically where high gradients occur), and the solution is recomputed only in these zones. This allows to refine the solution without having to recompute it on the entire domain, which saves time and computational costs. BoxLib can solve problems with simple geometry (i.e., boxes), in 2D and 3D, and in either Cartesian and cylindrical coordinates; it supports hybrid MPI and OpenMP parallel programming.
Results were obtained with the existing LMC code for a premixed and diffusion flame respectively; in both cases, it can be noticed that the different levels of refinement are located primarily close to the flame zone. The temperature profile for a premixed flame obtained with the existing 1D code was found without the AMR.
The current study is focused on understanding the effects of an electric field on hydrocarbon flames; to take into account these effects, the Poisson’s Equation has to be added to the set of conservation equations (mass, momentum, energy, and species) already implemented in the low Mach number combustion (LMC) code. The first case under development consists in modifying an existing 1D code, which works for the case of unitary Lewis number and without AMR; this is the simplest case scenario. Once this code will be ready, the next steps will be: include the AMR into the 1D code (including non unitary Le), and then modify the 2D code.
