Task Description:
NOTE this is a successor agreement to "Applications of Electric Fields in Microgravity Combustion Science (NNX07AB55A)," per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving the performance of energy conversion systems. As an actuator, electric fields can affect flame stability and soot formation; while as a sensing device, the electrical response at saturation is a flame characteristic. In addition to preparing for the proposed ACME E-FIELD experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS), we are currently studying electric field effects on quenched jet flames, partially-admixed air/fuel jet flames, and their associated dangers. This report summarizes recent findings. Specific activities include:
1.) Study electric field control of flames with wall effects near quenching. The experiment involves flow field imaging, along with OH chemiluminescence and OH planar laser induced fluorescence (PLIF) techniques. Measurements include thermal emission and carbon monoxide emission, and analyses evaluate thermal emission.
2.) Characterize time-scales related to the interaction between ions and neutral molecules within the burner/mesh electrode gap. These time-scales provide information into how an electric field affects combustion related parameters. These times-scales were determined using high-speed schlieren imaging and ion current/applied voltage measurements.
Our understanding developed in these areas may improve kinetic mechanisms for diffusion flame modeling (including charged species), help clearly identify the risk of CO emission from quenched flames, and help determine if electric fields can actively control the release of carbon monoxide from flames.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight-based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The control of combustion has the potential to improve efficiency and reduce emissions from burning fuels. Since high power density often requires combustion, these improvements will be important no matter what the fuel source. Electric fields acting on flames have the potential to aid in combustion control. In addition, electrical properties of flames can identify poor performing boiler flames that release poisonous carbon monoxide. Our studies show that a flame's electric signature can capture incipient quenching before dangerous emissions result. Understanding the links between electrical character and flame behavior may allow improved sensing of poor performing combustion systems.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2016
Task Progress:
In addition to preparing for the proposed ACME E-FIELD experiments aboard the ISS, we are currently evaluating an experimental method of measuring ion number density in a flame using a Langmuir probe, the dynamic interaction between the flame and chemi-ions, and the use of electric fields to control flames impinging on a surface. This report summarizes recent findings. Specific activities include:
1.) Study the electrical behavior of a non-premixed co-flow flame. This is done by measuring the ion current that is collected by a Langmuir probe placed into the flame. The ion current gives insight into the production and transportation of chemi-ions due to a natural occurring methane combustion process without the effects of an external electric field.
2.) Study the dynamic interaction between the flame and the electrical body force created by a flux of chem-ions. This is done by comparing transient flame behavior using a high speed camera and the transient ion current collected when an electric field is turned on.
3.) Study electric field control of flames with wall effects near quenching. The experiment supplements our earlier measurements of OH PLIF with 2-line OH temperature measurements and 2-photon CO PLIF to confirm the findings that electric fields can moderate carbon monoxide release from flames impinging on surfaces.
Summaries of these findings appear in this report with the details of all the work appearing in the publications and conference proceedings identified in the Bibliography section. This year the project produced 1 peer-reviewed journal article (with 2 others in preparation); 12 conference papers/presentations; 4 M.S. thesis documents; and 1 Ph.D. dissertation.
All ground-based experiments were performed using a coflow burner that is dimensionally similar to the proposed ISS coflow burner and that uses a fuel jet matching the dimension of the ISS jet burner. The burner consists of two stainless steel plenums threaded together. Fuel, introduced in the bottom plenum, is passed through a stainless steel tube (2.13 mm ID) and exits the top surface fully developed. Air entering the top chamber passes through flow straightening beads and a honeycomb mesh. The air exits the top surface with a top hat flow profile at the exit. A variable high-tension power supply connected between the burner and downstream mesh electrode produces the applied electric field. The electric field distribution is deformed by the flame’s space charge. Regardless, defining an applied field strength, E = V/D, is a useful approximation when describing experimental results. Ion current is computed using Ohm’s law and the measured potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground. An acrylic chamber shields the flame from room currents. A Faraday cage was also added to isolate the measurements from EMI radiating outside of the experimental volume.
(1) Langmuir Probe Studies
The object of this study is to evaluate the method of using a Langmuir probe to determine the ion number density produced by the flame. The short-term goal is to determine the naturally occurring ion number density (without an external field) while the long-term goal is to apply the Langmuir probe study to a flame with an external field. With the ion number density in the presence of an external field known, the electrical body force (ion-wind force) can be calculated.
Electric probes have a long history within the field of plasma diagnostics. They are simple to build and are easily implemented into plasma experiments. However, the results they provide are not so easy to analyze. A particular type of electric probe, the Langmuir probe, has found its way into combustion research in order to study naturally produced flame ions. In the present work, a small potential is applied to a Langmuir probe with respect to ground (burner). This procedure is known as the single-probe method.
For the geometry of the plasma (i.e., the flame) in this experiment, the best choice is to use a spherical tip Langmuir probe because it will have the minimum impact on the heated flow of gas inside the flame and because it provides a relatively simple means of calculating the ion flux from the measured ion current. The spherical shape reduces the complexity of the problem studied.
In combustion environments, CH* is predominately formed from C2H and atomic oxygen. Previous E-FIELD Flame investigations have suggested that there exists a high correlation between CH* and H3O+. However, this was shown at a global level. The current results show the correlation (if any) between CH* and ion current collection locally.
Probe System
A co-flow burner was used for creating a small methane/air diffusion flame. A simple Langmuir probe was used for ion current detection. It was made of stainless steel and insulated with a tube of alumina silicate to avoid melting, electric arcing, and electric transmission. Stainless steel was chosen because of its low resistivity and high melting point (1680 K).
The probe dimensions are a length of 6 inches (152.4 mm) and a tip of 1 mm of diameter. The probe was attached to two motor driven Velmex sliders for 2-axis control. One axis refers to the vertical axis Z (symmetry axis of revolution) and the other to the radial position r. The probe was swept radially from R=-19 mm to R-19 mm for different heights. However, an ion current was only detected within the range of R=-6 mm to R=6 mm, representing the extent to which the charged species can diffuse from the flame sheet radially. Positive potentials of 40 V, 80 V, and 120 V (generated by the high performance laboratory grade device: TREK Model 609A-3) were applied to the probe to attract negative charge carriers and to repel positively charged species.
Probe potentials that are too high run the risk of creating ion winds, which would disturb the flame from its natural state. It was found that at potentials above 400 V, the flame began to bend. The generated ion current that flows through the shunt resistor to the ground was measured and related to voltage using Ohm’s Law. From preliminary tests, it was determined that a Faraday cage was necessary to isolate the probe from external noise. The flow rate used was 26.9 mL/min. The ion current signal shows good symmetry across the flame with the peak in the reaction zone.
Chemilumenscence System
Chemiluminescence is radiation emitted from electronically excited molecules as they return to their lower energy state. The wavelength of the radiation that is emitted is characteristic of the particular molecule and the particular transition the molecule undergoes. Since the amount of radiation observed in the flame at a particular wavelength is proportional to the concentration of the associated excited molecule, a measurement of the radiation can be directly related to the concentration of the excited molecules.
In hydrocarbon combustion, the most common electronically excited species are OH*, CH*, and C2*. In the early 1970s chemiluminescence was identified as a marker for heat release, reaction zone, and equivalence ratio, thereby providing a relatively easy diagnostic alternative for the measurements in practical combustion applications and an inexpensive diagnostic tool that avoids expensive instrumentation, e.g., lasers. The present work is focused on the detection of CH* at a wavelength of 431 nm.
A bandpass interference filter was used to collect the appropriate wavelength range of the light emitted from the flame. The present work is focused on the emission of light from CH* which is a known precursor for positively charged species such as CHO+ and H3O+. H3O+ is known to be the only positively charged species that is able to survive outside the flame to any substantial extent. Since CH* is an accepted precursor to ion formation it is important to describe one of the paths for the formation of H3O+ from CH and CH*. CH* is produced chemically via the reaction of the ethynyl radical with monatomic and diatomic oxygen. Destruction reactions occur by spontaneous emission and by collisional quenching. There are two reactions that give rise to chemi-ions. The second reaction is more likely to occur in flames if the concentration of the excited CH can exceed the thermal equilibrium populations by several orders of magnitudes. Finally, H3O+ is formed from CHO+ by the addition of water. Pictures were taken from the flame and then post-processed with Matlab to compute the intensity.
Results and Discussion
The objective of this experiment is to determine what height above the nozzle produces the maximum collection of ion current. The probe swept the space several times at different heights from H=0.5 mm to H=6.5 mm with increments of delta H=1 mm. The potential applied to the probe is 40 V, 80 V, and 120 V and three different flow rates are used (26.9 mL/min, 40.4 mL/min, and 53.8 mL/min).
Images were taken of the flame using a 430 nm bandpass interference filter to capture the luminosity from the flame due to CH*. Two images were also taken using 440 nm and 420 nm filters. The purpose for these two extra images was to determine if there was any contribution to the detected light from any source other than CH* (e.g., soot). The results of these images concluded that the 430 nm filter was capturing only CH* chemiluminescence. Several pictures of the flame are taken and then averaged.
A three-point inverse Abel deconvolution method is applied for deconvolving CH* chemiluminescence images. Assuming that the plasma sheath created by the Langmuir probe is much smaller than the dimension of the probe, the results show that the ions have the highest concentration in the flame (compared to the location of CH*) but that they are transported far outside the flame.
A pixel intensity map is compared with ion current peaks position and amplitudes, and ion current peak positions and are gathered and correlated with pixel peak position and pixel intensity peaks for the corresponding heights (from H=0.5 mm to H=4.5 mm) for the three sampled probe potentials. Ion current and pixel intensity values are normalized by their corresponding maximum value. From these experiments it can be seen that the overall maximum correlation is achieved for Vp=40 V and for H-1.5 mm to H=3.5 mm; above H=3.5 mm this position correlation disappears. As the probe voltage increases, the location of peak ion current moves outward away from the CH* band. This is reasonable since higher probe voltage encourages the charged species to move toward the probe. In addition, as the probe potential increases the correlation is also reduced. There exists a poor correlation between the pixel intensity and the collected ion current from the probe for different probe potentials except for H=1.5 mm where the correlation is reasonable. The probe potential which best correlated is for Vp=40 V and for H-1.5 mm. The results also suggest that the ions are evenly distributed throughout the flame region.
Calculating Ion Number Density
For a spherical probe, the conservation of charge is mathematically expressed as a gradient of ion flux. Then, a relationship between the charge flux anywhere in the plasma sheath can be related to the charge flux at the sheath edge. The velocity of ions entering the plasma sheath is approximated to be the Bohm velocity. Combining these equations, the number density of chemi-ions as a function of ion current can be expressed. The only unknown left is sheath diameter. A thin sheath approximation can be used. Using the characteristic values consistent with the experimental parameters, it is found that there is sufficient evidence that a thin sheath approximation can be used. It is found that in the region of highest ion current collection by the Langmuir probe the ion number density is close to that found by others.
While this simple analysis produces reasonable results, it is very well known that Langmuir probe theory is notoriously very complicated and an analysis for the case that the plasma sheath is not thin should be performed. By inspection of the experimental results it could be seen that the maximum possible sheath diameter that could be produced by the flame plasma/Langmuir probe interaction is 5 mm. Using this in calculation produces an ion number density of around the same order.
(2) Dynamic Flame Response
The application of an external electric field to a flame is well-known to effect the flame's behavior. Previous E-Field Flame studies have visualized the dynamic effect an electric field has on the flow field by using high-speed schlieren imaging. These studies revealed the time-scales involved during the process of manipulating the flame with an external field. The results of the time-scales suggests that the full process can be qualitatively described by the following steps:
i) Ions are immediately collected (1-2 ms after the electric field is initiated) at the electrodes. However, the full ion flux that is produced by the field is not reached until 8-10 ms after the field is initiated. The cause of this time difference is most likely that the collection of ions is being restricted by the flame's own plasma sheath adjusting to the external field. This flame sheath behavior is not a new concept, however, is rarely accounted for in electric field flame studies in the literature.
ii) The flow field was seen to begin to change approximately 2-3 ms after the field was initiated. Even though the full ion flux is not reached within this time-scale, enough ions are extracted from the flame to produce an ion-wind force sufficient enough to manipulate the bulk gas. The difference in the two time-scales indicates the time it takes to produce enough ion/neutral collisions to produce this ion-wind body force. The change in the flow field was shown to originate near the base of the flame and progress its way up downstream from the burner exit.
iii) It was also shown from high-speed imaging of the flame itself that the first signs of the flame being manipulated by the field is 2-5 ms after the field is initiated. This suggested the flame is reacting to the change in the flow field and not by electric field/chemi-ion flux directly.
Steps i-iii describe the initial steps of how the electric field is able to manipulate the flame. What was also shown from these studies was that the flame/electric field interaction is not a simple one-direction process. This is because the flame is not only the object being controlled by the electric field but also the source of ions (i.e., the source of the ion-wind). In fact, the time-scale involved with the entire environment going from its initial state to final state can be described by these three major elements (electric field induced chemi-ion flux, neutral gas flow field, and flame/chemi-ion source) reaching an equilibrium state with each other.
A final interesting result from these studies was the existence of field strengths that produced final states that were non-steady and oscillatory in nature. It was observed that at high enough fields the transient ion current measurements and the transient thermal plume boundary began to oscillate with a frequency 74hz. This unsteady behavior is exemplary of the how the three elements described above are coupled above.
This objective of the current study is to characterize the unsteady behavior at high electric field strengths to determine what are the important parameters controlling the oscillations.
Determining Flame Height from Flame Videos
Further evidence of flame dynamics was obtained from high-speed video taken before and after the electric field was initiated. Each video was recorded at 500 frames per second (fps). Higher than 500 fps, the small amount of light produced by the flame is too weak to capture videos sufficient enough to analyze. For each video, an LED light is used to time the moment that the electric field is initiated. The time indicated by t=0 ms is the defined to be the frame just before the LED light turns on (in other words, the first frame in the video that the LED is turned on is considered t=2 ms).
Because the light from the flame was weak, light filters were not used to isolate at a particular wavelength. Hence, the camera also captures light emitted by soot particles. This is not easily noticeable from the black and white images but it does add difficulty in defining the location of the flame height based purely from pixel intensity. Even when soot does not seem to be present, defining flame height based on maximum pixel intensity, in many cases, produces pixel locations significantly far from where the human eye would locate the flame height in the image. A more reliable method was to choose the maximum gradient of the pixel intensity along the centerline of the burner. A 5-point moving average smoothing curve of the pixel intensity further cleaned up the flame height location. For selected videos, using the gradient of smoothed pixel intensity gave pixel location results no more than 2-3 pixels from where the human eye would define the pixel height location. After calibration (calibration factor of 70 microns/pixel), this results in a -0.2 mm difference from the location determined by the human eye. Also, it should be noted that when the electric field is turned on, the flame luminosity increases, which makes the pixel intensity profiles of each frame appear more distinct.
Transient Ion Current Measurements
A shunt resister was wired in series in between the burner and high voltage power supply. The transient ion current was determined by measuring the voltage drop across the shunt resistor and using Ohm's Law to determine the current. The ion current was sampled by at data acquisition at 1000 samples per second. The timing of the ion current measurements was defined similar to the flame height. The time, t=0 ms, is defined as the sample reading just before the command signal is sent to the high voltage power supply (i.e., t=1 ms is the sample in which the data acquisition reads the first high voltage measurement). Because the data acquisition has a better temporal resolution than the high-video camera, the timing of the data acquisition is considered to be the baseline timing source. Assuming the LED emits light much less than 1 ms after it feels a potential difference across its leads, t=0 ms is known within 1 ms between both the high-speed videos and the ion current measurements. Based on this experimental unknown, this error (-1 ms) would shift the transient flame heights up to 1ms to the left from their current temporal locations.
Results and Discussion
The oscillations in ion current and luminosity were faintly observable in the measurements at voltage steps as low as -6.1 kV but were not observable in the flame height measurements until -6.4 kV. This is because the small random fluctuations in the flame height position (±0.12 mm from the mean flame height) exceeds the amplitude change caused by the electric field below -6.4 kV. An amplitude of about 0.05 µA (±0.05 µA from the mean ion current) causes a significant enough effect for the oscillations to be observable in the flame height. As the intensity of the voltage steps increase above -6.3 kV, the amplitude of ion current oscillations increases, as well as, the amplitude of the flame height oscillations up till -6.8 kV. This step voltage produces the largest oscillations in the both the ion current and flame height. At a step voltage of -6.9 kV, the oscillations begin to disappear.
The 74 hz oscillations are easily observable. The amplitude of the ion current is ±0.1 µA from the mean ion current and the amplitude of the flame height is ±1 mm from the mean flame height. It is also interesting to point out that when the flame height reaches a high value the magnitude of the ion current is also high but out of phase by 1ms behind the flame height. This is most likely because a higher flame height decreases the distance between the flame and the downstream electrode (i.e., lower resistance), therefore, increasing the ion current.
As stated above, the uncertainty in the temporal calibration of the flame height produces a phase shift in the flame height profile up to 1 ms to the left. Accounting for this uncertainty, the ion current is between 1 and 2 ms behind the flame height. This suggested that (assuming the transportation of ions from the flame to the downstream electrode is the time limiting mechanism) when ion flux from the flame is increased (or decreased) it takes between 1-2 ms for it to be transported to the downstream electrode in order for an ion current to be measured by the shunt resistor. The hypothesis that the electrical resistance can be treated as a function of flame height for increasing/decreasing the ion current, seems reasonable enough to explain the unsteady ion current vs flame height profiles but does not explain what causes the flame height to oscillate. In order to do this, further studies of unsteady schlieren behavior is needed.
(3) Impinging Flames
There were two major accomplishments regarding the effect of electric fields on impinging flames subsequent to the last annual report. The first accomplishment is the use of 2-line OH thermometry to non-intrusively measure the temperature profile of the flame even when under the influence of an electric field. The second accomplishment was to use 2-photon planar laser induced fluorescence (PLIF) to measure the concentration of carbon monoxide (CO) in the impinging flame. The impinging flame study was the topic of Dr. Yu-Chien Chien’s Ph.D. dissertation completed as part of this project.
As in all prior studies, the experiments are conducted with a coflow burner and a 2 mm thick stainless steel plate progressively lowered toward the burner surface so that it gradually quenches the flame. The stainless steel coflow burner is 13 cm tall and has a 4 cm outer diameter. At the exit, the burner has a 2 mm inner diameter center tube carrying fuel, and air is provided separately through a concentric outer ring. The air is designed to have a uniform laminar flow distribution at the exit after it passes through a bed of beads and a honeycomb mesh close to the exit. Inside the burner, the length of the tube is sufficient to ensure fully developed laminar flow at the exit for the range of desired Reynolds numbers. The metal plate used as the quenching surface is 50 mm square. It is indirectly connected onto a vertical-axial translation stage through two cylindrical ceramic threaded posts. The diffusion flame used for this work had flow rates equivalent to a constant nominal speed of 20 cm/s for both methane and air at the burner exit.
The 2-photon CO signal depends on a wide range of parameters. Although complex, many of these values can be determined, at least for relative conditions, permitting CO fluorescence to provide a clear qualitative view of the spatial distribution of this important molecule. The wavelength chosen for the experiment is 230.034; the wavelength was monitored and calibrated with a Xenon lamp and a 1-meter spectrometer. This wavelength belongs to the transitions in the Q branch with a rotational quantum number around J=11.
A Nd:Yag laser offering 850 mJ at 1064 nm, provided, after doubling and mixing, 250 mJ at 355 nm with 5 ns duration at FWHM. The pumping energy at 355nm goes into a dye laser (Vista) with Coumarin 460 diluted in methanol. After the laser energy at 460nm is doubled and separated from the fundamental with a Pellin-Broca prism. The system is optimized for maximum output energy at 5 mJ per pulse. The laser beam is converted into a laser sheet using a quartz 100 mm focal length convex cylindrical lens that focusses the light into the burner. The lens has been chosen as a tradeoff between the energy density of the flame and the Rayleigh range, both of them have to be maximized for a good signal. For correcting the images for the intensity distribution of the laser sheet, a gas cell with CaF2 windows and estimated concentration of CO around 300 ppm was used as a uniform sample target. The detection system used to take the images is an emICCD PI-MAX4 with a 75 mm lens and a filter centered at 486 nm with a 50% transmission window of 10 nm. The gate for the images is 100 ns.
Three positions were studied with the burner at different distances with respect to the plate. An average of 1000 frames was taken for each position for both the laser intensity profile and the fluorescence signal. The cylindrical lens was selected to be 100 mm focal length in order to stay in the linear regime of the CO fluorescence, that is, the regime where the CO ionization dominates. The beam waist is estimated to be about 50 µm in thickness, and the average power density is approximately 0.5 GW/cm2. This power density is enough to ensure that ionization dominates the depopulation of the upper state, giving an approximate linear behavior with intensity for atmospheric pressure conditions.
The two-line OH thermometry measurements use the same apparatus but a different dye system and wavelengths. The basis for two-line OH temperature PLIF is the ratio of signal strength from two spectral lines. Where the ratio at every pixel of the camera is a function of several constants, temperature, laser intensity, both overlap integrals, and the ratio of both quantum fluorescent yields. The spectral overlap between laser profile and absorption line profile is assumed to be the same for both transitions, which is a source of a small systematic error, even though the laser profile is very similar for both transitions. The linearity of the signal was checked by comparing the overall integrated signal of the fluorescence images from the camera with the average energy power from the laser used for the images. The transitions selected from the A-X (1,0) band are the P1(3) and P1(10) around 283 nm.
200 images are averaged before ratioing to obtain a better signal to noise image. The averaged image is weighted with the laser intensity mapping obtained from a fluorescent dye diluted mixture. The images are aligned one by one since the laser intensity mapping is taken for every transition due to nonlinear behaviors in the doubling processes. The images are corrected using the average of the images (instead of 2 images) by using the overall integrated signal for each sequence of pictures. Finally, isolating temperature from the previous equation, a temperature ratio is obtained for each pixel. In order to only obtain meaningful temperatures, a product of both averaged intensity transitions is computed, and a constant is used to limit the low end in the not meaningful temperature data, assigning 0 K where it is not meaningful. The lower temperature limit is 1000 K because OH only exists at temperatures above 1000 K. All the measurements are repeated for different relative positions of the flame with respect to the plate.
Key results of the study show images for similar flame conditions of: two-photon CO, chemiluminescence, and two-line OH PLIF temperature measurements. Qualitative two-photon CO PLIF measurements in a non-premixed coflow impinging flame with a plate downstream the flow were obtained. The temperature dependence of the wavelength used has been studied in order to understand the images better. The intensity dependence of the signal has been corrected and additional corrections have been applied in order to account for the complex intensity dependence of the fluorescence signal. Contribution from C2* in the flame studied are larger than in premixed flames, but distinct images of CO without C2* interference were obtained through averaging and a narrow bandpass filter.
These results show that absolute flame temperature is not affected by the plate location but the extent of the hot zone of OH is affected. In addition, it is clear that when the plate is very close to the burner that CO is able to escape along the surface of the plate rather than being confined within the flame zone. Future work is to confirm the relationships between OH location and temperature, the boundary layer flow along the plate surface, and the release of carbon monoxide from impinging flames. The preliminary findings of this more complete study shows that electric fields can reduce CO release from impinging flames when the flame is at the cusp of its separation from a closed to open tip flame, which, coincidentally, is the condition where maximum heat transfer from the flame is achieved.

Task Description:
NOTE this is a successor agreement to "Applications of Electric Fields in Microgravity Combustion Science (NNX07AB55A)," per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving the performance of energy conversion systems. As an actuator, electric fields can affect flame stability and soot formation; while as a sensing device, the electrical response at saturation is a flame characteristic. In addition to preparing for the proposed ACME E-FIELD experiments aboard the ISS, we are currently studying electric field effects on quenched jet flames, partially-admixed air/fuel jet flames, and their associated dangers. This report summarizes recent findings. Specific activities include:
1.) Study electric field control of flames with wall effects near quenching. The experiment involves flow field imaging, along with OH chemiluminescence and OH PLIF techniques. Measurements include thermal emission and carbon monoxide emission, and analyses evaluate thermal emission.
2.) Characterize time-scales related to the interaction between ions and neutral molecules within the burner/mesh electrode gap. These time-scales provide information into how an electric field affects combustion related parameters. These times-scales were determined using high-speed schlieren imaging and ion current/applied voltage measurements.
Our understanding developed in these areas may improve kinetic mechanisms for diffusion flame modeling (including charged species), help clearly identify the risk of CO emission from quenched flames, and help determine if electric fields can actively control the release of carbon monoxide from flames.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The control of combustion has the potential to improve efficiency and reduce emissions from burning fuels. Since high power density often requires combustion, these improvements will be important no matter what the fuel source. Electric fields acting on flames have the potential to aid in combustion control. In addition, electrical properties of flames can identify poor performing boiler flames that release poisonous carbon monoxide. Our studies show that a flame's electric signature can capture incipient quenching before dangerous emissions result. Understanding the links between electrical character and flame behavior may allow improved sensing of poor performing combustion systems.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2015
Task Progress:
UCI Coflow Burner--All ground-based experiments were performed using a coflowing burner that is dimensionally similar to the proposed ISS coflow burner. The burner consists of two stainless steel plenums threaded together. Fuel, introduced in the bottom plenum, is passed through a stainless steel tube (2.13 mm ID) and exits the top surface fully developed. The air entering the top chamber passes through flow straightening beads and a honeycomb mesh. The air exits the top surface with a top hat flow profile at the exit. A variable high-tension power supply connected between the burner and downstream mesh electrode produces the applied electric field. The electric field distribution is deformed by the flame’s space charge, but defining an applied field strength, E = V/d, is a useful approximation when describing experimental results. Ion current is computed using Ohm’s law and the measured potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground. An acrylic chamber shields the flame from room currents.
Quenching studies--The effects of quenching on flame structure study was initiated by Professor Felix Weinberg at Imperial College in order to predict the hazardous conditions created by poorly tuned industrial boilers. The ultimate practical aim of this series of experiments is to use electrical aspects of flames to reduce the incidence of CO poisoning caused by the quenching of natural gas flames in malfunctioning burners. We investigate, for example, how the flow of charge can be employed to signal the onset of hazardous conditions before any CO release can occur. This research has now shifted entirely to UC Irvine as Professor Felix Weinberg passed away last year.
The work involves the examination of the electrical properties of partially quenched flames. Our work at Imperial College illuminated the potential dangers of improperly tuned boilers and the high concentration of carbon monoxide and hydrogen potentially emitted when quenched. This portion of our research was aimed at understanding the electrical behavior of a flame as a plate was incrementally lowered toward it by measuring the corresponding ion current. The study was a proof of concept to explore the potential of detecting flame impingement electrically without visual inspection. The work has shown that ion current sharply increases and finally saturates when lowering the plate toward the jet flame exit. The ion current decreases as the flame temperature and ion production fall.
We continued this work to study the phenomena occurring on the quenching plate as the flame approached it. Different quenching surface materials have various emissivities and thermal properties that lead to different equilibrium temperatures. Preliminary research involves identifying the thermal emission from the plate at different heights when lowered towards the flame (or when the flame sheet is interrupted).
A z-type Schlieren imaging technique is used to understand how the flow field changes with electric field control. The results of CO emission and flame imaging show that the electric control of flames has a clear effect when H/D (H – distance to the plate; D – fuel jet diameter) values are larger than 4.5, while the cases with smaller H/D create complex flow regions because they are dominated by the jet momentum. Schlieren images with and without electric field applied to the flame show steady laminar flow fields, with a typical stagnation point flow boundary layer shape extending radially outward on the plate to its edge.
An infrared camera (FLIR SC620) measures radiative emission and is situated directly above the quenching plate at normal incidence to avoid complications associated with Lambert’s cosine law. The quenching plate is painted with black paint and is considered a blackbody object. This assumption has been confirmed as reasonable using thermocouple temperature comparisons at a few spot locations. By using the heat map to characterize the spatial concentration of the heat balance on the plate helps describe how electric fields can control the concentration of the heat. Thermal maps from the 2-D image are converted into a radial temperature profile across the plate for comparison at H/D 4.5 (9 mm). The overall temperature distribution is approximately Gaussian. With negative field, the peak temperature is lower and profile is broader while the positive field produces higher peak temperature and narrower profile. This information suggests strongly that the heat transfer over the quenching plate can be altered or improved by an electric field and in so doing may provide much better thermal heating efficiency, particularly if the target plate is small.
Previous results convey the information that the total heat transfer is not affected substantially by the electric field near quenching at cases below H/D at 4.5 (9 mm); so, another assumption needs to be applied for these cases. The temperature profile in thermal maps indicates that the temperature profile does change with electric field. Therefore we assume that the field affects the local heat flux distribution rather than the total flux to the plate when the gap distance is small. The concentration of heat over the plate can be analyzed in the following way; there are six rings mapped from the hottest spot, these six rings are different percentages of the total heat loss (and thereby heat gain at steady state) from the plate. We next study how the heat flux changes with electric field strength. The heat flux is growing as the rings moves close toward the hot center. The heat flux variation under electric field effects at 80% to 50% is around 400 to 700 W/m2, the 40% ring is 800-900 W/m2, the 30% ring is 1000-1100 W/m2, and at 20% the flux can be up to 1400 W/m2 change in the flux when an electric field is present. These results show conclusively that the electric field can change the local heating from a flame in a significant way, particularly near the center cone, as expected.
A close look of the 20% heat loss with normalized heat flux at zero-field at each height shows the effect of plate location. The electric field seems to have the strongest effects at the larger distance of H/D = 5.5. This seems to occur because the tradeoff between directing the heat and quenching the flame begins to occur at approximately this height. The H/D 1.5 (3 mm) case is very complex since the plate is very low and the plate impeded flow field interacts with the flame in some way. We need to examine these extreme cases in more detail. The temperature and heat transfer over a quenching plate with the effect from electric field flames is investigated from H/D 5.5 to 1.5 (plate location 11 mm progressively lower down to 3 mm) with the maximum electric field that can be applied without breakdown. The plate has a broadened profile and lower peak temperature at the negative field; with the increasing of the field to the positive the plate has higher peak temperature. The overall heat flux to the plate before quenching increases with the field. Under conditions where the flame is being quenched by the plate, it is interesting to note that the variation with the electric field decreases. For example, at the 20% ring, the heat flux is increasing from 2400 W/m2 up to 3850 W/m2 at H/D 5.5 (11 mm) as the field focuses the flame. Similar phenomenon can be observed during flame quenching but these changes are smaller as compared to the cases without any flame/plate interaction. Further exploration is required such as on how does the heat propagate and distribute at the bottom side of the plate.
An initial measurement to understand the overall carbon monoxide emission inside a chamber shows how the combustion reaction alters under electric field control. Reactions consuming hydroxyl compete with each other layer by layer within methane/air flames, and carbon monoxide often employs hydroxyl to oxidize. OH planar laser induced fluorescence (PLIF) shows that OH location and concentration during flame quenching correlate strongly with carbon monoxide release. The PLIF measurements follow generally recommended practice and are conducted by pumping OH at 282.0 nm in the A-X(1,0) band and detecting fluorescence in the A-X(0,0), (1,1) band. The system is composed of a Nd:YAG laser (YAG) and a pulsed dye laser (PDL) with a wavelength extender (WEX). Being a legacy laser system, it is not automated and the experiment requires manual tweaking of the crystals to find and maintain good performance. The requirement for continuous adjustment makes precise quantification difficult but, as shown by the results, the manual effort produces very clear evidence of OH distributions in the impinging diffusion flames. The pulse energy was kept below 1 mJ to stay in the linear regime of the fluorescence. A high speed Phantom camera (v4.3) and a HiCaTT intensifier equipped with a P24 phosphor collected the images. A band pass filter centered at 320 nm was used (Semrock FF01-320/40-25) which offers 70% transmissivity to collect the light from the A-X(0,0) transition. The main peaks that are found and suitable for PLIF imaging are the stronger ones that start at 282.0 with the Q1(1) transition followed by the Q1(2), Q1(3). Though it is more sensitive to temperature changes than the most used transition Q1(8), the combination of lines still makes a very good choice for 2D temperature PLIF measurements if used in combination with other very sensitive temperature transitions. In addition, this transition range allowed less intensifying, leading to a better signal to noise ratio, and for the purposes of the current study, the 10% variation is not significant relative to the natural variations that occur in the electrically-driven flames being measured.
OH* natural chemiluminescence images in the band from 300 nm to 340 nm (using the same filter as before) are also recorded at gating around 10 microseconds. The images are processed through an Abel transform to reveal tomographically reconstructed local distributions. The reconstructed images are after averaging 200 pictures taken at a rate of 100Hz and after filtering with its background. The transformed images show a clear region of the reaction zone. In general, the overall OH intensity decreases as the plate approaches the burner, which implies that OH radical concentration decreases at smaller quenching distance. This, combined with the fact that the velocities were kept low so the flow behaves with similar characteristics of a laminar stagnation flow, gives a reason for the overall oxidation of the CO molecule to decrease, due to the lower OH concentration and less residence time for reaction through the OH layer as the plate approaches the burner. The tip of the OH radical zone opens because the plate acts a chiller for the flame, radiating energy and bringing the surface temperature to approximately 500K. Other work mentions that the OH radical is not expected to exist below 1000K, which is why the tip of the OH reaction zone opens in the cool gas layer near the surface even before the HR zone changes its shape. In addition, the overall OH fluorescence changes with electric field and distributes outwardly with negative fields while it gathers with a positive field. At relatively high burner to plate spacing the electric field has minor influence on the OH PLIF intensity but it does affect the location of the OH as the field affects the location of the flame sheet. When the electric field is applied upward, the ion driven wind pulls the flame in the direction of the flow field and the reaction became vigorous toward the plate. OH distributes strongly near the plate in this case. At closer plate distances the field affects the OH intensity as well as its position. When the electric field is negative, the downward directed positive ions produce a downward blowing wind that causes the reaction sheet to widen. When H/D at 3.5 (7 mm), there is the most dramatic effect of the electric field as regards the relative magnitude of OH fluorescence but relatively little change in the location of the OH relative to the flame sheet. This result is reflected in the large relative change in CO for the case with negative fields applied. As with the CO measurements, these images show that the effects of changes in plate height have a larger effect on the OH distribution than does the electric field.
Chemi-Ion Driven Flows in a Time-Varying Electric Field--For similar current densities, a flux of H3O+ ions through a gas, such as air, will produce body forced per unit volume about three orders of magnitude greater than a flux of electrons. In order to test this theory an experiment was needed to measure the velocity field within the electrode space region. A simple schlieren system is employed to visualization of the thermal plume within the electrode space. In the absence of an electric field, the thermal plume is buoyantly driven due to the pressure forces of the cool ambient gas environment acting on the hot combustion gases. The buoyancy force acting on the bulk gas can be described by the Boussinesq approximation. The upward motion of hot exhaust gas has been known to entrain ambient gas horizontally from the environment in order to satisfy mass conservation. With the presence of an electric field, the thermal plume is driven by both buoyancy and electrical body forces. An electrically driven thermal plume has been shown to entrain ambient gas similar to buoyancy driven thermal plumes but is expected to be higher by an order of magnitude for low heat release rates (i.e. low fuel flow rates). Schlieren technique is providing insight into time-scales related to the electro-hydrodynamic parameters that are being investigated in this study.
A brief theoretical analysis of the time-scales is performed before proceeding to the results of the schlieren experiment. The first time-scale is the time it takes to pull a charged particle from the flame and retrieve it downstream at the mesh electrode. For a positive field, H3O+ is the primary ion thought to exist within the electrode gap. The velocity of a single H3O+ ion travels through the electrode space at its drift velocity is equal to the product of its mobility, K, and the field strength, E. The time it takes for an H3O+ ion to travel from its place of origin, the flame, to the downstream electrode is then defined by the length of the electric field line divide by KE. Since the flame remains attached to the burner, it is assumed that the burner and flame have the same potential. The charge density only effects the local electric field lines near the flame where the lines are given a small radius of curvature but become parallel lines quickly downstream. This curvature slightly alters the length of the field lines, thus, altering their local magnitude. Since the order of magnitude of the analysis is less important compare to the whole scale of the flow field, the length of the field line will be taken as the length from the base of the flame up to the downstream mesh electrode. This is a good approximation, since it is thought that the highest concentration of H3O+ is located near the base of the flame. The electric field strength will be defined as the applied voltage difference between the two electrodes divided by the length of the electric field line. This analysis uses the applied voltage at saturation to produce the maximum, purely chemi-ionization effect. The length of the electric field line is 3.2cm, K is 2.9cm^3/V and the applied voltage as measured from the downstream electrode with respect to the burner is 5x10^3 V. Then we get the drift velocity 4530 cm/s and the time that the ions travel is 1ms. The next time-scale is the time it takes a volume of gas driven by a current of chemi-ions to travel from the flame to the downstream electrode. For simplification, this analysis will be performed for a one-dimensional system neglecting, viscosity, buoyancy, and pressure gradients within the ion stream. The rate of change of momentum along the axis is equal to the body force acting on the gas integrated over the volume between the flame and the downstream electrode. The maximum velocity due to the ion wind is also calculated as 187cm/s and the average velocity is 124 cm/s. The calculated time a volume of bulk gas to travel through the electrode space is ~34 ms. The analysis neglects buoyancy forces in the bulk gas. For the experiments performed in this study, buoyancy forces cannot be neglected. However, considering buoyancy and ion wind forces together leads to an extremely difficult mathematical problem. Therefore, an analysis of time-scales for buoyancy is performed next for reference. The velocity of a buoyantly driven gas is also approximated by velocity equation, and we get the maximum value 50 cm/s at T=1800K. The average value is 34cm/s. As expected, these values are of the same order but somewhat less than the velocities due to an ion wind. The time for a volume buoyantly driven gas to travel through the electrode space is also calculated around 125ms.
The first test was to test the voltage current response of the electrical/burner system. The voltage vs current of the system with and without the flame curve has characterized. The horizontal axis is the applied voltage on the mesh electrode with respect to the burner and has units of kilovolts. The vertical axis is the measured ion current measured through the shunt resistor and has units of microamperes. The test was for a methane flame with a fuel flow rate of 7cm/s. The co-flow was not used during this test. The negative field shows a saturation current of 1.25 microamps and the positive field shows 1.75 microamps. One last note that should be made is the ion current past the negative saturation point decreases and then increases very quickly. This is most likely due to thermal effects of hot metal surfaces (burner/mesh electrodes) releasing electrons past this high voltage range, i.e. thermal ionization. The applied voltage and ion current versus time in milliseconds are measured during this test. High-speed schlieren video also shows that the thermal plume starts at steady state where the gas velocity is driven only by buoyancy forces in the hot gas. At this state, the plume boundary has ~12mm diameter thickness downstream of the burner. The base of the plume boundary covers most of the extruded fuel tube. After the electric field is switched on, no noticeable movement occurs in the plume boundary till t=10ms. It should be noted that by comparison to ion current versus time curve, the ion current has become fully established just a few milliseconds prior to the 10ms mark. This shows that the interaction between chemi-ions and bulk gas is
For a negative field, the positive ions are pulled toward the burner while electrons are pulled downstream. Near the flame, the positive ions are forced to collide with the gas exiting from the fuel tube. This decreases the axial velocity of the bulk gas in this region, which explains the widening of the plume boundary near the flame. Further downstream, the plume boundary is thinner. An ion-wind effect is occurring in this region due to the current of electrons being collected at the downstream electrode. The ion-wind effect due to electrons is not as significant as seen with positive ion due to electron's higher mobility. At 92ms the ion-wind effect cannot be disregarded. The transient applied voltage and current measurements versus time in milliseconds are recorded during this video. An interesting thing to note in the curve is the slow decay in the ion current measurement. The ion current measured in positive field shows a very fast settling time while the ion current in negative field has a very long drawn out decay.
A high speed video of the methane flame during a negative field step is analyzed to explain this decay. The video starts from the flame at its initial state before the electric field is switched on. It takes ~8ms for a noticeable change in the flame structure. The initial change shows the flame height decrease as the diameter increases. As this happens, the glowing soot region increases from 0 to 40ms. Around 40ms the flame reaches a minimum height and then reverses direction till 136ms. The flame structure continues to expand up to ~130ms where its final shape is formed. The soot region was also seen to drastically decrease between 40ms and 136ms. In fact, the soot region continues to decay very slowly even after the flame structure has reached its final shape. This slow decay ends ~350ms after the electric field was initially turned on. The final state of the flame has a larger surface area and is less luminous than the original state. Visual traces of soot have completely disappeared. It is also interesting to point out that the slow decay of the soot region corresponds extremely well with the slow decay in transient ion-current measurement versus time curve. The overall flame shape has more of a "half-egg" shape compared to the initial shape. More will be done in the coming cycle to understand this soot disappearance.
