Task Description:
NOTE this is a successor agreement to "Applications of Electric Fields in Microgravity Combustion Science (NNX07AB55A)," per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
This report summarizes recent findings from a joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London on the use of electric fields in combustion systems, including preparations for experiments in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS) that will elucidate the fundamentals of chemi-ionization and the potential applications of ion-driven winds for combustion sensing and control.
Activities in this review period include:
1.) Determining the dynamic response of compact high-voltage power supplies for electric field generation (both for the ISS experiments and for potential terrestrial applications), and the flame’s behavior when subjected to these power supplies,
2.) Determining the effects of electric fields on flames that are impinging on quenching surfaces, including controlling the release of carbon monoxide (CO) and directing thermal convective flux,
3.) A detailed diagnostics study on CH* chemiluminescence in sooting flames both for use in analyzing the ISS xperiments and for quantifying a possible relationship between CH* emission and ion current, and
4.) Developing a ground-based apparatus to provide a refined understanding of how changes in hardware performance may affect the optimal test matrix for flight experiments.
Our understanding developed in these areas may improve kinetic mechanisms for diffusion flame modeling (including charged species), help clearly identify the risk of CO emission from quenched flames, and help determine if electric fields can actively control the release of carbon monoxide from flames.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The control of combustion has the potential to improve efficiency and reduce emissions from burning fuels. Since high power density often requires combustion, these improvements will be important no matter what the fuel source. Electric fields acting on flames have the potential to aid in combustion control. In addition, electrical properties of flames can identify poor performing boiler flames that release poisonous carbon monoxide. Our studies show that a flame's electric signature can capture incipient quenching before dangerous emissions result. Understanding the links between electrical character and flame behavior may allow improved sensing of poor performing combustion systems.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2014
Task Progress:
Flame Dynamic Response to High-Voltage Power Supplies--A portion of our research this year was directed toward characterizing a pair of High Voltage Power Supplies (HVPS) manufactured by UltraVolt because these supplies are the proposed high voltage source for a future space flight experiment aboard the ISS. Since our laboratory experiments were completed using a larger more robust power supply from TREK, it was valuable to evaluate possible differences. The results show thatTREK takes a few milliseconds (order of magnitude) rise time, while the HVPS takes approximately 100 ms. This could be an important issue since we are expecting the flame to have a response time on the order of 100 ms as well, and so determining electric field dynamics can be complicated by the slow rise time of the HVPS. By characterizing the power supply dynamics we can potentially deconvolve the flame response analytically. It is also possible that the power supply dynamics will not be as dramatic for ramps and smaller step changes, which are also important planned ISS experiments. On the ramp response, a 1kV square wave signal with different cycle times, 200 ms, 100 ms, and 50 ms is used. The results show that the HVPS exhibits about 0.2 kV overshoot after it reaches the desired 1 kV and then ripples down toward 1kV. On the TREK side, the overshoot is much smaller and can be neglected (about 10V). Although there is an overshoot, in the mean value the HVPS maintains agreement with the requested voltage for 200 ms and 100 ms cycles, and the response starts delaying for 50 ms steps. The TREK is able to work with accurate response for nearly all conditions and serves an ideal baseline result for comparison. Another response when asking for 5kV and back to 0V (in a large triangle profile) with 500V increments taken stepping up and down is also tested. This series mimics what will be a voltage-current characteristic curve sweep in the E-FIELD experiment. Results present that with the requested step getting smaller, the HVPS responds slower with higher cycle rates. The voltage overshoots and starts to fall before the value has converged to the request value; the step shape is no longer a square in both 10 ms, and 7.5 ms cases. The TREK can reach the requested voltage, and its value converges immediately. Its voltage is a little higher than the requested voltage but the difference is not significant.
As mentioned before, the HVPS shows good agreement on 100 ms timescales. However, this timescale is approximately same as that associated with the buoyant flows, making it difficult in 1g to distinguish the effects of the power supply and that of the flame. Fortunately, with a continuous measure of the current and voltage we expect to be able to deconvolve the effects. Some zero-g drop tower tests are planned to confirm this deconvolution approach. The ion current is one of the significant characteristics describing the flame in an electric field since it reflects the resistance to current flow at a given voltage. The maximum or saturation ion current for the small diffusion flame of these experiments is on the order of a few micro-amps. The steady ion current with five different flow conditions, starting at 10 cm/s with 5cm/s as increments, are measured and plotted as VCC (Voltage-Current Characteristic) curves. The VCC curves shows the typical distinct three regions of the ion current behavior in a flame. At first, the ion current rises (or falls) following a quadratic curve with increasing field strength. Then it reaches a plateau region and stops rising. With increasing field strength, the ion current rises again, following a parabolic curve until the flame blows off (upward directed ion driven wind – negative mesh) or is extinguished (downward directed ion driven wind – positive mesh). Those three regions are called the subsaturation region, the saturation region, and the supersaturation (or secondary ionization) region, respectively. The supersaturation region is often complicated by corona discharge effects from the burner and mesh so it often better to avoid the extreme voltages when trying to understand the electrical aspects of the flame alone.
The results demonstrate that the power supplies correspond to each other in the saturation region. However, there are considerable differences in the other regions. The ion current measured using the HVPS rises (or falls) with smaller field strength in the subsaturation and supersaturation regions. Therefore transition points in between the regions appear at lower field strength with the HVPS. It appears that the presence of the current sink component in the power supply affects the ion current. That trend is more significant under the higher flow condition. The power supplies are in good agreement with each other under the lower flow speed condition. This is a promising finding for the zero-gravity studies planned because electrical effects and their competition with buoyancy are much more pronounced when there is lower forced convective momentum. The flame response in terms of ion current is examined following a step input from 0 V to 5 kV. The initial spike observed in the TREK case corresponds to the capacitance of the burner/mesh electrode system. The current then decays to a steady value representative of the flame/electrode gap space. This phenomenon was characterized fairly extensively in prior work in this project. The rising ion current after the initial spike is likely due to the flame finding a new accommodation with the ion driven wind. The flame then settles to a steady condition after 30-40 ms. The HVPS results show a much less prominent spike because the slower response time does not engage the small system capacitance. It is very interesting to note, however, that the settling time of the ion current, and its ultimate value matches very well the results obtained when using the TREK. The insensitivity results because the requested voltage of this measurement is in the saturation region where the ion current does not rise with electric field strength. Therefore, the electric response is largely unaffected by the power supply response time. This a fortuitous condition that provides an important opportunity to maximize the understanding of flame behavior even when using a slow responding power supply. That is, operating with step changes between saturated regions can create more rapid response changes in the ion current than is strictly available in the voltage.
While there is experimental verification that the ion current response between the two power supplies is quite similar in time, the connection between this ion current and the flame behavior is still needed. Visualized flame response following steps of voltage using the TREK and the HVPS are captured with a camera filming at a rate of 300 fps. The mesh polarity is initially negative then a positive step voltage is applied, producing an increasing voltage range from -9 kV to +9 kV.
The results show that the TREK takes about 20 ms while the HVPS takes 130 ms to reach +9 kV. Generally, the flame is stabilized while the high voltage is applied. When the mesh is negative, the flame is extended vertically upward, and it becomes thinner. Conversely, while the mesh is positive, a downward wind is imposed, opposing natural convection. While only qualitative, it appears that with a simple time stretching the flame character matches between the two power supplies. This is slightly different from the ion current finding, which would have indicated that the flame response time should be unaffected. The difference is that in the -9 kV to 9 kV test the step is not into a saturated ion current condition but between two conditions in the supersaturated regions. In this circumstance, there will be sensitivity in the ion current. In any case, the still images are slightly misleading, and the high speed movies show more dynamic processes. In the TREK case, for example, the video shows that the flame is stabilized just 10 ms after the polarity is reversed. The flame transitions smoothly with little fluctuation from the narrow stretched shape with the upward wind to the flattened shape with the downward wind. On the other hand, when using the HVPS, the flame takes more than 100 ms to stabilize, and it continues to exhibit oscillations. With the slower responding power supply, the flame development seems separated into two stages where the flame reacts quickly at first and then slowly widens. This behavior corresponds to the electric response of the HVPS in step input responses. The oscillations are probably caused by the high voltage ripple in the output. The ripple does not affect the steady state ion current results because they are average values. Further study is needed but the dynamic differences noted above are consistent with considering the flame an active element of the system with a response time on the order of 30 ms. In the TREK case, the flame finds itself instantaneously facing an electric field condition that it then accommodates with a self-consistent change in shape and ion current generation. In the case of the HVPS the environment conditions (i.e., the electric field imposed) is continually changing as the flame tries to ccommodate the variation. This leads naturally to a more unstable behavior, particularly when the field is coupled with the ion current response. Again, further study in 1-g and zero-g will help sort out these effects.
UCI Coflow Burner--All ground-based experiments were performed using a coflowing burner that is dimensionally similar to the proposed ISS burner. The burner consists of two stainless steel plenums threaded together. Fuel, introduced in the bottom plenum, is passed through a stainless steel tube (2.13 mm ID) and exits the top surface fully developed. Air entering the top chamber passes through flow straightening beads and a honeycomb mesh. The air exits the top surface with a top hat flow profile at the exit. A variable high-tension power supply connected between the burner and downstream mesh electrode produces the applied electric field. The electric field distribution is deformed by the flame’s space charge. Regardless, defining an applied field strength, E = V/d, is a useful approximation when describing experimental results. Ion current is computed using Ohm’s law and the measured potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground. An acrylic chamber shields the flame from room currents.
Effects of Electric Fields on Impinging Flames--The ultimate practical aim of this series of experiments is to reduce the incidence of CO poisoning caused by the quenching of natural gas flames in malfunctioning burners. Concern about CO emission initially arose after we observed appreciable concentrations of CO within the luminous boundaries of our flames during experiments conducted at Imperial College, London, under the direction of Professor Felix Weinberg. These results prompted the question of how much carbon monoxide would escape into the atmosphere if quenching disrupted the flame. We studied CO release for a variety of quenching surfaces, using an exhaust system that aspirated the emerging product gases, along with much ambient air. In addition to our efforts at Imperial College, parallel studies are underway at UC Irvine, studying the properties of partially quenched flames. This portion of our research is aimed at understanding the electrical behavior of a flame as a plate is incrementally lowered toward it by measuring the corresponding ion current. The study explores the concept of detecting flame impingement electrically without visual inspection. Previous work has shown that ion current sharply increases and finally saturates when lowering the plate toward the jet flame exit. The ion current decreases as the flame temperature and ion production fall. Further details on this topic appear in the publications (Chien and Dunn-Rankin, 2013; Chien et al., 2013).
We continued the work to study the phenomena occurring on the quenching plate as the flame approached it. Different quenching surface materials have various emissivities and thermal properties that lead to different equilibrium temperatures. Preliminary research involves identifying the thermal emission from the plate at different heights when lowered towards the flame (or when the flame sheet is interrupted). In order to understand the thermal phenomenon, a FLIR camera is used. The FLIR camera uses a thermography technique for taking thermal images. The test ran with a stainless-steel plate that had been painted with a layer of non-gloss heat resistant paint to prevent reflections. The FLIR camera was located above the plate while a flame quenched underneath the plate. The microgravity relevance of this work is that convective heating in microgravity will depend on jet convection and ion-driven winds, rather than the combination of these flows and natural convection. To be clear, in this research all of the definitions of positive or negative electric field are based on the polarity of the burner relative to the downstream plate electrode. At 9 mm, the plate is very close to touching the outer dim luminous region of the zero-field flame but it does not reach the brightest flame front tip. For this plate location on the positive field side, the electric field drives positive ions and the ion wind toward the plate so that the flame is pulled up and the top of the flame narrows. The luminous zone at the flame front is brighter, presumably because the ion drift wind (also called Chattock wind) has entrained more oxidizer and shifted the reaction zone. When the flame is in positive field strength 6kV/0.9cm, the flame quenches. On the negative field side, the flame is pushed down gradually as the negative field strength grows. The downward ion wind spreads the flame and opens it. As in the case of the positive field, the flame quenches at approximately 6kV for the negative field but the extinguishment process is different. For the negative field, an arc develops between the plate and burner, and the arc disrupts the flame sufficiently to quench it. Similar phenomena can be seen when the plate is located at 5 mm, except that the flame is already open with zero field. The flame opens wider with increasing negative field strength, with the bottom rim of the flame close to the burner exit. This opening behavior results from downward directed positive ions producing a downward blowing wind when the burner is negatively charged.
To determine the effects of surface flame quenching on the electrical properties, the downstream plate is moved to different heights above the burner as the voltage is varied. At each different height of the plate above the burner, the range of electric field that is able to operate on the flame without extinguishing it or without generating an arc varies. The limits of the electric field become narrower as the gap between the plate and the burner decreases.
CO detection with high voltage control--Measurement of CO released from the flame with an electric field applied at different heights between the burner and the plate provides an indication of the potential for CO emission control of quenching flames.
The experiments are conducted for plate spacing from 3mm to 7mm, where the amount of CO generated is over one hundred ppm. The results show that CO concentration is affected significantly by the plate to burner quenching distance. Interestingly, CO concentration also varies with electric field. Normalized curves of this effect at each height with each measured value divided by the appropriate zero-field CO concentration is plotted. As the negative field grows, the CO level rises. In the positive field side, CO does not show a significant change but it still grows slightly just before falling near the breakdown or extinguishment limit.
The normalized results show a consistent trend that can possibly relate to unsteady fluctuations in the combustion driven by the electric field. With the plate progressively quenching, it is possible to estimate that the average CO concentration rises at larger negative field strength compared to the no-field case. There still exist mysteries on the effects of positive electric field strength to uncover any feasibility for CO control, but these preliminary findings suggest that electric field control near a quenching plate will have relatively minor positive influence on CO reduction. Electric fields may therefore be more important for sensing and for heat flux control of flames near surfaces.
Temperature measurement – FLIR camera--Temperature and species concentration measurements in flames that have an electric field applied have been a challenge for exploring local property distribution because probes of any kind disrupt the electric field significantly. The camera (FLIR SC620) measures radiative emission in the range from 7.5 to 13 microns, and it is situated directly above the quenching plate at normal incidence (to avoid complications associated with Lambert’s cosine law). The camera is controlled by its native commercial software (ExaminIR). The quenching plate is painted with black paint and is considered a blackbody object. This assumption has been confirmed as reasonable using thermocouple temperature comparisons at a few spot locations.
The RGB image taken at thermal equilibrium shows a well-distributed temperature change on the plate. The temperature shown in the image does not represent a local temperature of the plate or the flame temperature. It is measuring the temperature of a thin layer of the heat resistant spray paint. The overall heat transfer includes forced convection of hot flame products onto the bottom surface of the plate, conduction through the plate, and then to the paint, the heat convection out of the surface into the air, and radiation from the surface, as the system reaches thermal equilibrium. Based on straightforward heat transfer analysis it is easy to conclude that the radiation from the paint provides a reliable measure of the impinging heat from the flame on the backside of the plate. It feasible, therefore, to use the FLIR camera to characterize a quenching flame and to acquire a temperature distribution using 2-D image technology. The thermal was recorded 60 seconds after changing the electric field, by which time the temperature is steady. The pressure drop during the experiment can affect the flow rate as a result of the small jet impinging on the plate, and the different flow rate affects slightly the temperature measured from the infrared camera, showing that about 1 ml/min change in the maximum plate temperature 2 Celsius degree. Therefore all experiments conducted with IR imaging experiment use a fuel flow rate of 37.7ml/min (which is 20m/s) ± 0.6ml.
Measurement at various heights (3, 5, 7, 9, 11 mm) show that temperature decreases with the field strength. Maximum temperature of each condition at each height and field strength is recorded, and the relative maximum temperature at zero electric field at each distance between the plate and the burner is also plotted. On the positive field strength side, the maximum temperature increases quickly in the beginning at 2kV/cm and keeps rising with the field strength applied. The reaction zone is narrowed due to the ion wind and the flame’s hot gas being pulled up toward the plate. Both of these effects produce an increased local heat flux. On the negative field strength side, the reaction zone of the flame is shifted wider with the increasing of the field strength. Therefore, the maximum temperature decreases. The curve shows that the reducing trend initially decreases with similar slope until -3kV/cm, and then drops more rapidly with more negative field applied. As the plate reaches 3mm, the lowest limit of its position, the electric field effect on the maximum temperature of the plate does not vary as dramatically as for plate positions that permit more electric field influence on the flame. This is because the plate is so close to the flame that the reaction zone of the flame has already opened widely. That is, the jet momentum modification caused by the proximity of the quenching plate is more substantial than the momentum modification caused by the ion driven wind. Since we have seen that the ion-driven wind effects decrease with decreasing plate height and the physical effects of the plate increase with decreasing plate height it is clear that there will be a trade-off between these two influences. These results need more evidence and a theory to explain how the electric field is able to control and manipulate the flame’s heat flux to the plate.
CH* Chemiluminscence Measurements in Sooting Flames--The utility of chemiluminescent emission as a diagnostic tool is compromised in flames containing additional background radiation, particularly from soot. That is, a measurement of CH* chemiluminescence, even when using a narrowband interference filter, is obscured by incandescent particles in a sooting environment. The increased noise from soot affects the use of chemiluminescence as a quantitative marker and limits numerical validation of gas phase chemistry and soot oxidation mechanisms in these regions. This project effort utilized a filtering method employing three narrowband optical filters in order to subtract soot interference, and produce a soot-free CH* mage. Most of the key aspects of the method and findings were reported in the last annual report. The progress was refinement of the method, a conference paper and a journal paper that contain the details. Ultimately, by using the twin-filter method, the effect of soot temperature on the subtraction of soot luminosity was reduced below 1%. Developments toward Refined Test Matrices and Analysis for ISS Experiments--A ground-based experiment is being designed and built at UCI so that tests can be performed in preparation for analyzing ACME’s E-Field Flames flight experiments. A single burner is being constructed to match the ISS system. The burner will act as both a co-flow and gas jet burner with interchangeable fuel tubes matching the 1.3 and 2.1 mm gas jet nozzle diameter requirement. The mass flow controllers (MFCs) units being used to supply the fuel, air, and N 2 gas streams to the burner are SFC 2010 from Semiflow Engineering, matching the performance of those selected for the ACME CIR insert. These three MFCs are being calibrated and programmed to supply the flow rates stated in the E-Field test matrices in the ACME SRD. While not ideal (as described earlier), the two Ultravolt 20A12 power supply units chosen for the flight experiment will be used to power the electrode mesh and burner electrode for the preliminary experiments so we can prepare a data analysis process that minimizes uncertainty in ion current dynamics. The electric circuit and data acquisition for the entire experiment is being designed to incorporate the control of the three MFCs and dual Ultravolt power supply units, as well as acquiring measurement data for electrode voltages and ion current.
Imperial College, London--The ultimate practical aim of the experiments begun at Imperial College was to reduce the incidence of CO poisoning caused by the quenching of natural gas flames in malfunctioning burners. The work examined the interaction of a flame with a quenching surface and the potential for using electric fields to detect the proximity of the surface and to control the CO release by inducing an ion-driven wind at the appropriate time. Sadly, Professor Felix Weinberg, the lead investigator at Imperial College and the pioneer in electrical effects applied to flames, passed away in December of 2012. The flame quenching studies (and they have been described above) have now been moved to UC Irvine.

Task Description:
NOTE this is a successor agreement to "Applications of Electric Fields in Microgravity Combustion Science (NNX07AB55A)," per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving the performance of energy conversion systems. As an actuator, electric fields can affect flame stability and soot formation; while as a sensing device, the electrical response at saturation is a flame characteristic. In addition to preparing for the proposed ACME E-FIELD experiments aboard the ISS, we are currently studying quenched jet flames, partially-admixed air/fuel jet flames, and their associated dangers. This report summarizes recent findings. Specific activities include:
1) Characterizing the high voltage power supplies planned for experiments aboard the ISS.
2) A study on CH* chemiluminescence and soot pyrometry. This includes understanding the relationship between CH* emission and ion current.
3) Quantifying the risk of CO emission from quenched jet flames and identifying a flame’s “electrical boundary.” The boundary is defined as the location of a first detectable ion current.
4) Experiments designed to measure the ion current and the thermal emission of a flame as it is progressively quenched at a surface.
Progress in these areas may improve kinetic mechanisms for modeling and help reduce the risks of CO poisoning from quenched flames.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The control of combustion has the potential to improve efficiency and reduce emissions from burning fuels. Since high power density often requires combustion, these improvements will be important no matter what the fuel source. Electric fields acting on flames have the potential to aid in combustion control.
In addition, electrical properties of flames can identify poor performing boiler flames that release poisonous carbon monoxide. Our studies show that a flame's electric signature can capture incipient quenching before dangerous emissions result. Understanding the links between electrical character and flame behavior may allow improved sensing of poor performing combustion systems.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2013
Task Progress:
High Voltage Power Supply (HVPS) Study
A portion of our research this year was directed toward characterizing a pair of High Voltage Power Supplies (HVPS) manufactured by UltraVolt. The combined supply is the proposed high voltage source for a future space flight experiment aboard the ISS. Although selected for its small size and specifications, it is necessary to validate the supply performance under the proposed spaceflight conditions. NASA provided the power supply circuit diagram. In order to understand how the HVPS controls a process, a simple, basic approach on its output response is used and compared to a high-performance TREK supply used in experiments at UC Irvine.
The test consisted of applying a voltage step from -10kV to +10kV and measuring the time required for the output voltage to change between 10% and 90% of the requested voltage. The measured rise time of the UltraVolt supply (~85ms) is considerably longer than that TREK supply (~0.9 ms). It should be noted that both supplies have a short time delay of about 4ms from the time of the request to when the voltage begins to rise. This is a negligible effect and likely an error introduced by the data acquisition hardware. The results indicate that further evaluation is needed before we can accept the performance of the current power supplies. A follow-on study will investigate the system response for additional step and ramp functions, and an evaluation of noise. The effect of these non-ideal behaviors on the flame response will be evaluated.
UCI Coflow Burner
All ground-based experiments were performed using a coflowing burner that is dimensionally similar to the proposed ISS burner. The burner consists of two stainless steel plenums threaded together. Fuel, introduced in the bottom plenum, is passed through a stainless steel tube (2.13 mm ID) and exits the top surface fully developed. Air entering the top chamber passes through flow straightening beads and a honeycomb mesh. The air exits the top surface with a top hat flow profile at the exit. A variable high-tension power supply connected between the burner and downstream mesh electrode produces the applied electric field. The electric field distribution is deformed by the flame’s space charge. Regardless, defining an applied field strength, E = V/d, is a useful approximation when describing experimental results. Ion current is computed using Ohm’s law and the measured potential drop across a shunt resistor placed between the electrically isolated burner and the building ground. An acrylic chamber shields the flame from room currents.
Flame chemiluminescence and ion current
Results from a previous annual report discuss the strong relationship between the measured CH* chemiluminescence and the saturation ion current in non-sooting flames. The data suggested a bi-directional coupling between the luminous emission and the measured ion current. That is, the resultant ion wind modifies the flame structure, which influences ion production. This change in ion concentration intensifies the strength of the electrical body force and the measured ion current. At the saturation condition, the measured ion current can be related to the rate of ion production. However, because a flame must be altered by an electric field in order to measure the saturation current, a non-intrusive alternative may be possible using CH* chemiluminescence.
During the current reporting period we have expanded the conditions of the prior study to include sooting flames. In flames that produce incandescent soot, the emission spectrum from carbon, which is broad, interferes with CH* emission (~431 nm). In some cases, the soot spectrum collected through a narrowband filter centered at 430 nm contributed over 80% of the total emission measured. To filter out this noise, we investigated a method designed to remove the contribution of soot near the CH* emission line. The method involves measuring the emission through a pair of narrowband filters centered above and below this region. The scaled average of this measurement is proportional to the soot emission collected by a 430 nm filter to within 1%. The method was possible because of the near linear region in the broadband emission curve at 430 nm. After removing this contribution to the measurement, the remaining emission collected at 430 nm corresponds to CH*.
In lightly sooting methane flames, the method successfully removed the soot contribution from the flame image, and the resulting images reveal a previously obscured CH* distribution. In non-premixed ethylene flames, the method successfully removed the brightest portions of soot from the flame, leaving behind a luminous ring around the soot border. We originally suspected that this ring was an artifact of unsteadiness in the flame, but so far our careful repeated measurements suggest that this is not the case and that the signal does reflect CH*.
Because images are taken in sequence, this method is limited to steady flames. Follow on studies will explore tracking the CH* boundary in an unsteady sooting flame. If used with a calibrated PMT or a digital camera, this method may help determine the ratio of CH* radicals that eventually produce H3O+ ions, as well as identifying factors that influence the ratio. A calibration of the CH* emission was accomplished by Walsh et al., 2005, in determining the absolute CH* concentration (as compared to that of unexcited CH). We intend to use a similar approach.
Quenching studies
Professor Felix Weinberg at Imperial College is currently studying the effects of quenching on flame structure in order to predict the hazardous conditions created by poorly tuned industrial boilers. The ultimate practical aim of this series of experiments is to reduce the incidence of CO poisoning caused by the quenching of natural gas flames in malfunctioning burners. All the work involves progressively increasing proportions of air added to a constant fuel flow, so as to maintain a constant power input. The quenching measurements focus on compositions ranging from pure diffusion flames to progressively increasing air admixtures. The reason is that such burners (e.g., boilers) are designed to operate under near-stoichiometric conditions, and when they malfunction due, say, to an obstruction in the air supply, they tend to burn rich. Finally, we investigate how the flow of charge can be employed to signal the onset of hazardous conditions, before any CO release can occur.
Quenching
Concern about CO emission initially arose after observing appreciable concentrations of CO within the luminous boundaries of our flames. These results prompted the question of how much carbon monoxide would escape into the atmosphere if quenching disrupted the flame. We studied CO release for a variety of quenching surfaces, using an exhaust system which aspirated the emerging product gases, along with much ambient air.
The quenching bodies were clamped in a vernier positioner and the height of the quenching surface above the burner was recorded for each CO measurement. Of the numerous results, some show specific aspects of quenching behaviour. Although the Al grid, for example, also shows a small subsidiary peak that coincides with a maximum within the flame, it is clear that, close to the burner, quenching by some metals can generate CO from the reactants in excess of the amount present in the unperturbed flame. This is not surprising since Ni and Al have been used as constituents of catalysts for the production of syngas from natural gas. It implies that the use of new alloys in boiler tubing, and also metal impurities, may need to be scrutinized from that viewpoint.
We found no CO present from the products released beyond the region of luminosity which extends to about 16mm above the burner for diffusion flames and some 5 mm less for near stoichiometric premixed flames. This is worth bearing in mind, since all the parameters that follow are here plotted against H, the height above the burner.
The measurements imply that as much as 6% of the CH4 feed may be converted to CO. This is equivalent to 3 – 5 L/min for the 30kW recommended for a 1 bedroom flat. During 1999–2004, CO poisoning caused 16,447 deaths in the United States, the principal cause being incomplete combustion in malfunctioning heaters/boilers.
Electrical detection of proximity of quenching surface
The facility of monitoring flame – solid surface interactions electrically may have a variety of applications, not necessarily linked to quenching. In the present context, however, our chief objective was its use to detect the proximity to the flame of a quenching surface, well before any hazard of CO escape could arise. All the aforegoing measurements indicate that such a warning device should be based on a negatively charged burner to utilize the farther electron penetration. Comparison of the results already shows that as a ''quench detector" the current with the burner negative, signals the approach to a quenching surface at a height which is more than 30 mm in excess of that at which any quenching is ever recorded.
In practice, of course, quenching may occur by surfaces not directly above the flame. To explore the loci of electrical quenching detection, a rod with a rounded end was used as the positive electrode. It was clamped in the x-y-z positioner and manipulated to approach the flame orthogonally at locations all around the flame periphery. The contours of first detection of a current for both a pure fuel diffusion flame and a near-stoichiometric premixed flame at two potentials (37 and 56 V) were determined. Interestingly, the contours are remarkably similar to each other, in spite of the circumstance that the flow rate in the latter is ten times greater. They lie massively outside the regions in which CO is seen or detected in the products of quenching.
We conclude that detecting the proximity of quenching surfaces from a flame, to alert the user before any carbon monoxide is released, is feasible and requires only the use of small batteries. The detection is particularly effective in the hot post-flame region of the flow. It could readily be developed into a system which would give warning of hazardous conditions arising, say, from an unexpected elongation or change in flame shape due to, for example, an obstruction in the feed.
Near quenching
In addition to our efforts at Imperial College, parallel studies are underway at UC Irvine, studying the electrical properties of partially quenched flames. Our work at Imperial College has illuminated the potential dangers of improperly tuned boilers and the high concentration of carbon monoxide and hydrogen potentially emitted when quenched. This portion of our research is aimed at understanding the electrical behavior of a flame as a plate is incrementally lowered toward it by measuring the corresponding ion current. The study is a proof of concept to explore the potential of detecting flame impingement electrically without visual inspection. Previous work has shown that ion current sharply increases and finally saturates when lowering the plate toward the jet flame exit. The ion current decreases as the flame temperature and ion production fall.
We continued the work to study the phenomena occurring on the quenching plate as the flame approached it. Different quenching surface materials have various emissivity and thermal properties that lead to different equilibrium temperatures. Preliminary research involves identifying the thermal emission from the plate at different heights when lowered towards the flame (or when the flame sheet is interrupted). In order to understand the thermal phenomenon, a FLIR camera is used. The FLIR camera uses a thermography technique for taking thermal images. The test ran with a stainless-steel plate that had been painted with a layer of non-gloss heat resistant paint to prevent reflections. The FLIR camera was located right above from the top view of the plate while a flame is quenched underneath the plate. The image shows the plate’s temperature varies between 42 and 208 C, and the average is 112 C, when the emissivity is set as 0.98 and there is no viewing angle difference from the observed position. The next phase of this work will involve measuring electrical properties and their relationship to carbon monoxide release near quenching.

COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Combustion science
Task Description:
NOTE this is a successor agreement to "Applications of Electric Fields in Microgravity Combustion Science (NNX07AB55A)," per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
This joint project between the University of California, Irvine and Imperial College, London explores the use of large electric fields in combustion for the purpose of improving the performance of energy conversion systems. Electric fields have been shown to affect flame stability and soot formation; while as a sensing device, the flames electrical response can describe flame characteristics. In the past year, we have continued electric field testing on a coflow burner and jet diffusion burner for both methane and ethylene, which are proposed for the ISS experiment along with fundamental studies involving partially-admixed air/fuel jet flames. Specific activities over the year included:
1) Participating in the Requirements Definition Review to finalize requirements for our experiment and assure they are within CIR capabilities.
2) Irvine/NASA Glenn testing included, measuring the flame’s electrical response and voltage-current characteristic under various conditions, and reduced gravity testing at the NASA Glenn 2.2-s Drop Tower.
3) Experiments and numerical simulations of CO, H2, and ion formation in flames with varying levels of aeration.
4) Experiments designed to measure the ion current of a flame as it is progressively quenched.
5) Blackbody calibration of cameras for ground-based studies and development of algorithms to process color-filtered images from hardware expected for the ISS experiment for soot pyrometry.
Task Description:
The overall goal of this project is to understand the behavior of chemi-ionization in flames and to demonstrate the use of this understanding to manipulate combustion in beneficial ways (including enhancing flame stability and reducing flame soot). The project uses detailed measurements of electrical properties of flames in several ways.
First, we can create a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front; this is one of the rare and important action-at-a-distance effects on flames that can be used as a localized actuator. The effect of the wind has been demonstrated with a candle flame in parabolic flight based microgravity and in a spherical cage drop tower, but there has been no systematic study of the ion wind effect in the absence of the confounding effects of the approximately equal influence of buoyancy.
Second, we can use electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions. It is possible, therefore, to modify soot formation and to use charges attached to soot to affect soot transport. By adjusting the soot trajectory through the reaction zone it is possible to affect the oxidation of soot to prevent its eventual release or to modify the residence time of soot in different zones of the flame. It is also possible to use the neutral ion wind to change the mixing behavior of the flame and reduce soot in this way.
Finally, we can use the electrical properties to characterize the flame – there is a quantifiable relationship between the carbon content of a fuel and the ion current it can produce at saturation. This relationship is already exploited in a typical flame ionization detector (FID) analyzer for hydrocarbon emission where the carbon is burned in a hydrogen flame to create an ion current in proportion to the carbon influx. In direct flame interrogation, however, there are several confounding variables that can affect the ion current, including flame temperature (which generally affects the O atom concentration) and the reaction zone volume. Flame temperature can in turn be affected by levels of premixing, diffusion rates, fuel composition, and radiative loss. It is possible, therefore, to determine flame character from the ionization curve response.
Task Significance:
Understanding electric field interactions with flames is central to combustion control, particularly in situations near limit operation of the flame where small effects are amplified dramatically. Electric fields have been shown to modify burning rates as well as to enhance and reduce flame propagation even to the point of flame extinguishment. Our experiments provide a unique ability to make simultaneous measurements of both physical and electrical properties of flames.

Task Description: The experiments include the use of a counterflow burner apparatus, equipped with several diagnostic instruments such as Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV), Digital Particle Image Velocimetry (DPIV), thermocouples, and real-time flame visualization, for the study of strained reacting dusty flows. The counterflow system provides an ideal environment for the systematic study of the effect of strain rate on the particle dynamic response. The numerical aspects of this program include the development and use of quasi-one-dimensional and fully axisymmetric, two-phase modeling of the counterflow, with the use of detailed description of molecular transport and chemical kinetics in both phases. Experiments are conducted at normal and micro-gravity by utilizing the KC-135 aircraft. To obtain qualitative and quantitative information about the ignition, propagation, structure, and extinction behavior of reacting dusty flows at normal and micro-gravity, and gain physical insight into the controlling physico-chemical mechanisms. The research will allow for the systematic study of the effects of gas phase stoichiometry, strain rate, particle type and size, thermophoresis, and gravity on the ignition and burning characteristics of reacting dusty flows. The results are expected to be of interest to solid fuel combustion applications, explosions, material synthesis, and LDV and DPIV gas flow velocity measurement techniques. The understanding of the behavior of solid particles in reacting environments is very important. Inert particles can be present in reacting gas phase mixtures whose burning intensity can be affected. From a safety point of view, it is very important to understand how inert particles both hot and cold, can affect the ignitability and flammability limits of reacting gases. The understanding of the behavior of reacting particles is also very important, given that solids can be used in numerous earth- and space-based combustion processes. There is increased interest in clean solid burning for power generation in the not-very-distant future. Solids are also the chief candidates for space propulsion including future spaceships that will fly to Mars and return, utilizing the Martian carbon-dioxide. Furthermore, accidents can occur when a reacting dust accumulates in air and, in the presence of an ignition source, can result in explosion. Such explosions can occur during lumber milling, in grain elevators, and in mine galleries. Gravity forces particles to settle out of a gas flow. At normal gravity both gravity and the particle inertia can cause a non-convergence of the particle and gas flow fields, as is the case for large particles and low velocity gas flows for which gravity may dominate the hydrodynamic effects. Performing the experiments in micro-gravity allows the gravitational settling to be eliminated leaving only the hydrodynamic effects. Comparison between the normal and micro-gravity results will allow gravitational effects to be understood.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress: Within the scope of this work, an experimental combustion apparatus was developed in laboratory consisting of opposed-jet and stagnation type burners. A particle-seeding unit, which would work both at 1-g and µg was developed and manufactured. An experimental combustion rig, similar to the laboratory one, was designed and built for experimentation in µg environment. In this way, the stagnation flow type system, which is considered as one of the best techniques to perform systematic study on flames was introduced, for the first time, to a relatively long µg period facility, in this case the KC-135. The extinction characteristics of dusty premixed and non-premixed systems were investigated experimentally in 1-g and µg. The extinction conditions of flames seeded with inert or combustible particles were investigated as a function of strain rate (flow rate), particle type, particle diameter, particle delivery rate to the flow, gas-phase chemical composition and temperature, flame thickness and orientation. A CHEMKIN-based quasi-1D stagnation flow flame numerical code incorporating the presence of particles was developed to advance the current understanding of the physics behind these flows. Numerical simulations were performed to simulate the 1-g and µg extinction experiments and the adequacy of available theoretical models were assessed. The effects of Stokes drag, gravity and thermophoresis on particles in typical reacting flows were studied. The underlying physics of the counter-intuitive differences between the extinction behaviors of flames in 1-g and µg were explained, and the effects of relatively small and large particles were addressed. It was demonstrated that meaningful scaling of interactions between the two phases is not possible due to complex couplings between thermal and dynamic parameters of two-phase flows. A numerical investigation on the ignition behavior of premixed and non-premixed flames by hot inert particles in opposed-jet configurations was conducted. The effects of reactant-composition, strain rate, orientation of particle seeding, particle injection temperature and velocity were demonstrated. The differences with the ignition achieved by the interaction of combustible gases with hot gases were identified. The chemical pathways were analyzed and sensitivity analysis was performed, both for the first time, to determine the dominant kinetic paths of this unique type of flows.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
In FY 99 and FY 00 it had been shown numerically and experimentally that at low strain rates, extinction could be achieved more readily by injecting equivalent masses of larger inert particles rather than smaller particles. However, numerical results had also predicted that at higher strain rates smaller particles lead to extinction more readily. In FY 01 this result was confirmed experimentally, suggesting that the numerical code is predicting complex two-phase flow behaviors for a wide range of conditions. Simulations of the experimental data on flame extinction were also performed for the first time. Results were found to be in close agreement with experiments, again suggesting the reliability of the various models that have been introduced in the code. It was also found that the strain rate is not the only parameter that can determine what size particle cools more efficiently the gas phase.
In FY 02 the investigation was concentrated in three different areas. First, the effect of combustible particles on flame extinction was studied in normal gravity both experimentally and numerically for the first time. Second, the ignition of combustible gaseous mixtures by hot inert particles was investigated through detailed numerical simulations. Third, the detailed modeling of the flow around a single inert/reacting particle has been initiated.
Flame Extinction by Combustible Particles: The interaction of combustible solid particles (50 micron glassy-carbon) with atmospheric, strained, laminar premixed methane/air and propane/air flames in normal gravity was studied experimentally and numerically. It was found that at low strain rates, the particles could effectively burn within the gaseous flame zone and thus enhance the overall reactivity of the system and resistance to extinction. At high strain rates, however, the particles are rapidly transported through the flame and their ignition is delayed until they are well downstream of the flame and so have no effect or at best a minor one on the gaseous flame. If no ignition occurs, the combustible particles act simply as heat sinks, promoting extinction. It was found that the flame enhancement by the particles is more profound for Le
The experimental results for the twin-flame premixed case and Le 1 flame, however, the effect is similar to that of single-flames as the hot post-flame region is larger compared to Le
Flame Ignition by Hot Inert Particles: Ignition by sparks, glowing embers, or other hot particulate materials present serious safety hazards. In order to identify the mechanisms that control such events, a numerical study was conducted on the bulk ignition of premixed and non-premixed atmospheric methane flames by hot inert particles. For both premixed and non-premixed cases, increasing the amount of methane was found to inhibit ignition under all conditions considered. Analysis showed that the H-production is sensitive to the CH4 -> CH3 -> CH3O -> H path that is strengthened under fuel-lean conditions. While premixed ignition by hot particles was found to be similar to ignition triggered by impinging a mixture on heated air or oxygen, differences were observed for non-premixed systems. For non-premixed particle ignition, increasing the fuel concentration was found to always inhibit ignition, while in non-premixed gas-phase ignition this inhibiting effect was found to reverse at very low fuel concentrations. This is a result of the noticeably different gas phase temperature profiles that are induced during particle and gas-phase ignition. Finally, there is a major alteration in the ignition response of non-premixed particle ignition caused by moving the particle seeding from the fuel to the oxidizer side. This is attributed to the different thermal properties of the air and fuel that result in different heat transfer rates between the particles and air, in turn, affecting the kinetic paths leading to the production of H radicals.
Detailed Numerical Modeling of Flow Around a Single Inert/Reacting Particle: The ability of inert and/or reacting particles to ignite and extinguish the gas phase has been so far investigated numerically by only considering the particle as inert and by only considering its effect on the bulk behavior of the gas phase. However, under certain conditions the thermo-chemical events taking place at the immediate vicinity of the particle can modify the behavior of the bulk. For example, in our ignition studies of reacting gases by hot inert particles the main assumption is that ignition does not initiate at the particle surface but instead the gas is heated to the point of ignition.
Performing detailed numerical simulations of isolated particles that are exposed in convective streams will further assess the range of validity of such assumption. The simulation will be two-dimensional and will include detailed description of chemical kinetics and molecular transport. The equations have been formulated and the code will be first tested for pure heat conduction around a sphere. Subsequently, the effects of convection and chemical kinetics will be added.
In FY 03 the investigation was furthered in two main directions. First, a detailed numerical study was conducted on the ignition of non-premixed atmospheric methane/air flames containing inert aluminum-oxide particles in counterflow configurations. Second, the experimental and numerical study on the effect of combustible particles on flame extinction, which was initiated in FY 02 was extended to include the parameters which had not been considered earlier.
Hot Gas Flame Ignition in the Presence of Inert Particles: A detailed numerical study was conducted on the ignition of dilute non-premixed atmospheric methane/air flames containing inert aluminum-oxide particles in counterflow configurations. The injection temperatures of the fuel-side, the air-side, or both sides were increased separately until ignition was observed. The coupled conservation equations were solved for both phases along the stagnation streamline, with detailed descriptions of gas-phase chemical kinetics, molecular transport, and radiative heat transfer. The reactant injection temperature and orientation, strain rate, orientation of particle seeding, and injection particle number density and temperature were varied. Results showed that particles drastically modify the temperature field and thus the ignition temperature. It was found that when particle number densities are relatively high, the velocity field is also affected due to the momentum exchange between the two phases. Thus, the local strain rates and ignition temperatures are modified. Noticeable differences were observed among the three cases for which the injection temperatures of the fuel side or the air-side, or both sides were increased due to the different temperature fields generated. When particles are injected from the hot air-side rather than the cold fuel-side, lower ignition temperatures are observed. Also, flames were determined to ignite easier as the particle number density increases. These were found to be due to the effects that the particles have on the heat transfer at the vicinity of the ignition kernel. The effects of particle injection temperature on the hot gas ignition were investigated. It was demonstrated that the problem becomes a matter of competition between heating and cooling at various locations and the conditions under which particles assist ignition or retard it cannot be readily predicted without performing detailed analysis.
Flame Extinction by Combustible Particles: An experimental and numerical study was carried out on the effects of combustible solid particles on the extinction of atmospheric, strained, laminar premixed methane/air and propane/air flames in normal and micro-gravity. The study was conducted in the stagnation flow configuration by stabilizing single flames either below or above the gas stagnation plane by counter-flowing a reacting mixture against ambient-temperature air. Spherical 50 micron glassy-carbon and 32 micron Lycopodium particles were injected from either the mixture or the air-sides and the flame extinction states were experimentally determined. The data were analyzed to provide insight into the effects of gravity, strain rate, particle type, and injection orientation.
It was found that the presence of the particles does affect the reactivity of the gas phase negatively or positively depending on the strain rate. However, it was also determined that the particles have a more profound on extinction if they enter the flame from the upstream. This finding suggests that adding energy to the system before the gas reaction zone (upstream) is dominant over adding energy to the downstream of a flame, which, upon particle ignition, simply decreases the downstream heat loss from the flame. It was found that when carbon particles are injected into the downstream at low strain rates, they do not ignite and just cool the downstream, thus, increasing the heat loss from the flame, eventually facilitating extinction. It was determined that for moderate strain rates particle ignition occurs only in normal gravity but not in micro-gravity. When particles are seeded into the upstream of the flames, ignition happens only after particles pass the flame, reverse direction in the opposing jet and re-enter the flame from the downstream the second time. At low strain rates, however, ignition occurs both in normal and micro-gravity and occurs upstream of the flame making, thus, the effect of particles on extinction of gaseous flames more apparent.
Comparisons were made between the effects of glassy-carbon and Lycopodium particles. Lycopodium ignites at lower temperatures and it was found that its presence always enhances the overall reactivity of the system. This behavior was found to be more profound at high strain rates, which is in contrast to the behavior of glassy-carbon particles.
In our previous efforts on the understanding of the effects of combustible particles on flame extinction, we have treated the particles to be chemically “inert” in our numerical simulations and extracted insight based on the observed trends up to the location of predicted particle ignition, relying on the assumption that they would behave as inert up to that point. In FY04 we attempted to determine the validity of this assumption and dealt directly with the solid phase chemistry for the first time.
Independent detailed numerical simulations were performed for single glassy-carbon particles embedded into a stagnant gas using a previously reported one-dimensional sphero-symmetric transient code (SRPC, Single Reacting Particle Code). Its partner, the stagnation (SFC) code provides the gas-phase conditions and far field boundary conditions corresponding to different locations along the path of the particles. This provides an estimate of the reactivity of the particle and reveals the limits of the "inert" assumption.
The time integration in the SRPC was carried out until the particle's quasi-steady gasification rate was reached and the steady-state regression rate, RRp=dDp/dt, was determined. Then, by utilizing these RRp's the reduction of Dp can be calculated through time integration along the Lagrangian path of each particle calculated by assuming the particles to be inert. In the worst case examined, Dp had decreased by only 3%, thus, we found that the inert calculations can be relied on to accurately predict the trajectories and thermal histories of the particles.
As mentioned above, our previous studies on ignition had concentrated on the understanding of the gaseous flame ignition by means of injecting hot inert particles into combustible mixtures. We had also determined the differences between this type of ignition and the ignition of gaseous flames by impinging (hot or cold) fuel or fuel/air mixture against a hot air jet. We had also looked into cases where particles, which are not hot enough to ignite the gas by themselves, were injected into the gas and ignition was achieved by increasing the temperature of both or any of the two gas jets impinging on each other in oppose-flow configuration. However, this study was limited to non-premixed methane/nitrogen/air systems. In FY04, we have furthered this latter numerical investigation by looking into for the first time, premixed systems, and this time with hydrogen rather than methane as the fuel.
It was found that the ignition temperature (defined as the temperature at the hot boundary/boundaries at the point of ignition) increases with particle number density for all cases where particles are injected with the mixture, regardless of whether the temperature of the mixture side, the air side or both sides are increased to attain ignition. But the increase is much more notable for the case where only the air temperature is increased to achieve ignition. Ignition temperatures were found to be very similar for the other two cases. Similarly, the results for cases where the particles are injected with the air rather than the mixture, the ignition temperatures increase with particle number density, regardless of whether the temperature of the mixture side, the air side or both sides are increased to attain ignition. But this time much more notably for the case where only mixture temperature is increased to achieve ignition. Ignition temperatures for the other two cases were found to be very similar.
It was found that whether the mixture side or the air side temperature is increased does not matter for particle-free cases however, for higher particle number densities, ignition becomes much harder for the case where particles are injected with the mixture and the air temperature is increased for ignition compared to the case where particles are injected with the air and the mixture temperature is increased for ignition. This revealed that particles have more significant influence for the former case. The reason was determined as that the flames always try to ignite at the hottest location in the flow and in the latter case this is at the mixture nozzle. However, for the former case mixture is not injected hot and is heated by the hot opposing air-jet. Thus any mechanism that cools the air-jet at the interface of both jets (i.e. particles) requires that the air temperature is higher at the air nozzle, so that ignition can be achieved.
Our understanding of the behavior of combustible particles had been previously derived from their effects on the extinction of gaseous flames. Due to the relevance of combustible particles (especially metals such as Aluminum, Magnesium etc.) as propellants for future Mars missions, where the planet’s atmosphere is 95% carbon-dioxide and these metals are readily available on the surface, a new investigation was initiated in FY04, in which metal particle ignition and burning are studied in carbon-dioxide environment and in stagnation flow configurations. Various types of metals are being injected with a carbon-dioxide jet from the bottom burner against a stoichiometric carbon-monoxide/air or carbon-monoxide/oxygen premixed flame stabilized above the gas stagnation plane, where the product of combustion is largely carbon-dioxide. In this way, particles (that are small enough in size not to cross the GSP) are exposed to a hot carbon-dioxide environment that also provides the thermal energy required for the ignition of the particles.

Task Description:
The objectives of this program are twofold. The first is to utilize the results of the previous NASA support programs to continue to produce reference experimental data on near-limit flame propagation and extinction that will be of fundamental and practical importance. All experiments were performed for atmospheric flames in the counterflow configuration. The second objective is to compare the experimental data against numerical predictions and through such comparisons to validate current models describing the processes of chemical kinetics and thermal radiation and also gain insight into the mechanisms controlling the response of near-limit flames.
Task Objective:
To obtain quantitative information about the characteristics of weakly burning flames in microgravity, and to use this information to analyze near-limit phenomena at normal gravity and microgravity conditions.
The research will allow for the study of weakly burning flames without the complications of buoyancy, wall heat loss or time varying strain. It will provide fundamental data about the flammability limits, and has applications to turbulent combustion.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
It will provide fundamental data about the flammability limits, and has applications to turbulent combustion and space fire safety.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
Progress was made in four areas:

The cake flames are characterized by very small Karlovitz numbers and the obtained results are close to previous measurements. This approach may be appropriate for use in micro-gravity facilities.
2. The laminar flame speed has been traditionally used for the partial validation of flame kinetics. In most cases, however, its accurate determination requires extensive data processing and/or extrapolations, thus rendering the measurement of this fundamental flame property indirect. Additionally, the presence of flame front instabilities does not conform to the definition of the laminar flame speed. This is the case for Le
3. The lean flammability limits of CH4/air and C3H8/air mixtures were numerically determined for a wide range of pressures and unburned mixture temperatures in order to assess the near-limit flame behavior under conditions of relevance to internal combustion engines. The study included the simulation of freely propagating flames with the inclusion of detailed descriptions of chemical kinetics and molecular transport, radiative loss, and a one-point continuation method to solve around singular points as the flammability limit is approached. Results revealed that both pressure and unburned mixture temperature have significant effects on the lean flammability limit as well as the attendant limit flame temperature. Specifically, the lean limit was found to first increase and then decrease with pressure, while the limit temperature decreases with pressure in general, and can be reduced to values as low as 900 K under engine-like conditions. Through sensitivity and species consumption path analyses it was further shown that the chain mechanisms that control the near-limit flame response critically depend on the thermodynamic state of the mixture. Thus, mechanisms that are identified as important at near-atmospheric conditions may not be relevant at higher pressures and unburned mixture temperatures. In particular, the response of near-limit flames was found to resemble the homogeneous explosion limits of hydrogen/oxygen mixtures in that while at low pressures the main branching and termination reactions are respectively H + O2 --> OH + O and H + O2 +M --> HO2 +M, at the elevated pressures relevant to internal combustion engines the system branching is controlled by the HO2-H2O2 kinetics. Potential avenues for extending the lean operation limits of internal combustion engines are suggested based on the understanding gained herein.
4. The flame stability was assessed under normal gravity by using variable density inert gases. The hypothesis was that even under normal gravity flame stability could be enhanced for near-limit flames if the density gradients are minimized through the use of light inert gases such as helium whose density is seven times less than air and nearly equal to the density of typical combustion products. The studies were conducted in the opposed-jet configuration by counterflowing helium exiting the top burner against a hydrocarbon/air jet exiting the bottom burner. Helium was used also as the ambient gas. Experiment confirmed that by counterflowing methane/air or propane/air flames against helium extends the flame stability limits compared to using air instead of helium. This is due to the fact that by using helium the density gradients downstream of the flame are nearly eliminated and light gas always resides over heavy gas.
The H2/CO/C1-C4 kinetic model (111 species and 784 reactions), applicable to a wide variety of combustion scenarios, incorporates the recent thermodynamic, kinetic, and species transport updates relevant to high-temperature oxidation of hydrogen, carbon monoxide, and C1-C4 hydrocarbons was developed. Task Description:

The research will allow for the study of weakly burning flames without the complications of buoyancy, wall heat loss or time varying strain. It will provide fundamental data about the flammability limits, and has applications to turbulent combustion.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
It will provide fundamental data about the flammability limits, and has applications to turbulent combustion and space fire safety.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
In FY06, our research effort focused on (1) a new approach for the determining laminar flame speeds in a convenient manner especially under microgravity conditions, and (2) on the numerical determination of lean flammability limits under engine-like conditions.
Laminar flame speeds have been widely used to (partially) validate chemical kinetics. Experimental techniques for determining laminar flame speeds include among others: the Bunsen flame, the counterflow, the porous burner, the spherical flame, and the transition from Bunsen to flat flame techniques. With the exception of the transition one, all these approaches need either extrapolation or extensive data processing. The transition technique on the other hand requires a very special set of conditions that allow for stable flame transition, and such conditions may not be met during the short times available at reduced gravity facilities. In the present study, the “Cake-Flame Technique” is introduced, which allows for stabilizing flame at ultra-low strain rates and subsequently measuring its propagation speed. It was found that the propagation speeds of cake flames are rather close to the laminar flame speeds determined by the counterflow technique after invoking appropriate extrapolations. The strain rates of cake flames were found to be very low, with attendant Karlovitz numbers of the order 10^-2 ~ 10^-3. Compared to other techniques, the cake flame one is much simpler and can be performed in short times.
The determination of lean flammability limits under engine-like conditions were determined numerically using detailed kinetics and it was shown that a recent proposition that relates fundamental flammability limits to failure of engine operation below certain temperature is invalid.
