Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
In FY04, our research effort was made on the following aspects:
The rig has been re-organized and updated. Our experiments will include the determination of laminar flame speeds and extinction states for near-limit mixtures. For these measurements that DPIV technique will be employed. The variation of the mass flow rate is a very important aspect of the experimental procedure during the 2.2-sec drop time. To achieve flow rate adjustment a PID unit is employed and had to be integrate into the drop rig. In the previous design, the control circuit for the PID was not adjustable, but recently it was realized that, given the difference of flow rate change needed for different fuel/air mixtures and/or different equivalence ratio, the control circuit for the PID had to be adjustable. A new design of the control circuit has been finalized. The PID unit with the new adjustable control circuit is about to be tested. Additional improvements of the rig have been implemented.
Near limit, ultra-lean H2/air premixed flames were systematically studied at normal gravity. A significant discrepancy between experimental and predicted extinction strain rates was identified. The possible reasons that could cause such a discrepancy were determined through the use of sensitivity analysis. As this mathematical tool is not readily available in the existing stagnation flow codes, a "brute force" approach was implemented for performing sensitivity analyses. The effect of uncertainty associated with both kinetics and molecular diffusion process on the extinction strain rate was systematically assessed. For the sensitivity on rate parameters, the pre-exponential factor, A, of each reaction was perturbed by ±25% and the Kext was subsequently determined. For the sensitivity on the mass diffusion coefficients, the mass diffusivity of each species i to the mixture, Di,m, perturbed by ±25% and the Kext was subsequently determined. In both cases, logarithmic sensitivity coefficients were formed by determining the derivatives d(lnKex )/d(lnA) and d(lnKext)/d(lnDi,m) respectively for kinetics and diffusion.
As expected, the sensitivity analysis showed that the extinction strain rate is positively sensitive to the reactions H2 + O = OH + H , H2 + OH = H2O + H , HO2 + H = OH + OH , and the radical chain branching reaction H + O2 = OH + O. As also expected, the reaction H + O2 (+M) = HO2 (+M) exhibits a large negative sensitivity along with other radical-termination reactions, HO2 + OH = O2 + H2O HO2 + H = H2 + O2.
It is reasonable to attribute a part of the observed discrepancies to uncertainties associated with the rate parameters of the aforementioned reactions. However, the influence of kinetic uncertainties cannot be adequately assessed without considering the uncertainties in the diffusion coefficients. The sensitivity analysis showed the diffusivity of four species had a notable effect on Kext, namely H2, O2, H2O, and H. More interesting, the logarithmic sensitivity coefficients for diffusion are not only comparable to the ones of reaction rates, but in the case of the H2 are nearly 3 times larger that those of reaction rates. Additionally, the logarithmic sensitivities on the diffusivities of other species such as H and O2 while smaller than that of H2 are still of the order of those of reaction rates. Obviously, the discrepancies between experiment and simulation cannot be conclusively viewed as the kinetics being deficient, because the diffusion uncertainties may be solely responsible for the discrepancies. That validating kinetics mechanism against Kext’s without considering uncertainties related to diffusivities could result in the falsification of rate constants. It is important that the validation of models against flame data of such highly diffusive mixtures must be done by considering the uncertainties associated with both kinetics and molecular diffusion.

Task Description:
A technology roadmap developed in 1999 by the industrial combustion community under funding from the Department of Energy identified three core R&D needs for industrial combustion over the next 20 years. The highest priority needs were identified to be burner technologies, boiler systems and process heating systems. These technologies impact a wide range of industrial applications, such as power generation, heat treatment, kilns, drying, copper smelting and glass melting. Burners represent a cross-cutting technology and improvements in burner technology will have major payoffs. The industrial combustion roadmap identifies constraints and requirements for next generation burners that include emissions constraints, stabilization issues, and economical premixing mechanisms. The roadmap further states that the advanced burner of the future “would also be able to change the flame pattern or heat delivery from the burner” and that “one concept of a ‘smart’ burner incorporates non-steady-state combustion where fluctuations are controlled rather than random.” There is a clear need to scientifically explore all innovative burner concepts since it is not obvious what directions in burner designs will prove fruitful in the future. We are investigating an essentially unexploited burner strategy that uses high-intensity, high-frequency forcing of a fuel jet to achieve substantial partial-premixing of initially nonpremixed reactants. Our results show that it is possible to produce dramatic changes in the structure and luminosity of a turbulent nonpremixed jet flame with the application of strong forcing of the jet flow. For example, a turbulent nonpremixed methane jet flame, which exhibits substantial yellow luminosity due to emission from soot, can be made to turn completely blue and to shorten to about 1/3 of its original length, by the application of the forcing. These intense pulsations are achieved by modulating the fuel flow with a high-speed valve at a frequency that coincides with the organ-pipe resonance frequency of the fuel tube. The combination of rapid fuel flow rate modulation, coupled with the organ pipe resonance of the fuel tube results in very large amplitude, high –frequency modulation of the fuel gas pressure and velocity. The resulting flow exhibits a high degree of partial premixing of the fuel and air. Using direct flame photography, hotwire velocity measurements, planar laser induced fluorescence, and planar laser mie scattering we find that the changes in flame properties are due to ingestion (sucking) of ambient air into the fuel tube, vortex-ring entrainment, and turbulence generated by the unsteadiness. This form of high- amplitude, high-frequency forcing of the fuel jet differs significantly from most other forcing schemes, which tend to use low-amplitude, high-frequency (e.g. with a speaker) or high-amplitude, low-frequency (e.g. flame puffs) forcing.
In this project we will study and detail the mechanisms responsible for significant partial premixing in resonantly driven, transitional and turbulent jet diffusion flames. The ability to predict the flame length, and lifted flame length for these pulsed flames, and also the ability to discuss transitions between the luminous and nonluminous flame conditions requires careful experimental work. These experiments are to be divided between low gravity and normal gravity conditions. Differences in flame properties between the low gravity conditions and normal gravity conditions will help us to decouple buoyancy-induced modifications to mixing and flame length from acoustically-induced modifications. Some normal gravity experiments will use conventional measurements of gas species simply to establish the basic characteristics of this type of flame. Numerical modeling will be used to better understand the experimental results.
The objectives of this research are to: 1) characterize the mechanisms for increased near field mixing in strongly pulsed high frequency jet flames, 2) use the microgravity environment to develop an understanding of the role of buoyancy for near field mixed flames in modifying flame characteristics,
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The research has the potential to substantially reduce pollutants formed in jet diffusion flames which benefits our national goals towards a cleaner environment.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
Control of nonpremixed flames for tunable radiative and emissions properties represents an ambitious goal for combustion science. One mechanism to control flame properties is the use of fuel flow pulsing. In order to generate sufficiently strong pulsations over a wide frequency range, it has been useful to use the organ pipe resonance of the fuel tube to drive the fuel flow oscillations. Over the past three years of NASA funding we have experimentally and computationally investigated the effects of buoyancy on the pulsed flow control of nonpremixed flames. We found that radiative emissions associated with soot production is strongly tied to residence time in either soot growth promoting or soot growth inhibiting zones of the flame. The level of forcing impacts the relative amount of air (and oxygen) mixed with the fuel flow, and this ultimately affects the environment that the soot particles evolve in. A difference between normal gravity and reduced gravity flames pulsed at a similar level is that the reduced gravity flames appear to be broader and more luminous at the flame base. The higher luminosity of low-gravity flames has been observed previously in laminar flames and is typically considered to be due to increased soot formation resulting from the lower strain rates associated with the absence of buoyant acceleration. We should emphasize, however, that it has been established that this resonantly-forced jet exhibits significant partial premixing of non-fuel gas into the fuel stream, and it is believed that the premixing plays a significant role in the reduction in the soot luminosity of the forced (as compared to unforced) conditions. Therefore, it is possible that the increase in the soot luminosity could have to do with the modification of the partial premixing mixing in the absence of buoyancy. For example, in low gravity it is likely that the combustion products in the region near the tube exit are not convected away. In this case, the reverse flow may not be as efficient at bringing oxygen into the fuel tube, but instead entrains combustion products.
Summary and Objectives
In this project we studied and detailed the mechanisms responsible for significant partial premixing in resonantly driven, transitional and turbulent jet diffusion flames. The ability to predict the flame length, and lifted flame length for these pulsed flames, and also the ability to discuss transitions between the luminous and nonluminous flame conditions has required the combination of careful experimental and computational work. Experiments were divided between low gravity and normal gravity conditions. Differences in flame properties between the low gravity conditions and normal gravity conditions helped us to decouple buoyancy-induced modifications to mixing and flame length from pulsed-flow-induced modifications. Some normal gravity experiments used conventional measurements of gas species simply to establish the basic characteristics of this type of flame. Numerical modeling was used to better understand the experimental results.
The objectives of this research were to:
1) characterize the mechanisms for increased near field mixing in strongly pulsed high frequency jet flames,
2) use the microgravity environment to develop an understanding of the role of buoyancy for near field mixed flames in modifying flame characteristics,
Summary of Findings
Experimental Work
We designed a system to include our resonant acoustic burner into our existing drop rig. The development time for incorporating the burner into the rig was somewhat longer than we anticipated because of space restrictions in the drop rig. Dozens of drops were performed for the resonantly-forced jet flames at three different mean-flow Reynolds numbers (850, 1250, and 1850). In each case, the jet was fully-modulated at the organ-pipe resonant frequency of the tube. As discussed earlier, the strongly forced flames are blue and hence are not highly luminous; therefore, the imaging had to be performed at relatively low framing rates (500 Hz) and low shutter speeds. For both cases of normal and low gravity, as the Reynolds number is increased the flame appears shorter but wider. At the lower Reynolds number conditions, the structure of the flames is similar across gravity level over the lower half of the flame; however, the low-gravity flame becomes significantly more luminous farther downstream. The higher luminosity of low-gravity flames has been observed previously in laminar flames and is typically considered to be due to increased soot formation resulting from the lower strain rates associated with the absence of buoyant acceleration. We should emphasize, however, that it has been established that this resonantly-forced jet exhibits significant partial premixing and it is believed that the premixing plays some role in the reduction in the soot luminosity of the forced (as compared to unforced) conditions. Therefore, it is possible that the increase in the soot luminosity could have to do with the modification of the partial premixing mixing in the absence of buoyancy. For example, in low gravity it is possible that the combustion products in the region near the tube exit are not convected away. In this case, the reverse flow may not be as efficient at bringing oxygen into the fuel tube, but instead entrains combustion products. The clarification of this issue was a major goal of this research project.
Computational Work
We applied a finite volume CFDC (Computational Fluid Dynamics with Chemistry) code – UNICORN to study and simulate the strongly forced CH4–air diffusion flames. UNICORN (UNsteady Ignition and COmbustion with ReactioNs) solves the equations for the conservation of mass, momentum, individual species and energy in the unsteady formulation. The cylindrical form of the conservation equations are solved on a 2D axisymmetric staggered grid.
When going through the complete forcing cycle, the simulations clearly reveal that the forcing action serves to premix the fuel and air. The vortices generated by the forcing action bring in the cold air from the surroundings into the fuel stream, and thus premix the fuel and air. The reaction zone or the flame forms a cylinder, which surrounds the fuel-air mixture. The presence of oxygen in the internal part of the flame serves to oxidize the soot particles and thus result in dramatic soot reduction.

Task Description:
A technology roadmap developed in 1999 by the industrial combustion community under funding from the Department of Energy identified three core R&D needs for industrial combustion over the next 20 years. The highest priority needs were identified to be burner technologies, boiler systems and process heating systems. These technologies impact a wide range of industrial applications, such as power generation, heat treatment, kilns, drying, copper smelting and glass melting. Burners represent a cross-cutting technology and improvements in burner technology will have major payoffs. The industrial combustion roadmap identifies constraints and requirements for next generation burners that include emissions constraints, stabilization issues, and economical premixing mechanisms. The roadmap further states that the advanced burner of the future “would also be able to change the flame pattern or heat delivery from the burner” and that “one concept of a ‘smart’ burner incorporates non-steady-state combustion where fluctuations are controlled rather than random.” There is a clear need to scientifically explore all innovative burner concepts since it is not obvious what directions in burner designs will prove fruitful in the future. We are investigating an essentially unexploited burner strategy that uses high-intensity, high-frequency forcing of a fuel jet to achieve substantial partial-premixing of initially nonpremixed reactants. Our results show that it is possible to produce dramatic changes in the structure and luminosity of a turbulent nonpremixed jet flame with the application of strong forcing of the jet flow. For example, a turbulent nonpremixed methane jet flame, which exhibits substantial yellow luminosity due to emission from soot, can be made to turn completely blue and to shorten to about 1/3 of its original length, by the application of the forcing. These intense pulsations are achieved by modulating the fuel flow with a high-speed valve at a frequency that coincides with the organ-pipe resonance frequency of the fuel tube. The combination of rapid fuel flow rate modulation, coupled with the organ pipe resonance of the fuel tube results in very large amplitude, high –frequency modulation of the fuel gas pressure and velocity. The resulting flow exhibits a high degree of partial premixing of the fuel and air. Using direct flame photography, hotwire velocity measurements, planar laser induced fluorescence, and planar laser mie scattering we find that the changes in flame properties are due to ingestion (sucking) of ambient air into the fuel tube, vortex-ring entrainment, and turbulence generated by the unsteadiness. This form of high- amplitude, high-frequency forcing of the fuel jet differs significantly from most other forcing schemes, which tend to use low-amplitude, high-frequency (e.g. with a speaker) or high-amplitude, low-frequency (e.g. flame puffs) forcing. In this project we will study and detail the mechanisms responsible for significant partial premixing in resonantly driven, transitional and turbulent jet diffusion flames. The ability to predict the flame length, and lifted flame length for these pulsed flames, and also the ability to discuss transitions between the luminous and nonluminous flame conditions requires careful experimental work. These experiments are to be divided between low gravity and normal gravity conditions. Differences in flame properties between the low gravity conditions and normal gravity conditions will help us to decouple buoyancy-induced modifications to mixing and flame length from acoustically-induced modifications. Some normal gravity experiments will use conventional measurements of gas species simply to establish the basic characteristics of this type of flame. Numerical modeling will be used to better understand the experimental results.
The objectives of this research are to: 1) characterize the mechanisms for increased near field mixing in strongly pulsed high frequency jet flames, 2) use the microgravity environment to develop an understanding of the role of buoyancy for near field mixed flames in modifying flame characteristics, 3) develop scaling relationships that can be used to design burners for practical applications.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The research has the potential to substantially reduce pollutants formed in jet diffusion flames which benefits our national goals towards a cleaner environment.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
We have been making low gravity experiemntal runs in the UT-drop tower. The experimental measurements are primarily luminosity measurements. As expected, these measurements show that there is considerably more residence time in the low gravity flames than in the enormal gravity flames. The impact of residence time is explored in the soot luminosity and also in the transport of the large soot structures. These experiments make clear that even with strong pulsing of these effectively turbulent flames, the buoyant flows responsible for sweeping the low velocity regions of the flame flow field downstream have a significant effect on flame properties. We are processing these measurements to better define scaling parameters for these systems.
In computational work we have submitted a cold flow manuscript to the AIAA Journal, and have begun testing of the detailed chemistry model. We find from preliminary work on the detailed chemistry model that oxygen leakage may be a much more important mechansim for changes in the flame properties than we previously thought. We are presently introducing a simplified soot evolution model into the single step formulation.

Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Flame Measurements The effects of acoustic pulsations on the global parameters of methane jet diffusion flames like flame length and luminosity can be obtained from the flame measurements. To this effect flame measurements were made using a digital camera at resonant and non-resonant pulsing conditions of the fuel flow issuing out of the nozzle at different flow-rates. The luminosity and the flame length of the diffusion flames show a dramatic change as the flow is pulsed near resonant pulsing conditions, suggesting intense and localized mixing of the fuel and the surrounding air. Velocity Measurements Velocity measurements were made at the nozzle exit as well as at several downstream distances using a single-wire, constant temperature hotwire anemometer for air flow through the nozzle. Due to the use of single-wire hotwire probe, the velocity signal shows a large peak and then a small peak when pulsed at resonance frequency corresponding to the positive peak and negative peak, respectively. When pulsed at the second resonance frequency the velocities are still large compared to the un-pulsed velocity, however, the positive as well as the negative velocities are smaller than those of the first resonance frequency. For non-resonance pulsing, we found that the positive velocity increases to about twice that of the peak velocity at the un-pulsed condition. However, there is a negligibly small negative velocity which might be the reason for the non-resonantly pulsed flame looking similar to the un-pulsed flame. Power spectral desnity calculations were performed. These show that the distance where the coherent structures break down depends on the Reynolds number of the flow and the frequency of forcing. When the coherent structures break down, the spectral density shows a power law variation with a power law scaling of -5/3. Planar Laser Induced Fluorescence and Planar Laser Mie Scattering Using laser based diagnostic techniques like planar laser induced fluorescence (PLIF) and planar laser Mie scattering (PLMS), we investigated the physical mechanisms that lead to enhanced partial-premixing. Further insight into the mechanisms responsible for the effects due to pulsing of the flame was gained by imaging the light scattered from glycerol fog fed into the jet. This planar laser Mie scattering (PLMS) images were obtained at a rate of 8000 frames per second. The PLMS data showed that when the forcing frquency exceeded a critical value, the vortices generated at the nozzle exit plane were unable to separate from the nozzle. Numerical Analysis Simulations have been performed using a high-order finite difference code. These simulations have helped clarify the experimental findings. A limitation of the simulations is that only laminar flows can be simulated. Nevertheless, the laminar unsteady dynamics have clarified how the vortex formation and convection processes are modified by the unsteady flow. Both combustion and cold flow simulations have been performed to uncover the dynamics of the pulsed operation. With higher frequency forcing at the same amplitude level, we find that the vortex never escapes the nozzle region. This is similar to the experimental findings at the second resonance. If we push the amplitude even larger at the frequencies where the vortex does not initially escape for low amplitude forcing, we are able to dislodge the vortex.

Task Description:
This research investigates the effects of chemically-passive flame suppressants on the properties of laminar premixed flames at normal earth and microgravity conditions: considering various simple fuels for computational tractability with properties exhibiting various preferential-diffusion stability conditions that are known to affect laminar premixed flames (hydrogen and methane that are unstable at lean conditions, ethane that exhibits neutral stability and propane that is stable at lean conditions); various oxygen/nitrogen mixtures, fuel-equivalence ratios and pressures (to simulate spacecraft environments); and various chemically-passive flame suppressants (argon, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and water mist). The measurements will be reduced to find effects of test conditions on fundamental unstretched laminar burning velocities as well as simple concepts of flame suppression effectiveness such as minimum oxygen indices, laminar burning velocities, flame temperatures, etc.
The objectives of this research are: (1) to measure the effect of typical chemically-passive flame suppressants on laminar premixed flames at microgravity conditions relevant to spacecraft, and (2) to use the measurements to evaluate both detailed numerical simulations of the flames as well as simplified concepts of flame suppressant effectiveness such as minimum oxygen indices, laminar burning velocities, flame temperatures, etc., in order to provide rational rules for developing practical flame suppressants for spacecraft.
The significance of this research stems from the justification for limiting the study to consideration of effects of chemically-passive suppressants on the properties of laminar premixed flames. First of all, only chemically-passive suppressants are considered because chemically-active suppressants, such as Halons, generally are not allowable for spacecraft applications due to problems of astronaut health concerns and potential poisoning of spacecraft life support systems. Next, although most practical flames are turbulent, turbulent flames are difficult to study because experimental conditions are substantially complicated by the need to describe turbulence properties. In addition, turbulent flames cause turbulence-induced stretching and quenching, making them less conservative indicators of flame extinction than corresponding laminar flames. Another advantage of laminar flames is that they generally are tractable for detailed numerical simulations, unlike turbulent flames, enhancing capabilities to use computations to supplement directly measured properties. Laminar flames also are relevant to practical turbulent flames based on widely-accepted laminar flamelet concepts of turbulent flames. Finally, due to the complexities of turbulent flames, it seems unlikely that understanding of turbulent flame suppression will precede understanding of laminar flame suppression. Thus, for these reasons, it seems prudent to consider the suppression of laminar flames at the outset.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research benefits both the advancement of fundamental combustion science and the terrestrial fire suppression engineering community and industry.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Work during this report period involved experimental and computational evaluation of the effects of chemically-passive suppressants on laminar premixed hydrogen/oxygen/nitrogen/ suppressant flames at conditions where laminar flame speeds are reasonably fast so that effects of earth gravity are small; and the design/development of the short-drop free-fall apparatus for experiments to find flammability limits for various suppressants when effects of earth gravity are invariably important.
The studies of hydrogen/oxygen/nitrogen/suppressant flames involved experiments and numerical simulations for the following conditions: premixed hydrogen/air suppressant and hydrogen/30% oxygen and 70% nitrogen (by volume)/suppressant (the EVA-preparation atmosphere) flames; normal temperature (300 K); fuel-equivalence ratios of 1.0 and 1.8; pressures of 0.5, 0.7 and 1.0 atm; gaseous flooding type suppressants including helium, argon, nitrogen and carbon dioxide; and suppressant concentrations of 0-40% (by volume) which implies oxygen indices of 30-10. Major findings were that the suppressants increased in effectiveness in the order helium, argon, nitrogen and carbon dioxide, which reflects their progressively increased capabilities to either quench the reaction zone by their increased specific heats or to reduce flame velocities due to their reduced transport rates; the addition of chemically-passive suppressants generally decrease flame Markstein numbers which made them more susceptible to preferential-diffusion instability which increases flame speeds and counteracts effects of suppressants; hydrogen-fueled flames are unusually robust and still exhibit rapidly-propagating flames at oxygen indices smaller than ten; and predictions and measurements were in excellent agreement.
With the study of hydrogen/oxygen/nitrogen/suppressant flames completed, current work is concentrating on the development of a short-drop free fall facility needed for measurements of the effect of chemically-passive suppressants on flammability limits. Completing the development of this apparatus and initiating tests to find flammability limits for typical fuels, ambient atmospheres and passive suppressants will be the main focus of work during the next report period.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Initial numerical simulations of the effects of suppressants on laminar diffusion flames were carried out using the SANDIA code OPDIFF. Reactants of interest include hydrogen, wet carbon monoxide as fuels, with helium, argon, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide as suppressants. Oxidizing atmospheres include air and EVA-preparation atmospheres. These computations considered wet carbon monoxide flames, involving fuel mixtures of carbon monoxide and 3%, 5%, 10%, and 20% (by volume) hydrogen burning in oxidant mixtures of air and 0%, 10%, 20%, and 30% (by volume) suppressant.
Initial computations were undertaken to base line present work with the earlier computational and experimental work of Hassan et al. (1997) for the same wet carbon monoxide fuel mixtures but burning in pure air as premixed flames. In this case, the numerical algorithm was the SANDIA code PREMIX involving the wet carbon monoxide/air chemical kinetics of Kim et al. (1994) and Wang and Rogg (1993). The results of these baseline calculations are satisfactory thus far.
The test apparatus was assembled and some initial check-out tests were completed considering wet carbon monoxide as the fuel burning in air. These tests were quite successful with flame extinction conditions measured as a function of strain with little difficulty.
It was decided to use premixed hydrogen/carbon monoxide fuel mixtures and premixed air/suppressant oxidant mixtures in order to minimize reactant mixture blending errors by flow metering. This is important for the present test series because fuel and oxidant mixture flow rates to the opposed jet diffusion flame apparatus must be increased, while keeping the mixture compositions and the flame position unchanged, until quenching conditions are reached. In particular, initial attempts to do this while controlling four reactant streams (carbon monoxide, hydrogen, air, and suppressant) proved to be very difficult. Finally, all the flow meters were calibrated for the reactant mixtures of interest during the current series of test using wet-gas meters.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
Abstract. Work during this report period involved both flight- and ground-based experiments. Activities for the flight-based experiments consisted of reducing measurements of flame shapes and the distribution of soot properties within steady nonbuoyant soot-containing laminar jet diffusion flames during Space Shuttle Columbia flights STS-83, STS-94 and STS-107. These results were used to successfully evaluate a simplified model of the structure of these flames; subsequent application of this model suggested that soot properties within these flames should be universal functions of the degree of mixing of the fuel and the oxidant; these functions (called soot property state relationships) then provide a simplified and robust way of estimating soot properties in practical turbulent diffusion flames that otherwise would be computationally intractable for some time to come. This finding from the simplified model of flame structure was then confirmed by measurements of soot concentrations and continuum radiant emission from soot at wavelengths of 650 and 850 nm obtained from the observations of steady nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames. These findings show that steady nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames are the proper paradigm for soot processes in practical turbulent diffusion flames providing an experimentally tractable way to study soot processes in turbulent flames that will not be experimentally tractable for some time to come. The ground-based experiments involve detailed measurements of flame and soot properties in premixed and diffusion flame environments considering a variety of hydrocarbon fuels (CH4, C2H2, C2H4, C3H6, C3H8 and C6H6), gas temperatures of 1500-2350 K and pressures of 0.1-1.0 atm. In all cases, reaction rate properties were similar in premixed and diffusion flames and were independent of fuel type. Other conclusions of these measurements were as follows: primary soot particle surface growth rates were proportional to the product of the concentrations of C2H2 and H, and could be successfully correlated using existing Hydrogen-Abstraction-Carbon-Addition (HACA) mechanisms in the literature with steric factors on the order of unity, as expected; primary soot particle nucleation rates are crudely first-order with respect to the concentration of C2H2 and second-order with respect to the concentration of H, suggesting that nucleation is dominated by the formation of large PAH molecules via a HACA mechanism; and primary soot particle surface oxidation rates are dominated by the reaction with OH with a collision efficiency of 13%. Current work involves extending the range of the soot reaction property measurements to consider pressures of 1.0-10.0 atm and PAH as fuels in order to disclose any direct PAH reaction channels parallel to the HACA mechanism for soot surface growth.
Flight-Based Experiments. The flight-based experimental apparatus (called the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) Experiment) was successfully operated on the orbiting Space Shuttle Columbia during flights STS-83 in March 1997, STS-94 in July 1997 and STS-107 in January 2003. The test apparatus operated flawlessly and we were able to complete twenty-one (21) flame tests during flights STS-83 and STS-94, and twelve (12) flame tests during flight STS-107. No data was lost during flights STS-83 and STS-94, however, half the normally downlinked data and all of the sampling data was lost due to the unfortunate loss of the Space Shuttle Columbia and its crew during Space Shuttle Flight STS-107. Measured properties included flame images (lengths, diameters, and shapes), and distributions of soot properties in the flames (soot volume fractions, soot temperatures and soot radiative emission properties at two wavelengths based on imaging data and soot structure based on thermophoretic sampling and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)). The test conditions considering all three flights were unusually broad and involved ethylene- and propane-fueled laminar jet diffusion flames burning in still air at pressures of 35-130 kPa, for burner diameters of 0.4-2.70 mm, and for burner exit Reynolds numbers of 46-1186. These conditions yielded steady nonbuoyant round laminar jet diffusion flames whose lengths ranged from soot-free (blue) flames to flames near the laminar smoke point. The first stage of data reduction involved evaluation of the classical analysis of the structure of steady nonbuoyant round laminar jet diffusion flames due to Spalding (1979), after empirically extending this analysis to account for luminosity due to the presence of soot within the flames. It was found that the extended Spalding (1979) analysis provided excellent predictions of the shape properties of the test flames, when radiative heat losses were small so that the intrusion of effects of thermal quenching were avoided. This analysis also shows that flame properties are identical functions of time along all soot paths emanating from the jet exit and subsequently convecting at the local velocity within the flame through the flame sheet to the ambient environment. In addition, the universality of flame properties as a function of time is also preserved even when jet exit velocities are varied. These characteristics imply that the soot properties of these flames are universal functions of the extent of mixing of the flow because soot particles convect through flames at local gas velocities, as well. As a result, soot in steady nonbuoyant round laminar jet diffusion flames should satisfy soot property state relationships in contrast to the behavior of soot properties in steady buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames where the intrusion of effects of buoyancy due to earth’s gravity prevents behavior that satisfies soot property state relationships. The existence of soot property state relationships was subsequently confirmed by direct measurements of soot volume fractions, and continuum radiant intensities at wavelengths of 650 and 850 nm, from the flight-based flames. Finally, the existence of soot property state relationships has four (4) important implications for practical applications, as follows: (1) it helps explain the surprising universality of soot properties within large hydrocarbon-fueled buoyant turbulent diffusion flames; (2) it helps explain why buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames do not exhibit soot property state relationships whereas these properties are observed for nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames, which implies that only the latter are the proper laminar flame paradigm for the soot properties of practical turbulent diffusion flames; (3) it provides a tractable and robust way to develop methods of computational combustion for nonpremixed turbulent flames involving the combustion of hydrocarbons; and (4) it provides insight concerning the way that modifying the mixing properties of turbulent flames (e.g., by using air atomization for liquid-fueled propulsion systems) reduces the amount of soot formed and emitted from practical combustion processes. Finally, work during the next report period will involve extending the direct evaluation of the existence of soot property state relationships based on the imaging data available for laminar soot property flame experiments during Space Shuttle Columbia flights STS-83, STS-94 and STS-107.
Ground-Based Experiments. Development of a fundamental understanding of the reaction properties of soot particles continued, based on detailed measurements of the structure of steady buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames. Earlier measurements involved both premixed and nonpremixed (diffusion) flame environments, a variety of hydrocarbon fuels (CH4, C2H2, C2H4, C3H6, C3H8 and C6H6), gas temperatures of 1500-2350 K, and pressures of 0.1-1.0 atm. These measurements were used to study primary soot particle surface growth rates, primary soot particle nucleation rates and primary soot particle early oxidation rates (before 70% of the maximum soot mass is oxidized after which the soot surface becomes porous and internal soot oxidation becomes a factor). These results showed that fundamental soot particle reaction properties were independent of flame type (premixed or diffusion), fuel type, temperature and pressure (in the range 0.1-1.0 atm). In particular, primary soot particle surface growth rates satisfied existing Hydrogen-Abstraction-Carbon-Addition (HACA) mechanisms due to Kazakov et al. (1995) and Colket and Hall (1994), with unknown steric factors in these mechanisms having values on the order of unity, as expected. In addition, primary soot particle nucleation rates were correlated effectively by assuming that the rate of development of large PAH molecules by the Hydrogen-Abstraction-Carbon-Addition (HACA) mechanism controlled primary soot particle nucleation rates having first and second molecular orders with respect to the concentrations of acetylene and H, respectively. Finally, early primary soot particle surface oxidation rates for all the flames were found to satisfy the OH/O2 surface oxidation mechanism that Neoh et al. (1980) established based on measurements in the post-flame region of laminar premixed flames with a collision efficiency of OH for early soot oxidation of 13% and a relatively weak direct O2 reaction pathway based on the classical results of Nagle and Strickland-Constable (1962).
Given these results concerning primary soot particle surface growth rates, primary soot particle nucleation rates and early primary soot particle oxidation rates in laminar premixed and diffusion flames, for various hydrocarbon fuels (CH4, C2H2, C2H4, C3H6, C3H8 and C6H6), gas temperatures of 1500-2350 K, and pressures of 0.1-1.0 atm, information needed to simulate soot reaction properties in flame environments is generally in hand. There are two areas, however, where additional information is needed, as follows: (1) the potential effect of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) fuels, which could enhance primary soot particle surface growth and nucleation rates compared to the flame environments considered thus far; and (2) effects of pressure on soot particle reaction rates at pressures greater than atmospheric pressure that are relevant to numerous practical combustion applications. In order to fill these gaps in the literature detailed measurements of flame structure and soot properties are being undertaken to consider a typical PAH fuel (toluene) burning in an air coflow at atmospheric pressure, and acetylene fueled flames burning in an oxidizing coflow at pressures of 1.0-10.0 atm. The specific test conditions involve a total of seven (7) steady round buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames, with the fuel jets directed vertically upward and soot and flame structure measurements limited to various positions along the axes of the flame, similar to past work. The measurements are also similar to past work: soot volume fractions using deconvoluted laser absorption, primary soot particle diameters using thermophoretic sampling and analysis by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and High Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy (HRTEM), flow (soot) temperatures using deconvoluted multiline emission, flow velocities using laser velocimetry, concentrations of major stable gas species by isokinetic sampling and analysis using gas chromatography, and concentrations of some radial species (H, OH and O) using the deconvoluted Li/LiOH atomic absorption technique.
Observations for the seven new flames will be combined with past observations of the twenty-two (22) earlier flames in order to study effects of local flame properties on soot surface reaction properties.
Work completed thus far has involved establishing test conditions for the three toluene-fueled flames at atmospheric pressure and the four (4) acetylene-fueled flames at pressures of 1.0-10.0 atm. Complete measurements for each series of flames, along with data reduction and analysis of the measurements, takes roughly one man year. We are well along with the measurements of both series of flames and will complete this phase of the investigation during the next report period.
Understanding the mechanisms of soot reactions in flame environments on earth has significant relevance to society. Several specific effects of soot are important to both public health and combustion technologies, as follows: pollutant soot emitted from combustion processes causes more deaths than any other pollutant, comprising roughly 60,000 premature deaths each year in the US alone; carbon monoxide emissions intrinsically associated with soot emissions from flames cause 80 percent of the fatalities of unwanted fires, comprising roughly 4,000 deaths each year in the US alone; continuum radiation from soot is mainly responsible for the growth and spread of unwanted fires, causing 5,000 deaths each year in the US alone; particulate soot emitted from combustion processes has recently been identified as a major contributor to global warming; particulate soot emitted from combustion processes has recently been shown to cause melting of ice and snow in arctic regions by settling on their surfaces and increasing their absorption of solar radiation; and successful development of computational combustion is improbable without an understanding of soot reaction properties in flame environments. These observations amply motivate study of soot reaction properties in flames.

Task Description: The current proposal will explore the aspects of flame dynamics and ultimate fate of an already ‘established droplet cool flame’ under external thermal and convective perturbation through multi-physics based multi-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis addressing the variability observed in the International Space Station (ISS) experiments. Here, we will investigate the two extremities of n-heptane droplet sizes pertaining to droplet combustion -- (a) large diameter (typical to that of NASA FLame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) experiments, 1-4 mm) and (b) small diameter (submillimeter dimension, ~0.5 mm). The discovery of n-heptane droplet ‘cool flame’ on board the International Space Station (ISS) has introduced new research thrust in understanding the intricate behavior of ‘cool flame’ for diffusion control environment. Even though these studies were targeted to be performed in near-absence external convection influence, perturbations in the experiments resulted in slow drift of the droplet thereby generating an unintentional convective field. The role of this convective field on the observed “cool flame” dynamics is not quantified and determined. Additionally, to address the design of next generation combustor deploying cool flame and/or low temperature (LT) kinetics, a better understanding about how quasi-steady ‘self-sustained’ cool flame behave in response to induced convective perturbation is important and critical. The objective of the proposed research is to determine the role of thermal and convection influence on the cool flame dynamics – analyzing and interpreting the ISS data and hence extending the interpretation to submillimeter sized droplets. In order to achieve the proposed objectives, multi-dimensional multi-physics OpenFOAM (Foam Optics And Mechanics) based CFD platform will be utilized incorporating detailed combustion chemistry and associated fluid physics under the influence of convection and thermal field. ISS FLEX cases performed under microgravity will serve as base comparison case. Subsequently, three possible fluid fields (with convection influence, with heat flux influence, and combination thereof) for single droplet will be considered. For initial model development in OpenFOAM, simplified reaction kinetics will be deployed and subsequently the computation effort will be casted towards the incorporation of reduced kinetics. The proposed hybrid multi-physics model will be developed to get deeper insight into the FLEX cool flame experimental observation exploring the influence of external perturbation to cool flame itself. Therefore, any constitutive analysis, conclusion, and/or hypothesis drawn from such numerical works will directly and coherently support the title objective of the NASA Research Announcement (NRA) Appendix B solicitation, i.e., ‘reusability’ of the available database. Furthermore, these detailed analyses will help NASA in developing test matrix for large diameter cool flame experiments under external perturbation. Lastly, ozone assisted small diameter investigations using the proposed computational strategies can assist NASA in designing experimental test matrix for observing first ever submillimeter sized droplet cool flame and its interaction with external perturbation.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Low temperature combustion (LTC) and its association with cool flame kinetics have recently become leading research topics of interest due to their relevance to achieving high thermal efficiency, fuel flexibility, and low pollutant emissions for both advanced and legacy internal combustion engine applications. Despite promising lab-scale demonstrations of LTC technologies (e.g., homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) and reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI) engines)), the lack of fundamental understanding of the associated chemical kinetics continues to limit implementation of LTC technology in reciprocating engines and the interpretation of near-limit behaviors in gas turbine engines (e.g., lean blow off). A clearer understanding of the kinetics on pressure, temperature, equivalence ratio, and fuel structure is critical for enabling these new technology developments. Considering the fuel injection techniques commonly utilized in the aforementioned engine technologies, understanding how the dynamics and chemistries of LTC depend on fuel physical properties and distillation characteristics is also critical for these multi-phase, multi-component applications.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
The tasks completed resulted in 5 papers (4 published and 1 in review). The major tasks accomplished:
Task 1: Oscillatory cool flame combustion behavior of submillimeter sized n-alkane droplet under near limit conditions
This task reports simulation results of oscillatory cool flame burning of an isolated, submillimeter sized n-heptane droplet in a selectively ozone seeded nitrogen-oxygen environment at atmospheric pressure. An evolutionary one-dimensional droplet combustion code encompassing relevant physics and detailed chemistry was employed to explore the roles of low temperature chemistry, ozone seeding, and dynamic flame structure on burning behaviors. For XO2=21% and a range of selective ozone seeding, near-quasi-steady cool flame burning is achieved directly (without requiring hot flame initiation and radiative extinction). Under low oxygen index conditions, but with significant ozone seeding, a nearly quasi-steady cool flame is initially established that then transitions to a dynamically oscillating cool flame burning mode until the droplet is completely consumed. It is found that the oscillation is initiated by the depletion of a fuel vapor-oxidizer layer evolving near the droplet surface and its dynamic re-establishment through liquid vaporization and vapor/oxidizer transport. A kinetic analysis indicates that the dynamic competition between the reaction classes – (a) degenerate chain branching, and (b) chain termination/propagation – along with continuous fuel and oxygen leakage through the flame location contributes to an oscillatory burning phenomena of ever-increasing amplitude. Analysis based on a single full-cycle of oscillatory burning shows that the reaction progression matrices (evolution of heat and species) for hydroperoxy alkyl (QOOH) chain propagation/termination reactions directly scale with the gas phase temperature field. On the contrary, the hydroperoxy alkyl (QOOH) degenerate branching reactions undergo three distinct stages within the same cycle. The coupled flame dynamics and kinetics suggest that in the oscillatory burning mode, kinetic processes dynamically cross through conditions characterizing the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) turnover temperature separating low temperature and NTC kinetic regimes. In addition, a parametric study is conducted to determine the role of ozone seeding level on the observed oscillation phenomena.
Task 2: Dynamics of cool flames
Cool flames play a critical role in ignition timing, burning rate, burning limits, engine knocking, and emissions in conventional and advanced combustion engines. [Ed. Note. Reference: Ju Y, Reuter CB, Yehia OR, Farouk TI, Won SH. “Dynamics of cool flames.” Progress in Energy and Combustion Science. 2019 Nov;75(100787):1-39.] This paper provides an overview of the recent progress in experimental and computational studies of cool flames. First, a brief review of low temperature chemistry and classical studies of cool flames is presented. Next, the recent experimental and computational findings of cool flames in microchannels, microgravity droplet combustion, counter-flow flames, and turbulent combustion environments are reviewed. The flammability diagrams of different low temperature flames and their relations to hot flames in premixed and nonpremixed systems are discussed. The impact of cool flames on turbulent combustion and knock formation is also highlighted. Finally, future avenues in cool flame research, including the use of cool flames as a new platform for low temperature kinetic model validation, are presented. It is concluded that the understanding and control of low temperature combustion is critical for the development of future advanced engines and new fuels.
Task 3: Initial diameter effects on combustion of unsupported equi-volume n-heptane/iso-octane mixture droplets
Combustion of stationary fuel droplets comprised of an equi-volume mixture of n-heptane and iso-octane with initial diameters (Do) ranging between 1 mm and 6 mm was studied under this task. The intent was to show that by increasing Do to large enough values the burning mode would transition to a “Cool Flame” (CF) regime. The principle mechanism for the transition is radiative losses from the droplet flame that dominate the thermal field for large droplets. Unsupported or free-floating and droplets were probed in experiments carried out on board the International Space Station to promote spherical symmetry and a one-dimensional transport process in the standard atmosphere. The simulations employed a kinetic mechanism comprised of 298 species and 1916 reactions which included radiation, variable transport properties, and unsteady liquid and gas phase transport. Radiative losses from the droplet flame were unimportant for Do
Task 4: Sub-millimeter sized multi-component jet fuel surrogate droplet combustion
Isolated droplet burning behaviors of real jet fuel surrogates that all share the same kinetic behaviors for predicting fully pre-vaporized combustion behaviors of “global” Jet-A real fuel are investigated numerically. The three multi-component surrogate fuels (Surrogate-1: n-decane/iso-octane/toluene 42.7/33.0/24.3, Surrogate-2: n-dodecane/iso-octane/1,3,5 trimethyl benzene 49.0/21.0/30.0 and Surrogate-3: n-hexadecane/iso-octane/1,3,5 trimethyl benzene 36.5/31.0/32.5 molar ratios) have disparate distillation curve and other physical properties. Isolated droplet burning computations are used to compare and analyze the coupled effects of physical and chemical properties on predictions in comparison to microgravity data previously published in the literature. Simulations are performed using a transient one-dimensional sphero-symmetric model, involving numerically reduced detailed chemical kinetics, and multi-component gas-phase diffusive transport. Predictions agree well with microgravity experimental data published previously for surrogates 1, especially by including sooting effects in the computations. The interactions among the different liquid-phase components are modeled using UNIFAC activity coefficient methodology. [Ed.Note: UNIFAC is the UNIversal quasichemical Functional group Activity Coefficients method.] Stagnant and internally mixed liquid-phase behaviors are considered. The roles of preferential vaporization behavior are comprehensively evaluated by varying fuel composition, droplet size and ambient pressure conditions. Impacts of preferential vaporization on observed behaviors are highly sensitive to the droplet size, and thermodynamic conditions of the surrounding ambient. An expression for the degree of preferential vaporization effects is proposed, expressed in terms of average, maximum, and ignition burning rate. Preferential vaporization was found to have a strong non-linear dependence on initial droplet diameter, as well as operating pressure conditions. This implies that the preferential vaporization might have significant and dominant impact on multiphase/spray combustion of multicomponent fuels.
Task 5: Extinction characteristics of isolated n-alkane fuel droplets during low temperature cool flame burning in air
Large carbon number n-alkanes are notable components in all real transportation fuels, and their chemical structures foster substantial low temperature kinetic reactivity. Normal alkanes have been studied in various canonical configurations but rarely in systems with strong coupling between low temperature chemistry and transport for pure as well as for multi-component n-alkane mixtures. The Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experiments on board the International Space Station have provided a unique platform for investigating low temperature multi-phase n-alkane and iso-alkane combustion. Among the many interesting phenomena experimentally observed, cool flame extinction can occur, accompanied by the concurrent formation of a surrounding cloud of condensed vapor. In this work, we conduct numerical simulations of high and low temperature combustion of large, initially single-component n-heptane, n-decane, and n-dodecane droplets. The role of initial droplet diameter, operating pressure, and n-alkyl carbon number on the extinction of hot and low temperature flames is investigated and compared against the available experimental data. While all three fuels exhibit similar hot flame behavior, cool flame activity increases with the carbon number, resulting in an increased cool flame temperature and decreased extinction diameter. Multi-cyclic “hot/cool flame transitions” are found in air as pressure is slightly increased above one atmosphere. The cyclic behaviors correspond to continuously varying hot and cool flame transitions across the high, low, and negative temperature coefficient (NTC) kinetic regimes. Further increase in pressure results in a second stage steady “Warm flame” transition. The extinction of hot and cool flame has a strong non-linear dependence on ambient pressure; but as the hot flame extinction diameter increases with pressure, the extinction diameter of the cool flame decreases. The computational results are compared with a recent asymptotic analysis of FLEX n-alkane cool flames.

The three multi-component surrogate fuels (Surrogate-1: n-decane/iso-octane/toluene 42.7/33.0/24.3, Surrogate-2: n-dodecane/iso-octane/1,3,5 trimethyl benzene 49.0/21.0/30.0 and Surrogate-3: n-hexadecane/iso-octane/1,3,5 trimethyl benzene 36.5/31.0/32.5 molar ratios) have disparate distillation curve and other physical properties. Isolated droplet burning computations are used to compare and analyze the coupled effects of physical and chemical properties on predictions in comparison to microgravity data previously published in the literature. Simulations are performed using a transient one-dimensional sphero-symmetric model, involving numerically reduced detailed chemical kinetics, and multi-component gas-phase diffusive transport. Predictions agree well with microgravity experimental data published previously for surrogates, especially by including sooting effects in the computations. The interactions among the different liquid-phase components are modeled using UNIFAC activity coefficient methodology. Stagnant and internally mixed liquid-phase behaviors are considered. The roles of preferential vaporization behavior are comprehensively evaluated by varying fuel composition, droplet size and ambient pressure conditions. Impacts of preferential vaporization on observed behaviors are highly sensitive to the droplet size and thermodynamic conditions of the surrounding ambient. An expression for the degree of preferential vaporization effects is proposed, expressed in terms of average, maximum and ignition burning rate. Preferential vaporization was found to have a strong non-linear dependence on initial droplet diameter as well as operating pressure conditions. This implies that the preferential vaporization might have significant and dominant impact on multiphase/spray combustion of multicomponent fuels.

Task Description:
The current proposal will explore the aspects of flame dynamics and ultimate fate of an already ‘established droplet cool flame’ under external thermal and convective perturbation through multi-physics based multi-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis addressing the variability observed in the International Space Station (ISS) experiments. Here, we will investigate the two extremities of n-heptane droplet sizes pertaining to droplet combustion -- (a) large diameter (typical to that of NASA FLame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) experiments, 1-4 mm) and (b) small diameter (submillimeter dimension, ~0.5 mm). The discovery of n-heptane droplet ‘cool flame’ on board the International Space Station (ISS) has introduced new research thrust in understanding the intricate behavior of ‘cool flame’ for diffusion control environment. Even though these studies were targeted to be performed in near-absence external convection influence, perturbations in the experiments resulted in slow drift of the droplet thereby generating an unintentional convective field. The role of this convective field on the observed “cool flame” dynamics is not quantified and determined. Additionally, to address the design of next generation combustor deploying cool flame and/or low temperature (LT) kinetics, a better understanding about how quasi-steady ‘self-sustained’ cool flame behave in response to induced convective perturbation is important and critical. The objective of the proposed research is to determine the role of thermal and convection influence on the cool flame dynamics – analyzing and interpreting the ISS data and hence extending the interpretation to submillimeter sized droplets. In order to achieve the proposed objectives, multi-dimensional multi-physics OpenFOAM (Foam Optics And Mechanics) based CFD platform will be utilized incorporating detailed combustion chemistry and associated fluid physics under the influence of convection and thermal field. ISS FLEX cases performed under microgravity will serve as base comparison case. Subsequently, three possible fluid fields (with convection influence, with heat flux influence, and combination thereof) for single droplet will be considered. For initial model development in OpenFOAM, simplified reaction kinetics will be deployed and subsequently the computation effort will be casted towards the incorporation of reduced kinetics. The proposed hybrid multi-physics model will be developed to get deeper insight into the FLEX cool flame experimental observation exploring the influence of external perturbation to cool flame itself. Therefore, any constitutive analysis, conclusion, and/or hypothesis drawn from such numerical works will directly and coherently support the title objective of the NASA Research Announcement (NRA) Appendix B solicitation, i.e., ‘reusability’ of the available database. Furthermore, these detailed analyses will help NASA in developing test matrix for large diameter cool flame experiments under external perturbation. Lastly, ozone assisted small diameter investigations using the proposed computational strategies can assist NASA in designing experimental test matrix for observing first ever submillimeter sized droplet cool flame and its interaction with external perturbation.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Low temperature combustion (LTC) and its association with cool flame kinetics have recently become leading research topics of interest due to their relevance to achieving high thermal efficiency, fuel flexibility, and low pollutant emissions for both advanced and legacy internal combustion engine applications. Despite promising lab-scale demonstrations of LTC technologies (e.g., homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) and reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI) engines), the lack of fundamental understanding of the associated chemical kinetics continues to limit implementation of LTC technology in reciprocating engines and the interpretation of near-limit behaviors in gas turbine engines (e.g., lean blow off). A clearer understanding of the kinetics on pressure, temperature, equivalence ratio, and fuel structure is critical for enabling these new technology developments. Considering the fuel injection techniques commonly utilized in the aforementioned engine technologies, understanding how the dynamics and chemistries of LTC depend on fuel physical properties and distillation characteristics is also critical for these multi-phase, multi-component applications.

We had used computations over the past year to:
• characterize the dynamics of cool flame for a Primary Reference Fuel (PRF) droplet containing 50% n-heptane and 50% iso-octane mixture
• investigate the effect of droplet diameter on the cool flame behavior of PRF droplets
• analyze the role of multicomponent liquid droplet on the overall combustion behavior
• investigate the influence of sooting behavior on multicomponent droplet combustion.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
The first phase of this project encompasses three different studies pertaining to smaller droplet (Do = 0.5 mm), those that are amenable to perform terrestrial drop tower based tests-- (1) Initiation of directly established cool flame for sub-millimeter sized droplet utilizing selective ambient O3; (2) Mechanistic understanding of direct cool flame initiation for higher flash point fuels; (3) Dynamics of continuously expanding oscillatory cool flames.
In the first study, isolated n-alkane droplet combustion was numerically studied for different initial diameters (Do = 0.1, 0.5 mm), ambient pressures (1, 25 atm) with selected levels of O3 in the surrounding. This study primarily focuses on the exploration pathway to introduce directly established cool flame for sub-millimeter sized n-alkane droplets. It was found that the required initiation energy for igniting low and high flashpoint (relative to ambient temperature) fuel droplets differ due to the difference in fuel vapor accumulation near the liquid surface vicinity as a result of disparate flash point temperature. This results in a different strength (fuel mole fraction) of combustible partially premixed flammable vapor mixture. The rapid combustion of the premixed mixture provides additional energy feedback to sustain combustion during the transition from partially premixed to diffusive burning. In the case of high flash point fuel, the condensed phase droplet must be heated above its flash temperature by the initiation energy, which must also provide the energy to sustain the transition to diffusive burning.
In the second study, we extended the concept of ozone-assisted, directly induced cool flame combustion of the submillimeter-sized droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) for n-C10H22 and n-C12H26. It is found that simply modulating the ignition energy alone, especially for low flash point fuels, is an ineffective means of directly establishing cool flame burning. However, a combination of selective O3 loading and ignition energy have the potential to directly initiate cool flame for all three fuels at atmospheric pressure and temperature condition and for droplet sizes commensurate with ground-based experimental techniques. The absence of sufficient fuel vapor around the droplet for heavier n-alkanes compared to its low flash point counterpart prohibits the direct establishment of cool flame. Upon ignition, the fuel vapor is quickly consumed, which is inadequate to supply necessary energy feedback to the droplet, triggering multiple dumped cool flame oscillation before entering quasi-cool flame burning. In addition, the computational comparison among three different kinetic models for n-C12H26 demonstrated significant model to model prediction discrepancies suggesting the future need for large scale reevaluation of kinetic coefficients. The findings from these two studies were presented at the 10th US national Combustion Meeting 2017 and 33rd ASGSR Annual Meeting 2017.
As a continuation of the aforementioned two studies, we then explore the dynamics of oscillatory cool flames for n-C7H16 droplet. The dynamics of the near-limit cool flame burning of isolated submillimeter sized n-heptane droplets was numerically investigated. To provide the necessary near limit condition, the oxygen in the ambient was set to a value that is lower than the limiting oxygen index for n-C7H16, and ozone was seeded to the ambient to accomplish cool flame combustion initiation. The predictions show that at low oxygen indices, a quasi-steady cool flame burn is unattainable and the system transitions to a continuously pulsing, cool flame droplet combustion mode. Analyses further indicate that the dynamic interaction of degenerate chain branching and chain termination/propagation reaction classes of QOOH associated with the low temperature and negative temperature coefficient (NTC) kinetic regimes, and continuous fuel leakage across the flame location contribute to the ever-increasing trends of the oscillation magnitude.

Task Description:
Fuel cell based portable power sources offer opportunities for high efficiency and ultra-high density distributed power generation, which is essential for enhanced capabilities and survivability of the future long duration space missions as well as for extra vehicular activities (EVA) of astronauts. A key element of the fuel cell power sources is the fuel processor, which should have a capability to produce hydrogen from a variety of hydrocarbon fuels stored in a liquid phase for highest power density. To this end, this project focuses on the novel portable MEMS hydrogen generator with improved functionality and low cost achieved through innovative system integration approach and by exploiting advantages pertinent to fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, and catalysis on micro/nano scale. The proposed microreactor has multifuel processing capability achieved by using unique piezoelectrically-driven fuel atomization technology, it operates in autothermal regime that does not require external heating, it exhibits high fuel conversion and selectivity to hydrogen, and it features low “skin” temperature which is essential from thermal management prospective. To establish the fundamental bases for optimal design and operation of the proposed catalytic microreactor, a ground-based three-year experimental study of the microreactor and its key components is undertaken. The key objectives include (1) design, fabrication, and testing of the autothermal MEMS catalytic reactor integrated with hydrogen separating membrane, (2) design, fabrication, and experimental characterization of the novel micromachined fuel ejector array for energy-efficient atomization and mixing of liquid fuels, and (3) integration and experimental characterization of an integrated microreformer that combines a microreactor, a hydrogen separating membrane, and an atomizer/droplet ejection array.

Task Progress: We developed and characterized novel MEMS-enabled technologies for fuel processing for portable power generation and demonstrated the unique advantages offered by intimately integrating a microreactor with a micromachined ultrasonic atomizer for efficient dispersion of liquid fuels, and a micromachined Pd/Ag membrane for highly selective hydrogen separation. Periodic flow reversal at the appropriate frequency has been shown to be more robust to changes in operating conditions compared to a steady-state unidirectional flow. A valve-less flow reversal scheme integrated with a microchannel reactor has been developed to realize these advantages. Incorporating the hydrogen separation membrane in the reactor delivers pure hydrogen directly to the fuel cell anode and shifts the reaction equilibrium to increased hydrogen production. Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Fuel cells offer opportunities for high efficiency and ultra-high density distributed power generation, which is essential for many aerospace and terrestrial applications. A key element of the fuel cell power sources is the fuel processor, which should have a capability to produce hydrogen from a variety of hydrocarbon fuels. To this end, we are developing a novel MEMS hydrogen generator with improved functionality achieved through innovative system integration approach by exploiting advantages of transport and catalysis on micro/nano scale. The microreactor has multifuel processing capability achieved by using unique ultrasonic fuel atomization technology; it operates in autothermal regime without external heating with high fuel conversion and selectivity to hydrogen; and it utilizes in-situ separation of hydrogen from the reaction products via reactor-integrated sub-micrometer thick Palladium-Silver membrane. The key project objectives (sub-tasks) include (1) design, fabrication, and testing of the autothermal MEMS catalytic reactor and hydrogen separating membrane, (2) design, fabrication, and characterization of the micromachined fuel ejector for atomization of liquid fuels, and (3) integration and experimental characterization of an integrated microreformer that combines a microreactor, hydrogen separating membrane, and an atomizer. During the reporting period, we have achieved a number of critical advances in all three key aspects of the project. In particular, the first prototype of the MEMS microreactor has been designed and fabricated for the experimental performance characterization of the reverse-flow operation. In parallel, a theoretical analysis of the reactor operability and optimal operation has been performed that revealed the unique advantages of the reverse-flow autothermal microreactors as compared to the unidirectional counterparts. Of those, an unlimited reactor throughput while maintaining an autothermal (i.e., self-sustained without external heating) operation and its robustness (i.e., little dependence of the hydrogen yield on small variation in the feed composition) are the two main advantages that provide strong impetus for pursuing the reverse-flow microreactor concept. We have also perfected the fabrication process for ultra-thin (nanoscale) Pd-Ag membranes suitable for highly selective separation of hydrogen from the reaction mixture. This resulted in repeatable manufacturing of membranes which meet stringent requirements of structural and chemical stability to be suitable for experimental testing. To support the experimental work, a theoretical model of hydrogen permeation has been developed. The results of the analysis indicates that desorption of hydrogen on the low pressure side of the membrane may become the rate limiting step, rather than solid-phase atomic hydrogen diffusion as commonly thought for the conventional (macroscale) membranes. Finally, we have continued our work on understanding the fluid physics and performance optimization of the ultrasonic MEMS ejectors needed for fuel atomization prior to introduction to the reactor. The scaling law governing transition from drop-on-demand to continuous jet operation of the ejectors has been discovered through combination of high resolution visualization and theoretical analysis. Furthermore, a novel approach for improving power transfer efficiency for running the ejectors at low power input has been developed and experimentally demonstrated.
