Task Description:
The experiments described here are based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft. If this hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of safety provided NASA-STD-6001 Test #1.
There are important differences in the suppression of fires in space compared to on Earth. On Earth it is understood that best results are generally obtained when the extinguisher “attacks” the base of the flame, which is both the stabilization point and the point of fresh air entrainment. For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen.
There are two main objectives:
1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Space Applications: The current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
Earth Applications: BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2013
Task Progress:
Microgravity combustion tests burning thin and thick flat samples, acrylic spheres, and candles were conducted aboard the International Space Station. The samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose air flow speeds up to 40 cm/s. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. The effects of air flow speed, fuel thickness, and fuel preheating on flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent-flow configuration.
For thin fuels in the opposed-flow configuration, the flame quickly reached steady spread for each flow speed, and the spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed. These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in the opposed-flow geometry (downward flame spread). In the concurrent-flow configuration, flame size grew with time during the tests. A limiting length and steady spread rate were obtained only in low flow speeds (= 10 cm/s) for the short-length samples that fit in the small wind tunnel. For these conditions, flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow. This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity. In addition, by decreasing flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s), quenching extinction was observed. The valuable results from these long-duration experiments validate a number of theoretical predictions and also provide the data for a transient flame growth model under development.
For thick fuels, microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cm/s. The gas phase response is much faster compared to the solid and so as the flow speed is changed, the flame responds with almost no delay. At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cm/s) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time. At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cm/s) the flame continually heats the solid fuel resulting in an increasing fuel temperature, higher rate of fuel vaporization, and a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses. Only the smallest flames burning acrylic slabs appeared to be adversely influenced by solid conductive heat loss, but even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing. This has implications for spacecraft fire safety since a tiny flame might be undetected for a long time. While the small flame is not particularly hazardous if it remains small, the danger is that it might flare up if the air convection is suddenly increased or if the flame spreads into another fuel source.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2012
Task Progress:
The BASS hardware launched on STS-133.
We reviewed still camera tests by Jay Owens and Mike Johnston burning 1-g PMMA and Delrin. The intention was to create very dim blue flames to mimic the dimmest microgravity flames expected. Camera settings were determined for these flames as the starting point for the flight experiment.
Photographs of the BASS igniter wires were sent to CWRU for the purposes of the model. The geometry of the wire as well as the power as a function of time are needed to capture the ignition properly in the model. One difficulty is accounting for the relative fraction of (energy radiated)/(energy convected) from the wire. Simple heat transfer arguments show that half of the electrical energy deposited in the wire is radiated away at the typical wire temperatures.
We conducted PMMA sphere combustion drop tower tests. Modeling results of sphere drop tests show qualitative agreement of the flame structure. Both the 1-g and 0-g flames as well as the transition are captured. The modeling is performed using the FLUENT software by Sam Hsu at CWRU. Results were presented at the 7th US National Technical Meeting of the Combustion Institute in March 2011.
We conducted crew training with astronauts Ron Garan and Mike Fossum at JSC. While in Houston, we took the opportunity to review and modify the crew procedures with Carol Reynolds (MSFC). A description of the 1-g applications of the BASS experiment were submitted to astronaut Ron Garan.
Crew training was conducted for astronaut Don Pettit. At that time, it appeared unlikely that he would perform the experiment, so science support for his crew training session was cancelled. Chuck Bunnell proceeded with training anyway so that Don is familiar with BASS. At the present time, it appears that Don Pettit will indeed perform BASS operations starting in March 2012.
Crew training for Astronauts Joe Acaba (Increments 31-32) and Sunita Williams (Increments 32-33) as well as supporting MSFC operations staff was completed.
We provided input to the Microgravity Science Glovebox Investigation Operations Lead for more information on the test matrix plan, including: the actual test order for each point in the test matrix; desired groupings of specific points; and an estimation of the time needed need after a group of tests for analysis before the next group.
It appears that we will not have access to a dedicated combustion gas analyzer for use in the glovebox. However, Carol Reynolds (MSFC) has been working to assure that we will be able to get cabin oxygen concentration measurements before and after our tests. These are important to quantify any flame changes which might be attributed to variations in cabin oxygen. In addition, there are some fuels we prefer to burn if the cabin oxygen is on the high-end (e.g. 22%).
The BASS project description was reviewed and modified, then submitted to Peter Boul (JSC) who is supporting the Office of the ISS Program Scientist. The BASS project description now appears on their “toolbox” website. In addition, the web description for the GRC ISS experiments website was updated.
Procedures were reviewed in advance of the Joint Integrated Training.
A request for an undergraduate student to help in the spring of 2012 has been submitted.
We participated in Payload Expert Training to ensure proper communication techniques when operations begin. An estimate for a re-flight of BASS to burn additional fuel samples was submitted.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2011
Task Progress:
The work was initiated with a Science Team Kickoff meeting, at which the investigators met with the engineers to discuss hardware changes anticipated.
Early tests examined the feasibility of using the current SPICE igniter to burn thick solid samples. Good results were achieved as long as the igniter was close to the fuel (approximately 1mm) without touching it. Ignition of the PMMA occurred in less than 20 seconds. We characterized the SPICE igniter in the engineering hardware. We were able to achieve 3.5 amps at 3.75 volts through a 29-gage Kanthal wire, and verified that drawing this power was not harmful to the hardware circuit. The SPICE engineering unit igniter power characteristic curve was measured using a range of igniter with resistances from 0.5 to 2 ohm.
Some precursor tests using platinum ignition wires were conducted and they were very promising. The catalytic effects of platinum could aid ignition. Also platinum will not oxidize as readily as Kanthal. However, the available electrical current from SPICE is too low to use platinum effectively.
BASS fuel samples consist of 1.) Flat sheets of cotton-fiberglass fabric, Nomex, and Ultem; 2.) Cast PMMA spheres of two different diameters; 3.) Flat slabs of both PMMA and wax-soaked fiberglass fabric; and 4.) Shrouded candles (candle within a ceramic tube).
Zero Gravity tests were conducted using the BASS fuel and suppression system in Sandra Olson’s combustion tunnel. A rotary solenoid was used to retract the igniter once a flame was achieved in 1-g (before the drop). During the drop, a nozzle at the base of the duct could be turned on to extinguish the flame with nitrogen. Tests demonstrated that a 2-cm diameter PMMA sphere burning in 5 cm/s air flow can be extinguished with the planned flow rate of nitrogen within 4 seconds after application of the nitrogen (all during the available drop time). However, in 30 cm/s flow, extinguishment was not achieved within the available drop time, although there is a large hole in the flame at the stagnation point region. The shrouded candle fuel sample was also ignited, burned, and extinguished in during the drop test.
Tibor Lorik (ZIN Technologies) suggested mounting samples off a replaceable top window for the flight experiment. This was proposed instead of mounting the samples on the nozzle. A conceptual design was made consisting of posts that come off the window extending into the duct. Individual fuel samples (cylindrical or flat) could easily mount to these posts. This concept was chosen for the experiment.
The BASS SRD (Science Requirements Document) was completed.
Jay Perry (MSFC) provided some information about the current means for measuring and maintaining oxygen concentration on ISS. There are several mass spectrometers and one hand-held chemical oxygen sensor being used. Data indicates that the oxygen concentrations generally vary between about 20% and 22% oxygen, with some periods when the oxygen is even higher or lower. Our concern is that the flammability of many of our materials is quite sensitive over this range of oxygen concentration. As a result, we will require a reading of oxygen at the time of each test, and request that the tests be done when the oxygen is at a particular level (e.g., greater than 21%). This is stated in the procedures.
Several tests examined wake flames stabilized on PMMA spheres. There was a question whether the front half of the sphere needs to be an inert material (to inhibit forward flame spread), or whether the entire sphere can be made out of PMMA. Based on 1-g tests, the latter option was deemed to be adequate for the flight experiment.
The igniter design for the flat cards was completed. The igniter element is made of Kanthal crimped to copper wires, which run toward the back of the duct and then down and out of the way to the igniter connector. The copper wire is fed along the edge of the card to minimize obstruction of the flame in the camera view.
We submitted fuel types and amounts to be burned for all samples for safety calculations. Safety calculations were submitted to JSC toxicology for evaluation. Subsequently, safety calculations to include contingency samples were submitted to JSC toxicology for evaluation.
We passed the first and second System Acceptance Review (SAR-1 and SAR-2) held at GRC.
We passed the Phase II/III Flight Safety Review.
Graduate student Mike Johnston (CWRU) performed flow visualization tests using a smoke wire in the engineering hardware. Flow resistance at the inlet was added to achieve a smaller flow range in the duct. In addition, Mike performed 1-g tests in the BASS engineering hardware to work on the ignition of the fuels. Touch temperatures and time to cool were determined. Flow resistance consisting of 2 fine-mesh screens will be added to the hardware. This will effectively lower the flow speed range within the duct. Flow speeds of as small as 1 cm/s are of interest for selected tests. Finally, Mike performed a wide range of camera tests (still and video) to work out the anticipated camera settings required.
Undergraduate student Dennis Siedlak (CWRU) performed an extensive series of 1-g baseline burns in the engineering hardware, and analyzed the images.
We received the flight samples and igniters for inspection. Final hardware adjustments were made and the hardware was shipped to KSC for launch.
We met with Chuck Bunnell (ZIN Technologies) to go review and develop crew procedures. Crew training is scheduled for late October 2010.

Task Description:
The Forced flow Ignition and Flame Spread Test (FIST) aims to study the effects of gravity on the flammability diagrams of solid combustible materials, and the fire properties derived from them. The final objective of the research is to develop a new flammability apparatus that would better reflect the potential ambient conditions of space-based environments, i.e., microgravity, low velocity flow, oxygen concentrations below and above that of air, reduced pressure, and use it to obtain more appropriate flammability diagrams for practical materials (plastics, cable jackets, electronic circuit boards, etc.) that will be found in space-based facilities. The strong possibility of an accidental fire occurring in a space-based facility during a long mission is a primary safety concern. Consequently, it is of critical importance to characterize the fire properties of materials that are used.
FIST is similar to the ASTM E-1321 LIFT apparatus, except the fuel sample is mounted in small-scale wind tunnel so that a low-velocity oxidizer flow of specified oxygen concentration can be forced over the sample surface during the test.
The FIST protocol includes both ignition and flame spread testing. For an ignition test, a 30 mm by 30 mm test specimen is embedded flush in the substrate of the wind tunnel so that the gas flow boundary layer generated over its surface is not disrupted. Two radiant heaters are used to irradiate the sample with an approximately uniform heat flux of known intensity. Ignition is induced at fuel sample’s trailing edge with an electrically heated wire coil that acts as a pilot. Measured quantities for a particular material include the time to ignition as a function of ambient oxygen concentration and flow velocity, as well as the critical (minimum) mass and heat flux for ignition. Alternatively, flame spread tests can be conducted using larger samples (100 mm long by 30 mm wide). The sample is exposed to a heat flux that decays in the longitudinal direction. The sample is ignited locally at one end, and a flame spreads over teh sample surface. The rate of flame spread is measured by digitizing infrared images and taking the slope of the flame position vs. time. The ignition and flame spread data are plotted on a flammability diagram which is a measure of a material’s overall flammability.
To complement the experimental program, theoretical modeling of the ignition, burning, and flame spread process is performed. This modeling includes a description of the solid-phase heating and fuel generation process through a customized pyrolysis model. The pyrolysis model is coupled to the CFD-based Fire Dynamics Simulator for calculation of gas-phase phenomena (fluid mechanics, combustion, heat transfer, radiation, etc.). The combined model is used to calculate ignition, burning, and flame spread processes for different materials, environmental conditions, and geometries. One of the principal purposes of the modeling effort is to extend via modeling the experimental FIST results to other conditions that have not been tested, i.e. different O2, velocity, or gravity levels.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Composites are finding increased use in the transportation and construction industries. One barrier to their widespread adoption is the increased flammability of polymer based composites when compared with other materials. In the process of developing a test methodolgy for flammability of composites intended for use in space structures, the FIST project is developing a better understanding of composite materials' flammability useful to ground based design and manufacture.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
Flame spread modeling work during FY2007 focused on simulation of the KC-135 flame spread experiments conducted in October 2004. At lower heat flux levels, the modeled flame spread rate is underpredicted but matches the experimental data reasonably well (within 35%). However, at higher heat flux levels, the experimental flame spread rate is overpredicted by almost a factor of 2. This overprediction may be partially due to a discrepancy between the experimental preheat procedure and its representation in the simulations. It is anticipated that a multi-step gas-phase combustion mechanism and incorporation of the effect of ambient oxygen concentration into the condensed-phase decomposition model could improve model predictions. While inclusion of a comprehensive gas-phase reaction mechanism into a flame spread model is not feasible, a three or four-step mechanism that could account for (at least approximately) the effect of ambient oxygen concentration on the combustion process would be quite useful. Similarly, a simplified model that can account for the effect of ambient oxygen concentration on the thermo-oxidative decomposition of solid fuels could also potentially improve model predictions.
During FY2007, the focus of the pyrolysis modeling was to account for the effect of oxygen on the thermo-oxidative decomposition of combustible solids. The pyrolysis model was extended to solve the gas-phase energy equation (inside the decomposing solid, not in the “ambient” gas-phase outside of the decomposing solid because that is handled by a CFD code). In previous versions of the model, thermal equilibrium was assumed between the solid and gas-phase, making it unnecessary to solve the gas-phase energy equation. However, by solving the gas-phase energy equation, it becomes possible to consider thermal disequilibrium between the gas-phase and the condensed-phase inside the decomposing solid. More importantly, the heat released due to the gas-phase combustion of pyrolysate inside the decomposing can now be included in simulations because the model was also extended to include a user-specified number of homogeneous gas-phase reactions. This addition has made it possible to simulate the effect of ambient oxygen concentration on the thermo-oxidative decomposition of solids. Efforts have been made to extend the pyrolysis model to “practical” materials. Preliminary modeling of a laminated polyester composite has been conducted, with encouraging results.
In the FY2006 report, it was stated that an analytical model for opposed-flow flame spread rates was under development. This model predicts that flame spread is a balance between the heat-transfer to the solid ahead of the pyrolysis front and finite-rate chemical kinetics. This model was applied to existing, well-known flame spread data as well as the flame spread data gathered on the KC-135 with excellent agreement. In order to fully understand the predictive capabilities of this analytical model, additional flame spread experiments at high opposed-flow velocity subject to the heat flux levels used in the microgravity experiments were needed. Flame spread experiments in FY2007 were focused on obtaining this data. To gain some estimate of the experimental error, each test was performed a total of 3 times. The average percent variation from the mean was 21% for PMMA and 14.2% for PPG 30%. Clear trends in the experimental data were seen and matched by the analytical model. As the external heat flux level is increased, the flame spread rate increases for the same opposed-flow velocity. At lower heat fluxes, the spread rate behaves much as it does in the case with no heat flux. For a range of opposed-flow velocities, the spread rates are insensitive to changes in opposed-flow velocity due to the dominance of buoyancy-induced flow. The maximum flame spread rate occurs in this buoyancy-driven range and is therefore not seen experimentally in normal gravity. However, it does seem as if increasing the heat flux level has the same results as increasing the ambient oxygen concentration – the maximum spread rate shifts to the right, occurring at higher and higher opposed-flow velocities. Not only did the analytical model qualitatively match the trends in the experimental data for a wide range of test conditions, it was seen that the average difference between the model and the data over both materials and all conditions is 20%.
During FY2007, a new focus area for the FIST project was introduced: the ignition delay of polymeric materials in exploration atmospheres. Because future space vehicles will operate with a total cabin pressure of 8.5 psia with an oxygen concentration of 32%, it is crucial to understand fire behavior in this atmosphere. To accomplish this, a pressure chamber with the ability to control the ambient oxygen concentration will be used. The CIR chamber, previously used on the KC-135, was transported from Lawrence Berkeley Labs to the UC Berkeley campus with this goal in mind. In order to perform ignition delay tests in “exploration atmospheres,” the FIST tunnel was modified so that it fit inside the chamber and a frame was built to support the tunnel within the chamber. A heater mounting system was manufactured, along with a sample holder. Feedthroughs were obtained to connect the fan power, igniter power, heater power, and thermocouples to the power supplies and data acquisition equipment located outside of the chamber. In order to sense and control the pressure in the chamber, an appropriate pressure transducer and vacuum pump were obtained. The chamber was also connected to an oxygen supply to control the concentration inside. A system for the extinguishment of the flame has also been implemented. Ignition delay tests in regular atmospheric conditions have begun to serve as a basis of comparison for later tests. Once this series of baseline tests are completed, tests will be done in low pressure/normal oxygen, normal pressure/high oxygen, and low pressure/high oxygen environments with both PMMA and PPG 30%. To date, ignition delay tests in standard air have been performed with PMMA for heat flux levels of 9 to 12 kW/m2 with airflow velocities of 0.4, 0.7, and 1 m/s.
In FY2006, it was decided that the FIST apparatus should be modified to gain the ability to perform heat release rate measurements. Before heat release rate measurements can be performed, some modeling was done to understand how to setup the FIST tunnel to obtain the best accuracy and to determine the appropriate additional equipment needed. The focus was on two main aspects: how and where to sample the combustion gases. The measurement precision can vary whether we measure only oxygen, both oxygen and carbon dioxide, or oxygen, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. Because the carbon monoxide generation rate is very low for PMMA, the third method does not really improve the accuracy; results found with the first two methods are similar. For simplicity, the first experiments will focus on only oxygen measurement. An initial theoretical calculation was performed to determine the expected oxygen depletion in the outflow during combustion. Using equations of reaction, combustion, and the duct characteristics, we found that the oxygen will decrease from 21 to 20.07 percent in volume which, using the oxygen consumption method, corresponds to a heat release rate of approximately 1,100 kW/m². Based on these results, a short calculation shows that an error of ± 100 ppm in the oxygen concentration measurement results in an acceptable error in the heat release rate value of less than 2% error. An oxygen sensor with this level of accuracy was recently obtained. However, in order to obtain the best measurement accuracy, it is necessary for the combustion gases be thoroughly mixed. In order to determine the necessary modifications to the FIST tunnel, a model of the duct was created using FDS and Smokeview. Different duct designs were modeled to determine which was the most effective at mixing the exhaust gases and it was found that the least expensive and easiest to implement is to simply increase the duct length by about 30 cm.
SUPPLEMENTAL REPORTING FOR FINAL TASK BOOK REPORT
Continuing work begun at the end of FY2007, the ignition delay of polymeric materials in exploration atmospheres was explored. Because future space vehicles will operate with a total cabin pressure of 52.7 – 58.6 kPa with an oxygen concentration of 30 – 34%, it is crucial to understand fire behavior in this atmosphere. To accomplish this, a pressure chamber with the ability to control the ambient oxygen concentration was used. In these tests, polymethylmethacylate (PMMA) was exposed to a range of oxidizer flow velocities from 40 to 100 cm/s and externally applied heat fluxes from 8 to 14 kW/m2. Tests were conducted for a baseline case of normal pressure and oxygen concentration, low pressure (58.6 kPa) with normal oxygen (21%), and low pressure with 32% oxygen concentration conditions to determine the individual effect of pressure and the combined effect of pressure and oxygen concentration on the ignition delay.
Overall, it was found that reducing the pressure to 58.6 kPa while keeping the oxygen concentration at 21% reduced the ignition time by 17% on average. Increasing the oxygen concentration to 32% at 58.6 kPa reduced the ignition time by an additional 10%. The critical heat flux for ignition was also found to decrease in exploration atmospheres. These results show that tests conducted in standard atmospheric conditions will underpredict the ignition of materials intended for use on spacecraft and that, at these conditions, materials are more susceptible to ignition than in current spacecraft atmospheres. These results seemed counterintuitive at first, but they can be explained by considering the effect of pressure on the convective heat transfer coefficient and the mass loss required to reach the lean flammability limit. For forced flow over a flat plate, the convective heat transfer coefficient is proportional to the square root of the pressure. Pressure also affects the required mass loss to reach the lean flammability limit. Ignition occurs when the fuel and air mixture near the igniter reaches the lean flammability limit. As the pressure is reduced, the amount of air is reduced, so less fuel is required for the mixture to be at the lean flammability limit. Because the pyrolysis process has an Arrhenius dependence on temperature, ignition can occur at a lower temperature. When the oxygen is increased, the surface temperature at ignition is even lower because an elevated oxygen concentration can increase the rate of pyrolysis at a given temperature.
In order to more fully understand the effect of pressure on ignition delay, and perhaps find a less hazardous alternative to the proposed space exploration environment, another three series of tests were performed. In all three sets of experiments, the forced flow was fixed at 30 cm/s and the heat flux fixed at 14 kW/m2. In the first set, the pressure was lowered from atmospheric (101.3 kPa) until no ignition occurred with air (21% O2) as the oxidizer. As the pressure is decreased below atmospheric, the ignition delay time decreases. The delay time continues to decrease until about 28 kPa (4 psi) where a minimum occurs. The minimum observed ignition time is 22% lower than the ignition time in sea-level air. If the pressure is decreased below 28 kPa, the ignition time sharply increases until no ignition is seen at a pressure of 7 kPa (1 psi). By looking at the surface temperature traces, three regimes were identified. As the pressure is reduced from atmospheric to about 50 kPa, both the reduction in heat transfer coefficient and in the mass loss required to reach the lean flammability limit are dominant and the ignition time decreases rapidly. Below 50 kPa, the surface temperature at ignition begins to increase, implying that the chemistry time is becoming noticeable. Between pressures of 50 kPa and 27.6 kPa, the reduction in the heat transfer coefficient is competing with the increase in the chemical time so the ignition time still decreases as the pressure is reduced but not as quickly. Below 34.5 kPa, the heat transfer coefficient remains nearly constant as the pressure is decreased. It follows then that the increase in the chemical time is the sole mechanism controlling the ignition time below 27.6 kPa, the pressure where the minimum ignition time occurred.
In order to better understand the combined effect of reduced pressure and elevated oxygen concentration, the second series of experiments were performed in pressures from atmospheric down until no ignition occurred with the oxidizer of air enriched to 30% oxygen. The same trends seen with air as the oxidizer are also seen with oxygen-enriched air. The ignition delay time decreases, reaches a minimum, then begins to increase until no ignition occurs. However, when the oxygen concentration increases the pressures at which the minimum and no ignition occurs are different. The minimum ignition time occurred at a higher pressure of 41 kPa and the no ignition point occurred at a lower pressure of about 3.4 kPa. An elevated oxygen concentration changes the controlling mechanisms. Increasing the oxygen concentration may increase the pyrolysis rate at a given temperature, but it also increases the mass of fuel required to reach the lean flammability limit. The latter effect of oxygen may be responsible for shifting the pressure at which the minimum ignition time occurs. By looking at the surface temperature histories, it is estimated that the influence of oxygen on the pyrolysis rate is strong only at pressures above 70 kPa. At lower pressures, the collision frequency is perhaps small enough that this effect is masked by the increase in the required mass loss to reach the lean flammability limit. The gas-phase reaction rate is increased with the increase in oxygen so it is expected that the increase in the chemical induction time will occur at a lower pressure than in air. The change in heat transfer coefficient with pressure is not influenced by the oxygen concentration, so the range of pressures where this mechanism should be considered does not change. In order to fully understand these controlling mechanisms, however, it is necessary to examine the mass loss rate at ignition and is a subject of future research.
The third series of experiments were aimed at understanding ignition delay in low-pressure environments where humans could live. In this series, the pressure was reduced while keeping a constant partial pressure of oxygen of 21.3 kPa, in other words, “normoxic” equivalent environments. The ignition delay time is decreased when the oxygen concentration is increased from air at 21% to 30%. However, if the oxygen is increased further no additional decrease in the ignition time is seen. In fact, the normoxic curve follows the curve for 30% oxygen for all but the atmospheric pressure tests. For pressures below atmospheric, the normoxic oxygen concentration varies from 24 to 77%, indicating that any increase in oxygen concentration beyond 24% does not further reduce the ignition delay time because the chemical kinetics are fast, regardless of pressure.
Theoretical work in FY2008 focused on integrating the pyrolysis model with FDS 5.2.3. The coupled code, a user’s guide, and a technical reference can be downloaded here: http://code.google.com/p/gpyro/. Since many materials and practical systems exhibit two-dimensional behavior while undergoing pyrolysis, the solid-phase model has been extended to two dimensions. The code now includes an option to solve fully two-dimensional conservation equations for species, energy, mass, and momentum. This also makes it possible to account for the effect of buoyancy on pyrolysis and smoldering. Thus, the code can now explicitly account for the effect of gravity level on smoldering and pyrolysis.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
During FY2006, studies were conducted to examine the variation of the critical mass loss rate at ignition with freestream oxygen content, flow velocity, and applied radiative heat flux. The critical mass loss rate at ignition is primary component of a material’s overall ignitability and has important implications for microgravity fire safety. Experimental data were compared to a simplified theoretical model with good agreement between the predicted and measured values. This model was described and its predictions were presented in the FY2005 report. Although the theoretical model successfully predicted the variation of the critical mass loss rate at ignition with freestream oxygen content and velocity, it predicted no variation of the critical mass loss rate at ignition with heat flux. However, experimental FIST measurements clearly showed an increase in the critical mass loss rate at ignition with heat flux, a trend also observed by other researchers.
Since the model predicted no variation in the critical mass flux at the fire point with heat flux level, but the experimental FIST results showed an increase in the critical mass flux at the fire point with the applied heat flux level, additional experiments were conducted to isolate the influence of temperature and oxygen as factors in fuel production. PMMA samples 3 mm and 10 mm thick were used to study the effect of temperature. The role of oxygen was studied by modifying the surface of the 10 mm thick PMMA samples with 1 mm diameter (0.5 mm deep) dimples spaced at approximately 5 dimples per sq cm. At low heat flux levels, modifying the surface results in only a mild reduction in the critical mass loss rate at ignition. For higher heat flux levels, these modifications result in a significant lowering of the critical mass loss rate at ignition. This is explained on the basis of oxygen participation in the polymer decomposition process, which is known to produce radical species. Specifically, the enhanced formation of these radical species attributed to increased oxygen access may enhance ignition.
Work related to flame spread involved analysis of the microgravity flame-spread experiments conducted on the KC-135 aircraft in October 2004. These results demonstrate that microgravity flame spread rates may be faster than those under normal gravity conditions when exposed to an external heat flux at oxygen concentrations of 24%. These elevated flame spread rates result from a decrease in oxidizer velocity below that induced by gravity which increases residence time, thereby minimizing kinetic effects associated with short chemical times. This allows the flame to propagate in a region where the flame spread mechanism is dominated by heat transfer effects. As a complement to the flame spread experiments, simplified analytical and theoretical models have been developed. A simple analytical theory based on transition from a heat-transfer controlled regime and a chemical kinetics controlled regime has been used to predict normal gravity flame spread rates as well as microgravity KC-135 experiments with excellent agreement between the predictions and the experimental data. A numerical flame spread model is currently being developed. The model involves using the CFD-based Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) code developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) coupled to a pyrolysis model developed in our laboratory to simulate the effects of oxygen concentration and freestream velocity on opposed flow flame spread rates over thermally thick samples of PMMA. The FDS thermoplastic pyrolysis model was replaced with a model that considers subsurface pyrolysate generation by incorporating a distributed pyrolysis reaction. Additional modifications were made to reduce the over-predicted flame radiation (which resulted in unreasonably low flame temperatures) and to reduce CPU time by adopting a quasi-steady formulation. Calculations were conducted under forced flow conditions only, i.e. in the absence of gravity. Good agreement between the model predictions and the experimental data was obtained at an oxygen concentration used for model "calibration", but the flame spread rate is underpredicted at higher oxygen mass fractions and underpredicted at lower oxygen mass fractions. Future work during FY2007 will involve modeling oxygen concentration effects on gas and solid-phase kinetics to improve model predictions.
The numerical flame spread modeling described above used a generalized pyrolysis model that has been developed over several years. During FY2006, work continued on development of this model, intended for simulating the gasification of noncharring, charring, and intumescent materials, as well as smoldering in porous media. Conservation equations are solved for gaseous and condensed phase mass and species, solid phase energy, and gas-phase momentum. An arbitrary number of gas-phase and condensed-phase species can be accommodated, each having its own temperature-dependent thermophysical properties. The user may specify any number of reactions. Both in-depth radiation transfer through a semi-transparent medium as well as radiation transport across pores are considered. Melting is modeled using an apparent specific heat. All volatiles generated inside the solid escape to the ambient with no resistance to flow unless the pressure solver is invoked to solve for the pressure distribution in the solid, with the resultant flow of volatiles calculated according to Darcy’s law. The user may invoke a gas-phase convective-diffusive solver that determines the composition of the volatiles, including diffusion of species from the ambient into the solid. Thus, the actual composition of the pyrolysate vapors escaping from the solid can be predicted.
To aid in determination of the required material properties, the model has been coupled to a genetic algorithm optimization procedure that can be used to estimate material properties from laboratory tests. The genetic algorithm has been parallelized and run simultaneously on as many as 50 networked PCs to reduce CPU time. As mentioned earlier, the model has been integrated with NIST Fire Dynamics Simulator v4.06 so that it may be applied as a boundary condition in 2D and 3D simulations of ignition, flame spread, and fire growth. Although the pyrolysis model is one-dimensional, when it is applied as a boundary condition in FDS, two-dimensional heat conduction effects can be calculated.
The standalone pyrolysis model has been used to simulate the gasification of a noncharring solid, a charring solid, an intumescent coating, and smoldering combustion in a porous medium, with generally good results. The flexibility of this model to simulate different materials is important for space-based applications where a variety of materials are encountered. A paper describing this work is currently being prepared.

Task Description:
The objective of the program is to develop a new flammability apparatus and a bench-scale flammability test, FIST (Forced Ignition and Spread Test), that reproduces the environment that is expected in a manned space-based facility, i.e., microgravity and low velocity gas flows of variable oxygen concentration. The FIST would subsequently be used to obtain “flammability diagrams” of practical materials (plastics, composites, etc.) that are expected in these facilities. The research could eventually provide NASA with a test methodology to complement the existing protocol and provide a more comprehensive assessment of material flammability for space applications. Theoretical modeling, an extensive normal gravity data bank, and a few validation space experiments will support the testing methodology. This protocol could lead to better determination and ranking of the fire hazard characteristics of potential materials to be used in space-based environments, which are necessary criteria for an adequate fire protection design for space-based facilities.
The FIST apparatus is similar to the ASTM E-1321 LIFT apparatus, except the fuel sample is mounted in small-scale wind tunnel so that a low-velocity oxidizer flow of specified oxygen concentration can be forced over the sample surface during the test. The oxidizer (air or a N2/O2 mixture of prescribed oxygen concentration) is forced through a rectangular duct at a known velocity. The duct is 56 cm in length, 10 cm high, and 12.7 cm wide. Its two side walls are clear Pyrex and its bottom surface is an insulating substrate (mica). A 30 mm by 30 mm test specimen is embedded flush in the substrate so that the boundary layer is not disrupted. Two radiant heaters are used to irradiate the sample with an approximately uniform heat flux of known intensity. Ignition is induced at fuel sample’s trailing edge with an electrically heated Kanthal wire coil that acts as a pilot. Measured quantities for a particular material include the time to ignition as a function of ambient oxygen concentration and flow velocity, as well as the critical (minimum) mass and heat flux for ignition.
Alternatively, a larger sample 100 mm long with a width of 30 mm can be fit in the tunnel. The sample is exposed to a heat flux that decays in the longitudinal direction. The sample is ignited locally at one end, and the rate of flame spread can be measured by digitizing infrared images. The ignition and flame spread data are plotted on a “flammability diagram” which can be used quantify a material’s overall flammability.
To complement the experimental program, theoretical modeling of the ignition and flame spread process is performed. One of the principal purposes of the modeling effort is to extend the test results to other conditions that have not been tested (different O2 or gravity levels) via modeling. The proposed research program will study the effects of microgravity on the flammability diagrams of solid combustible materials, and the fire properties derived from them. The final objective of the research is to develop a new flammability apparatus that would better reflect the potential ambient conditions of space-based environments, i.e., microgravity, low velocity flow, oxygen concentrations slightly below and above that of air, and use it to obtain more appropriate flammability diagrams for practical materials (plastics, cable jackets, electronic circuit boards, etc.) that will be found in space-based facilities. The strong possibility of an accidental fire occurring in a space-based facility during a long mission, is a primary safety concern, and consequently it is of critical importance to characterize the fire properties of materials that are used.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Composites are finding increased use in the transportation and construction industries. One barrier to their widespread adoption is the increased flammability of polymer based composites when compared with other materials, particularly metals and concrete. In the process of developing a test methodolgy for flammability of composites intended for use in space structures, the FIST project is developing a better understanding of composite flammability useful to ground based design and manufacture.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
During FY05, considerable effort was devoted to developing modeling tools that can be used to calculate the ignition time of an irradiated solid fuel in microgravity environments. Conventionally, a solid-phase pyrolysis model is used to calculate the transient temperature distribution and mass loss rate of an irradiated solid. Ignition is assumed to occur when the mass loss rate reaches a critical value known as the critical mass loss rate at ignition. The primary shortcoming of this approach for predicting ignition times of a solid fuel in microgravity is that it is difficult to estimate how this critical mass loss rate at ignition varies with forced flow velocity, ambient oxygen concentration, heat flux level, and from fuel to fuel.
For these reasons, a large number of FIST experiments were conducted to measure the critical mass loss rate at ignition of the polypropylene/glass composite (PP/GL) and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) fuels as a function of oxygen concentration, heat flux level, and forced flow velocity. Heat flux levels were varied from 10 to 35 kW/m2, oxygen concentrations from 15-30%, and forced flow velocity from 0.5 m/s to 1.75 m/s. Data was collected on continuous mass loss with precision of +/- 0.05 mg at 0.5 second intervals. Front and backside surface temperature measurements were made with Type K thermocouples at 0.5 second intervals and providing +/- 5% precision. Values of dm/dt were calculated using a linear fit over an interval of 10-15 seconds around the timed point of observed ignition.
As a complement to the experimental measurements of the critical mass loss rate at ignition, a simple theory was developed that can be used to predict the critical mass loss rate at ignition as a function of fuel properties (heat of combustion and stoichiometric oxygen to fuel ratio), forced flow velocity, and ambient oxygen concentration. This work was submitted to the 31st International Symposium on Combustion. Good agreement between the experimental measurements and the model predictions were obtained.
In addition to measuring the critical mass loss rate at ignition, long-duration mass loss experiments were conducted with the igniter de-energized to help understand how the forced flow velocity and oxygen concentration affect the mass loss rate at a given heat flux.
A major part of the theoretical work during FY05 involved development of a comprehensive pyrolysis model to simulate the heating and gasification (i.e. mass loss) processes that occur in combustible solids. The model simulates the relevant physical processes that occur during the gasification and burning of complex solids, particularly charring or intumescent (swelling) materials and composites (due to their widespread use in the aerospace industry). Although the model has been developed with complex materials in mind, it can also be used to simulate simple noncharring solids such as thermoplastics.
The governing solid-phase conservation equations describing the pyrolysis of a charring/intumescent material have been formulated and implemented into a numerical model. The numerical model solves conservation equations for a user-specified number of solid and gas-phase species. For example, in simulating the thermal decomposition process in a charring material, conservation equations would be solved for the virgin material, the char, and the oxidized char (ash). Each solid species has its own temperature-dependent thermophysical properties (thermal conductivity, density, specific heat, radiation absorption coefficient, surface emissivity, etc.). The user may also specify an arbitrary number of solid to gas, solid to solid, or solid to solid + gas chemical reactions, each having its own Arrhenius reaction rate. Melting is handled using an apparent specific heat wherein the latent heat of melting is added to the specific heat of the matrix in the vicinity a “melting temperature”; it is assumed to follow a Gaussian distribution. Additional physics incorporated in the model include in-depth radiation absorption according to the Beer/Lambert law, in-depth radiation transport across pores using the “radiant conductivity” approach, gas-solid heat transfer, and Arrhenius reactions having arbitrary reaction order. Due to its generality, the model may be applied to thermoplastic fuels (PMMA, PP), charring fuels such as wood and fire-retarded polymers, intumescent solids, blended composites, laminated composites, melting polymers, non-homogeneous solids having layered composition, etc.
As part of the model verification process, the temperature profiles predicted by the model have been compared to exact solutions for two cases. The first is a semi-infinite solid heated by a constant incident heat flux with surface losses by convection only. The second is the classical “Stefan problem” which describes the propagation of a solidification front into a semi-infinite medium initially in the liquid state. The model accurately reproduces the temperature profiles for both exact solutions examined. No analytical solutions are available for the cases where pyrolysis occurs or the thermal properties vary with temperature. However, the model has been exercised quite vigorously and integral balances on the solid as a whole have confirmed that the model strictly conserves energy, mass, and species. This indicates that the model equations have been correctly implemented.
Due to the level of detail included in the pyrolysis model, a particular material must be characterized by specifying a large number of “material properties”, most of which cannot be directly measured or inferred from existing small-scale fire tests. For this reason, a procedure has been developed to extract the material properties required to characterize a material from existing bench scale fire tests (such as FIST). The methodology works by finding a combination of material properties (thermal properties, reaction kinetics, enthalpies of reaction, etc.) that provide optimal agreement between the model predictions and experimental data, which consists of temperature and mass loss rate measurements for a radiatively heated solid. Since a charring or intumescent material may require specification of more than 20 material properties, conventional search methods are not appropriate due to the large search space and the inherent nonlinearity. For this reason, the optimization procedure uses a genetic algorithm, which uses techniques rooted in “survival of the fittest” or Darwinian evolution to find an optimal solution (set of material properties providing the best agreement between model predictions and experimental data). A paper describing this methodology has recently been accepted for publication in Fire Safety Journal and will appear in 2006. To reduce the required CPU time, the genetic algorithm has been parallelized using Message Passing Interface (MPI) and the code has been successfully run in parallel on UCB computer clusters.
The pyrolysis model described above is coupled to NIST’s Fire Dynamics Simulator v4.05, a CFD code geared toward simulation of fire phenomena. The combined pyrolysis model/CFD code has been used to simulate opposed flow flame spread, including the effect of environmental variables on the predicted flame spread rate. It was found that at a fixed velocity the predicted flame spread rate is quite sensitive to the ambient oxygen concentration, increasing with O2 concentration. However, at a fixed oxygen concentration it was found that the predicted flame spread rate is not sensitive to the freestream velocity. This may correspond to the “flat region” seen at relatively low oxygen concentrations in the Fernandez-Pello opposed flame spread curves where the opposed flow flame spread velocity is independent of the freestream velocity.
A three-dimensional CFD model of the KC-135 FIST insert has been developed and coupled to the custom pyrolysis model being developed as part of the FIST project. The three dimensional model makes it possible to investigate the effects of the flow enclosure on the ignition and flame spread behavior in reduced gravity environments. The model is being used to better understand the effects of flow velocity, oxygen concentration, and gravity level on opposed flow flame spread rates. A limited number of three-dimensional calculations were performed with an infinitely fast gas-phase combustion reaction to investigate the effects of the flow enclosure. More recently, modeling efforts have been focused on 2D calculations using a finite-rate one step combustion reaction. Computer power limitations prevent 3D finite rate chemistry calculations from being performed. The experimental flame spread data obtained from the October 2004 KC-135 flame spread campaign are being used to “calibrate” the flame spread calculations.
The FIST team was trained by a representative from TSI Incorporated on use of the PIV system now temporarily installed on the FIST duct. Images of velocity vectors were obtained but considerable work needs to be done to give useable data on velocity fields near the reaction zone.
Analysis of flame spread images from the KC-135 are underway with successful extraction of flame spread velocities using SPOTLIGHT Image Analysis Software. Continuous burning mass loss measurements have begun in order to provide data to heat release rate calculations underway.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Experimental Subtask Ignition delay:
A type K thermocouple welded to the igniter has allowed for direct thermocouple measurements of igniter temperatures. These measurements have proven to be more stable and reproducible than the IR camera measurements conducted previously. A series of tests using these measurements have provided a minimum igniter temperature of 1105 C above which no further changes in ignition delay time is seen with increases in igniter temperature.
A series of tests were run to examine the effect of oxygen concentration on the ignition delay time of PP/30%GL. These tests were conducted at a flow rate of 1 m/s, at O2 concentrations of 17-24% and under variable heat fluxes. Tests showed an increase in ignition delay times with decreases in oxygen concentration and a limiting oxygen index for lower heat fluxes. Test results will be used to draw the ignition delay branch of flammability diagrams under variable oxygen concentrations and determine the limiting oxygen index for PPG for a range of heat fluxes.
Weight loss measurements of PP/30%GL and PMMA flame spread samples and ignition delay samples were forwarded to NASA GRC for use in filter design. This work led to development of a continuous mass loss measurement system, which measures mass changes in samples during the heating, ignition and mass burning phases of ignition delay tests. Work to date has focused on development of a Phlogopite Mica sample holder, which accommodates the polypropylene and polymethylmethacrylate samples while providing stability during mass loss measurements and thermal insulating conditions similar to those in current use in the FIST development tunnel at NASA GRC.
These tests are used to obtain information on the critical mass flux for ignition, examine the protective effects of blowing on oxidative pyrolysis and heating of the surface, support the numerical modeling of the FIST process through determination of mass loss rate, surface temperature, and back face temperature histories and to provide more accurate information about total mass loss for use in filter design. Analysis of the mass flux rate at the time of ignition gives good repeatability and has demonstrated an increase in mass flux rate at ignition with increasing heat flux for PPG. There does not appear to be a strong relationship between oxygen concentration in the induced flow and critical mass flux at ignition and work is underway to examine the effect of oxidizer velocity on critical mass flux at ignition.
A series of KC-135 tests of ignition delay with samples in the intended configuration for flight were completed. Examination of thermocouple readings showed consistency with microgravity tests completed on the KC-135 with larger sample sizes. IR and video imagery provided information on necessary improvements to the image acquisition systems intended for flight.
The UC Berkeley lab purchased a supply of black type G PMMA and PP/30%GL (PF062-3). A portion of each material has been forwarded to NASA GRC to maintain material consistency between NASA GRC and UC Berkeley.
The FIST tunnel has been modified with a particle seeding system and mounting hardware to accommodate a particle image velocimetry (PIV) system.
Flame spread:
The FIST tunnel has been modified allowing for easier transitions to the flame-spread configuration. PP/30%GL and PMMA flame spread tests were filmed using an IR camera and these digital IR images were processed using the SPOTLIGHT 1.0 image analysis software provided by NASA. This ground based analysis demonstrated that the SPOTLIGHT software allows for velocity measurements of the flame front under a variable heat flux while quantifying surface temperatures of the fuel ahead of the flame front.
Flame spread tests conducted on the KC-135 were evaluated using the methods developed in ground tests using the SPOTLIGHT software. Flame spread velocities for periods of microgravity and the 1.8 g pull-up period were quantified and analysis of IR imagery has provided information on necessary improvements to the image acquisition system.
Theoretical Subtask
As reported in FY03, a model that calculates the transient heating and gasification of a solid material exposed to thermal radiation has been combined with a model that provides a detailed description of phenomena occurring in the gas phase. A Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) code developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) known as Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) was used as the starting point. The FDS code numerically solves a discretized form of the “mildly compressible” Navier Stokes equations, which have come to be called the “low Mach number combustion equations”. In this way, a detailed spatial description of the flowfield (velocity, temperature, heat release) is obtained.
The combined solid and gas phase model was used to predict the ignition time of polypropylene/30% glass composite samples in normal and reduced gravity, and the results were compared with available experimental data. The reduced-gravity data were obtained during an earlier KC-135 flight campaign. Good agreement between the prediction and experiment was obtained. Both the experiment and prediction suggest that materials are easier to ignite in reduced-gravity low speed flows such as those that exist in manned space-based facilities. The numerical predictions also indicate that the pyrolysis rate and surface temperature at ignition are both considerably lower in low speed microgravity flows than in normal gravity flows where the minimum velocity is limited by buoyancy. This has important fire safety implications because it suggests that solid combustibles are easier to ignite under the conditions expected in space-based facilities (low-velocity ambient oxidizer flows and reduced gravity). These findings were submitted to the journal Combustion Science Technology. The paper was accepted and is currently in press.
The model was also used to examine the influence of ambient oxygen concentration on the calculated ignition delay time for the polypropylene 30% glass composite material. As a first approximation, the effect of oxygen concentration on the solid-phase decomposition rate was not included. Thus, any change in the predicted ignition time with ambient oxygen concentration is solely due to gas-phase effects. It was found that the model’s predictions are quite insensitive to ambient oxygen concentrations over the range 18%-30%, whereas the experimental measurements show that the ignition time decreases as ambient oxygen increases. However, recent mass loss rate measurements in our laboratory (as well as several papers in the literature) suggest that the rate of solid-phase polypropylene degradation is quite sensitive to the ambient oxygen concentration, increasing with oxygen level. As mentioned above, this phenomenon (more rapid decomposition at higher oxygen levels) has not yet been included in the model but could be approximated quite simply using a solid-phase activation energy that decreases with ambient O2 level. Recent experimental mass loss rate measurements made in our laboratory suggest that the freestream oxygen concentration influences the ignition time mostly by increasing the rate at which the solid material decomposes rather than through gas-phase effects because the mass loss rate at ignition was found to be relatively insensitive to ambient oxygen concentration. This is consistent with the modeling results.
The combined solid/phase and gas-phase model was used to calculate opposed flow flame spread rates on polypropylene/glass and polymethylmethacrylate samples. The available experimental data and trends are captured qualitatively by the model. A comprehensive comparison of model predictions to experimental data has not yet been performed, but is planned for FY05. The experimental data sets will include normal-gravity ground-based measurements made in our laboratory as well as microgravity flame spread data obtained on KC-135 flights in October 2004.
During FY04, several important improvements were made to the solid-phase model. It was modified to use a highly efficient recursive algorithm for solving the heat conduction equation. The computational cost of the model was reduced by several orders of magnitude, particularly for thick materials where several hundred cells may be required. The new algorithm was verified by comparison with an analytical solution for a semi-infinite solid exposed to a constant net heat flux.
The reduced computational cost of the new model makes it possible to apply stochastic search methods for optimization of input parameters. With this approach, the thermal properties and decomposition kinetics of a particular material can be estimated by finding the set of properties that minimizes the error between experimental measurements and the model predictions. However, several hundred thousand trial solutions are typically required, and this approach was not practical with earlier versions of the solid-phase model due to computational cost. An optimization technique was developed that uses a self-adaptive genetic algorithm based on the principles of Darwinian natural selection in combination with the solid phase-pyrolysis model. The genetic algorithm is essentially an optimization tool that is used to find the combination of material properties that provides the best agreement between model prediction and experiment. The required experimental measurements are mass loss rate, surface temperature, and back face temperature histories. Preliminary results are very encouraging. This method will allow us to apply the solid-phase model to other solids for which the required material properties are unknown and not available in the literature because they can be inferred from experiments in the FIST apparatus. Finally, work was started to extend the existing solid-phase model to handle charring and intumescent materials that may actually be used in extraterrestrial habitats. Due to the increased complexity of the underlying physical models for charring materials, the number of required material properties will be increased. However, the genetic algorithm optimization technique should make it possible to estimate the required material properties, even for complex charring or intumescent materials.

Task Description:
Funding is for Prof. Fernandez-Pello's role as U.S. Co-Investigator for the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)-sponsored project, “Flammability Limits At Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE)." JAXA International Announcement of Opportunity (AO) to fund experiments to be conducted aboard the Japanese Experiment Module, Kibo, 2012.
The objective of the proposed research program is to continue the experimental study of the flammability of wire materials in space exploration atmospheres and associated computational/theoretical tools to aid interpretation of test results.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Studying materials flammability in spacecraft allows us to accurately elucidate the effect of the environment parameters on the ignition and flame spread over combustible material, and through them their potential fire hazard. Particularly important is the determination of the Limiting Oxygen Concentration (LOC) on flame extinction under spacecraft environments. The anticipated improved methodology should reduce time and cost for the spacecraft material screening. Another important aspect of the research is the effect of melting and dripping of plastic insulation in normal gravity in comparison with microgravity. The results are relevant because dripping will not occur in microgravity and consequently could impact their burning and methodology to screen. The investigation and results have also benefits for terrestrial fire safety by providing further information about the flammability of materials under a variety of environments.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
During this reporting period, melting and dripping behavior during the opposed flame spread over horizontal and vertical polyethylene (PE) insulated wires were investigated. Two different wire dimensions – core/wire diameter of 3.5/8.0 and 5.5/9.0 mm – and three different insulations – low-density polyethylene (LDPE), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), and black LDPE (B-LDPE) – were tested. In order to identify the effect of the core, wires with solid copper core (Cu), hollow stainless steel core (SS), and without core were tested. Experimental results showed that a high-conductance copper core acted as a heat source downstream to increase the flame spread rate. However, in the upstream burning region, the copper core acted as a heat sink, cooling and reducing the mobility of the melting insulation. As a result, the copper core extended the insulation’s residence time in the flame to facilitate burning and reduce dripping. Moreover, in the vertical downward flame spread, the insulation drips flowed downward to preheat the wire, and this heating dominated over the heating by the core. As a result, higher dripping fraction for wires with lower thermal conductance resulted in faster flame spread. This is the first time that the simultaneous dual effect of heat source and sink for wire core was observed, and the influence of dripping on flame spread over wire was discovered.
NOTE that this project is continued by "Wire Combustion with External Radiation in Support of the JAXA Project Fundamental Research on International Standard of Fire Safety in Space"; grant number 80NSSC19K0331 with the same Principal Investigator, Prof. Carlos Fernandez-Pello. See that project for subsequent reporting.

Task Progress:
The research has one primary goal: to understand the changes in electrical wire flammability in the environment expected in space-based facilities. An aspect of the problem is that if the insulation material melts during the wire burning, major differences in flammability may occur between normal and microgravity, because the molten material will not drip in microgravity. Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
A program to study the flammability characteristics of electrical wiring insulation materials that will complement the existing JAXA project entitled “Fundamental Research on International Standard of Fire Safety in Space” (FLARE) so as to provide an assessment of wire materials flammability in the conditions expected in “Space Exploration Atmospheres” (SEA) has been continued at University of California (UC) Berkeley under NASA sponsorship for the last year. A summary of the research conducted during the period March 1, 2016 to February 28, 2017 is reported here.
The research has one primary goal: to understand the changes in electrical wire flammability, specifically the LOI-LOC (Limiting Oxygen Index-Limiting Oxygen Concentration), in the environment expected in space-based facilities, particularly those at exploration atmospheres (elevated oxygen concentration and low pressure). To date, flammability testing has focused mostly on atmospheric conditions. Work conducted at NASA Glenn Resarch Center (GRC) and at the combustion laboratories at UC Berkeley indicate that materials are more flammable in SEA atmospheres. However, considerable work remains to understand how the new cabin environment influences material flammability, particularly that of electrical wires.
The project experimental methodology consists of obtaining flame spread flammability boundaries (LOI-LOC) of electrical wires and wire insulation materials (primarily those being studied in Hokkaido University) in SEA environments and under external radiation. To conduct the experiments, an experimental apparatus and a bench-scale flammability test were developed during the previous grant period. This apparatus was used during the present period to continue the studies of LOC of wire insulation for flame spread at different environmental conditions and external radiation. The testing methodology is supported with theoretical modeling of the ignition and flame spread process.
While carrying out the flame spread tests it was observed that melting and dripping of the wire insulation had an important role in the process and that it influenced both the rate of flame spread and the LOC of the material. For this reason a subproject was initiated to study the role of wire insulation melting and dripping on the wire ignition and flame spread process. This is very significant because the burning characteristics of the wire insulation would be drastically different in normal and microgravity. Studies related to this subject comprised most of the work conducted during this reporting period. We feel that the findings to date are both novel and important to spacecraft fire safety. The research primarily supports the above mentioned JAXA program but also could lead to better determination and ranking of the fire hazard characteristics of potential wire insulation materials to be used in spacecraft.
