Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
High temperature air combustion technology has been accepted and now utilized by many countries around the world for significant energy savings, pollution reduction, and better quality of product produced from the process since the temperature in the entire combustion zone is very uniform (better than 40degrees C). Ultra low NOx, and carbon monoxide are produced with negligible unburnt hydrocarbons. Such achievements are new and provides a basis for many new applications.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Experimental
The experiments were conducted using a 1 sec drop tower facility. The experimental burner consisted of a 0.686 mm diameter fuel jet that was centrally located in a 12.7 mm diameter air jet. The combustion air in the outer jet could be maintained at any temperature, up to about 1100oC using electrical heating. The experiment test rig consisted of burner, voltage regulator, electrical air preheater, combustion chamber, color CCD camera and digital camcorder, and gas cylinders for fuel, combustion air, and burner cooling. The flame images were captured using a CCD camera in the emission mode at a framing rate of 30 frames per second and then recorded onto a digital camcorder. Several experiments were conducted under microgravity conditions at normal pressure and normal oxygen concentration air using propane as the fuel at a flow rate 0.02 SCFH. The flame photographs, recorded with the color CCD camera and camcorder, were analyzed to determine the flame shape (length and width) and color.
Results and Discussion
The results are presented at two air preheat temperatures of 900oC and 1000oC. The experiments were conducted with combustion air preheated to temperatures in the range of 900oC (for experiment #3) to 1000oC (experiment #4) at a propane gas flow rate of 0.02 SCFH. Preparation for the experiments involved turning on the air preheater to get the desired air preheats temperature. In this paper results from two specific experiments (experiments #3 & 4) are reported to provide the effect of air preheat temperature on flame size, shape and color (hybrid) under microgravity and normal gravity conditions. Before the drop the video camera was turned on to record the flame features at 1-g. The time sequence photos of flame during drop were separated from the recorded images onto the video camera at a speed of 30 frames/s. The results show that in both cases the flames are of hybrid color consisting of initial blue color flame followed by a yellow color flame downstream of the burner. The length of the yellow color flame is higher at higher air preheat temperature (compare flame photos from experiments #4 with #3). The yellow portion of the flame with experiments # 4 (having higher air preheat temperature) is higher. A close examination of the entire flame length (blue and yellow portion) shows that the length of flame in experiment #4 is shorter as compared to flames produced in experiment #3. The flames photographs were further analyzed with respect to the total length and width as well as the length and width of the blue and yellow portion of the flames during the entire time duration in the microgravity environment. The results show shorter flame at higher air preheats temperatures. Immediately after the onset of drop (very low microgravity conditions) the flame length for experiment #4 (with high air preheats) is smaller. This suggests that higher temperature air reduces the flame length in microgravity.
Our results obtained at 1-g conditions also showed that the flame length decreases with increase in air preheats [20, 21] using normal air. In contrast the flame width increases with increase in air preheats under microgravity conditions (compare flame width from t =0 to about t = 0.1 for the two cases). At the onset of microgravity the flame with high air preheats temperature experiences a rapid increase in flame width (experiment #4) as compared to low temperature air case (experiment #3). The rate of increase of flame width is higher with higher air preheats at t =0.1 to about t = 0.2. After t = 0.2 sec both flames reach the maximum width due to lower gravity field. The change in gravity with time during the drop was calculated by balancing the force on the entire drop package (i.e., drag and gravity = mass x acceleration).
At higher residence times (t) under microgravity conditions the flame length increases because of the drag and hence a higher gravity values as compared to that obtained at the onset of drop. This suggests that under microgravity conditions the flames are smaller and wider with increase in air preheats. At higher air preheats the yellow portion of the flame becomes higher and the blue portion of the flame becomes smaller. Hotter flames (with higher air preheats) affect the shape more (with regard to their length and width) in the presence of microgravity. These results are in agreement with the studies carried out at normal gravity conditions. The fuel flow rate and temperature of the air calculated results was taken as 0.02 ft3 /hr. (i.e., same flow rate as in the measurements). While the trends for the flame width are similar, the predicted length of the flame is higher. This shows that high temperature air has significant effect on reducing the flame length. This observation has also been made in 1-g experiments. The relative change in flame width and length during the microgravity test duration is consistent with the change in microgravity conditions during the drop, i.e., smaller length and larger width with increase in microgravity during the drop. Global features on the change in flame length and width as affected by gravity and air preheat temperature show that high air preheats further widens the flame width and reduces the flame length in microgravity conditions.
Conclusions
1. Flame length decreases and the width increases under microgravity conditions.
2. At higher air preheat temperatures the flame length decreases under microgravity conditions. Under microgravity conditions at high air preheat temperature, the flame width is even wider as compared to normal temperature air and normal gravity conditions.
3. The flame luminosity as measured by the yellow color of the flame increases with increase in air preheats temperature under microgravity conditions. This is consistent with the findings at the normal gravity conditions.
4. The correlations provide reasonably good agreement on the flame width at high air preheats with that observed under microgravity conditions.
5. The data obtained provides useful information for model validation and model development.

Task Description:
Abstract
The characteristics of gaseous diffusion flames have been obtained using high temperature combustion air under microgravity and normal gravity conditions. The time resolved flame images under free fall microgravity conditions were obtained from the video images obtained. The tests results reported here were conducted using propane as the fuel and about 1000oC combustion air. The burner included a central fuel jet injected into the surrounding high temperature combustion air. The fuel jet exit Reynolds number was 63 with a nozzle diameter of 0.686 mm. Several measurements were taken at different air preheats and fuel jet exit Reynolds number. The resulting hybrid color flame was found to be blue at the base of the flame followed by a yellow color flame. The length and width of flame during the entire free fall conditions has been examined. Also the relative flame length and width for blue and yellow portion of the flame has been examined under microgravity conditions. The results show that the flame length decreases and width increases with high air preheats in microgravity condition. In microgravity conditions the flame length is larger with normal temperature combustion air than high temperature air. Correlations used to predict the shapes of round non-buoyant laminar flames have been used to examine the shapes of high temperature air flames under microgravity conditions. The results show favorable predictions for the flame width during the microgravity conditions.

Task Description:
A series of measurements and calculations have been undertaken in an effort improve the understanding of the suppression of low strain rate flames by an agent in microgravity. The current study extends a previous investigation by developing and comparing a two-dimensional numerical simulation of flame structure and extinction to measurements made in micro-gravity and normal gravity for methane-air non-premixed flames with Nitrogen added to the reactants. Additional measurements and calculations are planned to consider non-premixed methane and propane flames suppressed by CO2 and CF3Br. It is anticipated that a database of suppression requirements for a matrix of fuels and suppressants will be useful to NASA for determining agent mass requirements for fire protection applications. Diagnostic capabilities will be added to the current microgravity experimental rig.
Task Objective: To investigate the effects of buoyancy on the structure and extinction of low strain rate flames through experimentation and computer simulation.
The project is relevant from both a fire safety and a fundamental perspective. Unwanted fires typically occur due to non-premixed combustion. The agent concentration required to achieve the suppression of non-premixed flames is an important consideration in design of total flooding fire protection systems. The initial stage of an unwanted fire in a microgravity environment, such as an orbiting space platform, will likely occur at a low strain rate. A primary motivation of this proposal is to measure the agent concentrations that are required to achieve extinction of counterflowing non-premixed (or diffusion) flames at low strain rates, measurements that are not possible to perform in normal gravity due to buoyancy induced flame instabilities. For this reason, there is a gap in knowledge regarding the suppression effectiveness of agents on diffusion flames for strain rates below approximately 20 s-1.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
New knowledge generated from this project could impact the search strategy for halon fire suppression replacements for fires in normal gravity, that is typical fires on Earth.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
The final report describes the study that has been supported through the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) microgravity grants program. This work was a continuation of a NASA microgravity grant that was active from February 1999 through September 2003. The work has used computations and measurements to investigate the structure and suppression of low strain rate non-premixed flames. This final report, on the latest grant, includes a summary of the work done on the contract and a list of publications.
The work during this grant period focused on both measurements and calculations and included the following:
• Continued development of the two-dimensional simulation with finite rate chemistry. [Hamins et al., 2007; Oh et al., 2007]. These publications are listed in the Bibliography section below. These calculations considered extinction of methane-air diffusion flames with N2 added to the fuel stream. The work compares calculations with our earlier measurements made in normal gravity and in microgravity using the NASA 2.2 s drop tower.
• Two-dimensional calculations were completed that considered the extinction of methane-air diffusion flames with CO2 added to the fuel stream in normal and microgravity. The computations were compared to the N2 addition results described in Hamins et al., 2007; Oh et al., 2007. Complete citation information is listed in the Bibliography section below.
• Flame extinction studies on the normal gravity extinction of propane were conducted.
• Finally, spectroscopic measurements were conducted on key flame intermediates to support detailed modeling of radiative exchange in near-extinction flames. Wakasuki et al. [2005] developed a method to estimate the temperature dependence of absorption coefficients through an extrapolation algorithm. This publication is listed in the Bibliography section below.
Spectroscopic measurements are important to understand the mechanisms of extinction associated with flames being suppressed by agents. CF3Br (Halon 1301) is one of the most important suppressants and has been used on space platforms for many years. Suppression studies often use CF3BR as a reference or baseline in considering the effectiveness of alternative agents. As part of this study, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements were made on CF3Br at elevated temperatures. Similar spectral measurements and analysis for propane, heptane and propylene were also conducted. The manuscripts mentioned above are listed in the Bibliography section below.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
MODELING The research this year has focused on developing an improved two-dimensional simulation – with finite rate chemistry. A transient two-dimensional flame simulation code based on a finite chemistry was developed to simulate the microgravity and 1-g counterflow nonpremixed flames. The simulation is able to predict the flame shape and the transition from a 1-g to microgravity, which occurs when performing drop tower experiments. The model also predicts the critical nitrogen volume fraction in the fuel stream needed for flame extinction (“extinction limit”) and the structure of near-extinction microgravity and 1-g flames. The code is based on a two-dimensional direct numerical simulation (DNS) method incorporating a 3-step global reaction mechanism [Dryer and Glassman, 1972] for methane oxidation. Detailed transport properties are considered. The buoyancy term was included in the governing equations to simulate the 1-g flame properly. A predictor-corrector method was used to integrate the governing equations explicitly. The time step was controlled such that a stable solution was obtained during the computation. An optically-thin radiation model was adopted due to computational cost.
EXPERIMENTS The research this year has also focused on analyzing the microgravity measurements previously obtained at the NASA 2.2 s drop tower. Particular attention was paid to the analysis process ing of the SiC fiber intensity measurement results, which are being used to determine flame temperature in near extinction flames. In addition, similar experiments in normal gravity were conducted using a 23.1 mm diameter counter-flow burner. These measurements were conducted to compare the microgravity results with those of normal gravity and to clarify the velocity ratio effects and the multi-dimensional effects due to effects associated with a finite burner diameter. The experimental conditions were carefully selected to avoid heating the burner duct.
SUMMARY Development of the two dimensional simulation has been very important in understanding flame structure and extinction phenomena, phenomena that were not fully understood using the popular one-dimensional flamelet models. The interpretation of the experiments by Maruta et al. [1998] can only be completely understood if multi-dimensional effects are considered. For the low strain rate microgravity flames studied by Maruta et al. [1998] in a small diameter burner, the turning point cannot be attributed purely to radiative loss -lateral heat loss must also be considered. Interpretation of the experiments by Bundy et al. [2003] also requires consideration of multi-dimensional effects. In that case, however, the buoyancy induced flow field with its varying strain rate is mainly responsible for the observed turning point behavior. In summary, interpretation of flame extinction phenomena has been greatly aided by the 2D simulation developed in this study.

Task Description:
Strongly-pulsed turbulent flames are studied by the injection of a fuel jet of unheated gaseous hydrocarbon fuel (ethylene) into a co-flowing oxidizer. In all cases the flames are fully-modulated, with the fuel jet completely shut off between injection intervals. Optical diagnostics and probes are used to determine the flame length, the dynamics of the large-scale flame puff structures, the velocity field and the rate of oxidizer entrainment, the combustion temperatures, flame radiation, and the exhaust emissions of the pulsed and steady flames. Experiments to study the pulsed flame structure and thermal characteristics are conducted in reduced gravity using the NASA GRC 2.2 second Drop Tower. Laboratory experiments to examine the flame structure and exhaust emissions are performed at the UW (University of Washington); velocity field measurements are undertaken at WPI (Worcester Polytechnic Institute). The combustion characteristics of fully-modulated diffusion flames are also investigated by three-dimensional, unsteady computations using both direct numerical and large eddy simulation approaches. The overall objective of this research program is to determine the behavior of strongly-pulsed and steady turbulent diffusion flames in both normal and reduced gravity. Emphasis is placed on examining the effects of buoyancy on the development and interaction of the turbulent flame structures over a wide range of injection conditions, ranging from isolated, non-interacting flame puffs to flames with steady injection. The implications of the dynamics and interaction of the burning fuel puffs for fuel/air mixing, combustion, and exhaust emissions are to be established. Combustion is critical to many systems essential to the technical infrastructure of the United States and of the world. Examples of important applications of combustion technology range from domestic furnaces and water heaters to large-scale central power stations. Turbulent combustion, which involves the complex coupling of chemical and fluid mechanical processes, is a critical fundamental problem for combustion processes. Specifically, combustion devices that are based on unsteady, turbulent flow appear to have the potential to achieve the low levels of emissions required to meet increasingly stringent environmental regulations, as well as economical savings that might derive from the use of more compact combustors.
However, the physical phenomena responsible for the enhanced mixing in unsteady, reacting flows are not currently well understood (the mechanisms operative in steady, turbulent jet flames are also not completely understood). Part of the difficulty in either case stems from the presence of buoyancy, which significantly complicates the turbulent mixing in flames in normal gravity. By the use of the microgravity environment to effectively remove the effects of buoyancy, an improved fundamental understanding of the fuel/air mixing and combustion characteristics of both fully-modulated and steady-state combustion systems can result. The resulting new fundamental knowledge may then lead to improved combustor designs for higher efficiency, more economical operation, and lower emissions for numerous applications on earth.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This work to date suggests that there are apparently specific injection conditions where the emissions of fully-modulated flames are comparable to those of the steady flame while the flame length is significantly shorter. This points to the potential utility of this technique in the development of compact, low emissions combustors involving turbulent diffusion flames.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Activities over the past year included: 1) pulsed-flame experiments in microgravity in the 2.2 s Drop tower at NASA Glenn Research Center; 2) measurements of pulsed-flame emissions in the laboratory, 3) surveys of turbulent puffs using Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV); and 4) numerical modeling of pulsed jet diffusion flames.
The combustor contains a fuel nozzle with inner diameter of 2 mm centered in a square duct 20 × 20 cm in cross section and 52 cm in length. The fuel is pure ethylene (C2H4) and the oxidizer co-flow consists of either air (lab experiments) or 30% O2 and 70% N2 by volume (Drop Tower tests). The gaseous fuel flow is controlled by a fast-response solenoid valve actuated in an on-off fashion. A continuously-energized, heated-wire igniter situated a few millimeters downstream of the nozzle exit ensures the ignition of each fuel puff upon injection. Experiments have been performed with a nozzle exit Reynolds number of 5000 and injection times ranging from 6 ms to 303 ms with jet off-times from 5 ms to 300 ms. Flame imaging is performed using a CCD array at a framing rate of 400 Hz. The mean flame lengths are determined using NASA's Spotlight image tracking program. The celerity (bulk velocity) of the turbulent flame puffs is determined by cross-correlating the temperature signals between a pair of type-R thermocouples at the location of the visible flame tip. Measurement of exhaust emissions are performed within the combustor and at the combustor exit using an aspirated sampling probe and standard emissions analyzers.
Reducing the jet-off time, for a fixed injection time, leads to a significant increase in the degree of flame puff interaction and results in an increase in the flame length. The high-speed imaging results reveals details of the flame structure and the onset of flame puff interaction as the jet off-time is decreased. The structure of fully-modulated flames is seen to be generally similar for normal gravity and microgravity, with the microgravity flame puffs persisting for a slightly longer time and advecting more slowly downstream than their normal-gravity counterparts. The measured puff celerity varied from a maximum value of c = 3.2 m/s to a minimum of c = 0.86 m/s (the injection velocity was 22 m/s). Three trends are apparent: 1) an increase in the puff celerity as the jet off-time is decreased, 2) a higher celerity for a lower value of the injection time, and 3) a higher celerity in normal gravity than in microgravity. The puff celerity in normal gravity exceeds that in microgravity by as much as 40% for the shortest injection time; a similar increase was recorded for both gravity levels as the injection time parameter decreased from 46 ms to 6 ms. The celerity of the most strongly-interacting flame puffs was as much as 2.8 times greater than for the case of isolated flame puffs. This increase in celerity is consistent with a decreased rate of momentum exchange, per amount of injected fuel, between the flame puffs and the oxidizer co-flow. Although buoyancy results in only a modest change in the flame length (6-20%), there is a consistently positive effect of buoyancy on the celerity of the flame puff structures.
For these strongly-pulsed flames, the values of the CO emission index (EICO) are generally higher than that of the steady flame. For sufficiently long injection time the EICO becomes comparable to the steady flame value for all values of the jet-off time. The EICO is highest for flame puffs with the shortest injection time. The observed decrease in the emission index of CO with decreasing jet-off time is consistent with the increased structure/structure interactions, which result in a longer flame length and a longer flame residence time due to a decreased rate of air entrainment per amount of fuel injected. For most injection conditions the measured exhaust-point NO concentrations are below those of the steady flame, and become comparable to the steady flame values for sufficiently short jet off-time. The increase in NO level with decreasing jet-off time is most pronounced for short injection times. The increase in the NO emission index (EINO) for short off-times is consistent with the greater flame puff interaction which leads to a slower rate of excess air dilution for a given amount of injected fuel, leading in turn to a longer flame length and a higher residence time.
The emission index of CO correlates well with a global residence time based on the observed variation of flame length. The EINO by contrast does not correlate with residence time for all values of injection time. The EINO does increase with increasing residence time for a fixed value of injection time. Temperature changes that accompany changes in the rate of air entrainment per volume of injected fuel could explain why the amount of NO emitted per mass of fuel injected is strongly dependent both the flame structure as well as the residence time. There are injection time and jet-off time combinations where the emissions of fully-modulated flames are comparable to those of steady flames, but with a shorter flame length. These results point toward potential benefits of the fully-modulated injection technique in the development of compact, low emissions combustors involving turbulent diffusion flames.
PIV investigations of strongly-pulsed, non-reacting jets have been conducted in a similar configuration as the combustion experiments. In this case the chamber was 30 × 30 cm in cross section and the nozzle diameter was 5 mm. Puffs were generated by injecting room temperature air through the nozzle into a flow chamber with a seeded, weak air co-flow. The seed particles were either 40 micron or 9 micron diameter aluminum oxide particles. The injection conditions were similar to the combustion experiments. Isolated jet puffs were examined at a location roughly 50 jet diameters downstream of the injection nozzle, at which location the puffs mixed sufficiently with the co-flow so that there is sufficient seeding within the puff for PIV data acquisition. The flow field was illuminated by a laser sheet from a double-pulsed Nd:YAG laser at a wavelength of 532 nm and a pulse energy of approximately 10 mJ/pulse. Images were recorded by a progressive scan CCD camera with a 60 Hz frame rate and a 640 × 480 pixel resolution. The time separation between successive pulses was on the order of 0.5 ms to 1 ms. The field of view for the velocity measurements was approximately 34 jet nozzle diameters in the radial direction and 25 diameters in the axial direction. Conditional averaging methods were developed and utilized to remove the spatial jitter resulting from the turbulent nature of the flow. The location of maximum velocity within each isolated puff used to align the velocity fields from different runs. The position of peak vorticity within the primary vortex core of the puff was used to align the vorticity fields.
The vorticity measured by PIV is confined primarily within the axially-elongated vortex cores. The peak vorticity occurs approximately 5 jet diameters from the centerline at a downstream distance of 50 diameters. Relatively little vorticity resides in the wake of the vortex core. Conditional averaging significantly smoothes the average vorticity, yielding significantly lower levels of maximum vorticity than observed in the instantaneous case. The rms of the vorticity fluctuations appears to be is mainly limited to the vortex core region, and can reach as much as 50% of the peak values within the core. The turbulent shear stress distribution is quite complex for this flow field. The axial velocity fluctuation has a ring type structure similar to the vorticity field; the radial velocity fluctuation is more elongated in the axial direction.
An existing computer code for steady jet diffusion flames has been modified to simulate strongly-pulsed flames. This code employs Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) using a low Mach number approximation applied to the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, combined with a single-step, Arrehenius-type reaction scheme. A massively parallel implementation of this code has been developed and run on the Cray X1 at the Arctic Region Supercomputer Center. Pulsed jet simulations have been performed for a Reynolds number of 1000 and an injection time of 0.6 ms. This very short injection time results in a "micro-puff" configuration, which exhibits the puff-like structure of these flames. The computational domain is being extended to simulate flames over the parameter range corresponding to the experiments. This implies significantly increased numerical resolution, a large computational domain, and calculations over longer time scales. Currently, two approaches are being pursued for this purpose. The first involves implementing a non-uniform mesh, which will enable the computational resolution to be concentrated only where it is needed. The second candidate approach is to apply monotonically integrated large eddy simulation (MILES).

Task Description:
Fully-modulated fuel jets consisting of unheated gaseous hydrocarbon fuel (ethylene) are injected into a co-flowing or stagnant oxidizer. Optical diagnostics and probes are used to determine the flame length, the velocity field and the rate of oxidizer entrainment, the combustion temperatures, flame radiation, and exhaust emissions of pulsed and steady flames in both normal and reduced gravity. Experiments are conducted in the laboratory to characterize the baseline flame behavior at normal gravity conditions and in microgravity using the NASA GRC 2.2 second Drop Tower and the 5.18 s Zero-Gravity Facility. Laboratory experiments to examine the flame structure and exhaust emissions are performed at the UW; laboratory velocity field measurements are undertaken at WPI. The combustion characteristics of fully-modulated diffusion flames are also investigated by three-dimensional, unsteady computations using both direct numerical and large eddy simulation approaches. The overall objective of this research program is to determine the behavior of fully-modulated (i.e., fuel completely shut off during part of each pulsing cycle) and steady turbulent diffusion flames in both normal and reduced gravity. Emphasis is placed on examining the effects of buoyancy on the development and interaction of the turbulent flame structures over a wide range of injection conditions, ranging from isolated, non-interacting flame puffs to flames with steady injection. The implications of the dynamics and interaction of the burning fuel puffs for fuel/air mixing, combustion, and exhaust emissions are to be established. Combustion is critical to many systems essential to the technical infrastructure of the United States and of the world. Examples of important applications of combustion technology range from domestic furnaces and water heaters to large-scale central power stations. Turbulent combustion, which involves the complex coupling of chemical and fluid mechanical processes, is a critical fundamental problem for combustion processes. Specifically, combustion devices that are based on unsteady, turbulent flow appear to have the potential to achieve the low levels of emissions required to meet increasingly stringent environmental regulations, as well as economical savings that might derive from the use of more compact combustors.
However, the physical phenomena responsible for the enhanced mixing in unsteady, reacting flows are not currently well understood (the mechanisms operative in steady, turbulent jet flames are also not completely understood). Part of the difficulty in either case stems from the presence of buoyancy, which significantly complicates the turbulent mixing in flames in normal gravity. By the use of the microgravity environment to effectively remove the effects of buoyancy, an improved fundamental understanding of the fuel/air mixing and combustion characteristics of both fully-modulated and steady-state combustion systems can result. The resulting new fundamental knowledge may then lead to improved combustor designs for higher efficiency, more economical operation, and lower emissions for numerous applications on earth.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This work to date suggests that there are apparently specific injection conditions where the emissions of fully-modulated flames are comparable to those of the steady flame while the flame length is significantly shorter. This points to the potential utility of this technique in the development of compact, low emissions combustors involving turbulent diffusion flames.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The combustor from an existing Drop Tower Rig has been installed and is operational in a new Combustion Laboratory at the UW. The combustor (10 x 10 cm cross section and 52 cm in length downstream of the nozzle tip) is supplied by ethylene fuel and house compressed air. Fully-modulated flames have been generated over the full range of pulsing conditions (injection times ranging from 6 ms to steady flames).
A high framing rate CCD camera is operational and provides for imaging of the laboratory pulsed flames at up to 400 frames/second. High-speed images of the pulsed flames are currently being acquired. A pair of thermocouples with known separation has been configured to measure directly the celerity of flame puffs in normal gravity. A suite of emissions instruments is being assembled to measure CO, CO2, O2, and NOx concentrations; this includes an existing unburned hydrocarbons analyzer.
In order to enhance the temporal resolution of the Particle Imaging Velocimetry (PIV) for velocity-field measurements, a reduced nozzle exit velocities and increased injection times are desired. The nozzle diameter in an existing combustor at WPI has been increased to 5 mm, resulting in a 2.5-fold decrease in the nozzle velocity compared with previous experiments. To accommodate the larger nozzle, the co-flow chamber has also been enlarged to a 30 x 30 cm square. An added benefit of the larger nozzle is that a much longer injection time (over 6-fold longer than previously) can be obtained for the same normalized puff injection volume used in previous experiments. The larger combustion chamber with glass walls, pulsing system, and fuel jet and air supplies has been assembled.
Computations has been carried out to assess the Stokes number of various sized particles to be used in conjunction with the PIV system suggests and optimum particle size of 20 microns. To avoid clogging the small orifice pulsing valve, seed particles are injected into the combustion chamber co-flow. A cyclone seeder has been designed and constructed to introduce alumina particles into the air co-flow. The seeder can handle particle sizes in the range of 1 to 40 microns.
The feasibility of performing emissions measurements in microgravity using the NASA GRC Zero-G Facility (ZGF) is being studied. Analysis indicates that, for most conditions, the ppm concentration levels of emissions in the entire ZGF chamber after one drop will not be sufficiently high to enable reliable measurements of the concentrations of CO and unburned hydrocarbons (UHC). Options for providing for a centerline-mounted, aspirated sampling probe, coupled with an initially evacuated vessel mounted external to the ZGF chamber are currently being evaluated.

Task Description: The detection of fires is very important within closed environments such as the Space Shuttle and International Space Station. Fires need to be detected within such areas as soon as possible, preferably before combustion has taken place. Previous research performed at KSC has shown that the multi-sensor technology commonly known as the electronic nose (e-nose) is able to detect the offgassing products from the insulation of heated wires well before combustion starts. Note that e-nose technology is not concerned with identifying in an analytical sense the chemicals being detected, but with classifying a mixture of vapors as coming from one source or another. This project would expand upon these results, and produce an integrated system of sensors and software which would not only provide a pre-combustion alarm, but also identify what kind of material is being overheated (wire insulation, printed circuit board, etc.). Metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensors are low cost, available in numerous miniature configurations, have a wide range of selectivity to various vapors, and are simple to operate. To that end, commercially available MOS sensors will be incorporated into a sensor array and exposed to thermal out-gassing products of electrical components. In addition, conventional circuit board components (e.g., IC chips-usually encapsulated in resins) will be subjected to heat cycles to mimic catastrophic failure with a potential fire hazard. Pattern recognition techniques will be developed at KSC to identify those commercially available sensors which provide the most sensitivity and reliability to detection and identification. It is recognized that other sensor technologies (e.g., SAW, quartz micro-balance, etc.) could potentially increase the identification power of the array, and so other sensor types will be tested and incorporated into the array if they are found to be useful. While this technology would be designed with flight consideration in mind, the result of this project will not be a flight-ready system, but one or two prototypes whose sensors have been partially screened for flight qualification.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Fire detection systems.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
The electronic nose has been adopted for use as a pre-combustion fire detection system that would specifically look for faults electronic components and electrical wiring. Specifically, the Airsense Enose has been selected and 4 classifiers have been trained to look at 9 different electrical components and wiring. For components in a 1’x1’x1’ volume, the Enose/Classifers can detect the presence of pre-combustion gases within 2 minutes. Additionally, it is most likely possible to identify the source of the gases (e.g. heated wire, resistor, inductor, etc…).
A prototype portable unit has been developed that implements the fire detection mechanisms. This unit is self-contained, operates on standard 120V 60Hz AC, and can audibly, visually, and electrically alarm upon the detection of pre-combustion components. Varying background gas and pre-combustion gas concentration would likely limit the operation of this technology to very specific, well controlled environments. However, given those more specific, well controlled conditions, the Enose would successfully work as a pre-combustion fire detection system.

Task Description:
Cool flames have significant implications for the control of engine knocking, ground and space fire safety, and combustion emissions. The recent International Space Station (ISS) combustion science experiments on flame extinguishment discovered the existence of cool flames for both large single droplets and droplet arrays after radiative extinction. Numerical simulations of droplet combustion also provide an explanation for the transition of hot flame to cool flame after radiative extinction. However, it remains unclear at what conditions the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. It is also not clear how oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition. More importantly, due to limits of space and payload, the ISS experiments did not provide detailed speciation and temperature distributions of cool flame structures for quantitative validation of kinetics and radiation model.
By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, we propose to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to * develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection ; * bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames ; * predict and answer the question at what conditions the transition from hot flame extinction to cool flames is possible and verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments ; * obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames ; * extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry. The proposed new ground-based experiments and data analysis are complimentary to and not directly linked with the science objectives from the original ISS combustion science investigation, and will significantly advance the understanding of near-limit cool flame dynamics and contribute to the future control of engine knocking, ground and space fire safety, and combustion emissions.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
An experimentally validated dimethyl ether (DME) and methane cool flame kinetic model was developed. The results showed that the existing kinetic model significantly over-predicts the cool flame extinction limits. Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
The extinction limits and cool flame radical index of non-premixed cool flames of large n-alkanes ranging from n-heptane to n-dodecane were measured in an atmospheric counterflow burner. The results demonstrate that an increase in fuel and oxygen concentration increases the cool flame extinction limit. In addition, with the increase in the carbon chain length of the n-alkane, the cool extinction limit also increases. The results also demonstrate that the dependence of cool flame extinction limit on ambient oxygen concentration for different n-alkanes is similar. The results are consistent with the measurements of extinction conditions in FLEX microgravity n-alkane-droplet experiments. The results also demonstrate that, due to the combined effects of multi-oxygen addition processes and the negative temperature coefficient effect, the cool flame low-temperature reactivity of n-alkanes is proportional to nth power of oxygen mole fraction, [O2]n. In this study, we measured n = 1.7, which is greater than n = 1.5 derived from the microgravity droplet experiment. The increase is due to the estimated NTC crossover temperature and radical dissociation being higher than the peak cool flame temperature predicted with detailed chemistry and transport effects.
Furthermore, we also found that the transport-weighted enthalpy and radical index proposed for non-premixed hot flames are not directly applicable to the cool flames because of the existence of fuel and oxygen leakage in cool flames and the location of the flame with respect to the stagnation plane. By accounting for the cool flame thermal and mass transport effects with a mass-weighted enthalpy, a cool flame radical index was proposed to evaluate the cool flame reactivity and to correlate the extinction limits of large n-alkanes with different carbon lengths. The results showed that the cool flame extinction limits of n-alkanes collapse for the combination of the cool flame radical index and the mass-weighted enthalpy. In addition, the results showed that, with the increase of the chain length of the fuel molecule, the cool flame radical index increases. The derived scaling relation and radical index provide an alternative and convenient metric to evaluate low-temperature reactivity for new fuels and surrogate fuel mixtures. Further work to extend the current results to fuels with different moieties (and hence radical indices) is warranted and is of practical relevance.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
In Year 4 (2019-2020), we conducted three research projects. Firstly, we used the experimental conditions of FLEX flight and conducted a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames. The results showed that the counterflow diffusion cool flame extinction limits are significantly affected by the oxygen concentration on the oxidizer side. However, different from the NASA FLEX data, counterflow diffusion cool flame extinction limit is more sensitive to the oxygen concentration.
Secondly, we conducted experimental studies of NO kinetic effects on the n-dodecane cool and warm diffusion flames. It was observed that NO addition reducing narrows cool flame extinction limits, inhibiting inhibits the transition from warm flame to cool flame, and promoting promotes the ignition transition from warm flame to hot flame. In addition, jet-stirred reactor (JSR) experiments of n-dodecane oxidation without and with NO addition were also performed. A validated low temperature n-dodecane/NOx kinetic model was developed.
Thirdly, autoignition-assisted nonpremixed cool flames of diethyl ether (DEE) are investigated under both laminar counterflow and turbulent jet flame configurations. The results show that below a critical mixture condition, the cool flame extinction limit and the low-temperature ignition limit merges at highly diluted DEE conditions, leading to an autoignition-assisted cool flame stabilization without hysteresis. By using a Co-flow Axisymmetric Reactor-Assisted Turbulent (CARAT) burner, the lift-off heights of auto-ignition assisted turbulent cool flame are quantified using formaldehyde planar laser-induced fluorescence. A correlation is proposed such that the autoignition assisted cool flame lift-off height scales with the product of the flow velocity and the square of the first-stage ignition delay time. The scaling results indicated that the correlation is valid with a chemical kinetic model which most reasonably predicted the cool flame stabilization limits of the laminar experiments.

Progress
We made two main progresses in Year 3 of our research: (1) An experimentally validated dimethyl ether (DME) and methane cool flame kinetic model was developed; and (2) we established successfully diffusion warm flames of n-alkanes.
In this first task, the extinction strain rates of hot flames, cool flames, and ozone-assisted cool flames have been measured in a counterflow burner. The reactivity of the hot flames is promoted by methane addition on a fuel mass fraction basis. However, the reactivity of cool flames (both ozone-less and ozone-assisted) is inhibited by methane, even when exchanged for inert nitrogen. Moreover, the ozone-assisted cool flames are found to reduce the sensitivity of cool flame extinction to the fuel concentration. A rate constant sensitivity analysis reveals that the CH3OCH3 + OH = CH3OCH2 + H2O and CH2OCH2O2H = CH2O + CH2O + OH reactions are disproportionally important to cool flames over homogeneous reactors, especially when considering their exothermic nature. These reactions are then modified (along with other reactions) based on the present experimental cool flame extinction data as well as reaction rates in the literature to produce an updated chemical kinetic model. The updated model is then validated using a combination of homogeneous reactors and flames at both high and low temperatures. Due to the increase in the rate constant of the CH3OCH3 + OH = CH3OCH2 + H2O reaction, the current model successfully predicts the cool flame extinction strain rate within ±20 s-1 of the experiments for DME/CH4 mixtures. The other experimental validation targets see differences between the original model and the updated model which are on the same order as the experimental uncertainties. A path flux analysis performed for cool flames reveals that the addition of methane scavenges OH and HO2 radicals, which is the reason behind its inhibition at low temperatures. This study shows the value of the ozone-assisted counterflow cool flame platform in chemical kinetic model development through its coupling of low-temperature chemistry, transport, and heat release. Specifically, it acts to constrain reactions that contribute significantly to the heat release and are subject to radical diffusion.
In the second task, we demonstrate experimentally, for the first time, the existence of multistage low-temperature diffusion flames in the counterflow configuration at terrestrial conditions. Such flames are defined by two distinct sequential oxidation zones, where the parent fuel peroxy chemistry governs the primary stage and the subsequent oxidation of the intermediates produced sustains the secondary stage, for sufficiently large Damköhler number. Specifically, the intermediates produced through the degenerate branching pathway and the decomposition of the alkylketohydroperoxide oxidize and partially replenish the radical pool and consume the fuel in the secondary stage. The reaction zone structure of multistage flames is dramatically influenced by the fuel inlet temperature, where the primary oxidation stage is dominant at lower temperatures while the secondary stage is dominant at elevated temperatures. However, as both structures are coupled, the reactivity of the multistage flame is dictated by the primary stage, except when the branching and heat release are supported externally, as in the case of ozone-doping. The results suggest that such multistage character likely manifests in flow fields with sufficiently long residence times, such as microgravity environments and highly turbulent flow fields. The present work contributes directly to the understanding of low-temperature flames.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Combustion science
Task Description:
Cool flames have significant implications for the control of engine knocking, ground and space fire safety, and combustion emissions. The recent International Space Station (ISS) combustion science experiments on flame extinguishment discovered the existence of cool flames for both large single droplets and droplet arrays after radiative extinction. Numerical simulations of droplet combustion also provide an explanation for the transition of hot flame to cool flame after radiative extinction. However, it remains unclear at what conditions the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. It is also not clear how oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition. More importantly, due to limits of space and payload, the ISS experiments did not provide detailed speciation and temperature distributions of cool flame structures for quantitative validation of kinetics and radiation model.
By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, we propose to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to * develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection ; * bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames ; * predict and answer the question at what conditions the transition from hot flame extinction to cool flames is possible and verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments ; * obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames ; * extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry. The proposed new ground-based experiments and data analysis are complimentary to and not directly linked with the science objectives from the original ISS combustion science investigation, and will significantly advance the understanding of near-limit cool flame dynamics and contribute to the future control of engine knocking, ground and space fire safety, and combustion emissions.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Numerical calculations of dimethyl ether (DME) radiative flames in the counterflow geometry found three distinct flame regimes at elevated pressures—hot flames, warm flames, and cool flames. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.
At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion.
These calculations served to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.
The warm diffusion flame was then revealed to occur in counterflow burner experiments using dibutyl ether (DBE). The two-stage flame structure was confirmed. Therefore, warm flames serve as a bridge between cool flames and hot flames.
The warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
We made two main progresses in Year 2 of our research: (1) we performed numerical calculations of dimethyl ether (DME) radiative flames in the counterflow geometry, discovering the “warm flame” in the process, and (2) we confirmed these warm flames experimentally using dibutyl ether (DBE).
While recent calculations have shown that cool premixed flames can extend the conventional lean and rich flammability limits of the hot flame, the flame regimes and burning limits of diffusion flames have not been as thoroughly investigated, especially at increased pressures. Therefore, the objective of the first study was to investigate the extinction and ignition transitions between different diffusion flame regimes at elevated pressures and to obtain a general diffusion flame flammability diagram which includes both hot and cool flames.
Specifically, the impacts of radiation, pressure, and reactant concentration on the extinction limits of different DME flame regimes were examined computationally with and without thermal radiation. A general €-shaped flammability limit diagram for diffusion flames was then obtained. In addition, the existence of a DME warm flame regime with a double reaction zone structure was demonstrated, and its flame structure and chemistry were compared with that of cool and hot flames.
It was shown that there are three possible cool flame transitions: (1) radiative extinction of hot flame to cool flame, (2) stretch extinction of hot flame to cool flame, and (3) stretch extinction of warm flame to cool flame. Moreover, there are also two different ways to form a warm flame by (1) radiative extinction of a hot flame and (2) ignition of a cool flame. The identification of these three flame regimes helps to understand near-limit flame transitions and to guide experimental observation of warm and cool flames.
In the second study, we reported on experimental evidence of the existence of a new self-sustaining low-temperature multistage warm diffusion flame, existing between the cool flame and hot flame, at atmospheric pressure in the counterflow geometry. The structure of multistage DBE warm diffusion flames was examined by using thermometry, laser-induced fluorescence, and chemiluminescence measurements.
It was confirmed that the warm diffusion flame has a two-staged double flame structure. A leading diffusion cool flame stage is present on the fuel side with a second intermediate stage on the oxidizer side. The second stage has a strong heat release that can be comparable to that of the first stage.
Furthermore, the analysis revealed that with the increase of fuel concentration, a single-stage cool flame can ignite to a warm flame or a hot flame. Moreover, a warm flame can extinguish into a cool flame or ignite to a hot flame when the fuel concentration is substantially reduced or increased, respectively. Finally, under certain conditions, a hot flame can extinguish directly into either a warm flame or a cool flame. Hence, the results suggest that the multistage warm flame can act as a critical bridge between cool flames and hot flames.

Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The cool flame extinction limit measurements for C7 to C12 n-alkanes showed that cool flame extinction experiment is a new platform to study the low temperature reactivity of transportation fuels and can provide crucial experimental targets for rapid screening of alternative fuels.
The results also showed cool flame extinction limits is a critical validation target of low temperature chemistry because of the lack of information of the cool flame heat release rates in other experimental systems.
The results also provide a new flammability limit diagram for both hot and cool premixed flames. The results showed that both the exhaust gas recirculation and the engine pressure dramatically affect the burning limits of cool flames. This is critical to the lean burn engine design.
The counterflow cool flame extinction provides a good validation target and explanation for the NASA droplet cool flame extinction limit.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
We made two progresses in year 1 research. In the first research, the low-temperature oxidation of hydrocarbon fuels has received increasing attention as advanced engines seek to operate in less conventional combustion regimes. Large n-alkanes are a notable component of many real transportation fuels and possess strong reactivity in this important low-temperature range. These n-alkanes have been studied extensively in various canonical kinetic experiments but seldom in systems with strong coupling between low-temperature chemistry, transport, and heat release. To address this issue, the present study investigates self-sustaining n-alkane cool diffusion flames in a counterflow burner. The extinction limits of both hot diffusion flames and cool diffusion flames are measured at atmospheric pressure for a range of n-alkanes from n-heptane to n-tetradecane. It is observed that while these fuels behave similarly for hot flames, the larger n-alkanes are substantially more reactive in the low-temperature cool flame regime. Moreover, ozone addition strongly enhances the low-temperature chemistry to the point where the differences in fuel reactivity are nearly suppressed.
The experimental measurements are compared with numerical simulations employing both detailed and reduced chemical kinetic models of various sizes. Although the different kinetic models adequately predict the extinction limits of the hot flames, a large scatter is present in the model results for cool flames, and a general overprediction of the measured cool flame extinction limit is observed for all of the fuels studied. This implies that the cool flame heat release is not well agreed upon by the current chemical kinetic models, despite their capability to reproduce many homogeneous reactor experiments at low temperatures. Furthermore, it is observed that the cool flame heat release is spread over a substantial number of reactions involving large molecules, a trait that makes it particularly difficult to create reduced kinetic models that can accurately describe cool flame behavior. The results of this study suggest that the cool flame platform can provide crucial validation of the coupling between chemistry, transport, and heat release in flames at low temperatures.
In the second research, the flame speeds and propagation limits of premixed cool flames at elevated pressures are numerically modeled using dimethyl ether mixtures. The primary focus is paid on the effects of pressure, mixture dilution, computation domain, and heat loss on cool flame propagation. The results showed that cool flames exist on both fuel lean and fuel rich sides and dramatically extend the lean and rich flammability limits of conventional hot flames. There exist three different flame regimes: the hot flames, lean and rich cool flames, and double flames. A new flame flammability diagram including both cool flames and hot flames at elevated pressures is obtained. The results show that pressure significantly changes cool flame propagation and burning limits. It is found that the increase of pressure affects the propagation speeds of lean and rich cool flames differently due to the negative temperature coefficient effect. On the lean side, the increase of pressure accelerates the cool flame chemistry and shifts the transition limit of cool flame to hot flame to a lower equivalence ratio. At lower pressure, there is an extinction transition from hot flame to cool flame. However, above a critical pressure, the hot flame directly transfers to a cool flame without hot flame extinction. Moreover, increases in dilution reduce the heat release of the hot flame and promote cool flame formation. Furthermore, the results show that a smaller downstream computation domain and higher heat loss also extend the cool flame transition limit and promote cool flame formation.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:

Task Description:
The effect of CO2 addition on flame speed and flammability limit of methane-air and methane-oxygen mixtures will be measured by a spherical propagating and counterflow flames. The spectral radiation will be detected and analyzed by using an infrared spectrometer and the InSb detector. An fitted statistical narrow band correlated-k (FSNB-CK)radiation model will be developed for spectral radiation prediction by comparing the predicted and measured radiation flux at given spectral wavelength.
Task Objectives
1. Measure the effect of CO2 addition on flame speed and flammability limit of methane-air and methane-oxygen.
2. Develop a new flame initiation theory.
3. Measure the the flame spectral radiation by using a spectrometer and InSb detector.
4. Develop an optimised radiation model
5. Design and build a drop module (rig).
Task Significance:
1. Provide the first hand data of the effect of CO2 addition on fire control and burning limit.
2. Establish a new model for spectral radiation computation.
3. Provide flame radiation database for microgravity experiment
4. Established a new flame theory for fire suppression.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
1. Establish a simplified model for fire initation and extinguishment.
2. Enable modeling of fire spreading in microgravity and normal gravity enviroment.
3. Establish an accurate method for flame speed and flammability measurement.
4. Provide experimental data of CO2 radiation in flames and its impact on flammability limit.
5. Provide fire detection capability using a CO2 radiation sensor.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
1. The effects of spectral radiation absorption on flame speeds at normal and elevated pressures were experimentally and numerically investigated using the CO2 diluted outwardly propagating CH4-O2-He flames. Experimentally, the laminar burning velocities of CH4-O2-He-CO2 mixtures at both normal and elevated pressures (up to 5 atm) were measured by using a pressure-release type spherical bomb. The results showed that radiation absorption with CO2 addition increases the flame speed and extends the flammability limit. In addition, it was also shown that the increase of pressure augments the effect of radiation absorption. Computationally, a fitted statistical narrow-band correlated-k (FSNB-CK) model was developed and validated for accurate radiation prediction in spherical geometry. This new radiation scheme was integrated to the compressible flow solver developed to simulate outwardly propagating spherical flames (a software for simulations of unsteady reactive flow using adaptive grids (SURFA-1D)). The comparison between experiment and computation showed a very good agreement. The results showed that the flame geometry had a significant impact on radiation absorption and that the one-dimensional planar radiation model was not valid for the computation of the flame speed of a spherical flame. An effective Boltzmann number was extracted from numerical simulation. Furthermore, the FSNB-CK model was compared with the grey band SNB model. It was shown that the grey band SNB model over-predicts the radiation absorption. It is concluded that quantitative prediction of flame speed and flammability limit of CO2 diluted flame requires accurate spectral dependent radiation model. The results were reported on the 31st International Symposium on Combustion (2006).
2. Dynamics of flame kernel evolution with and without thermal radiation and external energy addition was investigated analytically and numerically. Emphasis was placed on the effects of radiation heat loss, ignition power, and Lewis number on the correlation and transition between the initial flame kernel, the self-extinguishing flame, the flame ball, the outwardly propagating spherical flame, and the propagating planar flame. The present study extended previous results by bridging the theories of the non-adiabatic stationary flame balls and traveling flames and allowing rigorous consideration of radiation heat losses. The results showed that the effects of radiation heat loss played an important role in flame regimes and flame transition and resulted in a new isolated self-extinguishing flame. Furthermore, it was found that radiation heat losses significantly increased the critical ignition radius and resulted in three different dependences of the minimum ignition power on the Lewis number. Comparisons between the transient numerical simulations and the quasi-steady state analytical results showed a good agreement. The results suggested that prediction of flame initiation without appropriate consideration of radiation is not acceptable. The results were published on Combustion Theory and Modeling (2006).
3. The combined effects of flame stretch, curvature, and radiation on the extinction and flammability limit of premixed tubular flames are investigated by using the large-activation-energy asymptotic method. An analytical expression for flame speed, flame temperature and extinction limits is obtained and used to study the combined effects on flame dynamics. The flame isola for near limit radiative tubular flames is predicted and compared with that of the counterflow planar flames. It is found that the flame curvature has great effects on both the stretch extinction limit and the radiation extinction limits. By varying the radiation intensity, the results showed that the combined effects of radiation and curvature lead to various flame bifurcations. Comparisons among tubular flames of different flame radii as well as counterflow flames, all at the same stretch rate and radiation intensity, indicate that the premixed flame can be strongly affected by flame curvature. Furthermore, the effects of Lewis number are examined. The results also demonstrate a significant influence of preferential diffusion on the extinction limits of tubular flames at different flame curvatures. These results are accepted for publication on the International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer (2008).
4. The trajectories of outwardly propagating spherical flames initiated by an external energy deposition and radiation are studied theoretically, numerically, and experimentally by using hydrogen/air mixtures. Emphasis is placed on how to accurately determine the laminar flame speeds experimentally from the time history of flame fronts for mixtures with different Lewis numbers and ignition energies. The results show that there is a critical flame radius only above which are the linear and non-linear extrapolations for flame speeds valid. It is found that the critical radius depends strongly on the Lewis number. At large Lewis numbers, the critical radius is larger than the minimum flame radius used in the experimental measurements, leading to invalid flame speed extrapolation. The results also show that there is a maximum Karlovitz number beyond which propagating spherical flame does not exist. The maximum Karlovitz number decreases dramatically with the increase of Lewis number. Furthermore, the results show that the ignition energy has a significant impact on the flame trajectories. It is found that the unsteady flame transition causes a flame speed reverse phenomenon near the maximum Karlovitz number with different ignition energies. The occurrence of flame speed reverse greatly narrows the experimental data range for flame speed extrapolation. The strong dependence of flame trajectory on ignition energy and the existence of flame speed reverse phenomenon are also confirmed by experimental results. The results will be reported at the 32nd International Symposium on Combustion (2008)
5. To accurately measure the flame speeds, the effects of flow compression and flame stretch on the accurate determination of laminar flame speeds at normal and elevated pressures using propagating spherical flames at constant pressure or constant volume are studied theoretically and numerically. The results show that both the compression-induced flow motion and flame stretch have significant impacts on the accuracy of flame speed determination. For the constant pressure method, a new method to obtain a Compression-Corrected Flame Speed (CCFS) for nearly constant pressure spherical bomb experiments is presented. Likewise, for the constant volume method, a technique to obtain a Stretch-Corrected Flame Speed (SCFS) at elevated pressures and temperatures is developed. The validity of theoretical results for both constant pressure and constant volume methods are demonstrated by numerical simulations using detailed chemistry for hydrogen/air, methane/air, and propane/air mixtures. It is shown that the present CCFS and SCFS methods not only improve the accuracy of the flame speed measurements significantly but also extend the parameter range of experimental conditions. The results can be used directly in experimental measurements of laminar flame speeds.
6. In order to experimentally validate the theory, the impact of thermal radiation and non-spherical flow geometry on the accuracy of flame speed measurement using a spherical combustion chamber is analyzed. The results showed that flame speed measurement based on the conventional assumptions without appropriate corrections of thermal radiation and volume confinement cause 10% or more errors. A new criterion for flame speed measurements using spherical bomb is presented. The results were presented at the 5th National Combustion Meeting (March, 2007) at UCSD and submitted for publication on Combustion and Flame (2008). Specifically, the effect of flow compression and stretch on flame speed measurements and the effect of non-spherical flow field on flame speed measurements were investigated experimentally. Effect of flow compression and stretch on flame speed measurements: Pressure waves produced in the experiments of flame speed measurement using a spherical bomb will induce an inward flow velocity in the burned gas region. This inward burned gas velocity will affect the measured flame speeds. Discussions of the compression effects on flame speed measurement were either missing or neglected in the previous studies. For the measured flame speed of a stoichiometric hydrogen-air mixture on the range of flame radii used in the experiments, the results show that due to the flow compression effect, the error of the measured flame speeds could be larger than 15% depending on range of flame radii chosen in the experiment. The correction of the flow compression effect by using an analytical expression significantly improved the accuracy of the flame speed measurements (less than 5%). To measure the flame speed at both high pressure and high temperature, a constant volume spherical flame bomb has been used. In this approach, the transient flame propagation speed was used directly as the flame speed of the mixture and the effect of flame stretch on the flame speed was neglected. The results also show that as the flame propagates outward, the flame speed obtained without flame stretch correction does not agree with the unstretched planar flame speed until the flame radius is larger than 60% of the chamber size. However, by considering the flame stretch effect, the agreement between the flame speeds computed from the planar flame and the spherical flame was improved significantly in a broader range of pressure and flame radius. Effect of non-spherical flow field on flame speed measurements: In addition to the compression and stretch effects, the non-spherical flow field in the cylindrical bomb also produced errors of flame speed measurement. An analytical relation to correct for the flow field effect in the cylindrical bomb was derived by using the potential flow analysis. The flame speeds of hydrogen/CO-air mixtures were measured at 1, 10, and 20 atm. The measured flame speeds were compared to the existing data and model predictions. For the comparison of the measured flame speeds with other experimental data and numerical predictions, the results show that the data reported in the literature are much lower than the present results. The comparison also shows that the present data agree well with the modeled results using the detailed hydrogen-CO mechanism. The results clearly demonstrate that the experimental accuracy of flame speed is a key issue for the validation of kinetic mechanism.

Task Description:
The effect of CO2 addition on flame speed and flammability limit of methane-air and methane-oxygen mixtures will be measured by a spherical propagating and counterflow flames. The spectral radiation will be detected and analyzed by using an infrared spectrometer and the InSb detector. An optimised radiation model will be developed for spectral radiation prediction by comparing the predicted and measured radiation flux at given spectral wavelength. A drop module will be designed and built.
Task Objectives
1. Measure the effect of CO2 addition on flame speed and flammability limit of methane-air and methane-oxygen.
2. Develop a new flame initiation theory.
3. Measure the the flame spectral radiation by using a spectrometer and InSb detector.
4. Develop an optimised radiation model
5. Design and build a drop module (rig).
Task Significance:
1. Provide the first hand data of the effect of CO2 addition on fire control and burning limit.
2. Establish a new model for spectral radiation computation.
3. Provide flame radiation database for microgravity experiment
4. Established a new flame theory for fire suppression.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
1. Establish a simplified model for fire initation and extinguishment.
2. Enable modeling of fire spreading in microgravity and normal gravity enviroment.
3. Provide fire detection capability using a CO2 radiation sensor.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
1.1 We have measured the effect of CO2 addition on the flammability limits and flame speeds of CH4-O2-CO2-He mixtures at normal and elevated pressures using the outward propagating flames in a pressure-release type spherical bomb. The measured data were compared with numerical simulations utilizing a detailed emission/absorption statistical narrow band model. It was found that reabsorption can increase burning velocities of CH4-O2-He-CO2 mixtures and extend flammability limits. Furthermore, it is found that radiation reabsorption effect increases with the increase of environmental pressure. It is shown that for optically thick flames with CO2 dilution, reabsorption effects must be considered to correctly predict flame speeds and extinction limits in simulation. The work was presented at 43rd AIAA Aerospace Sciences Meeting and Exhibit on Jan.10, 2005 and at The 20th International Colloquium on the Dynamics of Explosions and Reactive Systems, Aug.1-5, Mcgill, Canada.
1.2 A theory to predict fire initiation from an external energy addition was developed. Emphasis was placed on the effects of the radiation heat loss, ignition power, and mixture Lewis number on the correlation and transition between the initial flame kernel, the self-extinguishing flame, the flame ball, the outward propagating spherical flame, and the planar propagating flame. The resent study extended the previous results by bridging the theories of the non-adiabatic stationary flame balls and traveling flames and allowing rigorous consideration of radiation heat losses. The results showed that the effects of radiation heat loss played an important role on flame regimes and flame transition and resulted in a new isolated self-extinguishing flame. Furthermore, it was found that radiation had significantly reduces the critical ignition radius and resulted in a three different dependences of the minimum ignition power on the Lewis number. Comparisons between the numerical simulations and the analytical results showed a good agreement. The results suggested that prediction of flame initiation without appropriate consideration of radiation is not acceptable. The work is submitted to Combustion Theory and Modeling and will be presented at the 44th AIAA Aerospace Sciences Meeting and Exhibit on Jan.9, 2006.
1.3 We developed a new Statistical Narrow Band-Correlated K (SNBCK) model to simulate the spectral radiation for spherical propagating flames. This algorithm has a better prediction accuracy than the previous SNB model developed by the PI and significantly improved the agreement between the prediction and the experimental results. The radiation model is integrated with a compressible reactive flow code to calculate ignition, flame speed, and flammability limits. This code is one of the most advanced computation codes available in combustion society. The work will be submitted to the next International Symposium on Combustion (2006).
1.4 We have set up an optical measurement system for spectral flame radiation. The system includes a spectrometer (SpectraPro 2500i, 200nm-10um), an infrared Detection assembly (InSb) for 1.5 to 5.0 microns, and a lock in amplifier amplifier (Stanford Research). Flame radiation from counterflow flame has been measured and calibrated.
1.5 We also visited NASA-Glenn Research Center to arrange microgravity experiments in this May.
