Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Major accomplishments and summaries are listed below:
1. We developed a new pressure release type high pressure spherical flame facility for the measurements of the laminar burning velocity with increased radiation optical thickness. It enables flame experiments in a pressure range between 0.001 and 30 atm. Xiao Qin and Yiguang Ju presented a paper entitled “Measurements of burning velocities of dimethyl ether and air premixed flames at elevated pressures” at the 30th International Symposium of Combustion in Chicago, IL in July 2004. In this paper, dimethyl ether and air flames, which allows high CO2 recycle, was studied. Experiments were conducted at pressures up to 10 atm. The measurement system was validated using laminar burning velocities of methane-air flames. A Comparison with the previous experimental data shows an excellent agreement and demonstrates the accuracy and reliability of the present experimental system. The flame speeds of dimethyl ether and air flames were measured and compared with the predictions using both full and reduced kinetic mechanisms. It was found that flame speed decreases considerably with the increase of pressure and the measured flame speeds are significantly lower than the predictions based on the available kinetic models. These results suggest that the existing kinetic models have to be significantly modified to predict reasonable flame propagation of dimethyl ether flames. Markstein lengths and the overall reaction order at different equivalence ratios were extracted from the flame speed data at elevated pressures. Therefore, the present study yields valuable flame speed data and submodels for high pressure dimethyl ether and air combustion.
2. Yuan Xue and Yiguang Ju presented a paper entitled “Extinction and flame bifurcations of stretched dimethyl-ether premixed flames” at the 30th International Symposium of Combustion in Chicago, IL in July 2004. In this paper, the combined effects of radiation and flame stretch on the extinction and flammability limits in the counterflow flames were studied. The major conclusions are as follows: a) Markstein length of lean dimethyl ether-air premixed is extracted from the counterflow flames using a method based on the flame front. The predicted positive Markstein length agrees well with the experimental data. The results showed that flow stretch significantly reduces the flame speed and narrows the flammability limit of the lean dimethyl ether-air flame. b) The combined effect of radiation and stretch results in a new flame bifurcation and multiple flame regimes for dimethyl ether-air flames. At equivalence ratio slightly higher than the flammability limit of the planar flame, the distant flame regime appears at low stretch rate. With an increase of equivalence ratio, in addition to the distant flame, a weak flame also appears at moderate stretch rates. With a further increase of equivalence ratio, the distant flame and the weak flame merge together which leads to the splitting of the weak flame branch into two new flame branches, a low stretch weak flame and a high stretch weak flame. c) Flame stability analysis demonstrated that the high stretch weak flame is also stable. A K-shaped flammability diagram showing various flame regimes and their flammable regions are obtained. The results demonstrated for the first time that the complicated bifurcations predicted using the one-step chemistry really happen for the DME-air flames.
3. Conducted flame speed measurements of CO2–He diluted methane-oxygen flames at atmospheric and elevated pressures (10 atm) at normal gravity with CO2 up to 50%. The results were compared with predictions with a newly developed spherical flame propagation code. A paper entitled “Experimental and numerical study of spectral dependent radiation on flame propagation” will be presented at the 43rd AIAA Aerospace Sciences Meeting and Exhibit on Jan.10, 2005.
4. Designed and fabricated a pair of nozzle burners and established methane air counterflow flames at normal gravity. The counterflow experiment setup was tested by measuring the extinction limit and temperature of methane air nonpremixed flames. The measured limit and flame temperature excellently matched the results reported in the literature, which validated the system. The spectral radiation properties of CH4-O2-CO2-He counterflow flames will be measured in this system.
5. Preparation for spectral dependent radiation measurements. We have ordered the following optical measurement system from Princeton Instruments for radiation detection: a) Spectrometer (SpectraPro 2500i, 200nm-10um) b) Infrared Detection assembly (InSb) for 1.5 to 5.0 microns c) Lock in amplifier (Stanford Research)
6. Development of code: a) A code package for simulating spherical flame propagation with narrowband radiation model and adaptive grids was developed. Using premixed hydrogen-air flames at normal gravity and pressure, the grid independency and accuracy of the code was tested. b) A spectral narrow band based correlated K model is currently underdevelopment for optimization.

Task Description:
Conducting space-based testing of fire suppression in large compartments is a daunting task from both the safety and the cost points of view. Simulations using a validated and verified numerical tool will provide valuable information that can complement and reduce the number of tests needed as well as help design better and safer experiments for testing fire-safety policies and practices. The primary objective of this research effort is to develop and demonstrate a computational tool for predicting the suppression of small or incipient fires in large (rack-scale) compartments. A secondary objective was to use this tool to understand and quantify the relative suppression effectiveness of CO2 and water-mist on fires in different gravitational environments.
Over the years, a unique capability has been developed at the Naval Research Laboratory to simulate both the detailed physics and chemistry of flames and fires as well as the flows in and around complex geometries such as those inside a space habitat. Previously, we have also used our models to study fire dynamics and suppression in a surface ship compartment. The approach we have adopted in this project is to modify, adapt and develop further the numerical simulation tool originally developed for compartment fire and shipboard smoke transport simulations. The original simulation tool included only a simple heat release model, simplified transport and other physical models and did not allow for any local mesh refinement. These are areas of improvement needed before use of the tool effectively for predicting fire suppression in normal and reduced gravity environments. The droplet and particulate transport sub-models and solution approaches also needed further verification and validation. Aspects of the model and simulation results for specific conditions were validated using experiments conducted at and by the Center for Commercial Applications of Combustion in Space (CCACS) of the Colorado School of Mines.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research has both basic scientific value and direct application to NASA goals to develop "effective methods of extinguishments of fires with minimal residual damage" and "maximize fire safety on orbiting vehicles." It specifically addresses several issues identified during a NASA Workshop on Spacecraft Fire Safety. These include: characterizing the flow field in spacecraft compartments, investigating the transport of fire-fighting agents and their interaction with the air and fuel surrounding a fire. This research also provides additional basic information on fire suppression and thus enhances our knowledge base for fighting fires on Earth and in Spacecraft and extraterrestrial environments. Thus, it also addresses one of the goals of NASA: to "enhance the knowledge base that contributes to earth-based technologies".
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
During this time period, we have made further developments of NRL's Fire and Blast Mitigation code, FBM, conducted numerical simulations, compared the results of the simulations to experimental data from CCACS. Further developments to the code include better transport and chemistry models; inclusion of a soot and radiation model and implementation of an Eulerian sectional approach to simulate the transport of water-mist droplets.
A simple and cost-effective approach for calculating transport properties is to use the Sutherland’s law for viscosity and derive the other diffusive transport properties using constant Prandtl and Schmidt numbers. However, in our preliminary simulations and verification studies, this resulted in large changes in the maximum temperature for small changes in these numbers. Therefore, a more detailed transport module has been incorporated into the code. In this approach, we calculate the transport properties for individual species and then use this information to compute the mixture transport properties for viscosity, thermal conductivity, and diffusion coefficients. We have retained the simpler approach as an option, just in case we can calibrate it with experimental data and use it when approximate but quick turn-around answers are needed.
The simpler flame sheet approximation used initially for the chemistry has been replaced with a finite rate two-step model. The chemistry integrator has also been upgraded with that used previously in our NRL FLAME3D model. In this approach, the actual species production and destruction rates are calculated on a local basis and will allow us to incorporate other multi-step chemistry models, if available for simulation of specific fire scenarios of interest to NASA.
A simple soot model (including soot radiation) has been included. This model solves two transport equations for the number density of soot particles and the volume fraction of soot. Source terms representing soot nucleation, coagulation, surface growth, and oxidation then complete the model. In addition, an optically thin radiation model was also incorporated, based on CO2, H2O and Soot radiation. The thermodynamics model has been changed from constant ratio of specific heats, to temperature-dependent curve-fits for the individual species enthalpies. The code now uses the thermodynamic curve-fits that are set up using the Chemkin translator.
The geometry modeled in the simulations was that of a small co-flowing burner within the larger CCACS enclosure with methane flowing through an inner tube and air flowing through an outer tube. The focus of the first set of simulations was to establish the level of detailed physics required in the simulations to achieve satisfactory comparisons with the experiments. The result of this study showed that the two-reaction global model and the more complex mixture-dependent properties are both vital in predicting a reasonable flame shape and unsteadiness. Thermal properties also contribute to a lesser extent to the flame shape and dynamics. In particular, the onset of unsteadiness is intricately linked to all three models.
Then experiments and simulations were carried out for a range of flow conditions. The flame height was found to grow linearly with flow velocity up to 4 cm/s, after which the flames became unsteady and tended to flicker. Although the exact location of the visual flame height is hard to determine in the simulations and compare, the trend in the simulations follows the experimental trend very closely.
The final set of simulations was focused on the suppression of these jet diffusion flames using water-mist. Both a steady flame as well as a pulsating flame were studied. Water-mist was injected off-axis from above the burner. In addition to the effect of vaporization and heat extraction, the downwash created by the mist injection has a dramatic effect on the flame. Even the nominally steady (without water-mist injection) flame stretches away from the mist and becomes partially detached from the burner lip.
In summary, a fully three-dimensional, unsteady, multiphase simulation tool has been developed for the studying the suppression of small flames in a large, complex enclosure with obstructions. The challenge has been to retain a sufficient level of detail to accurately model the small fire and still keep the problem of simulating the fire in a large enclosure computationally tractable. Additional studies are needed to characterize the relative effectiveness of various fire suppressants injected from arbitrary locations within the enclosure.

Task Description:
The Laboratory for Computational Physics and Fluid Dynamics (LCP&FD) of the Naval Research Laboratory proposes to investigate the effects of reduced gravity on the suppression of compartment fires. The objectives of the proposed investigation are to understand and quantify: 1) the relative importance of various postulated suppression mechanisms, and 2) the relative suppression effectiveness of CO2 and water-mist on both gas-jet and liquid-pool fires in different gravitational environments. These objectives will be achieved by developing a numerical simulation tool for predicting fire suppression in reduced gravity environments in large (rack-scale) compartments; conducting experiments to validate the results of the simulations for specific conditions; and then using the validated simulation tool to predict the effects of reduced gravity on fire suppression. The validation experiments will be conducted at the Center for Commercial Applications of Combustion in Space (CCACS) of the Colorado School of Mines.
The proposed effort has both basic scientific value and direct application to NASA-OBPR goals to develop "effective methods of extinguishments of fires with minimal residual damage" and "maximize fire safety on orbiting vehicles." It specifically addresses several issues identified during a NASA Workshop on Spacecraft Fire Safety. These include: characterizing the flow field in space compartments, investigating the transport of fire-fighting agents and their interaction with the air and fuel surrounding a fire. It will also provide additional basic information on fire suppression and thus will enhance our knowledge base for fighting fires on Earth and in Space. Thus, it also addresses one of the goals of NASA's Physical Sciences Research Division: to "enhance the knowledge base that contributes to earth-based technologies".
While this is not a follow-on proposal of any current or past investigations, the key investigators have made significant contributions in the past to NASA’s Microgravity Science Programs. Numerical simulations conducted at NRL have elucidated the role of gravity in the structure, dynamics and extinguishment of flames. Experiments and theoretical analysis at the Colorado School of Mines have provided valuable information on water mist/flame interactions. Over the years, a unique capability has been developed at LCP&FD to simulate both the detailed physics and chemistry of flames and fires as well as the flows in and around complex geometries such as those inside a space habitat. Recently, we have used our models to study fire dynamics and suppression in a surface ship compartment. We propose to modify and adapt this model to simulate the suppression of fires in reduced gravity environments. We will conduct verification studies to establish the credibility of the numerical simulation tool for conducting simulations of microgravity phenomena. Validation experiments will establish the quantitative accuracy of the simulation tool for fire suppression. By directly comparing the results of simulations and experiments, fundamental knowledge as well as practical information will be gained on the suppression of fires. In addition, numerical simulations, in which several parameters can be controlled independently, will provide added insight into the various mechanisms involved in fire suppression. A direct payoff from the proposed project to NASA will be an assessment of the relative effectiveness of CO2 and water-mist for spacecraft applications.

Fundamental knowledge as well as practical information will be gained on the suppression of fires.

Task Description: A series of experiments and extensive numerical calculations was conducted to study localized spot ignition and the subsequent transition to flame spread over thin plastic and paper sheets in different gravity levels including zero gravity and normal gravity. The intended fire scenario is ignition and subsequent fire growth over a thin polymeric material close to a very limited heat source such as the momentary burning of a small overheated wire in various different gravities. The results are intended to help insure a fire safe environment in spacecraft, the International Space Station, and future lunar and Martian habitats. This project focuses on two separate regimes: one is the early stage of localized spot ignition and the other is a later stage of fire growth from that ignition. With a thin polymeric sheet, two ignition events are observed and predicted; one is ignition on the surface exposed to an external heat (frontside ignition) and the other is ignition over the backside surface (backside ignition). In microgravity, the frontside ignition delay time of a polymeric material tends to monotonically increase with an increase in imposed flow velocity in the range simulating ventilation flows in these confinements. However, in normal gravity, in lunar gravity, or in Martian gravity, it is predicted that the frontside ignition delay time depends strongly on the sample orientation angle with respect to the gravitational direction due to buoyancy induced flow, even in a quiescent environment. Understanding the backside ignition process is important for fire safety because fire growth rate increases significantly with two simultaneous flames on both sides of the material. It is predicted that backside ignition occurs only after the formation of a small hole through the sample, after the sample is consumed locally. The formation of the hole has counteractive effects on both frontside and backside ignition; one is the consumption of the sample (tends to suppress both ignition) and the other is the fresh supply of air from the backside to the front side through the hole due to buoyancy induced flow (tends to favor ignition). Our preliminary calculation on fire growth shows that total heat release (which represents the size of a fire) from flame spreading over a thin polymeric sheet strongly depends on gravity level and the highest heat release would be between zero and normal gravity. Limited experimental results obtained in microgravity show that the size and the length of flame over a thin paper sheet drastically increases with an increase in external flow velocity. The objective is to conduct experiments on spot radiative ignition followed by transition to flame growth over different combustible solid surfaces (paper and plastics) in different gravity levels from microgravity to normal gravity. The transition phenomena of flame and sample surface temperature distribution are measured and the effects of sample thickness, oxygen concentration, imposed flow velocity, ignition configuration, and sample materials on the transition and flame growth characteristics are determined. In addition, numerical codes are developed for solving the time-dependent, three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations to describe spot ignition and subsequent transition to flame growth with various variables such as imposed external flow velocity, sample material and thickness, and oxygen concentration with different pressures by keeping partial pressure of oxygen at 0.21 in different gravity levels from zero gravity to normal gravity. The codes are validated by comparing the predicted results with the experimental data to determine the accuracy of the predicted results. The validated numerical model could be used for specific fire scenarios in spacecraft, ISS, lunar and Martian habitats. The numerical code could be used to estimate time-dependent heat release rate from the onset of localized ignition followed by subsequent flame growth over plastic materials in various gravities and also in various oxygen concentrations at various atmospheric pressures. With the material thermal properties measured in normal gravity as inputs to the code, the calculated results could be used as guidelines for the selection of materials and also as a part of overall fire safety evaluation of spacecraft, ISS, lunar and Martian habitats.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The numerical code developed under this project is general enough so that it can apply to fire scenario in normal gravity including buoyancy flow induced by gravity. The results could be used for improving public fire safety.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Numerical computations and a series of experiments were conducted in microgravity to study the ignition characteristics of a thin PMMA sheet (thicknesses of 0.2 mm and 0. 4 mm) using a CO2 laser as an external radiant source. Two separate ignition events were observed, including ignition over the irradiated surface (frontside ignition), and ignition, after some delay, over the backside surface (backside ignition). The results of our numerical study predict that frontside ignition delay time increases monotonically with an increase in imposed flow velocity in zero-gravity. However, in normal gravity, in lunar gravity, or in Martian gravity, it is predicted that the frontside ignition delay time depends strongly on the sample orientation angle with respect to the gravitational direction due to buoyancy induced flow even in a quiescent environment. Understanding the backside ignition process is important for fire safety because fire growth rate and heat release rate increase significantly with two simultaneous flames on both sides of the material. The backside ignition was achieved in two different modes. In the first mode, after the laser was turned off, the flame shrank and stabilized closer to the fuel surface. This allowed the flame to travel from the frontside to the backside through a small, open hole generated by the laser’s vaporization of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA). In the second mode, backside ignition was achieved during the laser irradiation. The numerical calculation simulating this second process predicts fresh oxygen supply flows from the backside gas phase to the frontside gas phase through the open hole, which mixes with accumulated hot MMA fuel vapor which is ignited as a second flame in the frontside gas phase above the hole. Then, the flame initiated from the second ignition travels through the hole to ignite the accumulated flammable mixture in the backside gas phase near the hole, attaining backside ignition. The first backside ignition mode was observed in 21 % oxygen and the second backside ignition mode for 35 %. The duration of the laser irradiation appears to have important effects on the onset of backside ignition. For example, in 21% oxygen, the backside ignition was attained after a 3 s laser duration but was not observed after a 6 s laser duration (within the available test time of 10 s in the drop tower). Longer laser duration might prevent two-sided ignition in low oxygen concentrations. The formation of a hole through the thin sample has two counteractive effects on the ignition process; one is reduction in fuel supply rate (suppresses ignition) and the other is an increase in oxygen supply from the back side to the irradiated side (promotes ignition).
Heat release rate is the most important measure representing the size of fire. Therefore, we are starting to investigate the effects of different gravity on heat release rate of a simple material using our numerical code. Our preliminary results of flame shape and distribution of local heat release rate .At the slow imposed flow of 2 cm/s, only flame spreading upstream is predicted in the gravity level from zero to 0.001 g because the downstream flame does not survive due to the oxygen shadow effects of the upstream flame. With a further increase in gravity, it is predicted that two flames simultaneously travel on opposite directions; one upstream and the other downstream. The downstream flame is supplied by oxygen from further downstream due to weak buoyancy induced flow. At the gravity level of 0.01 g, buoyancy induced flow overcomes the imposed flow and the size of the downstream flame is about the same as that of the upstream flame. With a further increase in gravity level, both flames become smaller but more intense. Total heat release is calculated by integrating the local heat release rate distribution for each gravity level . The results show that the maximum total heat release is predicted at around 0.02 g based on the conditions used in the calculation. However, the maximum local heat release rate monotonically increases with an increase in gravity due to higher oxygen supply rate via stronger buoyancy induced flow at higher gravity. These results might strongly depend on the imposed flow velocity, sample orientation, and oxygen concentration. Furthermore, the fire scenario shown in Figure 3 is based on a time-dependent flame spreading phenomena. Therefore, time-dependent heat release might show different dependency on gravity. More numerical study on this topic is needed.

The most favorable ignition configuration is the ceiling configuration (face down horizontal sample irradiated by upward laser beam). The formation of a hole through the thin sample due to consumption has two counteractive effects on the ignition process; one is reduction in fuel supply rate and the other is an increase in air supply from the side opposite to the irradiated side by the buoyancy induced flow through the hole. Task Description: To better understand particle formation processes and their coupling with flame propagation processes through detailed characterization of microgravity flames that produce copious amounts of particulate 'smoke'. The effects of silane/acetylene ratio and inert diluents on the burning velocities, flame temperatures, particle radiation, and silicon carbide (SiC) particle generation processes in premixed silane/acetylene flames will be measured in microgravity environments using flame diagnostics and analysis of flame products. These microgravity measurements will provide flame data uncomplicated by flame buoyancy and particle settling and thereby provide the opportunity to elucidate the couplings among particle formation, combustion enthalpy release/transport, and flame propagation. Comparisons of stoichiometric flames producing silicon carbide particles with acetylene-rich flames largely producing carbonaceous soot will advance the understanding of these processes and lead to better means for controlling them.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The planned approach to generating and studying premixed silane/acetylene 'vee' and/or cone flames supported above a nozzle burner during a 2.2 second drop tower experiment had been tested in laboratory experiments earlier in the program. The approach involves using a fixed inert gas flow to fill a bladder in a reservoir containing the premixed silane/acetylene reactants, and thereby feeding the reactants to the burner at the identical inert flow rate by displacement. This unconventional approach is required because of the limited drop time in which to stabilize separate reactant burner flows to produce a constant stoichiometric flame and because the total quantity of pyrophoric silane on board must be limited for overall safety reasons.
Safety requires that both the pyrophoric silane reactant and the flammable hydrogen flame product be protected from air exposure. Hence, the flame chamber can not be vented to the atmosphere, but rather must be sealed. Constant pressure operation then requires a rapid and reliable mechanism to compensate for the inflow of reactant gases and the expansion of hot flame product gases. Additional inert gas flow is necessary to dilute the hydrogen product beyond its flammability limits.
The approach adopted to maintaining constant pressure is to vent any excess gas into an evacuated chamber through a high flow back pressure regulator. The back pressure regulator can maintain a constant average pressure, but a limited response rate generates some pressure fluctuations. Laboratory tests confirmed that proper sequencing can minimize the effect of such pressure excursions on the flame response and stability. These tests were made using surrogate methane/air flames which have comparable burning velocities to those anticipated for the silane/acetylene flames. Some differences in flame response (to pressure variations) may arise due to differing transport properties of the reactants, but such differences in flame response are not expected to prevent flame stabilization in microgravity experiments.
The above approach was shown to be feasible, and design requirements were defined. The rig design was challenging due to the requirement of providing a completely contained, high flow rate, yet constant pressure, flame environment. Assembly of the experimental rig based on the completed design accepted in a review meeting at the NASA Glenn facility is nearly complete. An application for the required safety permit has been submitted, and the rig is expected to receive permits for use in both the 5 sec drop tower facility, and the 2.2 second tower. This will provide the rapid turn around times available with the 2.2 second tower, as well as the longer experimental times provided by the 5 second tower. Initial experiments are planned to be performed in the 2.2 second tower. If longer observation times are required under specific experimental conditions, the 5 second tower will be used. A no-cost extension in the performance period will be requested to facilitate completion of the planned experiments.
In preparation for analysis and interpretation of microgravity flame measurements, probable flame reaction mechanisms have been investigated using available data on silicon-carbon-hydrogen species energetics and reaction rate constants, as well as measured burning velocities and flame temperatures from our laboratory. This analysis has indicated that particle formation is the dominant energy-releasing process that generates the high flame temperature and drives the combustion wave. Considerable gas-phase pre-particle chemistry can occur rapidly at lower temperatures generating little net energy release. This suggests a simplified approach to modeling and gaining insight into the detailed flame chemistry. The approximation assumes energy from the high temperature particle growth region is transported toward the cool reactants and generates a hot bath gas with a fixed temperature profile in which most of the gas phase reactions occur nearly isothermally (at the local temperature). This approximation is currently being tested with kinetic modeling approaches.

Task Description:
To better understand particle formation processes and their coupling with flame propagation processes through detailed characterization of microgravity flames that produce copious amounts of particulate 'smoke'. The effects of silane/acetylene ratio and inert diluents on the burning velocities, flame temperatures, particle radiation, and silicon carbide (SiC) particle generation processes in premixed silane/acetylene flames will be measured in microgravity environments using flame diagnostics and analysis of flame products. These microgravity measurements will provide flame data uncomplicated by flame buoyancy and particle settling and thereby provide the opportunity to elucidate the couplings among particle formation, combustion enthalpy release/transport, and flame propagation. Comparisons of stoichiometric flames producing silicon carbide particles with acetylene-rich flames largely producing carbonaceous soot will advance the understanding of these processes and lead to better means for controlling them.

Task Description: The program consists of several parts, each of which consists of both experimental measurements and direct numerical simulation of microgravity flames: 1) Determination of the laminar flame speeds of gaseous fuels; 2) Determination of the corresponding Markstein lengths for these flames; 3) Determination of the extinction limits; 4) Investigation of Landau-Darrieus and diffusional-thermal flame surface instabilities; and 5) Recompilation of existing chemical kinetic mechanisms by using the high-pressure flame speed data as optimization points. The purpose of this research is to develop a fundamental understanding of premixed gas flame propagation, extinction and stability in high-pressure environments, where microgravity experiments will permit measurements undisturbed by convective effects. The chemical reaction mechanisms, which govern the various flame processes, are inherently nonlinear, and can cause non-monotonic variations of flame responses to increased pressure. Most practical combustion systems, especially internal combustion engines, operate at elevated pressures; while the fundamental information on flame chemistry were obtained at substantially lower pressures. Contributions to the fundamental understanding of flame processes at elevated pressures will have direct relevance to advances in the development of efficient and low-emission internal combustion engines.

Contributions to the fundamental understanding of flame processes at elevated pressures will have direct relevance to advances in the development of efficient and low-emission internal combustion engines.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
We have succeeded in experimentally observing pulsating spiral instabilities over propagating flames at elevated pressures, as well as in theoretically formulating a model that describes such spirals. Furthermore, we have experimentally demonstrated that the emergence of these spiral waves follow closely the right stability boundary governing the onset of diffusional-thermal pulsating instability, provided the evaluation of the reduced Lewis number is based on locally extracted thermokinetic parameters, and that these spiral waves exhibit many of the same characteristics such as meandering often observed in other excitable media, most notably the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction. It is also of interest to note that these spiral waves seem to initiate over surface elements. When hydrodynamic cells are formed, the outwardly propagating spirals are eventually absorbed at the cell boundary. Furthermore, mixed boundary conditions representing the presence of both diffusion and convection are needed to theoretically generate the spirals. The phenomenon appears to be quite rich, meriting further study.
While the present experiments were performed with rich hydrogen–air mixtures, the same phenomena of spiral flames could also exist for lean hydrocarbon–air mixtures with carbon numbers greater than two, such as propane, butane, and heptane, as the Lewis numbers for these mixtures of practical importance are also greater than unity. Indeed, computational studies of the one-dimensional planar propagation of lean heptane–air flames carried out in our lab have unambiguously shown the occurrence of pulsating instability prior to flame extinction. Furthermore, the sensitivity increases with leaner mixtures. The combustion and the associated unstable phenomena observed herein are hence of relevance to the utilization of petroleum fuels in internal combustion engines, especially for ultra-lean operations.
Experimental laminar flame speeds were accurately measured for CO/H2/air and CO/H2/He mixtures at different equivalence ratios and mixing ratios up to 40 atmospheres using the constant-pressure spherical flame technique. This adds to our already substantial database of high-pressure laminar flame speeds and Markstein lengths, enabling us to be leaders in the field in this aspect of combustion research. Further, the reaction rate constant of CO+HO2 ®CO2 +OH was calculated based on ab initio theory and canonical transition state theory. A kinetic mechanism based on recently published and calculated rate constants was presented to model the measured laminar flame speeds as well as the experimental data from counterflow ignition, flow reactor, and shock tube experiments in the literature. The comparison between the modeling results and the laboratory measurements suggests that accurate thermochemical data and the elementary rate constants are crucial to the satisfactory performance of the reaction mechanism.
Future work will continue to combine experimental, numerical, and theoretical work on high-pressure flame phenomena. We intend to increase the number of fuels in our database with higher hydrocarbon fuels, and use the experimental results to create and update comprehensive chemical kinetic mechanisms. Further, we will determine the effects on the flame speed of the cellular (increased) and pulsating (overall decrease) instabilities. Understanding the effects of these instabilities are key to improvement of internal combustion engines, as flame holding, extinction, knock, and chamber lifetime are all affected by fundamental flame instabilities not yet fully understood.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Markstein lengths and stretch-free laminar flame speeds were extracted for smooth acetylene, ethylene, ethane, propylene, propane, and dimethyl ether (DME) flames, nominally up to 10 atmospheres. These archival data are of relevance in the design of high-pressure combustion processes, and as target points for optimization of detailed kinetic mechanisms. Except for the results on DME, the experimental and numerical results show reasonable agreement for lean flames. The discrepancies for rich flames are larger, and in particular the rich ethylene chemistry was not well captured by the kinetic mechanism. Further, the pressure coefficients for the key reactions in the mechanism were not properly captured, yielding relative discrepancies between the different pressures for a given fuel and equivalence ratio. The scatter in the results for DME is subject to further research, both numerically and experimentally.
We have in addition conducted an experimental and theoretical investigation of the phenomenon of spontaneous cell formation on expanding acetylene, ethylene, hydrogen, propane, and hydrogen/propane spherical flames at elevated pressures. Critical conditions for the onset of instability were measured, and results were generally expressed in terms of a Peclet number, defined as the ratio of flame radius to the flame thickness. In addition, an asymptotic theory on the stability of spherically expanding flames was developed for a mixture consisting of two scarce fuels with distinct Lewis numbers. Predicted values of Peclet numbers for both pure fuels and fuel mixtures were shown to agree reasonably well with the measured values.
For the pure fuels, studying near-unity Lewis number flames of acetylene and ethylene isolated the effects of the hydrodynamic from the Lewis number dependent diffusional instabilities. It was shown that the flame thickness was the strongest governing parameter in the absence of significant diffusional-thermal instabilities. The study on pure fuels further yielded interesting results on the critical stretch rate for the onset of instabilities, and as such, non-equidiffusion was clearly shown through skew in these raw data. This result has not been observed for laminar flames before, but is often reported in turbulent flame studies as it is very relevant to the understanding of flames in the laminar flamelet regime of turbulent combustion modeling.
Finally, all the instability results were presented in a fully non-dimensional space, namely a Markstein-Karlovitz space. The results for both pure fuels and fuel mixtures fell on almost the same curve, indicating that the growth rate of instabilities was captured for the substantial variation in operating conditions, and only a function of the flame speed. This result may be somewhat fortuitous in that it was shown through a parametric study that the growth rate of the instabilities was not a strong function of the expansion ratio for the flames in the present investigation. Sivashinsky’s theory, however, predicts that the growth rate is a function of both the expansion ratio and the flame speed.
Given the shortcoming of the Wang-mechanism for the simplest reactions, new studies on, for example hydrogen with carbon monoxide, could possibly provide valuable target points for an improved optimization study. It is also clear that further investigation on the large discrepancies for dimethyl ether is needed, both experimentally and numerically. A major goal of our study is to use the knowledge gained to test outwardly propagating flames in a turbulent flow field. It has been shown to some extent that there is a strong influence of preferential diffusion/stretch interactions on turbulent flame front propagation and that the Markstein number determined from quasi-steady laminar flames is an adequate parameter to quantify the influence of integral strain rate on the space-averaged laminar burning velocity.
Mapping of cell size and evolution is a target for future research, both to elucidate the nature behind cellular instabilities and because of its obvious relevance to turbulent combustion. Palm-Leis & Strehlow noted a tendency for turbulence to be more effective in enhancing flame speeds when the flame was inherently unstable, and given our results from laminar flames, we expect this to be the case, actually, it is rather obvious. Further, Istratov & Librovich have suggested a sequential development of cellular structures in a spherical laminar flame that then becomes unstable, leading to turbulence generation and, ultimately, detonation, and explorations along this path would also be of great value to the combustion community at large.

The effort was divided into experimental and theoretical elements. The experimental effort consisted of using a porous spherical burner to issue fuel mixtures into an oxidizing environment. Different mixtures of fuel species permitted investigation of the phenomena of interest. The experiment effort was conducted primarily in the drop towers at the Glenn Research Center (GRC) and the NASA reduced-gravity aircraft. Space flight experiment was fully defined and approved during the program period. The theoretical effort consisted of the development of computational codes simulating the combustion phenomena of interest, and interpreting the calculated results on the basis of fundamental flame physics. The purpose of this flight definition task is to gain fundamental understanding of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in a simple, well-defined flow field. Using a spherical geometry this work considers: 1) gas-phase transient processes, including fuel vapor accumulation inside the flame and far-field diffusion, and their influence on flame movement and the achievement of steady flame behavior; 2) extinction boundaries of steady or near-steady flames and the identification of the associated chemistry at the global, reduced, and detailed levels; 3) the characteristics of partially-premixed flames; 4) flamefront pulsation and cellular instability especially near the extinction limits; 5) the dynamics of rotating flames; and 6) the behavior and structure of quasi-spherical flames in partial gravity environments. These studies are intended to significantly enhance the understanding of diffusion flames, especially providing capability for predicting flame behavior under varied conditions and configurations. As such, this work should contribute to engineering approaches to practical combustion systems, achieving increased energy conversion efficiencies and reductions in unwanted combustion emissions in both terrestrial and extraterrestrial environments.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Enhanced understanding of flame-flow vortical interaction could lead to improved burner design and operation in terms of energy efficiency and pollutant emissions.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2025
Task Progress:
The s-Flame experiment aimed to characterize and gain predictive capability of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in simple, well-defined flow fields such that the phenomena of interest could be studied without being complicated by various flow field effects. The basic flame configuration adopted was the spherically symmetric diffusion flame generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a quiescent, oxidizing ambient in microgravity. The theoretically one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation. The s-Flame experiment used the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the A dvanced Combustion Microgravity Experiment (ACME) hardware in the Destiny module of the International Space Station (ISS).
The s-Flames operations were conducted in two rounds of testing during Increments 60-63, where there was no testing during Increment 62 due to limited crew availability. More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Sept. 2019 to Jan. 2020, while the second round of testing – featuring helium rather than nitrogen dilution – occurred from May to July 2020.
Nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames in air seemed to demonstrate kinetic extinction at low flow rates (low system Da) and radiative extinction at high flow rates (high system Da). Radiative reabsorption extends flame size at extinction. Surprisingly, radiative extinction was a common event in ISS testing, which was predicted computationally but not previously observed for drop-tower or parabolic flight durations. Similarly, sufficient microgravity duration was needed to observe kinetic extinction because a near-steady flame must first be established before ramping down in flow rate to find the chemical kinetic extinction limit properly. Enriched O2 environments produced smaller characteristic flames; nonetheless, both extinction limits appeared to have been observed.
Ethylene flames, which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions, did not soot under microgravity conditions. Soot formation only occurred during forced ignition from the hotwire, but soon dissipated. Inherent sooting was also not found for enriched oxidizer conditions or the inerts, i.e., N2 and He, examined. Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames needed very large characteristic sizes to self-extinguish. Radiative extinction was not observed for the cases run, despite lowering the H2 concentration. However, kinetic extinction during ramp-down was exhibited for hydrogen flames.
Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen/methane mixture flames manifested radiative extinction, as predicted by computational simulations. However, kinetic extinction at low flow rates could not be identified conclusively. Helium-diluted cases had shifted extinction limits compared to the nitrogen-diluted cases. Ignition was also severely affected by using helium as a diluent. Helium-diluted cases were meant to isolate better pulsating instabilities, theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures above a critical Lewis number. However, at least from the video images, such thermal-diffusive instabilities were not conclusively proven in the ISS experiments, although flame oscillations prior to extinction were manifested. Flame luminosity does not necessarily correspond with flame strength. The highly thermal conductive nature of helium seemed to affect various processes, such as ignition and heat transfer to the burner (affecting isolation of kinetic extinction), despite higher characteristic flame temperatures.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
Given the amount of data, the bulk of the year was spent on developing programs to extract and plot the data automatically. Additional filtering was needed. Also, multiple programs were written to determine the temperature from the thin filament pyrometry (TFP) images. Still, more work needs to be done to understand the data, as well as filter the data better.
Initial observations showed that the concentricity of the flame with respect to the burner was not perfect. The degree of concentricity was not readily apparent until a polar coordinate transformation was applied to the images about the center of the burner. Further analysis and experimentation needs to be conducted in order to determine if the non-uniform flow field plays a critical role in the extinction of the flame and any further instabilities. This irregular flame geometry strongly impacts other facets of the collected data.
Using the calibration data and method provided by Dr. Marshall Long (Yale University), the temperature data was extracted from the TFP recorded in the NASA Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) [Data Camera] images. This process allowed a maximum temperature reading to be determined at a specific radial displacement from the burner center. Comparing this data to the simulation results shows some recurring differences between most cases.
The radiative and kinetic extinction times predicted by the simulation were within a few seconds of the experiments for the ethylene cases. The rapid decline in temperature (simulation) or the obvious cessation of temperature data (experimental) indicates the extinction point for the case. Although detailed experimental data points were unavailable, the predicted trend between the maximum temperature and its location are similar.
The experimental data often shows pulsations near extinction. However, the nature of these pulsations may be different from that predicted by the 1-D simulations. Other aspects of the instabilities were not well predicted, i.e., the size of the instability and the timing at which they occur. Further analyses are required to understand the phenomenon displayed in the experiments as related to the 1-D pulsations of the simulations. When comparing cases manifesting radiative or kinetic extinction, it has been shown that the current model is more accurate at predicting the extinction time of the radiative cases.
Currently, we are plotting other data from the experiments to compare with the simulations. Analyses are still ongoing, along with development of a quasi-steady code to plot the isola response for the cases.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
The s-Flame tests are intended to:
(i) Advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames; (ii) Obtain experimental data in simple, well-defined flow fields and understand various key elemental diffusion flame processes; (iii) Identify the extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damköhler numbers, respectively); (iv) Determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number; (v) Validate and/or improve accuracy of computational simulations, including detailed chemistry and transport.
The rationale for the matrix of experiments is to utilize various mixtures to assess both chemical and transport effects (including radiative) on flame behavior. Pure H2 and pure CH4 are utilized to assess kinetic mechanisms associated with each. Additionally, pure H2 only produces H2O as its radiative product, thereby isolating its radiative properties. Mixtures composed of both H2 and CH4 are used to examine their combined chemical and transport effects. N2 and He inerts, which affect characteristic flame temperature and transport (molecular and radiative), in the same mole fractions, are utilized for comparison.
The project has completed two (2) rounds of microgravity experimentation. Currently, detailed analyses of the acquired data, computational simulation, and theoretical analysis are ongoing. Interpretation of all phenomena will emphasize the simultaneous and coupled influence of chemistry and transport.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
During the reporting period, results from the following investigations have been obtained.
Initiation and Propagation of Laminar Premixed Cool Fames. Initiation and propagation of premixed cool flames for DME/O2/N2 mixtures are computationally studied in the 1-D planar configuration as well as the counterflow configuration. The results demonstrate that a residence time window exists for the occurrence of cool flames; external to this window a cool flame either cannot be initiated or will transition to a hot flame. Parametric study shows that the cool flame regime is sensitive to the amount of dilution in the flow, and that the cool flame becomes more intense at richer conditions. Global parameters such as the reference cool flame speed and cool flame temperature have been studied in a symmetric counterflow for various strain rates and equivalence ratios, with the controlling reactions identified. The results show that the premixed cool flame speeds are relatively low, around 6-7 cm/s, and are much less sensitive in terms of equivalence ratio variations. Experimental investigations have also been carried out in a counterflow, with a steady cool flame observed with a CCD camera with high sensitivity of the UV band. Such observations qualitatively demonstrate stronger cool flame chemiluminescence and insensitive change in the flame position with increasing equivalence ratios, which correspond well with the detailed numerical simulation.
This work is reported in: “Initiation and propagation of laminar premixed cool flames,” Peng Zhao, Wenkai Liang, Sili Deng, and Chung K. Law, Fuel 166 (2016) 477-487. [Ed. note: see Cumulative Bibliography]
Aspects of Colliding Spherical Flames: The morphology, corner dynamics, and flame-generated vorticity in colliding spherical flames are investigated. Schlieren images of the flame surface show that the morphology of the colliding process can be divided into three stages, which is further supported by simulations. Using experimental and simulation results, a comprehensive understanding of the collision dynamics is acquired, particularly the corner dynamics and the vortices generated near the corner. Regarding the former, we have identified strongly interacting factors, namely preferential diffusion and kine- matic restoration. Regarding the latter, we have demonstrated that the vorticity is generated by the baroclinic torque across the flame as a result of hydrodynamic pressure redistribution and density jump. The magnitude of the vorticity is estimated under quasi-steadiness assumption. By comparing the scales of the kinetic energy of the flame-generated vortices with those of the Kolmogorov eddies, it is suggested that vorticity at the flame corner could persist over dissipation and accumulate to a substantial extent to affect the turbulence spectrum as well as the local/global burning rate.
This work is reported in: “On Colliding Spherical Flames: Morphology, Corner Dynamics, and Flame-generated Vorticity,” Sheng Yang, Delin Zhu, and Chung K. Law, Combustion and Flame 167 (2016) 444-451. [Ed. note: see Cumulative Bibliography]
Extended Flammability Limits of n-Heptane/Air Mixtures with Cool Flames: A numerical and theoretical investigation has been conducted on the flammability limits of n-heptane/air mixtures by considering the role of the cool flame chemistry. It is found that the existence of the cool flame can substantially extend the lean and rich limits of the conventional high-temperature flame, with the extended limits being insensitive to pressure but sensitive to the extent of inert dilution. Different levels of kinetic criteria based on the controlling branching and termination reactions at low temperatures are derived and shown to agree well with the numerically simulated results at normal pressure. Furthermore, the critical temperature of cool flame flammability limits at normal pressure is found to be around 630 K and increases with pressure due to the shift of the NTC regime to higher temperatures.
This work is reported in: “Extended flammability limits of n-heptane/air mixtures with cool flames,” by Wenkai Liang and Chung K. Law, Combustion and Flame, Vol. 185, pp. 75-81 (2017). See Bibliography section below.
Theory of First-stage Ignition Delay in Hydrocarbon NTC Chemistry: The first-stage ignition delay of n-heptane/air mixtures is computationally studied using detailed mechanism and theoretically studied using eigenvalue analysis of simplified systems. Results show that the delay has a turnover behavior as temperature increases, being dominated by the competition of low-temperature branching and termination channels as well as the competition of forward and reverse reaction channels. As temperature increases to the intermediate range, the termination pathways result in a minimum in the delay, the state of which is theoretically derived.
The controlling kinetics of the first-stage ignition delay is found to be due to two types of competitions for the key intermediate species, namely the branching-termination competition and the forward-reverse competition. Between the two, the branching-termination competition is found to be the main reason leading to the turnover behavior around the regime transitioning from low to intermediate temperature. Furthermore, among all the branching-termination pairs, the competing channels of QOOH are found to be the most important for the minimum ignition delay. The validity of the derived analytical expression has also been tested and established for the large hydrocarbon fuels of n-octane and iso-octane, demonstrating the generality of the first-stage ignition concept.
This work is reported in: “Theory of first-stage ignition delay in hydrocarbon NTC chemistry,” by Wenkai Liang and Chung K. Law, Combustion and Flame, Vol. 188, pp. 162-169 (2018). See Bibliography section below.
Direct Numerical Simulation of Turbulent Nonpremixed "Cool" Flames: Applicability of Flamelet Models: “Cool” flames result from the coupling of low-temperature chemistry with molecular transport. These flames have been experimentally and computationally observed under laminar flow conditions but have not been isolated under turbulent flow conditions. A skeletal n-heptane chemical mechanism including low-temperature chemistry is used to conduct two-dimensional Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) of non-premixed “cool” flames subjected to unsteady, two-dimensional flow initialized from a plane of isotropic turbulence. Like conventional “hot” flames, at high Damköhler numbers, these “cool” flames are found to be adequately described by a steady flamelet model. However, at low Damköhler numbers, both non-premixed and premixed behavior are observed locally. When the combustion is locally non-premixed, these “cool” flames can be described by the unsteady flamelet model only if the correct scalar dissipation rate profile and associated boundary conditions are considered.
A comparison of two cases with varying Damköhler numbers showed that steady flamelet models are able to predict the behavior of the “cool” flame when the Damköhler number is sufficiently large, such that chemistry is faster than the flow timescales. In order to understand whether the lower Damköhler number case could be modeled with an unsteady flamelet model, a method was developed that could locally evaluate whether the combustion was locally non-premixed. Local increases in temperature above the steady flamelet model were then attributed to “premixed” effects rather than autoignition toward “hot” flames, which is too slow for the conditions considered. For points identified as locally non-premixed, the unsteady flamelet model was shown to be incorrect when a standard dissipation rate profile was considered. However, when the exact dissipation rate profile was considered, the unsteady flamelet model was shown to be consistent with the DNS data. These analyses indicate that conventional non-premixed combustion models developed for “hot” flames are equally applicable to “cool” flames as long as the underlying assumptions are satisfied.
This work is reported in: “Direct numerical simulation of turbulent nonpremixed "cool" flames: applicability of flamelet models,” by Alex G. Novoselov, Chung K. Law and Michael E. Mueller, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, Vol. 27, pp. 2143-2150 (2019). See Bibliography section below.
On Radical-induced Ignition in Combustion Systems: Theoretical developments based on eigenvalue analysis in assessing the state of incipient ignition induced by radical runaway with detailed chemistry of several classical problems are examined. The canonical ignition limits are analyzed, which are conventionally termed explosion limits, of hydrogen-oxygen mixtures, yielding explicit criteria that well reproduce their characteristic Z-shaped response in the pressure-temperature space. Subsequently, the role of hydrogen addition to the explosion limits of carbon monoxide-oxygen and methane-oxygen mixtures is evaluated, demonstrating and quantifying its strong catalytic effect, especially for the carbon monoxide mixtures. The role of low-temperature chemistry (LTC) in the autoignition of large hydrocarbon fuels is discussed, with emphasis on the first-stage ignition delay and the associated negative-temperature coefficient (NTC) phenomena. The analysis is extended to problems of nonhomogeneous ignition in the presence of convective-diffusive transport, using the counterflow as an example, demonstrating the canonical similarity between the homogeneous and nonhomogeneous systems.
Specific topics include hydrogen-oxygen ignition limits in homogeneous and nonhomogeneous systems, hydrogen-catalyzed ignition of CO- and CH4-oxygen mixtures, and the low-temperature chemistry in autoignition. The explosion limits of H2-CO-O2 and H2-CH4-O2 mixtures are examined at the next level of fuel complexity. Specifically, it shows that with only minute quantity of hydrogen addition, the explosion limits of the CO-O2 mixtures transition from monotonic to nonmonotonic behavior. The highly sensitive variation of the kinetic parameter characterizing the competition of O radical reacting with H2 and CO well explains such dramatic change. The H2-CH4-O2 mixtures show the transition by hydrogen addition with much less sensitivity. Such a difference is explained based on the competition of O and OH radicals by the branching and termination channels.
This work is reported in: “On radical-induced ignition in combustion systems,” by Wenkai Liang and Chung K. Law, Annu. Rev. Chem. Biomol. Eng., Vol. 10, pp. 199-217 (2019). See Bibliography section below.

NOTE: Continuation of Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames--NNX09AR03A
The effort was divided into experimental and theoretical elements. The experimental effort consisted of using a porous spherical burner to issue fuel mixtures into an oxidizing environment. Different mixtures of fuel species permitted investigation of the phenomena of interest. The experiment effort was conducted primarily in the drop towers at the Glenn Research Center (GRC) and the NASA reduced-gravity aircraft. Space flight experiment was fully defined and approved during the program period. The theoretical effort consisted of the development of computational codes simulating the combustion phenomena of interest, and interpreting the calculated results on the basis of fundamental flame physics. The purpose of this flight definition task is to gain fundamental understanding of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in a simple, well-defined flow field. Using a spherical geometry this work considers: 1) gas-phase transient processes, including fuel vapor accumulation inside the flame and far-field diffusion, and their influence on flame movement and the achievement of steady flame behavior; 2) extinction boundaries of steady or near-steady flames and the identification of the associated chemistry at the global, reduced, and detailed levels; 3) the characteristics of partially-premixed flames; 4) flamefront pulsation and cellular instability especially near the extinction limits; 5) the dynamics of rotating flames; and 6) the behavior and structure of quasi-spherical flames in partial gravity environments. These studies are intended to significantly enhance the understanding of diffusion flames, especially providing capability for predicting flame behavior under varied conditions and configurations. As such, this work should contribute to engineering approaches to practical combustion systems, achieving increased energy conversion efficiencies and reductions in unwanted combustion emissions in both terrestrial and extraterrestrial environments.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Enhanced understanding of flame-flow vortical interaction could lead to improved burner design and operation in terms of energy efficiency and pollutant emissions.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
Initiation and propagation of premixed cool flames for DME/O2/N2 mixtures are computationally studied in the 1-D planar configuration as well as the counterflow configuration. The results demonstrate that a residence time window exists for the occurrence of cool flames; external to this window a cool flame either cannot be initiated or will transition to a hot flame. Parametric study shows that the cool flame regime is sensitive to the amount of dilution in the flow, and that the cool flame becomes more intense at richer conditions. Global parameters such as the reference cool flame speed and cool flame temperature have been studied in a symmetric counterflow for various strain rates and equivalence ratios, with the controlling reactions identified. The results show that the premixed cool flame speeds are relatively low, around 6-7 cm/s, and are much less sensitive in terms of equivalence ratio variations. Experimental investigations have also been carried out in a counterflow, with a steady cool flame observed with a CCD camera with high sensitivity of the UV band. Such observations qualitatively demonstrate stronger cool flame chemiluminescence and insensitive change in the flame position with increasing equivalence ratios, which correspond well with the detailed numerical simulation.
The morphology, corner dynamics, and flame-generated vorticity in colliding spherical flames are investigated. Schlieren images of the flame surface show that the morphology of the colliding process can be divided into three stages, which is further supported by simulations. Using experimental and simulation results, a comprehensive understanding of the collision dynamics is acquired, particularly the corner dynamics and the vortices generated near the corner. Regarding the former, we have identified strongly interacting factors, namely preferential diffusion and kine- matic restoration. Regarding the latter, we have demonstrated that the vorticity is generated by the baroclinic torque across the flame as a result of hydrodynamic pressure redistribution and density jump. The magnitude of the vorticity is estimated under quasi-steadiness assumption. By comparing the scales of the kinetic energy of the flame-generated vortices with those of the Kolmogorov eddies, it is suggested that vorticity at the flame corner could persist over dissipation and accumulate to a substantial extent to affect the turbulence spectrum as well as the local/global burning rate.
A numerical and theoretical investigation has been conducted on the flammability limits of n-heptane/air mixtures by considering the role of the cool flame chemistry. It is found that the existence of the cool flame can substantially extend the lean and rich limits of the conventional high-temperature flame, with the extended limits being insensitive to pressure but sensitive to the extent of inert dilution. Different levels of kinetic criteria based on the controlling branching and termination reactions at low temperatures are derived and shown to agree well with the numerically simulated results at normal pressure. Furthermore, the critical temperature of cool flame flammability limits at normal pressure is found to be around 630 K and increases with pressure due to the shift of the NTC regime to higher temperatures.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2016
Task Progress:
During the reporting period, results from the following investigations have been obtained.
(1) Premixed Cool Flames in the Counterflow. Cool flames are essential features of chemical kinetics of large hydrocarbon fuels and are closely related to the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) phenomenon and engine knock. In this work, the coupling of cool flame chemistry and convective-diffusive transport is numerically and experimentally investigated for premixed flames in the counterflow, with heated N2 flowing against DME/O2/N2 mixture. It is found that low-temperature heat release is suppressed with high strain rate (short residence time), resulting in a stretched low-temperature S-curve response without a cool flame, and that the low-temperature chemistry induced ignition could transition to a high-temperature flame with low enough strain rate (long residence time). A steady-state premixed cool flame exists only with residence time in a strain rate window. Strain rate, dilution, and equivalence ratio effects on premixed cool flame characteristics were further identified. A symmetric counterflow configuration is then simulated to demonstrate the cool flame temperature and flame speed at fixed local strain rate, showing very different controlling chemistry and characteristics compared with the normal laminar flames governed by high-temperature chemistry. In addition, in a companion experimental investigation, premixed cool flames in counterflow were observed with a CCD camera with high sensitivity in the UV spectrum, corresponding to the characteristic wavelength of excited HCHO. The chemiluminescence from the cool flame is found to become more intense with increasing equivalence ratio, and the position of a cool flame is insensitive to variation in the equivalence ratio at the same flow rate. These observations qualitatively agree with the numerical simulations, demonstrating essential features of a new class of flames - the premixed cool flames.
(2) On Colliding Spherical Flames: Morphology, Corner Dynamics, and Flame-generated Vorticity. The collision of two identical spherical flames was studied for its relevance in flame interactions in various practical situations including those within turbulent flames. Experimentally, premixtures of fuel (H2, C3H8) and oxidizer were ignited by two synchronized sparks in a closed chamber under atmospheric pressure, with the subsequent flame-front evolution tracked by a Schlieren system with high-speed camera, as well as computationally simulated. Results show that development of the morphology of flame collision can be distinguished in three stages: independent propagation, strong interaction with flattened interfaces, and corner dynamics after merging of the interfaces. It is further demonstrated that propagation of the flame corner is controlled by the interacting mechanisms of preferential diffusion and kinematic restoration, that vorticity of considerable strength is generated downstream of the corner flame segment, and that the kinetic energy of the flame-generated vorticity is substantial as compared to those of the Kolmogorov eddies such that it could have strong influence on the turbulence energy spectrum and flame burning rate.
(3) Computational Simulation of Spherical Diffusion Flame Dynamics and Extinction. For the spherical diffusion flame experiments in microgravity slated to be conducted on the space station, numerical simulations have been conducted to refine the test matrix. The basic flame configuration is the spherically-symmetric diffusion flame generated by issuing a fuel mixture into a quiescent oxidizing environment. Upon ignition, the flame is initially located close to the burner surface, subsequently moving outward to reach the steady-state location. H2/CH4/N2 and H2/CH4/He mixtures are to be examined in the test matrix. Therefore, to guide the experiments, computational simulations are performed with detailed chemistry and transport, along with optically-thick and optically-thin radiation models, as well as with no radiative loss. Such flames allow for the investigation of transient flame extinction at the two limits, i.e., radiative and kinetic. A high flow rate can result in a maximum system extinction Damkholer number (Da) beyond which burning is not possible, caused by the reduction in the flame temperature due to radiative heat loss. By transitioning from a moderate flow rate (for which a diffusion flame can be established) to a low flow rate, a minimum system extinction Da may be reached, corresponding to the purely kinetic limit of burning. The dual diffusion- flame extinction modes for specific mixture compositions and initial ambient oxygen concentrations are obtained numerically.
For kinetic extinctions, a certain flow rate is applied to ignite and establish a quasi-steady flame, and then the flow rate is abruptly lowered (below the steady-state extinction limit) to seek the purely kinetic extinction limit, as the flame responds quasi-steadily. Dilution on oxidizer side is employed to ensure that the flame size just before extinction is about double the radius of the burner to be utilized. Effect of starting flow rate duration time to establish a quasi-steady flame is evaluated with respect to how the flame responds to flow rate reduction and subsequent extinction.
For radiative extinctions, H2/CH4/N2 and H2/CH4/He fuel mixtures are examined for different mole fractions compositions and issuing flow rates. Heat loss due to radiation is the dominant factor causing extinction as the flame spreads outwardly, when there is no steady solution for the given fuel and ambient mixtures. Extinction time varies less at high flow rates compared to low flow rates, for a given fuel mixture. High hydrogen concentration in the fuel mixture extends the extinction time, due to the high reactivity and diffusivity of hydrogen. For the same mole fraction of dilution in the fuel mixture and oxidizer mixture ambient, the one that is diluted by helium extinguishes sooner than the one contains nitrogen. Optically-thin models are shown to have shorter extinction times and bigger flame sizes than optically thick models due to more heat loss.
