Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2015
Task Progress:
NOTE: This project has been continued as a new grant--Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames--NNX15AC79A. See that task for subsequent reporting. (Ed., November 2015)
FINAL REPORT--During the reporting period results from the following investigations were published.
Effects of Soret diffusion on the minimum ignition energy of hydrogen/air mixtures by a heated kernel, and the associated flame structure, are investigated numerically with detailed chemistry and transport. Results show that Soret diffusion leads to larger (smaller) minimum ignition energy for relatively rich (lean) mixtures, and that this effect is mainly engendered by the Soret diffusion of H2, while that of the H radical is almost negligible. Mechanistically, Soret diffusion of H2 increases the fuel concentration entering the ignition kernel and consequently renders rich (lean) mixtures harder (easier) to ignite. The evolvement of the flame structure shows that before the H radical is substantially accumulated to exert an influence on the reaction zone, the high temperature gradient of the ignition initiation has driven H2 in the mixture moving towards the ignition kernel. For the stretched spherical flame of the ignition, it is shown that Soret diffusion of both H and H2 should be included such that the stretched flame speed can be accurately predicted. At small flame radius (large strain rate), the Soret diffusion of H2 is the dominant mode of Soret diffusion; at large flame radius (small strain rate), the influence of Soret diffusion is similar to that on the unstretched adiabatic planar flame where the Soret diffusion of H radical plays the major role.
Dynamics & Morphology of Colliding Spherical Flames: A preliminary experimental and computational study is conducted on the dynamics and flame morphology of two identical colliding spherical flames. Experimentally, premixtures of fuel (C2H6, C3H8) and air are ignited by two synchronized sparks in a closed chamber under atmospheric pressure, with the subsequent flame front evolution tracked by a schlieren system with high-speed camera. The images yield three distinctive stages during collision, namely: independent propagation, interface flattening and corner dynamics. The evolution of the total surface area and flame distortion is evaluated. Results show that the Lewis number dependence of the flame propagation speed at the corner is opposite to that expected of the thermal-diffusional effect, thereby demonstrating that Huygens’ propagation dominates over the effects of stretch-affected preferential diffusion. Simulation shows that the flow field is largely distorted around the flame corner, causing pressure redistribution and vorticity generation through the baroclinic force across the flame.
Weakly Buoyant Spherical Diffusion Flames: Properties of Hydrogen-CO/Ethylene Flames: Flame structure is strongly dependent upon the environment in which the flame is situated, in particular Earth's gravity. In a microgravity or microbuoyancy environment, natural convection due to the unidirectional gravity vector is largely suppressed. As buoyant effects are minimized, spherical symmetry of a fundamentally spherical phenomenon can be achieved. In particular, spherical flames present a unique opportunity for studying flame phenomena, as the spherical symmetry reduces complexity in analysis and interpretation of the controlling physical processes. In this study, weakly buoyant spherical flames are generated using a low pressure and low density fuel environment and a spherical porous copper burner. Flame testing is focused on mixtures of hydrogen and another fuel reacting with diluted oxygen. Ethylene-based fuels are first used, as ethylene is a more complex hydrocarbon than methane and exhibits sooting behavior. Syngas is also explored, for its potential in clean-burning technology. Five fuel mixtures are tested: hydrogen-methane, hydrogen-ethylene, helium-ethylene, nitrogen-ethylene and hydrogen-carbon monoxide. Through observation of flame shape and luminosity, the flames are tested for variations with pressure, oxidizer concentration, fuel concentration, and flow rate. Computational studies are also conducted to elucidate experimental results. This work is reported in: “Weakly Buoyant Spherical Diffusion Flames: Properties of Hydrogen-CO/Ethylene Flames,” Laurel Paxton, Princeton University Undergraduate Independent Work. Final Report, May 1, 2014.
Role of NTC Chemistry in Flame Phenomena: The phenomenon of negative temperature coefficient (NTC) is an essential feature of the chemical kinetics of large hydrocarbons at low to intermediate temperatures, and is practically relevant to the intrinsically low-temperature ignition processes governing engine knock, accidental explosions, and the recent development of the homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) engines. Furthermore, while fundamental studies of this phenomenon have mostly involved homogeneous systems such as the shock tube, flow reactor, and rapid compression machine, recent microgravity experiments and computational simulation by Dryer and William suggested that the NTC chemistry can also fundamentally affect the diffusion-affected phenomena of heptane droplet combustion. We have initiated a systematic investigation on NTC flames with various flame configurations, such as the counterflow premixed and diffusion flames, the doubly infinite planar premixed flame propagation, and the ignition of a premixture by a heated kernel. The understanding gained from such investigation will complement the microgravity studies of droplet combustion.
Self-acceleration of cellular spherical flames: The extent of rigor in the various claims of self-similarity in previous studies of the self-acceleration of expanding spherical flames is examined, particularly on the attainment of 3/2 for the power-law acceleration exponent. We find that the evidences presented in some of the prior studies were not rigorously interpreted, and as such the claim of the 3/2 exponent, motivated by the initial suggestion of Gostintsev et al. based on results of uncertain accuracy, and by the attractiveness of its potential implication on self-turbulization, is not justified. Our results suggest that self-acceleration definitely exists; and self-similarity, subsequent to the initial transient, most likely exists. Our power-law exponent, however, still seems to weakly depend on the system pressure and the intensity of the diffusional-thermal instability, and as such has not reached the hydrodynamic, flame-sheet limit. Further experiments with even thinner flames and longer observation times are needed to resolve this scientifically and practically important issue on flame propagation.This work is reported in: “An experimental investigation on self -acceleration of cellular spherical flames,” Fujia Wu, Grunde Jomaas and Chung K. Law, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 34 (2013) 937–945.
Theoretical analysis of low-Grashof number flames: The weakly-buoyant, quasi-steady burning of a spherical droplet in an infinite medium is studied theoretically for unity Lewis number and infinite chemical reaction rate, using the Boussinesq model. Approximate solution is given to the non-linear outer equations by applying the Oseen linearization to the unbounded low Grashof number (Gr) flow. This outer solution is then matched to the inner convective-diffusive solution treated with the Schvab-Zeldovich formulation. Half-order asymptotic expansions are adopted to describe the temperature and mass-fraction profiles. The flame-sheet position, as a function of polar angle and radial position, and mass burning rate are determined. The results compare favorably with experiments. In our perturbation analysis for small normalized density difference, flame characteristics are found to scale with Gr1/2.
Experiments on spherical flames in low pressure: Complementary low-pressure experiments are being used to examine the dynamics and flame structure of low-buoyancy, inverted, spherical diffusion flames. The effect of buoyancy is minimized in a low-pressure environment, typically down to 0.1 atmosphere, beyond which kinetic effects would become severe. However, since the flames examined have centimeter-order diameters, buoyancy can still be significant due to the large dimension. Therefore, to further reduce buoyancy, an additional arrangement is implemented, which involves injecting the oxidizer gas into an environment of low molecular weight fuel such as hydrogen and methane. Buoyancy is reduced because the hot, low-density flame sphere is now situated in an environment of low molecular weight gas. As such, spherical and rotating non-buoyant diffusion flames can be investigated, for extended durations. Detailed measurements are being made of the flame configuration, as well as its temperature and species (CH and OH) profiles, for different fuels and mixtures involving hydrogen, methane, and ethylene, along with inerts composed of nitrogen, helium, and carbon dioxide.
Transient numerical simulation: The transient numerical simulation of spherical flames developed as part of this program includes detailed chemistry and transport models, especially radiation mechanisms. The numerical simulations are being used as a predictive tool to assess the test matrix of the SRD for the space-based experiments. Specifically, cases of kinetic and radiative extinction are being investigated to assess the corresponding flow rates and times needed to achieve the phenomena. Only the cases which should reveal the phenomena will remain, along with some safety-factor redundancies. Due to time and g-jitter limitations, little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in the ground based test facilities, and the ACME definition will rely on the best effort in the modeling work. The experiments are meant to examine the relative importance of radiative emission and re-absorption, the adequacy of the detailed chemical kinetics mechanism and transport sub-models used, and the onset of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. Constant pressure and constant volume cases are also being compared.
Spherical diffusion flames under rotation: Microgravity experiments are conducted in the 2.2-second drop tower and zero-gravity facility at NASA-GRC to gain fundamental understanding of the effects of spinning on an otherwise spherical diffusion flame. The flames are generated by injecting either a fuel or an oxidizer mixture from a porous burner to a controlled ambient of either an oxidizer or fuel mixture, respectively. Results show that the polar flame location scales with the angular velocity monotonically as where a is greater and smaller than unity for small and large spinning velocities, respectively. On the contrary, the equatorial flame location responds nonmonotonically to increasing spinning velocity: first increasing and then decreasing. The experimental observations agree well with the computational simulation where the simulated results demonstrate that the nonmonotonic response of the equatorial flame location is caused by dilution of the reactant concentration in the outwardly-directed radial flow by the product and inert that are carried by the inwardly-directed polar flow upon traversing the flame segment in the polar region. This work was reported in: “Response of spherical diffusion flames subjected to rotation: microgravity experimentation and computational simulation,” by S. W. Yoo, S. Chaudhuri, K. R. Sacksteder, P. Zhang, D. L. Zhu and C. K. Law, Combustion and Flame, Vol. 159, pp. 665-672 (2012). (See FY2012 report Bibliography.)
Soret diffusion in heptane flames: The influence of Soret diffusion on the structure and response of n-heptane/air flames is investigated numerically with detailed reaction mechanism and transport. Unstretched freely-propagating planar premixed flames as well as stretched counterflow premixed and diffusion flames are studied, with emphasis on the separate and combined Soret effects of heptane and its oppositely-directed decomposition species H2 and H, as well as those of the major species O2, N2, CO2 and H2O. Results show that, in the unstretched case for which the flame temperature remains at its adiabatic value, Soret diffusion primarily affects the chemical kinetics embedded in the flame structure and the net effect is small; while in the stretched cases, its impact is mainly through those of heptane and the secondary fuel H2 in modifying the flame temperature, with substantial effects, while H2 and H also affect the chemical kinetics especially when the active reaction zone is localized. The dilution/enrichment of the reactant concentrations in the flame through the Soret diffusion of the major species O2, N2, CO2 and H2O further exert finite effects on the flame burning intensity. Self-acceleration of expanding spherical flames induced by flamefront instability: The cells that continuously develop over the flame surface of an expanding spherical flame increase its area and thereby the global propagation rate, resulting in the possibility of self-acceleration. The present study examines whether this self-acceleration could be self-similar, and, if so, whether it could also be self-turbulizing. Extensive experiments at elevated pressures and thereby reduced laminar flame thicknesses and enhanced propensity to exhibit Darrieus-Landau instability were conducted for hydrogen/air over an extensive range of equivalence ratios. The results demonstrate the strong possibility of self-similar flame acceleration, strong influence of the system pressure, moderate influence of diffusional-thermal instability, and a corresponding moderate spread in the power-law acceleration exponent.
Review on future fuel options: The state of research on developing fuel options for next generation chemical propulsion is reviewed for aviation fuels and energetic fuels. For aviation fuels, the development is based on considerations of cost, energy security and climate change, with Fischer-Tropsch synthetic fuels and biofuels hold potential as alternative aviation fuels. The need for basic research to develop predictive capability for the oxidative chemistry of evolving fuels in evolving engine designs is emphasized, illustrated by the intricate reaction pathways and the enormity of the reaction mechanisms involved. Recent research activities towards achieving the goal of fuel design are discussed through the development of detailed mechanisms, reduced mechanisms, and surrogate fuels. For the development of high-energy-density propellants, advances in several classes of materials are discussed, including metallized and hypergolic propellants, and propellants with strained and functionalized molecules as well as nanoparticle addition. The impact of the recent progress in chemical synthesis, materials science and nano science on these advances is noted. This work is reported in: “Fuel options for next generation chemical propulsion,” by C.K. Law, AIAA Journal, AIAA Journal, Vol. 50, No. 1, pp. 19-36 (2012). doi: 10.2514/1.J051328. (Reported in FY2012 Bibliography.)
Accelerating deflagration front: The formulation of Taylor on the self-similar propagation of an expanding spherical piston with constant velocity was extended to an instability-wrinkled deflagration front undergoing acceleration with RF (infinity) ta, where RF is the instantaneous flame radius, t the time, and alpha a constant exponent. The formulation describes radial compression waves pushed by the front, trajectories of gas particles, and the explosion condition in the gas upstream of the front. The instant and position of explosion are determined for a given reaction mechanism. For a step-function induction time, analytic formulas for the explosion time and position are derived, showing their dependence on the reaction and flow parameters including thermal expansion, specific heat ratio, and acceleration of the front.
Transient behavior of spherical diffusion flames: The transient behavior of burner-supported spherical diffusion flames was studied in the transport-induced limit of low mass flow rate and the radiation-induced limit of high mass flow rate which characterize the isola response of flame extinction. Oscillatory instability was observed near both steady-state extinction limits. The oscillation typically grows in amplitude until it becomes large enough to extinguish the flame. The oscillatory behavior was numerically observed using detailed chemistry and transport for methane (50%CH4/50%He into 21%O2/79%He) and hydrogen (100% H2 into 21%O2/79%He) diffusion flames where the fuel was issued from a point source, and helium was selected as an inert to increase the Lewis number, facilitating the onset of oscillation. In both methane and hydrogen flames, the oscillation always leads to extinction, and no limit cycle behavior was found. The growth rate of the oscillation was found to be slow enough under certain conditions to allow the flame to oscillate for over 450 seconds, suggesting that such oscillations can possibly be observed experimentally. For the hydrogen flames, however, the frequency of oscillation near the transport-induced limit is much larger, approximately 60 Hz as compared to 0.35 Hz for the methane flame, and the maximum amplitude of temperature oscillations was about 5K. The distinctively different structures of the hydrogen and methane flames suggest that while both instabilities are thermal-diffusive in origin, oscillations in the hydrogen flames resemble those of premixed flames, while oscillations in the methane flames are non-premixed in character.
Structure and extinction characteristics of counterflow diffusion flames: The structure and extinction characteristics of counterflow diffusion flames with flame radiation and non-unity Lewis numbers of the fuel and oxidant were examined using multi-scale asymptotic theory and a model expressed in terms of the jump relations and reactant leakages with the proper consideration of the excess enthalpy overlooked in previous analyses is developed. The existence of the dual extinction limits in the presence of radiative heat loss, namely the kinetic limit at small Damkohler number (high stretch rate) and the radiative limit at large Damkohler number (low stretch rate), are identified. It is found that the former one is minimally affected by radiative loss, while substantial amount of heat loss is associated with the radiative limit. The influence of radiative loss on the extinction Damkohler numbers is found to be through its effects on the flame temperature, excess enthalpy and the reduced extinction Damkohler number. At both extinction limits, the contribution from the flame temperature is always important and dominant. The contributions from the other two, however, could be important in some special cases. At small Le (fuel), the contribution from the reduced extinction Damkohler number is large and even dominant under small radiative loss. The contribution from the excess enthalpy is important for small Le (oxidizer) and it may be comparable to the contribution from the flame temperature when radiative loss is small. Thus, overlooking the excess enthalpy by previous analyses may result in rather large error in the predicted extinction Damkohler numbers, especially the kinetic one. Onset of flame oscillation: Using the results derived from a previous study, a linear stability analysis was conducted to study the onset of near-limit flame oscillation with radiative heat loss in 1-D chambered planar flames using multi-scale activation-energy asymptotics. The oscillatory instability near the radiation-induced extinction limit at large Damkohler numbers is identified, in additional to the one near the kinetic limit at small Damkohler numbers. It is shown that radiative loss assumes a similar role as varying the thermal diffusivity of the reactants. Thus, flame oscillation near the radiative limit is still thermal-diffusive in nature although it may develop under unity Lewis numbers. The unstable range of Damkohler numbers near the radiative limit shows quite similar parametric dependence on the Lewis numbers of reactants, Le (fuel) and Le (oxidizer), the equivalence ratio, and the radiative loss as that near the kinetic limit. They both increase monotonically with Le (oxidizer) and equivalence ratio and increase then decrease with Le (fuel). Increasing radiative loss extends the parameter range under which flame oscillations may develop. However, they show different dependence on the temperature difference between the supplying reactants. Unless radiative loss approaches its maximum value the system can sustain, flame oscillation near the radiative limit is only possible within a limited range of delta-T, whereas it is promoted monotonically with decreasing delta-T near the kinetic limit. Furthermore, while radiative loss shows small effect on the nondimensional oscillation frequency, the dimensional frequency of flame oscillations near the radiative limit can be substantially smaller than that near the kinetic limit.

Task Description:
The effort was divided into experimental and theoretical elements. The experimental effort consisted of using a porous spherical burner to issue fuel mixtures into an oxidizing environment. Different mixtures of fuel species permitted investigation of the phenomena of interest. The experiment effort was conducted primarily in the drop towers at the GRC and the NASA reduced-gravity aircraft. Space flight experiment was fully defined and approved during the program period. The theoretical effort consisted of the development of computational codes simulating the combustion phenomena of interest, and interpreting the calculated results on the basis of fundamental flame physics. The purpose of this flight definition task is to gain fundamental understanding of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in a simple, well-defined flow field. Using a spherical geometry this work considers: 1) gas-phase transient processes, including fuel vapor accumulation inside the flame and far-field diffusion, and their influence on flame movement and the achievement of steady flame behavior; 2) extinction boundaries of steady or near-steady flames and the identification of the associated chemistry at the global, reduced, and detailed levels; 3) the characteristics of partially-premixed flames; 4) flamefront pulsation and cellular instability especially near the extinction limits; 5) the dynamics of rotating flames; and 6) the behavior and structure of quasi-spherical flames in partial gravity environments. These studies are intended to significantly enhance the understanding of diffusion flames, especially providing capability for predicting flame behavior under varied conditions and configurations. As such, this work should contribute to engineering approaches to practical combustion systems, achieving increased energy conversion efficiencies and reductions in unwanted combustion emissions in both terrestrial and extraterrestrial environments.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Enhanced understanding of flame-flow vortical interaction could lead to improved burner design and operation in terms of energy efficiency and pollutant emissions.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2014
Task Progress:
FY2014 ANNUAL REPORT
The extent of rigor in the various claims of self-similarity in previous studies of the self-acceleration of expanding spherical flames was examined, particularly on the attainment of 3/2 for the power-law acceleration exponent. We find that the evidences presented in some of the prior studies were not rigorously interpreted, and as such the claim of the 3/2 exponent, motivated by the initial suggestion of Gostintsev et al. based on results of uncertain accuracy, and by the attractiveness of its potential implication on self-turbulization, is not justified. Our results suggest that self-acceleration definitely exists; and self-similarity, subsequent to the initial transient, most likely exists. Our power-law exponent, however, still seems to weakly depend on the system pressure and the intensity of the diffusional-thermal instability, and as such has not reached the hydrodynamic, flame-sheet limit. Further experiments with even thinner flames and longer observation times are needed to resolve this scientifically and practically important issue on flame propagation.

During the reporting period results from the following investigations were published.
1. Spherical diffusion flames under rotation. Microgravity experiments were conducted in the 2.2-second drop tower and zero-gravity facility at NASA-GRC to gain fundamental understanding of the effects of spinning on an otherwise spherical diffusion flame. This work is reported in: “Response of spherical diffusion flames subjected to rotation: microgravity experimentation and computational simulation,” by S. W. Yoo, S. Chaudhuri, K. R. Sacksteder, P. Zhang, D. L. Zhu and C. K. Law, Combustion and Flame, Vol. 159, pp. 665-672 (2012) ; publication was listed in the February 2012 Task Book Bibliography.

The influence of Soret diffusion on the structure and response of n-heptane/air flames is investigated numerically with detailed reaction mechanism and transport. Unstretched freely-propagating planar premixed flames as well as stretched counterflow premixed and diffusion flames are studied, with emphasis on the separate and combined Soret effects of heptane and its oppositely-directed decomposition species H2 and H, as well as those of the major species O2, N2, CO2 and H2O. The dilution/enrichment of the reactant concentrations in the flame through the Soret diffusion of the major species O2, N2, CO2 and H2O further exert finite effects on the flame burning intensity.
This work is reported in: “A comprehensive evaluation of Soret diffusion in heptane/air flames,” by Y. X. Xin, C. J. Sung and C. K. Law, Vol. 159, pp. 2345-2351 (2012).

This work is reported in: “An experimental investigation on self-acceleration of cellular spherical flames,” Fujia Wu, Grunde Jomaas and Chung K. Law, Proceeding of the Combustion Institute, in press.
4. Review on Future Fuel Options. The state of research on developing fuel options for next generation chemical propulsion is reviewed for aviation fuels and energetic fuels. For aviation fuels, the development is based on considerations of cost, energy security and climate change, with Fischer-Tropsch synthetic fuels and biofuels hold potential as alternative aviation fuels. The impact of the recent progress in chemical synthesis, materials science and nano science on these advances is noted.
This work is reported in: “Fuel options for next generation chemical propulsion,” by C. K. Law, AIAA Journal, AIAA Journal, Vol. 50, No. 1, pp. 19-36 (2012). doi: 10.2514/1.J051328 ; publication was listed in the February 2012 Task Book Bibliography.
During the reporting period, ongoing work consisted of the following.
1. Experiments on spherical flames in low pressure: Complementary low-pressure experiments are being used to examine the flame structure of low-buoyancy, inverted, spherical diffusion flames, using laser-based diagnostics. The effect of buoyancy is minimized in a low-pressure environment, typically down to 0.1 atmosphere, beyond which kinetic effects would become severe. However, since the flames examined have centimeter-order diameters, buoyancy can still be significant due to the large dimension. Therefore, to further reduce buoyancy, an additional arrangement is implemented, which involves injecting the oxidizer gas into an environment of low molecular weight fuel such as hydrogen and methane. Buoyancy is reduced because the hot, low-density flame sphere is now situated in an environment of low molecular weight gas. As such, spherical and rotating non-buoyant diffusion flames can be investigated, for extended durations. Detailed measurements are being made of the flame configuration, as well as its temperature and species (CH and OH) profiles, for different fuels and mixtures involving hydrogen, methane, and ethylene, along with inerts composed of nitrogen, helium, and carbon dioxide.
2. Transient numerical simulation: The transient numerical simulation of spherical flames developed as part of this program includes detailed chemistry and transport models, especially radiation mechanisms. Modification of the code for 2nd order accuracy in time marching is currently underway. The numerical simulations are being used as a predictive tool to assess the test matrix of the SRD for the space-based experiments. Only the cases which should reveal the phenomena will remain, along with some safety-factor redundancies. Due to time and g-jitter limitations, little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in the ground based test facilities, and the ACME definition will rely on the best effort in the modeling work. The experiments are meant to examine the relative importance of radiative emission and re-absorption, the adequacy of the detailed chemical kinetics mechanism and transport sub-models used, and the onset of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries. Constant pressure and constant volume cases are also being compared.

In terms of in-situ diagnostics, the associated equipment include an injection-seeded Spectra-Physics LAB-170-10 Nd:YAG laser and Spectra Physics CSTR-G-532 Nd:YAG-pumped dye laser, an Acton SpectraPro 500i Imagning Monochromator/Spectrograph, Roper Scientific PIMAX 1300HQ-25-FO digital UV-to-near-IR ICCD camera, Hamamatsu R928 photomultiplier, Agilent 54845A Infiniium 1.5GHz digital oscilloscope, Kaiser Optical 2.0” holographic SuperNotch-Plus Filter at 532nm, and Berkeley Nucleonics Model 555-4C 4 channel digital delay generator. The system is used for spontaneous Raman spectroscopy (SRS), laser-induced fluorescence (LIF), and filtered Rayleigh scattering (FRS) to probe the flame for gas-phase temperature and major/radical gaseous species concentrations. Particle imaging velocimetry (PIV) is utilized to map the aerodynamic flow field. As such the controlling mechanisms (for 1D and 2D axisymmetric spinning flames) can then be unambiguously identified, analyzed, modeled, and compared with detailed computational simulation for quantitative realism, fundamental understanding, and predictive capability.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
The transient behavior of burner-supported spherical diffusion flames was studied in the transport-induced limit of low mass flow rate and the radiation-induced limit of high mass flow rate which characterize the isola response of flame extinction. Oscillatory instability was observed near both steady-state extinction limits. The oscillation typically grows in amplitude until it becomes large enough to extinguish the flame. The oscillatory behavior was numerically observed using detailed chemistry and transport for methane (50%CH4/50%He into 21%O2/79%He) and hydrogen (100% H2 into 21%O2/79%He) diffusion flames where the fuel was issued from a point source, and helium was selected as an inert to increase the Lewis number, facilitating the onset of oscillation. In both methane and hydrogen flames, the oscillation always leads to extinction, and no limit cycle behavior was found. The growth rate of the oscillation was found to be slow enough under certain conditions to allow the flame to oscillate for over 450 seconds, suggesting that such oscillations can possibly be observed experimentally. For the hydrogen flames, however, the frequency of oscillation near the transport-induced limit is much larger, approximately 60 Hz as compared to 0.35 Hz for the methane flame, and the maximum amplitude of temperature oscillations was about 5K. The distinctively different structures of the hydrogen and methane flames suggest that while both instabilities are thermal-diffusive in origin, oscillations in the hydrogen flames resemble those of premixed flames, while oscillations in the methane flames are non-premixed in character.
The structure and extinction characteristics of counterflow diffusion flames with flame radiation and non-unity Lewis numbers of the fuel and oxidant were examined using multi-scale asymptotic theory and a model expressed in terms of the jump relations and reactant leakages with the proper consideration of the excess enthalpy overlooked in previous analyses is developed. The existence of the dual extinction limits in the presence of radiative heat loss, namely the kinetic limit at small Damkohler number (high stretch rate) and the radiative limit at large Damkohler number (low stretch rate), are identified. It is found that the former one is minimally affected by radiative loss, while substantial amount of heat loss is associated with the radiative limit. The influence of radiative loss on the extinction Damkohler numbers is found to be through its effects on the flame temperature, excess enthalpy and the reduced extinction Damkohler number. At both extinction limits, the contribution from the flame temperature is always important and dominant. The contributions from the other two, however, could be important in some special cases. At small Le (fuel), the contribution from the reduced extinction Damkohler number is large and even dominant under small radiative loss. The contribution from the excess enthalpy is important for small Le (oxidizer) and it may be comparable to the contribution from the flame temperature when radiative loss is small. Thus, overlooking the excess enthalpy by previous analyses may result in rather large error in the predicted extinction Damkohler numbers, especially the kinetic one.
Using the results derived from the previous study, a linear stability analysis was conducted to study the onset of near-limit flame oscillation with radiative heat loss in 1-D chambered planar flames using multi-scale activation-energy asymptotics. The oscillatory instability near the radiation-induced extinction limit at large Damkohler numbers is identified, in additional to the one near the kinetic limit at small Damkohler numbers. It is shown that radiative loss assumes a similar role as varying the thermal diffusivity of the reactants. Thus, flame oscillation near the radiative limit is still thermal-diffusive in nature although it may develop under unity Lewis numbers. The unstable range of Damkohler numbers near the radiative limit shows quite similar parametric dependence on the Lewis numbers of reactants, Le (fuel) and Le (oxidizer), the equivalence ratio, and the radiative loss as that near the kinetic limit. They both increase monotonically with Le (oxidizer) and equivalence ratio and increase then decrease with Le (fuel). Increasing radiative loss extends the parameter range under which flame oscillations may develop. However, they show different dependence on the temperature difference between the supplying reactants. Unless radiative loss approaches its maximum value the system can sustain, flame oscillation near the radiative limit is only possible within a limited range of delta-T, whereas it is promoted monotonically with decreasing delta-T near the kinetic limit. Furthermore, while radiative loss shows small effect on the nondimensional oscillation frequency, the dimensional frequency of flame oscillations near the radiative limit can be substantially smaller than that near the kinetic limit.
We have performed microgravity experiments on the effects of rotation on spherical diffusion flames, with emphasis on varying Lewis numbers on both the fuel and oxidizer sides. The study was motivated by recent theoretical development on the effects of rotation on droplet- or burner-generated flames. The experiments were devised not only to verify the theoretical predictions, but also extend or supplement the theories to study the flame response at high angular velocities where the perturbation theory no longer applies. The experiments were conducted using the 2.2 second drop tower at GRC. The flames were generated by injecting either the fuel or the oxidizer mixtures through a bronze porous burner to a controlled ambient which also comprises either an oxidizer or fuel mixture. As the theory predicted, the flame strengthened either at the pole or the equator as the Lewis numbers of the ambient and burner mixtures were varied. Specifically, it was demonstrated that when subjected to rotation, the flame deformed into a pancake shape, flattened at the poles and protruding outward from the equator, regardless of Le (fuel) and Le (oxidizer). The deformation increased as the angular velocity increased but reached an asymptote at high angular velocities, at which the flame surface approached very close to the burner surface near the poles. The flame temperature, however, was noticeably influenced by the Le of the system. When the Le of the burner mixture was less than unity, the emission at the poles significantly became stronger as rotation increased, even though heat loss to the burner was increasing as the flame became more flat. When this fuel mixture was moved to the ambient, just the opposite was observed. In fact, if these spherical flames were rendered to be very weak, the current results indicate that rotation could give rise to local extinction either at the poles or the equator. Finally, the flame shape deformations were shown to increase linearly with mass flow rates. All these observations were in accordance with the results of our theoretical work, to be discussed next.
The configuration and extinction of diffusion flames generated by either a porous spherical burner or a fuel droplet in response to slow rotational motion were investigated through perturbation analysis, with emphasis on the effects of non-unity Lewis numbers for both fuel and oxidizer. It is shown that the rotational motion induces a secondary flow which is directed inward towards the poles and outward from the equator, which in turn distorts the otherwise spherical flame into a pancake shape that is flattened at the poles and protruding at the equator. The flame temperature is also affected, becoming more susceptible to extinction either at the poles or the equator, depending on the combined effects of Lewis numbers, flame stretch through local flow nonuniformity, and ambient oxidizer concentration. The differences and similarities between the responses of diffusion and premixed flames in response to rotation are discussed.
In the previous work, by assuming constant density a perturbation analysis was carried out to examine effects of the secondary flow induced by rotation on the response of spherical diffusion flames enveloping either a burner or a fuel droplet. Complete analytical solutions were found for all the relevant quantities, with explicit expressions derived for the burning rate and distorted flame shape. General Lewis numbers were considered, as were ambient oxidizer concentration. The effect of rotation on local extinction was also assessed.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Previously, the structure and extinction of diffusion flames generated by a porous spherical burner or a fuel droplet in response to rotational motion were investigated through perturbation analysis, with emphasis on the effects of non-unity Lewis numbers (Le) for both fuel and oxidizer. Constant density was assumed for simplicity of analysis, hence allowing decoupling of the flow from the thermal effects. Solutions were found for all relevant quantities, and explicit expressions were given for the burning rate and the distorted flame shape. While the constant density assumption simplifies the analysis considerably by decoupling the flow from the thermal effects and provides elegant analytical results, such simplification in the analysis is known to give an incorrect flame location compared to experimental results, which might possibly lead to over- or under-prediction the effects of rotation. To address this, we carried out the analysis without making such simplification and the solutions were obtained numerically. While it was shown that main feature of the problem was adequately described by the constant-density model, the variable-density formulation revealed two new insights: (1) perturbations due to rotation decrease substantially as compared with the constant-density formulation, suggesting that the perturbing effects of rotation are substantially absorbed and thereby mitigated by the density variation, (2) magnitude of the perturbations strongly depends on the ratio of the burner/droplet surface temperature to the ambient temperature.
Finally, microgravity experiments were conducted at NASA Glenn not only to verify the theoretical predictions but also to extend or supplement the theories to study the flame response at high angular velocities where the perturbation theory no longer applies. The experiments were conducted using both the 2.2 second drop tower and the 5 second zero-G facility at GRC. The flames were generated by injecting either the fuel or the oxidizer mixtures through a bronze porous burner to a controlled ambient which also comprises either an oxidizer or fuel mixture. In the low angular velocity limit where the perturbation analysis predictions are valid, no visible changes were observed, as the perturbations predicted by the theory were also small. In the other extreme, the effect of rotation was clearly visible and the response agreed surprisingly well for most conditions with the perturbation theory. The scaling for the deformation of the flame was also analyzed separately at the poles and the equator. In particular, the polar displacement of the flame as a function of the angular velocity scaled similarly as that established by the spinning disk.

Task Description:
The effort was divided into experimental and theoretical elements. The experimental effort consisted of using a porous spherical burner to issue fuel mixtures into an oxidizing environment. Different mixtures of fuel species permitted investigation of the phenomena of interest. The experiment effort was conducted primarily in the drop towers at the GRC and the NASA reduced-gravity aircraft. Space flight experiment was fully defined and approved during the program period. The theoretical effort consisted of the development of computational codes simulating the combustion phenomena of interest, and interpreting the calculated results on the basis of fundamental flame physics. The purpose of this flight definition task is to gain fundamental understanding of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames in a simple, well-defined flow field. Using a spherical geometry this work considers: 1) gas-phase transient processes, including fuel vapor accumulation inside the flame and far-field diffusion, and their influence on flame movement and the achievement of steady flame behavior; 2) extinction boundaries of steady or near-steady flames and the identification of the associated chemistry at the global, reduced, and detailed levels; 3) the characteristics of partially-premixed flames; 4) flamefront pulsation and cellular instability especially near the extinction limits; 5) the dynamics of rotating flames; and 6) the behavior and structure of quasi-spherical flames in partial gravity environments. These studies are intended to significantly enhance the understanding of diffusion flames, especially providing capability for predicting flame behavior under varied conditions and configurations. As such, this work should contribute to engineering approaches to practical combustion systems, achieving increased energy conversion efficiencies and reductions in unwanted combustion emissions in both terrestrial and extraterrestrial environments.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Enhanced understanding of flame-flow vortical interaction could lead to improved burner design and operation in terms of energy efficiency and pollutant emissions.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
With the knowledge and experience gained from previous 1D spherical diffusion flame studies, chemically and aerodynamically more complex, 2D axisymmetric flame was investigated. The response of the rotating spherical diffusion flames with general Lewis numbers (Le) was analytically studied and microgravity experimentation was conducted at NASA Glenn to validate the theoretical findings.
The rotational flow is induced by spinning the porous sphere along its axis. The flames are non-spherical because centrifugal force engenders outward flow from the burner equator, with mass continuity satisfied by inward flow to the burner poles. Such an experimental configuration assists in the studies of the effects of vortical motion in turbulent flows in flame responses, droplet spinning in the interior of combusting sprays, as well as localized flame extinction. Few analytical works have been published with no clear experimental validation. Specifically, Lozinski et al. [1] carried out an analytical work based on unity Lewis number and found strong evidence that small rotating perturbation can have significant effect on the flame dynamics as well as the extinction behavior. However since their analysis was restricted to unity Lewis number (Le), while the majority of the practical combustion systems involve hydrocarbon-based fuels that have Le that deviate from unity, it is imperative that non-unity Le analysis be carried out.
An analytical model has been developed based on constant-density assumption [2]. It is shown that the flame temperature can deviate from the steady-state spherical flame temperature. Particularly, it was found that when LeF > 1 or LeO 1, the opposite happens. This is a strong indication that just by varying the Le of the mixtures either at the ambient or at the burner mixtures, the flame can extinguish either at the pole or the equator when the flame is sufficiently close to the limit condition.
With the above theoretical development in mind, microgravity drop experiments were conducted at NASA Glenn to validate not only the theory but also to extend the theory by experimentally studying the flame response at high RPM, where the rotation is no longer a perturbation [3].
When subjected to rotation, it was observed that the flame deformed into a pancake shape, flattened at the poles and protruding outward from the equator, regardless of LeF and LeO. The deformation increased as the angular velocity increased but reached an asymptote at high angular velocities, at which the flame surface approached very close to the burner surface near the poles. The flame temperature, however, was noticeably influenced by the Le of the system. When the Le of the burner mixture was less than one, the emission at the poles significantly became stronger as rotation increased, even though heat loss to the burner was increasing as the flame became more flat. When this fuel mixture was moved to the ambient, just the opposite was observed. In fact, if these spherical flames were rendered to be very weak, the current results indicate that rotation could give rise to local extinction either at the poles or the equator. Finally, the flame shape deformations were shown to increase linearly with mass flow rates. All these observations were in accordance with the results of theoretical work [2], even though the theory assumes small rotational perturbations which are contrary to the large rotational velocities in the experiments. It is thus suggested that the theory does capture the essence of the effects of rotation on the flame response.

Task Description: The detection of fires is very important within closed environments such as the Space Shuttle and International Space Station. Fires need to be detected within such areas as soon as possible, preferably before combustion has taken place. Previous research performed at KSC has shown that the multi-sensor technology commonly known as the electronic nose (e-nose) is able to detect the offgassing products from the insulation of heated wires well before combustion starts. Note that e-nose technology is not concerned with identifying in an analytical sense the chemicals being detected, but with classifying a mixture of vapors as coming from one source or another. This project would expand upon these results, and produce an integrated system of sensors and software which would not only provide a pre-combustion alarm, but also identify what kind of material is being overheated (wire insulation, printed circuit board, etc.). Metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensors are low cost, available in numerous miniature configurations, have a wide range of selectivity to various vapors, and are simple to operate. To that end, commercially available MOS sensors will be incorporated into a sensor array and exposed to thermal out-gassing products of electrical components. In addition, conventional circuit board components (e.g., IC chips-usually encapsulated in resins) will be subjected to heat cycles to mimic catastrophic failure with a potential fire hazard. Pattern recognition techniques will be developed at KSC to identify those commercially available sensors which provide the most sensitivity and reliability to detection and identification. It is recognized that other sensor technologies (e.g., SAW, quartz micro-balance, etc.) could potentially increase the identification power of the array, and so other sensor types will be tested and incorporated into the array if they are found to be useful. While this technology would be designed with flight consideration in mind, the result of this project will not be a flight-ready system, but one or two prototypes whose sensors have been partially screened for flight qualification.

Task Description: With longer-duration human exploration missions to Mars, the moon, or on the International Space Station, the chances for an accidental fire increase. Despite much excellent and useful research to understand the behavior of laboratory flames in microgravity, virtually no work has been conducted to understand large fires in microgravity (?g). This undoubtedly results from the danger and difficulty of conducting such experiments. We propose to use detailed numerical modeling to understand large fires in the reduced gravity conditions (0 gn, 1/6 gn, and 1/3 gn) of a range of extraterrestrial missions (gn is used to represent the acceleration due to normal Earth gravity) . Recently, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) numerical simulation codes based on Large Eddy Simulation (LES) have emerged as excellent tools for understanding large fires in 1 gn. One such program, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), has increased in use world-wide by researchers, fire protection engineers, and others. The range of applications and the sophistication of its underlying engineering models are increasing at a rapid pace. Hence, it seems like an excellent time to start to adapt the code for understanding large fires in reduced gravity, and use this valuable tool to provide the first insights into the fundamental behavior of such fires. This project brings together leading researchers in developing 1 gn fire models with those in microgravity combustion research to examine and modify the sub-grid scale models in FDS for applying it to understanding large fires in reduced gravity. The modified code will then be used to determine the important parameters in spacecraft large-fire growth and spread, suppression, and detection, and for fire-fighting training and fire recreation.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Full-scale fire modeling is a very powerful tool for promoting fire safety in space. It facilitates the exploration of space on longer duration missions to the moon or Mars since it allows a better understanding of the microgravity behavior of large fires—which increase in likelihood as the time in space increases. This knowledge will allow improved methods for the prevention of large fires in microgravity and for suppressing such fires if they occur.
An ability to model large-scale fires in space vehicles and habitats will allow improved fire safety through: 1.) improved fire detection, 2.) better characterization of materials flammability in reduced gravity, and 3.) improved fire suppression under microgravity conditions. Improvements in the modeling capability will also lead to similar benefits for fire modeling in normal Earth gravity.
Human survival in space requires fire-safe design as well as an appropriate response in the event of an unplanned fire. A numerical code capable of describing fire dynamics in reduced gravity will aid greatly in these activities, allowing engineers to design for the actual performance of the materials and system during the fire, rather than relying only on prescriptive codes (which are currently based on 1 g qualification tests for materials to be used on spacecraft). An accurate reduced gravity fire dynamics code can also serve as the basis for a virtual reality training aid to acquaint astronauts to the behavior of large fires in space. These techniques are in development for 1 g application; however, they are of particular value for space applications since full-scale training with real fires is not practical. Finally, there are many materials that fail the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA ) flammability screening tests but are allowed onboard space craft via various waivers (which limit the times and ways that they can be present in the crew compartment). It would be very useful to model the behavior of these items if accidentally exposed to an ignition source.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
Progress was made in five distinct areas. Specifically, we examined: 1. Oxygen limitations to fire growth in reduced gravity environments; 2. FDS predictive capability for solid material burning rates in normal and reduced gravity; 3. Overall fire behavior in space habitation modules, and 4. Extinction in co-flow diffusion flames. Finally, we also undertook measurements and analysis to assess the use of 5. Flame size as a method to determine the heat release rate from a flame.
1. Oxygen Limitations to Fire Growth in Reduced Gravity Environments
This work investigated two aspects of the problem of predicting fires in variable gravity: 1.) validation of the sub-grid models of turbulence in FDS for conditions similar to those expected to be encountered in spacecraft; and 2.) exploration of the global effects of gravity and ventilation on the potential heat release from a fire.
The goal of the first part of the work was to validate the capability of FDS to predict the movement of the turbulent air streams in micro- and variable-gravity environments. Unfortunately, experimental data on ventilation flows in variable gravity are not yet available. Nonetheless, there are experimental data in the heating and ventilation literature for isothermal, low speed air flow in simple geometries; these are relatively close to the conditions expected for low-gravity vehicles and habitation modules. Using an available dataset on ventilation in a rectangular room (3m x 3 m x 9 m) with variable inlet and exit locations and air flows, FDS was used to predict the velocities for comparison with the data. For a range of vertical and axial locations in the room, with air flows of -0.2 m/s to 0.4 m/s, FDS predictions of the average gas velocities were in reasonable agreement with the measurements. The significance of the agreement goes beyond gas velocities since the turbulent motion which affects the development of the velocity profile is the same physical phenomena which affects mixing, which is crucial for fire growth and spread.
The goal of the second part of this work was to understand how the supply of fresh, unburned air to the fire location is affected by variable gravity and ventilation flow in a module. The calculations examined one question: Under what conditions will a large fire in low gravity be non-viable due to limitations on the transport of oxygen to the flame? The calculations indicate that for uniform, co-flowing, laminar inlet flow, and fuel sources of representative size (r=5 cm to r=15 cm), the heat release rate can be limited by the supply of air. For higher air flow and smaller flames, the flames reach near peak values after about 20 s, whereas for larger flames with lower airflow, the heat release can be oxygen limited. Nonetheless, with any level of gravity above 1/6 g , there is sufficient buoyancy driven flow to make the heat release rate comparable to 1 gn results. A most important conclusion, however, is that putting the same burner into a 0 gn module with representative turbulent flow provides sufficient air so that the flames behave much more like flames in 1 gn than laminar co-flow flames in 0 gn.
2. FDS Predictive Capability for Solid Material Burning Rates in Normal and Reduced Gravity
The above work on oxygen limitations to fire growth in low gravity used a fire of prescribed fuel addition rate. A real fire, however, typically depends upon the feedback of the heat from the fire to decompose the solid fuel into gaseous compounds which then burn in the flame. Hence, to predict fire growth and spread (in 1 gn or low-gn), FDS must be able to properly account for the decomposition and burning of solid-phase materials. While it is desired to make such comparisons between model prediction and experiment based on samples of representative scale, no such data for materials burning in 0 gn or low-gravity are available. Hence, as a first step, 1 g burning rate data were generated for intermediate-scale samples using the NIST cone calorimeter (a device for irradiating a 10 cm x 10 cm 2.5 cm thick polymer sample and measuring the burning rate), and FDS was used to predict the burning rate. This approach provides some measure of the model’s capacity for predicting fire growth, since an ability to predict the burning of such a simple configuration is a clear prerequisite for modeling large fires (which ultimately will also involve burning on the scale of cone samples). The goal of this work then was to assess the relative importance of various numerical, physical, and experimental parameters on the predicted burning of the sample.
It was found that to accurately predict the heat release rate of the burning polymer, it was important to properly specify the domain size and select a fine enough grid resolution. The material properties: heat of vaporization, ignition temperature, and the activation energy for decomposition all needed to be carefully specified, and some experimental configuration factors (e.g., lip on sample holder and presence of the cone heater) also needed to be accurately described. To get correct values for cases with low imposed radiant heat flux, the flame heat transfer to the sample needed careful attention. Of minor importance were the use of direct numerical simulation rather than large-eddy simulation, and use of 3-D instead of 2-D coordinates in the calculation method. Presence of either exhaust flow or backside insulation had little affect on the calculations. A major finding was that the empirically determined effective heat of gasification was the most important parameter necessary for accurate prediction of the burning rate, and that values of the heat of gasification extracted from the cone measurements did not yield a predicted heat release rate in agreement with those measured in the cone.
3. Overall Fire Behavior in Space Habitation Modules.
Work in this area focused on predicting the Mir fire and understanding any fire risk from it, and starting to understand how fires in an ISS module (as a representative case) might differ from a normal gravity room fire. First we used ground-based tests of a similar oxygen generator to estimate that the heat output for the Mir fire was about 5 kW, in a volume of about 0.2 m3. We tried to get the numerical code to simulate a 5 kW fire burning in 0 gn, but various limitations in version 4.0 of FDS did not allow us to achieve that (and still have the radiation transport part of the calculation working). Hence, we must wait for FDS version 5.0 to be released to continue the investigations. In lieu of simulating a fire itself, we performed equilibrium calculations to estimate the product gas temperatures downstream of the oxygen generator to start to get a sense of the fire threat from the burning stainless steel of the oxygen generator. The final product temperature, based on stoichiometric burning of iron with O2, is about 3040 K. Nonetheless, if the mixing fan flow (1333 L/min) is combined with these high-temperature products, the final temperature is near 500 K We then attempted to simulate the radiation from the Fe2O3 particles, but again, this was not possible with FDS 4.0. Our conclusion at this point was that if the mixing fan were operating, the fire threat from the hot product gases would be low; however, if hot glowing particles were present, they could be an ignition source.
4. Extinction in co-flow diffusion flames.
Eventually, FDS will need to have a modified extinction model for flames in reduced gravity. In support of that goal, we collaborated with F. Takahashi at NASA-GRC in work to understand stabilization and extinguishment of co-flow diffusion flames (formed over cup-burners) in normal and reduced gravity. Progress was made in numerical modeling of the influence of chemical inhibitors, flame oscillations, and fuel type on flame extinguishment, and how these change with gravity levels. For example, the limiting temperature for shutdown of the heat releasing reactions was found to be around 1300 K in 0 gn, vs. 1700 K in 1 gn. The next step is to try to generalize the findings and then incorporate the effects into large fire models.
5. Flame size as a method to determine the heat release rate from a flame.
A few experiments slated to fly on the International Space Station concern solid sample combustion. The hardware has already been built, but the researchers now feel that getting the value of the heat release of the burning sample would be of use. In order to allow the researchers to extract heat release rate data from their experiments, we developed an experimental technique for simultaneously obtaining the flame size, heat release and smoke point for flames over condensed-phase materials. From these, a correlation can be determined so that the heat release rate can be obtained solely from the optically measured flame area. The data show that recorded images of the luminous flame (from soot emission) and that from CH emission (approximating the stoichiometric contour) diverge above the smoke point fuel addition rate so that the smoke point is readily determined. The flame area from the stoichiometric contour are superior to the flame height based on the luminous flame for correlating heat release rate. In addition, there exist several important considerations with regard to the actual implementation of the technique in a screening apparatus. For the small flames used, account must be made of the unsteady and the multi-dimensional heat loss terms in the energy balance equation, since these can greatly reduce the effective heat input to the sample from the radiant source.

Task Description:
With longer-duration human exploration missions to Mars, the moon, or on the International Space Station, the chances for an accidental fire increase. Despite much excellent and useful research to understand the behavior of laboratory flames in microgravity, virtually no work has been conducted to understand large fires in microgravity mg. This undoubtedly results from the danger and difficulty of conducting such experiments. We propose to use detailed numerical modeling to understand large fires in the reduced gravity conditions (0g, 1/6g, and 1/3g) of a range of extraterrestrial missions. Recently, computational fluid dynamics CFD numerical simulation codes based on Large Eddy Simulation LES have emerged as excellent tools for understanding large fires in 1g. One such program, the NIST Fire Dynamics Simulator FDS, has increased in use world-wide by researchers, fire protection engineers, and others. The range of applications and the sophistication of its underlying engineering models are increasing at a rapid pace. Hence, it seems like an excellent time to start to adapt the code for understanding large fires in reduced gravity, and use this valuable tool to provide the first insights into the fundamental behavior of such fires. This project brings together leading researchers in developing 1g fire models with those in microgravity combustion research to examine and modify the sub-grid scale models in FDS for apply it to understanding large fires in reduced gravity. The modified code will then be used to determine the important parameters in spacecraft large-fire growth and spread, suppression, and detection, and can also be used for fire-fighting training and fire recreation.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Full-scale fire modeling is a very powerful tool for promoting fire safety in space. It facilitates the exploration of space on longer duration missions to the moon or Mars since it allows a better understanding of the microgravity behavior of large fires—which increase in likelihood as the time in space increases. This knowledge will allow improved methods for the prevention of large fires in microgravity and for suppressing such fires if they occur.
An ability to model large-scale fires space vehicles and habitats will allow improved fire safety through: 1.) improved fire detection, 2.) better characterization of materials flammability in reduced gravity, and 3.) improved fire suppression under microgravity conditions. Improvements in the modeling capability will also lead to similar benefits for fire modeling in normal gravity on Earth. Human survival in space requires fire-safe design as well as an appropriate response in the event of an unplanned fire. A numerical code capable of describing fire dynamics in reduced gravity will aid greatly in these activities, allowing engineers to design for the actual performance of the materials and system during the fire, rather than relying only on prescriptive codes (which are currently based on 1-g qualification tests for materials to be used on spacecraft). An accurate reduced gravity fire dynamics code can also serve as the basis for a virtual reality training aid to acquaint astronauts to the behavior of large fires in space. These techniques are in development for 1-g application; however, they are of particular value for space applications since full-scale training with real fires is not practical. Finally, there are many materials that fail the NASA flammability screening tests, but are allowed onboard space craft via various waivers (which limit the times and ways that they can be present in the crew compartment). It would be very useful to model the behavior of these items if accidentally exposed to an ignition source.

Task Description:
Editor's Note: Successor agreement to "Fuel Dilution Studies of Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames in a Microgravity Environment (NNX07AB33A)," per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To understand better the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum – namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This should provide an excellent platform to gain a better understanding of the factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off distance and extinction, and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth, and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The overall goals of the research are to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Combustion of fossil fuels is responsible for the majority of energy production in the world today and provides the power for transportation systems of all kinds. Effective modeling of combustion processes is critical to improving efficiencies and reducing pollutants in practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in diffusion flames will improve modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
Microgravity Experiments: SLICE and CLD Flame
The Structure and Liftoff in Combustion Experiment (SLICE) was carried out on board the International Space Station (ISS) early in 2012. SLICE was a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment, which is one of the experiments in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), slated to begin in 2017. As will be detailed in the following sections, we continued to build on techniques developed for SLICE in preparation for CLD Flame and ACME.
Extension of High Dynamic Range (HDR) Imaging Techniques
The HDR imaging concept, developed to analyze results from SLICE and described in last year’s report, was extended to Rayleigh measurements in time-varying/turbulent flows. Two sequential laser pulses were used as illuminating sources and the Rayleigh-scattered light was imaged and recorded using the double frame option of an interline transfer CCD camera. Laser energies were such that the first image covered the majority of the detector dynamic range without reaching any saturation, while the second one was partially saturated in order to increase the pixel counts of the low signal level regions; the inter-pulse separation was chosen to be smaller than the characteristic time scales of the phenomena. The reconstructed HDR image showed increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) when compared to the unsaturated one, and equal or better SNR when compared to a conventionally averaged image. Additionally, an alternative image readout approach was demonstrated to improve the signal-to-noise ratio in temporally resolved laser-based imaging experiments. This latter method exploited the temporal decay characteristics of the phosphor screen of an image intensifier when coupled to an interline transfer CCD camera operated in double-frame mode. The light emitted by the phosphor screen was equally distributed and recorded over the two sequential frames of the detector so that an averaged image could be reconstructed. Again, its applicability to reactive flows was verified using planar Rayleigh scattering and tested with the acquisition of images of partially premixed methane/air flames. The comparison between conventional Rayleigh results and the averaged ones showed that the SNR of the latter was 30% higher than the former. This work was published in the journal Experiments in Fluids.
CLD Flame Burner: Preliminary Characterization of the Flight and Ground Units
The first iterations of the flight and engineering copies of the ACME CLD Flame hardware have undergone preliminary characterization. Hot wire anemometry measurements have been performed to assess the symmetry of the flows according to the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (for various flow conditions and at different downstream positions), and images of nitrogen-diluted coflow laminar diffusion methane flames were taken as a function of flow rates and fuel dilutions. The unsatisfactory flame symmetry that was observed at high lift-off demanded a revision of the burner coflow internal components (flow straightener and honeycomb). Several component configurations were manufactured and tested in-house at Yale, and the most satisfactory one is currently being replicated in the flight and engineering units at NASA Glenn. A replica of the ACME CLD Flame burner has also been manufactured at Yale so that parallel measurements can be taken with the SLICE detector and used to corroborate the results obtained with the ACME color data camera. Images of nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames have been collected using the replica burner as a function of the predicted pressure increase inside the combustion integrated rack (from 1.0 to 1.3 atm, with 0.1 atm steps); the flame luminosity was then compared to the image exposure to derive a correlation between pressure and expected maximum camera counts for various flow conditions.
ACME Detector: Flight Unit Spectral and Absolute Light Calibration
The calibration of the signal from the flight version of the ACME detector to a source with a known intensity and spectral distribution is necessary for the determination of quantities such as soot volume fraction and CH* mole fraction. These calibrations were done off-site in conjunction with personnel at Zin Technologies. Two different approaches -- that span different temperature ranges -- were implemented, namely blackbody and thermocouple measurements. In both cases, images of a heated source (either a blackbody furnace or a thermocouple junction placed in a non-sooty premixed propane/air flame) were taken with the ACME setup. Color ratios were evaluated from the red/green/blue channels of the detector and compared with theoretical values obtained by employing Planck's law. When collected through a blue-green color filter (BG7), the comparison between the flight unit and the Yale detector showed a discrepancy between the detectors' spectral responses that can be addressed by adjusting the transmissivity of the red and blue channels through the use of a multiplier. The results obtained without the color filter do not agree with the theoretical predictions and an investigation of the reason is currently underway.
Software Development and Documentation
As part of our NASA diagnostics development work, we have implemented techniques for quantitative measurements of soot temperature, soot volume fraction, thin-filament fiber temperature, and concentration of CH* in axisymmetric flames. These techniques require software for image acquisition and processing as well as careful characterization of the detection systems used. The bulk of this is done using image processing software developed in our labs over a period of more than thirty years. The “OMA” software undergoes continuous revision and extension and a version of the software for the Mac operating system has been available as open source since 2005 ( http://oma-x.org ). All of the ACME experiments will use the same detectors and many will be able to use the same processing methods that we have developed to handle the raw data. Therefore, the detector calibrations and latest version of the processing software are now available to all ACME investigators (and others as well through our open source web site). We have prepared a User’s Guide that outlines the basic processing steps for soot temperature and volume fraction determination. The user’s guide includes examples of raw data and the steps required to obtain quantitative measurements as well as macro scripts consisting of basic OMA commands, which will streamline the data processing. While the most advanced user interface and display capabilities are for the Mac operating system, versions for the Linux and Windows operating systems are available that implement all of the image processing algorithms and basic display capabilities.
Due to the relatively low pixel density of the ACME detector, interpolating algorithms (a.k.a. demosaicing algorithms) have been tested as a way to maintain the original spatial resolution when converting raw images into color ones. The “bilinear interpolation” and the “Malvar algorithm” have been implemented and added to OMA and their effectiveness tested against soot temperature measurements in a reference nitrogen-diluted ethylene flame. The quantitative information returned by the demosaiced images was seen to be more accurate that the one computed without any interpolation, albeit with an increase in the overall image noise.
Finally, a copy of the ACME software was installed on two computers here at Yale to closely simulate the way the ACME images will be taken on board the ISS and to test the ability of the detector to be controlled remotely. Moreover, OMA is now capable of decoding the .hobj image format that will be used to save the raw microgravity images.
