Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2016
Task Progress:
Microgravity Experiments: SLICE and CLD Flame
The Structure and Liftoff in Combustion Experiment (SLICE) was carried out on board the International Space Station (ISS) early in 2012. The goal of SLICE was to investigate the structure of lifted and sooty coflow diffusion flames in a microgravity environment. The SLICE experiments provided a comprehensive data set with a variety of test conditions, including different hydrocarbon fuels with varying dilution levels, different fuel nozzle sizes and various flow conditions. SLICE was a precursor to the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment, which is one of the experiments in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), slated to begin in late 2016. As will be detailed in the following sections, we continue to analyze results from SLICE in preparation for CLD Flame and ACME.
Application of High Dynamic Range (HDR) Imaging
Among the thousands of images of microgravity coflow diffusion flames returned by the SLICE campaign, roughly one sixth of them were partially saturated. Microgravity flames, in fact, have been found to be sootier than their 1 g counterparts and saturated images, by themselves, are not useful for quantitative measurements. The High Dynamic Range (HDR) imaging technique that has been under study to exploit the information embedded in those saturated frames, was tested and successfully applied to temperature measurements using thin filament pyrometry (TFP) and soot color ratio pyrometry in non-sooty and sooty flames, respectively. Additional characterization of the SLICE Nikon camera was done to assess reciprocity and linearity of the detector over an extended dynamic range. Representative sooty flames from the SLICE database were selected as test cases and the flame temperature was inferred using soot color ratio pyrometry, while the soot volume fraction was quantified thanks to an absolute light calibration. Results showed that the HDR approach was able to return images with enhanced signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which in turn resulted in better-defined temperature and soot volume fraction spatial distributions. This work was presented at the 9th US Combustion Meeting and an Applied Optics paper was published.
The same linearity and reciprocity analysis done on the SLICE detector was also performed on the color camera selected for the ACME experiments. It was seen that for the ACME camera, pixel cross talk and blooming become significant when images are partially saturated, and specific measures must be taken to avoid corruption of the quantitative data if the HDR approach is implemented.
HDR imaging was also extended to Rayleigh measurements in time-varying/turbulent flows. Two sequential laser pulses were used as illuminating sources and the Rayleigh scattered light was imaged and recorded using the double frame option of an interline transfer CCD camera. Laser energies were such that the first image covered the majority of the detector dynamic range without reaching any saturation, while the second one was partially saturated in order to increase the pixel counts of the low signal level regions; the inter-pulse separation was chosen to be smaller than the characteristic time scales of the phenomena. The reconstructed HDR image showed increased SNR when compared to the unsaturated one, and equal or better SNR when compared to a conventionally averaged image.
Current efforts are focusing on an alternative way of increasing the SNR in laser-based imaging experiments when image intensifiers are used as gating devices. The Rayleigh-scattered light of a single laser pulse is recorded and imaged on the chip of an interline transfer CCD camera through the use of an image intensifier; by exploiting the long temporal decay of the intensifier’s phosphors, when compared to the laser pulse, the phosphors’ emitted light can be recorded over the two consecutive frames of the CCD. Depending on the frames’ exposures and their timing with respect to the phosphor decay curve, the recorded counts in the two frames can be made equal, allowing for an averaging of the two. Preliminary results showed that, when working in the linear regime of an intensifier, the SNR of the averaged image is higher that the one of a conventional Rayleigh result obtained with an equal laser energy.
Quantitative Measurements of CH* Concentration
As part of the ongoing analysis of the SLICE image database, we shifted our focus from temperature and soot volume fraction measurements in sooty laminar coflow diffusion flames to the study and quantification of the chemiluminescent CH* radical in the non-sooty ones. Chemiluminescence is often considered as a practical marker for flame heat release rate and the comparison with results obtained from numerical simulations of SLICE flames let us study the relation between the chemiluminescent emission and flame heat release rate. The spectral characterization of the DSLR color camera used to acquire the flame images allowed the signal collected by the blue channel to be considered representative of the CH* emission of the A2 delta --> X2 Pi transition centered around 431 nm, while the analysis of the spectral emission of a previously characterized nitrogen-diluted laminar diffusion methane flame accounted for the contribution of chemiluminescence from emitting species other than CH*. An Abel deconvolution of the line-of-sight chemiluminescence was used to obtain the intensity distribution in a cross section of the flame and a quantification of the CH* concentration was possible thanks to an absolute light intensity calibration. Comparisons with numerical results display reasonably good agreement between measured and computed flame shapes, and showed that the integrated CH* concentration is proportional to the integrated computed heat release rate. The two-dimensional CH* and heat release rate spatial profiles match in a satisfactory way, albeit with differences in gradients and intensity distributions.
CLD Flame Burner Tests in a Sealed Chamber
Unlike the previous SLICE experiments that were performed in a vented vessel (Microgravity Science Glovebox), the upcoming ACME CLD Flame experiments will be carried out in an enclosed environment (Combustion Integrated Rack). Tests have been performed using a copy of the CLD Flame burner placed inside a sealed chamber to assess the influence of increasing pressure on the sooting behavior (thus flame luminosity) of coflow diffusion flames. Given the fuel and oxidizer mass flow rates, and over the maximum two-minute duration of ACME test points, the pressure is expected to increase by no more than 30 KPa. In normal gravity, a 25 KPa pressure difference showed that the flame luminosity, for the case of partially sooty methane flames, could change by a factor of four. This characterization, despite being limited to a few representative test cases, will aid in choosing and adjusting the optimal exposure times during the two minute image acquisition period. Additionally, thermocouple temperature measurements inside the chamber provided a sense for what the ambient temperature surrounding the flame would be if the CLD Flame burner were tested inside the ground copy of the Combustion Integrated Rack.
Recent Computational Progress
Flames from the SLICE experiments have been investigated computationally using a formulation based on the MC-Smooth vorticity-velocity formulations of the governing equations. In the physical model, the chemically reactive mixture is treated as Newtonian with diffusion assumed as Fickian. The gas-phase chemistry is described with 42 species and 250 reactions, and it is based on the GRI 3.0 mechanism, with all the nitrogen-containing species removed, except N2. The axisymmetric structure of the flames allowed the implementation of a two-dimensional computational domain with boundary conditions chosen to match the experimental ones. The computational domain extends 4.29 cm in the radial direction and 12.20 cm in the axial direction, and it is spanned by a nonuniform tensor-product grid containing 167 x 289 points. The governing equations are discretized on this grid using a nine-point computational stencil. The resulting strongly coupled, highly nonlinear equations are solved simultaneously using a damped, modified Newton’s method with nested Bi-CGSTAB linear solver. Initial computations concentrated on the sooting behavior of the flames, with results published in the Proceedings of the Combustion Institute. More recently, we have turned our attention to the analysis of CH* concentration and flame heat release rate. A paper on that topic is in preparation.

Task Description:
Editor's Note: Successor agreement to Fuel Dilution Studies of Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames in a Microgravity Environment (NNX07AB33A), per D. Stocker, NASA Glenn Research Center.
Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To understand better the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum – namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This should provide an excellent platform to gain a better understanding of the factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off distance and extinction, and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth, and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The overall goals of the research are to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Combustion of fossil fuels is responsible for the majority of energy production in the world today and provides the power for transportation systems of all kinds. Effective modeling of combustion processes is critical to improving efficiencies and reducing pollutants in practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in diffusion flames will improve modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2015
Task Progress:
Quantitative Measurements with Simple Diagnostics
We have continued the refinement and characterization of diagnostics and flame configurations that will allow us to take greatest advantage of the long periods of high-quality microgravity that are available on the International Space Station (ISS). We have worked to develop techniques for making the comparison between experiments and computations as quantitative as possible, even with relatively simple diagnostic techniques. A technique utilizing a color digital camera has been developed that allows observation of flame shape, size, lift-off height, and measurements of temperature via soot and thin-filament pyrometry as well as quantitative determination of the soot volume fraction. Techniques for obtaining an absolute light calibration have also been developed, which is essential for measuring the absolute soot volume fraction and the number density of chemiluminescent species such as CH*. In an effort to improve the diagnostics, thin-filament pyrometry has recently been assessed against laser-based techniques. Several sources of error were identified and uncertainty analysis has been performed to estimate the measurement uncertainty and provide insight on error reduction.
The color camera to be used in the ACME experiments has been specified and we have purchased a copy of the detector. The spectral response and linearity of the detector have been characterized, which is essential for accurate temperature, CH*, and soot volume fraction measurements.
Microgravity Experiments: SLICE and CLD Flame
As a precursor to CLD Flame, the Structure & Liftoff in Combustion Experiment (SLICE) took advantage of the existence of a closely related set of experiments recently completed on board the ISS. The goal of SLICE was to investigate the structure of lifted and sooty flames. The SLICE experiments were carried out on board the ISS early in 2012. A comprehensive data set with a variety of test conditions, including different hydrocarbon fuels with varying dilution levels, different fuel nozzle sizes and various flow conditions, was obtained. A fully characterized color digital camera was used to image line-of-sight flame emissions to obtain flame properties such as the flame shape and size, lift-off height, as well as soot temperature and volume fraction. The data analysis that has been done includes quantitative determination of soot temperature and volume fraction for all sooty flames and lift-off height measurements for lifted flames. Similar tests using a copy of the SLICE hardware under normal gravity have also been performed, which enables direct comparisons of these flame properties between 0-g flames and 1-g flames. Numerical simulation of some of the flames has also been performed and compared with experimental results. This work resulted in two presentations at the 35th International Symposium on Combustion and two papers in the Proceedings of the Combustion Institute. Furthermore, the results provided important data for continued development of the computational model and soot sub-model, and gave experimental insights that will help minimize risk and maximize the scientific return of the CLD Flame Experiment.
The CLD Flame hardware is currently being developed, and we have worked to improve the design of the coflow burner. A series of refinements were made to the fuel nozzle and the flow straightener used in the coflow. Detailed velocity measurements were made, which will provide the boundary conditions needed for the computational modeling. The improved coflow provided lifted flames with a higher degree of symmetry than previous designs. Following construction and characterization of the new burner at Yale, it was shipped to NASA Glenn for testing in their drop tower facilities.
High Dynamic Range (HDR) Imaging
SLICE yielded thousands of images of coflow diffusion flames in a microgravity environment under different conditions. The database includes an assortment of microgravity flames that vary in liftoff height, soot load, and shape, depending on fuel type (CH4 or C2H4), dilution level (with N2), nozzle diameter, and gas velocity. SLICE employed a Nikon D300s digital camera as the principal diagnostic tool. Microgravity flames have been found to be sootier than their 1 g counterparts. Over a series of exposures of sooty flames, this often resulted in some saturated images that, by themselves, are not useful for quantitative measurements. Until recently, this limited the analysis to a subset of the SLICE data. However, development and testing of High Dynamic Range (HDR) imaging algorithms has proved successful in overcoming these limitations. By combining information from multiple exposures of the same flame (even partially saturated images), the overall signal/noise of the measurement can be increased, resulting in improved temperature and soot volume fraction measurements. Given the high number of unstudied cases left in the database, the new processing techniques will provide useful data for additional investigations. Moreover, these new approaches will likely be beneficial for flame analysis in ACME.
Recent Computational Progress
The computational models used in our earlier flame studies employed a velocity-vorticity fluid dynamic approach where the Navier-Stokes equations were replaced by two nonlinear Poisson equations and a vorticity transport equation for the axial and radial velocities and the vorticity, respectively. While excellent agreement with experimental results has been obtained for numerous coflow flame studies, there are cases in which the agreement is less satisfactory. These are typically flames in which large vorticity values are generated near the base of the flame. The result is that the flames can have small regions of mass loss or gain. This results from the fact that in a velocity-vorticity model, it is the gradient of the continuity equation that is solved to machine zero and not the continuity equation itself. To improve mass conservation, we have recently investigated modifications to our previous velocity-vorticity formulation whereby vorticity terms in the velocity equations are replaced with modified difference expressions. Mass loss/gain is reduced dramatically in these problems.
We have also continued our studies of sooting flames in both a normal gravity and a microgravity environment. Despite the complexities of modeling soot formation in flames using detailed chemistry, the linkage of soot production to radiation and bulk flame properties is so strong that the coupled treatment of this problem has become a necessity for quantitative modeling of flame structure. Refinements to an earlier version of our soot model have recently been implemented. In this work the soot volume fraction is predicted using a sectional representation where the model assumes that soot particles are approximated as carbon spheres and that they exist in the free molecular limit. Rather than letting the surface growth process continue without any restriction on the size of the particles, we limit the size of the primary particles to approximately 25 nm. A further assumption is that within a given section, spheroids of varying diameter do not exhibit vastly differing aerosol dynamical qualities. This assumption holds as long as the number of sections is sufficiently large. In our most recent computations, a total of 30 soot sections were employed.

Task Progress:
SLICE Experiments were carried out on board the ISS early in 2012. Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame had two main objectives as follows:
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution. B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of methane and ethylene diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution.
Through the three rounds of testing of CLD Flame, both objectives were achieved. The first round of testing began in January 2018 and concentrated on measurements in dilute methane flames, as well as characterization and calibration of the imaging systems. The second round of experiments began in May 2018, and provided results on sooting methane and ethylene flames, as well as some data on weak, lifted ethylene flames. Because of issues related to the stability of the mass flow controllers, the quality of data on the extinction limits of the dilute methane and ethylene flames was not optimal. Therefore, a third round of experiments began in February of 2021. Improvements in the mass flow controllers allowed us to establish extinction limits for both fuels under a variety of flow conditions.
The main product from CLD Flame is a comprehensive dataset of microgravity and normal gravity coflow methane and ethylene diffusion flames. These include weak, lifted flames near extinction, under a variety of fuel dilution levels and flow conditions. The highly diluted, lifted flames tend to be non-sooting and differences in liftoff height and flame stability between 1 g and 0 g are significant. This data will provide a stringent test for computational models seeking to predict flame extinction. At the other end of the fuel dilution spectrum, the dataset includes robust, sooting flames, with different flow conditions and dilution levels, which provide different flame heights and levels of soot loading. Once again, the contrast between 1 g and 0 g flames is remarkable and the lack of agreement between experimental and computational results points to deficiencies in current models of soot formation.
The raw image data from CLD Flame has been processed to provide quantitative data on temperature in both the non-sooting and sooting flames using thin-filament and soot pyrometry, respectively. An absolute light calibration of the camera and optical train allows further quantification of CH* chemiluminescence in weak flames, as well as soot volume fraction in the case of sooting flames. The flow conditions are matched in the 1 g and 0 g datasets, and in both cases, detailed near-field velocity measurements have been made. These boundary conditions are critical as input to computational models wishing to compare experimental and predicted results.
In addition to the raw data from 1 g and 0 g flames, processed data in the form of computer-readable data files, as well as final figures, have been uploaded to NASA.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
This past year significant advancements were made in thin filament pyrometry (TFP) processing and analysis. The TFP experiments provide the foundation for quantitative flame measurements because they allow an absolute light calibration of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) camera and optics. This is needed for calculating soot volume fractions, CH* mole fractions, and for improved signal-to-noise temperature measurements, by providing reference parameters for intensity-ratio pyrometry. The improvements to the TFP analysis are discussed below and have led to higher confidence in the calibration of quantitative microgravity measurements.
New Demosaicing Method for TFP Analysis
The color data camera used in the ACME experiments uses a Bayer color filter array, consisting of a repeated pattern of two-by-two matrices of red, green, green, and blue color filters. Since individual camera pixels only detect a single color, an interpolation must be done to infer all three color components at each pixel location – a process known as demosaicing. A common issue arises when imaging small objects whose image is near to or smaller than the pixel spacing. The SiC fiber used in the ACME experiments are 14 µm in diameter and, depending on the zoom and focus settings, the fiber image on the chip may be on the same order as the camera’s 6.5 µm pixel spacing. Because the pixels associated with the red and blue color channels are only present in every other row, the image of the fiber can be absent from these channels. Standard demosaicing algorithms (e.g., the bilinear method) interpolate in both the horizontal and vertical directions to fill in the missing pixels. Near the edge of the fiber image, this leads to an interpolation of both high and low signals and creates undesirable checkered patterns, which results in unreliable fiber temperature calculations.
Different methods have been used in the past to avoid these issues and to more accurately capture the fiber signal in all three color channels. The first method is to slightly defocus the camera so that the fiber image spreads across more rows of the camera sensor. This is a simple method and has proven to be useful for accurately calculating fiber temperatures. However, during some of the microgravity tests, the fiber was too well focused to provide accurate fiber temperatures. Another method was to avoid demosaicing altogether and to generate half-resolution color images with no interpolation. This method produces improved temperature measurements but some form of predicting the missing signal is still needed when performing a light calibration.
To resolve these issues, a new two-step linear demoscaicing method was developed. It is similar to the bilinear method but biases the demosaicing primarily in one direction. Choosing the direction along the length of the fiber avoids the checkered patterns that were created when using the bilinear method and still produces full resolution images. While the issue of unreliable temperature results when the fiber images are smaller than or equal to the pixel spacing is not eliminated, the method does expand the limits of how focused the fiber image can be to give quality fully demosaiced images that provide meaningful temperatures.
Improvements to the Fiber Light Calibration Analysis
Ground-based measurements on the Yale coflow burner were used to benchmark the light calibration analysis used in the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame microgravity experiments. The Yale coflow burner is known to produce stable flames and has a long history of being used in published combustion studies at Yale and other labs worldwide. Stable flame conditions that have already been studied were used so that results using the latest methods could be compared with those previously published. The tests involved varying the camera focus and fiber sweeping speed.
It was found that even the slightest bit of defocusing made significant improvements to the final results. When the fiber image was spread over one to three pixels, the light calibration results were poor and usually unreliable. However, fiber images spread over five to ten pixels were greatly improved. Increasing the level of defocusing further was found to have negative results. In these overly defocused cases, the fiber temperature vs green signal began to diverge from the theoretical values based on Planck’s Law. This especially becomes a problem when performing an intensity ratio pyrometry calculation since the calibration isn’t able to represent the data well through the entire temperature profile.
Decreasing the speed at which the fiber swept through the flame also improved the calibration results, since this created more overlap between sequential fiber images. The idea is to make sure the distance traveled by the fiber between images is smaller than the pixel spacing. This gives the reconstruction processing more values to average over and aids in cleaning the regions where fiber signals are missing when the camera is focused. This was found to produce cleaner signals and the fiber data matched more closely to theoretical values formulated by Planck’s Law.
The absolute light calibration was evaluated by plotting the fiber color-ratio temperature against the fiber green signal and comparing those results to theoretical formulations based on Planck’s law of gray body light emission. The light calibration constant was calculated from the fiber temperature and green signal data at each pixel using two methods: one based on taking the mean and another using a non-linear least squares formulation. While the least squares method did the best at fitting the data, it was determined that taking the mean actually did a better job of calculating the true calibration constant with fiber tests that used more focused images. For focused fiber images, the least squares method biased towards unreliable regions of the fiber image where missing signals were present. Therefore, it was decided that using the mean produced the most reliable results overall.
Preparation for CLD Flame Round Three
After it was announced that there would be a third round of CLD Flame testing, new test matrices were created. The new test matrices contain two days of highly diluted ethylene flame tests and two days of highly diluted methane flame tests. In both cases, the objective is to utilize more stable mass flow controllers so that the dilution limits of both fuels in microgravity can be obtained. This was not possible during the first two rounds due to unstable behavior of some of the mass flow controllers. Further, round three will allow filling in missing test points for weak flames that were unsuccessful due to the mass flow controller issues. The test matrix also contains fiber and flame tests using a 430 nm filter. Using this filter will improve the measurements of CH*, which emits light at a wavelength of 431 nm. The ACME camera’s blue channel naturally passes the majority of the light around 431 nm but transmits a broader spectrum than the 430 nm filter. This will be especially useful for the ethylene flames, which have a greener hue than the methane flames, caused by chemiluminescence from CO2*. Using the 430 nm filter will isolate the chemiluminescence from CH* and filter out other unwanted emissions. Testing with the ground copy of the ACME camera fitted with the 430 nm filter was done to determine what parameters should be used for the flight tests.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
Analysis of Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame Data from Rounds One and Two
With the end of two rounds of CLD Flame testing, efforts have turned to the analysis of more than 300 test points recorded. The images of methane and ethylene flames with varying levels of nitrogen dilution have been processed to characterize flame geometry and lift-off height. For methane flames, calculations of CH* concentrations have been made (CH* is responsible for the blue light emitted by these flames). Temperature profiles were generated from thin filament pyrometry (TFP) fiber sweeps on highly nitrogen-diluted flames of both methane and ethylene. Soot temperature and volume fraction distributions from sooting ethylene flames have also been calculated. Some observations on differences in these flames under normal and microgravity conditions are included below.
Normal Gravity Experiments using the CLD Flame Burner for Comparison with Microgravity Results
The Yale-based ground copy of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) CLD Flame experiment (including TFP fibers) was set up and matched as closely as possible to that on the International Space Station (ISS), to allow comparisons to be made between 1 g and 0 g results. This involved measurements on both methane and ethylene flames with varying levels of nitrogen dilution, selected to match closely the fuel concentrations and flow conditions of the microgravity data from the ISS experiments. Specific test cases investigated include soot free, highly nitrogen-diluted flames, and heavily sooting flames with low nitrogen dilution.
Soot free methane flames were found for a dilution range between 30% to 60% methane (in all cases the balance of the fuel mixture is nitrogen). In normal gravity, fuel mixtures with fuel concentrations below 40% methane were found to be highly unstable and, in most cases, unsustainable. Therefore, flames with fuel mixture concentrations of 40% methane were chosen for direct comparison with the near-dilution-limit microgravity data. The coflow and fuel mixture velocities ranged from 10 to 30 cm/s at this concentration. Above 30 cm/s, these highly diluted flames experienced blow out.
Ethylene flames possess far greater soot loading than methane flames. Therefore, ethylene flames with high fuel mixture concentrations were the focus of a heavily sooting flame investigation. The dilution ranges for these flames was performed from 40% to pure ethylene flames. The coflow and fuel mixture velocities ranged from 30 to 50 cm/s.
Comparison of Normal and Microgravity Results
Highly Diluted Methane Flames
Flame images were captured under a large variety of flow conditions. Comparisons were made between microgravity and normal gravity highly diluted flames with 40% methane. Since the recorded images are integrated along the line of sight, they must be deconvoluted to provide cross-sectional data. This is typically done using a three-point Abel-inversion algorithm. Of the two gravity conditions, the flame lift-off height is more sensitive to increasing flow rate in normal gravity. Past 30 cm/s, the normal gravity flames are very unstable and highly susceptible to extinguishment. Microgravity flames are more stable and much higher flow rates and lift-off heights could be reached. Microgravity flames were captured with gas velocities up to 45 cm/s. It is also found that at this concentration, the microgravity flames are able to maintain a more curved cone shape while the normal gravity flames possess more of a curved disk shape. It was found from the flame images that the dilution limits of methane flames were extended in microgravity. From the ground-based copy of the CLD Flame experiment, it was found that 30% methane flames were unsustainable in normal gravity but were sustainable in microgravity. Full flame temperature profiles were constructed using TFP for 30% and 40% methane microgravity flames. A direct comparison of 40% methane flames in microgravity and normal gravity at 25 cm/s shows that the lifted characteristic of the normal gravity flame creates a flatter profile with a lower peak CH* mole fraction.
Sooting Ethylene Flames
Images were also captured of ethylene flames with fuel mixtures containing low dilution with nitrogen. These images were also deconvoluted using a three-point Abel-inversion algorithm. The deconvoluted data was then used to calculate the soot temperature using two-color ratio pyrometry and soot volume fraction using well known relationships of the optical properties of soot and an absolute light calibration. At lower fuel concentrations, the soot region possessed a small-capped profile near the tip of the flame. But as the fuel concentration increases, the soot region elongates as the flame grows taller. The peak temperature also cools due to increased radiative cooling. With pure microgravity ethylene flames, the peak temperature transitions to the wings of the flame while the centers of the flame are found to be significantly cooler. The normal gravity flames never make a full transition to the wings under the fuel conditions investigated. The microgravity flames also grow taller faster than the normal gravity flames and peak temperature cools much quicker also. The structure of the soot volume fractions is similar to that of the soot temperature, where the maximum soot region possesses a capped profile at the lower fuel concentrations and transitions to the wings as the fuel concentration moves towards pure fuel. As the fuel mixture increases in ethylene concentration and the gas velocity increases, the soot volume fraction also increases. In all cases, the microgravity flames possess a much higher soot volume fraction than their normal gravity equivalents. In most cases, the microgravity flames are found to have a soot volume fraction with a factor of 6-8 times higher than the normal gravity flames.
Normal Gravity Experiments using the Standard Yale Coflow Burner for Verification of Processing of the ACME data
In addition to normal gravity tests on the ground copy of the ACME CLD Flame burner, our copy of the ACME color data camera was used for soot temperature and volume fraction measurements on the Yale standard coflow burner. Flames from this burner have well characterized temperatures and soot volume fractions, obtained over many years using multiple diagnostic techniques. Such testing allows for verification of calculations performed on the ACME experiments as well as characterization of the relative uncertainties and accuracies of measurements made with the ACME data camera. Specific issues investigated were the evaluation of the possibility of pixel cross-talk between color channels of the ACME color camera, most likely to occur when there is a large difference between signal intensities. Other tests were performed to evaluate the effect of the ACME color camera’s lower pixel resolution, dynamic range, and signal/noise ratio compared to previously used digital cameras. Fiber measurements were also made with flames on the Yale standard burner. The light calibration from these were made as a confidence check of the performance between the ISS hardware and the ground-replica hardware. Additional ACME color data camera tests were performed on the standard flames, both with and without BG-7 color filters, to characterize differences in the measured quantities.
Improvements to Data Analysis
Since the beginning of ACME ISS testing, the CLD Flame team has made advancements in processing the ISS data as it was being generated. That work has continued this year with several notable advances. Evaluations were done of the FliPPID method (J.A.H. Dreyer et al. Appl. Opt., 58(10), pp. 2662-2670, 2019) as an alternative to conventional inverse Abel transforms. For some cases, this method has been shown to be useful for improving calculations of soot temperature and volume fraction done in axisymmetric flames. It is especially important for our case where the limited signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution of the ACME data camera result in undesirable artifacts near the centerline of the flame when inverted with other Abel transform methodologies. A drawback of the original version of the published code was that it is written in Python and execution was very slow. The code was rewritten in C++ with fitting-function options expanded, resulting in a factor of 300 speed increase and greater functionality. The improved routines have been incorporated into the oma2 program. As an aid to the other ACME experiments, an updated quick-start guide to installing the oma software and using it for processing data from the ACME color data camera was posted on GitHub. That repository also hosts the latest software versions of oma2 (for MacOS computers), oma2cam (which allows image capture using GigE and DSLR cameras), and QtOma2 (for Mac, Windows, and Linux operating systems). The repositories are available at http://github.com/mblong .
New Test Matrices
New test matrices were created for possible bonus testing in case there is a gap between ACME and subsequent Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) solid fuel combustion experiments. These experiments would concentrate on taking additional data on sooting flames, mismatched fuel/coflow velocities, continued evaluation of the light calibration of the color camera, and filling in some missing data in our previous tests.

Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of "Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame" grant NNX11AP43A, with investigators Drs. Marshall Long and Mitchell Smooke.
Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To understand better the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum – namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This should provide an excellent platform to gain a better understanding of the factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off distance and extinction, and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth, and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The overall goals of the research are to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Combustion of fossil fuels is responsible for the majority of energy production in the world today and provides the power for transportation systems of all kinds. Effective modeling of combustion processes is critical to improving efficiencies and reducing pollutants in practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in diffusion flames will improve modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
Microgravity Experiments: CLD Flame Round One
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment, which initially began November 2017, continued operations with round one of testing going into the new year and was completed at the end of February. During round one, CLD Flame saw 19 test days, 12 of which occurred in 2018. The tests consisted of methane/air flames at extreme dilution limits as well as pure fuel sooting conditions. The initial tests from the months November and December 2017 found challenges with the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) flow and ignition hardware that needed to be addressed before the desired data could be obtained. Starting in January, CLD Flame and the NASA Glenn ops team employed new strategies to meet these challenges. An optimized igniter position was found to improve the success rate of flame ignition attempts. Improved mass flow controller (MFC) calibration settings and increased flow times during testing were used to improve the stability and predictability of the gas flows during flame measurements. A subsequent challenge related to the gas flow issues was the excessive use of air during experimentation. CLD Flame included several test points to determine if nitrogen, rather than air, could be used as the ambient chamber gas; it was found that the differences were indiscernible. Thus, nitrogen was used for the majority of CLD Flame testing as the chamber gas to better manage the amount of daily air use.
Highly diluted methane flames were tested as low as 25/75% methane/nitrogen. However, at this extreme condition, the flames were very weak and found to be very susceptible to blow out from flow instabilities. Because issues persisted with the MFC performance during flow transition stages, the CLD Flame team was unable to determine the dilution limit of these microgravity flame. Discussions between the investigating team and the NASA Glenn ops team resulted in the conclusion that a third round of CLD testing will be planned following the completion of other scheduled ACME tests. The task of determining the dilution limit would be a primary task of CLD Flame round three.
Flame images were taken of steady, diluted methane flames from 30/70, 40/60, and 50/50% methane/nitrogen. At these concentration conditions, no visible appearance of soot was found. At 60/40%, a slight bit of soot was starting to become visible and quickly transitioned to very sooty flames at the 80/20 and 100/0% conditions. Using the thin-filament pyrometry (TFP) fiber array, flame temperature measurements were taken at 30/70 and 40/60% at various flow velocity conditions. For the 80/20 and 100/0% concentration conditions, soot temperature measurements were taken from the unsaturated flame images. From the flame images, CH* number density and soot volume fraction can be calculated but require an absolute light calibration. The absolute light calibration was done using the radiative properties of the heated TFP fibers. Multiple test points could be used to perform this light calibration. The verification of the calibration is an on-going process.
Microgravity Experiments: CLD Flame Round Two
CLD Flame testing resumed for round two at the end of May of 2018 and continued up to September. During this period, CLD Flame saw 17 days of operation. This round of tests consisted of obtaining measurements of highly nitrogen-diluted and heavily sooting ethylene/air flames. This followed round one of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames).
At the beginning of round two, it was immediately apparent that a significant amount of soot had accumulated on the coflow burner. The accumulation occurred due to an error in the input parameters of one of the last E-FIELD Flames test points that caused an augmented flame soot production and subsequently the electric field caused the soot to migrate towards the burner. This accumulation of soot on the burner was originally overlooked during the transition between E-FIELD Flames and CLD Flame. Due to concerns that the soot would compromise the flow boundary conditions, the coflow burner was taken from the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and cleaned, removing all soot from the inside of the fuel tube and the coflow honeycomb.
Following the coflow burner cleaning, CLD Flame began with sooting flame images. As expected, the ethylene flames were extremely sooty and much taller than the comparable methane flames. In round one, the ACME digital color camera settings were all constant except for the exposure time. With these taller and brighter ethylene flames, new camera settings were required, and thus, new spatial and light calibrations were necessary. Multiple calibration test points were performed throughout both rounds one and two. Repeating the calibration over multiple days allowed for the characterization of the ACME camera’s performance over time.
Flame images were captured of ethylene/air flames with concentrations of 100/0, 80/20, 60/40, 50/50, 40/60, 30/70, 20/80, 15/85% ethylene/nitrogen. Soot remained visible in these flames until the concentration reached as low as 20/80%. Similar to the methane/air flames in round one, the soot temperature and soot volume fraction could be calculated from the sooting flames. But unlike the non-sooting methane flames, CH* could not be calculated from the ethylene flames at 20/80 and 15/85 since these flames had a greener hue which indicated that more than CH* chemiluminescence was being emitted from the flames. The TFP fiber array was used to measure flame temperature profiles in the non-sooting ethylene flames at 20/80 and 15/85%. The measurements were made at various gas velocity conditions where the coflow and fuel mixture velocities were both matched and mismatched to study the effect of the coflow air stream.
Microgravity Experiments: Planning for Round Three
During the first two rounds of CLD Flame testing, poor performance of the MFCs during the transition stages between changing velocities persisted. This prevented the investigation of extreme dilution limits of microgravity flames for both the methane and ethylene flames. It was unclear whether the extremely weak flames were blowing out because it reached its extinction limit or blown out due to the unpredictable behavior of the nitrogen and air MFCs. Discussions with the NASA Glenn ops team led to the decision that extreme dilution limits should be the primary goal of a third round of CLD Flame tests. Because the soot volume fraction and CH* number density calculations rely heavily on the absolute light calibration, additional light calibration testing will also be required to ensure the performance of ACME’s digital color camera is characterized and maintained over the time period between the conclusion of round two and the beginning of round three.
Post Microgravity Experiments: Data Analysis
Since the beginning of ACME International Space Station (ISS) testing, the CLD Flame team has made advancements in processing the ISS data as it was being generated. Many of these results have been presented at conferences throughout the year.
The flame images of methane and ethylene flames have been processed to characterize flame geometry and lift-off height. For methane flames, preliminary calculations of CH* mole fractions have been made of Abel-inverted flame images. Temperature profiles were generated from TFP fiber sweep tests on highly nitrogen-diluted flames at velocities ranging from 20 to 40 cm/s. The same was done for nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames, with velocities ranging from 30 to 50 cm/s. Most work has been focused on these fiber temperature measurements since the light calibration is dependent on them. Preliminary measurements have also been made of soot temperature and soot volume fractions from heavily sooting methane and ethylene flames.
Ground-Based Experiments
In the final months of 2018, work has begun on configuration of a Yale-based ground copy of the ACME CLD Flame experiment. The preparation includes reconfiguring the hardware to match more closely to the final ISS test point conditions and procedures. The ground copy testing will include flame images and TFP measurements of both methane and ethylene flames. Absolute light calibration tests will also be performed with the ground copy to allow quantitative measurements of CH* concentrations and soot volume fractions. In addition to normal gravity tests on the ground copy of the ACME CLD Flame burner, the color data camera will be used for soot temperature and volume fraction measurements on the Yale standard coflow burner. This will provide even further verification of the analysis methods by comparing to measurements done on a burner that has already been well characterized for many years through multiple diagnostic techniques.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
Microgravity Experiments: ACME and CLD Flame
The Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment is one of the experiments in the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), which began in late 2017. Much of our effort during the first part of the award period concentrated on preparation for the start of ACME and CLD Flame. Since ours is the first of five experiments that will use the new ACME insert, considerable time was spent on refinement and augmentation of the CLD Flame test matrices to include initial testing of the ACME insert. The preliminary ACME scripts were reviewed and, when possible, preliminary hardware settings were suggested based on normal gravity results.
In June, Davide Giassi and Marshall Long spent two days at NASA Glenn taking part in tests of the ground copy of the ACME insert. Sample data from the tests were made available on a NASA server and analysis of that data began. Processing software to handle data provided by ACME was refined. Tests mimicking those planned for the flight experiments showed that one of the mass flow controllers was prone to oscillations. This turned out to be an issue with the flight hardware as well.
In the time leading up to initial testing, refinements to the test matrix for CLD Flame were made, with spreadsheets updated to include graphical representations of the timing of flow changes and to contain entries needed for the scripts that will control the experiment. By September, updated test matrices for initial ACME insert testing and CLD Flame experiments were provided to NASA. Different scenarios were established for initial camera testing, ignition testing, fuel dilution testing, flow ramping, and CLD Flame operational tests.
A Ground-Based Copy of CLD Flame
In order to provide data under normal gravity for comparison with the microgravity results, as well as to help in planning tests on the International Space Station (ISS), hardware has been developed that closely mimics that of ACME. The ground copy of the CLD Flame burner, which was previously characterized in our laboratory, is enclosed in a pressure vessel. A color CCD camera and zoom lens system of the same make and model as that utilized in the ACME insert are used to collect images. Specific steps taken during this funding period to allow ground-based CLD Flame measurements in hardware as close to that of ACME as possible include the following:
• The chamber volume was increased to ~82 liters to mimic that of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), which houses the ACME insert.
• Additional software was developed to remotely control the mass flow controllers (MFCs) and simulate the flow ramping that will characterize the ACME experiments. The software runs as part of the OMA program, which we use for data acquisition and analysis and has been made available to all of the ACME experiments. A custom circuit was built to interface OMA and the MFCs.
• An igniter assembly, with a remotely operated arm, was manufactured and placed inside the chamber.
• Igniters similar to what will be used in ACME were fabricated and tested. Since no tests of the ability of the ACME igniters to light gaseous flames were done prior to testing on the ISS, a series of tests was undertaken to assess the ability of the igniters to light our flames, the voltage required to light different fuels (related to temperature and power), and their expected lifetimes. This latter is particularly important as changing igniters requires significant operational time, since the chamber must be opened.
For our igniters, the minimum voltage required to ignite flames with different fuels was determined. By imaging the igniter and measuring the color ratios (which depend on the temperature) with the color camera, we have a way of comparing the behavior of the ACME igniters with ours and extrapolating the optimal ignition voltages for the various fuel dilutions. Furthermore, our tests indicate that the lifetime is sensitive to the time the igniter is exposed to flame.
Normal Gravity Tests Using the Yale CLD Flame Rig
Using the ground copy of the CLD Flame burner inside our pressure chamber, we have successfully performed normal gravity tests for the different scenarios included in the CLD Flame test matrices. In addition to acquiring images with our copy of the color data camera, telemetry similar to that returned by ACME are recorded. A video of a 40% methane flame test is available at the following url:
http://guilford.eng.yale.edu/cldflame/CLD_Flame_40_percent_OPS_test.mp4
Temperature measurements in selected non-sooty flames were done using a SiC fiber and employing thin filament pyrometry. These tests were useful in determining the effectiveness and accuracy of temperature from images taken without the blue-green (BG) color filter. Additionally, these tests confirmed the need for image defocus when thin filament pyrometry is implemented with the ACME setup. Specifically, images of nitrogen-diluted methane flames (stabilized on the CLD Flame burner, flow velocity in the range 10 to 35 cm/s, and fuel concentration ranging from 40% to 100%) were collected as a function of time and chamber pressure. Due to the relation between test duration and chamber pressure, this helped determine suitable temporally-stable flames whose temperature can be measured using thin filament pyrometry.
While Phase One of the CLD Flame experiments will concentrate on weak, non-sooting flames, measurements were also made in sooting flames, which will be the focus of the second phase of the CLD Flame experiments. Images of nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames (stabilized on the CLD Flame burner, flow velocity in the range 10 to 50 cm/s, and fuel concentration ranging from 20% to 100%) were collected with the ACME color data camera without the use of the BG color filter to investigate the capability of the detector to return accurate soot temperature information when no filter is used. For selected flames, soot temperature was also evaluated with a Nikon D300s as a way to confirm the results.
Computational and Experimental Study of the Effects of Pressure and Fuel Dilution
Since the CLD Flame experiments are carried out in the enclosed pressure vessel, there is an increase in pressure during each test due to the addition of fresh gas into the chamber (primarily from the coflow). To understand better the effects of this increasing pressure, we have conducted a combined computational and experimental investigation to characterize the influences of pressure, as well as fuel stream dilution on the structure, shape, and sooting behavior of coflow CH4-air laminar diffusion flames. A series of 72 CH4-air coflow laminar diffusion flames with four levels of N2 dilution in the fuel stream (i.e., 50, 55, 60, and 65% CH4) and 18 levels of pressure (i.e., 1.0 to 2.7 atm in 0.1 atm increments) were assessed. In general, very good agreement between the computations and the experiments was achieved for the temperature, the flame shape, and the soot volume fraction, and the numerical model successfully captured the effects of varying pressure and fuel stream dilution. The major conclusions of this research were as follows:
• The maximum temperature increases with increasing CH4 concentration or pressure.
• The lift-off height decreases significantly with increasing pressure, the modified flame length is roughly independent of pressure, and the flame radius decreases with pressure.
• The pressure and fuel stream dilution significantly affect the spatial distribution and the peak value of the soot volume fraction.
Results of this study were published in Combustion Theory and Modelling.

Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This should provide an excellent platform to gain a better understanding of the factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off distance and extinction, and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth, and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The overall goals of the research are to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.

The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in diffusion flames will improve modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation, and radiative transfer take place.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
During the initial stages of our project, we continued the analysis of the data obtained in our previous microgravity work, which concentrated on the lift-off behavior of our coflow diffusion flames in both normal and microgravity environments. More recently, our experimental work has centered on the development of measurement techniques that use simple experimental configurations to study sooting tendencies of flames at normal gravity. These techniques can later be applied to measurements made in a microgravity environment. The focus of the computational work has been on improving the modeling of soot formation. Some of the details of these advances are given in the following paragraphs. Experimentally, we have improved and extended our work using a digital camera (the Nikon D70) as an optical pyrometer. Use of the built-in color filter array (CFA) of a digital camera allows for two-dimensional imaging of flame emission spectra at the wavelengths of the red, green and blue color filters, without the need to spatially match images taken at the different wavelengths. As a result, it is possible to determine soot temperature and concentrations using a single picture. Previously, the filter profiles of the CFA were characterized to provide a calibration for our instrument. Experimentally determined temperatures were found to be approximately 100 K higher than those calculated numerically. Though the data agreed with expected trends, it was difficult to conclude on the overall accuracy of the temperatures measured, as comparison to a source of known temperature was not available.
Currently, an independent blackbody calibration is under development. Images have been taken of an oven at varying temperatures. In order to check the consistency of the two independent calibration techniques, temperature values for the data from the oven were determined using the CFA calibration. The calculated temperatures were found to be 94 K higher, on average, than the temperature that was set on the oven. A sensitivity analysis of the CFA calibration, which depends on a number of different measurements, shows the determination of the measured filter profiles to be critical to the final temperatures calculated, e.g., a shift of the red-channel’s central wavelength of 5 nm corresponds to change in calculated temperature of 50 K. Therefore, a blackbody calibration can be considered more robust than a calibration of the camera’s CFA. Preliminary results from the blackbody calibration for ethylene flames of different fuel concentrations (32%, 40%, 60%, and 80% ethylene, diluted with nitrogen) are found to have the same qualitative behavior as with the CFA calibration, with temperatures from the blackbody calibration being almost 100 K higher overall.
Once the local temperatures have been determined, the blackbody calibration makes it possible to estimate the soot volume fraction of the test flames using the pyrometer data. Information of the radial signal intensity at a given color channel, coupled with the experimentally determined local temperature are used to calculate the local soot concentration. The resulting soot concentrations from the pyrometer data can then be compared to soot volume fraction measurements made previously using laser-induced incandescence (LII). Peak soot concentrations, as well as variations in concentration across each flame, show excellent agreement between both measurement techniques.
Progress in our LII measurements has been made through implementation of an on-line extinction calibration, which provided an improved optical calibration to the system. In addition, the use of a fast camera system removed a measurement bias towards larger particles. The use of this fast camera, which can be gated down to 5 ns, makes two-dimensional particle-sizing measurements possible by determining the cooling rate of particles that have been heated by the laser. This particle-sizing technique and further improvements to the LII system are currently under development. A recent LII workshop provided the opportunity for researchers around the world to discuss this measurement technique in order to provide consensus as to the best-practices, and to try and eliminate discrepancies in implementation that occur between different research groups. Conclusions and inputs acquired from this meeting will be added to our LII system.
Computationally, soot kinetics are modeled as particles consisting of isolated spheroids, which undergo surface growth and oxidation and coalesce with one another on impact. The particle mass range of interest is divided into sections and an equation is written for each section including coalescence, surface growth, and oxidation. For the smallest section, an inception source term is included. The transport conservation equation for each section includes thermophoresis, an effective bin diffusion rate, and source terms for gas-phase scrubbing. The gas and soot equations are additionally coupled through non-adiabatic radiative loss in the optically-thin approximation. In previous studies, as the fuel dilution increases, we have predicted the migration of the high soot regions from the centerline of the flame to the wings. To understand this behavior more completely, we have begun a detailed investigation of the relative rates of inception, surface growth, and oxidation, along with a particle residence time analysis, to explain the shift of soot away from the centerline as the fuel fraction increases. While inception tends to peak on the centerline, the maximum in surface growth migrates from the centerline to the wings of the flame as the fuel fraction increases. Concurrently, the relative importance of surface growth and inception reverses. This change in the relative importance of these two subprocesses is due to the significant increase in residence time available for soot growth in the flame wings. By altering the inlet velocities of the higher fuel fraction flame, we are able to modify the available residence time along the wings so as to generate soot profiles similar to those of a lower fuel fraction flame. The level of soot on the centerline increases with respect to that on the wings as the peak centerline to wing temperature also increases.
In modeling the growth of soot particles, it has been conventional to assume that the particles consist of isolated spheroids, which undergo surface growth and oxidation and coalesce with one another on impact. The experimental evidence, however, is that while the coalescing spheroid picture is accurate for very small, young, particles, older soot particles tend to consist of chainlike aggregates of primary spheroids which fuse together on impact without coalescing. The aggregation process is important in soot formation because it affects the particle surface area available for growth and oxidation. Further, the primary particles within aggregates do not grow indefinitely, but tend to reach a limited maximum size not strongly dependent on either the flame or the fuel. To have a more realistic description of particle structure, the sectional aerosol dynamics representation that has been used to model the growth of spheroidal aerosols needs to be extended to model soot aggregates, as well.
To remedy these deficiencies, we are in the process of employing a discrete-sectional aerosol dynamics model, which has the feature of predicting aggregate growth. The algorithm has provision for a “discrete” size range of precursor or nascent particles whose masses are multiples of some inception growth species. The discrete size range is joined to an isolated spheroid size range whose boundaries vary linearly on a logarithmic scale as in the conventional sectional model; these “liquid” particles are assumed to coalesce on collision. Beyond an arbitrarily determined size, particles are assumed to fuse with one another, leading to formation of chainlike aggregates of smaller primary particles. The conventional spheroid sectional analysis tracks the total mass density within set sectional boundaries; the extended sectional analysis tracks not only the mass density, but also the number of primary particles within an aggregate section. The transition from liquid to solid particles occurs at a particle diameter that is an input item, and the mass fractal dimension of the aggregates is also assumed. Aggregate-aggregate collisions leading to larger aggregates are prescribed at rates based on the assumed fractal dimension.
Once the model is completed and fully implemented, we will carry out a set of computations first on normal gravity flames for which we have an extensive set of LII measurements and then on zero-g flames.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2012
Task Progress:
Computational modeling
The computational models used in our early flame studies included the chemical mechanisms of both GRI Mech 2.11 and a simple 26-species, C2 hydrocarbon mechanism developed at Yale. Both mechanisms clearly showed that buoyancy plays a role in both the size and shape of the laminar diffusion flame. Good comparisons between computations and experiments were obtained using the 26-species C2 mechanism for our standard, moderately diluted flame consisting of 65% methane and 35% nitrogen. However, the agreement in lift-off heights deteriorated rapidly as the dilution level in the flame was increased. Analysis of this disagreement pointed to a need for improved chemical kinetics. A 35-species chemical kinetic mechanism was used to study formaldehyde concentrations in our standard flame configuration under normal gravity conditions with an eye toward understanding the relationship of formaldehyde production and heat release rates. A recent computational effort re-analyzed our standard flames at both normal and zero gravity using a more up-to-date kinetics scheme based on one of the more comprehensive and well-validated sets available for ethylene. The resultant mechanism contains 476 reactions and 66 chemical species.
Another area that requires further study in a microgravity environment is sooty flames. Despite the complexities of modeling soot formation in flames using detailed chemistry, the linkage of soot production to radiation and bulk flame properties is so strong that the coupled treatment of this problem has become a necessity for quantitative modeling of flame structure. Refinements to an earlier version of our soot model have recently been implemented. In this more recent work, as in a number of flame studies, the soot volume fraction was predicted using a sectional representation. The model assumes that soot particles can be approximated as carbon spheres and that they exist in the free molecular limit (i.e., the mean free path of the gaseous mixture is much larger than the largest soot spheroid). The approach specifies a minimum and maximum particle mass and divides the spheroid sizes logarithmically into a number of bins or sections. A further assumption is that within a given section, spheroids of varying diameter do not exhibit vastly differing aerosol dynamical qualities. This assumption holds as long as the number of sections is sufficiently large. In our most recent computations, a total of 30 soot sections were employed (rather than 20 in previous studies). The surface growth model used in the numerical simulations was also modified.
Quantitative Measurements with Simple Diagnostics
Our recent experimental efforts have concentrated on further refinement and characterization of diagnostics and flame configurations that will allow us to take greatest advantage of the long periods of high-quality microgravity that are available on the International Space Station (ISS). We have worked to develop techniques for making the comparison between experiments and computations as quantitative as possible, even with relatively simple diagnostic techniques. A technique utilizing a color digital camera has been developed that allows observation of flame shape, size, lift-off height, and measurements of temperature via soot and thin-filament pyrometry as well as quantitative determination of the soot volume fraction. Techniques for obtaining an absolute light calibration have also been developed, which is essential for measuring the absolute soot volume fraction and the number density of chemiluminescent species such as CH*.
Microgravity Experiments: SLICE and CLD Flame
Our Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame experiment (CLD Flame) is one of the four investigations that make up ACME. The experiments in ACME are currently in development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the ISS. As a precursor to CLD Flame, the Structure & Liftoff in Combustion Experiment (SLICE) takes advantage of the existence of a closely related set of experiments recently completed on board the ISS. The goal of SLICE is to investigate the structure of lifted and sooty flames. The results can provide a test case for developing the computational model and soot sub-model, and also be used to minimize risk and maximize the scientific return of the CLD Flame Experiment.
Another milestone for the ACME experiments was reached in May, 2010 when the Requirements Definition Review (RDR) was held in Cleveland, Ohio. The review process included a Science Review Board and a Technical Review Board. The Technical Review Board assessed “the state of the ACME requirements and engineering development as being largely at the state of readiness needed to proceed to preliminary design.” In discussing the CLD Flame experiment, the RDR Science Panel report stated “the experiments will provide a unique database for testing combustion simulations. Long time periods at low gravity are needed to reach steady-state flame conditions. These conditions allow for more precise measurements and simplify the comparison of simulation and measurement results. The camera-based, imaging diagnostics developed at Yale have been thoroughly tested and will provide a unique, high-quality data set for use in this project and in future simulation projects.”
