Task Description:
Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To understand better the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum – namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This should provide an excellent platform to gain a better understanding of the factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off distance and extinction, and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The overall goals of the research are to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical processes controlling diffusion (i.e., non-premixed) flame structure and lifting phenomena (i.e., stabilization) and to provide for rigorous testing of numerical models, including thermal radiation, soot formation, and detailed chemical kinetics.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Combustion of fossil fuels is responsible for the majority of energy production in the world today and provides the power for transportation systems of all kinds. Effective modeling of combustion processes is critical to improving efficiencies and reducing pollutants in practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in diffusion flames will improve modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation and radiative transfer take place.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2011
Task Progress:
Experimental Progress
Our recent efforts have concentrated on further refinement and characterization of diagnostics and flame configurations that will allow us to take greatest advantage of the long periods of high-quality microgravity that are available on the International Space Station (ISS). Using a relatively simple measurement technique of imaging line-of-sight flame emission using a color digital camera, it is possible to make a number of observations on the flame. Such things as flame shape and size, lift-off height, and qualitative distributions of CH* and soot can be observed. A paper and book chapter have been published describing techniques for making the comparison between experiments and computations as quantitative as possible, even with relatively simple diagnostic techniques. A technique utilizing a color digital camera has also been developed that allows quantitative measurements of temperature via soot and thin-filament pyrometry as well as quantitative determination of the soot volume fraction. A paper on this diagnostic (which will be used in our all of our forthcoming NASA experiments) was recently accepted for publication.
Our Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame experiment (CLD Flame) is one of the four investigations that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME). The experiments in ACME are currently in development for conduct within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the ISS. As a precursor to CLD Flame, the Structure & Liftoff in Combustion Experiment (SLICE) takes advantage of the existence of a closely related set of experiments recently completed on board the ISS. The goal of SLICE is to investigate the structure of lifting and lifted flames, where the flame detaches from the nozzle and stabilizes at a downstream position. The results will be used to minimize risk and maximize the scientific return of the CLD Flame Experiment. The SLICE investigation will be conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the Smoke Point In Coflow Experiment (SPICE) hardware, both of which are already on orbit.
Detailed test matrices and experiment procedures are currently being generated for the SLICE experiment, which is scheduled to be completed in 2011. The experiments will include flames of methane, ethylene, and selected dilutions of each fuel as a function of the nozzle size. Measurements of the flame shape and size, lift-off and extinction limits, and quantitative soot temperature and volume fraction are anticipated through the SLICE experiments. These experiments are expected to enable refinement of the flame diagnostic settings and test matrix for the CLD Flame experiment, and allow for a preliminary assessment of the numerical codes’ ability to predict the flame structure under the broader range of conditions that are only found in microgravity flames.
Another milestone for the ACME experiments was reached in May, 2010 when the Requirements Definition Review (RDR) was held in Cleveland, Ohio. The review process included a Science Review Board and a Technical Review Board. The Technical Review Board assessed “the state of the ACME requirements and engineering development as being largely at the state of readiness needed to proceed to preliminary design.” In discussing the CLD Flame experiment, the RDR Science Panel report stated that “the experiments will provide a unique database for testing combustion simulations. Long time periods at low gravity are needed to reach steady-state flame conditions. These conditions allow for more precise measurements and simplify the comparison of simulation and measurement results. The camera-based, imaging diagnostics developed at Yale have been thoroughly tested and will provide a unique, high-quality data set for use in this project and in future simulation projects.”
Computational Progress
The computational models used in our early flame studies included the chemical mechanisms of both GRI Mech 2.11 and a simple 26-species, C2 hydrocarbon mechanism developed at Yale. Both mechanisms clearly showed that buoyancy plays a role in both the size and shape of the laminar diffusion flame. Good comparisons between computations and experiments were obtained using the 26-species C2 mechanism for our standard, moderately diluted flame consisting of 65% methane and 35% nitrogen. However, the agreement in lift-off heights deteriorated rapidly as the dilution level in the flame was increased. Analysis of this disagreement pointed to a need for improved chemical kinetics. A 35-species chemical kinetic mechanism was used to study formaldehyde concentrations in our standard flame configuration under normal gravity conditions with an eye toward understanding the relationship of formaldehyde production and heat release rates. A recent computational effort re-analyzed our standard flames at both normal and zero gravity using a more up-to-date kinetics scheme based on one of the more comprehensive and well-validated sets available for ethylene. The resultant mechanism contains 476 reactions and 66 chemical species. Analysis of other dilution levels is ongoing.
Another area that requires further study in a microgravity environment is sooty flames. Despite the complexities of modeling soot formation in flames using detailed chemistry, the linkage of soot production to radiation and bulk flame properties is so strong that the coupled treatment of this problem has become a necessity for quantitative modeling of flame structure. Refinements to an earlier version of our soot model have recently been implemented. In this work, as in a number of flame studies, the soot volume fraction was predicted using a sectional representation. The model assumes that soot particles can be approximated as carbon spheres and that they exist in the free molecular limit (i.e., the mean free path of the gaseous mixture is much larger than the largest soot spheroid). The approach specifies a minimum and maximum particle mass and divides the spheroid sizes logarithmically into a number of bins or sections. A further assumption is that within a given section, spheroids of varying diameter do not exhibit vastly differing aerosol dynamical qualities. This assumption holds as long as the number of sections is sufficiently large. In our most recent computations, a total of 30 soot sections were employed (rather than 20 in previous studies). The surface growth model used in the numerical simulations was also modified. A comparison of the new modeling results and the soot volume fraction measurements made with the digital camera was presented in a recently accepted journal article.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2010
Task Progress:
Recent Progress
With the successful completion of the Science Concept Review for our experiments on coflow laminar diffusion flames to be performed on the International Space Station (ISS), we have concentrated on further refinement and characterization of flame configurations and diagnostics that will allow us to take greatest advantage of the long periods of high-quality microgravity that are available on the ISS. This must be done in a way that will ensure compatibility with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), which is now in place and running experiments on the ISS. A detailed examination of the flow fields and flames produced by a redesigned burner was undertaken. Velocity measurements were performed via a hot-wire anemometer in order to verify a top-hat profile exiting the burner coflow, ensure a fully developed flow exiting the fuel tube, and observe boundary-layer effects of differing burner configurations. Asymmetries in previous flame images have been investigated as well. Current work includes exploring other flame configurations that require a smaller amount of coflow air. We have also continued the measurement of sooting flames at normal gravity.
We have worked with researchers at NASA Glenn on the specification of the measurement techniques to be used in the proposed microgravity measurements aboard the ISS. Techniques include color imaging, UV imaging of chemiluminescence, soot pyrometry for temperature and soot volume fraction, thin filament pyrometry for flame temperatures in nonsooting regions of the flame, and laser extinction measurements for soot volume fraction. Color photography will be used to monitor the appearance and stability of the flames at the various dilution levels. These images can be compared with the results of the computations. Using a relatively simple measurement technique of imaging line-of-sight flame emission using a color digital camera, it is possible to make a number of observations on the flame. Such things as flame shape and size, lift-off height, and qualitative distributions of CH* and soot can be observed. A paper describing techniques for making the comparison between experiments and computations as quantitative as possible, even with relatively simple diagnostic techniques, has been published.
Microgravity Modeling
The computational models used in our early flame studies included the chemical mechanisms of both GRI Mech 2.11 and a simple 26-species, C2 hydrocarbon mechanism developed at Yale. Both mechanisms clearly showed that buoyancy plays a role in both the size and shape of the laminar diffusion flame. Good comparisons between computations and experiments were obtained using the 26-species C2 mechanism for our standard, moderately diluted flame consisting of 65% methane and 35% nitrogen. However, the agreement in lift-off heights deteriorated rapidly as the dilution level in the flame was increased. Analysis of this disagreement pointed to a need for improved chemical kinetics. A 35-species chemical kinetic mechanism was used to study formaldehyde concentrations in our standard flame configuration under normal gravity conditions with an eye toward understanding the relationship of formaldehyde production and heat release rates. A recent computational effort re-analyzed our standard flames at both normal and zero gravity using a more up-to-date kinetics scheme based on a 66-species C2H4 mechanism. Analysis of other dilution levels is currently underway.
To accommodate the constraints imposed by the ISS, the size of the fuel tube and the coflow needed to be changed. Implementing these changes in the computational model requires a multiple-step process to generate converged solutions for the new chemical and physical specifications. This process is now complete for our standard, moderately diluted methane flames.
Another area that requires further study in a microgravity environment is at the other end of the fuel dilution spectrum – namely pure fuel, sooty flames. Despite the complexities of modeling soot formation in flames using detailed chemistry, the linkage of soot production to radiation and bulk flame properties is so strong that the coupled treatment of this problem has become a necessity for quantitative modeling of flame structure. Recently, we have made significant progress related to the modeling of soot formation in diffusion flames. Computations agree well with experiments at normal gravity. Microgravity diffusion flames are of direct relevance to the study of soot formation/oxidation in turbulent diffusion flames as these systems are generally non-buoyant due to the large flow velocities. Additionally, microgravity flames have a significantly higher propensity to soot due to increased residence times. Consequently, a study of sooting tendencies at microgravity will provide invaluable information that can be used to improve further our soot formation model. Under normal gravity conditions, we have worked to validate further our soot formation model by studying the interdependency of soot and NOx formation and to investigate sooting tendencies in time-varying flames.
The soot growth model has now been implemented in our “zero-g” coflow diffusion flame program. Previous soot computations for methane were undertaken with an older version of our methane reaction mechanism. The computations have been updated using “San Diego Mech” by adding new species and pressure-dependent reaction rate coefficients to the program. Those computations are now complete for pure methane under both normal and zero gravity conditions.
Microgravity Experiments
We have been able to benefit from the existence of a closely related set of experiments recently completed on board the ISS. The Smoke Point In Co-Flow Experiment (SPICE) measures the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity conditions. These studies were designed to improve the understanding of heat transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions, provide insights into soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions, and devise better fire safety strategies in spacecraft. Dr. David Urban (PI) of NASA Glenn Research Center and Prof. Peter Sunderland (Co-PI) of the University of Maryland generously agreed to share some of their data with us and even allowed us to specify test conditions for further experiments related to our project goals. The similarity of the SPICE flame configuration to our own coflow flames provided an excellent opportunity for us to perform preliminary experiments in a high-quality microgravity environment and to test and improve our analysis strategies in order to obtain the most quantitative data possible from the diagnostics available on board the ISS.
While all of the fuel for the SPICE experiment has been consumed, we were able to define a new subproject entitled “Structure and Liftoff in Combustion Experiments” (SLICE) that will take advantage of the SPICE hardware that is already on orbit. The goal of the SLICE experiment is to investigate the structure of lifting and lifted flames, where the flame detaches from the nozzle and stabilizes at a downstream position. The results will be used to minimize risk and maximize the scientific return of the CLD Flame Experiment. This will enable refinement of the flame diagnostic settings and test matrix for the CLD Flame experiment. It will also allow for a preliminary assessment of the numerical codes’ ability to predict the flame structure under the broader conditions that are only found in microgravity flames.

Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of NNC04AA03A, Fuel Dilution Studies of Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames in a Microgravity Environment, with grants reinstatement in 2006.
Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To better understand the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum - namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames which have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This should provide an excellent platform from which to better understand the factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off distance and extinction and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth and oxidation processes in soot formation models The goals of the research will be the generation of modified kinetic mechanisms for hydrocarbon fuels that are able to model effectively diffusion flame structure under a larger parameter range than existing mechanisms and the development of submodels for soot formation that are capable of preditcting both high and low soot loading levels in hydrocarbon flames of various fuels (methane, ethylene and propane).
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Combustion of fossil fuels is responsible for the majority of energy production in the world today and provides the power for transportation systems of all kinds. Effective modeling of combustion processes is critical to improving efficiencies and reducing pollutants in practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in diffusion flames will improve modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation and radiative transfer take place.

Task Progress:
In a follow-up to our previous NASA-funded work, we have continued the measurement of sooting flames at normal gravity. COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Task Description:
Carbonaceous soot particles formed in hydrocarbon flames are highly efficient radiators of heat. Because of this, the particles act as heat sinks in the high temperature combustion gases, and the gas will respond by conducting heat into the particles. This conductive heat flux, in turn, results in a transport of particles by thermophoresis, which can drive the particles towards each other and into contact. Essentially, this coupled action of radiative emission and thermophoretic transport creates a coagulation mechanism in the flame. Recent experimental observations in sooting microgravity diffusion flames, as well as simple analytical models, indicate that this mechanism could result in a destabilization of the soot field and the formation of very large (super-micron) soot aggregates. This research project will examine, through a combined experimental and theoretical/numerical program, the effects of combined radiation/thermophoresis interactions on the evolution of aerosols in high temperature gases. The objective of our proposed work is determine the conditions under which coupled radiation and thermophoresis leads to large aggregate formation in flames. The research will be undertaken in three concurrent tasks. The first task will be an experimental examination of radiation/ thermophoresis effects in spherical, hydrocarbon/air diffusion flames that are formed in microgravity environments (using the 2.2 s drop tower). Microgravity is needed because 1) it provides a flame residence time that is comparable with our estimates of the characteristic coagulation times resulting from radiation/thermophoresis coupling; 2) it eliminates particle aggregation by fluid shear; and 3) large-scale aggregates are known to form in such flames. We will test the radiation/thermophoretic mechanism by controlling the radiation environment of the flame. Specifically, we will project a source of radiation into the soot-aggregating regions of the flame, the intensity of which will be sufficiently large so that radiation emission from the soot becomes balanced by radiative absorption. If radiation/thermophoresis is driving large-aggregate formation in the flame, then a balancing of radiative emission with absorption will arrest the aggregation. We will use direct imaging methods to determine the extent to which the radiative field alters the coagulation dynamics of the particles.
The second task of the proposed research is to develop a numerical model for predicting the effects of radiation/thermophoretic coupling on soot volume fraction in diffusion flames. We will base the model on the spherical, microgravity diffusion flame used in the experiment, and employ simplified, one-step kinetic models to describe soot formation and oxidation. However, the model will be fully 3D to account for the 3D restructuring of the soot field by the coupled mechanisms. The goals of this effort will be to identify conditions under which the soot field becomes destabilized (i.e., increasingly nonuniform) by radiative emission and thermophoretic transport.
The third task of the proposed research will be to develop accurate analytical models of the radiative emission, hydrodynamic drag, and thermophoretic properties of realistic, fractal-like aggregates of spheres. Such information is needed to accurately assess the effects of radiation/thermophoretic aggregation of soot (in particular) and overall convective/diffusive soot transport in flames (in general), yet a detailed understanding of these properties for soot particles is lacking. Observations of diffusion flames in microgravity flames, as well as simple theoretical models, indicate that the radiation/ thermophoresis mechanism can lead to a snowballing of aggregate growth (i.e., 'superaggregate' formation) in situations of sufficiently long residence time. A detailed experimental and theoretical examination is needed to fill in the understanding of this mechanism, i.e., under what flame conditions and time scales will it lead to soot field instability. Furthermore, the interaction of particle radiation and thermophoresis has relevance beyond that of 'natural' soot formation in flames. Unlike other coagulation mechanisms, radiation/thermophoresis could potentially be controlled by manipulation of the radiative field -- much as we are proposing to do in our experiments. This mechanism could therefore be exploited to either accelerate or arrest the coagulation of aerosols, and such an ability would have immense practical importance.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
One of the tasks in the project is to provide improved models of radiation absorption by soot aerosols. These methods will be of benefit to the prediction of the effects of soot on atmospheric radiation forcing, as well as the modelling of heat transfer from flames.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Ground--based experiments were conducted in the summer of 2004, with the objective of identifying soot coagulation effects resulting from radiation and thermophoretic interactions. The experiments utilized a coflow, sooting acetylene/air diffusion flame, with the soot plume maintained at a high temperature by a coannular, premixed methane/air flame. Gelation of the soot emitted by the acetylene flame was observed, although the rate of gelation was not apparently affected by the temperature environment of the soot. Furthermore, individual, large--sized soot particles did not appear to be attracted to each other, as predicted by the theory, when the slow--moving flowfield of the plume brought the particles into close proximity.
The experiments were therefore inconclusive with regard to identifying the presence of the hypothesized radiation--thermophoretic coagulation mechanism in sooting diffusion flames.
Analytical work has been completed to predict the absorption cross sections of fractal--like soot aggregates. The model uses an electrostatics formulation (Rayleigh limit) for neighboring spheres. Results show that the absorption cross section of aggregates can be 20--50 percent larger than that of the isolated primary spheres in the near to mid IR wavelengths. This effect is uniquely due to the aggregated sphere structure of the particles. A power--law formula was developed to provide a simple method of predicting the absorption cross sections of aggregates as a function of refractive index and number of primary spheres in the aggregate.
Analytical/numerical work has also been completed on a detailed model of momentum and heat transfer from fractal--like aggregates in the free molecular Knudsen regime. The objective of this work, which forms the basis of the MS thesis of a graduate student supported by the project, is to provide a detailed prediction of the thermophoretic forces between radiatively--heated or cooled aggregates and estimate the effect of these forces on the coagulation rates of the aggregates. This work complements the near--continuum model previously developed by the author.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
A Monte-Carlo method has been developed to predict the free--molecular--limit hydrodynamic drag and thermophoretic force properties of fractal-like aggregates of spheres. Results from the calculations have identified an effective hydrodynamic radius of aggregates based upon the aggregate fractal dimension and number of monomers. The predictions of the model are consistent with published experimental measurements of aggregate hydrodynamic radius. In addition, the results confirm that the thermophoretic velocity of an aggregate, in the free molecular limit, is largely unaffected by the aggregated structure of the particle, in that the thermophoretic velocity of the aggregate is essentially the same as the velocity of the isolated momomer spheres. This result indicates that thermophoretic sampling methods applied to soot in flames will not bias the measured particle size distribution, because the rate at which particles collect on the sampling grid will not be dependent on the size of the particles.
We have also performed detailed computations of the absorption properties of soot aggregates. Our calculations employed an exact electrostatics formulation for sphere clusters to predict Rayleigh--limit radiative absorption. In the near to mid IR wavelengths, it is shown that aggregation can result in absorption cross sections that are up to a factor of two greater than than that predicted by an independent--sphere (Rayleigh--Gans) model. The relative increase in absorption increases with the number of spheres in the aggregate, and reaches an asymptote for aggregates containing 100-200 spheres. A simplified correlation was developed to predict the aggregate absorption cross section as a function of number of spheres and refractive index.
A simplified bench-top experiment has been designed to produce a situation in which radiation and thermophoresis will act to compress particles into high local volume fraction. The experiment will produce a laminar, slow-moving flow of absorbing/emitting particles that are maintained in a high local gas temperature yet allowed to radiate to a cool radiation background.
Experiments have been conducted in which the stream of soot particles was produced by an underventilated acetylene--air flame. Still photographs and video pictures of the soot plume indicates that the plume can undergo a `collapse', in which the soot essentially coalesces into a single strand, upon quenching of the flame. We are uncertain at this point whether the effect is due to the radiation/thermophoresis interaction, or if it is a gelation effect. Additional experiments are currently underway.

Task Description: The task involves identifying and analyzing relatively simple models of combustion of non-premixed system; diffusion flame sheets and edge-flames. In particular, the task is to describe the development of intrinsic instabilities such as (i) spontaneous flame oscillations, the nature of the oscillations and the mechanisms responsible for such behaviors and (ii) cellular structures and how, in particular, they are affected by the flow field and the reactants compositions. Another objective is to investigate the effects of thermal expansion on diffusion flame instabilities. The objective of this work is to provide theoretical support to microgravity experimental studies of non-premixed combustion (diffusion flames) in an attempt to develop rigorous understanding of the effects of gravity, or the lack of gravity, on these processes. More specifically, the objective is to determine the conditions for the onset of flame instabilities, and identify the responsible physical mechanisms that lead to these modes of burning. Many practical applications and most fires consist of diffusion flames. Understanding fires is particularly important to NASA's missions because of its concern with the safety of future space explorations.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Although the current project focuses on configurations most relevant to microgravity studies, the results being fundamantal in nature are also relevant to to the understanding of the structure and dynamics of diffusion flames which are most relevant to many earth applications. Many practical applications of combustion, such as furnaces and diesel engines, involve diffusion flames and in most cases fires result from the combustion of non-premixed reactants. Better understanding leads to improvement in design, combustion efficiency and, indirectly, reduction of pollutants.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
1. A novel design was introduced for the realization of a planar unstrained diffusion flame. In the Porous Plug Counter Diffusion (PPCD) burner the fuel is supplied from the bottom of the chamber through a semi-permeable plate that maintains a uniform flow and prevents backward diffusion of products. The oxidizer is supplied through an array of hundreds of closely spaced hypodermic needles, allowing the products to escape vertically through the space between the needles. As a result, a uniform flow is maintained throughout the chamber except, perhaps, for a narrow region adjacent to the tip of the needles that does not exceed the size of one diameter. The realization of a planar unstrained diffusion flame is likely to increase the experimental data on diffusion flame instability and facilitate direct comparison with theory.
2. A comprehensive stability analysis of a planar diffusion flame was presented. It was shown that when instabilities exist they are necessarily associated with excess or deficiency in the available enthalpy at the reaction sheet. This occurs as a result of differential - nonunity Lewis numbers - and preferential - unequal Lewis numbers - diffusion, and at high flow rates, namely when the Damkohler number is sufficiently low. Diffusion flame instabilities, therefore, occur at near-extinction conditions. The various patterns that are likely to be observed at the onset of instability are summarized for a wide range of Lewis numbers and for various mixture strengths.
3. The general characterization described above remains qualitatively correct even when realistically accounting for density variations, an effect that has not been studied before. Thermal expansion was found to have a different influence on the various modes of instability, and its overall effect depends on the ratio of the stoichiometric and supply temperatures as well as on the temperature differential across the entire combustion layer.
4. The main consequence of non-unity Lewis numbers on the combustion field is that it yields temperature and concentration profiles that are non-similar. A volumetric heat loss term that affects the temperature but not the concentration fields also generates non-similar profiles that can promote diffusive-thermal instabilities. In the presence of gas-phase radiation, for example, it was found that flame oscillation can be triggered by appreciable heat losses even for unity Lewis numbers, and the instability is enhanced by heat losses when the conditions already favor oscillations.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Task Description:
The work associated with this project concentrates on understanding the mechanisms controlling diffusion flames, their flammability limits and the onset of instabilities. These issues, which are of fundamental importance to combustion science, could be best observed in a reduced gravity environment. Three configurations have been chosen for this investigation: (a) the jet diffusion flame, formed when a fuel jet issues from a relatively narrow nozzle into quiescent air, (b) the planar diffusion flame formed in the stagnation point flow of two opposed streams, one of fuel and the other of oxidant, and (c) the burner-generated spherical diffusion flame, formed surrounding a porous sphere into which gaseous fuel is internally supplied. These configurations have been chosen because of their relative simplicity that permits full parametric solutions, and because they have been extensively used in microgravity experimental studies, thus enabling comparison with experimental data. They are appropriate for investigating the effects of flow, stretch and curvature on the flame. The first task will be to describe the steady burning and the effects of hydrodynamics, differential and preferential diffusion, incomplete combustion, stoichiometry and gravity on the process. The second task will be to describe time-dependent phenomena such as the development of spontaneous oscillations, the mechanisms responsible for such behaviors and the nature of the oscillations. The third task will be to identify conditions for onset of other form of instabilities, such as cellular structure, and how, in particular, they are affected by the flow field. In all cases, a weak gravitational field will be introduced as an external disturbance to the system in order to assess its influence on the process and better understand the role of buoyancy on diffusion flames. The objective of this work is to provide theoretical support to microgravity experimental studies of non-premixed combustion (diffusion flames) in an attempt to develop rigorous understanding of the effects of gravity on these processes. Many practical applications and most fires consist of diffusion flames. Understanding fires is particularly important to NASA's missions because of its concern with the safety of future space explorations. Combustion processes are in general extremely complicated involving not only the complexities associated with multi-phase, multi-component flows of compressible gases, but also the coupled effects of chemical kinetic and physical transport. Gravitational forces complicate matters even further. The production of high-temperature gases give rise to a buoyant motion, which can strongly affect the flame structure and its endurance as well as the combustion efficiency. The microgravity environment provides the opportunity to develop "clean' experiments designed at studying fundamental combustion processes without the substantial distortion of gravity. Along with the experimental investigation there is a need for theoretical modeling aimed at explaining and guiding the observations and numerical simulations aimed at quantifying the predictions. This program is concerned with the development of simple models, and their analysis by means of approximate analytical techniques and numerical computations. The problems that will be studied, which are of direct relevance to ongoing microgravity experiments, are intended to elucidate on observed phenomena that are not completely understood. Available microgravity experiments provide ample of data against which the theoretical predictions can be compared. The program will thus benefit from the research collaboration of the PI with investigators carrying out experimental work that complement the proposed theoretical work. This also provides a feedback mechanism by which adjustment and improvement of the models can be made.

Task Progress:
A paper entitled, "On the transition from smoldering to flaming", coauthored by Profs. Matkowsky and Bayliss of Northwestern University and Dr. Anatoly Aldushin of the Russian Academy of Science's Insatitute for Structutal Macrokinetics and Materials Science, was published (Combustion and Flame, vol. 145 (2006), 579-606).
In addition, a version of the paper, entitled "On the mechanism of triggering the transition from smoldering to flaming" was presented at the 31st International Symposium on Combustion, held in Heidelberg, germany in August, 2006. It was accepted for publication in the Symposium Proceedings. The abstract for both papers reads: "We consider the transition from smoldering to flaming. Though there have been numerous experimental studies of this topic, it has been virtually untouched theoretically. Rather than investigating the details of either the transition process or the subsequent flaming, we focus on determining the mechanism and the conditions that trigger the transition. We employ both computations and approximate analytical approaches. We consider a planar, forward smolder wave driven by a constant forced flow of gas containing oxidizer. The chemical kinetic scheme employed consists of three reactions, namely, pyrolysis, fuel oxidation and char oxidation. There have been a number of speculations about the nature of the triggering mechanism, including the gaseous reactions, the char oxidation reaction, destruction of the porous matrix through which the smolder wave propagates, and others. However, no mechanism has, as yet, been theoretically demonstrated to be capable of acting as the triggering mechanism. We show that the char oxidation reaction hardly affects the characteristics of smolder wave propagation due to its small reaction rate, though under appropriate conditions, it can act as the trigger for the transition to flaming due to its ability to self-accelerate. Specifically, we introduce the concept of, and then compute, a quantity which we term the flaming distance L(F) . This is the distance that a steadily propagating smolder wave initiated at the gas flux inlet, travels inside the porous medium before the char oxidation reaction spontaneously self-accelerates, resulting in an eruption of the temperature in the smolder front. That is, the smolder wave propagates for a relatively long latent period of time until it reaches L(F) . A transition to flaming then occurs. The flaming distance L(F) depends on the physicochemical parameters of the fuel and the products as well as external parameters, such as the velocity and composition of the incoming gas, heat loss, etc. We show that smolder waves propagating in porous samples of length L do (do not) exhibit a transition to flaming if L(F) L)).
Finally, a new paper is currently in preparation. In contrast to the papers which consider forward smoldering, the new paper considers the possible transition from smoldering to flaming for reverse smolder waves.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
A paper "Effects of Gas-Solid Nonequilibrium in Filtration Combustion" appeared in Combustion Science and Technology 175, in 2003. The abstract of the paper reads: To determine the effects of gas-solid nonequilibrium on forced filtration combustion (FC) waves, a two-temperature model is employed, with separate temperature fields for the gas and solid particles. We consider heterogeneous (gas/solid) combustion in a porous sample with a prescribed gas influx at the inlet. If the combustion wave travels in the same direction (opposite to) the direction of the gas flux it is referred to as coflow (counterflow) FC. We determine the effects of gas-solid nonequilibrium on various aspects of forced FC waves. First, we consider coflow FC, in which case the gas infiltrating through the hot product region significantly enhances propagation of the wave. For a relatively small gas flux, the infiltrating gas delivers heat from the hot product layer to the combustion layer, thus increasing the combustion tempertaure and hence the reaction rate. Propagation of such waves is controlled by conduction of the heat released in the reaction, to the prehet zone. Conductively driven coflow FC waves have been extensively studied using one-temperature models, which assume a very large rate of interphase heat exchange between the solid and the gas, so that thermal equilibrium is rapidly attained. However, if the gas flux is sufficiently large, the phases do not have sufficient time to equilibrate and hence one-temperature models are no longer valid. For relatively large gas flux, using the two-temperature model, we show that an alternative mechanism of enhancement occurs whereby the combustion temperature increases as a result of increasing the effective initial temperature ahead of the reaction zone. Propagation of such waves is controlled by convection of heat stored in the product, to the preheat zone. Convectively driven coflow FC waves depend on a pronounced temperature difference between the phases and cannot be described by a one-temperature model. Employing the two-tempertaure model we describe both conductively and convectively driven FC waves. We compare and contrast the two wave structures and their combustion characteristics, including propagation velocity, extinction limit, and the ability of the wave to accumulate energy. We also discuss the transition between the two types of waves. Next, we consider the effects of nonequilibrium on counterflow FC waves, in which the solid near the reaction site loses heat to the cool infiltrating gas. Counterflow waves are necessarily conductively driven. Extinction can occur if the gas flux is sufficiently large. We find that thermal nonequilibrium has a significant effect on the extinction limit and on the combustion characteristics.

Task Description:
In the proposed study, which is a renewal of an existing project, a transient, fully three-dimensional simulation code will be developed to simulate the effects of realistic g–jitter on a number of combustion systems. Acceleration disturbances of realistic orientation, magnitude and time dependence can be easily included in the simulation. A number of microgravity combustion experimentalists have agreed to use a preliminary version of the code. The experience of these users will be essential to both fully debugging the code and making it more user friendly. At the end of the project the code will be made available for general use by the microgravity combustion community.
The simulation algorithm is based on techniques used in an existing large eddy simulation code which has successfully simulated fire dynamics in complex domains. This technique is very efficient computationally so that simulations of the entire experimental domain with one to two million grid cells can be performed on current single processor workstations. An efficient cell blocking method allows the user to easily define and modify the solid surfaces comprising the simulation domain and diagnostic equipment. To preserve computational efficiency, simple combustion models are used (e.g., flame sheet or highly reduced, finite rate, second order, global Arrhenius kinetics). A multiblocked grid approach will be implemented to allow regions requiring high resolution (i.e., the flame) to be covered by a fine grid while coarser grids cover the rest of the experimental volume.
Acceleration disturbances or g–jitter about the background level of reduced gravity exist in all the microgravity facilities. Low frequency g–jitter has been repeatedly observed to disturb a number of combustion systems. Guidelines regarding tolerable levels of acceleration disturbances for a given combustion system (i.e., flame balls, gas jet diffusion flames, etc.) have been developed for use in the design of ISS experiments. The validity of these guidelines, however, remains unknown. The proposed simulation code will allow users to assess the g-jitter effects on their flame for the microgravity facility in question. This will help investigators plan experiments and interpret their data. For example on the ISS an acceptable acceleration environment will be achieved through the combined use of a passive isolation system and scheduling appropriate crew/station activity (e.g., no ergometer exercise). Different flames are expected to have different acceleration environment requirements and, therefore, demands on crew/station activity. The proposed simulation code will provide one means of determining these requirements.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
During the first two years of the program the efforts were focused on developing a high pressure test rig with optical access for use in the ground based microgravity facilities. The primary issue with the design was selection of a non-reactive material or material coating that would withstand the targeted pressure range of the study and provide a non-catalytic surface. While our original design had proposed to use the pressurized quartz vessel-inside-a metal pressure vessel technique, which we have successfully utilized in our flow reactor facility, the possibility of rapid pressure rise inside the constant volume quartz reactor necessitated moving to an all metal reactor design which necessitated selection of an inert coating for the inner surface. Finding such a coating took much of our first eigthteen months time as no manufacturer would guarantee the passivity and the durability of their products over the temperature (600-900 K) and pressure (1-10 atm) ranges of the program. It was during this phase of the preliminary design that we began to work on simulations of the oxidation processes that would occur within the reactor. These simulations identified the risk of the rapid pressure rise and also the need to run multi-dimensional calculations. Such calculations required us to take detailed kinetic models and develop lower dimensionality chemical models, also known as “reduced” models in order to perform a realistic simulation. About the time that we had identified possible coatings for our metal reactor to test their applicability, it became obvious that by the time we identified the appropriate coating, designed the facility, ran through the appropriate safety certification, then begin fabrication that there was going to be a significant reduction in the availability of time with the microgravity facilities. At this point we got permission to change the focus of the research program from primarily an experimental program to a modeling study of hydrocarbon oxidation. This work would also support the experimental work underway under the direction of a Co-Investigator of this program, Dr. H. Pearlman. We also undertook the development of optical diagnostics for in-situ measurements that were initially planned in collaboration with the ZARM.
During the course of this work we have made significant progress, preparing five manuscripts for presentations which will ultimately be developed into archival publications and form the basis for dissertations. The work encompasses a range of models including detailed chemical formulations for propane, butane, n-heptane and iso-octane, the primary reference fuels (PRFs) for spark ignition engines, to explore the oxidation behavior of real size hydrocarbons, and reduced models for the propane and the PRFs to investigate mixtures, and global models of the PRFs to allow computations in two dimensions.
The first manuscript described a global kinetic model that simulated the autoignition and ultimate combustion of propane at temperatures from 600 – 1000 K, for pressures ranging from 1 – 10 atm and over the range 0.5
Later we compared a detailed kinetic model for propane with a skeletal model of 49 species and 80 reactions in 0D simulations in preparation for use in multidimensional calculations. The skeletal model was constructed entirely from elementary reactions and rate parameters were selected from the literature. The skeletal mechanism predicted the quantitative global parameters (pressure, temperature, and induction times) and species concentrations, such as carbon monoxide, hydroxyl radical, formaldehyde, and cool flame light intensity very well, within the accuracy targets for the study. The mechanism was also able to predict the qualitative features including the number of cool flames as well as prediction of the transition to hot ignition. The mechanism is valid across a wide range of equivalence ratios. The skeletal mechanism reduced the computation time by a factor of three and also required an order of magnitude less computer memory for the computation than a detailed propane model. The mechanism will be used to predict the spatio-temporal temperature and species distribution in unstirred cool flame experiments using a two dimensional CFD model.
As mentioned, in keeping with our plan of studying more realistic fuels than propane, we have developed detailed and skeletal models of the PRFs for spark ignition engines. We have used these models to explore the effect of the ignition promoting additive di-tertiary butyl peroxide (DTBP) on their preignition chemistry, which direct application to homogeneous charge compression ignition engines. Both models were able to reproduce existing experimental data on preignition reactivity for a range of n-heptane/iso-octane ratios with a without the addition of up to 1.5% (by volume) DTBP. A key question to be answered in this study was to identify the mechanism by which DTBP promotes ignition. The decomposition of DTBP generates both moderate heat release and a pool of highly reactive radical intermediates and there is disagreement as to which mechanism promotes ignition. By examining the results from the simulation, we determined that for mixtures which were primarily more than 50% n-heptane the key mechanism for promotion is the additional heat release; however, for the mixtures that were primarily iso-octane the mechanism is the generation of the radical pool. This illustrates the power of combining experimental work with modeling studies. Both models led to similar interpretations; however, the skeletal model was computationally efficient enough (cutting computational time by two orders of magnitude; memory allocation by three orders of magnitude) that we are trying to apply it to multidimensional computations as well.
Unfortunately, our optical diagnostic work has not been as successful. We have been faced with an irritating sequence of equipment failures that have essentially kept this portion of the work from moving forward.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The major goal of the first year was to refine the design parameters for the high pressure reactor and to design and construct the reactor and its supporting measurement and gas handling system. Progress has been made in each of these areas and will be discussed below.
Development of design parameters
As we worked to refine our design and as one of the Co-I’s (HP) underwent further safety reviews in his low pressure program, a major issue became the integrity and safety of the original “quartz sphere inside a pressure vessel” design concept. The major issues being the integrity of the metal to pyrex to quartz feed-throughs at our proposed pressures and the ability to match the internal reaction pressure profile in the pressurized annular region between the quartz reactor and the pressure vessel. Our concerns led us to investigate the use of coatings on the inside of a metal pressure vessel with the expectation that recent developments in material science and research in catalysis would yield appropriate coatings. An ideal coating would be just as inert as the present acid washed quartz surfaces and adhere to the inner walls of the metal reactor without cracking and flaking. A literature survey coupled with a search of possible vendors identified several promising coatings; however, most have not been used in our proposed temperature and pressure ranges. More importantly their traditional application, e.g., turbine blade coatings, has been to protect the wall surface from corrosion or thermal loads and not to ensure inertness of the surface. Therefore, we have identified leading candidates and are proceeding with a test program to determine how inert the surface really is. This requires fabricating some test coupons and sending them to be coated; followed by reactivity tests in our laboratories. We expect to complete these tests in the next quarter. While this redirection has delayed this part of our first year program, successful determination of an more robust reactor system should eliminate a major safety concern for the project.
Design and construct the reactor and its supporting systems
While the design of the actual reaction vessel depends on the determination of whether we can coat a metal sphere or we go with the original plan of a “quartz sphere inside a pressure vessel”, we have been working on the design of the test rig and supporting systems. The design roughly parallels the existing cool flame rig of one of the Co-PI’s; however, there are the additional complications of operating at elevated pressure and allowing provision for appropriate optical accessibility by the diagnostics being developed at the University of Bremin. Elevated pressure modifies the design in two crucial aspects. The first is that all of the fittings and hardware must be rated for the higher pressure and this quickly manifests itself in terms of mass and bulk. Hence every structural member of the test rig must be designed to withstand higher loads. The second impact is that since the reactor is roughly the same size as the low pressure reactor, in order to achieve the desired Rayleigh Number, it requires considerably more reacting mixture to reach the design pressures. This changes the size and pressure of the intermediate storage tanks and also impacts the diameter of the lines connecting the storage tanks to the reacting vessels. We have to consider the trade-offs between size and pressure of storage tanks (from a safety issue) and reactor fill time (from consideration of the time=0, start of reaction). Additionally we have to consider the maximum pressures possible due to hot ignition of our high pressure systems. We have performed both equilibrium and detonation calculations with our proposed mixtures to explore these extreme conditions. These results indicate that in order to achieve acceptably low maximum pressures, thereby reducing safety concerns and reducing the mass of the reactors and storage vessels, we will have to operate with significant dilution by nitrogen or other inert gas (helium or argon). We are in the process of mapping our operating mixtures.

Task Description:
In this task we research a catalytically stabilized, premixed flame in a jet configuration where the jet diameter is smaller than a typical macro-scale flame thickness. Both a nozzle stabilized flame with some of the combustion occurring inside of the catalytic delivery tube, as well as a stagnation plate and enclosed flame configuration, will be examined. The research will explore the potential for a microjet flame as a heater, a power source, or a torch capable of operation in the Martian atmosphere.
The basic concept is that of a small, pre-mixed fuel/oxidizer flow that begins combusting inside a capillary-size (1 mm diameter or smaller) delivery tube, the outlet section of which is a pure catalyst, and then completes combustion either as a free jet flame or impinging on a flat plate as a stagnation flame. The plate can also be catalytic to increase combustion efficiency and reduce the chance of reaction quenching. Of particular fundamental interest will be the flame structure and stability when the outlet tube diameter is on the order of or less than a typical premixed flame thickness.
The proposed program will consist of normal gravity experiments primarily in air and low-pressure carbon-dioxide atmospheres (i.e. Martian). Some exploratory work will investigate the feasibility of burning in a vacuum environment. The first stage of experiments will investigate the lower size limits of a premixed, catalyzed, partially-precombusted free jet flame, and gather fundamental combustion data on a scale where none currently exist. Fuels to be used include hydrogen, as well as fuels that may be made in-situ on Mars such as carbon monoxide, methane, and possibly methanol (all mixed with hydrogen to obtain the catalytic effect); the oxidizer will be oxygen partially diluted with an inert such as nitrogen or carbon dioxide to prevent catalyst burnout. The catalysts will be platinum and palladium. We will also measure the downstream combustion efficiency and its dependence on length of catalytic tube section (or the flow residence time in the catalytic section).
In the second stage a stagnation plate will be added to the flow to obtain data on the effect of heat loss from the jet and to evaluate the potential of the jet as a microtorch. A catalytic plate will also be studied to determine the flame structure in a stagnation flow field. The third stage of experiments will occur later in the program and involve integration of the impinging jet flat flame burner into a more realistic enclosed combustor, which will allow high-pressure operation. In addition to fundamental information on the flame structure, the experiments will provide operating characteristics and limits of a pre-mixed microjet flame. The heat transfer to the stagnation plate is of interest for heater applications.
The diagnostics for the experiments will include: 1. Standard and spectral imaging of the flame; 2. Temperature measurements of the solid plate and gas-phase flame using thermocouples, thin filament pyrometry and infrared imaging; 3. Particle Image Velocimetry measurements of the gas-phase flow profiles, and 4) Planar Laser Induced Fluorescence and Rainbow Schlieren measurements on the reacting flow field. Measurements will be made over a range of jet exit diameters, gas velocities, operating pressures, catalyst types, catalyst section lengths, external environments, plate-to-jet separation distances, equivalence ratios and types and percentages of diluent gases.
The program will also involve the development of a detailed numerical model, using a commercial code, to predict the behavior of the combustion. The model will be two-dimensional, axi-symmetric, and solve the full Navier-Stokes equations for momentum and the energy and species conservation equations, including surface radiation. We will use detailed chemistry for both the gas and surface reactions. Currently, detailed mechanisms (including surface chemistry) for most of the candidate fuels and catalysts are available in the technical literature. The objective is to determine the fundamentals of catalyzed premixed jet flames at sub-millimeter scales. Quantities such as flame shape, flammability limits, temperature, acoustic emission, catalytic effects, etc. will be measured as a function of equivalence ratio, velocity, pressure, and fuel type. NASA is in need of simple, small, power systems, and combustion offers a largely untapped technology that may have many advantages over the batteries technology currently used. The high power density offered by combustion systems, along with easy recharge, make the consideration of micro premixed flames for heating or conversion to power attractive.

Microcombustors have the potential to supply personal power for a variety of devices with advantage over current power sources like batteries. There is a lack of fundamental data on the characteristics of small-scale premixed flames, and this project will supply data useful for designing devices and verifying models. The resulting flame would have a wide range of potential applications as a heater, torch, or the basis for a microcombustor electrical generator.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Progress was achieved on both the experiment and the numerical model during this reporting period. We constructed an apparatus that allows the precise metering and mixing of oxygen and a fuel gas (methane or carbon monoxide) and the ignition of this mixture at the end of a small tube. A nitrogen co-flow shroud was built to shield the flame from the effects of ambient oxygen in the room. A camera with microscope lens recorded the flame size and shape, a microphone recorded the flame sound, and a video camera recorded the flame as it moved inside the tube. Three flame regimes were studied: a flame stabilized outside the tube, the flame stabilized just inside the end of the tube, and a traveling flame inside the tube. The tube diameter, wall thickness, and material were varied to determine their effects.
For the flame stabilized on the outside of the tube, the blow-off limits were determined and flame shape and size recorded and measured over a range of tube sizes, equivalence ratios and mixture velocities.
At low speed the flame forms a rounded cap on the tube outlet, while at higher speed the flame stretches out and more closely resembles a standard Bunsen flame. It appears that in some cases reaction continues to take place beyond the bright flame cone. The richer flames (e.g., phi = 1.3) move closer to the tube and heat it sufficiently that it glows slightly due to thermal emission. This may be due to air diffusing to the flame and providing extra oxygen. In the nitrogen shroud, the flame extinguished above phi = 1.3 for the tube size in these tests. In the air ambient, the flame made a gradual transition in intensity, becoming dimmer and larger as the equivalence ratio increased for the same outlet velocity. Most of the tests were run with the tube horizontal, and the flame appeared symmetric about the tube axis. As the flame became longer, the effect of buoyancy did begin to be obvious and the flame stretched vertically for phi = 4 for the velocities in this investigation.
For certain conditions we discovered the flame would move inside the tube and begin slowly traveling upstream toward the fuel source. At first, the flame stabilizes on the tube end. It heats the end of the tube, and when that is sufficiently hot the flame is able to go inside. Then the flame continues preheating the tube and advancing upstream. As the flame moves away from the end of the tube, the tube downstream of the flame cools and is no longer visible. The flame releases enough heat to cause the tube wall to glow brightly, making the flame location easy to determine.
The rate of flame propagation for flames in four different microtubes as a function of mixture equivalence ratio was measured. The upstream flow velocity is held constant at 2 m/s. The flame velocity was obtained by recording a standard video of the outside of the tube, which glowed very brightly in the flame location and then tracking the flame front using software developed at GRC. Once in the tube, all of the flames had a steady propagation rate, so the slope from a position vs. time graph yielded the velocity. Note that the tube diameters are all close to the conventional quenching diameter for phi = 0.8 (~ 500 micronmeters), but much smaller at phi = 1.2 (~700 micronmeters).
For tubes of the same material (alumina ceramic), the thicker walled tube yielded a higher flame propagation rate. There are two competing effects regarding conduction in the tube wall. Heat conducted radially is lost into the wall and eventually to the ambient, while that conducted axially assists in flame propagation. In this case, the thicker wall provides more cross-sectional area to conduct heat upstream, outweighing the effect of radial conduction. It is believed that this effect will only exist until a critical wall thickness is reached.
A high tube thermal conductivity also led to high flame propagation velocities. This is evident in the curve for the stainless steel tube. As the temperatures of the flame increases, the thermal conductivities of the alumina and stainless steel begin to depart. At high temperatures the stainless steel thermal conductivity increases while that of alumina decreases. At phi = 1.0, the fact that the wall thicknesses of the two tubes are similar is overwhelmed by the large difference in thermal conductivities. The flames in the ceramic tubes propagated with the highest velocities at an equivalence ratio just under 1.0. This may be due to kinetics, but may also be partly explained by the fact that the thermal conductivity of the ceramic Al2O3 achieves its lowest values at temperatures between 1300K and 1800 K. According to the model of the heat transfer in the tube, these are the temperatures the tube will be experiencing at an equivalence ratio of one. Lowering the temperature by decreasing the equivalence ratio below 1.0 causes the temperature of the tube to drop, but at the same time the thermal conductivity begins to increase. At these high temperatures a drop in temperature from 1300 K to 900 K could nearly double the thermal conductivity from approximately 4 to 8 W/mK. The drop in flame speed associated with a lean adjustment of the equivalence ratio may be overwhelmed by the increase in flame speed due to a large increase in thermal conductivity. It was also found that despite the fused silica having a lower thermal conductivity (1.4 W/mK), it supported higher propagation velocities than alumina. The reason for this is not obvious. More work is needed to untangle the effects of the wall thickness and material for cases where the thermophysical properties vary with temperature.
The silica tube has a transparent wall, allowing images to be obtained of a propagating flame. A numerical model developed by Lee and Tsai for larger tubes predicted either mushroom or tulip shaped flames, depending on the conditions. In these micro-tubes, the flame is neither, and takes on a fairly flat profile.
In contrast to the flame propagation above, at certain operating conditions, a flame stabilized just inside the outlet of a tube; the flame will travel neither upstream nor will it blow out the end. Such behavior was present with both ceramic and stainless steel tubes. With the fused silica tube rapid softening occurred and we could not test for a long enough time to stabilize the flame (some melting also occurred with the stainless steel tube, but not as rapidly). When the flame was inside the tube, no blue flame was visible outside, but the end of the tube glowed brightly. One mechanism of stabilization for the flames near the outlet of the tube is an asymmetry of heat losses. If a flame is in the middle of the tube, it can lose heat both upstream and downstream due to conduction in the tube wall. When the flame resides near the outlet of the tube, the major heat loss is upstream, since there is no tube downstream to act as a conduction path. This leads to an increase in the temperature of the tube near the outlet. The flame is able to heat the tube enough to propagate into it, but not enough to continue propagating upstream.
To better understand this effect, a numerical model of the heat transfer in the microtube was developed to predict tube wall temperatures, heat losses, etc. The steady state model accounts for axial conduction in the tube wall, radial convective and radiant heat losses to the environment, convective heat transfer to and from the flow, heat release in the gas via an energy source term based on complete combustion, and variable thermophysical and transport properties. The control volumes are defined using the SIMPLE algorithm and the coupled equations are solved iteratively. The effect of wall thickness in the model is apparent, with the thin walled tube getting hotter locally, but the temperature dropping off more quickly away from the region of heat release.
Further experiments with the microflames revealed it is also possible to manually force the flame to stabilize inside the tube. In certain conditions where the flame is close to entering the tube, but definitely stabilized outside the tube, one could manually preheat the tube with a match, which would cause the flame to move and stabilize inside the tube. Removing the match did not cause the flame to move back outside, indicating the presence of two stability points.
Fuel leakage underneath an exterior stabilized flame can lead to flame extinction and/or incomplete combustion. With the flame deep inside a microtube, however, much of the heat is lost due to conduction in the walls and subsequent radiation and convection to the environment. For a microcombustor application where outlet heat delivery is most important, it seems that having the flame stabilized just inside the end of the tube is optimal, as no fuel leakage can occur and the highest outlet temperature is at the end of tube.
At low velocities and slightly rich equivalence ratios, when the flame is stabilized inside the tube, significant acoustic emissions can be heard from the tubes. This sound tended to be of single frequency, and was loud enough to be heard through a closed door. Data acquired by the microphone was processed with a fast Fourier transform to obtain an amplitude vs. frequency plot. Typical frequencies obtained were about 1.8 kHz. Originally, we believed the emission was similar to that from an organ pipe, but experiments with different length tubes showed no frequency dependence on tube length. An investigation with the fused silica tube was performed to determine what the flame was doing inside the tube when sound was being emitted. The video showed that when the acoustic emission occurs, the flame appears to stretch out from a disk and fill a length of tube equal to many diameters, and the emitted frequency depended on the flame length. The flame appeared long in the video (captured at 30 fr/s), but this is probably due to the flame rapidly pulsing back and forth in the tube.
Regarding the numerical model, during this period we completed inclusion of the gas-phase reactions and added heat loss and axial conduction to the tube wall. The latter required a change in solution procedure from a marching scheme to one that accounts for downstream conditions (due to the axial conduction term). We have begun to run parametric cases with carbon monoxide and hydrogen to determine the effects of initial tube and gas temperature.
