Task Description:
NOTE (Ed., November 2019): Continuation of "Developing the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a NASA Standard Material Flammability Test," grant #NNX10AD96A, 1/1/2010 to 12/31/2014; and "Developing the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a NASA Standard Material Flammability Test (NNX14AC70A)," 2/1/2014 to 1/31/2017, with the same Principal Investigator Dr. Fletcher Miller.
The research proposed here is directed toward further development of a new apparatus to replace or augment the current NASA Standard 6001 Test 1 used to screen materials for space flight applications, and specifically the flight experiment that will allow us to obtain flame spread data on thick fuel. Test 1 is by far the most widely used test in the Standard, but does not take into account the influence of flow in a controlled manner, while flow has been shown to have a large (often dominant) effect on flame spread in microgravity. The ground-based apparatus described here, The Narrow Channel Apparatus, has been used by the author and collaborators for several years to study fundamental aspects of material flammability in reduced buoyancy conditions. Two new versions of the apparatus have been built that allow the study of flame spread on thick fuels under low pressure, high oxygen conditions such as being considered for new space craft, as well as allow examination of effects of apparatus orientation and sample width. Replacing the Test 1 apparatus with a Narrow Channel will allow for rapid, efficient testing, while also taking into account the low flows actually encountered in microgravity. By controlling the flow, it should be possible to approximate partial gravity conditions; although it is not a major part of this work, the possibility will be explored in the new vertical narrow channel.
This phase of the research continues to be devoted to ground-based testing while also preparing for the flight experiments. The work is conducted collaboratively at three institutions by investigators that have worked together for several years in this area (Dr. S. Olson at NASA Glenn Research Center and Dr. I. Wichman at Michigan State University are the other two investigators). The research at San Diego State University consists of five main tasks. The first task will be to make flame spread measurements in a Narrow Channel in low pressure, high oxygen (normoxic) conditions on thick Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) to match the planned flight test matrix. The second task involves extending our existing Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) and/or FLUENT model of flame spread in a Narrow Channel to evaluate the influence of heat loss to the upper wall as well as determine velocity and other field data not easily accessible experimentally. In this part of the research FDS will be run with Gpyro to determine the effect of solid-phase heat conduction. The model will also be run to predict differences between normal, partial, and microgravity including some runs with the fuel surface aligned with gravity. The third task will be to continue to work with NASA to develop and fly a flight experiment to test flame spread with forced flow over a thermally thick fuel in microgravity. In support of this effort, we may do some drop tower tests. There is a large data gap in this subject area, and true microgravity verifications tests are needed to prove the validity of the Narrow Channel Apparatus. After the flight, the data will be analyzed and compared to the model. The fourth task will be to perform Narrow Channel experiments on fuels/solids other than PMMA such as Nomex, Kapton, etc. in a higher oxygen, lower pressure environment. We have a selection of fuels based on discussions with NASA Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC). The last task was added new in 2020 and that was the development of a hybrid Test 1 that is conducted in a vertical orientation in a chamber, but with a low upward flow of the test atmosphere to purge combustion products and allow for a much small apparatus. This will provide comparison data to the Narrow Channel results as well as to tests run previously by NASA in the standard Test 1 apparatus.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research encompasses flame spread and material flammability in narrow channels or gaps. We use this geometry to simulate microgravity conditions. However, many fire situations involve flames in narrow gaps. TWA Flight 800, which crashed off the coast of Canada, was brought down by a small fire spreading through some narrow gaps in the walls and ceiling near the cockpit, for instance. Many building fires involve fire spread inside walls. Fires in computers likewise can occur between the printed circuit boards. Thus, information gained from experiments about how flames spread in various atmospheric conditions in narrow gaps is useful in areas well beyond spacecraft fire safety. The numerical model we are developing will be validated against our experiments and can also be used to study flame spread in these gaps.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2025
Task Progress:
GOALS AND OBJECTIVES
The major goals of this project are: • To develop the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a possible supplement or alternative to NASA Standard 6001B Test 1 (material ﬂammability). • To prepare for experiments on the International Space Station (ISS) in 2027 wherein thermally thick fuel slabs would be tested for the ﬁrst time in long-duration, true microgravity.
To accomplish these goals, a number of objectives are being pursued: • Conduct experiments in our existing Narrow Channel Apparatuses (NCA) on thermally thick and thin materials. Vary the oxygen, pressure, and opposed ﬂow velocities. • Measure the fuel surface temperature ahead of the ﬂame to determine the effect of conductive preheating by the ﬂame as it spreads. • Measure the gas-phase ﬂame temperatures for calibrating a numerical model. • Continue developing the numerical model of the ﬂame spread process in the NCA using computational ﬂuid dynamics. • Conduct tests in a modiﬁed chamber to produce NASA Test 1 results. • Make measurements in a replica of the ﬂow duct on the ISS to determine the effect of pressure on the fans and the ﬂow distribution. • Develop a new NCA that incorporates lessons learned from the ﬁrst generation NCAs.
ACCOMPLISHMENTS
During this reporting period we made progress on all of the objectives listed above. Experiments were conducted on 5 mm thick Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) in our NCA at oxygen levels from 21% (atmospheric) to 38.8 %, and pressures ranging from 8 psia to 14.7 psia. Flame extinction and ﬂame spread rate was quantiﬁed. The optical properties of PMMA were measured in a spectrometer to determine the emissivity so that an infrared camera could be used to measure the PMMA surface temperature during the spreading process; in addition, thermocouples were used for some tests and comparisons. Measurable preheating of over 20 mm was found, showing that for these very slow-moving ﬂames solid-phase conduction can play a role.
We also developed a technique for using thermocouples to measure the gas-phase temperature for the ﬁrst time. Results indicated that the computational model was overestimating the temperature so that we need to make modiﬁcations to that.
During this period signiﬁcant progress was made on further developing the numerical model in Ansys Fluent®. Our previous model treated only the gas-phase domain with the window and the fuel surface as boundary conditions. Now we have added both the fused silica window and the PMMA fuel to the model so that they play a role in distributing the heat from the ﬂame to environment and control the fuel vapor coming from the PMMA. Since our model is steady state (due to computer limitations), using an experimentally determined spread rate, we added motion to both the window and the fuel to simulate the movement of the ﬂame. This was shown to signiﬁcantly affect the thermal ﬁelds. We also added surface-to-surface radiation to the model to account for fuel radiative losses to the window.
Tests were conducted in our NASA Test 1 upward burning chamber. We modiﬁed the make-up gas inlet to occupy the entire bottom of the chamber (rather than small side ports) to allow a higher inlet mass ﬂow without increasing the inlet velocity. Tests were run using cotton samples at a variety of pressures and oxygen concentrations since those were the most readily available in the NASA Materials and Processes Technical Information System (MAPTIS) database to which we wanted to compare. We found that our results were more repeatable and consistent than those reported in the MAPTIS database, indicating that our modiﬁed Test 1 chamber (not only the NCA) may be of interest to NASA as well.
We made additional measurements on our Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) ﬂow duct replica using a mass-ﬂow controller as the gas inlet source (rather than the fans that we and SoFIE on the ISS use) and found discrepancies between the fan and the mass ﬂow controller. This could be due to a calibration issue, or due to a ﬂow maldistribution in the duct. To improve the calibration, we designed a new calibration nozzle, using a mix of analytical and numerical techniques, and are in the process of fabricating it. To test for a ﬂow maldistribution, we built a scanning system so we can measure across the entire duct cross-section once the sensor is calibrated.

Task Description:
NOTE (Ed., November 2019): Continuation of "Developing the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a NASA Standard Material Flammability Test," grant #NNX10AD96A, 1/1/2010 to 12/31/2014; and "Developing the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a NASA Standard Material Flammability Test (NNX14AC70A)," 2/1/2014 to 1/31/2017, with the same Principal Investigator Dr. Fletcher Miller.
The research proposed here is directed toward further development of a new apparatus to replace or augment the current NASA Standard 6001 Test 1 used to screen materials for space flight applications, and specifically the flight experiment that will allow us to obtain flame spread data on thick fuel. Test 1 is by far the most widely used test in the Standard, but does not take into account the influence of flow in a controlled manner, while flow has been shown to have a large (often dominant) effect on flame spread in microgravity. The ground-based apparatus described here, The Narrow Channel Apparatus, has been used by the author and collaborators for several years to study fundamental aspects of material flammability in reduced buoyancy conditions. Two new versions of the apparatus have been built that allow the study of flame spread on thick fuels under low pressure, high oxygen conditions such as being considered for new space craft, as well as allow examination of effects of apparatus orientation and sample width. Replacing the Test 1 apparatus with a Narrow Channel will allow for rapid, efficient testing, while also taking into account the low flows actually encountered in microgravity. By controlling the flow, it should be possible to approximate partial gravity conditions; although it is not a major part of this work, the possibility will be explored in the new vertical narrow channel.
This phase of the research continues to be devoted to ground-based testing while also preparing for the flight experiments. The work is conducted collaboratively at three institutions by investigators that have worked together for several years in this area (Dr. S. Olson at NASA Glenn Research Center and Dr. I. Wichman at Michigan State University are the other two investigators). The research at San Diego State University consists of five main tasks. The first task will be to make flame spread measurements in a Narrow Channel in low pressure, high oxygen (normoxic) conditions on thick Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) to match the planned flight test matrix. The second task involves extending our existing Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) and/or FLUENT model of flame spread in a Narrow Channel to evaluate the influence of heat loss to the upper wall as well as determine velocity and other field data not easily accessible experimentally. In this part of the research FDS will be run with Gpyro to determine the effect of solid-phase heat conduction. The model will also be run to predict differences between normal, partial, and microgravity including some runs with the fuel surface aligned with gravity. The third task will be to continue to work with NASA to develop and fly a flight experiment to test flame spread with forced flow over a thermally thick fuel in microgravity. In support of this effort, we may do some drop tower tests. There is a large data gap in this subject area, and true microgravity verifications tests are needed to prove the validity of the Narrow Channel Apparatus. After the flight, the data will be analyzed and compared to the model. The fourth task will be to perform Narrow Channel experiments on fuels/solids other than PMMA such as Nomex, Kapton, etc. in a higher oxygen, lower pressure environment. We have a selection of fuels based on discussions with NASA Kennedy Space Center (KSC) and NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC). The last task was added new in 2020 and that was the development of a hybrid Test 1 that is conducted in a vertical orientation in a chamber, but with a low upward flow of the test atmosphere to purge combustion products and allow for a much small apparatus. This will provide comparison data to the Narrow Channel results as well as to tests run previously by NASA in the standard Test 1 apparatus.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research encompasses flame spread and material flammability in narrow channels or gaps. We use this geometry to simulate microgravity conditions. However, many fire situations involve flames in narrow gaps. TWA Flight 800, which crashed off the coast of Canada, was brought down by a small fire spreading through some narrow gaps in the walls and ceiling near the cockpit, for instance. Many building fires involve fire spread inside walls. Fires in computers likewise can occur between the printed circuit boards. Thus, information gained from experiments about how flames spread in various atmospheric conditions in narrow gaps is useful in areas well beyond spacecraft fire safety. The numerical model we are developing will be validated against our experiments and can also be used to study flame spread in these gaps.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
This summary covers the period from August 2019 through August 2021. During this period there were three primary accomplishments. The first accomplishment was the continued development of a technique to use a commercial infrared camera to monitor the surface temperature of the combustible material while it was burning. A Master’s student and an undergraduate student worked on this together. They made careful measurements with both the camera and a thermocouple embedded in the surface that accurately measures temperature at a point to calibrate video images acquired by the camera from which the entire time-temperature history of the burning material could be determined. This allows us to understand the extent and mechanism of preheating of the material by the flame as might occur in microgravity. From these measurements we can predict the flame spread rate and use that in models that assess the danger of fire on board spacecraft. This activity was cut short in mid-Spring of 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic when we had to stop on-site work in the laboratory.
The second accomplishment was the initiation of a computational model of a flame on a surface burning in a low-speed airflow, similar to the ventilation flows on spacecraft. We had previously been using the Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) software written by the National Institute for Standards and Technology for this, but in this period we made the switch to FLUENT, a commercial software code. This package is general-purpose heat transfer and fluid flow software. FLUENT has not to our knowledge been used previously for simulating flames on solid materials, but it offers increased execution speed and can better simulate plastics that burn away leaving gaps or valleys in the burning surface.
We first created the geometry of our Narrow Channel experimental apparatus in the software and then tried cases of fuel/air mixing without combustion and finally some with combustion and successfully achieved a simulated flame stabilized above the surface. To represent the “valley” created when material burns away, we used experimental data from our partner at Michigan State University that measured the depth of the valley as a function of air velocity. Much of the work in this period has been devoted to obtaining the proper material and combustion properties for the simulations, and running test cases to be sure the results are correct and consistent. This activity has been supported by one graduate student since 2019, and joined by a second one starting in the spring of 2021. Since we can conduct these simulations remotely, this work has not been appreciably affected by COVID-19.
The third activity has been the design and construction of a variation of the standard NASA Test 1 apparatus. This was conducted by a team of five undergraduates who took this on for their Senior Design project for the calendar year 2020. We wanted a NASA Test 1 apparatus for our own use to provide comparison data to what we obtain from our own Narrow Channel Apparatus, which we believe is a more representative test for microgravity conditions. The standard NASA test involves a large pressure/vacuum tank that we did not have access to, so we designed a system that uses a much smaller tank and provides a low, make-up air flow that brings fresh oxygen to the flame while sweeping away combustion products. The test is still run in the vertical configuration like the NASA test, and it will be useful to compare results from this new, low-flow test to the NASA results that rely on buoyancy entirely. This may be a more efficient way to run the test since it avoids the long period needed to evacuate the refill in the large chamber. The new apparatus was mostly completed by the end of 2020, but due to COVID-19 restrictions we have not been able to test it yet in the laboratory.

Task Description:
This research will study flame spread over flammable solid materials such as plastic, paper, cloth, and hair, using a new apparatus designed to simulate microgravity flow conditions on Earth. We designed and built two new Narrow Channel Apparatuses at San Diego State, and one at Michigan State, that control environmental variables such as flow velocity, gas pressure, and oxygen concentration to reproduce space craft atmospheres. To accompany the experiments, we are developing a numerical model so that we can determine certain quantities such as heat loss to the channel ceiling that are difficult to measure.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2015
Task Progress:
[Ed. note October 2016: compiled from PI's final technical report]
This research objective was to examine the flame spread in a Couette channel and determine if it’s an adequate apparatus to simulate microgravity in the study of flame spread. This research was divided into two sections, the first dealing with cold flow in pure Couette channel, and the second covering combustion in a linear velocity profile. Data for the first section is summarized below.
It was apparent that a realistic finite length channel does not present us with a fully developed laminar flow profile that is exactly linear but is in fact slightly curved. This agrees well with other research done using Couette channels. The cause of this is the pressure differential along the entrance of the channel created by the top moving plate suction force on the fluid outside the channel as well as the pressure along the exit of the channel created by the flow leaving. The curviness of the profile is a function of Reynolds number and the length/height ratio of the channel.
The pattern observed and the effect of the channel’s length, plate velocity and gap height was examined. As the channel gets longer the velocity profile becomes more linear and less curved, while the increase in the height of the channel reduces the linearity of the u-velocity profile. For the one moving top plate case, the higher the plate velocity the more curved the fully developed u-velocity profile becomes. The two moving plate, the u-velocity profile acts in a manner similar to a Hagen-Poiseuille channel with an adverse pressure differential along the channel. This matched the pattern expected from the analytical fully developed laminar u-velocity profile that was also derived during this research.
The h, L and U0 were varied in such a manner to keep the h/L ratio and Re the same, the u-velocity and the pressure, did not change, which is what was expected. Only one ratio and one Reynolds number was utilized due to time restrictions. The entrance length was also examined and a relationship between it and the Reynolds number was determined for both the case at which only the top plate is moving and the case at which both top and bottom plates are moving at the same velocity. It was compared to the HP entrance length to find that.
The second part of this study was the flame spread in a Couette channel. The channel utilized by Hung was the baseline of the model. The gap height was kept constant while varying the top plate velocity which showed a pattern that is similar for both 1g and 0g as well as similar to the experimental results. For the larger gap heights utilized, the flame at 0g was longer and higher than that of the 1g. This is due to the fact that in the 0g flame, the fuel pyrolyzed in front of the flame remains close to the surface allowing the 0g to spread faster before burning all the fuel behind it, which will diffuse upward until it meets the oxygen and combusts creating a longer and higher flame. However, increasing the height will reduce the oxygen gradient and hence slows down and shrinks the flame at 0g while for the 1g flame buoyancy takes over and the flame spread levels off and the flame height increases.
Note that this work continues under NASA Cooperative Agreement NNX14AC70A, “Developing the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a NASA Standard Material Flammability Test,” which began in January 2014 with Dr. Fletcher Miller continuing as Principal Investigator.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2014
Task Progress:
The SDSU and MSU Narrow Channel Apparatuses were used to recreate spacecraft atmospheric conditions and study the burning of plastic samples subject to various pressures, oxygen levels, and flow velocities. As shown previously, the Narrow Channel also reduces the effect of gravity and simulates microgravity conditions by eliminating the tendency of hot air to rise. The samples burned were 2 inches wide and up to 10 inches long, with thicknesses varying from .002 inches to 3/8”.
A new filtering system was added to the back of the Narrow Channel Apparatus to remove particulate so that additional sensors could be added. These include CO and CO2 sensors to measure the product gases that are evolved in the simulated microgravity conditions. In addition, a new way to measure the surface temperature of the fuel material using an embedded thermocouple was developed.
Numerical modeling of the flow and combustion process was conducted for the first time using the Fire Dynamic Simulator software. A two-dimensional domain was created to model the Narrow Channel. Two channels were modeled, one with a moving top (a Couette Channel) and one with the flow being driven by pressure differences. Both of these channels have been built and tested experimentally. Flame spread rate and temperature were calculated using the software for a variety of conditions that matched some of the experiments. The numerical model takes over a week to run in most cases, so that simulating many cases is time consuming.
The experimental tests of the thin plastics in the Narrow Channel Apparatus showed good agreement with actual microgravity tests conducted in Japan and at NASA Glenn Research Center. Flame spread rates increased with oxygen level and with flow velocity up to about 15 cm/s. Both the 21% and 30% oxygen levels showed peaks, after which the flame spread rate fell as the flow velocity was turned up higher. The 50% oxygen flames kept spreading faster as the flow was increased. The agreement between the simulated and actual microgravity was very encouraging, indicating that this is a good test method for thin fuels.
The effect of channel height was also explored. The data show that for gap heights above about 14 mm, the flame spread rate is not too dependent on gap height. However, other tests show that the gap needs to be about 10 mm or less or buoyancy starts to influence the results. For that reason, a gap height of 10 mm was used for these tests, even though the flame does experience some heat loss to the top of the channel.
Experimental data from the thick fuel tests showed a strong variation with flow velocity, much more than for the thin fuels. A strong peak was reached about 20 cm/s. These data were corroborated by tests in the MSU Narrow Channel Apparatus as well. Tests there were also conducted with black and clear plastic to determine the difference.
Limited numerical model results were obtained due to the time it takes for each run. However, for those tests that were completed, the numerical model shows the same trends with flow velocity, but the flame spread rate is much higher (three or more times) than has been measured experimentally. The reason for that discrepancy is under investigation.

Task Description:
This research will study flame spread over flammable solid materials such as plastic, paper, cloth, and hair, using a new apparatus designed to simulate microgravity flow conditions on earth. We designed and built two new Narrow Channel Apparatuses at San Diego State, and one at Michigan State, that control environmental variables such as flow velocity, gas pressure, and oxygen concentration to reproduce space craft atmospheres. Additionally, the Narrow Channel suppresses buoyant flow by having a closely spaced ceiling on the channel, so that flow conditions closely resemble those found on space craft. The objective of the research is to prove the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a viable test method for opposed flow material flammability testing. This will allow NASA to screen materials in more realistic conditions than does the current NASA test which makes no account of microgravity. The experimental research consists of test wherein we ignite various solids in the channels and measure how fast the flame spreads in various conditions. To accompany the experiments, we are developing a numerical model so that we can determine certain quantities such as heat loss to the channel ceiling that are difficult to measure.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research encompasses flame spread and material flammability in narrow channels or gaps. We use this geometry to simulate microgravity conditions. However, many fire situations involve flames in narrow gaps. TWA Flight 800, which crashed off the coast of Canada, was brought down by a small fire spreading through some narrow gaps in the walls and ceiling near the cockpit, for instance. Many building fires involve fire spread inside walls. Fires in computers likewise can occur between the printed circuit boards. Thus, information gained from experiments about how flames spread in various atmospheric conditions in narrow gaps is useful in areas well beyond spacecraft fire safety. The numerical model we are developing will be validated against our experiments and can also be used to study flame spread in these gaps.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2012
Task Progress:
During the first year of this grant we designed and constructed three apparatuses to study how flames spread in narrow channels under varying atmospheric conditions. The fuels planned in the tests are those that would be of interest to NASA such as paper, plastic, cloth, and hair, so that material flammability can be determined. These narrow channels, due to their ability to restrict hot air rising, simulate microgravity conditions on spacecraft where heat also does not "rise," since there is no "up" in microgravity. The three channels are all different to allow different effects to be tested.
The first, the San Diego State University Narrow Channel Apparatus (SDSU NCA), allows sample materials 2 inches wide by up to 18 inches long to be burned. The channel is capable of being operated at low pressure up to 2 times atmospheric pressure and with oxygen concentrations from 85% to 21% (like on earth) to simulate different spacecraft atmospheres. An air flow over the sample simulates the spacecraft ventilation system. The airflow has a character like that found in a small gap, and therefore does not completely reproduce the flow in an open spacecraft cabin.
The second channel at SDSU can test samples the same size, but due to a moving top on the channel, it creates a flow much more like an open cabin flow that might exist in a space craft fire. It cannot, however, recreate pressure conditions on space craft. This is the first channel of its kind in the world, and it is still undergoing some trial tests.
The third channel, at Michigan State, is a much wider channel than the others so that it can test large samples up to 12 inches wide. It is not capable of reduced pressure, but can vary the flow velocity and oxygen level.
All three channels can have a variable gap height and flow velocity, and each is outfitted with a camera to record videos of the flame to determine how fast it spreads. The gap height is defined as the distance between the fuel and wall, and is approximately 1/4 inch.
During the second year of the study, velocity measurements have been made in each channel to calibrate them. Then, flame spread tests have been conducted using various paper fuels similar to those used by other investigators to see the effect of pressure, oxygen level, and flow velocity for a given gap height. Many of the conditions tested were obtained for the first time and new data were recorded. These data give a much clearer overview of flame spread in different conditions than had been available before.
Separately from the efforts above, the original Narrow Channel at NASA was used to test the effect of gap height and an optimized height was found that was used in the other tests. Also, a series of tests were conducted with trioxane as the fuel, since that was a possible fuel for microgravity tests on the International Space Station. These were the first flame spread tests known to be conducted over trioxane.

Task Description:
We plan to propose an extensive ground-based test program leading to a possible flight experiment to study flame spread over wax-impregnated inert porous media that simulates solid fuel combustion. The work will study fundamental flame spread and extinction but also be geared toward proving the narrow channel apparatus as a viable test method for opposed flow material flammability testing in microgravity. The work will also develop techniques, based on previous experience with liquid pool filling in microgravity, to provides a mechanism to replace the "solid" fuel in a space experiment without opening the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) chamber aboard the International Space Station. Modified Spread Across Liquids (SAL) flame spread hardware with a temperature controlled tray will be used to establish initial conditions at sub-flash temperatures for faster spread in the Zero Gravity Research Facility testing, and the Narrow Channel apparatus will be used in normal gravity testing. Normoxic atmospheres will be tested along with independent variation of oxygen, pressure, initial fuel temperature, and opposed flow velocity. The fuel will be thick enough to be considered thermally thick, and will only be burning on one side. A model of the flame spread and extinction will be based on the model developed for the SAL experiment by Prof. Sirignano at UCI (3D, transient) but we will modify it to better describe the wax fuel and inert porous media.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
[Ed. note: compiled from PI's final progress report submitted August 2017]
The SDSU NCA has been shown to successfully simulate microgravity for not only thin cellulose fuels, but also for thin Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) sheets at 1 atm pressure if the proper gap height is chosen. Tests completed in the SDSU NCA closely compare to actual microgravity conditions seen in drop tower experiments under otherwise the same conditions. Three oxygen mole fractions were tested where the NCA corresponded with true microgravity testing. Flame spread rate was shown to be extremely sensitive to oxygen concentration as experiments run at 50% O2 were many times faster than samples burned at 21% O2. These results provide further verification that the SDSU NCA is a viable option to complement or replace NASA’s Test 1 for material flammability testing.
While gap height experiments have shown 18 mm and 6 mm gaps to be unfit for the SDSU NCA, it is unclear what gap height produces the best compromise in buoyancy suppression and heat loss to the top and bottom plates of the NCA. Sidebotham suggests a full gap height of 10-12 mm for Whatman 44 filter paper using side view image analysis and quantitative methods. Future planned experiments will determine the best gap height for thermally thin PMMA in the NCA.
The SDSU NCA has been shown to match the thick PMMA data of the Michigan State University Narrow Channel Apparatus very well at an oxygen concentration of 21 percent with the minor differences being attributed to the false bottom material and the PMMA thickness. Only one true microgravity test was available for comparison. The flame spread velocity found using the SDSU Narrow Channel Apparatus fell close to the true microgravity data point near the lower flame extinction limit.
Larger differences in flame spread velocity were found at the extremes of the range tested (11 cm/s and 25 cm/s). At low opposed flow velocities the flame struggles to move forward and often shrinks away from the side walls making it difficult to get accurate measurements. Minor flaws in flow (caused by lifting and warping of the fuel bed) likely affect the flame spread rate more as gas velocity increases creating less precise results at higher speeds. Potential causes for scatter include performing a test while the channel is still warm from the previous test, effects from the aluminum tape used to hold down the sample, effects from the fuel lifting, or effects from the igniter wire being in different areas of the flow.
At 21 percent oxygen concentration the flame spread rate rises, reaches a peak, and then begins to once again drop off. This is expected as the flame experiences the three different opposed flow regimes. First, speeding up through the oxygen transport limited regime, followed by a more steady gas phase conduction limited region, and finally slowing in the residence time limited regime on its way to flame blow-off. This shows there is an optimal opposed velocity that maximizes the flame spread rate, or is the most hazardous fire condition. At higher oxygen concentrations the peak flame spread velocity is thought to be out of the range of the tested opposed flow velocity.
Oxygen concentration has the largest effect on flame spread rate; however, it has little effect on flame length. Because of this a higher oxygen concentration means a lower residence time. As the residence time increases, the depth of pyrolysis increases and less soot is created, resulting in a bluer flame.
In exploring the effect of 2-D conduction we found Fire Dynamics Simulator coupled with Gpyro does model the combustion of polymethyl methacrylate in a narrow channel well. It is shown that Gpyro models multidimensional conduction within solids well, and that it takes mass that is burned away into consideration.
In all 20 tests were done on the International Space Station and their results categorized according to the way the fuel sample was burnt, i.e., one sided or two sided. Oxygen concentration study was done for the experiments. From the results of the tests we observed width effects wherein for the same thickness the wider fuels (2 cm wide) showed a higher spread rate than the narrower fuels (1 cm wide). The 2 cm wide fuels spread faster by 0.045 mm/s on average. Also it was observed that the two sided burns spread faster than the one sided burns by 0.0275 mm/s on average. Agreement with results from the Narrow Channel apparatus was reasonable.
For the flame spread in vertical narrow channels, the spread rate monotonically decreased when convection was mixed but not when convection was natural. Flame extinction in a natural convection setting was mostly due to quenching under lunar gravity and perhaps a combination of blow-off and quenching under normal gravity. The vertical velocity values were sufficient to confirm that blow-off was partially responsible for flame extinction under normal gravity. The amount of heat lost to the atmosphere is known, but the cause of heat loss is still not certain. Rendering the right wall of the channel adiabatic accelerated the spread rate and prolonged combustion before imminent extinction.

Task Description:
NOTE (Ed., January 2014): Continuation of "Developing the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a NASA Standard Material Flammability Test", grant # NNX10AD96A with the same Principal Investigator.
This research will study flame spread over flammable solid materials such as plastic, paper, cloth, and hair, using a new apparatus designed to simulate microgravity flow conditions on earth. We designed and built two new Narrow Channel Apparatuses at San Diego State, and one at Michigan State, that control environmental variables such as flow velocity, gas pressure, and oxygen concentration to reproduce space craft atmospheres. Additionally, the Narrow Channel suppresses buoyant flow by having a closely spaced ceiling on the channel, so that flow conditions closely resemble those found on space craft. The objective of the research is to prove the Narrow Channel Apparatus as a viable test method for opposed flow material flammability testing. This will allow NASA to screen materials in more realistic conditions than does the current NASA test which makes no account of microgravity. The experimental research consists of test wherein we ignite various solids in the channels and measure how fast the flame spreads in various conditions. To accompany the experiments, we are developing a numerical model so that we can determine certain quantities such as heat loss to the channel ceiling that are difficult to measure.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our research encompasses flame spread and material flammability in narrow channels or gaps. We use this geometry to simulate microgravity conditions. However, many fire situations involve flames in narrow gaps. TWA Flight 800, which crashed off the coast of Canada, was brought down by a small fire spreading through some narrow gaps in the walls and ceiling near the cockpit, for instance. Many building fires involve fire spread inside walls. Fires in computers likewise can occur between the printed circuit boards. Thus, information gained form experiments about how flames spread in various atmospheric conditions in narrow gaps is useful in areas well beyond spacecraft fire safety. The numerical model we are developing will be validated against our experiments and can also be used to study flame spread in these gaps.

Task Description: The research will investigate the effect of an electric field on the dynamics of self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) waves and the effect of the field on phase formation and structure evolution in SHS. The planned work includes both terrestrial and reduced gravity experiments. The latter will be carried out in parabolic flights and in drop towers. The parabolic flight experiments will use existing facilities developed by Guigne International, Ltd. in NASA's KC-135 aircraft. Modifications were done to accommodate the requirements for application of an electric field application as well as instrumentation for temperature measurements and imaging. Drop tower experiments will be carried out in the NASA Glenn Research Center 2.2 s Drop Tower, and additional drop tower experiments will be carried out in Japan by one of the collaborating scientists. The research will employ systems that produce varied amounts of liquid. For example, the systems Si + C or Ti + Al allow investigation of the case where one reactant melts and the other does not, the system Ta + C allows investigation of a system where neither the reactants not the products melt, and the system FeAl allows investigation of the case where both reactants and products melt. These systems are expected to respond to the gravity level in different ways, e.g., through liquid transport effects. It is also planned that quenching experiments will be performed. This will be accomplished by turning off the electric field during the combustion process. The removal of the field will cause the deflagration wave to quench under certain conditions, essentially freezing the structure of the wave. Wave structure will be analyzed using XRD, SEM and EPMA. We plan to quantify heat losses from samples using several techniques. We will also pursue computational and asymptotic modeling efforts. The computational efforts involve extending previous numerical models to account for phenomena such as melting, capillary flows, buoyant flows and three spatial dimensions. Asymptotic studies will be concerned with determining influences of electric fields on stability and extinction of field-assisted SHS waves, taking into account capillary transport of liquids as well as local variations in surface tension and contact angles from thermal or electrical effects. This research program is focused on studying self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) under reduced gravity conditions. The broad objective of this research program is to understand the role of an electric field in SHS reactions under conditions where gravity-related effects are suppressed. The research will allow increased understanding of fundamental aspects of field-assisted SHS processes as well as synthesis of materials that cannot be formed in normal gravity. For example, the electric field has been shown to influence the nature of the product, the composition of phases in a composite, and the homogeneity (elemental distribution) in solid solutions. Furthermore, the field can influence other important SHS-related phenomena including capillary flow, mass-transport in porous media, and Marangoni flows. These phenomena are influenced by gravity in conventional SHS processes (i.e., without electric fields). As a result the influence of the field on SHS under reduced gravity is expected to be different than under normal gravity. It is also known that heat loss rates from samples, which can depend significantly on gravity, can influence final products in SHS. This research will provide new information on the effects of gravity on self-propagating high-temperature combustion synthesis with applied electric fields. The research will increase understanding of the effects of buoyancy, segregation, percolation and may potentially lead to new materials that cannot be formed under normal gravity conditions.

Task Progress:
The reactive settling in the system Al-W was investigated under different gravitational conditions and under the influence of an electric field. Compacted powder mixtures of 0.1W + 1.0 Al were reacted inside chemical ovens under conditions of 0 g (low gravity), 0.16 g (lunar gravity), 1.0 g (terrestrial gravity), and 1.8 g (high gravity). The chemical ovens selected were Nb + 2Si and Ti + Al which provided different temperatures. The elements reacted partially to form WAl4 under 0, 0.16, and 1.8 g conditions aboard NASA KC-135 plane. The effect of gravity on the microstructural distribution of the phases WAl4 and unreacted W and Al was investigated. In the 0 g case the unreacted W was randomly distributed throughout the sample and under 0.16 g partial settling of the W particles was observed. When the reaction was carried out at 1 g, the settling of W particles is virtually total. Similar microstructural distribution was observed in the case of 1.8 g. Settling of the WAl4 intermetallic phase was not observed even at the highest gravity condition. Moreover, the applied electric current did not affect the settling or the distribution of W grains; similar microstructures were found for each gravity condition with and without the electric current. The settling pattern showed no dependence on the direction of the combustion wave; bottom and top ignition samples exhibited similar microstructures. The reactive settling process was carried out under the influence of an electric field. It was seen that the field had no discernable effect on the resulting microstructure.
Furthermore in the Al-W system, the dissolution and precipitation was investigated. Once the reaction temperatures are reached, W will dissolve into liquid Al. In turn, WAl4 precipitates were found to form upon cooling of the sample. The precipitates grew larger with increasing gravity, due to the absence of unreacted W particles in 0.16, 1, and 1.8 g samples. Therefore gravity has been shown to affect the precipitate size indirectly. Electric current showed little effect on the precipitate length in terrestrial gravity. On the other hand, in microgravity, samples reacted at 200A and 350A showed about 40% and 36% increases in precipitate size, respectively. This is believed to be due to the increased availability of dissolved W in the 200A and 350A samples and due to the possibility of enhanced mass transport by electric current. Neither electric current nor gravity was found to affect the alignment, directionality, and distribution of the intermetallic phase. It was found that increasing gravity resulted in an increase in the dissolution of W, resulting in the formation of higher amounts of WAl4. This is believed to be due to an increase in dissolution rates created by the stirring effect of the settling motion of the unreacted W particles. Finally, increasing electric current was observed to enhance the W dissolution rate into liquid Al. Although the chemical oven combustion waves moved towards the top (warmer and less dense liquid at the bottom), unstable convection is shown to be absent even at the highest gravity condition.
In addition to the Al-W system, the possibility of settling was investigated in terms of density differences between the solid and the liquid phase, solubility and dissolution rate (temperature), and initial solid concentration for Ta, Ti and Ni in liquid Al. Although settling in isothermal systems is a well-understood phenomenon, it is quite difficult per above-mentioned parameters in the dynamic conditions present in SHS reactions. As previously mentioned in the W-Al system settling was only observed at high reaction temperatures when the Nb + 2Si chemical oven was used. At low temperatures the formation of the intermetallic phase (WAl4) was observed to prevent settling. On the other hand, for Ta and Ti settling was only observed at low reaction temperatures when the Ti + Al chemical oven was used. At high temperatures total dissolution was observed for Ta and Ti. Settling of Ti was found to depend on the grain size (Ti) due to the lower density differences between Ti and liquid Al. Total dissolution was the case for Ni even at the lowest temperature experimented. Only the intermetallic precipitates in the Ta-Al system showed settling behavior. The reactive settling behavior can be explained with the corresponding solubilities at different temperatures.
Reactive capillary infiltration experiments were performed in porous samples inside of thin graphite foil capsules, using the chemical oven technique. The capsules consisted of a single layer of Al and a single layer of Ni or Ti. In order to investigate the gravitational effects of the movement of the liquid, the Al was placed on the bottom or the top of the Ni or Ti. Experiments were performed in 0 and 1 g with and without electric current (0 and 350 A). Capillary infiltration distances were measured for the experiments under 0 A and were found to be larger under 1 g conditions for all four experimental cases. However, the distance of infiltration of the Al into the Ti was greater than into the Ni. This is contradictory to equilibrium contact angles reported in the literature. On the other hand, SHS reactions are, for the most part, under non-equilibrium conditions therefore such values should be considered. Experiments under 350 A showed complete infiltration of the liquid Al into the Ni or Ti for both 0 and 1 g.

The first flight campaign (KC-135) for the Microgravity Field Activated Combustion Synthesis (MFACS) experiments was completed with success on November 2003 at Johnson Space Center, Houston.After analysis it was found that the experimental temperatures and velocities in the Ti + Al system reached higher values under 1-g conditions compared to the 0-g conditions. Reaction temperatures and wave velocities increased in both cases with increasing currents applied, as expected. For this system it was found that the lowest current applied for the formation of stable combustion wave (threshold current) was higher during reduced gravity conditions, possibly affected by the decrease in the preheating of the sample due to the reduction of gravity driven convection effects. Average velocities were measured for the completed reactions in both 1-g and 0-g at 250A. It was found that the experiments in 1-g (1.92 ± 0.17 mm/s; ± standard deviation, s) had faster average velocities than the 0-g experiments (1.67 ± 0.06 mm/s; ± s).The Ti + 3 Al system was investigated to be able to understand the effects of different amounts of liquid involved in the reaction, with 3 times the aluminum compared to the Ti + Al system. Up until about 325A (threshold), terrestrial experiments displayed temperatures in excess of 375°C compared to reduced gravity experiments. A switch in this behavior was observed where the reduced gravity experiments showed a steep temperature increase up to about 600°C at 325A applied. After that, With increasing applied currents, the reduced gravity experiments had higher reaction temperatures up to highest current used in this study (550A). Microstructural evolution of the Ti + Al and Ti + 3Al systems have been investigated using SEM analysis and reaction sequences and zones have been identified in the quenched samples in both 1-g and 0-g.After ongoing analysis of the terrestrial and reduced gravity experiments it was hypothesized that increased percentage of the liquid phase compared to the solid phase would attenuate the effects of gravity or other phenomena at the absence of gravity. Problems with sample integrity and retaining constant contact with the electrodes simply limits the implementation of increased liquid phase. To avoid these factors, smaller samples that can contain up to 100% liquid were inserted into the center of a structurally stable green pellets. The exterior pellet is considered a chemical oven because it provides heat to the smaller insert by means of a combustion wave assisted by the electric current. Inserts composed of a heavy metal (W, Ta, TaC and Ti) and a low-density liquid (Al) investigated settling effects, which were mixed and pressed to full density. Percolation effects were studied by using inserts that consisted of loose powders of a metal (Ni and Ti) and liquid (Al). The removal of the field will cause the deflagration wave to quench under certain conditions, essentially freezing the structure of the wave. Wave structure will be analyzed using XRD, SEM and EPMA. We plan to quantify heat losses from samples using several techniques. We will also pursue computational and asymptotic modeling efforts. The computational efforts involve extending previous numerical models to account for phenomena such as melting, capillary flows, buoyant flows and three spatial dimensions. Asymptotic studies will be concerned with determining influences of electric fields on stability and extinction of field-assisted SHS waves, taking into account capillary transport of liquids as well as local variations in surface tension and contact angles from thermal or electrical effects. This research program is focused on studying self-propagating high-temperature synthesis (SHS) under reduced gravity conditions. The broad objective of this research program is to understand the role of an electric field in SHS reactions under conditions where gravity-related effects are suppressed. The research will allow increased understanding of fundamental aspects of field-assisted SHS processes as well as synthesis of materials that cannot be formed in normal gravity. For example, the electric field has been shown to influence the nature of the product, the composition of phases in a composite, and the homogeneity (elemental distribution) in solid solutions. Furthermore, the field can influence other important SHS-related phenomena including capillary flow, mass-transport in porous media, and Marangoni flows. These phenomena are influenced by gravity in conventional SHS processes (i.e., without electric fields). As a result the influence of the field on SHS under reduced gravity is expected to be different than under normal gravity. It is also known that heat loss rates from samples, which can depend significantly on gravity, can influence final products in SHS. This research will provide new information on the effects of gravity on self-propagating high-temperature combustion synthesis with applied electric fields. The research will increase understanding of the effects of buoyancy, segregation, percolation and may potentially lead to new materials that cannot be formed under normal gravity conditions.

Task Description:
The von Karman swirling flows are generated by spinning a fuel disk at different speeds. This geometry provides a unique way of establishing a desired stretch rate from very low to very high values. Also, the governing equation for this geometry reduces to an one-dimensional problem making it possible to include complex chemical and transport mechanisms. Also, close to the extinction boundaries the diffusion flame breaks symmetry and forms complex dynamic patterns some of which are similar to the patterns observed in biological and chemical systems. We examine pattern formation along the flammability boundaries using a gas-fueled, spinning porous-disk burner. Also, theoretical descriptions of these edge-flames are developed using activation energy asymptotic models.
The objective of this work is to investigate, both experimentally and theoretically, the effect of stretch on diffusion flames embedded in swirling flows. Theoretical models using asymptotic techniques (activation energy and rate ratio asymptotics) will be developed to interpret the experimental observations. Both the experiments and the theoretical models will be focused on the flammability boundaries in the low stretch and high stretch regimes. We have also discovered the existence of pattern formation in diffusion flames in von Karman swirling flows close to the extinction boundaries that exhibit many similarities to the patterns observed in biological systems. One of our objectives to understand the commonalities between these phenomena.
The motivation for this study comes from the need to understand material flammability conditions in the slow convective environments commonly encountered in spacecraft environments. Here, flames that would normally extinguish on earth may be sustained. It is also hoped that the results obtained from studies of laminar-flame extinction may be applied for predictions in turbulent situations through estimates of strain rates in turbulent fields.
Also, the pattern formation phenomena in diffusion flames was discovered during our previous NASA funded grant period. In the current study we further investigate this phenomena using a newly designed gas-fueled, spinning-disk burner. The rotating spiral flames observed in these experiments mimic electrical pulse propagation in heart tissues and exhibit similar dynamics. We hope to model these flame dynamics and try to identify the underlying commonalities behind these phenomena.

Task Description:
NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is the major method used to evaluate flammability of materials intended for use in habitable environments of U.S. spacecraft. The method is an upward flame propagation test initiated in a stagnant environment and using a well-defined igniter flame at the bottom of a vertically mounted sample. A material passes this test if the vertical burn length is less than 15.2 cm (6 inches) and there is no evidence of transfer of burning debris. The test is conducted in the most severe flaming combustion environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft, currently 30% oxygen at 10.2 pounds per square inch absolute (psia).
Recent research has shown that current normal gravity materials flammability tests do not correlate with flammability in ventilated, micro-, or reduced-gravity conditions. The materials selection for spacecraft is based on the assumption of commonality between ground test flammability results and spacecraft environments, which does not appear to be valid. To better understand the actual normal gravity flammability limits, a modified Test 1 protocol has been proposed that, as an alternative to qualifying materials as pass/fail in the worst-expected environments, measures the actual upward flammability limit (akin to the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI)) for the material so that a more accurate assessment of the margin of safety of the material in the real use environment can be made. The method allows the option of selecting better or best materials based on the margin of safety, as opposed to what would be considered just "passing" from a flammability point of view.
A research program is underway to correlate normal gravity flammability test data with data under ventilated reduced gravity or microgravity conditions. The program will determine materials suitability for microgravity and reduced gravity testing by evaluating oxygen concentration thresholds under various total pressures in normal gravity tests and in spacecraft-specific environments (ventilated microgravity or reduced partial gravity). The normal gravity data will be correlated with flammability data in microgravity environments and the safety factors involved when selecting spacecraft materials based on normal gravity testing will be evaluated.
Rigorous correlations between ground test flammability data and data in ventilated spacecraft environments would allow selection of materials with increased fire resistance, and thus decrease the fire risk in space systems. The operational flexibility will also increase since the safety factors will be assessable.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The identification of the fundamental limit in microgravity and its comparison with the normal gravity flammability limit will help us understand flammability in different configurations on Earth. It will help us understand the impact of buoyant flow on flammability, and help in evaluating flammability on the Moon or Mars.
It will improve the safety of astronauts during exploration missions so the mission can successfully be completed and the crew can return safely to Earth.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2023
Task Progress:
We completed a series of concurrent rod blowoff tests at variable gravity levels in the centrifuge drop vehicle in the Zero Gravity Research Facility. Testing was conducted with the 0.318 cm radius polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) rods in the 8.2 pounds per square inch absolute (psia) lunar exploration vehicle pressure. The flame stagnation region does not seem to be strongly affected by Coriolis forces.
The results to date of the experiment compare very well with the blowoff branch of the Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) flammability boundary we published in Combustion and Flame in 2017 (Olson S, Ferkul P. "Microgravity flammability boundary for PMMA rods in axial stagnation flow: Experimental results and energy balance analyses." Combustion and Flame. 2017 Jun;180:217-29). The buoyant flow is estimated using Ub = 25 (g/gEarth)^1/2 so the 1g (Earth g) buoyant flow is 25 cm/s for the stagnation geometry. The boundary is just slightly shifted down from the BASS-II boundary. The close alignment of the two boundaries indicates that the square root scaling appears to be valid. The stable flame at lunar g level and 13.8% O2 is very close to the minimum in the BASS-II flammability boundary. This would seem to support prior research which found materials are more flammable on the Moon than on Mars or the Earth. The results were presented at the American Society for Gravitational and Space Research (ASGSR) and a paper of the results is planned.
The Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) flight flow sensor was found to be unreliable due to damage it apparently sustained during high pressure Fuel Oxidizer Management Assembly (FOMA) calibrations. A ground flow sensor was fast-tracked to be flight qualified and calibrated. The Combustion Tunnel drop rig was used to calibrate the flow sensor against a known forced flow velocity in normal gravity. A preliminary analysis of the data has been conducted with additional analysis underway after receiving updated calibration data for the critical flow orifices used in the testing.

Task Description:
NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is the major method used to evaluate flammability of materials intended for use in habitable environments of U.S. spacecraft. The method is an upward flame propagation test initiated in a stagnant environment and using a well-defined igniter flame at the bottom of a vertically mounted sample. A material passes this test if the vertical burn length is less than 15.2 cm (6 inches) and there is no evidence of transfer of burning debris. The test is conducted in the most severe flaming combustion environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft, currently 30% oxygen at 10.2 pounds per square inch absolute (psia).
Recent research has shown that current normal gravity materials flammability tests do not correlate with flammability in ventilated, micro-, or reduced-gravity conditions. The materials selection for spacecraft is based on the assumption of commonality between ground test flammability results and spacecraft environments, which does not appear to be valid. To better understand the actual normal gravity flammability limits, a modified Test 1 protocol has been proposed that, as an alternative to qualifying materials as pass/fail in the worst-expected environments, measures the actual upward flammability limit (akin to the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI)) for the material so that a more accurate assessment of the margin of safety of the material in the real use environment can be made. The method allows the option of selecting better or best materials based on the margin of safety, as opposed to what would be considered just "passing" from a flammability point of view.
A research program is underway to correlate normal gravity flammability test data with data under ventilated reduced gravity or microgravity conditions. The program will determine materials suitability for microgravity and reduced gravity testing by evaluating oxygen concentration thresholds under various total pressures in normal gravity tests and in spacecraft-specific environments (ventilated microgravity or reduced partial gravity). The normal gravity data will be correlated with flammability data in microgravity environments and the safety factors involved when selecting spacecraft materials based on normal gravity testing will be evaluated.
Rigorous correlations between ground test flammability data and data in ventilated spacecraft environments would allow selection of materials with increased fire resistance, and thus decrease the fire risk in space systems. The operational flexibility will also increase since the safety factors will be assessable.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The identification of the fundamental limit in microgravity and its comparison with the normal gravity flammability limit will help us understand flammability in different configurations on Earth.
It will improve the safety of astronauts in spaceflight so they can return safely to Earth.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
The centrifuge drop vehicle in the Zero Gravity Research Facility was refurbished in early 2020 to conduct low pressure blowoff testing with 0.318 cm radius polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) rods to compare with the forced flow data. We completed just a few experiments prior to the pandemic mandatory telework in March 2020, and just began testing again in September 2021. The flame is all blue but is quite stable and does not seem to be strongly affected by Coriolis forces.
The results to date of the experiment compare very well with the blowoff branch of the Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) flammability boundary we published in Combustion and Flame in 2017 (Olson S, Ferkul P. "Microgravity flammability boundary for PMMA rods in axial stagnation flow: Experimental results and energy balance analyses." Combustion and Flame. 2017 Jun;180:217-29). The buoyant flow is estimated using Ub = 25 (g/gEarth)^1/2 so the 1g (Earth g) buoyant flow is 25 cm/s for the stagnation geometry. The boundary is just slightly shifted down from the BASS-II boundary. The close alignment of the two boundaries indicates that the square root scaling appears to be valid.
The stable flame at lunar g level and 13.8% O2 is very close to the minimum in the BASS-II flammability boundary. This would seem to support prior research that found materials are more flammable on the Moon than on Mars or the Earth. A few additional tests are planned to complete the testing. A paper of the results is planned.
During the pandemic, I spent time analyzing flight results from the Solid Inflammatory Boundary at Low Speed (SIBAL) fabrics, since I am burning SIBAL fabric as well as PMMA rods as part of my upcoming experiments on the International Space Station (ISS). I am working on a more traditional flame spread paper for that project, but I did develop a novel analysis of the post-flame smolder wave that developed behind flame, To analyze the smolder wave, I used a variety of techniques to measure the speed of the smolder wave, the number and size of the smolder spots, and the shape of the smolder wave distribution. A paper documenting this analysis is planned.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
Low-pressure blowoff experiments were conducted with a stagnation flame stabilized on the forward tip of cast polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) rods in a vertical wind tunnel. Pressure, forced flow velocity, gravity, and ambient oxygen concentration were varied. Both normal gravity and microgravity tests were conducted to determine the influence of buoyant flow velocity on the blowoff limits. A linear shift of a buoyant flow of ~25 cm/s was adequate to match the microgravity data. The flame standoff distance before blowoff varies with the inverse square root of pressure and stretch rate via the gas phase length scale d = (a/a)1/2, where the thermal diffusivity varies inversely with pressure. For a constant critical Damkohler number, the reaction rate must increase in tandem with the flow rate. The flame standoff distance responds to environment changes to maintain both the critical Damkohler number and the molar flux of oxygen along the blowoff boundary. These interdependencies result in the partial pressure of oxygen at blowoff being linearly dependent on the total pressure regardless of forced flow velocity and gravity level. At very low pressures, reactant leakage appears to cause a two-stage reaction zone. For very dilute oxidizer mixtures, an apparent high pressure blowoff limit is found, believed to be caused by chain-terminating three body reactions. A normal gravity materials flammability screening methodology is suggested for spacecraft exploration atmospheres where the blowoff partial pressure of oxygen versus total pressure blowoff limits are measured for the expected exploration atmospheres (oxygen concentrations). As long as the blowoff boundary is above the Earth-normal partial pressure of oxygen (21 kPa) threshold, the material is safe for use in spacecraft.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
Normal gravity flame blowoff limits in an axisymmetric polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) rod geometry in upward axial stagnation flow are compared with microgravity Burning and Suppression of Solids – II (BASS-II) results recently obtained aboard the International Space Station (ISS). This testing utilized the same BASS-II concurrent rod geometry, but was done in normal gravity mixed convective flow. Cast PMMA rods of diameters ranging from 0.635 cm to 3.81 cm were burned at oxygen concentrations ranging from 15% to 18% by volume. The forced flow velocity where blowoff occurrs was determined for each rod size and oxygen concentration. These blowoff limits compare favorably with the BASS-II results when the buoyant stretch rate is included and the flow is corrected by considering the blockage factor of the fuel. From these results, the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined to be linear, with oxygen concentration and flow velocity as coordinates.
We describe a new normal gravity ‘upward blowoff test’ method which extrapolates this linear blowoff boundary to the zero mixed stretch rate limit to resolve microgravity flammability limits—something current methods cannot do. This new test method can improve spacecraft fire safety for future exploration missions by providing a tractable way to obtain accurate but conservative estimates of material flammability in low gravity based on tests performed on Earth.
During the blowoff extinction of clear cast PMMA rods in concurrent axial flow for microgravity BASS-II experiments, a dynamic flame oscillation was observed after the flame was blown off of the stagnation point but briefly stabilized on the periphery of the rod. Complementary normal gravity experiments were conducted and flame oscillations were tracked using a high speed color camera at 240 frames per second. The side-stabilized flame oscillated up and down the rod with increasing amplitude until the entire flame extinguished. In none of the BASS-II or normal gravity tests could the side-stabilized flames persist (Hopf subcritical bifurcation). Since the oscillations occurred even in microgravity, the mechanism does not depend on gravity. For the larger fuel radius tests, the flame developed asymmetric oscillation (pitchfork bifurcation). The oscillation time and the number of oscillations scale with the inverse square of the rod radius (~ Fourier no.) for the preheated microgravity rods. The average flame oscillation frequency is found to be linearly dependent on the mixed convective stretch rate (inverse of the flow time). The flame intensity varied in concert with its direction, either increasing or decreasing as the flame moved upstream or downstream, respectively. The oscillation frequency decreased as the amplitude increased and the flame slipped slightly farther down the rod with each oscillation. The flame speed increased with each subsequent oscillation, both flashing forward upstream and retreating downstream. The oscillations were found to closely follow a power law log-periodic dependence similar to those that describe systems approaching a critical point, such as diffusion-limited aggregation clusters, earthquakes, ruptures, and even stock market crashes. The net flame speeds varied linearly with ambient oxygen concentration, and linearly with the mixed convective stretch rate. Based on these observations, a mechanistic theory of the oscillations is described, and is consistent with the thermodiffusive instability.
Low-pressure blowoff experiments were also conducted with a stagnation flame stabilized on the forward tip of cast PMMA rods in a vertical wind tunnel. Pressure, forced flow velocity, gravity, and ambient oxygen concentration were varied. Most of the tests were performed in normal gravity, but a handful of microgravity tests were also conducted to determine the influence of buoyant flow velocity on the blowoff limits. A linear shift of a buoyant flow of ~25 cm/s was adequate to match the microgravity data. The flame standoff distance before blowoff varies with the inverse square root of pressure via the gas phase length scale d=(a/a)1/2, where the thermal diffusivity varies inversely with pressure. The blowoff limits have a linear dependence between the partial pressure of oxygen and the total pressure, regardless of forced flow velocity and gravity level. Phenomenologically, the reaction rate is proportional to the oxygen flux to the reaction zone, so the flame surface area increases (via increasing d) as pressure is reduced, which compensates for the reduced partial pressure of oxygen for a given flow velocity. The flame standoff distance is also proportional to the inverse square root of the stretch rate (velocity), so the flame area decreases linearly with the mixed flow velocity. This reduced flame area results in a linear increase in the blowoff pressure so that the oxidizer molar flux to the smaller area maintained. The flow velocity (forced and/or buoyant) affects the blowoff pressure through the critical Damkohler number residence time, which dictates the partial pressure of oxygen at blowoff. This is because the critical stretch rate increases linearly with increasing pressure at low pressure (sub-atmospheric pressures) since a second-order overall reaction rate with two-body reactions dominates in this pressure range. A normal gravity materials flammability screening methodology is suggested for spacecraft exploration atmospheres.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
Normal gravity flame blowoff limits in an axisymmetric polymethylmethacrylate (pmma) rod geometry in upward axial stagnation flow were obtained in the laboratory apparatus. The blowoff limits are compared with microgravity Burning and Suppression of Solids – II (BASS-II) results recently obtained aboard the International Space Station. The lab testing used the same BASS-II concurrent rod geometry, but with the addition of normal gravity buoyant flow. Cast polymethylmethacrylate (pmma) rods of diameters ranging from 0.635 cm to 3.81 cm were burned in a vertical flow tube similar to an LOI device, but with the capability of varying the forced flow velocity. Oxygen concentrations ranging from 14 to 18% by volume were supplied from premixed bottles. The forced flow velocity where blowoff occurred was determined for each rod size and oxygen concentration. These normal gravity blowoff limits compare favorably with the BASS-II results when the buoyant stretch is accounted for and the flow is corrected by considering the blockage factor of the fuel. From these results, the normal gravity blowoff boundary for this axisymmetric rod geometry is determined as a function of oxygen concentration and equivalent stretch rate. The oxygen concentration at blowoff linearly increases as the equivalent stretch rate increases. This a new normal gravity ‘upward flame spread test’ method provides a flammability curve that can be extrapolated to the zero stretch limit to estimate the microgravity flammability limits—something current methods cannot do. This new test method can improve spacecraft fire safety for future exploration missions by providing a tractable way to obtain good estimates of material flammability in low gravity.
Low-pressure blowoff experiments were also conducted with a stagnation flame stabilized on the forward tip of cast PMMA rods in a vertical wind tunnel. Pressure, forced flow velocity, gravity, and ambient oxygen concentration were varied. Stagnation flame blowoff is observed from a time-stamped video recording of the test. The blowoff pressure is determined from test section pressure transducer data that is synchronized with the video time stamp. The forced flow velocity is also determined from the choked flow orifice pressure. Most of the low pressure tests were performed in normal gravity, but a handful of microgravity drop tests were also conducted to determine the influence of buoyant flow velocity on the blowoff limits. The blowoff limits are found to have a linear dependence between the partial pressure of oxygen and the total pressure, regardless of forced flow velocity and gravity level. The flow velocity (forced and/or buoyant) affects the blowoff pressure through the critical Damkohler number residence time. For a constant critical Damkohler number, the partial pressure of oxygen at blowoff varies with the equivalent stretch rate (flow velocity) to provide this linear dependence. This is because the critical stretch rate increases linearly with increasing pressure at low pressure (sub-atmospheric pressures) since a second-order overall reaction rate with two-body reactions dominates in this pressure range.
