Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2016
Task Progress:
Microgravity experiments burning cast Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cylindrical rods in axial stagnation flow were conducted aboard the International Space Station in 2014 as part of the BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids) experiment. The complete lower portion of the oxygen-stretch rate flammability boundary was obtained experimentally for PMMA in microgravity for the first time. Complementary 5.18-second Zero Gravity Facility blowoff drop tests were also conducted. A constant critical Damkohler number analysis has been applied to the data. For the blowoff branch, the boundary exhibits a linear dependence between oxygen concentration and stretch rate. For the quenching branch, the dominance of the exponential kinetics term indicates that the temperature is critical.
A Nusselt number heat transfer correlation has been used to estimate the heat flux to the rod along the flammability boundary. Oxygen consumption calorimetry is then used to estimate the flow radius needed to provide adequate oxygen. The thermal length, oxygen flow length, and measured standoff distance are all within 1 mm across the blowoff region, but the thermal and oxygen lengths diverge once flows drop to the order of diffusive velocities with the flame standoff distance between them.
A two zone surface energy balance uses the heat flux correlation and gas phase radiative feedback to evaluate relative importance of heat losses along the flammability boundary. At the bottom of the flammability boundary, heat losses amount to approximately 20% of the net heat flux to the surface. Quantitatively, heat losses are actually lowest along the quenching branch, but because of the low total flame heat flux, surface radiative loss becomes a dominant factor. Gas phase radiative feedback increases from 3% of the total heat flux at high stretch to 26% at low stretch. Measured rod regression rates agree with predicted values. A one-dimensional version of the model agrees with previously published stagnation flow regression rates.
In order to more accurately determine the relationship between the burning of solid materials under microgravity and normal gravity conditions, a series of normal gravity blowoff extinction tests were conducted to compare with BASS-II testing. This testing utilized the BASS-II concurrent rod geometry, with the addition of normal gravity buoyant flow. Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) rods of diameters ranging from 0.25” to 1.5” were tested at oxygen percentages ranging from 14-18% by volume. The forced flow where blowoff occurred was found for each rod size and oxygen concentration. These blowoff flammability limit results are currently being evaluated.
The blowoff flammability boundary when pressure and oxygen are varied instead of the forced flow was also investigated. The partial pressure of oxygen at blowoff increases linearly with total pressure, in a trend different from the simple volume fraction value.
Based on these results, it seems plausible that an improved test method that determines the normal gravity blowoff boundary can be used to extrapolate to the reduced gravity material flammability boundary, which will improve spacecraft fire safety for future exploration missions.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2015
Task Progress:
This year the BASS-II precursor experiments were conducted aboard ISS using the Microgravity Science Glovebox and the BASS hardware. For this project (SMµRF), acrylic cylinders in 3 diameters were tested in a concurrent (stagnation) flow to determine flammability limits as a function of flow and ambient oxygen level.
BASS-II Ops were completed from February to early August, 2014. Science data analysis is underway. A total of 24 SMµRF tests were conducted during BASS-II. Some samples were burned more than once. There are some samples that could be burned further, should future operational time become available. The Principal Investigator is busy analyzing the results of BASS-II, in preparation for a Requirements Definition Review in Dec. 2014.
For the first time on ISS, BASS-II utilized MSG working volume vitiation with GN2. We developed a perfectly stirred reactor model to determine the GN2 flow time and flow rate to obtain the desired reduced oxygen concentration in the working volume for the tests. This worked out extremely well for operations, and added a new vital variable, ambient oxygen level, to our test matrices.
We obtained blowoff and quenching extinction limits to define the flammability boundary for PMMA as a function of flow and oxygen concentration. The low flow boundary is a surprisingly steep threshold at very low flows, whereas blowoff is a more gradual slope. The 1g blowoff for the ¼” rod is at 16% oxygen, whereas we obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen in BASS-II. Thus the material has a negative Oxygen Margin of Safety of 2.4% O2, and the normal gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.
The minimum in the flammability boundary is at very low flows, on the order of diffusive flows. This minimum occurs in what is termed here the ‘Goldilocks’ zone of flow, where the oxygen flow is not too little to suffocate the flame, provides just enough heat release to sustain the flame but the flow is not so strong that it sweeps the fuel out of the hot flame zone before the reaction of Equation 1 can occur. As ambient oxygen is reduced, the flame temperatures are reduced, which slows down the reaction time. Thus the flow needed to blow off the flame becomes slower as oxygen decreases and the flame temperature is reduced.
Each test provides a wealth of information in addition to the extinction limits. This data includes flame size, standoff distance, spread rate, bubble layer thickness, tip regression shape, pre-extinction flame oscillations, and vapor jetting frequency and sample interactions. This data is still being analyzed.
Ground-based drop tower work and lab experiments have been conducted to develop an illumination technique to image the bubble layer in depth while still imaging the flame shape.
The Science Requirements Document for the flight experiment is being updated to reflect the knowledge gained from the BASS-II tests and the ground-based testing. A Requirements Definition Review is scheduled for December, 2014.

In FY 13, we successfully passed the Science Concept Review and completed a Science Requirements Document for the flight experiment. These are significant milestones on the path to flight hardware development.
I also successfully completed a number of 5.2 second drop tower tests with PMMA rods and cheesecloth fabric studying flame spread and flammability limits. In the drop tower, I was able to quantify the blowoff branch of the extinction curve, but the time is too short to obtain quenching extinction. In the cheesecloth tests, I tested a variety of area densities to determine the flame spread rate dependence on thickness for concurrent flame spread, to compare it to opposed flow inverse dependence. I am very interested in determining limits for both opposed and concurrent flame spread to determine which configuration is the worst case in spacecraft fires.
As part of this project, I defined 20 samples to be flown for BASS-II in the ISS MSG. We built and launched these samples, and testing has begun. On the second test, I was able to observe a quenching extinction process, which is quite different from the blowoff extinction. In blowoff extinction, the flame tip opens up and then the flame blows downstream to extinguish. In contrast, for quenching extinction, the flame shrinks toward the stagnation region (at the tip of the rod) and gets smaller and smaller until it disappears.
I was selected to participate as a Co-Investigator on a JAXA 2012 AO Selected experiment studying Fire Safety. I have been involved in defining the science requirements for the JAXA experiment hardware to be tested in the Kibo module on ISS.
Lastly, I defined a Normoxic Upward Pressure Limit (NULP) for NASA Test 1 tests, which takes advantage of the normoxic atmospheres for exploration missions to simplify the parameter space, in terms of pressure and oxygen, to evaluate the flammability limits of materials in Test 1. I also included a factor of safety on this NULP to account for the enhanced flammability in space.

Task Description:
NASA STD 6001 Test 1 is the major method used to evaluate flammability of materials intended for use in habitable environments of U.S. spacecraft. The method is an upward flame propagation test initiated in a stagnant environment and using a well-defined igniter flame at the bottom of a vertically mounted sample. A material passes this test if the vertical burn length is less than 15.2 cm (6 inches) and there is no evidence of transfer of burning debris. The test is conducted in the most severe flaming combustion environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft, currently 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia.
Recent research has shown that current normal gravity materials flammability tests do not correlate with flammability in ventilated, micro-, or reduced-gravity conditions. The materials selection for spacecraft is based on the assumption of commonality between ground test flammability results and spacecraft environments, which does not appear to be valid. To better understand the actual normal gravity flammability limits, a modified Test 1 protocol has been proposed that, as an alternative to qualifying materials as pass/fail in the worst-expected environments, measures the actual upward flammability limit (akin to the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI)) for the material so that a more accurate assessment of the margin of safety of the material in the real use environment can be made. The method allows the option of selecting better or best materials based on the margin of safety, as opposed to what would be considered just "passing" from a flammability point of view.
A research program is underway to correlate normal gravity flammability test data with data under ventilated reduced gravity or microgravity conditions. The program will determine materials suitability for microgravity and reduced gravity testing by evaluating oxygen concentration thresholds under various total pressures in normal gravity tests and in spacecraft-specific environments (ventilated microgravity or reduced partial gravity). The normal gravity data will be correlated with flammability data in microgravity environments and the safety factors involved when selecting spacecraft materials based on normal gravity testing will be evaluated.
Rigorous correlations between ground test flammability data and data in ventilated spacecraft environments would allow selection of materials with increased fire resistance, and thus decrease the fire risk in space systems. The operational flexibility will also increase since the safety factors will be assessable.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The identification of the fundamental limit in microgravity and its comparison with the normal gravity flammability limit will help us understand flammability in different configurations on Earth.
It will improve the safety of astronauts in spaceflight so they can return safely to Earth.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2013
Task Progress:
First and foremost, we seek to develop a fundamental understanding of how NASA’s material flammability test, NASA-STD-6001.A Test 1, relates to the actual flammability of materials in low- and partial-gravity. As part of this goal, we will obtain a better fundamental understanding of material flammability as a function of concurrent flow, oxygen, and pressure.
The hypothesis to be tested in this research is that a material’s flammability hazard in microgravity or partial gravity is at least equivalent to and may be greater than its flammability measured in normal gravity. We also hypothesize that most materials exhibit a similar flammability boundary as a function of oxygen and flow. These two hypotheses then imply that there may be a similar magnitude negative oxygen margin of safety for many materials. If true, a common factor of safety is could be defined for materials to ‘de-rate’ them for use in microgravity or partial gravity.
To better understand the actual normal gravity flammability limits, a modified Test 1 protocol has been proposed that, as an alternative to qualifying materials as pass/fail in the worst-expected environments, measures the actual upward flammability limit (akin to the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI)) for the material so that a more accurate assessment of the margin of safety of the material in the real use environment can be made. The method allows the option of selecting better or best materials based on the margin of safety, as opposed to what would be considered just “passing” from a flammability point of view.
We have been conducting drop tower tests of materials to evaluate their flammability boundaries in low gravity. We have found that a number of materials have a negative oxygen margin of safety in low gravity. However, drop testing is limited to 5.18 seconds, so only the thinnest of films can be tested, and even then the limits found may be lower than longer duration testing would find, where the flame just takes longer to go out than the drop time.
Recently, we have been focusing on defining a flight experiment that to correlate normal gravity flammability test data with data under ventilated microgravity conditions. The flight experiment will determine the minimum in the flammability map for select materials. An oxygen margin of safety will be evaluated. If it is negative, then a safety factor will be defined for the materials to ‘de-rate’ them for use in microgravity or partial gravity.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2011
Task Progress:
Currently, NASA STD 6001 Test 1 is the major method used to evaluate flammability of materials intended for use in habitable environments of U.S. spacecraft. The method is a 6” propagation pass/fail upward flame propagation test conducted over a 5 cm wide by 30 tall slabs of material exposed to the most hazardous environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft. Flow is buoyant only (no forced flow).
It is well known that in normal gravity, upward and downward flammability limits are different. The velocity and velocity gradient across surfaces is affected by the geometry of the surface. A slab has a leading edge that affects the development of the boundary layer, and the back edge step induces a recirculation zone where an opposed flow flame would stabilize; a sphere has a stagnation zone and a wake region; and a rod has a stagnation region, a boundary layer on the sides, and a wake region. Depending on where the flame ignites, the material may or may not be flammable.
It is not clear, however, if this test configuration is the worst case in zero gravity, where flow velocity is decoupled from oxygen concentration, pressure, and flame temperature. To compare the effect of geometry on the flammability of materials, flat slabs, spheres, and rods have been tested in both 1g and 0g to evaluate changes in the flammability limits. Testing and analysis of the results is still underway. The goal of the geometry variation is to define the ‘worst case’ geometry for zero gravity as well as to evaluate how sensitive the flammability limits are in normal g to geometry changes.
This year, the research results were presented at the Central States Section Meeting of the Combustion Institute in Champaign, IL in March, 2010, at the International Conference on Environmental Systems in Barcelona, Spain, and as a Work In Progress Poster at the International Combustion Symposium in Beijing, China in August, 2010. The Principal Investigator attended the June PI Kickoff meeting in Cleveland, OH, and the Co-Investigators visited NASA GRC in August to tour facilities and discuss test plans. The PI visited White Sands Test Facility in September, 2010 to meet with Co-Investigators to tour their facilities and discuss the research. The concept for a flight experiment is being developed.

Task Description:
In order to safely explore beyond our planet, we need to develop methods, data bases, and validating tests for material flammability characterization, hazard reduction, and fire detection/suppression strategies for spacecraft and extraterrestrial habitats. This work addresses these needs by applying the fundamental knowledge gained from low stretch experiments to the development of a low stretch material flammability test method that simulates low gravity or partial gravity levels to better evaluate fire hazards in these environments.
NASA's Cone Calorimeter Test 2 is required for major-use non-metallic panels and as an option for the retest of the flammability of a material which failed the Upward Flammability Test 1. The Cone Calorimeter is widely used ASTM standard test method because it evaluates the effects of preheating on flammability and it provides a wealth of data for evaluation. However, Test 2 has no pass/fail criteria at this point. The concept of the apparatus being developed uses the low stretch geometry to simulate the conditions of the extraterrestrial environment through proper scaling of the sample dimensions to reduce the buoyant stretch we have on Earth. The apparatus uses controlled forced-air flow to augment the low stretch to levels which simulate Lunar or Martian gravity levels. In addition, the effect of imposed radiant heat flux on material flammability can be studied with the cone heater, which simulates the hazard of a small fire spreading to adjacent materials. After breadboard testing, the apparatus will be integrated into NASA's White Sands Test Facility's Atmosphere-Controlled Cone Calorimeter for evaluation as a new materials screening test method.
Primary variables include material tested, imposed forced stretch rate (effective gravity level), radiant flux level, and oxygen concentration. Data from the Apparatus will include ignition delay time, mass loss rate, heat release rate (O2 consumption), and product generation rates (CO, CO2, soot, THC). Ignition limits and material flammability limits will be measured for selected ideal/practical materials. If extinction limits are determined in Earth-based low stretch experiments as a function of the percent of heat flux conducted into the solid, we can identify critical percent heat flux values for spacecraft.
In addition to the development of the apparatus, a predictive model will be developed to predict flammability limits for a given material, using specific material properties, desired atmospheric composition, and extraterrestrial gravity environments as inputs to the prediction. The experimental and predicted results will be compared to evaluate the test method and predictive capability. We are working to reduce the fire danger to astronauts by developing an earth-bound method of evaluating materials flammability in various gravitational environments from normal gravity to microgravity, including the effects of partial gravity low stretch rates such as those found on the Moon (1/6g) or Mars (1/3g).
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
ELSA (Equivalent Low Stretch Apparatus) is proposed as a new 1g test materials screening method that is has been designed to allow us to evaluate material ignitability and flammability in spacecraft and extraterrestrial environments based upon scaling of the velocity gradient in different geometries.
This test measures a number of parameters, many of which can be used to rank materials under given conditions.
- ignition delay time, - oxygen consumption, which is used to derive heat release rates, - mass loss rates (when used with O2 consumption, we get global equivalence ratios), - CO and CO2 production rates, - critical heat flux for ignition, - soot and total hydrocarbon (not measured to date, but could be added to exhaust system using COTS hardware),
This project addresses the following organizing question(s):
3) Is there a normal gravity test that can quantify material flammability in reduced gravity either by itself or in conjunction with NASA STD 6001, Test 1?
4) How does the flammability and ignitability of materials change in high O2 concentration low pressure environments (in reduced gravity)?
To date, the fundamental similarity scaling of the stretch rate (velocity gradient) of ELSA has been demonstrated in a prototype system at NASA Glenn. An engineering unit is currently being tested at WSTF, which includes many of the exhaust diagnostics not available at the Glenn facility.
A peer-reviewed article on this test method was presented at the 30th International Symposium on Combustion [4] and is available from the PI upon request.
Preliminary Scaling Comparisons with ELSA of Independent Low Gravity Tests.
Scaling Arguments: The ELSA concept is based upon scaling analysis that demonstrates buoyant stretch and forced stretch can be equated. This means that through scaling we can assess how materials will burn over a wide range of gravity levels.
The stretch rate is simply the velocity gradient as the flow decelerates toward the fuel surface. The velocity gradient for flame spread problems has been shown to be the important flow parameter [9], and the flame is spreading deep within the boundary layer where the velocity gradient is almost constant. For forced flow velocities of up to 20 cm/s (spacecraft ventilation), the velocity gradient (stretch rate) is of the same order for small fires. Thus a test method which varies the velocity gradient (stretch rate) will capture the essential flammability behavior of flame spread as well as stagnation point fires.
FIST Data
To demonstrate this scaling with experimental results, the ignition delay results of FIST[1] at different flow rates, including natural convection, are added to the ignition delay –stretch plot by estimating the Blasius boundary layer velocity gradient at the surface for the free stream flow based on their experiment geometry. The correlation holds up very well over a wide range of velocity gradient in cm/s per cm (flame stretch rate, s-1).
While the normal cone flow field is not well characterized, the flame is stabilized near a surface with a cross flow (entrained air), and velocity gradients in a laminar boundary layer near the surface are constant. For a 5 cm surface (1/2 sample) with an average velocity gradient near the surface of 33 s-1, the average entrained cross flow would be ~20 cm/s, which is reasonable.
Skorost Data
A flammability study of different materials, including PMMA, was conducted aboard Mir in their Skorost facility [2]. Rods of PMMA were burned in a concurrent airflow parallel to the rod axis. Interestingly, the rods developed large molten balls at their burning tips, and in the low flow environment provided by Skorost, the flames were stabilized at the stagnation point of the ball. They measured rod regression rates, molten ball diameters, and flame diameters. Using that information, we can estimate the stretch rates and burning rates for these PMMA ‘lollipops’.
Regression rates of molten spheres were calculated by converting the mass loss rate (g/s) determined from the rod regression rate into the same mass loss rate from the molten sphere. Equivalent stretch rates were determined by taking into account both the forced stretch around the sphere (af,sphere =3/2 U/Rsphere) and the curvature-induced stretch for the small samples (acurv =3 U/R *(Rflame-Rsphere)/Rsphere). The equivalent stretch is then aequiv = af,sphere+ acurv. As the flame standoff distance (Rflame-Rsphere) becomes small relative to the radius of curvature, curvature effects become negligible. 2) Ivanov, A.V., Balashov, Ye.V., Andreeva, T.V., Melikhov, A.S.; “Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space”, NASA CR-1999-209405, 1999.
3) Olson, S.L., and T’ien, J.S.; “Buoyant Low Stretch Diffusion Flames Beneath Cylindrical PMMA Samples”, Combustion and Flame, V.121, pp. 439-452, 2000.
4) Olson, S.L., Beeson, H.D., Haas, J.P., and Baas, J.S.; “An Earth-Based Equivalent Low Stretch Apparatus for Material Flammability Assessment in Microgravity and Extraterrestrial Environments”, Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, V30, 2004, to appear.
Plans
To continue the project through completion of a new test method, we envision the following tasks need to be conducted:
1) We need to complete the comparison of WSTF-GRC data for PMMA, so that we have confidence that our understanding of the test method is robust (ignition, flow, radiant heat, enclosure effects, etc).
2) We need to evaluate materials that may slump, swell, or display other behavior that may perturb the test. Materials that drip will be automatically eliminated (failed?) because the material will ignite when it hits the hot cone, thus disrupting the test and possibly damaging the hardware. Screens or meshes need to be tested in the inverted geometry (note: screens are used in the standard cone test for vertical samples as part of the ASTM test method).
3) We expect that via similarity scaling the 1g test will provide quantitative evaluation of a material’s reduced-gravity flammability characteristics. See figures at the end of the plan for some preliminary results of analysis to date. However, to demonstrate that more fully, we need to evaluate samples in different velocity gradient /geometries to test the stretch scaling correlation of data such as oxygen consumption, ignition delay times, critical heat flux for ignition, toxic product generation, etc. The most expedient and inexpensive way to do this over the velocity gradient range of interest is aboard the parabolic aircraft. There, we can fly low gravity trajectories at high heat flux levels (~50 kW/m2, velocity gradient 10-40 s-1). In addition, we can test the partial gravity scaling by testing samples under partial gravity parabolas with a relatively low forced convective stretch (~10 s-1). These experiments will likely use PMMA as the reference material, as is the case with the standard cone. This would most likely require a new parabolic aircraft rig buildup to accommodate the cone and large samples.
4) In addition, if/when a radiant ignition-type experiment flies on ISS, we can compare the results of the flight experiment with ground-based testing of the same material.
5) While we have been operating with the WSTF Cone facility, there are significant advantages to developing a custom ELSA facility that would eliminate some of the existing constraints of the current facility, such as the confined space of the enclosure. In addition, a custom unit would allow us to address a number of the organizing questions and deliverables: - testing in candidate atmospheres (lower ambient pressure, higher O2); - testing of detectors positioned in the exhaust system; - testing of suppression system(s) integrated into the system, tied in to the detectors if desired.
6) We need to develop a robust engineering model (as opposed to a scientifically cumbersome model) that uses material properties as input and predicts flammability behavior in the end-use environment. Simple FDS models have been developed, but a detailed study has yet to be conducted. This task may be folded into the evaluation of practical fire scenarios which is a task for the entire FPDS program. Several projects are starting to work on aspects of this. Once ELSA scaling is verified, the measured material properties would serve as input. Coordination of and funding for these efforts will be done within the FPDS program.)
7) The acceptance criteria for this test method need to be developed which address the varied exploration environments. We can address this when the scaling has been demonstrated. If possible, we should include the outcomes of the fire scenario modeling and/or performance-based risk assessments
Deliverables (schedule dependent on tbd funding)
1. Comparison and assessment of WSTF and GRC data for PMMA.
2. Work with FEANICS team to define the requirements that would have to be placed on a flight experiment that could be used in support of the stretch scaling verification. (flow characterization, gas sampling, etc).
3. Demonstration of the functional relationship between stretch rate and the measured quantities (tign, etc) for materials other than PMMA. This should be done for classes of materials to show applicability of the test method.
4. Comparison of the quantities measured in the normal gravity apparatus with similar quantities in the parabolic aircraft CIR(FEANICS) apparatus to verify low-stretch similarity with reduced gravity behavior. In other words, this will determine if the boundary-layer ignition tests are suitable to confirm the scaling. We would start with PMMA and then move to other materials, depending on the outcome of (2).
5. Planning/Design of an ELSA-type insert for the CIR-chamber aircraft rig.

Task Description:
In order to safely explore beyond our planet, we need to develop methods, data bases, and validating tests for material flammability characterization, hazard reduction, and fire detection/suppression strategies for spacecraft and extraterrestrial habitats. This work addresses these needs by applying the fundamental knowledge gained from low stretch experiments to the development of a low stretch material flammability test method that simulates low gravity or partial gravity levels to better evaluate fire hazards in these environments.
NASA's Cone Calorimeter Test 2 is required for major-use non-metallic panels and as an option for the retest of the flammability of a material which failed the Upward Flammability Test 1. The Cone Calorimeter is widely used ASTM standard test method because it evaluates the effects of preheating on flammability and it provides a wealth of data for evaluation. However, Test 2 has no pass/fail criteria at this point. The concept of the apparatus being developed uses the low stretch geometry to simulate the conditions of the extraterrestrial environment through proper scaling of the sample dimensions to reduce the buoyant stretch we have on Earth. The apparatus uses controlled forced-air flow to augment the low stretch to levels which simulate Lunar or Martian gravity levels. In addition, the effect of imposed radiant heat flux on material flammability can be studied with the cone heater, which simulates the hazard of a small fire spreading to adjacent materials. After breadboard testing, the apparatus will be integrated into NASA's White Sands Test Facility's Atmosphere-Controlled Cone Calorimeter for evaluation as a new materials screening test method.
Primary variables include material tested, imposed forced stretch rate (effective gravity level), radiant flux level, and oxygen concentration. Data from the Apparatus will include ignition delay time, mass loss rate, heat release rate (O2 consumption), and product generation rates (CO, CO2, soot, THC). Ignition limits and material flammability limits will be measured for selected ideal/practical materials. If extinction limits are determined in Earth-based low stretch experiments as a function of the percent of heat flux conducted into the solid, we can identify critical percent heat flux values for spacecraft.
In addition to the development of the apparatus, a predictive model will be developed to predict flammability limits for a given material, using specific material properties, desired atmospheric composition, and extraterrestrial gravity environments as inputs to the prediction. The experimental and predicted results will be compared to evaluate the test method and predictive capability. We are working to reduce the fire danger to astronauts by developing an earth-bound method of evaluating materials flammability in various gravitational environments from normal gravity to microgravity, including the effects of partial gravity low stretch rates such as those found on the Moon (1/6g) or Mars (1/3g).

Task Description:
The objective of the project is to develop a methodology to correlate material flammability limits in normal gravity and microgravity, which allows quantitative estimation of material flammability limit in microgravity based on the flammability data obtained on the ground. The project involves an international team including Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), NASA, ESA (European Space Agency), and universities in Japan, USA, and France. Dr. Olson is a U.S. Co-Investigator for the JAXA sponsored experiments to be conducted aboard the Japanese Experiment Module, Kibo.
To establish global standards for fire safety in space, we seek to develop a fundamental understanding of how NASA’s material flammability test, NASA-STD-6001.A Test 1, relates to the actual flammability of materials in micro and partial gravity.
The investigation strategy is to perform extensive research via ground-based experiments, including 1g and parabolic flight tests, and via theoretical formulations. Flight experiments on orbit in International Space Station (ISS)/KIBO will be performed to verify the correlation. The flight experiments on orbit are expected in 2018 or later.
By the end of the project, a new fire safety standard test method for screening spacecraft materials will be proposed that addresses the shortcomings of existing standard test methods such as NASA-STD-6001B.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Studying materials flammability in space allows us to accurately control the flow field and thus elucidate the importance of a critical Damkohler number (flow time /reaction time) on flame extinction. The anticipated improved methodology should reduce time and cost for the spacecraft material screening. Investigation and results have Earth benefits for terrestrial fire safety.

Task Progress:
ISS experiments are underway. Experiment 1-2 filter paper samples were completed in March 2024. The PMMA samples for Experiment 1-1 were conducted starting in March 2024. Since another experiment was scheduled to use the vacuum resources needed for the FLARE experiments in June 2024, the PMMA samples were finished in August 2024 and the rod samples for Experiment 2-1 were started in August 2024. International Standard ISO 4589-4 “Plastics – Determination of burning behavior by oxygen index – Part 4: High gas velocity test” was established on April 6, 2021 by the FLARE project. Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
The 2019 annual international Flammability Limits At Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE) January workshop was cancelled due to the Government shutdown. An expanded ‘Spacecraft Materials Flammability Workshop’ was held from May 20-22, 2019 at NASA Glenn Research Center's Guerin House. The workshop was an expansion of the JAXA flare experiment annual workshop, and included presentations on programs from international representatives from JAXA, German Aerospace Center (DLR), National Centre for Space Studies (CNES), ESA, NASA [Headquarters, Glenn Research Center (GRC), White Sands Test Facility (WSTF), and Johnson Space Center (JSC)], and a number of universities. Also at that meeting, the FLARE science teams presented their status to the group. In addition, results from parabolic aircraft campaigns were discussed. Workshop attendees toured the Zero Gravity Research Facility, the Telescience Support Center, and the Combustion Integrated Rack.
Low-gravity aircraft parabolic trajectories and microgravity drop tower experiments have been conducted to study blowoff extinction limits for thin sheets of bleached grade#90 cheesecloth. To avoid confusion with ignition limits, the flames were ignited under a flammable condition, and the conditions were changed (flow, oxygen) to determine if the flame would blow off. Preliminary blowoff boundaries were mapped for both opposed and concurrent flow. The concurrent blowoff boundary occurs at lower oxygen concentrations for the same ambient flow velocities than the opposed blowoff boundary, and the slopes do not appear to be parallel. This is hypothesized to be due to the a higher Damkohler number at the flame base of a concurrent flame (stagnation flow) than at the leading edge of an opposed flow flame (boundary layer flow) under the same flows.
Local blowoffs were observed during testing, where a significant fraction of the opposed flame width extinguishes, and where one whole side of the concurrent flame blows off. Often, the remaining flame will again spread to the affected area, only to have the event occur, often repeatedly, during the test. Due to the stochastic nature of the local extinctions along the 2D stabilization region [leading edge (opposed flow), flame base (concurrent flow)], they do not always result in total extinction of the flame, indicating the flammability boundary is a band rather than a sharp boundary of conditions (flow, oxygen concentration).

Task Progress:
An international workshop was held at Tsukuba, Japan in January, 2018. At that meeting, the science teams presented their status to the group. In addition, plans for a parabolic aircraft campaign were discussed.
A series of NASA Glenn Zero Gravity Research Facility (ZGRF) tests were continued this year to determine the approximate high velocity blowoff limits for thin cotton fabrics for both opposed and some concurrent flow conditions. Concurrent blowoff of thin cotton sheet occurs frequently on only on one side of the sample at near-limit conditions. Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
A successful TIM (technical interchange meeting) and Phase 0/1 Flammability hazard review was held at NASA White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) Dec. 6-8, 2016. Also discussed at that meeting was the FLARE project status and the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) standardization plan was updated. NASA has proposed an improved upward flame spread Test 1 of NASA STD 6001B which evaluates the upward limiting oxygen index and maximum oxygen concentration (ULOI/MOC) of a material in 1g. JAXA is pursuing a downward burning limiting oxygen index (LOI) method as a potential alternative index for flammability. For either of these methods, there is a discrepancy in the actual flammability limit in microgravity since material flammability can be higher in microgravity.
An international workshop was held at European Space Research and Technology Centre (ESTEC), in Noordwick, Netherlands in January, 2017. At that meeting, the science teams presented their status to the group. In addition, plans for a parabolic aircraft campaign were discussed.
A series of NASA Glenn Zero Gravity Research Facility (ZGRF) tests were continued this year with the updated Microgravity Wind Tunnel, which includes a new longer test section and two high resolution GIGE cameras. The tests were performed to determine the approximate high velocity blowoff limits for thin cotton fabrics for both opposed and some concurrent flow conditions. The materials were ignited in normal gravity and then the experiment was dropped. The ambient gas oxidizer concentration was switched to the test atmosphere to determine if the flame could survive in the reduced oxygen concentration during the 5.18 second drop.
For opposed flow flame spread, the lowest section of the flammability boundary is filled in with microgravity drop data, and the wings of the boundary include normal gravity blowoff data from Fernandez-Pello, Ray, and Glassman (18th Symposium on Combustion, 1981) and Solid Surface Combustion Experiment (SSCE) quiescent microgravity data from Ramachandra et al. (Combustion and Flame 100, 1995). The minimum in the flammability boundary is at an oxygen concentration of ~13% O2 at approximately 10 cm/s, which is in the range of spacecraft ventilation flow velocities.
The normal gravity buoyant only limit occurs at a limiting oxygen concentration of ~15.9% O2, significantly higher than the observed minimum in the flammability boundary. This demonstrates how a normal gravity test is not a conservative test to evaluate microgravity flammability. However, it may be possible to account for the buoyant flow and correct the data to predict a conservative microgravity limit, since the blowoff boundary is linear with flow down to very low velocities. If the blowoff boundary is determined via 1g testing, and the buoyant flow contribution is included, the minimum in the flammability boundary can be estimated by extrapolating to zero flow.
Some concurrent ZGRF tests have also been conducted near the bottom of the flammability boundary, and the blowoff limits are even lower than opposed limits.
Steady flames are obtained as low as 12% O2. The 12% O2 concurrent ZGRF flame spread tests were tracked to determine if they appeared to be stable. The flame length appears to grow linearly with flow, and the flame spread rate increases linearly with flow as well. This is in agreement with numerical modelling (Ferkul and T'ien, 1994). The flame length increases linearly with the flame spread rate, in agreement with the Markstein and deRis paper (1973) where they indicate a concurrent flame over a given material should have a constant burnout time (length/spread rate) for fixed oxygen and pressure.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Combustion science
Task Description:
The objective of the project is to develop a methodology to correlate material flammability limits in normal gravity and microgravity, which allows quantitative estimation of material flammability limit in microgravity based on the flammability data obtained on the ground. The project involves an international team including JAXA, NASA, ESA (European Space Agency), and universities in Japan, USA, and France. Dr. Olson is a U.S. Co-Investigator for the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)-sponsored experiments to be conducted aboard the Japanese Experiment Module, Kibo.
To establish global standards for fire safety in space, we seek to develop a fundamental understanding of how NASA’s material flammability test, NASA-STD-6001.A Test 1, relates to the actual flammability of materials in micro and partial gravity.
The investigation strategy is to perform extensive research via ground-based experiments, including 1g and parabolic flight tests, and via theoretical formulations. Flight experiments on orbit in International Space Station (ISS)/KIBO will be performed to verify the correlation. The flight experiments on orbit are expected in 2018 or later.
By the end of the project, a new fire safety standard test method for screening spacecraft materials will be proposed that addresses the shortcomings of existing standard test method such as NASA STD 6001B.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Studying materials flammability in space allows us to accurately control the flow field and thus elucidate the importance of a critical Damkohler number (flow time /reaction time) on flame extinction. The anticipated improved methodology should reduce time and cost for the spacecraft material screening. Investigation and results have Earth benefits for terrestrial fire safety.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2016
Task Progress:
An international workshop was held at Hokkaido University in Sapporo, Japan in January, 2016. At that meeting, the science requirements were reviewed and finalized. The science teams presented their status to the group. In addition, plans for a parabolic aircraft campaign were discussed.
A series of NASA Glenn Zero Gravity Research Facility (ZGRF) tests were performed this year with the updated Microgravity Wind Tunnel, which includes a new longer test section and two high resolution GIGE cameras. The tests were performed to determine the approximate high velocity blowoff limits for thin cotton fabrics. The materials were ignited in normal gravity and then the experiment was dropped. The ambient gas oxidizer concentration was switched to the test atmosphere to determine if the flame could survive in the reduced oxygen concentration during the 5.18 second drop.
For opposed flow flame spread, the low gravity blowoff limits were determined at three oxygen concentrations. These were compared to normal gravity data. The 1g data indicates the limiting (zero flow) oxygen concentration is ~15.9% O2, significantly higher than the observed ZGRF limits at ~13% O2. This demonstrates how the 1g test is not a conservative test to evaluate microgravity flammability. However, it may be possible to account for the buoyant flow and correct the data to predict a conservative microgravity limit.
Some concurrent ZGRF tests have also been conducted, and the blowoff limits are even lower than opposed limits, but further drop and 1g testing is required to determine if a similar shift in the limits is feasible for concurrent flow. Because concurrent flames grow rapidly, it is difficult to get a 1g flame blowoff before the flame exceeds the apparatus size.

Task Progress:
A workshop for the project was held January 2015 at NASA’s White Sands Test Facility. A presentation was made to the international team discussing the Burning and Suppression of Solids –II (BASS-II) test results obtained in 2014. In addition, pressure effects on flammability limits were examined.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Task Description:
This work is based on a micropropulsion idea generated from a relatively recent discovery concerning the behavior of laminar flames propagating in very narrow tubes. When a slow laminar flame is ignited near the closed end of a tube, the material ahead of the flame is accelerated and a boundary layer is formed along the walls in the unreacted material. Due to the presence of the boundary layer, the flow velocity changes across the channel, increasing from zero at the wall to a maximum in the middle of the tube. Previous simulations have shown that the nonuniform flow stretches the flame, so that the shape of the flame becomes similar to the velocity profile. This increases the flame surface area, thus accelerating the energy generation and the flow. There is little change in the laminar burning rate, but the speed of the flame that propagates with the flow grows very rapidly in the laboratory frame of reference, from centimeters per second to hundreds of meters per second for adiabatic walls.
The high-speed flow created by the accelerating flame has the potential to provide a significant thrust that can be further enhanced by attaching an appropriately shaped exist nozzle. The thrust will gradually increase as the flame and flow accelerate, and reach a maximum when the flame approaches the open end of the tube or the nozzle. We consider regimes in which the flame remains laminar until the end of the tube and does not produce strong shocks or detonations. In contrast to the majority of other combustion-based propulsion concepts, most of the thrust here can be provided by the material accelerated ahead of the flame. Therefore, a propulsion device could be only partially filled with a combustible mixture. The rest of the material can be an inert gas or combustion products from a previous pulse. Task Objective: To explore the possibility of using flame acceleration in narrow tubes for micropropulsion. This micropropulsion concept is of particular interest for low-gravity environments, where relatively small, controlled thrusts could be used for navigational corrections. In such cases, there might not be a need for the high repetition rates required for pulse combustion and pulse detonation engines.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The micropropulsion concept has a potential to provide significant benefits for space exploration and satellite navigation.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress: A flame propagating towards the open end of a partially obstructed channel filled with a gaseous combustible mixture can accelerate or oscillate, depending on the channel width and obstacle configurations. The accelerating flame is able to produce a high-speed flow at the open end of the channel that has the potential to provide significant thrust, and this can be used in micropropulsion devices. We study these phenomena for channels with obstacles using multidimensional reactive Navier-Stokes numerical simulations. Computations show that at initial stages, the flame and flow acceleration is caused by thermal expansion of hot combustion products. At later stages, shock-flame interactions, Rayleigh-Taylor, Richtmyer-Meshkov, and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, and flame-vortex interactions in obstacle wakes become responsible for the increase of the flame surface area, the energy-release rate, and, eventually, the shock strength. Computations performed for different channel widths d with the distance between obstacles d and the constant blockage ratio 0.5 reproduce the main supersonic regimes observed in experiments: choking flames, quasi-detonations, and detonations. For quasi-detonations, both the initial DDT and succeeding detonation reignitions occur when the Mach stem, created by the reflection of the leading shock from the bottom wall, collides with an obstacle. As the size of the system increases, the time to DDT and the distance to DDT increase linearly with d2. We also observe an intermediate regime of fast flame propagation in which local detonations periodically appear behind the leading shock, but do not reach it. Channels with obstacles are of a particular interest for micropropulsion because they can provide simple ways to control combustion regimes and trust development by changing the channel width, the obstacle spacing, or the fuel/oxydizer ratio.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
A laminar flame propagating towards the open end of a narrow channel filled with a gaseous combustible mixture can accelerate or oscillate, depending on the wall temperature and the channel width. The accelerating flame is able to produce a high-speed flow that has the potential to provide significant thrust, and this can be used in micropropulsion devices. We study these phenomena using multidimensional reactive Navier-Stokes numerical simulations, and show that for adiabatic walls, the maximum flame acceleration occurs when the the channel is about 10 times larger than the reaction zone of a laminar flame. In three-dimensional square channels, the flame speed increases roughly 2 times faster than in idealized two-dimensional channels. The accelerating flame generates weak compression waves that propagate with a local sound speed ahead of the flame. If the channel is long enough, the compression waves may converge to a strong shock, and eventually trigger a detonation that develops in the shock-compressed material near the wall. In shorter channels, the flame and the unreacted material ahead of it can accelerate to the velocities close to the sound speed without creating strong shocks. This combustion regime is of particular interest for micropropulsion because it allows an efficient use of fuel and a gradual development of the trust. The results of numerical simulations were used to determine key specifications for proof-of-principle experiments at NASA Glenn Research Center.

The high-speed flow created by the accelerating flame has the potential to provide a significant thrust that can be further enhanced by attaching an appropriately shaped exist nozzle. The thrust will gradually increase as the flame and flow accelerate, and reach a maximum when the flame approaches the open end of the tube or the nozzle. We consider regimes in which the flame remains laminar until the end of the tube and does not produce strong shocks or detonations. In contrast to the majority of other combustion-based propulsion concepts, most of the thrust here can be provided by the material accelerated ahead of the flame. Therefore, a propulsion device could be only partially filled with a combustible mixture. The rest of the material can be an inert gas or combustion products from a previous pulse. To explore the possibility of using flame acceleration in narrow tubes for micropropulsion. This micropropulsion concept is of particular interest for low-gravity environments, where relatively small, controlled thrusts could be used for navigational corrections. In such cases, there might not be a need for the high repetition rates required for pulse combustion and pulse detonation engines.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Work on the flame-vortex interaction project during this year has focused on the development and evaluation of systematically reduced kinetic-mechanisms for accurately simulating flame vortex-interaction in different gravitational environments. The systematically reduced mechanisms were incorporated into the FLAME3D code developed previously.
The main idea behind systematic reduction of mechanisms is to reduce a "starting" reaction mechanism by computing some of the intermediate species assuming quasi-steady-state (QSS) behavior. By doing this, we no longer need to solve a transport equation for these intermediate species, and do not include them in the energy balance or the transport property calculations. Systematically reduced mechanisms are detailed in numerous papers (Smooke, 1991) and will only be outlined here. The first step is to choose an appropriate starting mechanism for the given conditions you are interested in. For our studies, we used the methane Peters & Rogg (1993) mechanism as our starting mechanism. Intermediate species are then identified that can be approximated as QSS species. This is typically done by analyzing results using the starting mechanism and comparing temporal and spatial fluxes for candidate species. Once the QSS species are identified, a global mechanism is developed by determining the primary reaction chains and eliminating the fastest reactions using the steady-state approximations. Reaction rate for the global reactions are expressed as a summation of elementary reaction rates. The final step is to develop expressions for the QSS species using both the QSS assumption and also assuming specific reactions are in equilibrium.
The systematically reduced mechanism used for our current research follow the mechanisms used in Peters and Rogg (1993) and Chelliah (1993) for methane premixed and diffusion flames. These mechanisms use a four step global mechanism involving the transported species CH4, O2, H2O, CO, CO2, H, H2 and the QSS species OH, O, CH3, CH2O, CH2, HCO, HO2, and H2O2. We adjusted some of the expressions for the QSS species based on a series of one-dimensional premixed flame calculations computed using conditions similar to the flame-vortex conditions. We found that for most conditions we could obtain flame speeds to within 5% of the flame speed calculated using the starting mechanism, although we also found that the reduced mechanisms are generally valid for a much smaller range of conditions than the starting mechanism.
After the series of one-dimensional computations, we computed a series of two-dimensional computations with the flame-vortex interaction. In particular, we wanted to reproduce a series of cases that had been accomplished previously with weak, moderate, and strong vortices. The main emphasis of the research was to determine whether we could reproduce similar behavior with the reduced mechanisms as we saw with the starting mechanisms such as flame pinch.
From the studies, two main disadvantages were found with using systematically reduced mechanisms. The first disadvantage is that the range of conditions for which a given mechanism is valid is much smaller than with the starting mechanism. Care must be taken to ensure that the mechanism is valid in different regions of the flame. This can be difficult, especially for complex multi-dimensional flow-fields. Secondly, the QSS assumptions break down outside of the actual flame region. Because of this, the reduced mechanisms are less robust than the starting mechanism. In particular, careful attention must be given to generating valid initial conditions whether that initial condition is important or not in the subsequent studies.
In all cases, we were able to reproduce similar phenomena with the reduced mechanisms as was seen with the original starting mechanism in previous studies. The amount of CPU savings was about a factor of two better than the starting mechanism. However, for larger hydrocarbons, where the number of QSS intermediates should be much larger, there is a potential for much more significant CPU savings.

Task Description:
This ground-based (laboratory and KC-135 aircraft) study aims to (1) isolate the role of conduction heat loss on cool flame quenching and determine cool flame quenching distances (and their associated Peclet numbers) and (2) determine if cool flames can propagate through hot flame quenching distances (and vice versa) for conditions that support both cool and hot flame propagation. Buoyant convection in Earth-based studies affects the transport of heat and species, complicating the determination of the quenching distances. In the absence of buoyant flows, the quenching distances can be more clearly determined.
Various hydrocarbon-air premixtures will be tested in the laboratory, and those with chemical induction times that are sufficiently short (e.g., less than 20 s) will be tested aboard NASA's KC-135 microgravity (mg) aircraft. The results (quenching distance, flame speed near the limit of propagation, flame speed as a function of mixture Lewis number, and critical Peclet number) will be tabulated as a function of mixture stoichiometry, temperature, pressure, vessel size, and surface condition. An analytical model that includes thermal and species diffusion will also be developed and compared with the experimental results.
This proposed study fits well within NASA's strategic plan, building a foundation upon which the knowledge gained can then be applied to earth and space-based systems. Specifically, cool flames warrant special attention in reference to aircraft and spacecraft fire safety, since they occur in mixtures with compositions outside of the standard flammability limits and can transition to hot flames under appropriate conditions, i.e., multi-stage ignition. Most recently, the importance of understanding autoignition in static enclosures (e.g., fuel tanks) has been reiterated by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) (PR99-18) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), in response to the Trans World Airlines (TWA) 800 747 center wing tank explosion (FAA and DOT, 1999; NTSB, 1999). While the source of ignition aboard the TWA flight has not been definitively identified, autoignition was considered and not ruled out. It is therefore imperative that we understand the fundamental physicochemical processes and the critical parameters requisite for cool flames and autoignitions to occur to protect against them in undesirable situations. In addition, related research by the PI aims to exploited cool flames to reformulate fuels for fuel cell use as well as reduce industrial costs for gas generation.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The research is relevant to refine chemical kinetic models used to predict the autoigniton of hydrocarbon fuels for use in new engines (homeogeneous charge compression ignition engines), improve our understanding and improve the safety of fuel storage in fuel (aircraft) tanks to suppress low-temperature oxidation reactions, cool flames and autoignition.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
Cool Flames (Numerical Progress)
(1) A five-step, skeletal chemical kinetic mechanism including diffusive fluxes of heat and species has been extended to a two-dimensional, axisymmetric flames progataing in narrow channels. This model is able to provide a qualitative understanding of the structure (shape, temperature, and species profile) and stability of cool flames and low-temperature reactions. The role of the Lewis number on flame stability is also explored. In addition, the role of the characteristic vessel size and its role on the laminar to turbulent flow transition was explored (increasing vessel size increases the rise speed of the hot, less dense gas, i.e., Rayleigh number increases). In sufficiently large vessel, the flow is expected to transition to turbulence. This may be the first effort to better understand the role of weak turbulence on cool flame structure, stability and evolution.
(2) To provide a quantitative estimate of species concentrations for the proposed space-based Cool Flames Experiment, a PLUG flow reactor numerical computer model is being developed using the Centre national de la recherche scientifique (CNRS) detailed chemical kinetic mechanism for propane and/or n-butane-oxygen premixtures. Once perfected, this model will be used to predict the stable species concentrations appropriate to the proposed test points and used for both safety calculations associated with the exhaust / venting of cool flame products as well as support quantitative gc measurements. The values will be compared with gc stable species measurement accuracies to determine which species can be quantitatively measured in the space-based experiment.
Paper Presentation
A technical paper entitled “Cool Flames at Earth, Partial, and Reduced-Gravity” was presented at the Eastern States Section of the Combustion Institute at Pennsylvania State University, October 26-29, 2003. It discussed variable-gravity experiments conducted aboard NASA’s KC-135A and the effect of weak convection on cool flame stability, ignition limits and flame shape.
Papers In-Progress
A technical paper entitled “A Two-Dimensional Gray-Yang model in a rectangular enclosure including natural convection,” is being prepared.
Outreach to Undergraduate Students at Drexel University
An overview of select experiments and discussion of the research has been incorporated into an undergraduate course (UNIV 101) that Professor Pearlman teaches for incoming engineering students at Drexel University.

Task Description:
Solid fuel and premixed gas combustion exhibits some amazing self-organizaing patterns that rival those previously observed in the famous Belousov-Zhabotinskii liquid phase reaction and biological systems such as the electrical wave propagation observed in potential traces around the human heart. Such self-organizing patterns, including rotating spiral waves and target patterns, can produce instabilities and lead to nonuniform combustion and irregular pressure hstories. This can affect rocket motor thrust vs time profiles. Moreover, this study as much further reaching implications in that it may lead to an improved understanding of self-organizing structures that occur in a variety of chemical and physcal systems. Some have even suggested that such a mechanism may be responsible for LIFE on Earth and perhaps other planets! Understanding self-organizing structures is therefore imperative and will directly support our President's Exploration agenda.
In addition to understanding the mechanisms that lead to self-organization, cool flames are explored since they offer a new way to validate chemical kinetic mechanisms and an improve understanding is needed before newly developed engines (such as Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition Engines) developed by most auto manufacturers become a reality. These engines offer the high efficiency of a diesel engine with the low emmissions common to spark-ignition engines. Imrpved control, especially at high loads, is important and needs to be addressed before such revolutionary concepts become a reality. To understand cool flames, the Cool Flames Experiment haad successfully passed its science concept review several years back and was scheduled to be developed for the ISS. In the past year, little progress has been made on the development side, while significant progress has been made in modeling these phenomena.
The understanding of self-organization and cool flames are complimentary efforts with different objectives.
The first effort is directed at developing a greater understanding of the high-Lewis number diffusive-thermal instability in ground-based studies, exploring the role of Lewis number, gas mixtures, heat loss and dditives/inhibitors on system stability and reactive-diffusive structure. Experimentally, a large diameter tube filled with a mixture of known gases diluted with helium (one of the most prevalent the most prevalent elements belived to exist in the primordial gas that comprised Earth's atmosphere. The large diameter tube is important because the instability manifests itself as a long wavelength wave on the surface of an otherwise freely-propagating flame as the flame traverses the tube. To eliminate the complexities associated with the buoyant transport processes, reduced gravity testing is suggested to obtain an unobscured view of the competing diffusive processes of mass and heat.
The second effort aims to understand low-temperature oxidation reactions and cool flames. This is a flight-definition program. It considers a static reactor with prescribed mixture of known, premixed gases. The chamber and thus the gases are heated until a reaction, often a precursor to ignition, is initiated spontaneously, without spark or external ignition. In these systems, buoyancy alters the hydrodynamic, thermal and concentration fields. In turn, this alters the flame shape and reaction rate. Since the time required for reaction initiation can be on the order of minutes, or hours or even days(!), these experiments must be performed in long duration reduced gravity facilities. Such reactions have been the cause of extensive fire damage in art galleries, corn silos, grain piles, etc on Earth and it is critical to imporve our understanding of what conditions are safe and what conditions are not safe for short and long duration space flight. The amazing thing with cool flames is that the reactions can be extremely slow and take hours or days before the first sign of a fire is observed! During this time, however, ignition precursors are being formed, which can be detected in advance of the fire (autoignition event), thus preventing a fire in the first place. Prevention via early detection is no less important when it comes to fire safety then it is in medicine or other fields! Early detection saves lives!
Instabilities similar to the diffusive-thermal instability to be studied have been observed in combustion synthesis of materials, as well as a host of other chemical and biological systems, including electrical propagation of signals in and around heart tissue (note, breakup of spatially organized waves is believed to be responsible for heart problems, most notably sudden cardiac death). In material synthesis, burning of a solid is involved, which mandates that the combustion can only be understood on the surface of the material. Since the current investigation involves gaseous components, transport throughout the system can be observed and parameters more easily varied. The knowledge thus gained, which is not available in any other configuration, should be directly applicable to combustion synthesis of materials as well as a providing a fundamental understanding of the couplings between reaction and diffusion, common to all combustion systems. The cool flame investigation is aimed at understanding processes that occur leading to spontaneous ignition. As such, the investigation will lead to an increased understanding of the physics behind knock in engines, which fuel manufacturers avoid by using additives, control of newly developed efficient engines and safety related concerns in spacecraft. This is lacking in current combustion theory.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Refined chemical kinetic models can be baselined using the data obtained from this experimental program. These refined models will be used to more accurately predict the combustion behavior of hydrocarbon fuels at low temperatures. It is relevant to autoignition in newly developed Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition engines and also useful to mitigate potential fire hazards in space-based platforms. Prevention via early detection is no less important when it comes to fire safety then it is in medicine! Early detection saves lives!
In addition, the Cool Flames Experiment presented an altogether new way for chemists and combustion scientists to validate detailed chemical kinetic models that typically have 100's of parameters (activation energies, pre-exponential factors, temperature exponents) that must be validated and tuned to experimental data. These models can then be used to predict the temperature profiles in engines and the efficiencies that can be achieved as well as the pollutants produced. Unfortunately, NASA terminated this grant prematurely and without access to microgravity facilities, experimental data needed to validate these models cannot be obtained.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Numerical / Computation Results
1. A five-step, skeletal chemical kinetic mechanism based on the original Gray-Yang model (the first model to predict the negative coefficient behavior of low temperature oxidation of hydrocarbons) has been developed. The model includes diffusive fluxes of heat and two intermediate species (a free radical propagating species and a branching species) and allows for initiation, branching, propagating and termination steps. It is a time-dependent, two-dimensional (spherical) model with axisymmetry assumed about the vertical diameter (no azimuthal variation in species concentrations, temperature of velocity). In addition, buoyancy convection is incorporated using the Buossinesq approximation in an otherwise assumed incompressible flow. This model is numerically solved and used to gain qualitative information on the behavior of cool flames at reduced-gravity, partial-gravity, and terrestrial conditions.
2. The model described in (#1) has been solved. Numerical results have been obtained on the two-dimensional temperature contours as a function of time for prescribed Arrhenius parameters (pre-exponential factors of reaction rates for each of the five steps, and appropriate activation energies) and assumed constant properties (cp) and diffusivities for heat and species concentrations. Species concentrations and velocity profiles remain to be analyzed. Ground-based (1g) studies have been performed using propane-air and propane-oxygen gaseous mixtures at select test conditions. The data has been analyzed and plots detailing the pressure history for different reactor temperatures, flame diameter versus time, and the associated ignition diagrams have been developed. Temperature contours predicted using modified Gray-Yang skeletal kinetic model at different instants in time; Temperature scale in K.
3. A skeletal chemical kinetic mechanism developed by Wang and Mou to predict cool flame behavior in a CSTR (continuously stirred tank reactor) has been modified to include diffusive transport, a requirement for all unstirred, static reduced gravity studies. The model has been numerically coded and preliminary results have been obtained. For the first time, time-periodic, damped temperature oscillations are predicted at reduced-gravity. Experimentally, such temporal oscillations have been not (as yet) been observed at reduced-gravity for unity Lewis number within the available 20s on the KC135 aircraft, yet have been observed at high Lewis number (Le>>1) in butane-oxygen mixtures that have significant helium dilution. The oscillatory nature of cool flames at reduced-gravity is intricately linked with the conductive heat versus diffusive species transport. Additional experiments and numerical analysis is planned to further clarify the thermokinetic and diffusive couplings and explore the way these couplings lead to oscillations, sustained or damped.
Cool Flames (Experimental Progress) 1.Cool flames in propane-oxygen and propane-air mixtures, based on the experiments conducted during the May 12th KC135 flight week at NASA GRC were very difficult, if not impossible, to image with our intensified cameras. Only one cool flame was imaged for a range of pressures, temperatures and fixed mixture composition (50vol%propane: 50vol.% oxygen). A more sensitive camera (CIR LLL camera) was subsequently tested and found to be sufficiently sensitive to image most equimolar propane: oxygen cool flames.
2. To determine the light emission spectrum associated with cool flames in propane-oxygen premixtures, an emission spectrometer was mounted such that the light emission, as viewed from the side window of the furnace (looking through the furnace windows and reactor vessel wall), was collected via a fiber optic cable and lens coupling In preliminary tests conducted using an equimolar propane:oxygen mixture at sub-atmospheric pressures and a fixed temperature (320oC), the spectrum could not be determined since the signal-to-noise ratio was inadequate (less than one). Averaging and increased integration times were tested, yet the spectrum remains undetermined. Based on this study, a high temperature fiber optic that can be inserted directly into the reactor is being pursued to eliminate transmission losses associated with the furnace windows and flask walls.
3. The CIR LLL-UV camera was shipped, setup and tested at Drexel University to determine it's ability to image low-light level cool flames in propane-oxygen premixtures at laboratory conditions. For nearly all conditions in the lab, the cool flames were successfully imaged, albeit in some cases with image-enhancing software. A new rack is being developed for the camera and support hardware in preparation for the next KC-135 cool flame experiment campaign.
4. Select experimental test points were conducted aboard NASA's KC135 microgravity aircraft (2 flight weeks) during microgravity, Martian and Lunar parabolic maneuvers using the same test mixtures. This data is currently being analyzed and directly compared to the 1g (laboratory) data to help clarify the role of the diffusive fluxes and weak buoyant convection (weaker than that on Earth) on cool flames and auto-ignition flame structure, emission, induction period and stability.
5. Ongoing collaboration with Professor Griffiths at University of Leeds to develop a comprehensive 1-dimensional cool flame model for propane: oxygen at low pressures has continued. This is in support of the current KC-135 aircraft studies and the future space-based experiments.
