Task Description:
This grant considers high Lewis number premixed gas flames and cool flames at reduced gravity. The Cool Flames Experiment successfully passed the science concept review in 8/00 and preparation is in progress for RDR.
Description: This is a two part project. The first part aims to better understand the effect of Lewis number on the diffusive-thermal instability in premixed gas flames. In essence, the structure and stability of premixed flames is determined by the chemistry coupled with transport of heat and mass (chemical species). When the ratio of the rate of heat diffusion to mass diffusion is greater than one (i.e., a high Lewis number), the flame becomes unstable and develops spatio-temporal patterns that appear in the form of target and spiral waves. These flame instabilities were predicted in the late 1970's, but have only recently been observed in the lab, albeit highly distorted due to complications associated with buoyant convection. At microgravity, experiments will eliminate buoyant complexities and isolate the roles of heat and mass diffusion on the flame structure and stability, the system will be reduced to a tractable experiment and it will be modelled. This effort is a ground-based study.
The second part of the project aims to study cool flames, which are very weak flames that occur in almost all fuel-air mixtures when they are heated. For over thirty years, cool flames have been oberseved in closed reactors, yet complications associated with natural convection have prevented researchers from modelling these systems and quantitatively comparing experimental data. At microgravity, however, a unique environment exists where complications associated with natural convection can be mitigated and the structure, stability and evolution of cool flames can be determined. This effort encompasses two distinct investigations with complimentary but different objectives. The first effort is directed at developing a greater understanding of the high-Lewis number diffusive-thermal instability. This is a ground-based effort. The role of Lewis number, gas mixtures, heat loss and the role of additives/inhibitors are studied in both normal and reduced gravity. The system in which this instability will be investigated is a large diameter tube filled with a mixture of known gases that are ignited at one end. The large diameter tube is important because the instability manifests itself as a long wavelength wave on the surface of an otherwise freely-propagating flame as the flame traverses the tube. The buoyant rise of hot products due to gravity scales as the square root of g (earth’s gravity) multiplied by the tube diameter. To eliminate the complexities associated with the buoyant transport processes, reduced gravity testing must be conducted to obtain an unobscured view of the competing diffusive processes of mass and heat. The second effort is aimed at understanding low-temperature oxidation reactions and cool flames. This is a flight-definition program. It will focus on closed, static reaction vessels into which a mixture of known, premixed gases is introduced. The chamber and thus the gases are heated until a reaction, often a precursor to ignition, is initiated. In these systems, buoyancy alters the hydrodynamic, thermal and concentration fields. In turn, this alters the flame shape and reaction rate. Since the time required for reaction initiation can be on the order of minutes, hours or as long as days, these experiments must be performed in long duration reduced gravity facilities. In addition, all existing cool flame and thermal ignition models (e.g., Semenov, Frank-Kamenentskii, Gray-Yang) neglect natural convection and assume conduction heat transfer. While this is not a valid assumption for most unstirred, normal gravity cool flames and autoignitions, it is exclusively valid in unstirred reactors at microgravity.The current objective for this portion of the project is to provide technical direction to the engineering teams designing and fabricating the breadboards of critical systems prior to the Requirement Definition Review. Instabilities similar to the diffusive-thermal instability to be studied have been observed in combustion synthesis of materials, as well as a myriad of other chemical and biological systems, including electrical propagation of signals in and around heart tissue (note, breakup of spatially organized waves is believed to be responsible for heart problems, most notably sudden cardiac death). In material synthesis, burning of a solid is involved, which mandates that the combustion can only be understood on the surface of the material. Since the current investigation involves gaseous components, transport throughout the system can be observed and parameters more easily varied. The knowledge thus gained, which is not available in any other configuration, should be directly applicable to combustion synthesis of materials as well as a providing a fundamental understanding of the couplings between reaction and diffusion, common to all combustion systems. The cool flame investigation is aimed at understanding processes that occur leading to spontaneous ignition. As such, the investigation will lead to an increased understanding of the physics behind knock in engines, which fuel manufacturers avoid by using additives, together with safety related concerns in spacecraft. Such an understanding is lacking in current combustion theory.

These refined mdoels can then be used to more accurately predict the combustion behavior of hydrocarbon fuels at low temperatures. It is relevant to autoignition in newly developed Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition engines and also useful to mitigate potential fire hazards in space-based platforms.

EXPERIMENTAL PROGRESS Low pressure experiments using equimolar propane: oxygen and propane:oxygen:nitrogen premixtures were conducted during the August, 2004 KC-135 aircraft flight week at NASA GRC. Approximately 40 tests were conducted at four different temperatures ranging from 320 to 350C using a static, unstirred, quartz reactor. Radially-propagating, diffusive-controlled single cool flames, multi- and single-stage ignitions were observed following an induction period that is dependant on the mixture composition, temperature, pressure and gravity level. Using the CIR LLL-UV camera, spectral imaging of the light emission, owed to excited formaldehyde, was performed. Never before seen images of propane:oxygen cool flames at microgravity were obtained. Post-analysis of the spectral data will clarify the spatio-temporal formaldehyde concentration, which will be used to validate recently developed detailed low-temperature kinetic models of cool flames (Fairlie, Griffiths, Hughes, Pearlman, 2004). With refined kinetic models, an improved predictive capability will be acquired for possible use in a variety of industrial processes including auto-ignition in diesel engines and currently developed low-emission HCCI (homogeneous charge compression ignition) engines such as those under development at Sandia National Labs and by automotive manufacturers. Additional KC-135 aircraft testing is required to obtain data over a broader range of temperatures, pressures, and mixture compositions to improve our understanding of auto-ignition, help mitigate fire safety hazards in spacecraft, learn new ways to use cool flames to refine petroleum fuels and generate hydrogen gas for fuel cells (a new effort is being explored independently by our group at Drexel, DOE, and NASA GRC).
Representative cool flame experiments have also been conducted at Martian and Lunar gravity are shown below to demonstrate the importance of natural convection on the flame structure, temperature and species profiles. An understanding of these effects is important to mitigate fire hazards and optimize the combustion process of hydrocarbon fuels at different g-levels, including those associated with Mars and the Moon, in support of the President's new exploration vision.
Note also that the existing cool flame apparatus can also be used to support the President's Exploration vision to study partial oxidation of hydrocarbons as well as carbon monoxide oxidation (the primary Martian-derived fuel) at partial-gravity (Lunar and Matian ) conditions as demonstrated in KC135 tests. Knowing the manner in which convection and diffusion affect the heat release and loss rates in these systems, thus temperature of the reacting gas, the amount of heat, power and electricity (e.g., thermoelectrically-derived) that can be derived from reacting CO on Mars and/or the Moon can be determined.

OUTREACH An overview of NASA's Martian rover flights has been introduced in the Compressible Gas Dynamics course (MEM 320) taught by Professor Pearlman at Drexel University. NASA-relevant examples such as temperature, pressure and density changes on leading edges of supersonic aircraft are used to demonstrate the principles of compressible gases. Cool flame research conducted aboard NASA's KC135 aircraft and reduced-gravity facilities has also been introduced.

Task Description:
The tasks completed this year include the development of a catalyst and process for the direct conversion of methane to formaldehyde and optimization of a catalyst for the conversion of carbon dioxide to methane. The undergraduate student was involved with catalysts synthesis and optimization.
For conversion of CO2 to methane we have developed a catalyst that shows over 96% selectivity for methane and recently showed how reactor design improves yield. This is significantly better than traditional catalyts.
For the direct conversion of methane to formaldehyde we have developed a catalyst for high selectivity to formaldehyde allowing process optimization to yield a commercially viable process. This is an important process as it allows us to use methane as a precursor for producer chemical production. We have demonstrated over 56% selectivity at reasonable conversion, a significant achievement which would make this process commercially viable over the current two stage process (methane to methanol, then methanol to formaldehyde). Formaldehyde is a very large volume producer chemical so the new process when optimized is potentially valuable. Current commercial processes are multistep, not suited for use in a Mars environment and very waste intensive. A patent disclosure has been submitted. Our overall objective is to develop processes for producer chemical production in a Mars environment. We have been successful in engineering catalysts that are high selectivity for the desired products in the last part of the project we are further optimizing catalysts and focusing on reactor design. New catalysts and compact reactor designs have been demonstrated. Current processes are multistep and waste intensive. In particular the direct methane to formadehyde process is far less cumbersome and waste producing than traditional process and thus consistent with application in a Mars environment. Our process is made possible by our optimize vanadium incorporated MCM-41 catalyst. As noted below formaldehyde is a major producer chemical so this also has Earth applications.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Our one step methane to formaldehyde process has significant environmental implications. Current processes are multistep and waste intensive. Our process (made possible by our optimize vanadium incorporated MCM-41 catalyst) is clean and require less capital investment. Formaldehyde is a major producer chemical.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
We have met the goals listed in our initial proposal. We have optimized at catalyst for the conversion of carbon monoxide to methane and used a short contact time reactor for the synthesis. We have also optimized a new catalyst for the conversion of methane to formaldehyde.
Carbon Dioxide to Methane We have optimized a catalyst for conversion of carbon dioxide to methane in a Mars environment. The catalyst for this process is based on the incorporation of Nickel in an MCM-41 mesoporous silica framework in order to maintain high dispersion. Pretreatment in hydrogen resulted in the best yield. For 3% Ni incorporated Ni-MCM-41, 96% selectivity to the desired product (methane) was achived at a space time yield of 633gm/kgh.
An interesting feature of our catalyst system is that selectivity increases as conversion increases. Because the selectivity increases with conversion we can go to higher temperatures in Ni-MCM-41 catalysts with smaller pores and this will give us even better yields. (The reducibility of the Ni in the MCM-41 decreases as pore size is decreased so small metal particles will be stable at higher temperatures).
Methane to Formaldehyde The current state of the art for converting methane to formaldehyde involves cumbersome 2 and 3 step processes that would be difficult if not impossible to implement in space. We have developed a process that produces very high selectivity formaldehyde at yields making it a practical and economic process. A selectivity of 60% was achieved at a space hourly time yield of 1315g/kghr significantly higher than with any other catalyst system.
The catalyst that allows these results is based on the incorporation of Vanadium in an MCM-41 mesoporous silica framework in order to maintain high dispersion and optimize the stabilization of the isolated vanadium species that is most selective for formaldehyde production.
The very high yield to fomaldeyde allowed a simplified one step process for the production of formaldehyde from partial oxidation of methane to be developed and optimized. A paper was submitted and in the final review stages on the novel application of statistical multivariate analysis and prediction through the multi-regression model for the optimization of the processing parameters in the complex reaction process. This approach is advantageous, especially when experimental evaluation and optimization of a process is time consuming and expensive. By carrying out a finite number of experiments, statistical modeling in this work shows reasonable good prediction ability in terms of methane conversion, formaldehyde selectivity, and space time yield. Moreover, not only are the synergistic effects between reaction parameters revealed, but also a comprehensive understanding of the whole production process over variation of the all reaction parameters (within the phase space represented by the experimental grid) are allowed. The final process is simpler and less waste producing than the convential multistep.

Task Description:
A cylindrical burner will be studied under microgravity conditions in both the 2.2 second drop tower and the aircraft KC135. Diagnostic techniques under microgravity condition will include color video, (CH* and OH*) chemiluminescent imaging, and the Rainbow Schlieren method. Normal gravity investigations will also be performed at Vanderbilt University and will include detailed measurements of flame structure using combustion laser diagnostics. Three different kinds of fuels will be investigated in order to examine the effects of varying Lewis number.
Task Objective:
1. Examine the effects of curvature on the flame structure of laminar diffusion flames. 2. Investigate the effects of curvature on the extinction limit of laminar diffusion flames. 3. Improve either reaction rate data or transport data for flames with a high degree of curvature.
Practical combustion devices inevitably involve turbulence to some extent, which is characterized by the concurrence of stretch and curvature. In certain circumstances, curvature may be the dominant factor of some combustion phenomena, taking the extinction of the weak turbulent diffusion flame as an example. The unique geometry of the Vanderbilt cylindrical burner enables the separation of stretch effects and curvature effects, and therefore makes the investigation of these combustion phenomena possible. A comparison of the extinction stretch rate between counterflow flames and tubular flames can reveal the effects of curvature on the extinction limit. Assisted by numerical investigations, this result will reveal improved ways to prevent or even extinguish fire under microgravity. New insights to geometry-related fire safety concerns might also be introduced.
A recent numerical study showed the non-monotonous dependence on the stretch rate of the temperature of a negatively curved laminar flame with Lewis number less than one. Such phenomena can only be seen at very low stretch rate, where the gravity effects will compromise or even prevent the discovery of this phenomenon. Only under microgravity condition, such a flame can be established and thus make the study of such kind of curvature effects feasible.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Understand effect of flame curvature on flame stability and extinction which will aid in control of fires.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
The effect of curvature on laminar flames is studied in tubular flames. For non-premixed tubular flames, curvature effects are best studied in micro-gravity to avoid deleterious effects of buoyancy. For micro-gravity study, a drop tube experiment was developed around the Vanderbilt opposed tubular burner. The drop tube experiment included fuel/oxidizer, ignition, instrumentation, and data acquisition systems. The drop tube rig passed the design review in the first 9 months of the project and the rig was constructed by NASA and Vanderbilt over the next 15 months. Prior to the safety review at the start of the 3rd year of the project, NASA re-directed its research programs and the drop tube was no longer available as a government provided facility. Extensive experiments on the effect of curvature on laminar flames in normal gravity were performed using the opposed flow tubular burner. In flame structure studies, laser-induced Raman scattering was applied to measure the temperature and major chemical species concentrations in non-premixed opposed tubular flames burning hydrogen, methane and propane fuels. The measured temperature and chemical species concentration profiles in the tubular flames were compared to detailed transport, complex chemistry numerical simulations; good agreement was found between the measured and predicted results. The importance of curvature on the temperature and extinction of non-premixed flames was found to depend on the fuel Lewis number, Lef, that is the ratio of the bulk thermal diffusivity to the fuel mass diffusivity. For example, when compared to flat flames, for opposed tubular flames burning 15% hydrogen diluted in nitrogen (Lef=0.41; a value less than 1), convex curvature toward the fuel increased the flame temperature by 80K and the extinction stretch rate was 20% higher; the flame with concave curvature toward the fuel decreased the flame temperature by 80K and the extinction stretch rate was 50% lower. The opposite effect was found for flames with fuel Lewis numbers above one. The effect of curvature is greatest for sub-unity fuel Lewis number hydrogen flames.
The effect of flame curvature on extinction on non-premixed flames for hydrogen, methane and hydrogen fuels diluted by various inert gases (Ar, He, N2, CO2) burning in air was studied in the opposed flow tubular burner. For fuel mixtures with fuel Lewis number much less than one, convex flame curvature made the flame more difficult to extinguish (vice versa for concave curvature). The opposite effect was found for fuel mixtures with fuel Lewis numbers at or above one. Thus curvature can make flames harder to extinguish.
The cellular regions of non-premixed tubular flames for low fuel Lewis number hydrogen diluted in inert gas (He, N2, Ar, CO2) vs. air flames were mapped out. Two to eight cells were found along the circumference of the diluted H2 flames near extinction. Convex curvature promoted the cellular behavior and concave curvature suppressed the cellular behavior. These instabilities were due to thermal-diffusive effects since they were not found in near unity fuel Lewis number flames. The cellular structure of premixed tubular flames was also studied.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
• The PI team has finished construction of the ignitor assembly. Due to the accessibility to the ignition region, the ignitor needs to have the ability to move back and forth approximately 3 inches in a controllable manner. The desired control mechanism is the following: whenever the lever hits a limit switch, an external circuit will flip the polarity of the power supply. This results in a reversed moving. The timing to start each move is also controllable via this external circuit.
• The PI team has finished construction and testing of the thermocouple assembly. Thermocouple mounted on a mini-translation stage is intended to acquire a temperature profile in the radial direction during the drop. This translation stage will store a program that upon triggering can execute a sequence of actions to make the measurement (e.g. to move 100 ?m per step for 100 steps).
• NASA GRC finished the construction of the experimental rig. All the parts are mounted in position. The electrical systems are wired and past the initial testing. The rig was shipped to Vanderbilt University for testing on Sep. 14, 2005. An updated version of the electrical schematic was supplied by technician at GRC.
• The PI team finished setting up the Raman scattering experimental system for a detailed laser diagnostics on the curved laminar flames under normal gravity. The tubular burner is tested at the same time. Non-premixed tubular flames of hydrogen-air will first be studied by this non-intrusive technique (Hu, et al.).
• The PI team is conducting the necessary test on the drop rig. This includes testing (1) the flow system, (2) the electrical control system, (3) the camera system, (4) the thermocouple translation stage. Some minor upgrade is carrying out by the PI team, which includes:
1> Replace the pressure relief valves with ASME VIII certified Kunkle relief valves.
2> Install extension wire for the thermocouple probe used.
3> Install resistance wire on the ignitor assembly.
• The PI team is working closely with technical monitor at NASA GRC in preparing the pneumatic pressure test request as well as the safety review for the drop rig. The documents for the pressure test are ready.

Task Description:
Cool flames are important in knock formation in internal combustion engines and in modern engine concepts operating at low temperature to achieve high efficiency and low pollution. Cool flames have been observed on the International Space Station in droplet combustion in a quiescent chamber where cool flames appeared after the hot droplet flame extinguished due to radiation. Cool flames in practical devices are subject to flow unsteadiness that stretches and curves the flames. Under NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Research Announcement science, flat cool premixed and diffusion flames in the presence of fluid stretch have been studied in opposed-jet flames that feature the interplay of finite-rate chemistry, molecular transport, and heat transfer, including radiative extinction. In opposed-jet burners, flat cool flames can transition to warm flames and hot flames with each transition driven by different chemical reactions. Flame regimes have been determined in flat cool premixed and diffusion flames, including transitions between cool, warm, and hot flames, formation of multi-stage flames, and flame extinction.
Flames in nature are not flat. Studies in opposed-jet flat cool flames lack the presence of curvature found in practical internal combustion engines. The curvature of tubular flames is expected to change where the cool flames transition to warm and hot flames, as well as stretch rate extinction values. Curvature and stretch rate are also known to produce cellular structure in flames. In this study, cool premixed and diffusion flames in tubular flames will be investigated both computationally and experimentally to determine the effect of curvature on cool flame regimes, transition to warm and/or hot flames, flame structure, multi-stage flame formation, and extinction stretch rates.
The project will use data from PSI system listed as Investigation #12 in Table A of the Program Element entitled, “Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation/Stretch Extinction using Counterflow Flames” ( https://nspires.nasaprs.com/external/viewrepositorydocument/cmdocumentid=807808/solicitationId=%7B3B58C0CA-6FF7-C12A-B5F1-75920A1809B1%7D/viewSolicitationDocument=1/E.8%20Physical%20Sciences%20Informatics_Amend36.pdf ). The computational and experimental study will expand upon this original investigation to determine the additional effect of curvature on the cool flames in terms of their transitions and structure, including cellular formation. In this study, cool flames in the tubular flame geometry will be investigated both computationally and experimentally. Gaseous fuels (dimethyl ether) and liquid fuels (dibutyl ether) will be investigated in the tubular burner to parallel earlier studies in flat, opposed-jet cool diffusion and premixed flames. The regime diagrams, flame transitions, flame structure, multi-stage formation, and extinction conditions will be determined computationally using the Vanderbilt Tubular Flame Code as a function of pressure. The detailed numerical simulation (DNS) code includes detailed molecular transport, complex chemical kinetics, and radiation heat loss. The cool tubular flame structure will be measured with advanced laser diagnostics. Raman scattering will be used to measure the flame temperature and major species concentrations. Planar laser-induced fluorescence (PLIF) of CH2O and chemiluminescence will be used as a marker of the cool diffusion flame. The tubular flame experimental and computational results will be compared to the previous cool opposed-jet results to determine the effect of curvature on the cool flame transitions, structure, multi-stage flame formation, and extinction.
Cool premixed and diffusion flames are found in diesel engines and other modern internal combustion engine concepts such as homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI), reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI), and partially premixed compression ignition (PCCI). Understanding the effects of curvature and stretch rate on cool flame transitions and structure will lead to better insight into cool flame propagation in practical internal combustion engines.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Cool premixed and diffusion flames are found in diesel engines and other modern internal combustion engine concepts such as HCCI, RCCI and PPCI. Understanding the effects of curvature and stretch rate on cool flame transitions and structure will lead to better insight into cool flame propagation in practical internal combustion engines.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2026
Task Progress:
During the current reporting period, research at Vanderbilt University has focused on simulating premixed tubular flames fueled primarily by dimethyl ether (DME), with a particular emphasis on cool flames, and how they differ from hot flames, to investigate curvature effects in mixtures with fuel Lewis numbers above unity. While DME remains the primary fuel, efforts have been made to extend the study to dibutyl ether (DBE), which is expected to exhibit stronger curvature effects due to its higher fuel Lewis number. However, the larger chemical kinetic mechanisms required for DBE have presented significant convergence challenges.
To enable more detailed simulations, new high-performance Precision 5860 computers with upgraded CPUs and increased RAM were acquired. These systems have allowed the transition from one-dimensional to two-dimensional simulations, hopefully enabling the study of cellular structures and flame instabilities that are not captured in the 1D models. These 2D simulations aim to reveal how flame curvature influences the development of cellular patterns in both cool and hot premixed flames.
Earlier simulations using a starting temperature of 550 K had limited convergence and a restricted range of computational conditions. Based on insights from related studies, the starting temperature was increased to 600 K, significantly improving numerical stability and expanding the range of accessible flame conditions. This adjustment has allowed further exploration of equivalence ratios, stretch rates, and curvature effects for DME flames under both cool and hot regimes.
Although DBE simulations remain challenging due to the size and complexity of its reaction mechanisms, initial findings identify conditions where curvature effects may be more significant. The new computational resources and higher starting temperatures have improved convergence for DME flames and enabled exploration of a broader range of flame conditions, including both cool and hot regimes.
Future work will focus on achieving stable DBE simulations, conducting 2D simulations of DME flames to study cellular flame structures, and further examining the effects of curvature and stretch. Task Description:
Cool flames are important in knock formation in internal combustion engines and in modern engine concepts operating at low temperature to achieve high efficiency and low pollution. Cool flames have been observed on the International Space Station in droplet combustion in a quiescent chamber where cool flames appeared after the hot droplet flame extinguished due to radiation. Cool flames in practical devices are subject to flow unsteadiness that stretches and curves the flames. Under NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Research Announcement science, flat cool premixed and diffusion flames in the presence of fluid stretch have been studied in opposed-jet flames that feature the interplay of finite-rate chemistry, molecular transport, and heat transfer, including radiative extinction. In opposed-jet burners, flat cool flames can transition to warm flames and hot flames with each transition driven by different chemical reactions. Flame regimes have been determined in flat cool premixed and diffusion flames, including transitions between cool, warm, and hot flames, formation of multi-stage flames, and flame extinction.
Flames in nature are not flat. Studies in opposed-jet flat cool flames lack the presence of curvature found in practical internal combustion engines. The curvature of tubular flames is expected to change where the cool flames transition to warm and hot flames, as well as stretch rate extinction values. Curvature and stretch rate are also known to produce cellular structure in flames. In this study, cool premixed and diffusion flames in tubular flames will be investigated both computationally and experimentally to determine the effect of curvature on cool flame regimes, transition to warm and/or hot flames, flame structure, multi-stage flame formation, and extinction stretch rates.
The project will use data from PSI system listed as Investigation #12 in Table A of the Program Element entitled, “Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation/Stretch Extinction using Counterflow Flames” ( https://nspires.nasaprs.com/external/viewrepositorydocument/cmdocumentid=807808/solicitationId=%7B3B58C0CA-6FF7-C12A-B5F1-75920A1809B1%7D/viewSolicitationDocument=1/E.8%20Physical%20Sciences%20Informatics_Amend36.pdf ). The computational and experimental study will expand upon this original investigation to determine the additional effect of curvature on the cool flames in terms of their transitions and structure, including cellular formation. In this study, cool flames in the tubular flame geometry will be investigated both computationally and experimentally. Gaseous fuels (dimethyl ether) and liquid fuels (dibutyl ether) will be investigated in the tubular burner to parallel earlier studies in flat, opposed-jet cool diffusion and premixed flames. The regime diagrams, flame transitions, flame structure, multi-stage formation, and extinction conditions will be determined computationally using the Vanderbilt Tubular Flame Code as a function of pressure. The detailed numerical simulation (DNS) code includes detailed molecular transport, complex chemical kinetics, and radiation heat loss. The cool tubular flame structure will be measured with advanced laser diagnostics. Raman scattering will be used to measure the flame temperature and major species concentrations. Planar laser-induced fluorescence (PLIF) of CH2O and chemiluminescence will be used as a marker of the cool diffusion flame. The tubular flame experimental and computational results will be compared to the previous cool opposed-jet results to determine the effect of curvature on the cool flame transitions, structure, multi-stage flame formation, and extinction.
Cool premixed and diffusion flames are found in diesel engines and other modern internal combustion engine concepts such as homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI), reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI), and partially premixed compression ignition (PCCI). Understanding the effects of curvature and stretch rate on cool flame transitions and structure will lead to better insight into cool flame propagation in practical internal combustion engines.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2025
Task Progress:
During the recent reporting period, progress was made in simulating tubular diffusion flames at Vanderbilt University. Using an in-house code, simulations focused on one-dimensional radial flame propagation for a preheated (550 K) N2-DME mixture versus N2-O2, at pressures up to 8 atm and with various chemical kinetic mechanisms. The study covered cool, warm, and hot flame regimes, allowing comparison with Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data for low-stretch opposed jet diffusion flames. Tubular flames, due to their inherent curvature, can affect flame behavior in non-unity Lewis number flames. In dimethyl ether (DME)-fueled flames, where the Lewis number is above unity, previous research has shown that a concave (negative) curvature toward the fuel enhances the flame, while a convex (positive) curvature weakens it.
To represent the flame structure accurately at lower stretch rates, an expanded computational domain was used to capture the flame's full thickness while keeping boundary conditions constant. This increased the flame radius and reduced curvature effects, producing results consistent with other opposed jet flame studies in terms of temperature profiles and stretch extinction limits. Future work could benefit from the use of stronger flame curvature, achievable at higher pressures or stretch rates, to enhance curvature effects in a smaller domain. Increasing the curvature should further emphasize the effect of curvature on these above unity flames.
Further computational work is being done on premixed DME/O2/O3 vs heated N2 tubular flames. These flames have hot and cool stretch extinction limits higher than the diffusion flames previously mentioned and may be able to provide better results showing the effects of curvature.
Parallel experimental work included building multiple proportional-integral-derivative (PID)-controlled temperature boxes for precise heating of gas streams, with thermocouples and insulated heating tapes around both the N2 co-flow and preheated N2-DME inner nozzle lines. Teledyne Hastings mass flow controllers were also updated with DME-compatible Perfluoroelastomer (FFKM) O-rings and recalibrated to ensure accurate flow rates, critical for experimental accuracy.
A Raman spectroscopy system was also set up, using an Nd:YAG laser doubled to 532 nm and a 1:2:4 pulse stretcher to manage power and minimize laser-induced breakdown. Testing showed good correlation with past results for H2 and CH4 tubular flames, validating this setup for further flame diagnostics.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2024
Task Progress:
The primary task of the first year of this project was to investigate the effect of curvature on cool diffusion flames at high pressure and compare to previous Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) NASA Research Announcement (NRA) Science data involving the numerical study of opposed-jet cool diffusion flames. This investigation involves comparing both temperatures and specific species concentrations that play important roles in cool flames.
The in-house tubular flame code was modified to accept the larger chemical kinetic mechanisms associated with more complex fuels such as dimethyl ether (DME) and dibutyl ether (DBE). This code can simulate both negative curvature (concave to the fuel) and positive curvature (convex to the fuel) effects to further determine the important role curvature may play in non-unity Lewis number fuels. These simulations are underway for N2-DME vs. N2-O2 diffusion flames with multiple chemical kinetic mechanisms, and show promising results for cool, warm, and hot flame structure when compared to previous opposed-jet results from other research groups under similar conditions. The simulations cover a range of curvature values and pressures up to eight atmospheres. Continued computational work involves building a more complete dataset for cool flame regimes and transitions into warm or hot flames along with temperature and species profiles at the various cool flame conditions.
Initial equipment to experimentally produce tubular cool flames at atmospheric conditions has been acquired. This equipment includes in-line gas heaters and nozzles to deliver a uniform and consistent flow at the desired temperature to produce cool flames. The computational results will provide essential information in experimentally reproducing these cool flames.

Task Description:
Partially premixed flames contain a rich premixed fuel-air mixture in a pocket or stream, and, for complete combustion to occur, they require the transport of oxidizer from an appropriately oxidizer-rich (or fuel-lean) mixture that is present in another pocket or stream. Partial oxidation reactions occur in fuel-rich portions of the mixture, and any remaining unburned fuel and/or intermediate species are consumed in the oxidizer-rich portions. A detailed understanding of the structure of partially premixed flames is important from both practical and scientific considerations. Unwanted fires can originate in a partially–premixed mode when a pyrolyzed or evaporated fuel forms an initial mixture with the ambient air which is fuel rich. Partially premixed flames occur in many applications. We have developed and implemented new measurement techniques for microgravity experiments on open flames (such as analog and digital holographic interferometry, rainbow schleiren, and the use of Fourier optics) through previous NASA–funded research. We have made detailed measurements of normal gravity flames and simulations of partially premixed flames in both normal and microgravity. We have found that (1) heat transport from the nonpremixed to the premixed reaction zones in partially premixed flames, (2) mass transport of radical species among these reaction zones, (3) heat losses (e.g., their effect on pollutant formation) from the reaction zones, and (4) the wide transport region between these zones play an important role in partially–premixed flames. A careful investigation of the interactions between transport, buoyancy, and thermal radiation will increase our understanding of these flames, resulting in better combustor design and fire safety solutions. In general, if the transport zone thickness exceeds 4 mm (as is usually the norm), gravitational effects overwhelm transport effects. Likewise to investigated lifted or propagating flames, the maximum propagation or liftoff height that is uninfluenced by buoyancy effects must be lower than ?1.6 cm for methane–air flames. Clearly, these are restrictive dimensions in which to conduct measurements with suitable clarity and resolution. Furthermore, radiation effects in these flames can be investigated in detail only under microgravity conditions. The flame structure can be modified significantly by changing the level of partial premixing, while keeping other parameters, such as overall stoichiometry, Reynolds number, etc., fixed. Since the flame structure is also influenced by buoyancy (based on the comparison of the diffusive and buoyant time scales), the effect of partial–premixing on the structure can be isolated in a microgravity environment. This has important implications with regard to modifying the flame stability and pollutant emission characteristics of practical combustors. Finally, the investigation of diffusive-thermal instability in the context of partially premixed flames is greatly facilitated in the absence of gravity. The instability, which is related to flame stretch and non-unity Lewis number, is responsible for flame tip opening, and modifying the adiabatic flame temperature and flame speed. It is also directly related to flame liftoff and blowout phenomena. A four-year experimental–numerical investigation is being conducted to investigate these various issues. While premixed and non-premixed microgravity flames have been extensively investigated, the corresponding literature regarding partially premixed flames (PPFs) is sparse. We report the first experimental investigation of burner-stabilized microgravity PPFs. Partially premixed flames with multiple reaction zones are established in microgravity on a Wolfhard-Parker slot burner in the 2.2 second drop tower at the NASA Glenn Research Center. Microgravity measurements include flame imaging, and thermocouple and radiometer data. Detailed simulations are also used to provide further insight into the steady and transient response of these flames to variations in g. The flame topology and interactions between the various reaction zones are strongly influenced by gravity. The flames widen substantially in microgravity. During the transition from normal to microgravity the flame structure experiences a fast change and another relatively slower transient change. The fast response is due to the altered advection as the value of g is reduced, while the slow response is due to the changes in the diffusive fluxes. The radiative heat loss from the flames increases in microgravity. A scaling analysis based on a radiation Damköhler number is able to characterize the radiation heat loss.
This investigation has relevance to a variety of industrial applications.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The fire safety lessons learned in space have terrestial applications.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Partially premixed flames with multiple reaction zones have been established in microgravity on a Wolfhard-Parker slot burner in the 2.2 second drop tower at the NASA Glenn Research Center. Microgravity measurements include flame imaging, and thermocouple and radiometer data. Detailed simulations are also used to provide further insight into the steady and transient response of these flames to variations in g. The flame topology and interactions between the various reaction zones are strongly influenced by gravity. The flames widen substantially in microgravity. During the transition from normal to microgravity the flame structure experiences a fast change and another relatively slower transient change. The fast response is due to the altered advection as the value of g is reduced, while the slow response is due to the changes in the diffusive fluxes. The radiative heat loss from the flames increases in microgravity. A scaling analysis based on a radiation Damköhler number is able to characterize the radiation heat loss.
Our experiments are also considering the influence of other diluents on these lifted flames such carbon dioxide and argon. These diluents are the primary components of non-halon gaseous fire extinguishing agents. Both inert species behave uniquely and differently when used as diluents. One reason arises from their differing heat capacities. The diluents also influence the flame by inhibiting the burning intensity, since they increase the third body concentrations and, therefore, influence the combustion chemistry. Different diluents also have differing radiation emission properties, which impact the heat losses from these flames. Our investigation hopes to elucidate these issues in a fundamental sense in the hope of facilitating useful fire safety strategies.

Task Description:
Partially premixed flames contain a rich premixed fuel-air mixture in a pocket or stream, and, for complete combustion to occur, they require the transport of oxidizer from an appropriately oxidizer-rich (or fuel-lean) mixture that is present in another pocket or stream. Partial oxidation reactions occur in fuel-rich portions of the mixture, and any remaining unburned fuel and/or intermediate species are consumed in the oxidizer-rich portions. A detailed understanding of the structure of partially premixed flames is important from both practical and scientific considerations. Unwanted fires can originate in a partially–premixed mode when a pyrolyzed or evaporated fuel forms an initial mixture with the ambient air which is fuel rich. Partially premixed flames occur in many applications. We have developed and implemented new measurement techniques for microgravity experiments on open flames (such as analog and digital holographic interferometry, rainbow schleiren, and the use of Fourier optics) through previous NASA–funded research. We have made detailed measurements of normal gravity flames and simulations of partially premixed flames in both normal and microgravity. We have found that (1) heat transport from the nonpremixed to the premixed reaction zones in partially premixed flames, (2) mass transport of radical species among these reaction zones, (3) heat losses (e.g., their effect on pollutant formation) from the reaction zones, and (4) the wide transport region between these zones play an important role in partially–premixed flames. A careful investigation of the interactions between transport, buoyancy, and thermal radiation will increase our understanding of these flames, resulting in better combustor design and fire safety solutions. In general, if the transport zone thickness exceeds 4 mm (as is usually the norm), gravitational effects overwhelm transport effects. Likewise to investigated lifted or propagating flames, the maximum propagation or liftoff height that is uninfluenced by buoyancy effects must be lower than ?1.6 cm for methane–air flames. Clearly, these are restrictive dimensions in which to conduct measurements with suitable clarity and resolution. Furthermore, radiation effects in these flames can be investigated in detail only under microgravity conditions. The flame structure can be modified significantly by changing the level of partial premixing, while keeping other parameters, such as overall stoichiometry, Reynolds number, etc., fixed. Since the flame structure is also influenced by buoyancy (based on the comparison of the diffusive and buoyant time scales), the effect of partial–premixing on the structure can be isolated in a microgravity environment. This has important implications with regard to modifying the flame stability and pollutant emission characteristics of practical combustors. Finally, the investigation of diffusive-thermal instability in the context of partially premixed flames is greatly facilitated in the absence of gravity. The instability, which is related to flame stretch and non-unity Lewis number, is responsible for flame tip opening, and modifying the adiabatic flame temperature and flame speed. It is also directly related to flame liftoff and blowout phenomena. A four-year experimental–numerical investigation is being conducted to investigate these various issues. While premixed and non-premixed microgravity flames have been extensively investigated, the corresponding literature regarding partially premixed flames (PPFs) is sparse. We report the first experimental investigation of burner-stabilized microgravity PPFs. Partially premixed flames with multiple reaction zones are established in microgravity on a Wolfhard-Parker slot burner in the 2.2 second drop tower at the NASA Glenn Research Center. Microgravity measurements include flame imaging, and thermocouple and radiometer data. Detailed simulations are also used to provide further insight into the steady and transient response of these flames to variations in g. The flame topology and interactions between the various reaction zones are strongly influenced by gravity. The flames widen substantially in microgravity. During the transition from normal to microgravity the flame structure experiences a fast change and another relatively slower transient change. The fast response is due to the altered advection as the value of g is reduced, while the slow response is due to the changes in the diffusive fluxes. The radiative heat loss from the flames increases in microgravity. A scaling analysis based on a radiation Damköhler number is able to characterize the radiation heat loss.
This investigation has relevance to a variety of industrial applications.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The fire safety lessons learned in space have terrestial applications.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
Partially premixed flames with multiple reaction zones have been established in microgravity on a Wolfhard-Parker slot burner in the 2.2 second drop tower at the NASA Glenn Research Center. Microgravity measurements include flame imaging, and thermocouple and radiometer data. Detailed simulations are also used to provide further insight into the steady and transient response of these flames to variations in g. The flame topology and interactions between the various reaction zones are strongly influenced by gravity. The flames widen substantially in microgravity. During the transition from normal to microgravity the flame structure experiences a fast change and another relatively slower transient change. The fast response is due to the altered advection as the value of g is reduced, while the slow response is due to the changes in the diffusive fluxes. The radiative heat loss from the flames increases in microgravity. A scaling analysis based on a radiation Damköhler number is able to characterize the radiation heat loss.
Our experiments are also considering the influence of other diluents on these lifted flames such carbon dioxide and argon. These diluents are the primary components of non-halon gaseous fire extinguishing agents. Both inert species behave uniquely and differently when used as diluents. One reason arises from their differing heat capacities. The diluents also influence the flame by inhibiting the burning intensity, since they increase the third body concentrations and, therefore, influence the combustion chemistry. Different diluents also have differing radiation emission properties, which impact the heat losses from these flames. Our investigation hopes to elucidate these issues in a fundamental sense in the hope of facilitating useful fire safety strategies.

Task Description:
This proposal is a request for continued funding for an experimental and computational study that has been supported through the NASA microgravity grants program from February 1999 through February 2003. The work has investigated the structure and suppression of low strain rate non-premixed flames under normal gravity and microgravity conditions. The topic is relevant from both a fire safety and a fundamental perspective. Unwanted fires typically occur due to non-premixed combustion. In terms of fire protection, the agent concentration required to achieve suppression of non-premixed flames is important.
In the current study, a drop tower rig and associated diagnostics have been prepared to conduct suppression experiments in the 2.2 s NASA-Glenn drop tower. Preliminary experiments have measured the critical N2 concentration required for flame suppression when N2 is added to the fuel stream of methane-air diffusion flames. Normal-gravity measurements have been conducted for comparison with the microgravity results. In addition, the measurements have been compared to computational results. Measurements were compared to a previously developed one-dimensional flamelet code that was modified to include radiative heat loss by participating gas species. A transient axisymmetric flame simulation is being developed. The preliminary version of the code uses a mixture fraction approach to simulate the dynamics of flame transition from normal to microgravity in drop tower experiments.
The work proposed here is an extension of the current study. The proposed research addresses several areas beyond what is expected to be completed by the end of the current grant period. The proposed study includes: (1) broadening the scope of the tests to include a variety of fuels and agents. Fuels other than CH4 that are more representative of actual fires (higher sooting tendency) and agents other than N2 that are representative of suppressants in use on space platforms (CO2, CF3Br, etc) will be investigated. It is expected that a database of suppression requirements for a matrix of fuels and suppressants will be useful to NASA for sizing agent mass requirements for total flooding applications; (2) diagnostic capabilities will be added to the microgravity experimental rig including (a) the use of radiometers to measure radiative emission for comparison to the simulations and (b) the use of two-color pyrometry to measure soot volume fractions; (3) the flame simulations will be enhanced such that (a) the one-dimensional flamelet code will be modified to include soot and the radiative emission due to particulates when appropriate. The computed flame structure will be validated by comparison with the measured distributions of temperature, heat flux, and soot; and (b) The two-dimensional transient flame simulation will be improved by inclusion of finite rate kinetics and radiative flame emission. The proposed model would then allow insight into the dynamics of flame extinction. The objective is to characterize the influence of thermal radiation on flame extinction. The task will enable us to beteer engineer fire safety.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Fire safety is of concern in both space and earth enviironments.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress: We have characterized the influence of thermal radiation with various diluents on flame stability. How a thermally radiating diluent is introduced is important. For instance, we find that when carbon dioxide is injected directly into the fuel-rich central jet of a coflow flame, it is more effective at suppressing the flame than when it is introduced into the air coflow. This influence changes in normal and microgravity.

NOTE: Continuation of "Experimental Investigation of Emulated Burning Rate at Various Gravity Levels," grant NNX10AD98G, with the same Principal Investigator (PI) (Ed., 1/14/2015)
A novel experimental apparatus, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), was developed. This apparatus is capable of assessing ignitability, steady burning rate, and extinction characteristics of virtual solid and liquid fuels as a function of gravity level, flow characteristics, and orientation. By changing the fuel gas and its flow rate, it enables the emulation of steady combustion for a range of liquid and solid fuels having B numbers (mass transfer numbers) and radiation characteristics that fall anywhere within physically realistic bounds. Measurements of the critical mass flux at ignition can also be made. These measurements were conducted as a function of scale and orientation to assess turbulent and laminar burning in natural convection. The experiment is well suited to testing in the Combustion Integrated Rack aboard the International Space Station. The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) simulated the steady burning of liquids and solids using a rectangular porous burner fed by gaseous fuel and equipped with a total heat flux sensor. BRE controlled the fuel flow rate based on the measured heat flux at the burner and the measured surface temperature. This allowed it to use a small number of gaseous fuels to match the following four properties of a large number of condensed fuels: heat of combustion (LHV), heat of vaporization (L), surface temperature (Ts), and laminar smoke point. Extinguishment was considered via changes in fuel flow rate. Both low flow rates (for kinetic extinction) and high flow rates (for radiative extinction) were considered. The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5%; and 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project is expected to improve the understanding of fire and combustion processes in both microgravity and normal gravity. It also could advance the state of the art in the design of porous burners and simple heat flux meters.

Dehghani P, De Ris JL, Quintiere JG. "Demonstrating steady burning for small flat materials in microgravity in a quiescent ambient." Proceedings of the Combustion Institute. 2022 Nov 8. Online ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2022.08.107 , Nov-2022
The likelihood of steady burning in microgravity is examined with BRE using a gas burner with a flat 25 mm diameter porous surface with two embedded heat flux sensors. The data are greatly expanded from a previous work. The fuel mixture used in this analysis are ethylene and ethylene diluted with nitrogen, resulting in a range of heats of combustion from 12 to 47.2 kJ/g. An analytical solution of these flames was utilized to compute their steadiness, temperatures at flame sheet, and sizes. 103 flames were ignited in an ambient with nominal oxygen mole fractions of 0.21, 0.265, 0.34, and 0.40. 49 of those flames burned for the entire duration of the test before the fuel supply was terminated, while the remainder self-extinguished. The flames attained at least 90% of their asymptotic heights for all 49 fuel terminated flames. An estimated critical steady flame temperature ranging from 1100 to 1200 K was observed, segregating the sustained and self-extinguished flames. Flame temperatures for the 49 terminated flames were above the critical temperature range, indicating sustained steady burning, whereas below they self-extinguished. An empirical correlation of the radiative fraction, based on radiation theory with O, a dimensionless parameter, was used in prediction for real fuels at steady burning in microgravity. A flammability diagram, as a plot of the emulated fuel heat of gasification with its burning mass flux, for the range of steady data, was presented in technical reporting to NASA, comparing how real fuels might burn steadily in normal and microgravity conditions. The results suggest that fuel mass burning rates would be about 3 to 4-times higher in 1-g. The heats of gasification and combustion of some real fuels were presented and compared against the burner flames.

Task Description:
NOTE: New grant awarded 80NSSC20M0119 with new start/end dates 4/9/2020-10/08/2021; added on to existing grant NNX15AD06A per D. Stocker/GRC (Ed., 10/13/20)
NOTE: Continuation of "Experimental Investigation of Emulated Burning Rate at Various Gravity Levels," grant NNX10AD98G, with the same Principal Investigator (PI) (Ed., 1/14/2015)
A novel experimental apparatus, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), is being developed. This apparatus is capable of assessing ignitability, steady burning rate, and extinction characteristics of 'virtual' solid and liquid fuels as a function of gravity level, flow characteristics, and orientation. By changing the fuel gas and its flow rate, it will be possible to emulate steady combustion for a range of liquid and solid fuels having B numbers (mass transfer numbers) and radiation characteristics that fall anywhere within physically realistic bounds. Measurements of the critical mass flux at ignition can also be made. These measurements will be conducted as a function of scale and orientation to assess turbulent and laminar burning in natural convection. The experiment is well suited to testing in the Combustion Integrated Rack aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) will simulate the steady burning of liquids and solids using a rectangular porous burner fed by gaseous fuel and equipped with a total heat flux sensor. BRE will control the fuel flow rate based on the measured heat flux at the burner and the measured surface temperature. This will allow it to use a small number of gaseous fuels to match the following four properties of a large number of condensed fuels: heat of combustion (LHV), heat of vaporization (L), surface temperature (Ts), and laminar smoke point.
Extinguishment will be considered via changes in fuel flow rate. Both low flow rates (for kinetic extinction) and high flow rates (for radiative extinction) will be considered.
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows:
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5%; and 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project is expected to improve the understanding of fire and combustion processes in both microgravity and normal gravity. It also could advance the state of the art in the design of porous burners and simple heat flux meters.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
We completed the Round 2 testing aboard the International Space Station (ISS). We continued working on the data analysis of all Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) data.
Three journal papers and four conference papers and posters were published this year.
We have performed power-law regression analyses of radiation fraction and surface heat flux with test conditions, i.e., mass flux, surface temperature, the heat of combustion, oxygen mole fraction, and pressure.
Regression analyses were performed on the ISS measurements to examine correlations of burning rate. The best correlations obtained to date correlate burning rate with oxygen mole fraction and heat of gasification. Pressure has no statistical effect on burning rate. A flammability map is in progress in terms of heat of combustion vs. heat of gasification for each ambient condition. It will identify flammable regions.
We continued to analyze the thin-filament pyrometry (TFP) results, and the correlations between radiative loss fraction, adiabatic flame temperature, and peak temperature. We are collaborating with Alex Snegirev to obtain Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) runs of these flames. [Ed. Note: See bibliography.]
We extracted steady heat flux on the burner surface and flame radiation measurements analysis to report heats of gasification (which corresponds to a range of solids) and radiative loss fraction correlation with flame height.
We developed a MATLAB code to read an image sequence with an unlimited number of images and to measure flame dimensions for each image.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
We compared the calculated convective heat flux, flame height, and radius, from the ellipsoidal model, with the ISS measurements. These are documented in a summary spreadsheet for the round 1 tests.
We organized the existing ISS Round 1 data and also added to it to develop our “ISS summary spreadsheet,” which contains a summary of measurements and derived quantities.
We compared measured heat flux at the center of the burner surface, flame height, and radii with their theoretical counterparts.
We extracted steady heat flux on the burner surface and flame radiation measurements analysis to report heats of gasification (which corresponds to a range of solids) and radiative loss fraction correlation with flame height.
We began an analysis of the video records from all four cameras in Round 1.
We developed a Matlab code to read an image sequence with an unlimited number of images and to measure flame dimensions for each image.
We worked on radiation fraction correlations with a non-dimensional theoretical variable and corrected radiative heat flux to the bevel edge, which was used to also correct the calorimeter for the bevel edge effect.
We finalized the radiation dimensional analysis for prediction of flame radiative loss fraction. We are currently working on the uncertainty analysis.
We worked on the ISS test matrix and documentation for the second round of testing (i.e., parameters spreadsheet, ignition flow timing calculations, and estimation of the heat-flux/flame-size steadiness to obtain an appropriate burn time for the experiments with the 50 mm burner).
We performed RadCal calculations to determine absorption coefficients for varying oxygen mole fractions and fuel fractions for PMMA, POM, PP, and PS.
Two test days have been completed in round 2. In the first day the flow rates specified in the test parameters were not achieved. This has now been corrected. We have requested a make-up day, which will be day 9 if the request is granted.
We have made good progress analyzing the Day 1 and 2 results. We are converting the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) camera still images into color videos. Predictions made for these tests are being compared with the measured results.
We have continuously updated the Round 2 test matrix and parameters as tests are performed. This includes changing the test day order and the fuel bottles and flow meters associated with each day.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
Two journal papers were published in 2019, one was accepted, and a fourth was submitted. One M.S. student defended his thesis on BRE and graduated.
Round I of BRE testing on the ISS was performed in 2019 and is now complete. A total of 63 BRE flames were observed on the 25 mm burner during eight test days. The results are highly significant. Many flames were observed to burn steadily, which was not expected by most microgravity combustion experts.
We have been analyzing the data for all 63 ISS tests, including the radiometers, heat flux gauges, and calorimeter. We developed a flammability map for steady flames. We obtained heats of gasification for all 29 steady tests using the calorimeter.
On every ISS test the heat flux sensors in the burner surface experience discontinuities. These are upward jumps in sensor output, from typically 3-6 kW/m2, typically about 60 s after ignition. These jumps are attributed to water condensation and evaporation.
We performed normal gravity experiments to optimize the pre-flow sequence for Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) ISS tests. This is required owing to the large plenum in the BRE burners.
In normal gravity we successfully emulated methanol pool fires of methanol, acetone, and ethanol. For this we matched heat of combustion, smoke point, heat of gasification, and flame height. We began emulating several plastics. We continued to analyze normal-gravity tests with propane. This included fitting flame height correlations and analyzing the theoretical convective heat flux.
The heat flux readings and the temperatures of the heat flux sensors seem to be reversed from what is expected. We investigated if these wires could be crossed or the data reversed somehow. We performed paint degradation tests to study the heat treatment effect on the calibration constant. We repainted one of the heat flux sensors to investigate possible paint degradation. Any degradation has only a minor effect on the measurements.
We calibrated the top-plate calorimeters for the various burners in normal gravity and microgravity. This requires a detailed heat flux analysis and yields a set of calorimeter constants for each burner. We optimized the calorimeter calibration for the 25 mm ISS burner. This was confirmed by the center heat flux gauge and the radiant fraction.
We explored extensions to the Baum ellipsoidal model. This is now able to predict the transient shapes of the ISS flames.
We worked on the radiation analysis of the ISS tests with three different methods. These were Mean beam length; Thin hemispherical flame; and Thin ellipsoidal flame with considering the flame standoff distance. These analysis help estimate the radiant fraction and the radiative flux to the burner surface as a function of radius.
Alex Snegirev and his team continued to perform Fluent simulations of the BRE flames in microgravity.
Work continued in finalizing the ISS test matrix for Round II and a possible bonus round.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
One journal paper was published in 2018 and a second one was accepted. Three conference papers, posters, and abstracts were published and presented.
Akshit Markan defended his Ph.D. dissertation and graduated. He has started a position at Whirlpool Inc.
Parham Dehghani started his Ph.D. Eric Auth started his M.S.
Alex Snegirev and his team continued to perform Fluent simulations of the BRE flames in microgravity.
James Quintiere and Parham Dehghani visited NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) to learn about the flight hardware and operations.

We designed an igniter similar to that on ISS to study ignition conditions at different igniter locations/orientations. We created a Kanthal A1 igniter tip to mimic the one used by NASA and developed a Matlab code to predict igniter temperature with fuel flowing in normal gravity. The optimum radius for the ignitor position was tested.
The ISS radiometer diagnostics were reviewed. A similar system was configured for testing at University of Maryland.
We stripped the paint and repainted (with Rustoleum paint) several of our burners and heat flux gauges.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
One journal paper was published in 2017 [Ed. note: see previous year's Bibliography section] and a second one was submitted. Four conference papers or abstracts were published and presented.
The detailed calorimeter model has improved. This considers a heat balance for the copper slug of the burner and may provide more accurate measurements of heat feedback to the surface than the heat flux gages. This model has been validated for the UMD (University of Maryland) burners by conducting normal gravity tests. The model was also applied to drop-tower burn tests. We are able to predict the average heat flux for these tests. This alternative approach to calculate heat flux is compared to the theoretical heat flux predicted by the analytical model of H. Baum.
A heated sphere transient model was developed numerically and analytically (with Howard Baum) for the BRE burner. Two methods were tested to estimate the convective heat transfer coefficient (during drop tower tests) and compared to theoretical values. We are preparing an abstract for the National Combustion Meeting and a journal paper for Combustion and Flame.
The solution for the 1D transient combustion model has been derived. The solution contains expressions for the velocity field, temperature field, density and species mixture fractions.
The unsteady combustion model for the BRE burner is complete with the velocity field, temperature field, density and species mixture fractions derived. The model considers a porous ellipsoidal particle with fuel leaving its surface at a constant rate. The model has been tested against the 5 s drop tests and shows good agreement.
James Quintiere gave a plenary lecture at the 9th International Seminar on Flame Structure, Novosibirsk, Russia. Its title was, A Gas Burner Emulator for Condensed-Phase Burning.
Alex Snegirev’s team in St. Petersburg has completed their first CFD simulations of BRE flames. The UMD unsteady analytical model is being compared to the CFD simulations. The model is being modified to introduce radiative loss fraction as an additional parameter.
Akshit Markan was awarded the UMD Graduate School’s Outstanding Graduate Assistant Award for 2017. This was for his role as Graduate Research Assistant on the BRE project. Only the top 2% of Graduate Assistants were selected for this award.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
One journal paper was published in 2016 and a second one submitted last year has just been published in January 2017. Three conference papers or abstracts were published and presented.
Two BRE spaceflight burners were sent to UMD (University of Maryland) for flow and flame characterization and heat flux gauge calibration. This was for both transient and steady operation, and accounts for different paints on different surfaces. The burners were then returned to NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC). The spaceflight burners are sufficient to achieve the BRE flight objectives pending microgravity flame testing.
The 5 s BRE drop test program at GRC has completed. A total of 51 drop tests were performed. The results are being scrutinized to determine accurate rates of heat flux to the burner surface.
An improved calibration rig for heat flux meters was developed. Calibration of heat flux gauges was performed, particularly our standard meters traceable to NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) and MedTherm.
A model was developed to estimate the incident heat flux at the burner surface using the copper plate as a calorimeter. This will provide an independent measurement of heat flux to the burner surface (in addition to the heat flux gauges). The model considers transient heating, radiative emission, convection to the surroundings, conduction into the burner walls, and conduction into the heat flux gauges. The model has been applied to the spaceflight BRE burners and the UMD burners. Normal gravity tests were conducted on the UMD burners in order to validate the calorimeter model. The model was used to predict the average heat flux for the drop-tower tests. We are able to predict the average heat flux for these tests. This alternative approach to calculate heat flux is compared to the theoretical heat flux predicted by the analytical model of H. Baum.

Task Description:
A novel experimental apparatus, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), is being developed. This apparatus is capable of assessing ignitability, steady burning rate, and extinction characteristics of 'virtual' solid and liquid fuels as a function of gravity level, flow characteristics, and orientation. By changing the fuel gas and its flow rate, it will be possible to emulate steady combustion for a range of liquid and solid fuels having B numbers (mass transfer numbers) and radiation characteristics that fall anywhere within physically realistic bounds. Measurements of the critical mass flux at ignition can also be made. These measurements will be conducted as a function of scale and orientation to assess turbulent and laminar burning in natural convection. The experiment is well suited to testing in the Combustion Integrated Rack aboard the International Space Station.
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) will simulate the steady burning of liquids and solids using a rectangular porous burner fed by gaseous fuel and equipped with a total heat flux sensor. BRE will control the fuel flow rate based on the measured heat flux at the burner and the measured surface temperature. This will allow it to use a small number of gaseous fuels to match the following four properties of a large number of condensed fuels: heat of combustion (LHV), heat of vaporization (L), surface temperature (Ts), and laminar smoke point.
Extinguishment will be considered via changes in fuel flow rate. Both low flow rates (for kinetic extinction) and high flow rates (for radiative extinction) will be considered.
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows.
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5%; and 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
