Task Description:
A novel experimental apparatus, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), is being developed. This apparatus is capable of assessing ignition, steady burning rate, and extinction characteristics of 'virtual' solid and liquid fuels as a function of gravity level, flow characteristics, and orientation. By changing the fuel gas and its flow rate, it will be possible to emulate steady combustion for a range of liquid and solid fuels having B numbers (mass transfer numbers) and radiation characteristics that fall anywhere within physically realistic bounds. Measurements of the critical mass flux at ignition (flashpoint) and extinction (fire point) can be made. These measurements will be conducted as a function of scale and orientation to assess turbulent and laminar burning in natural convection. The experiment is well suited to testing in the Combustion Integrated Rack aboard the International Space Station and aboard parabolic aircraft. The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) will simulate the steady burning of liquids and solids using a porous burner fed by gaseous fuel and equipped with a total heat flux sensor. BRE will control the fuel flow rate based on the measured heat flux at the burner and record the measured surface temperature. This will allow it to use a small number of gaseous fuels, mixed with diluent, to match the following four properties of a large number of condensed fuels: heat of combustion, heat of gasification, surface temperature, and laminar smoke point. The gas flow rate will be adjusted such that the heat flux to the burner surface matches the heat required to vaporize the appropriate flow rate of liquid or solid fuel. Extinguishment will be considered via changes in fuel flow rate. Both low flow rates (for kinetic extinction) and high flow rates (for radiative extinction) will be considered. The flight objectives for BRE are:
1. Burn gaseous fuels in BRE to simulate the burning rates of condensed fuels in a quiescent microgravity environment. Instantaneous flame heat flux will be measured and used to control the rate of fuel supply. Fuels to be simulated include paper, plastic, and alcohols.
2. Burn gaseous fuels in BRE to estimate the ignition and extinction behavior of these condensed fuels in microgravity.
3. Use BRE to estimate the effects of burning at enhanced oxygen conditions in microgravity.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This project is expected to improve the understanding of fire and combustion processes in both microgravity and normal gravity. It also could advance the state of the art in the design of porous burners and simple heat flux meters.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2013
Task Progress:
Michael Bustamante received his MS degree, his thesis entitled: EXPERIMENTAL INVESTIGATION OF LIQUID AND GAS FUELED FLAMES TOWARDS THE DEVELOPMENT OF A BURNING RATE EMULATOR (BRE) FOR MICROGRAVITY APPLICATIONS, is available from the University of Maryland. A paper and presentation was made at the Dayton Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute April 22–24, 2012 entitled: Laminar Burning on Flat Wicks at Various Orientations by M.J. Bustamante, K.T. Dotson, Y. Zhang, P.B. Sunderland, J.G. Quintiere. The paper contains experimental and theoretical analysis on the burning of flat plates in natural convection at orientation angles of +90 to - 90 (with 0 being vertical). It also shows how a burner can emulate the burning of methanol and ethanol saturated on the plates. In addition aircraft flight and drop tower experiments explored the burning of these alcohols on flat plates. Quasi-steady flames were indicated in some cases, suggesting the possibility of steady burning in micro-gravity. A 50 mm diameter burner was designed and constructed to investigated the emulation of pool fires. Two heat flux meters recorded the flame heat flux at two point on the surface. By matching the flow rate of the burner fuel to the burning rate of the pool fire, and using a fuel and diluent mixture to best match the heat of combustion and smoke point, the heat of gasification was duplicated for methanol, heptane and PMMA. So three condensed phase fuels were emulated to demonstrate the validity of the burner concept.
In August a SRD report was presented for review, and the Committee gave positive feedback in supporting the project's continuation in the ACME space station experimental program.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2012
Task Progress:
• A second M.S. student joined this project: Yi Zhang.
• Michael Bustamante has been selected as a NASA Space Technology Research Fellow for 2011/2012. Bustamante’s application was entitled “Burning Rate Emulator Experiments for Spacecraft Fire Safety.” Bustamante’s fellowship includes a student stipend, faculty advisor funding, on-site allowance, and support for health insurance and tuition and fees. He will conduct research at NASA Glenn and NASA Johnson.
• A heat flux gauge was incorporated into the wick apparatus.
• An additional array of tests were performed with liquid wicks resulting in incident heat flux data, and flame standoff characterization through the full range of angles. A method was developed for consistent and accurate measurement of the standoff distance. Additional tests were also performed recording burning rate measurements to strengthen the previous data set.
• Findings were presented at U.S. National Combustion Meeting (see below).
• A basic gas burner was constructed capable of testing at all angles of orientation for the purpose of doing some preliminary testing to assist in the design of the next iteration of the BRE.
• Gas burner tests were performed matching the recorded mass loss rates per unit area of methanol during wick testing. Images of the resulting flames were taken, analyzed for flame standoff distance, and compared to the methanol results.
• An analytical model of the flames was developed. This predicts flame standoff distance and burning rate for laminar diffusion flames on planar wicks. Gravity can be included in any direction. The predictions are in reasonable agreement with the experiments.

Task Description:
A novel experimental apparatus, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), is proposed. This apparatus is capable of assessing ignitability, steady burning rate, and extinction characteristics of 'virtual' solid and liquid fuels as a function of gravity level, flow characteristics, and orientation. The BRE consists of a porous burner whose temperature is controlled by a heat exchanger. A total heat flux sensor is mounted in the surface of the burner to create a feedback loop where the gaseous fuel flow rate supplied to the burner is proportional to the measured heat flux. By changing the fuel gas, it is possible to emulate steady combustion for a range of liquid and solid fuels having B-numbers (mass transfer numbers) and radiation characteristics that fall anywhere within physically realistic bounds. Measurements of the critical mass flux at ignition can also be made. These measurements will be conducted as a function of scale and orientation to assess turbulent and laminar burning in natural convection. To assess gravity effects, an experiment insert will be developed for NASA parabolic trajectory aircraft that can, in principle, efficiently report the results for a range of gravity conditions, including microgravity combustion, in a single trajectory. The experiment is well suited to subsequent testing in the Combustion Integrated Rack aboard the International Space Station.

Task Description: We are applying three-dimensional direct numerical simulation and concurrent theoretical analysis to study turbulent jet flame liftoff and blowout for a variety of buoyancy conditions. There are competing theories regarding jet flame liftoff and blowout, and especially how this is influenced by buoyancy. Our objectives are to use numerical simulations and theoretical analysis to (i) test existing hypotheses, (ii) identify the governing mechanisms for liftoff and blowout, (iii) determine which of the various modeling approaches are most consistent with the governing mechanisms, and (iv) devise a means for controlling liftoff and blowout. Turbulent jet flame liftoff and blowout are of critical importance to the safety and reliability of a variety of combustion devices. Our research will help understand these phenomena, and better predict them. This information can then be used in the design of safer and more reliable combustion devices.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Our research objective is to study the process of liftoff and lifted flames in microgravity environments. Specifically, we are interested in the effects of buoyancy and forcing upon turbulent and transitioning lifted flames.
During the past year we have completed the development of our computer code for simulating buoyant and non-buoyant jet flames. The code has been developed to run on massively parallel computers, and employs state-of-the-art as well as newly developed numerical methods. This year we have applied this code to a study of the three-dimensional transitioning region of buoyant and non-buoyant jet flames. The simulations clearly show how the jet flame is strongly affected by buoyancy. We have also performed linear stability analysis, using a primitive variable formulation of the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. From this analysis it was determined that, below a certain threshold density ratio, the flows becomes absolutely unstable, in that it then supports sustained oscillations. Furthermore the Strouhal number predicted by the linearized theory correlates well with that observed in the direct numerical simulations. These theoretical and numerical results suggest optimal disturbance forcing of the jet flame in order to optimize mixing. We are presently attempting to exploit these results in further direct numerical simulations.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:
NOTE: Added to Task Book in 10/2006 per GRC
Task Description: Prediction of the optimum size and location of suppression systems for fire extinguishment in reduced gravity facilities requires either experimental measurements or computer simulations. The experimental approach requires reduced gravity testing facilities. Although this approach can generate reliable data, conducting experiments in reduced gravity is expensive, time-consuming, and only practical on a reduced-scale basis. The current experimental data available in the literature is not suitable for full-scale estimation of fire and smoke motion in space facilities, especially for determining placement of automatic suppression devices. An alternative solution to designing these systems is the use of computer modeling techniques to predict fire, smoke, and suppressant behavior in low gravity environments. The overall objective of this project is the development of an engineering tool that accurately predicts suppression agent dispersion and fire extinction for normal and low-gravity environments. To fulfill the overall objective, two computational tools, the Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) and a traditional commercial computational fluid dynamics software package (FLUENT) will be evaluated to determine if modeling of the suppression of fires can be validated for both normal and micro-gravity conditions. Experiments have been conducted to provide concentration and velocity data on suppression in normal gravity environments. The data is used to validate the computer modeling codes for the prediction of suppressant movement. Additionally, a model for local flame extinction based on a critical Damköhler number is developed for the prediction of suppression in both normal and low gravity environments.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The overall benefit of this research study will be the development of a computational tool that can be used to determine the optimum placement and use of suppression systems within any three-dimensional geometry. The immediate impact of this study will be through enhancing the total fire safety aboard the International Space Station, Crew Exploration Vehicle, and other space vessels. A secondary impact of this tool will be an optimization of suppression system placement that will allow a reduction of the amount of agent needed to extinguish fires, thus reducing the weight of the agent that must be transported to and stored on the space vessel. The use of the computational tool will not be limited solely to space vessels. Direct application of the computational tool in Earth-based facilities will have merit through the potential optimization of localized suppression systems to prevent the unacceptable spread of fire and resulting destruction. This computational tool will have the most value in facilities containing equipment that mimics the electronics and component-rich configurations of spacecraft. The Earth-based facilities most likely to benefit from an analysis using this computational tool will be telecommunication switching stations, telecommunication utility rooms, electronics utility rooms, electronics manufacturing facilities, computer networking facilities, and other such telecommunication, electronics, or computer facilities.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Through the 2006 work year, a series of experiments were conducted for validation purposes. To facilitate the validation experiments, the ground-based test mock-up construction was completed. The mock-up consisted of a reduced-scale simulated electronics rack that was one eighth of the volume of a typical rack found aboard a space vehicle such as the ISS. The dimensions of the mock-up were 0.5 meter by 0.5 meter by 1.0 meter.
The ground-based rig was designed to allow for the addition of internal obstructions to increase the complexity of the geometry. These obstructions consisted of two parallel plates, where the separation distance between the two plates could be adjusted to various widths. This mock-up design allowed for a challenging geometrical configuration for fluid flow and provided a systematic test for model validation. A gaseous agent, Nitrogen, mixed with a small amount of tracer gas, NO2, was introduced into the test apparatus through a mounted nozzle located in the center of one of the four sides of the rig. The nozzle was an exact replica of the International Space Station (ISS) CO2 extinguisher nozzle. Data acquisition for the test apparatus over the 2006 work year consisted of agent concentration measurements.
The concentration measurements were obtained in three distinct locations within the experimental apparatus during cold flow conditions (i.e., no flame and no fuel) using Planar Laser Induced Fluorescence (PLIF) of the tracer gas. By measuring the concentration level of the tracer gas, the concentrations of the suppression agent and local oxygen concentrations could be determined and compared with modeling predictions.
The test setup utilized a Nd:YAG laser beam that was turned into a sheet projected through the channel created by the parallel plates. The position and direction of the sheet could be easily changed, as could the channel gap distance and the direction of the gap (horizontal or vertical). Because of the relatively weak fluorescence of NO2, an image intensifier, including a filter to reject the incident laser light, was used. Through precise gating, the intensifier ignored the incident laser pulse but observed the fluorescence of the NO2, which has a significantly longer lifetime than the incident light.
A virtual representation of the ground-based test rig was composed using the Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST-USA). Modeling of the experimental data with the FDS code was used to determine if this code was appropriate for accurately modeling the suppression dispersion aspect of the problem.
The FDS model of the ground-based test rig was constructed to scale with the identical dimensions and layout. A layer of fluid cells was added around the rig with open pressure boundaries to ensure that the internal pressure of the model did not rise unrealistically. All obstructions present in the actual ground-based rig were accounted for and included in the model. Additionally, four vents were included in the model that represented typical vents found in space vehicle electronics racks. Overall, the model contained 518,400 cells. These cells were approximately 1.0 cm (0.4 in.) in length in the y and z directions, and 0.635 cm (0.25 in.) in the x direction to ensure accurate separation of the parallel plates so as to match the data taken via experimentation.
As mentioned above, the PLIF measurements allowed for obtaining the concentration of the tracer gas at locations between the parallel plates located within the ground-based test rig. Three test separations were chosen in an effort to determine a minimum spacing where entrance of the gas into the parallel plates would become more difficult. Due to constraints imposed by backscattering of the laser from the acrylic plates, 1.27 cm (0.5 in.) was found to be the smallest separation gap that still provided meaningful data. As such, in addition to the 1.27 cm (0.5 in.) gap, spacings of 1.91 cm (0.75 in.) and 3.18 cm (1.25 in.) were also examined in an effort to obtain concentration data.
As mentioned above, gas was injected into the test rig during testing via a nozzle that was identical to the CO2 extinguisher nozzles located aboard the ISS. This nozzle was designed with eight outlets surrounding the tip of the nozzle in a radial fashion. A ninth outlet was located directly at the tip of the nozzle. In the PLIF experiments, the testing agent was composed of a mixture of 1000 ppm NO2 mixed with a balance of N2. The test mixture was introduced into the rig at a pressure of 2.4 MPa (350 psi) over a blowdown period of approximately five seconds. After the blowdown period, concentration data was recorded for an additional 15 seconds. Results were obtained as images recorded by a digital camera with appropriate lens filters and were processed using a MATLAB routine.
A range of concentration values was obtained experimentally at the three separations tested. The peak concentrations ranged from 280 ppm of NO2 to 325 ppm of NO2. The smaller value was obtained at the 1.27 cm (0.5 in.) plate separation, and the larger value was obtained at the 3.18 cm (1.25 in.) plate separation. Predictions from the FDS modeling resulted in a fairly uniform concentration value of 400 ppm of NO2. This peak value did not vary greatly among the three plate separations. Comparison of the modeling results with the experimental results clearly shows marked differences. The modeling results produced by FDS overpredict the maximum concentration by approximately 120 ppm for the 1.27 cm (0.5 in.) case and by 75 ppm for the 3.18 cm (1.25 in.) case. The overall trends of the concentration histories are fairly similar, yet proper transport from the nozzle into the plates is not captured accurately.
Even with these differences, the FDS model only overpredicts the peak NO2 concentrations at the middle plate location by 35% at the 1.27 cm (0.5 in.) plate spacing and by 20% at the 3.18 cm (1.25 in.) plate spacing. If an average of the concentration is taken after the blowdown period has occurred, these predicted concentrations improve slightly to 30% overprediction for the 1.27 cm (0.5 in.) spacing and 18% overprediction for the 3.18 cm (1.25 in.) spacing. While these differences are significant, the results from the model still have the potential to be useful in examining the transport aspect of this problem.
Several issues will be explored in the 2007 work year in an effort to reduce the errors in the model predictions. First, a complete grid sensitivity analysis will be conducted to determine the effects of the grid. Second, a more detailed accounting of the difference between the ambient temperatures in the test rig and the inlet gases will be conducted. Within FDS, small differences in density due to temperature differences can have a significant impact. Third, the Large Eddy Simulation (LES) routine used to obtain results to date may not capture transport at an appropriate level of detail. An as alternative, a Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) solver is available and will be explored to determine if improved results can be obtained. Finally, a commercial computational fluid dynamics modeling package (FLUENT) will be used to analyze the distribution aspect of the problem in an effort to obtain more reliable results.

Task Description:
Fire Safety on spacecraft and in potential non-terrestrial environments (e.g. Mars) is an important consideration for any mission. Safety of the crew and spacecraft, as well as continuation of the mission is dependent on adequate prevention, detection and suppression of fires in low- and micro-gravity environments. Task Description:
The research is divided into three topics: 1) radiation-dominated flame spread over thick fuel beds, 2) concurrent-flow flame spread rates and extinction conditions effects of convective and radiative losses, and 3) addition of gaseous fuels to the oxidizing atmosphere.
Flame spread over flat solid fuel beds is a useful means of understanding more complex, two-phase, non-premixed flames, such as those found in fires in enclosures, e.g., manned spacecraft and terrestrial buildings. Both transport and chemical effects are well known to affect the characteristics of flame spread. Conductive, convective and radiative transport processes may couple to each other and to chemical effects in unusual ways. Consequently, the goal of this work is to extend previous studies by employing µg experiments with emphasis on the atmospheres and flow environments likely to be present in fires which might occur at µg. The goal of this work is to provide information that will enhance crew safety in manned spacecraft including the Space Shuttle, International Space Station, and potential future missions to the moon and Mars.
The understanding and control of accidental fires is a critical safety issue in both terrestrial and space-borne environments. Space environments are different from earth-based environments for several reasons. Of course, the major difference is the lack of buoyancy-induced convection. Another difference is that fires in spacecraft may occur in non-standard atmospheres because of the use of non-standard breathing atmospheres or the use of diluents as fire extinguishing agents. Consequently, the understanding of these effects is critical to understanding how fires might start, spread, and be extinguished at µg conditions. One of the tasks of this project, the study of CO2 as a fire extinguishing agent, is particularly relevant to fire safety on the International Space Station, whose fire suppression system uses CO2 as the extinguishing agent. Our experiments show that CO2 is less effective that other agents such as helium at microgravity, whereas the opposite is true at earth gravity.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Radiation is the main mechanism of fire spread between buildings, thus understanding radiation effects on fires is useful to fire prevention and suppression on earth as well as in space.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress: The rates of flame spread and minimum oxygen concentrations supporting flame spared over thermally-thick fuel beds were determined at earth gravity and microgravity for varying concentrations of a gaseous extinguishing agent (N2, CO2 or He) added to “baseline” O2-N2 atmospheres. Drop towers were used to obtain microgravity, and foam fuels were employed to obtain sufficiently rapid flame spread in these short-duration facilities. At earth gravity, CO2 was the most effective on a molar basis at reducing spread rate and causing flame extinction whereas at microgravity, He was the most effective. These findings are proposed to result from the transition from a high-speed blowoff-type limit at earth gravity to a low-speed radiative heat loss-induced limit at microgravity. CO2 is less effective as an extinguishment agent at microgravity because it re-absorbs radiation from flame and re-radiates it back to the fuel bed at microgravity, whereas with N2 and He this phenomena is not evident at microgravity because these two gases are radiatively non-participating. He is particularly effective at microgravity because its high thermal diffusivity leads to much larger flame thicknesses resulting in much greater volume for radiative heat losses. Radiative effects are unimportant at earth gravity because convective flow is significantly faster, leading to thinner flames with much lower ratios of radiative to conductive/convective heat transfer. These results are particularly noteworthy considering that the International Space Station employs CO2 fire extinguishers; our results suggest that helium may be a better extinguishing agent on both mass and mole bases at microgravity even though CO2 is much better on a mole basis at earth gravity.

Task Description:
The research is divided into three topics: 1) radiation-dominated flame spread over thick fuel beds, 2) concurrent-flow flame spread rates and extinction conditions effects of convective and radiative losses, and 3) addition of gaseous fuels to the oxidizing atmosphere. Flame spread over flat solid fuel beds is a useful means of understanding more complex, two-phase, non-premixed flames, such as those found in fires in enclosures, e.g., manned spacecraft and terrestrial buildings. Both transport and chemical effects are well known to affect the characteristics of flame spread. Conductive, convective and radiative transport processes may couple to each other and to chemical effects in unusual ways. Consequently, the goal of this work is to extend previous studies by employing µg experiments with emphasis on the atmospheres and flow environments likely to be present in fires which might occur at µg. The goal of this work is to provide information that will enhance crew safety in manned spacecraft including the Space Shuttle, International Space Station, and potential future missions to the moon and Mars. The understanding and control of accidental fires is a critical safety issue in both terrestrial and space-borne environments. Space environments are different from earth-based environments for several reasons. Of course, the major difference is the lack of buoyancy-induced convection. Another difference is that fires in spacecraft may occur in non-standard atmospheres because of the use of non-standard breathing atmospheres or the use of diluents as fire extinguishing agents. Consequently, the understanding of these effects is critical to understanding how fires might start, spread, and be extinguished at µg conditions. One of the tasks of this project, the study of CO2 as a fire extinguishing agent, is particularly relevant to fire safety on the International Space Station, whose fire suppression system uses CO2 as the extinguishing agent. Our experiments show that CO2 is less effective that other agents such as helium at microgravity, whereas the opposite is true at earth gravity.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Radiation is the main mechanism of fire spread between buildings, thus understanding radiation effects on fires is useful to fire prevention and suppression on earth as well as in space.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Flame spread tests were performed in the NASA-Glenn Zero Gravity Facility (ZGF) to define the test matrix for the REEFS space flight experiments in the FEANICS facility. Foam fuels were chosen for these tests to represent a thermally-thick solid fuel that could provide sufficiently high spread rates that meaningful data could be obtained within the µg time available in drop-tower experiments. Two types of thermally-thick, open-cell foams were tested: rigid polyphenolic (PP) foam and flexible polyurethane (PU) foam. Over 150 tests were conducted.
The salient features of these results are:
1. At earth gravity all three diluents have nearly the same efficacy in reducing flame spread rates and causing flame extinction, for total pressures and oxygen mole fractions tested. 2. At microgravity, for higher total pressures and lower oxygen mole fractions, all three diluents have nearly the same efficacy in reducing flame spread rates and causing flame extinction 3. Most importantly, at microgravity, for lower total pressures and higher oxygen mole fractions, CO2 is clearly the least effective of the three diluents tested and He appears to be the most effective. 4. The spread rates in undiluted atmospheres is higher at microgravity, but dilution has a stronger effect on spread rates at µg than at 1g.
At low pressures, at earth gravity, the spread rates are almost independent of pressure whereas at microgravity, the spread rates are substantially higher at higher pressure. This again shows the qualitative change in behavior between earth gravity and microgravity for thermally-thick fuels. At earth gravity, the efficacy of all three diluents for high O2 concentration / low total pressure conditions is similar, leading to speculation that again He may be the most effective diluent at µg.
The effect of opposed flow velocity (U) on flame spread rate was measured. With 35% O2 in CO2 at 2 atm total pressure, the spread rate shows a slight minimum at an intermediate value of U (˜ 1 cm/sec). A minimum spread rate at intermediate U is consistent with the predictions of a theoretical model developed for this purpose.
A series of tests were conducted to determine whether tests at earth gravity, for either upward or downward flame spread, are “conservative” in that the minimum oxygen mole fraction (LOI) supporting combustion is higher at microgravity than at earth gravity. If earth-gravity tests are “conservative,” then earth gravity flammability criteria may safely be used to screen materials to be used at microgravity conditions. Two different foam materials were used: polyphenolic green and polyurethane. A comparison of the LOI data for earth gravity (upward and downward flame spread) with microgravity conditions showed that of the cases tested only one, namely high-pressure O2-CO2 atmospheres, shows this non-conservative behavior. This is believed to be related to radiation effects, which are most prevalent at high pressure and with CO2 diluent.
Most potentially flammable materials of interest, with the exception of paper, are thick enough that the material can be considered thermally-thick, that is, the thermal penetration depth into the fuel bed is smaller than the physical thickness of the fuel sample. The difficulty in assessing the flammability of thermally-thick materials at µg is that long durations of µg are needed since spread rates are slow and the corresponding characteristic time scales are long. REEFS skirts this problem by employing foam fuels that have much lower density and thermal conductivity than fuels conventionally used in thick-fuel flame spread experiments (e.g. PMMA), and thus much faster spread rates. In this way, some meaningful results can be obtained even in short-duration drop tower experiments. Even in space experiments where µg time is less of a consideration, dense fuel experiments present difficulties. Because of the large length and time scales, ignition energy requirements are large, and available test facilities such as CIR may have inadequate size test sections. Some space experiments may continuously feed a roll of thermally-thin fuel (e.g. paper) into the test section, with a feedback mechanism to maintain the flame front at a specified location. By using "compressible," flexible foam fuel such as REEFS' polyurethane foam, it is proposed that the roll-fed apparatus could be modified to incorporate thermally-thick foam fuels. Consequently, tests using polyurethane foam were conducted to determine if this flexible fuel could be deployed in the roll configuration. Results show that foam density changes less than 10% compared to the original values for practically all conditions tested.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Earth gravity and drop-tower experiments have shown that for thermally-thick foam fuel beds, three fire extinguishing agents (helium, nitrogen and carbon dioxide) have nearly the same efficacy in reducing flame spread rates and causing flame extinction for a wide range of total pressures and oxygen mole fractions. Moreover, even at microgravity, for higher total pressures and lower oxygen mole fractions, all three agents have nearly the same efficacy in reducing flame spread rates and causing flame extinction. However, at microgravity, for lower total pressures and higher oxygen mole fractions, CO2 is clearly the least effective of these three agents tested and He is the most effective. The spread rates in undiluted atmospheres is higher at microgravity, but dilution has a stronger effect on spread rates at microgravity than at earth gravity.
On a simple heat capacity basis, one would expect CO2 to be the most effective extinguishing agent and He the least effective since CO2 has the highest heat capacity of the three extinguishing agents tested and He has the lowest. Thus, dilution by CO2 should lead to the largest reduction in flame temperature and thus the smallest spread rate. In contrast, the experimentally observed results show exactly the opposite trend at low pressures and high oxygen mole fractions. We believe there are three reasons for this behavior. First, the Lewis number of O2 in He is much higher than O2 than in N2 or CO2 (1.20 vs. 1.00 vs. 0.84), which, as previous work has shown, leads to significantly lower flame temperatures and lower spread rates for He than would be expected on a simple heat-capacity basis. Second, the dramatically higher thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity of He compared to N2 or CO2 (1.82 vs. 0.22 vs. 0.12 cm2/s) leads to much thicker flames and thus greater radiative loss for the same spread rate in the case of He. Third, unlike CO2, N2 and He are radiatively non-participating and thus no reabsorption or re-emission occurs. The reabsorption reduces heat loss to ambient and the re-emission increases the total heat flux to the fuel bed, both of which increase the spread rate in the case of CO2.
There are also other potential advantages to He as an extinguishing agent for spacecraft applications. For example, He is far more effective on a mass basis at both 1g and µg. Additionally, He has no physiological activity, unlike CO2 which affects human respiration. Moreover, as compared to N2 or CO2, He is not very soluble in water (about 8.6 ml/liter at 20°C, compared to 16.9 for N2 and 1019 for CO2) and thus has less tendency to cause bloodstream bubble formation following accidental or intentional spacecraft cabin depressurization. (The Space Shuttle uses intentional partial cabin depressurization, with a corresponding increase in O2 mole fraction, as a standard procedure for Extra-Vehicular Activity because it leads to a shorter period of time that the EVA astronauts need to pre-breathe pure O2 before suiting up and depressurizing to the 0.2 atm, pure O2 environment of the EVA suits.)
The effect of opposed flow velocity (U) on flame spread rate was also measure for foam fuels. With 35% O2 in CO2 at 2 atm total pressure, the spread rate shows a slight minimum at an intermediate value of U ( about 1 cm/sec). A minimum spread rate at intermediate U is consistent with the predictions of a simple model we developed. The theoretical predictions show that for denser fuels, the differences in spread rate between quiescent microgravity, microgravity with weak flow and earth gravity are more significant, indicating that for denser fuels, thus earth gravity data may be even more atypical of spread rate characteristics at quiescent or low-flow microgravity conditions.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
The effects of radiation heat transfer in microgravity were investigated for opposed-flow (downward) over thermally-thick fuel and were compared to convection heat transfer in earth gravity. Microgravity experiments on flame spread over thermally-thick fuels were conducted using foam fuels with lower density and thermal conductivity compared to denser fuels such as PMMA, and thus, larger flame spread rates were obtained. Hence, valid microgravity results were obtained even in 2.2-second drop-tower experiments, not to mention for the longer duration tests in Zero Gravity Facility. In contrast to the conventional understanding, it was found that steady flame spread can occur over thick fuels in quiescent microgravity environments, especially when radiatively-active diluent gases such as CO2 were employed. This result is proposed to be due to radiative heat transfer from the flame to the fuel surface, which could lead to steady spread even when the amount of the heat transfer via conduction from the flame to the fuel bed is negligible. Radiative effects are more significant at microgravity conditions because the flame is thicker, and thus, the volume of radiating combustion products is larger. These results suggested that helium may be a better extinguishment agent on both mass and mole bases at microgravity even though CO2 is much better on a mole basis at earth gravity. These findings are relevant to studies of fire safety in manned spacecraft, particularly the International Space Station that uses CO2 fire extinguishers. CO2 may not be as effective as an extinguishing agent at µg as it is at earth gravity in some conditions because of the differences in spread mechanisms between the two cases. In particular, the difference between conduction-dominated heat transport to the fuel bed at earth gravity and radiation-dominated heat transport at µg indicates that radiatively-inert diluent such as helium could be preferable in µg applications. Helium may be a superior fire suppression agent at µg on several bases. First, helium is more effective than CO2 on a mole basis (i.e., the product of pressure and storage volume is smaller) at µg, meaning that the size and weight of storage bottles would be smaller for the same fire-fighting capability. Second; helium is much more effective on a mass basis (by about 11 times) at µg. Third; helium has no physiological activity, unlike CO2 that affects human respiration. Fourth, as compared to N2 or CO2, helium is not very soluble in water, and thus, has smaller tendencies to cause bloodstream bubble formation following rapid spacecraft cabin depressurization.
A number of experiments have been done with different fuels for concurrent (upward) configuration with various widths and thicknesses at various pressure levels. Unsteady, “hopping” mode of flame spread was observed in such buoyancy-driven concurrent flame spread experiments when low-density, but thermally-thick foam fuels were used. This hopping occurred regularly, spatially and temporarily in narrow samples even under conditions far from the extinction limit. These behaviors were found for a wide range of fuel types, pressures, oxygen mole fractions, and fuel widths. Heat losses via conduction through the back plate and wall play an important role in the upward flame spread, whereas its effects are less important in the downward flame spread. Tranverse heat and momentum losses are also important contributing to unsteady “hopping”, “walking” behavior and its dependence on fuel widths. This “walking” behavior can be explained by local blow-off; i.e., when the oxygen mole concentration is not sufficient, flame cannot be sustained at the full width, and splits into smaller fronts propagating locally. This creates varying buoyancy forces along the fuel width, and as a result, the flame is extinguished locally. If oxygen mole concentration is high enough, the flame burns along the full fuel width; however, turbulence still breaks the flame during hopping. When the thermal conductivity of the fuel is close to that of the gas, then hopping may occur, but if the thermal conductivity of the fuel is sufficiently high, then the hot spot gets spread out before it has a chance to grow. These hot spots formed in upward cases can be an explanation of these hopping behaviors at near limit cases for both thermally thin and thick fuels. However, more complex factors such as heat losses to the side walls and entrained oxygen by buoyancy may also be responsible for the hopping behavior for thermally-thick fuels even under conditions far from the extinction limit.

Task Description: Several studies relating to premixed laminar and turbulent flames at microgravity are being pursued. The primary task is the space flight experiment entitled “Structure Of Flame Balls At Low Lewis-number (SOFBALL)” that is investigating spherical, stable, stationary flame structures (“flame balls”) at microgravity. In addition to the space experiment and supporting ground-based microgravity experiments on the KC-135 aircraft, numerical modeling of flame balls with detailed chemical, transport and radiation emission/absorption models is being conducted. Related projects include investigation of “flame tubes” that have been discovered in stretched counterflow flames at low Lewis number, edge flames, flame propagation in Hele-Shaw cells, and experimental simulation of premixed combustion using aqueous autocatalytic chemical reactions. The objective of this work is to obtain a better understanding of the mechanisms of flammability, instability and ignition limits of premixed-gas flames and the ways in which buoyancy affects these limits. The results of these studies will lead to an improved understanding of the fire hazards that may exist in orbiting spacecraft and of ways to minimize these hazards. In particular, the SOFBALL experiments provide the opportunity to study the interactions of the two most important processes necessary for combustion (chemical reaction and heat and mass transport) in the simplest possible configuration.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
These studies may lead to an improved understanding of the mechanism of combustion limits in Earth-based devices, which in turn could lead to the development of cleaner and more efficient engines through the use of lean premixed combustors.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
On STS-107 a total of 39 tests were performed in 15 different mixtures, resulting in a total of 55 flame balls, of which 33 were named by the crew. Most tests (by design) produced only 1 flame ball, though one test intentionally designed to produce a large number of flame balls resulted in 9 balls. The total burn time for all flames was 6 1/4 hours. Since flame balls are extremely sensitive to gravitational acceleration, all tests were conducted during orbiter free drift periods. The quality of the microgravity was found to be excellent, averaging less than 1 micro-g for most tests. Over half of the science data was downlinked during the mission, resulting in minimal loss of science despite the loss of Columbia and its crew.
Among the accomplishments of the experiment were • The weakest flames ever burned, either in space or on the ground. The weakest flame balls produced about 0.5 watts of thermal power. By comparison a birthday candle produces about 50 watts of thermal power. • The leanest flames ever burned, either in space or on the ground. The leanest hydrogen-air test points contained 3.2 mole percent H2 in air (equvalence ratio
Several issues not resolved during the previous space flight experiments on STS-83 and STS-94 in 1997 were addressed by experiments on STS-107:
• Can flame balls last much longer than the 500 sec maximum test time on STS-83 and STS-94 if free drift (no thruster firings) can be maintained for the entire test? Answer: not usually - some type of flame ball motion, not related to microgravity disturbances, causes flame balls to drift to walls within ˜ 1500 seconds. The only exception to this was the very last test in which 9 flame balls formed initially and extinguished one by one until only one (name “Kelly” by the crew) remained. Unexpectedly, Kelly survived 81 minutes, seemingly immune to drift, until it was intentionally extinguished due to operational limitations (it was still burning at the time). The mechanism responsible for the drift of isolated flame balls has not yet been identified, though some mechanisms have been proposed. The shorter-than-expected test times on most tests meant enough time for multiple reburns of each mixture within the flight timeline. • Can oscillating flame balls be observed in long-duration, free-drift conditions? Answer: Probably, but it is still necessary to determine if flame ball motion rather than inherent oscillations of stationary flame balls may have caused the observed oscillations). • Are higher Lewis number flame balls (e.g. H2-O2-He-CO2, Le ˜ 0.8) more likely to oscillate, as predicted theoretically? Answer: No. These flames were extremely stable. • Do the flame balls using methane (CH4-O2-SF6 mixtures) behave differently from those in hydrogen fuel (e.g. H2-O2-SF6 mixtures)? Answer: Yes. They frequently drifted in corkscrew patterns, though again the mechanism responsible for this drift is not clear.

The proposed devices are applicable to portable electronic devices, microcombustors, microreactors and micro propulsion devices on earth as well as in space.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
By use of a novel tetrahedral configuration that resulted in minimal heat losses, catalytic combustion of propane-air mixtures on the downstream side of the membrane was able to provide the thermal power for self-sustaining pumping of the reactants. This proof-of-concept apparatus demonstrates the first-ever example of a gas pump with no moving parts that derives its energy for pumping from the gas itself with no external energy source.
Transpiration properties of glass fiber discs were enhanced by coating the disc with either a traditional silica aerogel or a macroporous silica aerogel. These results show the advantages of using materials with designed microstructures. In particular, we have emphasized the development of macroporous aerogels in which the large pore volume is determined by templating methods. The macroporous aerogel material was far more effective than the traditional aerogel as the maximum flow rate of the macroporous aerogel coated discs was 11 mL/min at a temperature difference of 280°C. Unlike the uncoated glass fiber disc, the coated disc did not exhibit a decrease in flow rate at elevated temperatures. In addition, platinum catalytic particles were fabricated by the reduction of hydrogen hexachloroplatinate in ethylene glycol.

Task Description:
Combustion experiments using arrays of droplets seek to provide a link betwen single droplet combustion phenomena and the behavior of complex spray combustion systems. Both single droplet and droplet array studies have been conducted in microgravity to better isolate the droplet interaction phenomena and eliminate or reduce the confounding effect of buoyancy-induced convection. In most experiments involving droplet arrays, the droplets are supported on fibers to keep them stationary and close together before the combustion event. The presence of the fiber, however, disturbs the combustion process by introducing a source of heat transfer and asymmetry into the configuration. As the number of drops in a droplet array increases, supporting them on fibers becomes less practical because of the cumulative effect of the fibers on the combustion process. To eliminate the effect of the fiber, several researchers have conducted microgravity experiments using single unsupported droplets -- this is the first experiment using multiple unsupported droplets. The overall objective of this research is to extend the study of unsupported droplets by investigating the combustion of well-characterized drop clusters in microgravity. This will be accomplished by forming and stabilizing a cluster of droplets in an acoustic field prior to the microgravity and combustion event. The number and size of the drops in the cluster can be accurately controlled using a custom on-demand droplet generator and the size and shape of the cluster can be controlled through the design of the acoustic resonance chamber and selection of the resonance frequency. Additionally, group combustion numbers (ratio of the mass transfer between the phases in the cloud to the mass transfer between the ambiance and the cloud surface) between 0.1 and 100 can be obtained which encompasses the individual particle combustion, group combustion, and sheath combustion regimes. Because the presence of an acoustic field greatly influences drop combustion, the field will be turned off at the start of the microgravity period. The initial diagnostic capability to be incorporated into the experimental package includes multiview imaging to view the motion of the droplets and to view the position of the flame front. Initially, droplet clusters will be formed using methanol, n-decane, and heptane as many of the droplet array and group combustion studies have done. This will allow the droplet burning rates obtained from this research to be directly compared with results of isolated droplet and droplet array studies. The position and movement of the flame front will provide some of the first experimental data for comparison with group combustion models obtained using large numbers of drops. Data will be obtained as a function of group combustion number, drop size, number of drops, and drop size distribution. Several tests are also planned in which drops will be formed with binary fuels composed of heptane/methanol, heptane/ethanol, or heptane/hexadecane to experimentally investigate the effect of fuel volatility on cluster combustion and help define future research. These fuel compositions are the same as those used in other drop combustion research, immediately linking the current results to existing research.
The specific objective of this research is to study the combustion of well-characterized drop clusters to better link isolated droplet and droplet array studies with those involving spray flames. In this study, which will be conducted in a series of drop tower experiments, the formation of the drop clusters will be precisely controlled using an acoustic levitation system so that dilute, as well as dense clusters can be created and stabilized before combustion is begun. Tasks to be accomplished during this research include (1) the design and fabrication of a unique droplet combustion experiment using acoustic levitation to stabilize a droplet cluster prior to combustion, (2) investigation of droplet combustion in the individual particle combustion, group combustion, and sheath combustion regimes by varying the number of droplets, droplet size, and cluster diameter, and (3) investigation of the effect of drop size distribution, droplet composition, and continuous-phase oxygen concentration on cluster combustion.
Isolated drop and drop array studies have become common methods to isolate and investigate the many complexities of the drop combustion process. Accordingly, several isolated drop, drop array, and spray studies are currently in progress under the NASA Microgravity Science and Applications program. Results from these research programs indicate that even with the effects of buoyancy removed, the extrapolation of the results from droplet array studies to spray flames is difficult. The problem arises because even the simplest spray systems introduce complexities of multi-disperse drop sizes and drop-drop interactions, coupled with more complicated fluid dynamics. Not only do these features make the interpretation of experimental data difficult, they make the problem very difficult to analyze computationally. Group combustion models have become a popular method to investigate the behavior of large numbers of interacting droplets. In these models, the interaction between droplets is treated in a statistical manner rather than tracking and evaluating drop interactions using a Lagrangian approach. These models have allowed very comprehensive investigations of the combustion of multi-component drops, spray ignition phenomena, high-pressure combustion, etc. While these models idealize actual spray systems to a point where they can be treated computationally, the experimental analogy to these models is difficult to achieve. Therefore, even though these models have provided useful results, the verification of the results with direct comparison with experimental data is still lacking. Direct experimental measurements in well-defined droplet clusters would fill a large gap in our current understanding of droplet combustion. The results of this study will provide an intermediate link between droplet array studies and those performed using full combusting spray systems. They will also provide unique experimental data for the calibration, verification, and improvement of group combustion models that are currently being applied to complex flow situations.

Task Description:
The experiments are aimed directly at testing, understanding and improving NASA's existing policies and practices toward spacecraft fire safety. In this study, we examine several previously unaddressed issues regarding these fire safety practices and policies. Specifically,
a. NASA Test 1 (an upward flame spread test) is the primary qualification test for materials' use on spacecraft. NASA Test 1, however, does not consider some possible fire sources and some of its assumptions remain unvalidated. These include, among others: a) Premixed fires can occur and heat and ignite solid materials, but these are unconsidered in Test 1; b) Solid materials may be heated well above normal spacecraft air temperature at the time of an accidental exposure to an ignition source (again unconsidered) and; c) The effect of firebrands in 1g is assumed to be worst case.
b. Configuration control in microgravity is unvalidated. NASA requires that flammable materials be separated by 5 cm or more, so that fire from one material cannot ignite a neighboring material.
c. There are also concerns with the fire suppression practices and policies. For example, there is uncertainty about the time to extinguish a fire upon termination of ventilation. The application of a jet of suppressant may itself produce firebrands from molten or charring material, and cause an accidental spread of fire. Finally, carbon dioxide, the suppressant of choice for the International Space Station, behaves differently than other diluent, in regard to its impact on the range of oxygen concentrations that will support a flame.
The goal of the proposed research is to contribute to improved fire safety practices and policies for spacecraft and Martian habitat through the achievement of the following objectives:
1. Determine systematically the conditions that will ignite onboard flammable materials upon passage of an initial premixed gas, firebrand, or aerosol flame over these materials.
2. Test the effect of firebrands and configuration spacing.
3. Determine the effectiveness of the flow of CO2 extinguisher or other extinguishing agents.
Fire is among the most feared hazards of human space flight. These experiments address fire safety practices and policies that have heretofore not been tested under conditions of spaceflight, i.e., in a microgravity environment.
By performing parametric experiments both in normal gravity and reduced gravity on the KC-135 aircraft, as well as developing and analyzing related modeling, generality of the interpretation of the experimental findings will be pursued along with direct recommendations for fire safety practices and policies for fire safety on spacecraft and in Martian habitats. This is the principal value of the research.

Task Description:
Partial Gravity is the environment in which planetary exploration is to occur, yet little has been done to characterize the behavior of fluid, thermal and reacting systems under reduced, but non-zero, gravitational conditions. In the case of fire safety systems, simple laboratory fuels have been shown to be substantially more flammable in partial-gravity environments than in normal Earth gravity. Such experiments are limited to the few seconds duration available using aircraft flying parabolic trajectories. While more can be done using the aircraft capability, extended duration tests will be needed to adequately explore partial-gravity behavior, especially for realistic materials and fire fighting schemes.
With the exception of conducting tests on other planetary bodies, the only extended partial-gravity test capability currently envisioned is artificial gravity obtained using a low-speed centrifuge operated in an orbiting spacecraft such as the International Space Station. In contemplating using a centrifuge to obtain artificial gravity for fire related research, the Coriolis force will be present and will induce additional complexity into the behavior of flames and other fluid systems. Careful theoretical work accompanying artificial gravity experiments will relate the results to the genuine partial-gravity environment of planetary destinations, where Coriolis effects would be negligible. However, such work will also directly model behaviors within rotating spacecraft that are envisioned for long interplanetary missions to avoid the undesirable human physiology effects of microgravity. Before proposing to use a space-based centrifuge for fire research, ground-based facilities must be used to define meaningful flight test research.
The purpose of this proposed ground-based research effort is to begin and stimulate the use of centrifuge facilities for understanding flame and fire behavior in an artificial gravity. The effort consists four progressive parts: 1) participation in the design and construction of a partial-gravity centrifuge for use in the NASA ground-based reduced-gravity facilities; 2) a pilot study of a stabilized stationary diffusion flame in artificial partial gravity; 3) a more extensive study of a spreading flame over a solid fuel in artificial partial gravity in which Coriolis effects will be quantified; and 4) the development of an unsteady, three-dimensional model that includes the Coriolis force. In keeping with the practical objectives of direct support for fire safety in spacecraft flown beyond Earth orbit, the flame spreading research will extend current understanding into the use of non-standard habitable atmospheres proposed for such spacecraft and the use of proposed extinguishing agents as atmospheric diluents.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Surface combustion, shs, fire safety and smoldering
Task Description:
This task consists of both experimental and theoretical efforts. Flame spreading experiments will be conducted, burning thin fuels in purely-buoyant flows in partial-gravity aboard reduced-gravity aircraft facilities, mainly using existing equipment. An extensive numerical modelling effort will also be conducted to provide simulations of flame spread in purely buoyant and purely forced flows.
The purpose of this research effort is to examine flame spreading and material flammability in partial-gravity environments, extended as part of this effort to as low as 10-3 g/g Earth, with the objectives: 1) to determine the flame structure, flame spreading and material flammability characteristics of thin fuels burning in opposed, buoyant flows (downward spreading); 2) to determine the flame structure, flame spreading and flammability characteristics of thin fuels burning in concurrent, buoyant flows (upward spreading) over the entire expanded range of partial-gravity levels; 3) to identify the similarities and differences of flame spreading over simple fuels in forced versus buoyant flows to aid in predicting flammability limits and flame spread behavior in extraterrestrial environments; and 4) to advance the technology for conducting high-quality reduced-gravity aircraft experiments.
This effort will provide the first experimental data and theoretical background on the relative flammability of materials and corresponding fire hazards that will be encountered in Lunar and Martian environments.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
34 normal diffusion flames (NDFs) and 38 inverse diffusion flames (IDFs) were established in earth-gravity and their high resolution photographs were taken with a view to obtaining flame length information for verifying the applicability of the Roper flame length correlations for normal and inverse flames.
The total and spectral radiation properties of 16 NDFs and 7 IDFs were measured. This is one of the first studies on the total and spectral radiation properties of oxygen enhanced inverse diffusion flames. The total radiation was measured using a radiation flux meter and the spectral radiative intensity was measured using a fast infrared array spectrometer.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
SiC filaments were used to measure flame shapes of 21% and 30% O2 earth-gravity normal and inverse diffusion flames. The filaments oxidized in the higher oxygen flames. Contours of maximum soot volume fraction were also obtained for these flames based on deposits on the SiC filaments. Further diagnostics with these filaments are being investigated. Laser extinction-based soot volume fraction measurements are currently in progress after validation.
Detailed chemistry computations of earth-gravity and microgravity flames were completed and the flame shapes obtained using the maximum temperature contours of these cases were compared with the Roper shapes. These indicate reasonable agreement for the higher oxygen flames while the differences are larger for the lower oxygen flames. Further, computational results indicate that both earth-gravity and microgravity inverse diffusion flames are more sooting and emit harmful gases at high oxygen concentrations.
Radiation calculations were performed for all the inverse diffusion flames using optically thin behavior with CO2, H2O, CO and CH4 as the participating species. Some observations from the results are as follows:
1. As expected, heat release rate and radiation emission increase with oxygen enhancement.
2. Radiation emission increases significantly with decrease in gravity.
3. Amongst all the species considered for radiation emission, CO2 contributes the maximum radiation emission (about 50 - 60% of the total radiation emission)
The coupling of the flame structure and radiation calculations is in progress. An analytical model is being developed for radiation calculations in an optically thick medium.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The Principal Investigator team at IUPUI has been developing its combustion laboratory. An enclosure, an NDF burner and an IDF burner and flow system were built for the experiments by a graduate student at IUPUI. A digital camera was purchased and used to image NDFs and IDFs. The student did his summer internship at NASA Glenn under Dr. Sunderland’s supervision. The internship provided a valuable training opportunity for the student. Development of a numerical code to predict the analytical Roper flame shape this year has resulted in establishment of empirical parameters based on microgravity and normal gravity flames. Reasonable agreement is now being obtained between the Roper predictions and observed shapes of ethane NDFs and IDFs in normal gravity and microgravity. A new PhD student has been hired at IUPUI to continue soot extinction and radiometric measurements on flames run by the previous student and some new test conditions for producing sooting flames. An undergraduate student has also been working on an independent project to design a thermophoretic sampling probe for soot for these flames.
The Co-Investigator team at Purdue (West Lafayette) has performed global chemistry and detailed chemistry computations (involving 99 species and 1066 reaction mechanisms including PAH) for the NDF and IDF configurations for which experimental data on flame shapes are available. A Ph.D. student was hired to support this effort. Some local acceleration effects noticed for the IDFs in the global chemistry calculations were confirmed to be present in detailed chemistry calculations. Domain and grid independence studies were completed for global chemistry calculations for the test cases. The results of the investigations are being compared with the experimental and analytical results and being compiled into a journal paper for publication. The model will include multi-ray, coupled radiation heat transfer calculations.

Task Description:
While past studies and current tests for fire safety have focused on normal diffusion flames (NDFs), the inverse diffusion flame (IDF) configuration is related to possible fire scenarios in spacecraft and extra -vehicular activity (EVA) environments. IDFs also are a potential fire-safety concern for medical care involving enhanced oxygen.
In industrial furnaces using oxygenenhanced combustion, flame shape control is important for obtaining a desired heat flux and temperature profile. Flame radiation predictions are functions of the flame volume and surface area.
The main objectives of the study, which focuses on NDF and IDF shapes for oxidizer varying from 21% to 100% O2, are:
1. to examine the performance of shape predictions of NDFs and IDFs using the extended Roper model with experimental results by varying assumed velocities and temperatures as suitable for 1-g and 0-g.
2. to establish the limits of applicability of these analytical predictions.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This study is of relevance to fire safety in terrestrial environments where oxygen enhanced combustion is used and in emergency rooms in hospitals etc. where oxygen storage and use is common.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
Comparisons between steady-state computational results and experimental data showed some of the following major findings:
1. Oxygen-enhanced conditions resulted in increased flame temperatures and increased buoyancy effects for normal gravity flames of constant length.
2. The present experiments, analysis, and computations indicate that gravity has a relatively small effect on flame temperature, flame width and flame length of IDFs due to the dominance of convection over buoyancy. This indicates that our planned experiments in normal-gravity IDFs will be highly relevant to oxygen-related spacecraft fire safety.
3. Calculations reveal that buoyant acceleration plays the dominant role for earth-gravity NDFs and that centerline axial velocities can be approximated assuming constant acceleration.
4. Comparisons of maximum temperatures based on present thermo -physical properties and global kinetic rates with adiabatic (2000 species) equilibrium temperatures show that the computations may be overestimating the temperature by underestimating the rates of dissociation reactions. Temperature measurements and detailed chemistry and thermo -physical property calculations are necessary to address this issue.

Task Description:
The original objective of this research was to study the combustion of bi-component miscible droplets in reduced-gravity environments so that buoyancy effects are rendered negligible. The program was termed the Bi-Component Droplet Combustion Experiment (BCDCE). Of particular interest were the burning rate (droplet history), the time to flame contraction, potential microexplosions, Marangoni flows, and sooting behaviors. The experiments used liquid mixtures selected to display influences of large component volatility differences and liquid species diffusion on combustion phenomena. The program was both experimental and theoretical in nature. Experiments included reduced-gravity studies as well as normal-gravity comparison experiments.
In fall 2005, the BCDCE program was aligned with a different program that includes a team of investigators from different universities as well as from NASA. This program, which is termed the Flammability and Extinction Experiment (FLEX), is focused upon using droplets to study flammability and extinction under reduced-gravity conditions of relevance to spaceflight and human exploration of space. The FLEX program is both experimental and theoretical in nature. Experiments include reduced-gravity studies as well as normal-gravity comparison experiments. In the research, individual droplets are dispensed, deployed and ignited in reduced gravity (as well as normal gravity). Theoretical approaches include developing computational and analytical models, with a particular emphasis on evaluating influences of gas-phase diffusive transport as well as droplet internal flows, which may arise from Marangoni stresses as well as droplet deployment and ignition.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The BCDCE research extended previous research on combustion of pure liquid fuels to mixtures of pure fuels, which more closely approximate practical fuels. The results from this research program were relevant to design of practical combustion systems that employ liquid fuels such as engines and oil-fired burners.
The FLEX results will be useful for improving understanding of combustion and fire-related phenomena under reduced gravity conditions, e.g., influences of diffusive transport and droplet internal flows on flammability and extinction.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
Reduced gravity and normal gravity combustion experiments were performed with individual droplets that were initially about 1 mm in diameter. Most experiments were performed with propanol or heptane, but some data were also obtained with methanol. The environment was composed of an air-inert mixture at 0.1 MPa and about 298 K, where helium, carbon dioxide and xenon were separately used as inerts. The amount of inert was progressively increased until droplets could no longer be ignited. The amount of inert gas required to suppress combustion was generally higher in reduced gravity than normal gravity. The data show that ambient gas transport properties such as Soret transport play an important role in determining flammability of droplets. The data also showed that flammability characteristics depend on the gravitational level and fuel type.
Analysis of previous reduced-gravity experiments involved digitizing and analyzing video images from experiments on combustion of individual propanol droplets. These experiments were conducted in air at standard temperature and with pressures ranging from 0.1 MPa to 1.0 MPa. The data show that sooting characteristics, burning rates and flame shapes vary significantly with pressure. Calculations indicate that burning rates are controlled by the liquid temperature, which increases with increasing pressure.
Computational modeling involved extending a previous 1-dimensional numerical model to account for non-unity activity coefficients for propanol-water and propanol-water-glycerol mixtures. Calculations indicate that water absorption is very small for droplets burning in air at pressures ranging from 0.1 MPa to 1.0 MPa.
A multidimensional computational model was also further developed. The code is based on overset grid technology to allow modeling of a droplet on a fiber. The code was used for droplet evaporation or combustion studies, where capillary forces were accounted for in some calculations. Results demonstrate that droplet vaporization characteristics depend on the fiber diameter and that Marangoni stresses can also be important. Three-dimensional calculations of fiber supported, or unsupported, 100 micron methanol droplets burning at elevated temperature and pressure showed that flame shapes and the onset time for ignition depend on whether a support fiber is present.
Analytical modeling focused on predicting influences of fuel pyrolysis on droplet combustion characteristics. Transfer numbers, burning rates and quasisteady flame standoff ratios can be appreciably reduced when fuel pyrolysis effects are included in the analyses. It was also found that fuel pyrolysis can influence temperature gradients between droplets and flames, which influences formation of soot shells.
The NASA Tracker Station was used to capture and analyze 16 mm films from droplet combustion experiments. A high resolution digital camera and a macro lens were used to form an automated system where individual frames of film were converted into high-resolution digital images. Custom computer codes were written for analysis of the images. Parameters of interest such as droplet and flame diameters can be efficiently determined with high resolution.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Work has principally been in the following areas: reduced-gravity and normal-gravity experiments; development of a computational model; and development and use of the NASA Tracker Station for analysis of 16mm cine films of droplet combustion experiments. A summary of the progress is given below.
Reduced-Gravity and Normal-Gravity Experiments:
Reduced gravity and normal gravity combustion experiments were performed with individual fiber-supported droplets that were initially about 1 mm in diameter. Most experiments were performed with propanol, but some data were also obtained with heptane and methanol. The environment was composed of an air-inert mixture at 0.1 MPa and about 298 K, where helium, carbon dioxide and xenon were separately used as inerts. In the experiments, the amount of inert gas in the environment was progressively increased until droplets could no longer be ignited. Droplet ignitability depended on the gravitational level as well as the inert gas in the environment. In general, the amount of inert gas required to suppress combustion was higher in reduced gravity than normal gravity. Use of xenon required significantly higher mole fractions for suppression of combustion relative to helium or carbon dioxide. The data indicate that ambient gas transport properties such as Soret transport play an important role in determining flammability of droplets.
Computational Model Development:
Results for three-dimensional numerical calculations of vaporization histories of 25-100 micron methanol droplets supported on thin fibers were developed. These droplets were assumed to be spherical. Calculations were carried out for high temperature and high pressure external flow conditions, and droplets vaporized in air. Fiber diameters of 1/20 to 1/5 of the initial droplet diameters were selected to enable investigation of the influences of support fibers on the droplet behavior. A unique feature of these calculations is that effects of thermocapillary flows were considered. The effects of the fiber on droplet internal and external circulation at low and high Reynolds numbers were investigated. A thick fiber increases the net heat transfer rates to the droplet. Supported and unsupported droplets vaporize at similar rates at high Reynolds numbers. At lower Reynolds numbers, unsupported droplets vaporize faster.
Further three-dimensional numerical calculations involved modeling isolated 100 micron methanol droplets burning in microgravity environments at 1500 K and 50 atm [4]. Three flow configurations were considered: (1) a spherical unsupported droplet; (2) a droplet fully supported in the middle of a 10 micron quartz fiber with a solid-liquid contact angle of 30 degrees; and (3) a droplet suspended at the end of a 10 micron quartz fiber such that the droplet climbs up the fiber with a contact angle of 60 degrees. Cases (2) and (3) involved non-spherical droplets with droplet shapes determined by the liquid-fiber contact angle. Marangoni convection due to thermocapillary stresses was suppressed due to limitations of the speed of present-day desktop computers. Water condensation on the droplet surface was also suppressed. Ignition occurs the earliest in the suspended droplet, followed by the unsupported droplet and lastly for a fully supported droplet. It was found flame shapes and droplet heat transfer rates were different for the three conditions investigated.
Use of the NASA Tracker Station:
The NASA Tracker Station is being used at UC Davis for capture and analysis of 16 mm films from droplet combustion experiments. A high resolution Canon EOS 20D digital camera and a Canon MP-E macro lens are used in conjunction with the Tracker film transport system to form an automated system where frames of film are converted into digital images. The camera resolution is sufficient to allow individual film grains to be imaged, thus providing very high resolution images of droplets and flames. The Tracker system is controlled via a computer. The MATLAB technical computing software environment along with the Image Processing Toolbox is used to track droplet characteristics during combustion. The coordinates of droplet outlines are obtained and parameters of interest such as droplet diameter are calculated to plot time histories. The analysis method produces high resolution and accurate results in an efficient manner.
Other:
A paper describing theory to predict influences of thermal pyrolysis of fuel on soot shell locations was accepted by a journal. A paper describing experiments related to influences of pressure on reduced-gravity combustion of propanol droplets was accepted by a journal.
