Task Description:
The program is both experimental and theoretical in nature. The experiments will be conducted in ground-based facilities and on space-based platforms. Normal-gravity comparison experiments will also be performed. Bi-component droplets will be dispensed, deployed and ignited in reduced gravity. The droplet regression history will be measured by backlighting the droplet. An orthogonal view of the flame provides the flame history. Droplet interiors will be imaged, and flow visualization will be used to provide information on flowfields within droplets.
The ground-based experiments will be limited to smaller droplets. The space-based experiments will use the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus hardware to examine the combustion history of larger droplets with correspondingly larger time and length scales.
Theoretical and numerical studies will be used to model the combustion of the droplets in reduced gravity. The liquid phase transport processes will be of particular interest. The influence of surface tension driven flows on liquid phase transport will also be studied. The objective of this research is to study the combustion of bi-component miscible droplets in reduced-gravity environments so that buoyancy effects are rendered negligible. Of particular interest are the burning rate (droplet history), the time to flame contraction, potential microexplosions, Marangoni flows, and sooting behaviors. The experiments use liquid mixtures selected to display influences of large component volatility differences and liquid species diffusion on combustion phenomena. The research extends previous research on combustion of pure liquid fuels to mixtures of pure fuels, which more closely approximate practical fuels. Thus, this program should lead to a better understanding of the combustion of practical liquid fuels.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The research extends previous research on combustion of pure liquid fuels to mixtures of pure fuels, which more closely approximate practical fuels. Thus, this program should lead to a better understanding of the combustion of practical liquid fuels. Combustion phenomena of particular interest are burning rates (droplet histories), transport of mass and energy within droplets, flame size histories, bubbling within droplets, Marangoni flows, and sooting behaviors. The results from this research program are expected to be relevant to design of practical combustion systems that employ liquid fuels such as engines and oil-fired burners, e.g., by enabling the design of devices with higher efficiencies and reduced pollutant emissions. The results should also be useful for improving understanding of combustion phenomena under reduced gravity conditions, which is relevant to spacecraft fire safety.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Research was performed on to investigate aspects of combustion of isolated droplets burning under reduced gravity conditions. Analysis of reduced-gravity experiments involved digitizing and analyzing video images from experiments on combustion of propanol droplets, initially about 1 mm in diameter, in air at pressures from 0.1 MPa to 1.0 MPa. The results indicate that as the pressure increases, burning rates increase. Droplets did not soot at 0.1 MPa, but strong sooting was observed at 0.3 MPa and above. Theory indicates that increases in burning rates are caused by changes in properties, e.g., the liquid enthalpy of vaporization, as the pressure increases. Also, flames became less spherical at elevated pressures (from buoyancy influences), and data were obtained on flame aspect ratios and sizes as functions of time.
Computational modeling involved extending a previous numerical model to predict activity coefficients for propanol-water and propanol-water-glycerol mixtures. Calculations indicate that water absorption is very small (mass fractions generally less than 1 %) for propanol droplets burning in air at pressures ranging from 0.1 MPa to 1.0 MPa. A multidimensional computational model was also developed further. The code is based on overset grid technology and uses several meshes to resolve different parts of a droplet on a fiber. The code was used for mass-transfer studies (without combustion but with surface-tension influences). Surface tension forces were predicted to be important in terms of mass transfer and flowfield characteristics.
Analytical modeling focused on predicting influences of fuel pyrolysis on droplet combustion characteristics. Accounting for fuel pyrolysis changes classical expressions for the transfer number because the flame must supply energy for fuel pyrolysis, which requires the flame to be located closer to the droplet. Transfer numbers, burning rates and quasisteady flame standoff ratios can be appreciably reduced when fuel pyrolysis effects are included in the analyses. It was also found that fuel pyrolysis can influence temperature gradients between droplets and flames, which influences formation of soot shells.

Task Description:
These experiments involve burning unsupported and supported droplets within a pressure chamber. Droplets and flames are photographed with on-board video cameras (CCD and ICCD) to allow direct observation of liquid and gas behaviors. Data to be obtained will include transient droplet and gas-phase flame diameters, the occurrence of liquid bubbling inside droplets, the low- pressure deflagration limit, influences of fuel species on liquid consumption rates, radiant heat emissions, and gas thermal profiles.
Theoretical studies focus on extending previously developed analytical models of HAN-based liquid propellants to include phenomena such as non-equilibrium vaporization, bubbling, alternative chemical-kinetic schemes, gas-phase chemistry, and reactions of fuel species such as TEAN or methanol. The objective of this research is to study the combustion of monopropellant droplets and monopropellant droplet components in reduced-gravity environments so that spherical symmetry is strongly promoted. Hydroxylammonium nitrate (HAN) is a major constituent in a class of liquid monopropellants with many attractive characteristics and which display phenomena that differ from other liquid monopropellants. The research will involve studying combustion of droplets containing HAN (which is oxygen rich), water, and fuel species such as TEAN, glycine and methanol.
Droplets/particles initially in the mm size range are studied at pressures up to 30 atm. The experimental studies utilize reduced gravity to strongly promote spherical symmetry. This will allow observations of burning rates and flame structures to be made without the complicating effects of buoyant and forced convection. Normal gravity comarison experiments are also performed. The theoretical studies will complement the experimental work. HAN-based liquid monopropellant combustion is relevant to applications such as spacecraft thrusters and liquid-propellant guns. Fundamentally, there are processes associated with HAN-based liquid monopropellant combustion that are not well understood, e.g. laminar liquid surface deflagration rates, TEAN droplet combustion mechanisms and rates, and gas-phase flame extinction.

Task Description:
Soret transport, which is mass transport driven by thermal gradients, can be important in practical flames as well as laboratory flames by influencing transport of low molecular weight species (e.g, He, H and H2) and high molecular weight fuel species (e.g., C7H16) and O2. This research is concerned with investigating effects of Soret transport on combustion of liquid fuel droplets. Experiments will involve normal-gravity and reduced-gravity experiments on combustion of liquid fuel droplets in environments where Soret effects significantly influence transport of fuel and oxygen to flame zones. The experiments will employ pressures ranging from 0.3 to 10 atm, with extensions to 30 atm also being considered. Experiments will also be performed where Soret effects are not expected to be important. Droplets initially in the 0.5 to 1 mm size range will be burned. Data will be obtained on influences of Soret transport on combustion characteristics (e.g., droplet burning rates, droplet lifetimes, flame extinction, and transient flame behaviors) under simplified geometrical conditions that are most amenable to theoretical modeling (i.e., spherical symmetry). The experimental results will be compared with existing theoretical models as well as new models that will be developed as part of this program. The knowledge gained will be of use in evaluating combustion mechanisms under reduced gravity, which is of interest for spacecraft fire safety.
It is noted that in fall 2005, the PI became involved with a different program that includes a team of investigators from various universities as well as from NASA. This program, which is termed the Flammability and Extinction Experiment (FLEX), is focused upon using droplets to study flammability and extinction under reduced-gravity conditions of relevance to spaceflight and human exploration of space. The FLEX program is both experimental and theoretical in nature. Experiments presently include reduced-gravity studies as well as normal-gravity comparison experiments. In the research, individual droplets are dispensed, deployed and ignited in reduced gravity (as well as normal gravity). Theoretical approaches include developing computational and analytical models, with a particular emphasis on evaluating influences of gas-phase diffusive transport as well as droplet internal flows, which may arise from Marangoni stresses as well as droplet deployment and ignition. The present research on influences of Soret transport on droplet combustion is strongly complementary to certain aspects of the FLEX program, e.g., research on influences of gas-phase transport properties on flammability and extinction of droplets.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research has the potential to produce new and useful information on influences of Soret transport combustion mechanisms, both in normal gravity as well as reduced gravity. For example, Soret transport can be important in low-gravity flames by significantly influencing transport of O2 to a flame zone when low molecular weight (e.g., He) or high molecular weight (e.g., SF6) species are present in the gas phase. Low gravity combustion characteristics such as flame sizes, flame temperatures and sooting can be significantly influenced by Soret transport. Increasing knowledge about these effects is important for applications such as spacecraft fire safety.
Soret transport can also influence transport of high molecular weight fuel species, which are commonly employed in terrestrial engines. The present research has the potential to provide new information that will increase understanding of combustion mechanisms that are relevant to terrestrial applications that involve use of liquid fuels.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
Work has principally involved performing normal-gravity and reduced-gravity experiments, analyzing data from these experiments and performing theoretical analyses. Summaries of the progress are given below.
Normal-Gravity and Reduced Gravity Experiments:
Reduced gravity and normal gravity combustion experiments were performed with individual fiber-supported droplets that were initially about 1 mm in diameter. These experiments were performed with a goal of investigating influences of Soret transport and multicomponent diffusion on droplet flammability characteristics. Droplets composed of heptane, methanol or propanol were investigated and a thermocouple and radiometer were employed in conjunction with video cameras to obtain data on flammability behavior. The gas temperature is predicted to be strongly influenced by Soret effects under certain circumstances, e.g., when xenon or helium are used as a diluent, and as a result it is useful to be able to measure the gas temperature in a non-intrusive manner. Efforts were directed towards development of a simple low-power diode laser system than could be potentially used on the UCD drop rig for measurement of gas temperature and concentrations of selected species, e.g., CO or H2O, via tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS). Task Description:
Soret transport, which is mass transport driven by thermal gradients, can be important in practical flames as well as laboratory flames by influencing transport of low molecular weight species (e.g, He, H and H2) and high molecular weight fuel species (e.g., C7H16) and O2. This research is concerned with investigating effects of Soret transport on combustion of liquid fuel droplets. Experiments will involve normal-gravity and reduced-gravity experiments on combustion of liquid fuel droplets in environments where Soret effects significantly influence transport of fuel and oxygen to flame zones. The experiments will employ pressures ranging from 0.3 to 10 atm, with extensions to 30 atm also being considered. Experiments will also be performed where Soret effects are not expected to be important. Droplets initially in the 0.5 to 1 mm size range will be burned. Data will be obtained on influences of Soret transport on combustion characteristics (e.g., droplet burning rates, droplet lifetimes, gas-phase extinction, and transient flame behaviors) under simplified geometrical conditions that are most amenable to theoretical modeling (i.e., spherical symmetry). The experimental results will be compared with existing theoretical models as well as new models that will be developed as part of this program. The knowledge gained will be of use in evaluating combustion mechanisms under reduced gravity, which is of interest for spacecraft fire safety.
It is noted that in fall 2005, the PI became involved with a different program that includes a team of investigators from various universities as well as from NASA. This program, which is termed the Flammability and Extinction Experiment (FLEX), is focused upon using droplets to study flammability and extinction under reduced-gravity conditions of relevance to spaceflight and human exploration of space. The FLEX program is both experimental and theoretical in nature. Experiments presently include reduced-gravity studies as well as normal-gravity comparison experiments. In the research, individual droplets are dispensed, deployed and ignited in reduced gravity (as well as normal gravity). Theoretical approaches include developing computational and analytical models, with a particular emphasis on evaluating influences of gas-phase diffusive transport as well as droplet internal flows, which may arise from Marangoni stresses as well as droplet deployment and ignition. The present research on influences of Soret transport on droplet combustion is strongly complementary to certain aspects of the FLEX program, e.g., research on influences of gas-phase transport properties on flammability and extinction of droplets.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research has the potential to produce new and useful information on influences of Soret transport combustion mechanisms, both in normal gravity as well as reduced gravity. For example, Soret transport can be important in low-gravity flames by significantly influencing transport of O2 to a flame zone when low molecular weight (e.g., He) or high molecular weight (e.g., SF6) species are present in the gas phase. Low gravity combustion characteristics such as flame sizes, flame temperatures and sooting can be significantly influenced by Soret transport. Increasing knowledge about these effects is important for applications such as spacecraft fire safety.
Soret transport can also influence transport of high molecular weight fuel species, which are commonly employed in terrestrial engines. The present research has the potential to provide new information that will increase understanding of combustion mechanisms that are relevant to terrestrial applications that involve use of liquid fuels.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
Work has principally involved performing normal-gravity and reduced-gravity experiments, analyzing data from these experiments and performing theoretical analyses. Summaries of the progress are given below.
Normal-Gravity and Reduced Gravity Experiments
Reduced gravity and normal gravity combustion experiments were performed with individual fiber-supported droplets that were initially about 1 mm in diameter. These experiments were performed with a goal of investigating influences of Soret transport and multicomponent diffusion on droplet flammability characteristics. Droplets composed of heptane, methanol or propanol were investigated and a thermocouple and radiometer were employed in conjunction with video cameras to obtain data on flammability behavior. The environment was composed of an air-inert mixture at 0.1 MPa and about 298 K, where helium, carbon dioxide and xenon were separately used as inerts. In the experiments, the amount of inert gas in the environment was progressively increased until droplets could no longer be ignited. Droplet ignitability depended on the gravitational level as well as the inert gas in the environment. In general, the amount of inert gas required to suppress combustion was higher in reduced gravity than normal gravity. Use of xenon required significantly higher mole fractions for suppression of combustion relative to helium or carbon dioxide. The data indicate that ambient gas transport properties play an important role in determining flammability of droplets. For example, Soret diffusion likely promotes transport of O2 to flame zones when Xe is used, delaying extinction. Conversely, use of He as an inert will likely promote extinction, with Soret transport playing a significant role by inhibiting transport of O2 to flame zones. Analysis of the experimental data has also indicated that droplet burning rates depend significantly on the ambient gas conditions as well as the gravitational level.
Theoretical Modeling
Efforts were directed towards development of theoretical models to predict the influences of Soret transport on combustion behavior. These efforts involved computational modeling of diffusion flame behaviors for the opposed-flow configuration, which is a one-dimensional situation (with planar or cylindrical symmetry), where use was made of CHEMKIN software. Calculations were performed for various fuel and oxidizer combinations with chemical kinetic mechanisms of varying complexity. Some calculations included Soret transport while others did not. Results indicate that Soret transport can play an important role for these opposed-flow configurations, but that the influences of Soret transport may be weaker than for the spherically-symmetric case that corresponds to droplet combustion in reduced gravity. An important variable in the opposed-flow calculations is the strain rate, and the calculations have suggested that Soret transport may be most important at the low strain rates that would likely prevail in low-gravity situations with low-speed flows.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
Individual methanol or propanol droplets, initially about 1 mm in diameter, were burned in normal gravity in O2/inert atmospheres at pressures ranging from 0.03 MPa to 0.3 MPa. The inert gases used were N2, Ar, He and CO2 and the O2 mole fraction in the environment was 0.21. The flames showed strong influences of buoyancy on flame shapes at 0.1 MPa and 0.3 MPa; at 0.03 MPa. Droplet flames were oftentimes significantly dimmer in reduced gravity (relative to normal gravity). Preliminary analysis indicates that normal-gravity burning rates were appreciably larger than for reduced gravity.
Reduced-gravity experiments investigated the combustion characteristics of individual droplets initially composed of methanol. Droplets initially in the 1 mm size range were burned under reduced-gravity conditions using facilities available at the NASA Glenn 2.2 Second Drop Tower. The droplets were burned in O2-inert environments, where He, Xe, Ar, CO2 and N2 were used as inerts, and the O2 mole fraction in the environment was 0.21. The ambient pressure ranged from 0.03 MPa to 1 MPa. Flame behaviors, e.g., sooting and flame brightness, depended strongly on ambient conditions. Burning rates are presently being evaluated.
Further reduced-gravity experiments will be performed after submission of this report (but during the current reporting period). These experiments will investigate influences of Soret transport and multicomponent diffusion on the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) and the Minimum Extinction Concentration (MEC). The experiments will involve burning individual droplets (e.g., alkane or alcohol) in O2-inert environments, where the inert is varied until LOI or MEC conditions are attained. The gases to be used as inerts include He, Ar, N2, CO2, Xe, and possibly SF6, and in some cases mixtures of these gases will be used. The pressure will be varied over the range 0.03 MPa to0.3 MPa (and perhaps as high as 1.0 MPa). It is anticipated that the experiments will show significantly differences between the LOI and MEC conditions as the inert gas is varied. For example, Soret diffusion will likely promote transport of O2 to flame zones when Xe or SF6 are used, delaying extinction. Conversely, use of He as an inert will likely promote extinction, with Soret transport playing a significant role by inhibiting transport of O2 to flame zones.
Analytical theory to predict influences of Soret transport and multicomponent diffusion on flame extinction will be developed after submission of this report (but during the current reporting period). It is anticipated that Soret transport and multicomponent diffusion will strongly influence droplet radiant heat losses as well as extinction conditions through variations in the O2 Lewis number between the flame and the environment.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Research was performed to investigate influences of Soret transport on combustion characteristics of liquid fuels, specifically liquid fuel droplets. The research over the period of this report was principally in two areas: (1) reduced-gravity experiments; and (2) analysis of the reduced-gravity experimental results. The reduced-gravity experiments involved burning individual propanol droplets that were initially about 1 mm in diameter. The environment was composed of an oxygen-inert mixture, where helium, argon, xenon and nitrogen were used separately as inerts. The oxygen mole fraction in the environment was 0.21 (similar to air) or 0.50. The pressure ranged from 0.3 atm to 10 atm. Analysis of data from the experiments indicates that combustion characteristics depend significantly on the inert species. Helium appeared to produce larger and cooler flames while xenon produced flames that were significantly smaller and hotter (for approximately the same initial droplet diameter). Nitrogen and argon produced intermediate results. These findings are relevant to spacecraft fire safety in that that they show that inert gas transport properties can influence combustion characteristics of flames under reduced-gravity conditions.

Task Description:
A large body of experimental data has been accumulated with NASA funding under +1g, -1g and micro-g conditions which show the effects of buoyancy on premixed combustion processes. The purpose of this investigation is to model these data numerically and thereby test their adequacy and also to help elucidate the mechanisms by which buoyancy interacts with premixed laminar and turbulent flames.
Turbulent combustion processes account for approximately 90% of the power and heat generated worldwide but remain among the most significant unresolved problems in combustion science. In these processes mass and momentum fluxes, chemical kinetics and heat release are coupled in complex ways over a wide range of time and length scales. With the increased computational power now available formerly intractable difficulties can be addressed and the Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) codes being developed will become useful design tools for the practical engineer and, to a significant extent, obviate the need for often expensive, and time consuming empirical work. However, due to the current incomplete state of knowledge of turbulent combustion processes a close coordination of experimental and computational approaches is necessary for advances to be made.
Combustion research and technology is also directed at reducing pollution formation by burning at lean stoichiometries. Under these conditions flame instability, blow-off and flashback become safety concerns. Buoyancy has been observed to have a significant effect on flame stability and on conditions in the far-field burnt gas which, through the pressure field, affect flow both upstream and downstream of the flame. The temperature increase across a typical hydrocarbon flame is large (factors of ~6-8) and so the flow field consists predominately of hot, light products downstream and cold, dense reactants upstream in the reactants. The buoyancy affects the downstream flow by accelerating the products and has a large impact on the boundary conditions of the flow.
These large scale effects associated with the interaction of buoyancy with laminar and turbulent flames have yet to be adequately simulated. This is primarily due to the necessity of modeling a large physical domain so as to be insensitive to boundary conditions associated with buoyancy. In this study the near and far field of premixed laminar and turbulent flames will be simulated using a local adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) technique. The advantage of this technique is that it is capable of modeling large domains without sacrificing numerical resolution where it is required. The purpose of this study is, by numerical simulation of premixed flames, to elucidate the mechanisms by which buoyancy effects in the far field can modify premixed flame structure and dynamics. The work ise based on, and attempts to simulate, experimental work previously obtained under NASA funding. Collecting experimental data under microgravity conditions is a difficult and expensive enterprise and so the numerical simulations while aiding in the interpretation of experimental data but are at the same time be able to supplement those measurements. Furthermore, study of the boundary conditions associated with buoyant interactions provides insight into the modeling of the more complex boundaries of, for example, walls and physically confined flows. This is a problem of practical importance as the interaction of buoyancy and walls in forming the boundary conditions of large industrial flames often has to be dealt with in an ad hoc manner. The buoyancy/premixed flame interaction could be considered, therefore, a paradigm for large-scale pressure effects and so the results of this study will be relevant not only for combustion science but also for technological development.

1) Flame tip flicker in premixed conical laminar methane/air flames has been simulated. These simulations, using a reduced chemical scheme, are performed with an inlet flow of 0.73 m/s and equivalence ratio, phi=0.8. The phase-averaged velocity data provided an excellent means for following the evolution of the flow field but a more detailed investigation of the flicker process was also performed. Two types of vortex evolution were observed as alternate vortices were entrained leading to regular variations in the maximum flame tip height.
2) A study of buoyancy affects under gravity conditions characteristic of lunar and Martian conditions was started. Two aspects were investigated: flame licker frequency and inverse gravity fields. The affect of the reducing buoyant forces is clear from the lowered flicker frequency and flicker amplitude.
3) Work is continuing on the flame flicker phenomenon with a much wider range of initial conditions. Close comparisons with the experimental data already obtained with NASA funding is a central concern of this study.
4) The ‘funnel’ flame, an axiymmetric V-flame for which experimental data is available is also being studied. Of particular interest is the affect of buoyancy on the included flame angle under normal and inverse gravity conditions for which a large experimental data base exists.

A large amount of experimental data for microgravity combustion has been obtained form drop-tower experiments, specifically from the drop-tower in NASA-Glenn. A concern with these experimental results is the affect of the transition from 1g to 0g and how long the induced stabilities take to damp out. Only after this has happened are reliably microg results obtained. Our numerical approach provides a good means to investigate these phenomena.

Task Description:
A large body of experimental data has been accumulated with NASA funding under +1g, -1g and micro-g conditions which show the effects of buoyancy on premixed combustion processes. The purpose of this investigation is to model these data numerically and thereby test their adequacy and also to help elucidate the mechanisms by which buoyancy interacts with premixed laminar and turbulent flames.
Turbulent combustion processes account for approximately 90% of the power and heat generated worldwide but remain among the most significant unresolved problems in combustion science. In these processes mass and momentum fluxes, chemical kinetics and heat release are coupled in complex ways over a wide range of time and length scales. With the increased computational power now available formerly intractable difficulties can be addressed and the Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) codes being developed will become useful design tools for the practical engineer and, to a significant extent, obviate the need for often expensive, and time consuming empirical work. However, due to the current incomplete state of knowledge of turbulent combustion processes a close coordination of experimental and computational approaches is necessary for advances to be made.
Combustion research and technology is also directed at reducing pollution formation by burning at lean stoichiometries. Under these conditions flame instability, blow-off and flashback become safety concerns. Buoyancy has been observed to have a significant effect on flame stability and on conditions in the far-field burnt gas which, through the pressure field, affect flow both upstream and downstream of the flame. The temperature increase across a typical hydrocarbon flame is large (factors of ~6-8) and so the flow field consists predominately of hot, light products downstream and cold, dense reactants upstream in the reactants. The buoyancy affects the downstream flow by accelerating the products and has a large impact on the boundary conditions of the flow.
These large scale effects associated with the interaction of buoyancy with laminar and turbulent flames have yet to be adequately simulated. This is primarily due to the necessity of modeling a large physical domain so as to be insensitive to boundary conditions associated with buoyancy. In this study the near and far field of premixed laminar and turbulent flames will be simulated using a local adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) technique. The advantage of this technique is that it is capable of modeling large domains without sacrificing numerical resolution where it is required. The purpose of this study is, by numerical simulation of premixed flames, to elucidate the mechanisms by which buoyancy effects in the far field can modify premixed flame structure and dynamics. The work ise based on, and attempts to simulate, experimental work previously obtained under NASA funding. Collecting experimental data under microgravity conditions is a difficult and expensive enterprise and so the numerical simulations while aiding in the interpretation of experimental data but are at the same time be able to supplement those measurements. Furthermore, study of the boundary conditions associated with buoyant interactions provides insight into the modeling of the more complex boundaries of, for example, walls and physically confined flows. This is a problem of practical importance as the interaction of buoyancy and walls in forming the boundary conditions of large industrial flames often has to be dealt with in an ad hoc manner. The buoyancy/premixed flame interaction could be considered, therefore, a paradigm for large-scale pressure effects and so the results of this study will be relevant not only for combustion science but also for technological development.

A full simulation can take up to approximately one month. The phenomenon of flame tip flicker observed experimentally was reproduced in these simulations and the flicker frequency was found to match those found empirically.
Software development activities focused primarily on modifications to the code necessary to generalize the allowable orientation of the gravitational acceleration with respect to the inlet flow, and appropriately model the interaction of the computational domain with the ambient laboratory environment, especially in the case of an inverted conical flame (-g). Simulation of the inverted configuration involves a number of adjustments, primarily to the inflow/outflow boundary conditions. The inflow rate of fuel-air mixture was the same as the +g case but the direction of the gravitational force in the simulation is reversed. Successful simulations of this system have been performed. In the laboratory, a large-scale, very low velocity flow of ambient air is induced by the buoyantly driven upward flow of the burnt gases and so the heat conducted across the stagnation surface from the burnt gas to the ambient air below it is convected upward and radially outward along with the hot products. A physically consistent approach to simulate these boundary conditions in the -g case is recovered computationally by adding a small upward flow of ambient air through the downstream (bottom) boundary. A small amount of numerical experimentation indicated that the stagnation point is not very sensitive to the velocity of this flow indicating that the dynamics of this system are being controlled primarily by the buoyant interactions.

Task Description:
The four separate global tasks have to be completed to meet the technical objectives of the proposed investigation are: (1) System design and integration of the Fan Beam Emission Tomography (FBET) system for use in the reduced gravity facilities at NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) including the 2.2 second and 5.0 second drop towers and possibly the KC-135 parabolic aircraft, (2) Development of the deconvolution algorithm and demonstration with synthetic data and a normal gravity test fire, (3) Experimental evaluation of the Fan Beam Emission Tomography System in the reduced gravity facilities at NASA Glenn Research Center, and (4) Preparation of final report and Science Requirements Document (SRD) for hardware and software for use on International Space Station (ISS).
The objectives of the research are to (1) develop instrumentation for obtaining emission signatures at multiple view angles from a non-symmetric and transient laminar fire, and (2) develop a deconvolution algorithm to obtain the local gas species and soot concentrations and temperature from the emission signatures.
It is critical that advanced optical instrumentation be developed for microgravity combustion research on the ISS. This proposed instrument, which enables measurement of temperature and species in a plane, holds great promise to be widely used and important instrument for space-based research. The project involves developing an entire system that is flight worthy, including hardware and analysis software, and then to deliver the system to NASA for use by other researchers. The research involves conducting demonstration experiments in the drop tower at NASA Glenn Research Center with SAL, TIGER-3D, and LSP.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The diagnostics developed for this project is currently used to study rocket engine combustors.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The first task for the project was to review fires for which microgravity data was available so that the proposed FBET system could be evaluated. Based on the literature survey of quantitative measurements available in normal and reduced gravity experiments, it was decided to evaluate the FBET system using laminar diffusion flames burning ethylene, methane, acetylene, and mixture of these fuels with nitrogen and hydrogen.
The second task of the project was to design and fabricate optical scanners to be used in the FBET system. The fabrication of an optical scanner using a computer controlled stepper motor was completed in the fourth month of the project, and the spectrometer with scanner was displayed at the Sixth International Microgravity Combustion Workshop in Cleveland. The scanner provides the path-integrated intensity at 30 angles in the plane of the optical axis. Data was collected at three different heights above the burner for these flames. The data acquisition system logged the data continuously for a period of thirty seconds. The ES100 spectrometer and scanner were successful in obtaining data required for emission tomography.
The third task of the project was to procure and integrate the spectrometer and scanner into a drop rig. The spectrometer and scanner was delivered to NASA where it was integrated into a drop rig. In addition, a four channel thermocouple tree for obtaining temperature measurements from the laminar diffusion flames in the drop rig was designed and integrated into the drop rig by NASA. A total of 73 drop tests were conducted during the second year. 31 of these drop tests were conducted with the spectrometer, and 42 drop tests with the thermocouple.
The fourth task was to obtain data from a GRC provided combustion chamber at En’Urga Inc. This task was designed to calibrate the spectrometer with 8 mm thick sapphire windows that are currently used in the ISS combustion module. The chamber is not required to calibrate the FBET system with an 8 mm thick sapphire window. Therefore, En’Urga Inc. utilized only the windows and a Santoro type burner (without the combustion chamber) during the second year of the project. The intensities measured from flames were to be corrected for transmission of the windows. This was successfully accomplished during the second year.
The fifth task of the project was to review new detectors that could serve as a replacement for the 160 element PbSe array used in the spectrometer. A TE cooled HgCdTe array, manufactured by Sofrad-IR was found to be the only alternative to the current system. However, the HgCdTe array is not available any longer. Therefore, the ES100 with scanner currently offers the best hope of obtaining spectral images from transient flames.
The sixth task of the project to develop the deconvolution algorithm required for the FBET system. Forward calculations of the equation of radiative transfer were completed during the first year to obtain synthetic data to be used for the deconvolution algorithm. Deconvolution of the synthetic data so as to obtain temperature and gas species concentrations was completed during the second year of the project. The deconvolution recovered temperatures and gas concentrations with 0.1%. Addition of random noise of 1% in intensity and 10 nm in wavelengths was introduced into the synthetic data. The deconvolution algorithm still allowed for recovery of gas temperatures and gas concentrations within 1% at most locations in the flame. At the center of the flame, the error in the deconvolution procedure was approximately 20%.
The seventh task of the project was to obtain data from axisymmetric flames under normal gravity. Normal gravity experiments were conducted at En’Urga Inc. The spectral radiation intensities obtained from the normal gravity experiments were deconvoluted to provide local temperatures, gas concentrations, and soot volume fractions in methane and ethylene flames. For non-sooting flames, reasonable estimates of temperatures and gas concentrations were obtained using the FBET system. For sooting ethylene flames, reasonable estimates of temperatures and soot volume fractions were obtained. However, the gas concentrations could not be retrieved from the deconvolution procedure due to the masking effects of the soot layer.
The eighth task of the project was to obtain data from axisymmetric flames under reduced gravity using the 2-second and 5-second drop towers. Two second drop tower experiments were conducted during the third year. Reasonable estimates of temperatures and gas concentrations were obtained from the drop tower experiments for a non-sooting methane flame. For sooting flames, the time required for obtaining data with very high signal to noise ratio was too short. Therefore, it was not possible to obtain reasonable estimates of either temperature or soot volume fractions from these measurements. It was decided to utilize the five second drop tower to obtain data with greater SNR.
Five second drop tower tests were conducted and local temperatures, gas concentrations, and soot volume fractions were estimated using the FBET system. The system worked successfully in providing local gas concentrations, temperatures, and soot volume fractions in a non-intrusive manner from microgravity flames for the first time ever.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:

Task Description:
There are four specific tasks associated with achieving the technical objectives of the project. The first task is to design, fabricate, and calibrate a small angle multi-wavelength scattering instrument. The second task is to develop an algorithm to obtain particle size distribution, number density, refractive indices, and fractal dimension from the measured intensities. The third task is to validate the measurement and data reduction scheme using well characterized normal gravity and reduced gravity fires. The last task is to obtain signatures from a variety of particulate, both from combustion of common materials as well as from nuisance sources. These tasks will form the basis of a science requirement document proposing the instrument be evaluated in the Space Station CIR module. The project was limited to three years and therefore reduced gravity data was not obtained.
There are two key objectives to the proposed work. (1) The first is to utilize advances in measurement and data interpretation technologies to develop a small angle scattering system that can be used in combustion science studies. (2) The second is a systematic study of the scattering signatures of a wide variety of combustion generated particulate and particulate that are present in the environment with a view of augmenting current fire safety systems utilized in the space station.
It is critical that advanced optical instrumentation be developed for microgravity combustion research on the ISS. The proposed instrument, which enables characterization of combustion generated particulate, holds great promise to be widely used and is an important instrument for space-based research. An additional benefit of the project is that the fundamental science for developing false alarm free fire detection systems for spacecraft will be completed. The project involves developing an entire system that is flight worthy, including hardware and analysis software, and delivering the system to NASA for use by other researchers.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The small angle scattering sensor will form the basis for an advanced, low false alarm rate fire detector system. Such low false alarm rate fire detector systems will have immediate acceptance in the protection of high value (museums, bank vaults, etc.) and confined (interior of submarines, airplanes, etc) spaces.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2007
Task Progress:
During the first year of the project, the design of a bench top small angle scattering system was completed. Components of the system were purchased and assembled on an optical bench. The system was calibrated with 10 mm single slit. During the first year the system was calibrated with a 514 nm TE cooled diode laser. Based on the calibration, it was ascertained that the system can provide accurate data from 0.05 degrees to 10.5 degrees with an increment of less than 0.1 degrees.
During the second year, the design and fabrication of the two wavelength small angle scattering system (SASS). The system was designed using ProEngineer solid model package. The optical design was completed using Zemax Optical Design software. The system was calibrated using a 10 micron slit. Scattering signatures were obtained from burning PVC (electrical wire), rubber, and paper. Simulations of the expected scattering from soot particles were also calculated using the The Rayleigh-Debye-Gans Fractal Aggregate (RDG-FA) theory.
During the final year of the project, additional evaluation of the system was completed. It was found that the optical design had some problems with not providing correct signatures when the particles are not within a narrow range of distances from the imaging lenses. Attempts to correct this problem were not successful. A deconvolution algorithm was developed during the final year of the project and tested with synthetic data. The data collected from the burning samples were not deconvoluted due to the uncertainties arising identifying the particle. Additional resources are required to correct the optics for the scattering system before it can be utilized with confidence.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:
NOTE: End date changed to 8/29/2022 per NSSC information; original end date was 6/4/2021 (Ed. 12/14/21)
Task Description: We plan to combine computational and experimental methods to generate temperature and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data sets. A series of computations incorporating a soot model in which the dynamical equations for particle production are coupled to the flow and gaseous species conservation equations with modifications to account for the large soot loadings of the SPICE flames will be employed. Specifically, we will include the effects of thermal radiation re-absorption in the model and we will allow aggregate formation using a discrete-sectional size representation. For the heavy soot loading flames to be considered in this study, the balance between soot production, soot oxidation, and radiative temperature reduction will need to be examined more closely to help assess the various modes for smoke point development. To ascertain the importance of the various parameters in the model/kinetic mechanism, a first-order sensitivity analysis will be employed. The raw data from SPICE that we will concentrate on consists of more than 1600 images from the Nikon D300s DSLR camera, stored in a lossless, compressed format (Nikon .nef). These will be decoded to the three color channels and used to determine soot temperature from color ratio pyrometry. In the initial work, we will assume optically thin behavior, which will likely be accurate for some, but not all, of the fuels and flow conditions. The temperature distribution will then be used, along with the absolute light calibration that is available for the SPICE setup, to determine the soot volume fraction. This initial processing will provide valuable information on flame size, shape, and soot loading trends. This, along with the measured flow boundary conditions, will guide the computations. For the flames with the highest soot loading, the soot luminosity and spectral distribution will be affected by absorption and scattering. This in turn will affect the temperature and soot volume fraction calculated from the raw data. Taking optical properties of soot from similar flames in normal gravity, we will investigate the influence of extinction on the derived temperature and soot volume fraction.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2023
Task Progress:
Compiled from final technical report submitted to NASA (Ed., 3/5/24):
The global pandemic and COVID-19 issues made it difficult to keep the work going in a steady manner. Nevertheless, progress was made, and in the No Cost Extension (NCE) year, we obtained a much better understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames.
For some choices of model parameters, it proved possible to generate rather large soot loads, especially in microgravity and for lower values of the sectional coalescence cutoff. Unfortunately, however, the goal of replicating the significant discrepancies in peak soot when going from 1g to 0g remained elusive. Many uncertainties remain, and one in particular is already under investigation: we have focused on the surface growth model for surface-growth-dominated flames, but there could be interactions that we are missing with the soot inception model. At present, our soot model does not include large soot precursors such as pyrene; we plan to address this in future research.
Results of this investigation were published in Combustion Science and Technology (see Cumulative Bibliography):
Dobbins RR, Tinjero J, Squeo J, Zhao X, Hall RJ, Colket MB, Long MB, Smooke MD. A combined experimental and computational study of soot formation in normal and microgravity conditions. Combust. Sci. Technol. 2022 Mar 29. https://doi.org/10.1080/00102202.2022.2041621

Task Description:
This project concerns the development of two diagnostics for application to microgravity combustion experiments. These diagnostics are particle image velocimetry (PIV) and two-wavelength thin-filament pyrometry (TFP). The diagnostics will be used to measure velocities and temperatures in laminar gas jet diffusion flames in the GRC 2.2-Second Drop Tower. 1. Measure the velocity fields in microgravity laminar jet diffusion flames using particle-image velocimetry in the 2.2-Second Drop Tower.
2. Conduct full-field temperature measurements of the same flames using two-wavelength thin-filament pyrometry.
3. Compare the measurements with predictions from analytical and numerical models. These measurements will support the evaluation of analytical and numerical combustion models. Such models furnish velocity predictions, which are crucial to the analysis of past flight investigations of both laminar and turbulent jet diffusion flames.

Task Description:
The proposed program addresses the need to understand the physics and chemistry involved in propellant combustion processes in micro-scale combustors for propulsion systems and energy conversion devices on micro-spacecraft. These spacecraft are planned to have a mass less than 50 kilograms with attitude control estimated to be in the 10 milli-Newton thrust class. Combustors of this size are expected to benefit significantly from surface catalysis processes. Therefore, the proposed program specifically aims to gain a fundamental understanding of the ignition conditions, flammability limits, combustion efficiency, and modeling of propellant combustion in heated microtubes fabricated from known catalyst materials. The data and models generated will form a micro-combustor database, which is applicable to MEMS based chemical thrusters and energy conversion devices.
The present study is broken down into the following four major projects: (1) experimental determination of the ignition and flammability limits as functions of Reynolds number, pressure, preheat temperature, catalyst type, and tube length to inside diameter ratio; (2) experimental mapping of wall temperature distribution and exit profiles of temperature and species; (3) experimental assessment of performance and efficiency for various micro-combustors; and (4) detailed modeling of catalytic combustion including gas phase kinetics and surface chemistry. They are selected because their non-toxic character will aid in the human exploration of space. It is noted that the productions of the aforementioned fuels are near-term top priorities of in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) technologies.
These proposed studies are anticipated to engender significant impacts on fundamental understanding and predictive capabilities regarding catalytic combustion in general and micro-propulsion devices using non-toxic propellants of importance to human space flight in particular. Ultimately, the studies will provide insights into approaches for achieving ignition and increased energy conversion efficiencies leading to technological advances in various combustion processes/devices in terrestrial, space-based, and extraterrestrial surroundings.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This research is directly relevant to the development of micro-satellites, which are important for Earth weather and resource reconnaissance. The present investigation can also improve the efficiency and lower the emissions of combustion devices on Earth for more efficient resource utilization with less adverse environmental impact. The micro-scale devices developed will greatly aid the portability of power supplies for field applications on Earth.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
A versatile test facility has been established, including a vacuum chamber, microtube reactors, mass flow control system, data acquisition system, power supply for heating the microtube, vacuum pump, and infrared camera. The vacuum chamber was outfitted with a test stand to hold the experimental setup. The test stand included ceramic insulators for mounting the microtube and a bulkhead to hold the flow connections. The chamber was also equipped with a feedthrough that includes thermocouple leads and pressure transducer wiring as well as a ZnSe window for taking IR images and several observation windows.
The present study characterized the combustion of rich hydrogen/oxygen propellant mixtures and rich methane/oxygen propellant mixtures in platinum microtubes with inside diameters of 0.4 and 0.8 mm. All the mixtures tested had equivalence ratios beyond the corresponding rich flammability limits. Experimental results showed that catalytic reactions could support combustion in mixtures even when gas phase chemistry does not play a significant role. The effects of varying equivalence ratio, pressure, mass flow rate, and tube diameter on the critical temperature leading to catalytic ignition were systematically investigated. Furthermore, the effects of doping the methane/oxygen mixture with hydrogen were explored, demonstrating a substantial reduction in the ignition temperature with hydrogen addition. Microtube performance in terms of available thrust, specific impulse, and power required for preheating the microtube were also discussed. Utilizing a plug flow model, the experimental conditions were simulated with detailed gas phase/surface chemistry, thermodynamic properties, and transport properties. The computational results generally supported the experimental findings.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Experimental efforts have been devoted to complete the investigation on catalyzed combustion of hydrogen-oxygen in platinum and palladium tubes at varying sub-atmospheric pressures. In addition, we designed and built an in-house vacuum test cell and the associated data acquisition system. Subsequently, we systematically investigated catalyzed ignition of methane-oxygen in microtubes.
Modeling efforts have been focused in two areas. The first area involves a critical evaluation of Navier-Stokes, boundary-layer, and plug-flow models for reacting flows in a catalyst microtube. In the second area, unsteady term was added in the model to allow a reliable prediction of catalytic ignition.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
Micro-propulsion devices behave differently than macro-scale devices because of the differences in magnitude of flow rates and heat transfer. Reducing the combustor size increases the relative surface area, increasing the heat loss, and as combustors are continuously reduced in size, they approach the quenching dimensions of the propellants. Combustors of this size are expected to benefit significantly from surface catalysis processes. A miniature flame tube apparatus is chosen for this study because microtubes can be easily fabricated from known catalyst materials and their simplicity in geometry can be used in fundamental simulations for validation purposes. Experimentally, we investigated the role of catalytically active surfaces within 0.4 and 0.8 mm internal diameter microtubes, with special emphases on ignition processes in fuel rich gaseous hydrogen and gaseous oxygen. Calculations of flame thickness and reaction zone thickness predict that the diameters of our test apparatus are below the quenching diameter of the propellants in most atmospheric test conditions. The temperature and pressure rise in resistively heated platinum microtubes and the exit hydrogen concentration were used as an indication of exothermic reactions. Data on imposed heat flux/preheat temperature required to achieve ignition versus mass flow rate are presented. With a plug flow model, the experimental conditions were simulated with detailed gas-phase chemistry and surface kinetics. Computational results generally support the experimental findings.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:
Note: Original end date was 12/30/2007.
Task Description:
This research relates to technology development efforts of both fire-extinguishing systems in human exploration of space and various combustion systems for terrestrial applications. The practical considerations are based on the fact that most uncontrolled fires and combustion systems are diffusion flame type combustion. Fire safety issues include flame stability, spread, and suppression phenomena aboard spacecraft in microgravity (ug) and on planetary surface bases in low gravity (the moon, 0.165g; Mars, 0.380g) as well as on the Earth (1g).
As a result of flame-surface interactions, the diffusion flame often forms an edge, which may attach to burner walls, spread over condensed fuel surfaces, jump to another location through the fuel-air mixture formed, or extinguish by destabilization (blow-off). Furthermore, local extinction and re-ignition processes can occur in both fires and combustors as a result of interactions between the flame zone and vortices or fire-extinguishing agents. Flame spreading and secondary fires, where fires jump from one location to another, will lead an initially small ignition source to a dangerous established fire. In such circumstances, the dynamic behavior of edge diffusion flames may play a key role in a fate of fires. Because of various levels of buoyancy in low-gravity, fires in space behave differently from those on Earth. This research at NASA Glenn addresses edge diffusion flame stability, spread, and suppression, which is of essential importance in space-based fire safety and Earth-bound combustion systems.
The structure of edge diffusion flames, stabilized on various geometries are studied experimentally and computationally. The experiments include both 1g and low-g tests in the 2.2 s Drop Tower at Glenn and the C-9 Reduced-Gravity Aircraft. Diagnostics include video observations, the Mach-Zehnder Interferometry (MZI) for temperature measurements, and the particle image velocimetry (PIV) for velocity measurements.
The fundamental aspect of the proposed program relates to recent advancement in numerical simulations. As a result of significant progresses in the development of detailed combustion reaction mechanisms and computer technologies over the last decade or two, it is now feasible to simulate various transient combustion phenomena in simple configurations (burner geometry, flow, and fuel) with confidence, leading to deeper understanding of physical and chemical unit processes taking place during the phenomena under investigation. Direct numerical simulations are performed by solving the time-dependent full Navier-Stokes equations along with energy- and species-conservation equations, including a detailed reaction mechanism for C1-C3 hydrocarbon combustion (33 species, 112 elementary steps) and radiative heat losses from CO2, H2O, CO, and CH4.
The objectives of this research are:
1. To elucidate flame stability, spread, and suppression mechanisms of edge diffusion flames of gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels using various fire-extinguishing agents in 1g and low-g by revealing internal flame structure. The edge diffusion flame geometries to be used include axisymmetric fuel jets, candles, and cylindrical fuel surfaces in a low-speed coaxial oxidant stream in 1g and low-g with the oxygen concentration, oxidant velocity, pressure, fuel type, and agent type as independent variables.
2. To provide rigorous testing of the fidelity of the computational models, including detailed chemical reaction mechanisms and the radiative heat-transfer sub-models, in the simulations of the subject phenomena: unsteady flame stabilization, spread, and suppression, for various edge diffusion flame geometries, environments, fuels, and agents.
This research is important in relation to fire safety in space exploration. The diffusion flame stability mechanism is more complicated and less understood than that of premixed flames because the reaction rates in diffusion flames are transport-limited and complex flame-structure dependent. A conventional view of diffusion flame stability in normal gravity, where a buoyancy-driven flow exists, or for forced-convection conditions assumes that there exists a small premixed flame at the flame base, which propagates against the mixture flow, thus preventing the flame from lifting. This research thus far has revealed that the speculation of premixed flame base formation is unrealistic, particularly in diffusion dominant micro gravity flames, and a newly conceived concept based on the reaction kernel replaces the conventional view. Direct numerical simulations with a detailed reaction mechanism and radiative heat losses provide precise flame structure information on radical species transport and reactions, which cannot be obtained by experiments or theories. Thus, this research contributes to expand our understanding of diffusion flame stabilization, particularly into a previously unstudied diffusion-dominant regime in microgravity.
Furthermore, flame spread over condensed fuel surfaces and flame suppression have rarely been viewed from the point of stabilization and destabilization of edge diffusion flames. This research uniquely addresses to the edge diffusion flame phenomena in relation to the internal flame structure of the reaction kernel (peak reactivity spot) at the flame edge. The effects of various fire-extinguishing agents on the flame stability, spread, and suppression will be revealed on a step-by-step basis by systematic experiments and computations . Therefore, this research, which capitalizes the unique microgravity environment, benefits development efforts of fire-extinguishing systems to enable safe and productive human space explorations of the moon and Mars through fundamental understanding of the edge diffusion flame characteristics.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Underlying physics and chemistry of edge diffusion flames are relevant to the performance of Earth-bound combustion systems, including gas turbines, diesel engines, and industrial burners. Flame holding in combustors is necessary to achieve design performance and safe operation of the system. Therefore, this research is also beneficial for improvements and further developments of Earth-bound combustion technologies and certainly contributes to a progress in fundamental combustion science.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
The structure and stability of laminar jet diffusion flames of gaseous hydrocarbon fuels in co-flowing air at normal earth gravity have been investigated experimentally and computationally. Measurements of the critical mean jet velocity of methane, ethane, and propane at lifting or blowoff were made as a function of the air velocity. Computations using an implicit, third-order accurate numerical scheme simulated the internal structures of the stabilizing region (base) of methane and propane flames. A reaction mechanism, including 33 species and 112 elementary steps for C1-C3 hydrocarbons, and a broad-band radiation heat-loss model assuming optically thin media, were used. For methane and propane, the simulated flame base moved downstream toward lift-off under flow conditions close to the measured lifting limit. A peak reactivity spot (i.e., reaction kernel) formed in the stabilizing region is responsible for the flame attachment and detachment. The flame lift-off occurs due to flame-base destabilization (detachment), rather than extinction. An increase in the entrained velocity (decrease in the residence time) moves the flame base downstream, in search of a new balancing point between the residence time and overall reaction time, while still maintaining vigorous burning at the reaction kernel.
SUPPLEMENTAL RESEARCH PROGRESS FOR FINAL REPORTING
The structure, stabilization, and extinguishment of a low-speed co-flow diffusion flame in normal earth gravity (1g) and microgravity have been studied experimentally and computationally. In addition to a circular tube burner, a cup burner, which was used in a previous effort, and cylindrical burner geometries were used. For the tube and cup-burner configurations, methane, ethane, propane, or n-heptane was used as the fuel and an inert or chemically active gaseous agent was added to the coflowing air. The microgravity cup-burner flame extinguishment testing was conducted using standard and pre-extravehicular-activity (EVA) oxidizing atmospheres (21 % O2 in N2 at 101 kPa and 30 % O2 in N2 at 70.3 kPa, respectively) aboard the NASA Reduced-Gravity Aircraft (C-9) in March and October 2006.
For the cylindrical configurations, three types of flames were used: (I) burning in a middle cylinder section, (II) around a downstream-end section, and (III) around an upstream-end section. Methane-blowing porous cylinders and cylindrical samples of polymers (polymethyl-methacrylate, high-density polyethylene, and polyoxymethylene) were used as the fuel source. A gaseous fire-extinguishing agent or water mist was added gradually to the oxidizer flow to measure the critical volume fraction of agent at extinguishment. The methane cylindrical flames extinguished via blowoff processes (in which the flame drifted downstream), whereas the polymer flames receded downstream and shrank, while the flame base kept attached to the surface, until extinguishment. The agent concentration in the oxidizer required for extinguishment was fairly independent of the mean oxidizer velocity (3 to 16 cm/s). By contrast, the water mist droplet mass fraction at extinguishment in cylindrical burners decreased substantially with increasing the mean oxidizer velocity.
Numerical simulations with full chemistry were performed to reveal the detailed flame structure and to predict the minimum extinguishing concentrations (MECs) of gaseous agents for a comparison with the experiment. Despite the complexity of chemistry and flame-flow interactions in the blowoff processes, the numerical predictions of MECs were in fair agreements with the measurements. The MECs in microgravity were, in general, substantially larger than those in earth gravity, and the MECs in the pre-EVA condition were significantly larger than those in the standard atmosphere in microgravity. The relative ranking of agent effectiveness depended on the agent’s ability to reduce the flame temperature to a threshold range through the heat capacity and thermal conductivity of the agent-laden oxidizer.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Flight Assignment/Project Notes:
Note: Original end date was 12/30/2007.
Task Description:
This research relates to technology development efforts of both fire-extinguishing systems in human exploration of space and various combustion systems for terrestrial applications. The practical considerations are based on the fact that most uncontrolled fires and combustion systems are diffusion flame type combustion. Fire safety issues include flame stability, spread, and suppression phenomena aboard spacecraft in microgravity (ug) and on planetary surface bases in low gravity (the moon, 0.165g; Mars, 0.380g) as well as on the Earth (1g).
As a result of flame-surface interactions, the diffusion flame often forms an edge, which may attach to burner walls, spread over condensed fuel surfaces, jump to another location through the fuel-air mixture formed, or extinguish by destabilization (blow-off). Furthermore, local extinction and re-ignition processes can occur in both fires and combustors as a result of interactions between the flame zone and vortices or fire-extinguishing agents. Flame spreading and secondary fires, where fires jump from one location to another, will lead an initially small ignition source to a dangerous established fire. In such circumstances, the dynamic behavior of edge diffusion flames may play a key role in a fate of fires. Because of various levels of buoyancy in low-gravity, fires in space behave differently from those on Earth. This research at NASA Glenn addresses edge diffusion flame stability, spread, and suppression, which is of essential importance in space-based fire safety and Earth-bound combustion systems.
The structure of edge diffusion flames, stabilized on various geometries are studied experimentally and computationally. The experiments include both 1g and low-g tests in the 2.2 s Drop Tower at Glenn and the KC-135 Reduced-Gravity Aircraft. Diagnostics include video observations, the Mach-Zehnder Interferometry (MZI) for temperature measurements, and the particle image velocimetry (PIV) for velocity measurements.
The fundamental aspect of the proposed program relates to recent advancement in numerical simulations. As a result of significant progresses in the development of detailed combustion reaction mechanisms and computer technologies over the last decade or two, it is now feasible to simulate various transient combustion phenomena in simple configurations (burner geometry, flow, and fuel) with confidence, leading to deeper understanding of physical and chemical unit processes taking place during the phenomena under investigation. Direct numerical simulations are performed by solving the time-dependent full Navier-Stokes equations along with energy- and species-conservation equations, including a detailed reaction mechanism for C1-C3 hydrocarbon combustion (33 species, 112 elementary steps) and radiative heat losses from CO2, H2O, CO, and CH4. The objectives of this research are:
1. To elucidate flame stability, spread, and suppression mechanisms of edge diffusion flames of gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels using various fire-extinguishing agents in 1g and low-g by revealing internal flame structure. The edge diffusion flame geometries to be used include axisymmetric fuel jets, candles, and cylindrical fuel surfaces in a low-speed coaxial oxidant stream in 1g and low-g with the oxygen concentration, oxidant velocity, pressure, fuel type, and agent type as independent variables.
2. To provide rigorous testing of the fidelity of the computational models, including detailed chemical reaction mechanisms and the radiative heat-transfer sub-models, in the simulations of the subject phenomena: unsteady flame stabilization, spread, and suppression, for various edge diffusion flame geometries, environments, fuels, and agents. This research is important in relation to fire safety in space exploration. The diffusion flame stability mechanism is more complicated and less understood than that of premixed flames because the reaction rates in diffusion flames are transport-limited and complex flame-structure dependent. A conventional view of diffusion flame stability in normal gravity, where a buoyancy-driven flow exists, or for forced-convection conditions assumes that there exists a small premixed flame at the flame base, which propagates against the mixture flow, thus preventing the flame from lifting. This research thus far has revealed that the speculation of premixed flame base formation is unrealistic, particularly in diffusion dominant micro gravity flames, and a newly conceived concept based on the reaction kernel replaces the conventional view. Direct numerical simulations with a detailed reaction mechanism and radiative heat losses provide precise flame structure information on radical species transport and reactions, which cannot be obtained by experiments or theories. Thus, this research contributes to expand our understanding of diffusion flame stabilization, particularly into a previously unstudied diffusion-dominant regime in microgravity.
Furthermore, flame spread over condensed fuel surfaces and flame suppression have rarely been viewed from the point of stabilization and destabilization of edge diffusion flames. This research uniquely addresses to the edge diffusion flame phenomena in relation to the internal flame structure of the reaction kernel (peak reactivity spot) at the flame edge. The effects of various fire-extinguishing agents on the flame stability, spread, and suppression will be revealed on a step-by-step basis by systematic experiments and computations . Therefore, this research, which capitalizes the unique microgravity environment, benefits development efforts of fire-extinguishing systems to enable safe and productive human space explorations of the moon and Mars through fundamental understanding of the edge diffusion flame characteristics.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Underlying physics and chemistry of edge diffusion flames are relevant to the performance of Earth-bound combustion systems, including gas turbines, diesel engines, and industrial burners. Flame holding in combustors is necessary to achieve design performance and safe operation of the system. Therefore, this research is also beneficial for improvements and further developments of Earth-bound combustion technologies and certainly contributes to a progress in fundamental combustion science.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
The task progress has been published in two papers in the Proceedings of The Combustion Institute and a paper in the Proceedings of the Central States Sections/The Combustion Institute Meeting.
The structure of axisymmetric laminar jet diffusion flames of ethane, ethylene, acetylene, and propane in quasi-quiescent air has been studied numerically in normal earth gravity (1g) and zero gravity (0g). The time-dependent full Navier-Stokes equations with buoyancy were solved using an implicit, third-order accurate numerical scheme, including a C3-chemistry model (32 species, 112 reactions) and an optically thin-media radiation model for heat losses. Observations of the flames were also made at the NASA Glenn 2.2-Second Drop Tower. For all cases of the fuels and gravity levels investigated, a peak reactivity spot, i.e., reaction kernel, was formed in the flame base, thereby holding a trailing diffusion flame. The location of the reaction kernel with respect to the burner rim depended inversely on the reaction-kernel reactivity or velocity. In the C2 and C3 hydrocarbon flames, the H2-O2 chain reactions were important at the reaction kernel, yet the CH3 + O --> CH2O + H reaction, a dominant contributor to the heat-release rate in methane flames studied previously, did not outweigh other exothermic reactions. Instead of the C1-route oxidation pathway in methane flames, the C2 and C3 hydrocarbon fuels dehydrogenated on the fuel side and acetylene was a major hydrocarbon fragment burning at the reaction kernel. The reaction-kernel correlations between the reactivity (the heat-release or oxygen-consumption rate) and the velocity, obtained previously for methane, were developed further for various fuels in more universal forms using variables related to local Damköhler numbers and Peclet numbers.
Furthermore, direct numerical simulations with the C3-chemistry model have been performed to investigate the transient behavior and internal structure of flames propagating in an axisymmetric fuel jet of methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, or propane in 1g and 0g. The fuel issued from a 3-mm-i.d. tube into quasi-quiescent air for a fixed mixing time of 0.3 s before it was ignited along the centerline where the fuel-air mixture was at stoichiometry. The edge of the flame formed a vigorously burning peak reactivitiy spot, i.e., reaction kernel, and propagated through a flammable mixture layer, leaving behind a trailing diffusion flame. The reaction kernel broadened laterally across the flammable mixture layer and possessed characteristics of premixed flames in the direction of propagation and unique flame structure in the transverse direction. The reaction kernel grew wings on both fuel and air sides to form a triple-flame-like structure, particularly for ethylene and acetylene, whereas for alkanes, the fuel-rich wing tended to merge with the main diffusion flame zone, particularly methane. The topology of edge diffusion flames depend on the properties of fuels, particularly the rich flammability limit, and the mechanistic oxidation pathways. The transit velocity of edge diffusion flames, determined from a time series of calculated temperature field, equaled to the measured laminar flame speed of the stoichiometric fuel-air mixtures, available in the literature, independent of the gravity level.
