Task Description:
In the exploration of space, longer duration missions to the moon, to Mars, and aboard the International Space Station (ISS) increase the likelihood of fire events. NASA's fire safety program for manned space flight is based largely upon controlling the flammability of the material on board and removing ignition sources. There is ongoing research to improve the flammability characterization of materials in low gravity. However, very little research has been conducted on fire suppression in a low-gravity environment. Although the existing suppression systems aboard the Space Shuttle (halon 1301, CF3Br) and the ISS (CO2 and water-based form) may continue to be used, alternative effective agents or techniques are desirable for long-duration missions.
In this study, both experimental and computational approaches are pursued. The experiments include both normal- and reduced-gravity tests using the NASA Glenn's drop tower and the KC-135 aircraft. The critical extinguishment mole fraction of fire-extinguishing agents will be measured using a cup burner, which is the industry-standard burner apparatus most widely used for agent effectiveness in fire safety engineering. The cup-burner forms a laminar co-flow diffusion flame with a circular fuel source (2.8 cm diameter, either a liquid pool or a low-velocity gas jet) inside a co-axial chimney with an oxidizer flow. Because its structure resembles a fire, great faith has been placed in agent extinction concentrations determined in the cup burner experiment, and many codes and standards are based on the cup-burner values. Major parameters to be varied are the gravity level, oxygen mole fraction in the oxidizer, oxidizer velocity, and types of fuel, agent, and diluent. Fuels include methane (CH4), heptane (n-C7H16), methanol, and trioxane (3[CH2O]). In addition to chemically passive agents (N2, CO2, Ar, and He) we will also study agents which have an increasing chemical contribution; (i.e., CF3H, CF3Br, and Fe(CO)5). Direct numerical simulation will be performed to capture unsteady fire suppression processes in various gravity and oxygen levels using comprehensive reaction mechanisms for the CH4-O2 combustion (GRI Mech) and halogenated agent chemistry (NIST CKMech).
The objectives of this study are as follows.
1. Obtain fundamental knowledge of physical and chemical processes of fire suppression, using gravity and oxygen concentration as independent variables to simulate various environments in spacecraft and surface bases in Mars and moon missions.
2. Provide rigorous testing of numerical models, which include comprehensive descriptions of chemistry and radiative heat losses.
3. Provide basic research results useful for technological advances in fire safety, including the development of new fire-extinguishing agents and approaches, in the microgravity environment associated with ISS and in the partial-gravity Martian and lunar environments.
This research is important in relation to NASA's long-term goals in fire safety for long-duration missions in the exploration of space. First, this research contributes to the area of space fire suppression, which has not yet been fully studied. This research addresses such practical problems through fundamental scientific approaches. By using gravity and oxygen levels as independent variables, this research provides better understanding of the physical and chemical mechanisms involved in suppression of fires in space and gives more rigorous testing of numerical models. Basic results obtained by this research may lead to technological advances in fire suppression, e.g., new fire-extinguishing agents and/or approaches, particularly suitable for fires in space. Thus, this research contributes to the development of improved strategies and procedures for fire suppression in microgravity environment associated with the ISS or spacecraft and the reduced-gravity lunar and Martian environments.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Although the cup-burner apparatus has been used for determining the minimum extinguishing concentration of fire-extinguishing agents as described in national and international standards, fundamental understanding of this apparatus has been vertually null. This research provide the details of the flame extingushment process in the cup burner experiment, thus benefitting the terrestrial fire suppression engineering community and industry.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
The structure and suppression of laminar methane-air co-flow diffusion flames formed on a cup burner have been studied experimentally and numerically using physically acting fire-extinguishing agents (CO2, N2, He, and Ar) in normal earth (1g) and microgravity (ug). The low-g extinguishment testing of the flame with CO2 was conducted aboard the NASA Reduced-Gravity Aircraft (KC-135). The computation uses a direct numerical simulation with detailed chemistry and radiative heat-loss models.
An agent was introduced into a low-speed coflowing oxidizing stream by gradually replacing the air until extinguishment occurred under a fixed minimal fuel velocity. The suppression of cup-burner flames, which resemble real fires, occurred via a blowoff process (in which the flame base drifted downstream) rather than the global extinction phenomenon typical of counterflow diffusion flames. The computation revealed that the peak reactivity spot (the reaction kernel) formed in the flame base was responsible for attachment and blowoff of the trailing diffusion flame.
The minimum extinguishing concentration (MEC) determined experimentally in 1g were CO2, 15.7+/-0.6 %; N2, 25.9+/-1.0 %; He, 26.7+/-1.1 %; and Ar, 37.3+/-1.5 %. The extinguishing agent volume fraction in 1g for CO2 was nearly constant over a wide range of the oxidizer velocity (3 to 18 cm/s), exhibiting a “plateau region,” and steeply decreased as the velocity was decreased to approach the over-to-under-ventilated flame limit (~1 cm/s). The ug extinguishment data for CO2 acquired aboard the KC-135 were within 20 % to 24 %, but required further refinement. The numerical simulation performed thus far predicted the extinguishing agent volume fractions as: CO2, 14.5 % (or 16.1 % with different kinetic parameters for a methyl-H atom reaction step) in 1g and CO2, 19.1 %; N2, ~38 %; He, 30.7 %; and Ar, ~49 % in 0g. The buoyancy-induced flame flickering in 1g and thermal and transport properties of the agents affected the flame extinguishment limits.

Task Description:
In early 2012, the Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Methane, ethylene, or a selected nitrogen dilution of each fuel issuing from a burner tube in coflowing air was ignited to form a laminar diffusion flame. The structure of the flame was characterized and the liftoff velocity limits were determined as a function of the fuel and burner diameter. The flame temperature, soot, and CH* radical concentrations were measured and compared with computation. Although the lifted flame far from the burner (~10 cm) might be stabilized with a triple-flame structure, i.e., a stoichiometric diffusion flame base with fuel lean and rich premixed branches, the stabilizing and lifting mechanisms of burner-rim-attached flames were still largely left unstudied.

The overall merit of the proposed research is fundamental contributions to combustion science and NASA’s microgravity combustion research, through the effective use of underutilized SLICE data on the liftoff limits and the rigorous validation of the numerical methods, including reaction mechanisms, soot formation, and radiation models.

If successful, the proposed research will give a significant impact on the research area of flame stabilization, which has been one of major subjects of interest since the early days of modern combustion research, started several decades ago. Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
A laminar jet diffusion flame is formed by igniting a gaseous hydrocarbon fuel issuing from a small stainless-steel burner tube (0.4 to 2.5 mm i.d.) in coflowing air through a coaxial glass chimney (95 mm i.d.) or a converging nozzle (25 mm i.d.). As the fuel or air velocity is increased gradually, the flame base detaches and lifts off the burner rim, stabilizes at a new position downstream, and blows out eventually due to the finite rate of chemical reactions. This study investigates the stabilizing mechanism of laminar jet diffusion flames in normal Earth gravity (1g) and microgravity (ug) experimentally and computationally.
During the reporting period, we have performed the following tasks.
(1) Measured the stability limits of laminar coflow jet diffusion flames of propene in 1g for the fuel tubes with inner diameters of 0.8 and 1.6 mm, in addition to the fuels investigated previously (i.e., methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, propane, butane, butene).
(2) Performed the computation using the in-house numerical code (UNICORN) with a newly incorporated chemical reaction mechanism applicable to C1 to C4 hydrocarbons. Successfully revealed the structure of a butane jet diffusion flame, for the first time, as the flame base lifted off the burner rim gradually until blowout, in response to incremental increases in the coflowing air velocity. The predicted flame stability limit was in good agreement with the measurement.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2020
Task Progress:
In early 2012, the Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) aboard the International Space Station [1]. A gaseous hydrocarbon fuel (methane, ethylene, or a selected nitrogen dilution of each fuel) issuing from a small burner tube in coflowing air was ignited to form a laminar diffusion flame. As the fuel or air velocity was increased gradually, the flame base detached and lifted off the burner rim, stabilized at a new position downstream, and blew out eventually due to the finite rate of chemical reactions. In this study, the stabilizing mechanism of laminar diffusion flames has been examined further in normal Earth gravity (1g).
During the reporting period 12/13/2018 to 12/12/2019, we have performed the following tasks:
(1) By using the engineering model of the Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) experiment assembly, loaned from the NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC), the stability limits (lift-off and blow-off) of laminar diffusion flames have been measured in 1g [2, 3]. The fuels are methane, ethane, ethene, propane, butane, 1-butene, 70% methane in nitrogen, and 20% ethane in nitrogen. The fuel tube inner diameters are 0.4 mm and 0.8 mm. In general, the critical fuel jet velocities at the flame stability limits are larger for a larger fuel tube diameter, for alkenes than alkanes (due to the higher reactivity), and for a lower number of carbon atoms (due to the lower fuel density).
(2) Furthermore, by using a newly fabricated experimental apparatus, the stability limits have been measured over much larger ranges of the fuel and air velocities as well as the fuel tube diameter than those of the SPICE rig. The apparatus consists of a stainless-steel fuel tube (0.4 – 3.2 mm i.d.) coaxially installed in a glass chimney (95 mm i.d.). In addition to the pure C1 – C4 hydrocarbons mentioned above, acetylene is also used as the fuel.
(3) The computation with detailed chemistry to reveal the diffusion flame structure and flame-flow interactions leading to the flame stability-limit conditions has been initiated. A chemical reaction mechanism for butane has newly been incorporated in the in-house numerical code, especially capable of simulating unsteady flame-flow interaction phenomena such as the flame stabilizing process.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
During the reporting period 12/13/2017 to 12/12/2018, we have performed the following tasks:
(1) Hand-carried an engineering model of the Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) experimental assembly from the NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) to the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) on 3/23/18. After setting up and running the experiment over the spring/summer, the apparatus was returned to the GRC on 8/31/18, in response to a request by NASA. Additional experiments are needed.
(2) Measured the stability limits (lift-off and blow-off) of laminar diffusion flames in the Earth gravity (1g) in the SPICE apparatus for various fuels using various burner tube diameters. The fuels tested thus far include ethane, propane, butane, and 1-butene and the burner tube diameters used are 0.4 mm and 0.8 mm. In general, the critical fuel jet velocity at the flame lifting is larger for a larger fuel tube diameter, for alkenes than alkanes (due to the higher reactivity), and for a lower number of fuel carbon atoms (due to the lower fuel density). The critical fuel jet velocity for ethane with 0.8 mm dia. fuel tube in the present experiment is approximately 21% higher than that obtained in the SLICE’s 1g test in 2012 [Takahashi et al., 2012]. The calibration of the fuel mass flow controller and the air fan need to be completed. Other fuels planned to be tested include methane, ethylene, acetylene, and propene. However, because of the SPICE apparatus’s upper limits of the mass flow controller for fuel (500 sccm in N2) and the coflowing air speed (~65 cm/s), the lifting limit could barely be reached for the fuel with a high reactivity such as ethylene even using the smallest burner tube diameter (0.4 mm). For a highly reactive fuel such as acetylene and/or for a larger diameter will require an experimental apparatus capable of wider fuel and air flow rate ranges.
(3) Initiated the fabrication of a new burner system for studying the structure and stabilization of laminar diffusion flames in 1g at the CWRU campus. The burner consists of a stainless-steel fuel tube (0.4 – 2.1 mm i.d.) and a coaxially installed contour nozzle (~25 mm i.d. exit) for the coflow air. Four mass flow meters (Hastings, HFM-200 and HFM-201) have been purchased for the flow ranges of 500 sccm N2 for the fuel, 200 sccm N2 for an additive to the fuel, 50 slpm for the coflow air, and 15 slpm for an additive to the air. The burner assembly will be installed on a 3D translational stage for the diagnostic measurements.
(4) Made an oral presentation of the results of the stability limits, obtained using the SPICE experimental apparatus, at the 34th Annual Meeting of the American Society for Gravitational and Space Research, Bethesda, Rockville, MD, October 31-November 3, 2018.
Reference: Takahashi, F., Kulakhmetov, R., Stocker, D.P., Ma, B., and Long, M.B., Microgravity Enhances the Stability of Gas-Jet Diffusion Flames, 28th Annual Meeting of the American Society for Gravitational and Space Research, New Orleans, LA, November 28-December 2, 2012.

Flight Assignment/Project Notes:

Task Description:
This task consists of ground-based experiments using low-gravity aircraft and continued development of a comprehensive predictive model of flame spread and extinction over solid fuels.
The overall objectives of the research program are to understand the flame spread and extinction phenomena of solids in low-speed forced concurrent flows in microgravity and in upward buoyant flows in partial gravity. Specifically, we are interested in knowing how gravity affects the flammability limits and spread behaviour of solid materials and how to infer the combustion behaviour of these materials in low gravity from test results in normal gravity.
The significance of the task is to understand the material flammability in reduced gravity and material screening tests for low gravity applications; this can contribute to a safer space exploration mission.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This study on the basic mechanism of material flammability contributes to the fire safety of human both on earth and in space travel and exploration. The PI has served as a member of the National Academy of Engineering (NRC) committee to identify innovative research needs to foster fire safety in the US.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2010
Task Progress:
This research program is concerned with the effect of low-speed flow on the spreading and extinction processes over solid fuels. Specifically, we are interested in the Solid Inflammability Boundary At Low-speed (SIBAL). The project has passed the Science Concept Review and the experiment was originally scheduled to be performed in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack. However, with a shift of NASA prority, the original space experiment has been cancelled and the project became a ground-based investigation. Despise this change the overall objectives of the project remain the same. But, due to the lack of experimental platform in space, emphases have been shifted to modeling and normal gravity tests.
The hypothesis (more accurately the prediction from the theoretical model) is that due to radiative loss from the flame, a quenching limit exists in low-speed flow. The complete flammability boundary consists of a low-speed quenching branch and a high-speed blowoff branch. The merging point of the two branches defines the fundamental flammability limit. The flammability boundary is expressed mainly as a function of oxygen percentage and flow velocity. The original objectives of the flight investigations as stated in the 2002 SIBAL SCR are:
1) Experimentally verify the model predictions by measuring the extinction limits in low-speed concurrent flow at several oxygen percentages, flow velocities and sample widths.
2) Verify the existence and quantitatively determine the fundamental low-oxygen limit.
3) Measure the steady flame spread rates and visible flame lengths. Measure the 2-D surface temperature distribution in the pre-heat and the pyrolysis zones. Measure flame (gas-phase) temperatures at selected locations. Measure radiation from the flame and the solid.
4) Compare the experimental data with model predictions.
It is very clear that these original objectives are directly related to spacecraft fire safety. Two new objectives are added in this proposing period in order to answer an important question on the practical material flammability screening process and to address the possible different environment for fire safety in space exploration:
5) Evaluate the present NASA 6001 material flammability test #1 and to establish the relationship between its test results in normal gravity with material flammability characteristics in micro- and partial gravities.
6) Investigate material flammability in low pressure and high oxygen environment.
Accomplishment
1. A summary of the design and the testing of a novel solid burning device for the original SIBAL project were given in the journal paper (J1). This includes related experimental and computational results.
2. Gas radiation effects and the influence of Fuel vapor Lewis number on flame spread and extinction were investigated theoretically in (J2) and (J4).
3. One-sided flame spread over a composite fabric was studied in detail in (J3) and cyclic flame spread over Nomex was discovered in (J6) and in Kleinhenz’s Ph.D. thesis (P2).
4. Results of detailed measurement of radiation properties of thin cellulosic fuels were presented in Pettegrew’s Ph.D. thesis (P1).
5. The behavior of flammability limit at low oxygen atmosphere was investigated theoretically for thick solid slabs in both normal and micro-gravities. It was discovered that a hysteresis phenomenon exists between the side and the wake stabilized flames (J5).
6. Pressure modeling as a simulation tool for estimating the rate of upward flame spread in partial gravity was proposed (J7). Other scale modeling issues were discussed in the book article (B1).
7. The mechanisms leading to pressure flammability limits were examined in (J8).
8. Development of three-dimensional steady concurrent flame spread model over solids with radiation in both forced and buoyant flows were advanced in (P3) and (P4). The latter includes detailed comparison with three sets of experimental data.

Task Description:
This task consists of ground-based experiments using low-gravity aircraft and continued development of a comprehensive predictive model of flame spread and extinction over solid fuels. The overall objectives of the research program are to understand the flame spread and extinction phenomena of solids in low-speed forced concurrent flows in microgravity and in upward buoyant flows in partial gravity . Specifically, we are interested in knwing how gravity affects the flammability limits and spread behaviour of solid materials and how to infer the combustion behaviour of these materials in low gravity from test results in normal gravity. The significance of the task is to understand the material flammability in reduced gravity and material screening tests for low gravity applications; this can contribute to a safer space exploration mission.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This study on the basic mechanism of material flammability contributes to the fire safety of human both on earth and in space travel and exploration -The PI Has served as a member of the National Academy of Engineering (NRC)committee to identify innovative research needs to foster fire safety in the US.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
1. A preventive approach to fire safety is proper material selection based on the flammability characteristics. One such measure of flammability is the Limiting oxygen Index (LOI). This is a commonly used numerical flammability index for relative grading and selecting materials. The test measures the extinction limit of a downward spreading flame over a finite size (rectangular slab or rod) fuel specimen. In this work [1], a two-dimensional numerical model was used to study the flame stabilization and extinction characteristics over a thick model solid fuel, which resembles a specimen burning near extinction limit in an LOI testing procedure. The computations were preformed for mixed buoyant-forced flow environment prevailing in the LOI test at normal gravity. At sufficiently high oxygen level (far away from flame extinction limit) the flame is anchored on the sides of the fuel slab (side-stabilized flame), but as the oxygen level is reduced, at a certain value the flame stabilization point abruptly shifts from the sides of the specimen to the wake region (wake flame). The structural details of these two modes of flame stabilization are discussed. The computations also show that the shift in the flame anchoring position with oxygen level exhibits hysteresis, i.e. multiple flame solutions may exist for a given environmental condition of flow and oxygen. The flame extinction limits and flame-shift limits (side-stabilized flame to wake flame and vice versa) in ambient oxygen percentage are presented for different forced flow velocities. Over the velocity range studied here, the side-stabilized flame (similar to flames over of thin fuels) becomes less flammable (higher LOI) at higher velocity whereas, the wake stabilized flame becomes more flammable (lower LOI) with increase in forced flow velocity. To understand the implication of this earth based measurement to material selection for space application, additional computations were performed for pure-forced flow environment in zero gravity. Stabilization and extinction behavior of the flames at normal gravity is compared with that in zero gravity. The computations in pure forced flow environment show that the two modes are also present in zero gravity environment but only above certain minimum flow velocity. Below this velocity only single flaming solution was obtained. In the present computations, the LOI values at zero gravity were lower than those at normal gravity. For zero gravity the LOI based on side stabilized flame (for thin fuels) shows a non-monotonic behavior, there is a minimum LOI which for the present set of property and kinetic parameter values occurs at forced velocity of about 3-5cm/s. The LOI based on wake flame extinction, at zero gravity decreases rapidly with flow velocity for small velocities but with further increase in velocity the LOI value stays approximately constant.
2. The Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) apparatus has traditionally been used to quantify flammability characteristics of the materials numerically. The testing procedure consists determining the minimum concentration of oxygen in a mixture with nitrogen that when passed through the column will support combustion of solid fuel ignited from the top. Although a simple device, the flow pattern inside the device could be complicated by buoyant velocity induced under the influence of earth’s gravitational force field. This in turn could affect the measured LOI value. So far the experimental studies are limited to global measurements and there is no detailed study on this device. In this work [2], the LOI test apparatus is numerically studied using a three-dimensional model for downward flame spread over a film type solid fuel. The model capability is exploited to investigate the mixed buoyant-forced flow field in the test column, the solid fuel combustion details and flame extinction behavior. The computations show that buoyancy effects can result in the ambient air from outside to be drawn into the column. The degree of entrainment decreases as the gas mixture mass feed rate at the base of the column is increased. Over the velocity range 0.5cm/s-15cm/s, the LOI values are almost constant to change in the column base inlet velocity. In the absence of buoyant force (which has implication to the zero gravity space environment) the flow field is drastically different from that in normal gravity, and the computed LOI values for the chosen fuel are lower than those for normal gravity cases and exhibited a non monotonic trend with a minimum LOI. The LOI was found to be independent of specimen width for width greater than 1cm.
3. In the enclosed environment of a manned space habitat, fire safety becomes a major concern. Though various combinations of pressure and oxygen can be used to support human habitation, the bulk of flammability testing for materials is done at standard atmospheric conditions. This study focuses on the flammability and flame spread in these potential space habitat environments [3 and Kleinhenz’s PhD thesis]. Pressures were kept below 1 atm, Oxgyen/Nitrogen mixtures between 21% and 30%, and gravity levels of 1 g/ge (Earth), 0.38 g/ge (Martian), and 0.16 g/ge (Lunar) were used.Two materials were examined. Part 1 of this report discusses Kimwipes®, a thin tissue paper, which was better suited for the reduced gravity experiments. A scaling relation that predicts upward spread rate as a function of pressure, gravity, and width, is introduced and experimentally verified. Nomex® fabric, practical material commonly used in the space program, is the focus of Part 2. Nomex has a lower oxygen limit for upward spread than for downward spread. A unique phenomenon was observed during experimentation, whereby the continually elongating flames broke off in the middle into two smaller upward propagating flames. One flame would then extinguish, and the remaining flame would repeat this cycle. The process was documented in detail and is believed to be a function of a two stage pyrolysis occurring in the fuel.In order to enhance the capability of flame-spreading model as a predictive tool, especial in microgravity, we have performed radiation property measurement, spreading tests in normal gravity, and model calibration exercises for a specific cotton-fiberglass composite fabric. The paper gives details of how these are done and some of the special features of the burning of a composite fuel [3].
4. Using a detailed three-dimensional model, the effects of gas-phase chemical kinetic rate and pressure on flame-spread rates are investigated for both buoyant upward and concurrent forced flow flame spread over thin solids [4]. For wide (two-dimensional) samples, varying the chemical kinetic rate alone has a negligible effect on spread rate in forced concurrent flow spread; it has a small but finite influence on upward buoyant spread rate. The latter is thought to be through the increasing buoyant velocity at higher flame temperature when the kinetics becomes faster. In narrow samples, the influence of kinetics is increased, thought due to the side quenching influence from kinetic rates. However, pressure has a much larger influence on concurrent flame spread rate than that from kinetics alone. This is primarily through the pressure effect on flame standoff distance that affects the fuel burning and heat release rate. Based on this sensitivity study, the possibility of pressure modeling is examined. Comparing with a previously proposed scheme of pressure modeling derived from reduced gravity experiment, a small discrepancy has been found. It is suggested that this discrepancy is due to the lack of flame radiation in the flame spread model.
5. A three-dimensional concurrent flame spread model that includes a gray gas radiation model has been solved for 5 cm/s purely forced flow over a thin cellulosic fuel [5]. Cases are compared for full Planck mean radiation, no radiation, and an intermediate case which is thought to better represent the radiative energy interaction. Results show that the radiation decreases the flame temperature, flame length and spread rate. Flame profiles, heat fluxes, and additional structural details are presented.
6. The importance of radiation effects in the combustion of solid fuels means that surface radiative properties must be well known under a variety of conditions to allow accurate numerical modeling. This paper [6] and Pettegrew’s PhD thesis provide partial results (both spectral and band-integrated) from an experimental effort that determined the radiative properties of a thin cellulosic fuel as a function of viewing angle at discrete levels of pyrolysis.
7. Flame spread over a thermally-thin solid fuel is numerically investigated under various boundary conditions using a detailed two-dimensional, opposed-flow model with gas-phase radiation and the latest Kimwipe pyrolysis kinetics data [7]. The effects of solid virgin fuel temperature, external radiation and fuel vapor doping in opposed air flow are systematically studied because of their importance in room fires (flashover) and in spacecraft fires (overheated equipments). The numerical results show that all of these elemental factors involved in a room fire can enhance the flame spread rate but their mechanisms of enhancement are not the same. This paper will present the detailed flame responses to each individual factor [7].
8. Additional reduced gravity experiments on flame spreading and upward oxygen flammability limits have recently been carried out on C-9 mission aboard the KC135 airplane in March 2006. The data are still being analyzed. The first part of the data should reinforce the pressure-gravity modeling relationship proposed previously. The second part of the data will be useful in assessing the effect of partial gravity on upward flammability limit and the effect of sample length (relative to width) in performing the upward burning experiments.

Task Description:
This task consists of the development and flight of a space-based experiment, the continued pursuit of ground-based results in drop towers and aircraft experiments, and the continued development of a comprehensive predictive model of flame spread and extinction over solid fuels. The overall objectives of the research program are to understand the flame spread and extinction phenomena of a thin combusting solid in low-speed forced concurrent flow. Specifically, we plan to carryout a space experiment: (1) to determine the low-speed flammability boundary of a selected thin solid fuel or fuels. To verify the existence of and quantify the reasons for the critical low oxygen limit, (2) to measure the flame spread rate, flame size, and selected specific aspects of flame structure in low-speed flow, and (3) together with model predictions, determine the mechanisms controlling the behavior of flame spreading and extinction of thin solids in low-speed forced flow. In normal gravity, buoyant air motion in flames is at least 20 to 30 cm/sec. Flame spreading mechanisms that are present only in lower flow velocities, such as spacecraft air-ventilation currents, cannot, therefore, be studied in normal gravity. This research seeks to contribute to fundamental combustion science, and to improve the basis for engineering improved spacecraft fire safety.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2005
Task Progress:
Modeling
(1) A Computational Study of Low Oxygen Flammability for Thick Solid Samples
The LOI apparatus is a standard device commonly used for numerical flammability ranking of the solids. The standard specimens used in the test are thick (in the form of rods and bars). The specimens are ignited at the top in normal gravity (directed downwards) and imposed forced flow of known mixture of oxygen and nitrogen. As oxygen level in the flowing gas mixture is reduced, the flame, which is normally anchored on the sides of the fuel, retreats to the wake region behind the flattened top end of the specimen (if given sufficient experimental time). The flame in the wake eventually extinguishes on further reduction in oxygen level. Here in this work, a two-dimensional numerical model is used to study the flame stabilization and extinction characteristics over a thick solid fuel.
In a mixed buoyant-forced flow environment considered here, it is observed that at higher flow velocities or gravity and at low oxygen levels the flame stabilization point shifts from the sides of the wick to the wake region. The structural details in the two modes of flame stabilization are discussed. The shift in the flame anchoring position with oxygen level exhibits a hysteresis, i.e. multiple solutions may exist for a given environmental condition. The flame extinction limits and flame-shift limits (form sides of the solid fuel to the wake region or from the wake region to the sides of the fuel) in oxygen percentage are presented for the environmental parameters, forced flow velocity and gravity level.
(2) Effects of Fuel Lewis Number on the Flame Spread over Solids
Using a detailed two-dimensional numerical model, a systematic investigation has been made to study the effect of fuel Lewis number (LeF = ? / DF) and mass transfer on flame spread over thin solids. The fuel Lewis number affects the flame spread rates for both concurrent and opposed flames over thin fuels. The dependence of the flame spread rate on fuel Lewis number for these two spreading modes are, however, not the same. In opposed flame spreads (zero-gravity, self-propagation and normal gravity downward propagation), the flame spread rate vs. the fuel Lewis number curve is non-monotonic. In the high fuel Lewis number range, increasing fuel Lewis number decreases the opposing spread rate whereas in the low fuel Lewis number range, decreasing fuel Lewis number decreases the opposing spread rate. In steady, concurrent spread in zero-gravity with low-speed flow and a constant flame length, the flame spread rate decreases with fuel Lewis number in a monotonic manner. By using the computational model as a tool, the effects of fuel mass diffusion perpendicular to and parallel with the solid surface are isolated to obtain more physical insight on the two-dimensional aspect of fuel mass transfer on flame spread. In addition, the model has also been used to decouple the solid evaporation process so that the fuel diffusion effect in the gas phase can be isolated. Both of these theoretical exercises contribute to the understanding of mass transfer effects on the flame spreading phenomena over solids.
Experimental (1) Solid Combustion Experiments Using a Continuous Fuel Dispenser for Use in Microgravity and Associated Model Computations
The conventional way of determining the flammability characteristics of a material involves a number of tedious single-sample tests to distinguish flammable from non-flammable conditions. A novel test device and fuel configuration has been developed that permits multiple successive tests for indefinite lengths of thin solid materials. In this device, a spreading flame can be established and held at a fixed location in front of optimized diagnostics while continuous variations of test parameters are made. This device is especially well-suited to conducting experiments in space (e.g. aboard the International Space Station) where the limited resources of stowage, volume, and crew time pose major constraints. A prototype version of this device was tested successfully in both a normal gravity laboratory and during low-gravity aircraft trials. As part of this ongoing study of material flammability behavior, a numerical model of concurrent-flow flame spread is used to simulate the flame. Two and three-dimensional steady-state forms of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations with chemical reactions and gas and solid radiation are solved. The model is used to assist in the design of the test apparatus and to interpret the results of microgravity experiments. This paper describes details of the fuel testing device and planned experiment diagnostics. A special fuel, developed to optimize use of the special testing device, is described. Some results of the numerical flame spread model are presented to explain the three-dimensional nature of flames spreading in concurrent flow and to show how the model is used as an experiment design tool.
(2) One-sided Flame Spread Phenomena of a Thermally Thin Composite Cotton/Fiberglass Fabric
As an experimental necessity, past flame spread studies have relied on fast burning cellulosic papers. For longer duration tests planned for the International Space Station a 50% fiberglass, 50% cotton composite fabric is better suited for the novel fuel feeding system in the compact hardware design of a current microgravity combustion experiment. The fabric’s combustion characteristics in normal gravity include unexpected cases where a flame can be sustained on one side of the fuel. One-sided flames are smaller in size than their two-sided counterparts, and propagate at half the speed. Surface temperature distributions were measured using infrared imaging and indicated a high temperature region caused by the non-flammable fiberglass. Breaching the fiberglass matrix made it possible for the flame to transfer to the other side of the fuel, suggesting that the fiberglass matrix acts as a flame arrester.

Task Description:
This task consists of the development and flight of a space-based experiment, the continued pursuit of ground-based results in drop towers and aircraft experiments, and the continued development of a comprehensive predictive model of flame spread and extinction over solid fuels. The overall objectives of the research program are to understand the flame spread and extinction phenomena of a thin combusting solid in low-speed forced concurrent flow. Specifically, we plan to carryout a space experiment: (1) to determine the low-speed flammability boundary of a selected thin solid fuel or fuels. To verify the existence of and quantify the reasons for the critical low oxygen limit, (2) to measure the flame spread rate, flame size, and selected specific aspects of flame structure in low-speed flow, and (3) together with model predictions, determine the mechanisms controlling the behavior of flame spreading and extinction of thin solids in low-speed forced flow. In normal gravity, buoyant air motion in flames is at least 20 to 30 cm/sec. Flame spreading mechanisms that are present only in lower flow velocities, such as spacecraft air-ventilation currents, cannot, therefore, be studied in normal gravity. This research seeks to contribute to fundamental combustion science, and to improve the basis for engineering improved spacecraft fire safety.

Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of "Flame spread and extinction over solid materials," grant NNX10AD99A. [Note: Grant NNX10AD99A has been renamed, "Research Opportunities in Combustion Science," per NSSC information (Ed., 1/5/24).]
Flammability of solid materials is of interest to NASA as a first line of defense in spacecraft fire safety efforts. In micro- or partial-gravity, the reduced buoyant flows, coupled with low-speed air circulation currents, create an environment quite different than that in normal Earth gravity. In addition, there are several oxidizer atmospheres under consideration for crew vehicles and habitats, which expand the scope of the problem. A fundamental understanding of solid flammability as a function of gravity, flow velocity, oxygen percentage, pressure, and sample configuration can be an important contribution both to combustion science and to the NASA space exploration initiatives.
This proposed experiment will concentrate on the flame growth, decay, and extinction over the surface of a non-flat thick solid in microgravity. In particular, a solid sphere of substantial size (i.e., 4 cm diameter) is chosen as a representative of non-flat samples. In addition to the parameters influencing the flammability of thin solids, the degree of interior heat-up is an important parameter on the solid burning characteristics of thick specimens. For spherical samples, the degree of interior heating is always changing. The problem is therefore unsteady in nature. In addition, flow around a sphere is different from that around a flat surface. The existence of a forward stagnation point, and shoulder and wake regions results in a different local flow pattern, hence a different flame-solid interaction. These can affect the burning and extinction characteristics.
In the proposed experiment, cast Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) spheres will be instrumented with five embedded thermocouples to record the interior temperatures during the preheating and the combustion processes. The project objectives are (1) Experimentally determine the flame growth characteristics (growth rate, flame shape, and dimensions) over a thick solid fuel as a function of flow velocity, oxygen percentage, pressure, and the degree of internal heating; (2) Experimentally determine the flame extinction characteristics (quenching and blowoff limits) over a thick solid fuel as a function of flow velocity, oxygen percentage, pressure, and the degree of internal heating; and (3) Establish a high-fidelity numerical model that can be compared with the microgravity results and serve as a tool connecting normal gravity and microgravity performance.
The microgravity experiment using the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) in the International Space Station (ISS) has started in February 2023. It is expected to continue until June 2023 followed by data analysis under a renewed grant.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This is a fundamental study on the flammability of solids. The understanding to be achieved will help us to deal with fire safety on Earth and in space.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2023
Task Progress:
In this past year, our major effort is to prepare the Growth and Extinction Limit (GEL) microgravity experiment in the International Space Station (ISS). The progress in this period includes ignition and flame-quenching extinction. Though these works were restricted either by normal gravity buoyancy-induced flow or limited experiment duration (5.2 s) in the drop tower, supplemented by numerical model and theoretical analysis, they still provided significant data to prepare for the upcoming ISS GEL experiment.
Ignition delay and ignition boundary in normal gravity
In this work, the ignition limits and the ignition delay times of the GEL sphere were investigated with the 10 mm – B type SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction) igniter in normal gravity. The igniter wire’s electrical current and power-on time, its distance from the sample surface, the forced flow velocity, oxygen percentage, and pressure were systematically varied. Two ignition delay times were determined: igniter-assisted ignition and self-sustained ignition. The solid temperature profiles were measured and used to determine the sub-surface temperature gradient at ignition. A numerical model was developed to study the heat transfer mechanism between the igniter and the solid surface during the pre-pyrolysis heat-up period. In addition to its scientific value in fundamental research of blunt body Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) samples’ ignition with heated wire, by using the equivalent flow strain rate, this research also provided valuable data in the preparation of the GEL experiment. For the ISS experiments, it is important to ensure that the sample can be ignited, but on the other hand, the igniter is not to overheat the sample leading to a too strong initial flame that shortens the flame growth period. To understand the details and the mechanisms of heat transfer between the igniter and the solid sample in the preheating phase, a numerical model was developed and solved with ANSYS Fluent to study the fluid-thermal processes between the igniter and the solid sample. The heat transfer modes include convection and radiation between the igniter and the sample (solid-to-solid) and heat conduction inside the solid. Pyrolysis is ignored during this pre-ignition period. The computation shows that at the stagnation point, radiative heat transfer is, in general, more important than convective heat transfer, and constitutes about 60% of the net total heat flux. The numerical model was also used to predict the ignition delay and heat transfer under microgravity.
The numerical model was also used to predict the ignition delay and heat transfer under microgravity. In the absence of gravity-induced buoyant flow, the convective heat transfer is weaker but the heat flux at the stagnation point region gets stronger. It leads to shorter time delay to heat the solid surface to the pyrolysis temperature. Another utilization of the normal gravity data for the ISS GEL microgravity experiment is to employ the equivalent stretch rate concept. For example, the 5 cm/s flow rate at normal gravity is equivalent to a 26 cm/s pure forced flow rate at microgravity. This provides guidance in the microgravity experiments.
A complete document of the normal gravity ignition work can be found in: Li C, T’ien JS, Johnston MC, Olson SL, Ferkul PV. "Ignition of thermally thick blunt body PMMA samples using a heated wire." Fire Saf. J. 2022 Oct;133:103663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.firesaf.2022.103663
Dynamic response and induced quenching extinction in normal to zero gravity transition
The transient response of the diffusion flame over the stagnation region of the GEL sphere to an abrupt transition to zero-gravity was investigated experimentally in the NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) 5s drop tower. A corresponding numerical modeling effort was carried out by Professor Sheng-Yen Hsu and his student Ching-Wei Wu. One of the objectives of this effort is to locate the flame extinction boundary during the 1g-0g transition. These data, although transient, can help us to locate the range of parameters in the determination of the quenching limits in the ISS GEL experiment.
In this experiment, an initial flame was established in normal gravity in a 17% oxygen atmosphere before the sudden release in a 5.18-second drop tower for zero gravity. Two parameters were investigated: the forced flow velocity and the degree of preheating in the surface layer of the GEL sample. The amount of preheating was controlled by monitoring the embedded thermocouples reading and adjusting the time of normal gravity burning before releasing to microgravity. The experimental results showed that the flame tip retreats by the end of the 5.18-second drop, and the flame may either survive or die depending on the controlling parameters. The experiments also showed rapid and dynamic flame changes, both in shape and color, in response to the changes of flow patterns when the buoyant driving force is suddenly removed. A numerical model was developed and implemented with ANSYS Fluent to gain more insight on the transient flow pattern and the solid-gas energy balance at the solid surface during the transition. The model solves full two-dimensional transient Navier-Stokes momentum, species, and energy equations with direct numerical simulation. Zeroth-order Arrhenius reaction is assumed for the solid pyrolysis at the solid surface. The produced Methyl Methacrylate (MMA) monomer reacts with oxygen in the gas phase through a one-step overall combustion reaction. The solid phase solves the two-dimensional transient heat conduction. Gas-phase radiation is ignored but solid surface radiation is considered. Solid phase is coupled with the gas phase though solid surface energy balance. Ignition is through external energy input in a small volume (0.0264 cm3) in the upstream forward stagnation point region with a total heat input of 2.64 W in 10 s.
An extinction map is presented using the experimental and the numerical data. Most of the work has been carried out previously but the results have been written up in this period. A manuscript has been submitted for journal publication and is under review.
Preparation of test samples for ISS experiment
Custom made 4-cm diameter cast PMMA sphere samples with 5 embedded thermocouples have been provided to NASA. All samples have been CT x-rayed in the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) Case Center for Imaging Research to determine the positions of each thermocouple. The measured solid in-depth temperatures are to be used to evaluate the sub-surface temperature gradient.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
1. Ignition Tests
Properly controlled ignitions are critical to the success of the Growth and Extinction Limit (GEL) space experiment. Many parameters need to be quantified in the proposed ignition process using heated hot wires. A systematic experimental and modeling study has been carried out. Ignition limits and ignition delay times of a large polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) sphere (4-cm diameter) and cylinder (5.08-m diameter) are investigated by placing an electrically-heated wire coil beneath the sample in a slow forced flow. The wire serves both as a heater for the solid sample and as a gas-phase hot spot to ignite the air-fuel vapor mixture. In the experiment, the wire electrical current and energizing duration, the wire placement distance from the sample surface, the forced flow velocity, oxygen percentage, and pressure are systematically varied. Ignition limits as a function of oxygen percentage, pressure, and igniter current are determined. Two ignition delay times are determined: Igniter-supported ignition and self-sustained ignition. These critical times are also functions of the degree of heat-up of the sample interior. Solid temperature profiles are measured using imbedded thermocouples to determine the sub-surface temperature gradients at the moment of ignition. The heat transfer modes from the igniter to the solid sample are investigated using a numerical analysis on the igniter and its interaction with the solid during the pre-pyrolysis heat-up period. At the flow stagnation-point region where the ignition is to occur, radiative flux is greater than convective flux. This is consistent with the experimental finding on ignition delay times and heat flux measurements. 2. Modeling Extinction Limits in Stagnation-point Diffusion Flame with Heat Loss to Solid Interior
The planned microgravity experiment, Growth and Extinction Limit (GEL), is designed to study the material flammability and extinction of thermally thick solids with an emphasis to quantify the effect of conductive heat loss into the solid interior by measuring the in-depth temperature profile. To obtain a more detailed understanding of the extinction phenomena, a previously developed one-dimensional axisymmetric stagnation-point diffusion flame model is expanded to account for the excessive heat loss into the solid beyond steady burning state. This is important because for thick solids, the burning period can have a long and slow solid transient with a quasi-steady gas-phase. A non-dimensional excessive conductive heat loss parameter is defined in the paper, and extensive numerical computations have been performed to determine the extinction boundary and the characteristics of near-limit flames. The classical U-shaped flammability boundary in the oxygen vs. stretch rate plot now becomes a series of U-shaped boundaries as a function of this heat loss parameter. For a given oxygen ambient, extinction boundary is a function of the heat loss parameter. The boundary consists of a blowoff branch and a radiative quenching branch. Detailed flame structures and energy balances are discussed along the extinction boundary. In this model, the non-dimensional gas-phase reaction rate (ratio of residence time to reaction time) has the classical Damköhler number character. Along the extinction boundary, the maximum non-dimensional reaction rates are approximately constant and of the order unit across the entire range of stretch rates.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2021
Task Progress:
1. PMMA sample fabrication. Last year, 30 thermocouple-instrumented PMMA spheres were ordered from our vendor, Meisner Galley, Inc. at New York state. Out of these, 15 were not made properly. The vendor promised to re-make 15 samples free of charge. But, we need to prepare again the pre-cast kits ourselves without ZINN’s support. This year, the order was further delayed by the shutdown of vendor’s lab due to COVID-19. We eventually received the re-made samples in August, 2020. Out of the 15 re-cast samples, only 9 are deemed good. Since these are used as the spared samples for 1-g testing, we felt 9 were adequate. We also ordered 30 un-instrumented PMMA sphere samples for ground testing (cheaper to make).
The newly received instrumented samples have been CT-scanned to precisely determine the thermocouple positions.
2. Ignition Test. Properly controlled ignitions are critical to the success of the Growth and Extinction Level (GEL) space experiment. Many parameters need to be quantified in the proposed ignition process using heated hot wires. A systematic experimental study has been carried out to investigate the igniter current level, igniter-sample separation distance, flow velocity, and oxygen percentage on ignition delay times and ignition limit. These normal-gravity ignition tests have been conducted using the variable oxygen tunnel at Case Western Reserve University.
Two ignition times were identified: the first appearance of igniter-assisted gas flame and the minimum igniter energizing time for self-sustained solid ignition. Two types of PMMA samples were used--a circular cylinder and a GEL sphere. The commercially available cylinders were tested first before the custom-made sphere samples became available. Un-instrumented spheres were used for the majority of tests. TC-instrumented samples were employed later only when solid temperature data is needed. The results of the ignition tests have been reported previously in SoFIE monthly meetings.
Ignition of two-step heating using hot wire has also been tested. In this series, a low-current heating was first applied until one embedded thermal couple reaches a pre-determined temperature before the higher ignition current is employed. The objective is to test whether an additional preheating method will provide useful insight on the ignition, extinction, or flame spread.
Using heat flux sensors, heat flux to the sample surface was measured using cylindrical sample. The variables in these tests are igniter distance, flow velocity, and pressure. The igniter current is kept at 4A.

Task Description:
NOTE: Continuation of "Flame spread and extinction over solid materials," grant NNX10AD99A.
Flammability of solid materials is of interest to NASA as a first line of defense in spacecraft fire safety efforts. In micro- or partial-gravity, the reduced buoyant flows, coupled with low-speed air circulation currents, create an environment quite different than that in normal Earth gravity. In addition, there are several oxidizer atmospheres under consideration for crew vehicles and habitats, which expand the scope of the problem. A fundamental understanding of solid flammability as a function of gravity, flow velocity, oxygen percentage, pressure, and sample configuration can be an important contribution both to combustion science and to the NASA space exploration initiatives.
This proposed experiment will concentrate on the flame growth, decay, and extinction over the surface of a non-flat thick solid in microgravity. In particular, a solid sphere of substantial size (i.e., 4 cm diameter) is chosen as a representative of non-flat samples. In addition to the parameters influencing the flammability of thin solids, the degree of interior heat-up is an important parameter on the solid burning characteristics of thick specimens. For spherical samples, the degree of interior heating is always changing. The problem is therefore unsteady in nature. In addition, flow around a sphere is different from that around a flat surface. The existence of a forward stagnation point, shoulder and wake regions result in a different local flow pattern, hence a different flame-solid interaction. These can affect the burning and extinction characteristics.
In the proposed experiment, cast Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) spheres will be instrumented with five embedded thermocouples to record the interior temperatures during the preheating and the combustion processes. The project objectives are (1) Experimentally determine the flame growth characteristics (growth rate, flame shape, and dimensions) over a thick solid fuel as a function of flow velocity, oxygen percentage, pressure, and the degree of internal heating; (2) Experimentally determine the flame extinction characteristics (quenching and blowoff limits) over a thick solid fuel as a function of flow velocity, oxygen percentage, pressure, and the degree of internal heating; and (3) Establish a high-fidelity numerical model that can be compared with the microgravity results and serve as a tool connecting normal gravity and microgravity performance.
The proposed experiment is to be conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) because ground-based microgravity facilities cannot provide the test time duration needed for thick samples.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This is a fundamental study on the flammability of solids. The understanding to be achieved will help us to deal with fire safety on Earth and in space.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
One-g to micro-g drop tests of PMMA spheres under different degrees of preheating and forced air flow has been performed. Embedded thermocouples enable the quantification of the degree of subsurface preheating. A quenched (within the 5-s drop duration) vs non-quenched corridor has been identified in a map with forced velocity and solid sub-surface temperature gradient as coordinates. The transient flame response in this step g-decrease has been found to be highly dynamic with multi-dimensional features. A corresponding numerical model has been formulated and solved by our colleagues, Professor Sheng-Yen Hsu and graduate student, Ching-Wei Wu, which provided additional details of the transient flame and solid responses.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2018
Task Progress:
The PhD dissertation by Michael Johnston summarized the work performed recently. This is broken into multiple related sections culminating in support of the space flight experiment Growth and Extinction Limits (GEL). GEL is a solid fuel combustion experiment in microgravity which intends to study the significant effect of solid fuel preheating on ignitability, flammability, flame propagation, and extinction. It is part of the combined Solid Flammability, Ignitability, and Extinction (SoFIE) project which is planned to operate in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) aboard the International Space Station (ISS). As part of this work,
1. A ground based test device was designed and constructed to measure the real time burning rate of solid fuels through gravimetric analysis within an upward facing low speed variable oxygen tunnel, similar to a commercial limiting oxygen index device. This device is described in detail in Johnston’s PhD dissertation and journal publication #2.
2. The validation of the above device using ethanol tea lamps was presented.
3. Direct measurement of the local burning rate in the forward stagnation region of thick polymethyl methacrylate spherical shells in a low stretch flame configuration (similar to those expected in the GEL flight experiment) was presented as a function of heat loss to the solid and gas feed oxygen concentration. The existence of minimum critical local burning rate as a property of the material alone had been suggested by previous works due to the desire for simplification in crude numerical models. This was not the case, and burning rate was found to be a parameter of flame heat loss to the solid and ambient oxygen concentration.
4. The design and construction of spherical PMMA samples for the GEL flight experiment, with thermocouples embedded into the solid interior was discussed.
5. A ground testing campaign of GEL sample prototypes in the NASA Zero-G Facility was discussed as the flame transitions from 1G to 0G near the low oxygen burning limit with transition triggered when a prescribed internal temperature profile was reached. An approximate extinction boundary was determined using this procedure.
6. The design and construction considerations for the Growth and Extinction Limits experimental apparatus in ISS were discussed, including the proposed test matrix, igniter testing, and gaseous oxidizer resource consumption.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2017
Task Progress:
1. Numerical modeling for Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiments
1.1 Flat SIBAL samples: Flame growth, spread, and quenching extinction over a thin composite cotton-fiberglass fabric blend (referred to as the SIBAL fabric) were studied in low-speed concurrent purely forced flows aboard the International Space Station. The tests were conducted in a small flow duct within the Microgravity Science Glovebox. The fuel samples measured 1.2 and 2.2 cm wide and 10 cm long. Ambient oxygen was varied from 21% down to 16% molar concentration and flow speed from 55 cm/s down to 1 cm/s. A slow purely forced flow resulted in a small flame, enabling us to observe the entire history of flame development including ignition, flame growth, steady spread (in some cases), and decay at the end of the sample. In addition, by decreasing flow velocity during some of the tests, low-speed flame quenching extinction limits were determined as a function of oxygen percentage. The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher extinction speeds in lower oxygen atmospheres. The shape of the quenching boundary supports the prediction by earlier theoretical models. These long duration microgravity experiments provide a rare opportunity for solid fuel combustion since microgravity time in ground-based facilities is generally not sufficient. This is the first time that a low speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread is mapped in a clean and unambiguous manner. A previously developed three-dimensional transient model is modified to compare with the experiment. The modification includes the use of two-step SIBAL fabric pyrolysis kinetics where the rate constants are determined using Thermo-Gravimetric Analysis data. The model yields good quantitative comparison on the quenching boundary, the flame transient development, and the steady flame spread rates.
1.2 Radiation Model and Spherical PMMA samples: Gas phase radiative heat transfer becomes especially important for flame spread over solid fuel in microgravity near the low velocity quenching limit, also known as radiative quenching limit. Near this limit the flame color of PMMA is blue due to the low soot content and therefore, spectral dependency of the radiative heat transfer becomes important. Commonly used radiation treatments such as gray gas model and wide band model face difficulty in obtaining accurate results in such condition. Moreover, being a diffusion flame prevents the usage of some of the popular special approximations such as spherical harmonics method since the absorption coefficient becomes zero in some wave lengths. This research overcomes such challenges by solving the radiation field around a PMMA sphere by Statistical Narrow-Band Correlated-k (SNB-CK) spectral model combined with three dimensional discrete ordinate method.
The model is applied to an experimental configuration from the recent microgravity BASS project aboard the International Space Station. A PMMA sphere (initial diameter of 2 cm) is placed in a small wind tunnel (8 cm x 8 cm x 17.5 cm) within the microgravity glovebox where flow speed and oxygen percentage are varied. The recorded flame spread rate after ignition at the forward stagnation point and radiative quenching limiting flame when flow velocity is reduced are compared with the model results.
2. Ground based Experiments
2.1 Droptower tests of instrumented PMMA sphere samples: A technique of making cast PMMA sphere sample with 5 small thermocouples embedded at different locations has been devised and three proto samples have been made by an outside manufacturer. One of the most recently made samples has been tested in the 5-s droptower. This is a transient experiment where a sample is ignited in normal gravity, left burning for a period of time until the prescribed sub-surface temperature gradient is reached before dropped in microgravity. Transient flame development is recorded. Three tests have been performed in 17% O2 with a forced 2 to 6 cm/s flow. Flames go out during the drop in all the three cases. To determine the flammable limits, more tests will be conducted once additional fabricated samples arrive. One of the purposes of this series of tests is to help us to define the preheating levels to be used in the flight experiment.
2.2. Gravimetric Measurement of Solid and Liquid Fuel Burning Rate near and at the Low Oxygen Extinction Limit: A precision mass balance coupled with a variable oxygen flow tunnel/nozzle enables us to measure the burning rate of solid and liquid fuels as a function of ambient oxygen percentage all the way to the extinction limit. Two sample configurations have been studied. The first is a liquid-fueled wick flame (ethanol tea lamp). The total burning rates (mass/time) are measured as a function of wick length and oxygen percentage. Near the low oxygen limit, limit-cycle flame oscillation has been found that can last for many minutes to an hour. The averaged mass burning rate of the oscillatory flame is about one-half of that of the neighboring steady flame. In the second configuration, local burning rates (mass/area time) of two Polymethylmethacrylate spherical samples have been measured in the flame stabilization zone. Each sample has a different amount of heat loss and a different oxygen limit. The critical burning rate at their respective oxygen limit are different. This implies that critical burning rate is not a property of the material alone and it should not be used as the only criterion to judge the extinction or the ignition of materials.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2016
Task Progress:
1. Numerical modeling for BASS experiments
1.1 Flat SIBAL samples
Flame growth, spread, and quenching extinction over a thin composite cotton-fiberglass fabric blend (referred to as the SIBAL fabric) were studied in low-speed concurrent purely forced flows aboard the International Space Station. The tests were conducted in a small flow duct within the Microgravity Science Glovebox. The fuel samples measured 1.2 and 2.2 cm wide and 10 cm long. Ambient oxygen was varied from 21% down to 16% molar concentration and flow speed from 55 cm/s down to 1 cm/s. A slow purely forced flow resulted in a small flame, enabling us to observe the entire history of flame development including ignition, flame growth, steady spread (in some cases), and decay at the end of the sample. In addition, by decreasing flow velocity during some of the tests, low-speed flame quenching extinction limits were determined as a function of oxygen percentage. The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher extinction speeds in lower oxygen atmospheres. The shape of the quenching boundary supports the prediction by earlier theoretical models. These long duration microgravity experiments provide a rare opportunity for solid fuel combustion since microgravity time in ground-based facilities is generally not sufficient. This is the first time that a low-speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread is mapped in a clean and unambiguous manner. A previously developed three-dimensional transient model is modified to compare with the experiment. The modification includes the use of two-step SIBAL fabric pyrolysis kinetics where the rate constants are determined using Thermo-Gravimetric Analysis data. The model yields good quantitative comparison on the quenching boundary, the flame transient development, and the steady flame spread rates (References #1 and #2).
1.2 Radiation Model and Spherical PMMA samples
Gas phase radiative heat transfer becomes especially important for flame spread over solid fuel in microgravity near the low velocity quenching limit, also known as radiative quenching limit. Near this limit the flame color of PMMA is blue due to the low soot content and therefore, spectral dependency of the radiative heat transfer becomes important. Commonly used radiation treatments such as gray gas model and wide band model face difficulty in obtaining accurate result in such condition. Moreover, being a diffusion flame prevents the usage of some of the popular special approximations such as spherical harmonics method since the absorption coefficient becomes zero in some wave lengths. This research overcomes such challenges by solving the radiation field around a PMMA sphere by Statistical Narrow-Band Correlated-k (SNB-CK) spectral model combined with three dimensional discrete ordinate method.
The model is applied to an experimental configuration from the recent microgravity BASS project aboard the International Space Station. A PMMA sphere (initial diameter of 2 cm) is placed in a small wind tunnel (8 cm x 8 cm x 17.5 cm) within the microgravity glovebox where flow speed and oxygen percentage are varied. The recorded flame spread rate after ignition at the forward stagnation point and radiative quenching limiting flame when flow velocity is reduced are compared with the model results. (PhD dissertation by Makoto Endo and Reference #3)

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2015
Task Progress:
BASS-II experiment aboard the International Space Station was conducted successfully. By August, 2014, all the samples have been burnt.
(a) Flame spread rate and extinction limits were obtained in purely forced flow in zero-gravity under various oxygen percentage for narrow Sibal fabric samples in a small wind tunnel inside the Microgravity Glovebox. Data are being analyzed and used to compare with model and to calibrate the model parameters.
(b) Ignition test on 4-cm partial sphere was conducted in BASS II. Sustained ignition requires more than 1 minute application of the present igniter. Such a long time is necessary because of the long heat-up time of the bulk solid. This test will help us to device ignition strategies in the GEL experiment.
(c) There is a plan to perform more tests using the partially burnt Sibal and PMMA sphere samples from the BASS I and II tests in ISS.
(d) Two cast 4-cm spherical PMMA samples with 5 embedded thermocouples were customarily made. Preliminary tests in a flow tunnel with variable oxygen percentage showed the thermocouples behaves properly.
Theoretical effort on the modeling of gas-phase radiation with spectral dependence is continuing. Requirement Definition Review (RDR) was conducted and completed in December 2014.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2014
Task Progress:
During this period, the following tasks have been performed:
(1) Prepare the Science Requirement Document (SRD) of GEL for the Science Concept Review (SCR) which is a part of the Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE) project. The review was held on July 9-10, 2013. The review panel recommended the continuation of the development toward the space experiments. In their report, the panel provided substantial comments and recommendations. To respond to the panels comments, a revised SRD for GEL was prepared. It will facilitate the writing of the consolidated SRD (combining all five project within SoFIE) to be drafted by the SoFIE project scientist Dr. Ferkul.
(2) The GEL experiment requires a PMMA spherical sample be instrumented with 5 internal thermocouples. Substantial effort was made to identify a vender who can custom cast the sample with thermocouple rake prepared by us. A scheme of making the rake has been designed and tested. We are currently waiting to the see the prototype be fabricated.
(3) Because gas phase radiation is important in combustion in space, a numerical model including flame radiation is needed. Previously we have used the commercial FLUENT code to model for the PMMA sphere combustion without flame radiation. Commercial codes are generally not easy to do detailed data analysis which is crucial in scientific research. To add flame radiation, Makoto Endo has chosen to develop his own combustion code. This work is in progress.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2013
Task Progress:
1. Ground-based experiment and numerical modeling
Ignition of a PMMA sphere using a hot wire igniter in normal gravity followed by transition into a forced convective microgravity environment has been studied experimentally in NASA’s 5.18 second drop tower and modeled using a transient numerical code. The flame is ignited at the forward stagnation region, and then the igniter is retracted. The flame is allowed to spread around the PMMA sphere before release into microgravity. The flame transitions to the new environment quickly, although the solid phase response time is longer than the available drop time. Depending on the oxygen concentration, the forced flow velocity and the degree of solid interior heating, the transition flame is either stabilized around the sphere or shrinks toward the forward stagnation point in a decaying mode. The transient numerical model reproduces the experimental sequences and provides more insight as microgravity computation can be performed in longer time durations. A direct comparison of the model and experiment has been made. The model predicts a slightly larger flame standoff distance, but the flame length and curvature is captured well.
2. Space experiment in BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids)
BASS is a rapid turnaround low budget experiment on the combustion of solid fuels currently being performed in the International Space Station. Small size samples are used in a small wind tunnel within the glove box. Among the several types of fuel samples, PMMA spheres with initial diameter of 1 and 2 cm were tested. In one of the BASS case, it took initially 25 sec for a PMMA sphere with 2-cm diameter to ignite. After some flame spread, the flame was extinguished by reducing the flow speed. When we re-ignited the sphere after some time, it took only 15 sec. Clearly there is an effect of pre-heating of the solid on ignition. In the spreading case, the initial flame is blue and weak in appearance. As the flame spread, the color becomes brighter and yellowish. This apparently stronger flame has an irregular flame shape due to fuel vapor sputtering. Both the ignition and the flame growth processes show that in-depth heating has a large effect on the flame characteristics. It should be noted that in the BASS experiment, the air is limited to ISS atmosphere which is 21±1% and one-atmosphere pressure. There is no monitoring of the internal sample temperature. In addition, the sample size is relatively small.
3. Numerical modeling of the burning of 4-cm spherical PMMA sample inside the CIR (Combustion Integrated Rig) chamber
As a preparation for experiment in the CIR chamber, graduate student Makoto Endo modeled the flow pattern in the entire chamber including a recirculation tube (for flow creation) and a 4-cm diameter PMMA sphere sample. The combustion model followed Sheng-Yen Hsu's with improved parameters. Besides the flame spread and solid heat up phenomena, it showed the ability of capturing the recirculation occurring in the CIR chamber which will affect the duration of experiment. This model is going through multiple updates and currently it takes the surface regression into account. The computed results show a complex flow pattern but the flow is well behaved near the test sample. In an example, the flame grows after ignition with a 20 cm/s flow with igniter on. At 60 seconds, the igniter is turned off. The advance of pyrolysis front slows down initially but resumes its rate later. At 90 s, the flow rate is reduced in several numerical experiments. When the flow is reduced to 10 cm/s, the flame retreats initially but resumes growth with a slower rate later. If the flow is reduced to 2 cm/s, the flame shrinks and becomes extinct. At the intermediate 7 cm/s, the flame front is stationary thus yielding a dividing limit between flame growth and extinction. This is of course a function of internal heating. This simulation demonstrated the capability that with computational fluid mechanics and computational combustion, the flow pattern in the entire test chamber can be included in the study of the combustion behavior.
