Task Description:
A ground-based experimental and theoretical project for flame spread and extinction over solid materials is proposed with the intention of leading to a flight experiment in the space station. The research will be fundamental in nature but has practical applications to spacecraft fire safety. The objectives are (1) to determine the flame spread and growth characteristics of solids in concurrent flow in reduced gravity, (2) to determine the mechanisms of flame decay and extinction, (3) to establish a high-fidelity numerical model that can simulate both normal and reduced gravity flames, including the interpretation of the results of NASA-STD-6001A test 1. We intend to study both fabric and thick solid samples. This ground-based research is to extend the previous experimental works on solid flame spread in reduced gravity that were almost exclusively limited to very thin samples and to enhance the model capability to a three-dimensional transient formulation. The ground-based experiments will utilize both the normal-gravity and zero-gravity facilities at NASA Glenn Research center. Considerable effort will be spent to plan a space experiment that has to be carried out in the currently available facility in the International Space Station (i.e. CIR). In addition to James T'ien (PI), Dr. Paul Ferkul (NCSER) and Dr. Sandra Olson (NASA GRC) will participate as Co-Is in the project.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
This is a fundamental study on the flammability of solids. The understanding to be achieved will help us to deal with fire safety on earth and in space.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2011
Task Progress:
Ignition of a PMMA sphere using a hot wire igniter in normal gravity followed by transition into a forced convective microgravity environment is studied experimentally in NASA’s 5.18 second drop tower and modeled using a transient numerical code. The flame is ignited at the forward stagnation region, and then the igniter is retracted. The flame is allowed to spread around the PMMA sphere before release into microgravity. The flame transitions to the new environment quickly, although the solid phase response time is longer than the available drop time. Depending on the oxygen concentration, the forced flow velocity and the degree of solid interior heating, the transition flame is either stabilized around the sphere or shrinks toward the forward stagnation point in a decaying mode. The transient numerical model reproduces the experimental sequences and provides more insight as microgravity computation can be performed in longer time durations.

NASA’s fire safety standards have not confirmed scientifically that they are always conservative for fire safety in space because the test is based on the flammability in the normal gravity. It is already known that a solid material’s flammability in microgravity may be greater than in normal gravity for some conditions. Therefore, whether the NASA's standards will be applied for future space missions by individual countries, or if better general standards for fire safety (e.g., oxygen index method) would be better for fire safety in space should be studied. This work aims to determine what standards are adequate for the evaluation of fire safety and material flammability in space.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Studying materials flammability in space allows us to accurately control the flow field and thus elucidate the importance of a critical Damkohler number (flow time /reaction time) on flame extinction. The anticipated improved methodology should reduce time and cost for the spacecraft material screening. Investigation and results have Earth benefits for terrestrial fire safety.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2022
Task Progress:
The Flammability Limits At Reduced-g Experiment (FLARE) project is a collaborative effort involving an international team, including the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA) and universities in Japan, USA, and France. The objective is to develop a method to correlate material flammability limits in normal gravity and microgravity. A quantitative estimation of material flammability limit in microgravity, based on the flammability data obtained on the ground, can then be generated. The NASA White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) role in this effort is to provide the ground testing used in the quantitative estimation. NASA/WSTF is also participating in the review and execution of the newly created ISO-4589-4 standard (Plastics – Determination of burning behavior by oxygen index – Part 4: High gas velocity test).
Tests performed by NASA/WSTF are also to evaluate the difference, if any, between the NASA-STD-6001 igniter and a hot wire igniter comparable to flight experiments. Comparison between the standard ignition and the proposed hot wire ignition methods is being performed for each of the test configurations (standard flat, rod, and wire samples). All testing with the exception of tests performed on the high gas velocity oxygen index (HOI) were executed using the Maximum Oxygen Concentration (MOC) test method. This method establishes a threshold oxygen concentration that represents the maximum oxygen concentration a material passes the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 criteria with a discrete test interval of 1% oxygen by volume.
In the beginning of 2019, JAXA personnel met with NASA/WSTF to discuss the progress of the project. Prior to JAXA’s visit, the HOI test system (ISO-4589-4 Test apparatus) and auxiliary equipment were shipped to NASA/WSTF and received in late 2018. During JAXA’s visit in January of 2019, WSTF personnel were trained on the function, calibration, and performance of the test method per JAXA’s instructions. During this visit, a draft of the ISO-4589-4 standard was also provided to WSTF personnel for review. At this point, WSTF personnel agreed to perform a minimum of two replicate test series for each material at each of three flow conditions (60, 80, and 100 cm/s) for a total of 30 test series. All samples were prepared by JAXA personnel and were provided to the NASA/WSTF team at the time the training was administered. All test data was provided to JAXA throughout the following months at the time of completion.
Several of the original materials first proposed by JAXA for 1-G NASA-STD-6001 (flat sheet, standard configuration) testing were determined too thick and cancelled during fiscal year 2019. Other materials were added to the test matrix to better align with the flight and parabolic flight experiments performed by JAXA. Final testing concentrated on thinner materials to reduce the ignition time, prolong hot wire igniter life, and reduce test variability by use of a single ignition profile for all materials within a given test method.
During the FLARE Technical Interchange Meeting (TIM) at the beginning of calendar year 2020, JAXA further expanded the test matrix utilizing the HOI apparatus. Materials added during this meeting included specimens used in the 1-G ground, flight, HOI, and parabolic flight tests. As in the previous year, the materials were added to the test matrix to better align the various test methods under evaluation. The beginning of calendar year 2020 also marked the beginning of the pandemic, during which limited site access to mission essential work. Progress on FLARE did not continue until the summer of 2021.
Upon commencement of the remainder of the flat specimen 1-G Test 1 materials, progress was made on the performance of flat specimens in the NASA-STD-6001 fixture. Additional material will be required to perform some of the 1-G NASA-STD-6001 Rod testing as well as the Rod and Wire testing to be performed in the HOI apparatus. These materials, in final configuration, will be supplied to NASA/WSTF by JAXA. Raw material may need to be supplied, dependent on current inventory, to JAXA by NASA/WSTF to produce the test specimens in the final configuration.
Currently, work has not started on the wire samples. Performance of the wire samples using a J-configuration is being investigated as a means to provide the most conservative ground test possible. Preliminary results on several materials, conducted by NASA/WSTF comparing the 15° and J-configuration surface ignition methods, indicate conservatism when using the J-configuration surface ignition method. No Rod or Wire testing has been performed in the HOI apparatus. JAXA is currently investigating the method of performing such tests and will communicate with NASA/WSTF once a procedure/test matrix is determined. This work is anticipated to begin later in calendar year 2022.
NASA/WSTF has reviewed ISO-4589-4 as part of JAXA’s standard creation process. NASA/WSTF has agreed to include a reference to the ISO document in the NASA-STD-6001 as a potential supplemental flammability test method. At this time, there is no plan to make ISO-4589-4 a required test per NASA-STD-6001.

The team is a combination of NASA Glenn Research personnel with experience in microgravity combustion and researchers from the National Institute for Standards and Technology who have extensive experience in smoke detection. The investigation will define an experiment that will make measurements of the particle size distribution of spacecraft smoke from a variety of spacecraft materials. The overall project objective is to improve the reliability of spacecraft fire detection by making measuremstns of the particle size distribution of spacecraft smoke. The smoke detectors currently used in NASA spacecraft are based upon understanding from 1-g smoke measurements. Experiments conducted aboard the space shuttle in 1996 demonstrated that the particle size distribution for various materials can change substantially and that smoke detector sensitivity in 1-g is not necessarily a good indicator for performance in low-gravity. This suggests that the reliability of spacecraft smoke detectors can be substantially improve dif they are designed based upon the smoke particulate properties of spacecraft smoke.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
Science concept definition: The investigation is in the science concept definition phase. A final draft of the Science Requirements Document has been written and subjected to internal review. At this point the project is ready for peer review once the panel is selected by Headquarters.
Development of flight diagnostics: One of the critical diagnostics for the Smoke experiment is a particle number counting device. Numerous systems exist but are limited by potential gravitational susceptibility. Working with the project team, a modified P-Trak- a type of CNC (condensation nuclei counter) has been developed which is believed will operate effectively in low-gravity. Specifically, the condenser in the unit has been modified to induce the flow of liquid alcohol back towards the saturator, largely independent of gravitational forces. This is accomplished through a series of precisely machined grooves which encourage the wicking of the liquid alcohol in the proper direction along the condenser’s inner wall. The design was developed following an analysis to measure the contact angle of isopropyl alcohol on the aluminum surfaces of the condenser. The hardware has been prepared for flight as a risk mitigation experiment and is ready for launch when upmass becomes available.
Aerosol Dynamics modeling: Two aerosol growth dynamics model have been developed at NIST. One model is a zero-dimensional model for a nucleating/condensing vapor that is isothermal and spatially uniform and the other model employs the NIST Fire Dynamics Simulator code. Both models have been used to predict smoke growth in the experiment hardware and have produced mutually consistent predictions of the condensation rate. Corresponding validation experiments are underway.

Task Description:
The basic experimental approach will be to use one flame to synthesize soot with subsequent injection into a second flame. Variations of flame conditions and geometries will provide for a selection of soot processes by which the objectives can be realized. Optical methods will be used to measure soot concentration, pyrommetry for soot temperature and gas temperatures using thermocouples. Velocity information, critical for determining residence time, will be obtained by PIV while key radical concentrations, such as OH and O2 will be measured by diode laser absorption spectroscopy.
Electron spectroscopic and microscopic techniques will be used to characterize the soot nanostructural evolution prior to and during growth, thermal and oxidative densification and oxidation. Analysis of the high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) image data will quantify changes in the soot graphitization level and be used to correlate both the development of nanostructure upon growth, temperature and oxidation conditions. Combined with primary particle size measurements, the impact of nanostructure upon these processes will be assessed.
To analyze soot nanostructure, assess its evolution, to synthesize and characterize fullerenes and fullerenic structures and investigate soot oxidation as a function of oxidant, temperature and nanostructure.
Specific objectives will be to show that a) soot growth conditions affect the resulting nanostructure (graphitization level and fullerenic structures), b) the initial soot nanostructure will impact the rate of soot oxidation, and c) oxidation in turn will alter the soot nanostructure, the degree depending upon the oxidation conditions. A final objective will to demonstrate that soot nanostructure, both nascent and as altered by oxidation will affect subsequent soot (re)growth.
Soot impacts the performance of power and propulsion systems, is a hazard of unwanted fires and is the main combustion generated pollutant. Responsible for an estimated 60,000 deaths per year in the United States alone, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)’s new Particulate Matter (PM) 2.5 criteria for particulate matter reflects increasing recognition of the health hazards associated with soot. Combustor ignitors and fuel injectors can become fouled with flame generated soot. Continuum radiation from soot is the main heat load upon combustor components and linings and is ultimately responsible for their failure. The spread of unwanted fires largely occurs through preheating from soot radiation. While an unwanted pollutant, soot also causes the release of substantial CO (carbon monoxide) emissions from fires and unburned hydrocarbons in engines. In contrast to seeking control of soot inception and growth, an alternative strategy is to focus on soot removal through oxidation. Current models for soot oxidation are inhibited by widely varying values for soot oxidation rates, differing by a factor of 20.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
By applying our fringe analysis algorithms to the soot samples from our collaborators, we believe we can use our results to both understand the combustion process by which the soot was formed, and identify the source of the soot.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2004
Task Progress:
The progress below covers the duration of the grant.
Title: Soot Oxidation: Dependence Upon Initial Nanostructure
Conclusions
The work reported here illustrates a dependence of the soot particle nanostructure upon synthesis conditions; namely temperature, time and initial fuel identity. Such structural variations in the graphene layer plane dimensions necessarily alters the ratio of basal plane versus edge site carbon atoms. A corresponding variation in the overall reactivity, reflecting an average of the different reactivities associated with these specific atomic sites arises. This variation is illustrated here between a disordered soot derived from benzene and a graphitic soot derived from acetylene. Their oxidation rates differ by nearly 5-fold. Curvature of layer planes, as observed for an ethanol derived soot, is found to substantially increase oxidative reactivity. Relative to fringe length as a manifestation of graphitic structure, curvature more effectively increases reactivity towards oxidation. Larger variations in oxidation behavior may be expected, depending upon the soot synthesis conditions. Other physical properties may similarly be affected.
Title: Soot Nanostructure: Dependence Upon Synthesis Conditions
Conclusions
As the results show, the nanostructure of soot does indeed depend upon its formation conditions. Fuel identity governs the soot nanostructure under specific combinations of temperature and residence times as dictated by flow rates. At 1250 ºC, fuel structure effects are hidden, as all fuels, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) tested produced an amorphous soot regardless of the flow rate. These results are interpreted as soot mass growth being dominated by PAHs.
An increased flow rate results in soot nanostructure that is controlled largely by the pyrolysis kinetics for the pure hydrocarbon fuels. Variation of the flow rate alters the pyrolysis chemistry; specifically the species that add mass to the soot particle. These in turn are dependent upon the temperature.
Title: Carbon Nanostructure Examined by Lattice Fringe Analysis of High Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy Images
In conclusion, a lattice fringe analysis program has been developed to quantify the data conveyed by HRTEM images. By providing a direct measure of the molecular level of graphitic structure, it is expected that its application could provide predictive capabilities for carbon reactivity, particularly towards oxidation. The robustness of this program is demonstrated by using a series of carbon blacks possessing different levels of graphitic structure, prepared at different heat treatment temperatures. Its credibility is benchmarked against a traditional measure of graphitic structure, as provided by Raman analysis. Lattice fringe length is found to be monotonic with the level of graphitic structure as provided by the ratio of the integrated intensities of the G/D spectral peaks in the Raman spectra. Reciprocally, for production purposes, the G/D band intensity ratio can serve as a direct measure of the lattice fringe reactivity.
Title: Analysis of HRTEM Images for Carbon Nanostructure Quantification
Conclusions
Our image processing algorithm has been expanded to extract fringe separation and tortuosity in addition to fringe length from HRTEM images. An image analysis algorithm has been developed to extract the different measures of lattice fringe length, separation distance and tortuosity from HRTEM images. Validation of the lattice fringe separation distance has been tested against a series of heat-treated carbon blacks representing samples possessing different levels of graphitic structure. The results are compared to X-ray Powder Diffraction (XRD) data and found to be in reasonable agreement. The ability of this algorithm to further distinguish soots based on fringe length and tortuosity is tested using a series of soots synthesized by pyrolysis of hydrocarbon fuels at different flow rates and temperatures within a tube furnace. Amorphous soots produced at low temperatures are contrasted with those produced using high synthesis temperatures. Fringe length increases and interlayer spacing decreases with the observable increase in graphitic structure and order. Alteration of fuel or mass growth species (achieved by varying flow rate in the pyrolysis process) produces significant curvature within the carbon lamella. The curvature is shown to result in an increase in the fringe spacing. Tortuosity provides a measure of the curvature of the layer planes which further distinguishes the nanostructure of these carbons from those with graphitic structure.

Task Description:
Fire protection on the Space Shuttle and International Space Station has been developed primarily through the modification of standard practices in terrestrial fire safety applications and experience gained throughout the history of the U.S. manned space program. The primary feature of a spacecraft fire protection strategy is material control and elimination of potential ignition sources. Underlying this strategy is that any ignition event that does start a fire will remain "small" and not spread until the fire is detected and the crew has time to respond. The fact that the ISS has only portable fire extinguishers is testimony to the role of the crew in the fire protection system. In the 20 years of Shuttle operation, there have been five potential fire-causing incidents of component overheating or electrical short-circuiting. In all of these incidents, the crew recognized and corrected the problem before the smoke detector actuated. While these incidents can be considered a success for the fire protection system, one has to wonder how long the event would have continued before the smoke detectors reached the alarm threshold. The current era of larger spacecraft with fewer crew members increases the likelihood that a pre-fire incident will occur in an unoccupied module.
Obviously, if the crew can detect the fire before the smoke detectors, fire precursors are present in the atmosphere that an appropriately designed and placed sensor could detect. The trick is knowing what compound or compounds to look for and in what concentrations. Smoldering and pyrolysis, common pre-fire events, generate substantial yields of volatiles (partial decomposition products) that could be used as pre-fire signatures. There are currently at least three research projects aimed at developing techniques for improved fire detection, all based on the measurement of gaseous products of combustion such as CO, NOx, HCN, HCl, and total hydrocarbons. These include several SBIR projects developing sensitive laser absorption techniques as well as the development of MEMS gas sensors being conducted at the NASA Glenn Research Center. While these sensors are promising for use in spacecraft because of their small size and low power requirements, a more basic problem exists – to make use of these sensors to detect a fire, one must know what chemical species and concentrations to look for.
Studies conducted in 1-g environments have measured the yield and identity of partial decomposition products as function of the rate of heating and oxygen concentration. Though insightful, buoyancy convolves the rate of heating with oxidizer entrainment and combustion product removal. Thus variability in partial decomposition products (identity and yield) and occurrence of secondary reactions of evolved volatiles can be obscured. The non-buoyant or weakly convective flows characteristic of a microgravity environment will alter the rates of oxidizer entrainment and combustion product removal. The tenet of this proposal is that the specific chemical reactions (and their products) can differ substantially in such environments. With smoldering or pyrolysis events as characteristic pre-fire and "fire" events, variability in the evolved partial decomposition products and their concentration has consequences for both fire detection and toxicological assessment.
The proposed study seeks to investigate the differences (identities and relative concentrations) of the volatiles produced by pyrolyzing and/or smoldering materials in a microgravity environment. Test materials will be representative of typical spacecraft materials and, where possible, will be tested in appropriate geometries. Wire insulation materials of Teflon, polyimide, silicone, and PVC will be evaluated using either cylindrical samples or actual wire insulation. Other materials such as polyurethane, polyimide, melamine, and silicone-based foams will be tested using cylindrical samples, in addition to fabric materials, such as Nomex. Electrical components, such as resistors, capacitors, circuit board will be evaluated.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Several design considerations for both detectors, fire suppression and materials (both structural and cosmetic) have been illuminated by these studies.
Specific recommendations follow:
Materials that evolve substantial particulate or CO under any conditions of pyrolysis of smoldering present either a direct health risk under such conditions or during extinguishment actions. Production of organic compounds such as carboxylic acids or inorganic acids such as HF or HCl will cause corrosion and quickly render environments non-habitable at very low (10’s ppm) concentrations. Given the low levels for toxicity associated with HF and HCl, coupled with relatively large amounts of such materials aboard a confined volume, advanced alternative wire insulation materials ought to be sought. So-called oily smokes or aerosols will pose daunting cleanup challenges. Other materials producing aerosols or particulate of unknown composition or with morphologies analogous to nanomaterials with known biological effects could pose long-term chronic toxicity. Advanced materials could mitigate these risks. For example, new clay-polymer or carbon-polymer composites not only have higher glass transition temperatures and depressed heat release rates but can even be rendered inflammable. Moreover our own measurements to be reported elsewhere have shown that release of toxic byproducts from smoldering or pyrolysis to be substantially mitigated by incorporation of these nanofiller materials.
Suppression activities ought to be thoroughly investigated. Altered temperatures and ambient environments will change pyrolysis and combustion modes leading to potentially drastic changes in byproduct identities and concentrations. For the materials studied here fire suppression could create a more hazardous environment than the original fire. Fortunately the effects associated with such transient actions associated with suppression can be adequately tested in low-gravity emulators such as drop towers and aircraft.
Side effects associated with particulate matter must be considered. Organic and elemental carbon particulate can clog filters and coat the interior of air-handling systems. Moreover high smoke concentrations can limit if not eliminate visibility and thereby inhibit or prevent evacuation.
Finally the health effects of these materials ought to be evaluated. The tar-like compounds could contain aromatic or highly substituted aromatics possessing –F, -OH, -COOH or other functional groups. Such chemical functionalities are known to be irritating to lung and epithelial tissue.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
Introduction
In complimentary work Thermal Gravimetric Analysis – Fourier Transform Infrared (TGA-FTIR), a so-called hyphenated technique was used to identify the gases evolved during smoldering and flaming combustion of polymers approved for spacecraft use. Performed at a constant heating rate, gases evolved during the temperature ramp are detected by FTIR. Comparison against reference library spectra permits identification of the various functional groups of gaseous components and molecular identification of smaller species. In this work segment FTIR spectra were collected at several points along the TGA curve beginning with the initiation of sample weight loss and at subsequent points in the temperature ramp. Conclusions are drawn summarizing the changes which occur in the stages of decomposition of the resins.
Conclusions
Evolved fire signatures from the combustion of six polymers approved for spacecraft were determined through two techniques. The gases produced at different stages of the fire were identified by TGA/FTIR and the quantification of specific gases was performed after the smoldering and flaming of these materials in the vertical furnace following the chromatographic analysis of the gas sample.
Among the great number of gaseous products identified by IR and quantified by GC, CO2 appears to be the predominant species corresponding to the complete thermal degradation in the atmosphere of air. However, this signature is produced in the middle and end of a fire event. We observed that clearly no single species serves as a consistent indicator for the detection of the initial fire. The most conservative sensor design should take in account the detection of more than one fire signature.

Underlying this strategy is that any ignition event that does start a fire will remain "small" and not spread until the fire is detected and the crew has time to respond. The fact that the ISS has only portable fire extinguishers is testimony to the role of the crew in the fire protection system. In the 20 years of Shuttle operation, there have been five potential fire-causing incidents of component overheating or electrical short-circuiting. In all of these incidents, the crew recognized and corrected the problem before the smoke detector actuated. While these incidents can be considered a success for the fire protection system, one has to wonder how long the event would have continued before the smoke detectors reached the alarm threshold. The current era of larger spacecraft with fewer crew members increases the likelihood that a pre-fire incident will occur in an unoccupied module.
Obviously, if the crew can detect the fire before the smoke detectors, fire precursors are present in the atmosphere that an appropriately designed and placed sensor could detect. The trick is knowing what compound or compounds to look for and in what concentrations. Smoldering and pyrolysis, common pre-fire events, generate substantial yields of volatiles (partial decomposition products) that could be used as pre-fire signatures. There are currently at least three research projects aimed at developing techniques for improved fire detection, all based on the measurement of gaseous products of combustion such as CO, NOx, HCN, HCl, and total hydrocarbons. While these sensors are promising for use in spacecraft because of their small size and low power requirements, a more basic problem exists – to make use of these sensors to detect a fire, one must know what chemical species and concentrations to look for.
Studies conducted in 1-g environments have measured the yield and identity of partial decomposition products as function of the rate of heating and oxygen concentration. Though insightful, buoyancy convolves the rate of heating with oxidizer entrainment and combustion product removal. Thus variability in partial decomposition products (identity and yield) and occurrence of secondary reactions of evolved volatiles can be obscured. The non-buoyant or weakly convective flows characteristic of a microgravity environment will alter the rates of oxidizer entrainment and combustion product removal. The tenet of this proposal is that the specific chemical reactions (and their products) can differ substantially in such environments. With smoldering or pyrolysis events as characteristic pre-fire and "fire" events, variability in the evolved partial decomposition products and their concentration has consequences for both fire detection and toxicological assessment.
The proposed study seeks to investigate the differences (identities and relative concentrations) of the volatiles produced by pyrolyzing and/or smoldering materials in a microgravity environment. Test materials will be representative of typical spacecraft materials and, where possible, will be tested in appropriate geometries. Wire insulation materials of Teflon_, polyimide, silicone, and PVC will be evaluated using either cylindrical samples or actual wire insulation. Other materials such as polyurethane, polyimide, melamine, and silicone-based foams will be tested using cylindrical samples, in addition to fabric materials, such as Nomex_. Electrical components, such as resistors, capacitors, circuit board will be evaluated.

Task Description: The detailed characterization of metal particle ignition and combustion requires spatial and temporal resolutions that can be achieved only with relatively larger particles (1-5 mm). To avoid the natural convection and liquid flow effects, experiments on combustion of such particles will be conducted in microgravity environment. Since duration of the investigated process is between 5 and 20 s, we plan to conduct experiments by using reduced-gravity research aircraft of NASA. The ignition and combustion will be studied by using a high-speed video camera, thermocouples and product composition analysis. The obtained experimental data will be used to model ignition and combustion of complex metal particles, accounting for characteristic features such as inter-metal reactions, cracking of solid shells, etc. This research is aimed at understanding fundamental problems in combustion of metals related to a number of applications, such as propulsion and power, Mars in-situ resource utilization, and advanced materials synthesis. Specifically, we plan to study combustion of complex particles involving two different metals, one of which forms the core (Al), and the other a thin shell (Ni, Co, Fe, Cu, etc.). It is important that the particles exhibit high combustibility in both oxidative and inert ambient atmospheres. In the latter case, combustion proceeds due to a high exothermic reaction between the metals, with the formation of solid products (e.g. intermetallics). The main goal of the project is to establish ignition and combustion mechanisms of single complex metal particles in inert (Ar, He) and oxidizer (O2, air, CO2) atmospheres. We plan to determine the ignition (e.g. temperature, delay time) and combustion (e.g. burning rate, flame structure) characteristics of single complex metal particles under different experimental conditions, such as particle composition and size, nature (inert or different oxidizing) of ambient gas. Special attention will be devoted to elucidating the roles of inter-metal reaction and physical processes in surface layers (e.g. cracking of the shell, melt spreading) in the ignition process of complex metal particles. The use of complex metal particles, instead of pure metals, in solid rocket propellants is a promising approach for the enhancement of engine performance due to easier ignition and reduced agglomeration. Further, the decrease in ignition temperature of metal fuel in Mars atmosphere is important for propulsion and power systems using Martian CO2 as an oxidizer.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
Combustion of complex metal particles is a novel method for production of a variety of materials, including intermetallics and ceramics. The knowledge obtained from this project will allow development of new technology for synthesis of advanced materials with tailored microstructures and properties.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress:
The experimental setup for studies on combustion of single complex metal particles under microgravity (parabolic flights) was completed. Structural analysis of the setup was made to confirm that the setup met the NASA requirements. Test Equipment Data Package was prepared and submitted to NASA along with the report on structural analysis. The setup passed safety review by NASA for experiments onboard C-9B aircraft.
The ignition of Ni-coated Al particles in Ar and CO2 atmospheres was studied under normal and reduced gravity conditions. The ignition temperature of single Ni-coated Al particles was found to be independent of the atmosphere (CO2 or Ar) and Ni content (provided enough Ni is present). This is the result of a common ignition mechanism, which relies on the sequential formation of NiAl3, Ni2Al3 and NiAl. It was further determined that melting of NiAl3 at 854°C plays a critical role in ignition, leading to self-acceleration of the reaction. Finally, despite the heterogeneous nature of the original particles (Al core and Ni shell), it is remarkable that the product phases are well-mixed. Experiments with Fe-coated Al particles were also conducted and, as a result, some specific features of the Fe coating were revealed.
Experiments in microgravity during parabolic flight were performed using both Ni-coated and Fe-coated Al particles. In total, 84 experiments were successfully completed, and analysis of the results is in progress. The work supported by this grant has been described in four journal articles, including two invited, and presented at five scientific conferences.

Task Description:
The detailed characterization of metal particle ignition and combustion requires spatial and temporal resolutions that can be achieved only with relatively larger particles (1-5 mm). To avoid the natural convection and liquid flow effects, experiments on combustion of such particles will be conducted in microgravity environment. Since duration of the investigated process is between 5 and 20 s, we plan to conduct experiments by using reduced-gravity research aircraft of NASA. The ignition and combustion will be studied by using a high-speed video camera, thermocouples and product composition analysis. The obtained experimental data will be used to model ignition and combustion of complex metal particles, accounting for characteristic features such as inter-metal reactions, cracking of solid shells, etc.

Task Description:
The goal of ATHINA is to examine the transition of flame fronts to flamelet spread. This occurs in low gravity near-limit conditions. In addition, for Fire Safety reasons it is necessary to examine the reverse transition, from flamelet spread to active flame spread. This might occur when a fresh quantity of air enters the region, and poses a serious fire hazard aboard spacecraft. ATHINA thus has a basic science component and a definite Fire Safety component.
The objective of ATHINA is to conduct basic science and applied engineering research on the flame-to-flamelet (and vice-versa) transition process. Experimental, theoretical, and numerical means are to be employed to that end. Fire Safety in space has become a larger concern as NAS has become more mission-oriented.
The significance of ATHINA appears in both its basic science implications (the flamelet regime being a troublesome intermediate between flaming and quenching in which the flame very capably "adapts" to maximize its survival in adverse conditions), and in its engineering implications (being directly concerned with fire and flame spread in near-limit microgravity environments). The importance to Fire Safety is the largest element of significance in this project.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits:
The device developed for ATHINA (earth-based), alternatingly called a "hele-Shaw" facility and a "Turing" facility (thus presently unnamed) is useful for assessing the fire hazard in tight spaces, such as narrow ducts and walls, where fires may be initiated.
Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2008
Task Progress:
Theoretical Progress: Theoretical work was carried out on two projects: (1) The “Fire Dynamics Simulator” (FDS) code of NIST, adapted to simulate flame to flamelet transitions on burning thin samples; (2) The 2-D physics based simulation of the ignition-to-flame-spread-transition problem, which was carried out in order to explore fundamental unsteady flame spread processes; This work was carried out by MSU graduate student Mr. Y. Long and PI I. S. WIchman. For (1) the NIST Fire-Dynamics Simulator (FDS) code was adapted to conduct a transient 3-D simulation of the transition from flame fronts to flamelet fronts. The goal was to simulate the experiments and to describe the flamelet transition processes, including flamelet formation, flamelet bifurcation and extinction. Certain features of the flame-to-flamelet transition, including the eventual bifurcations and extinctions that occur in real tests, were relatively successfully simulated in the numerical work. We were able in the simulation to examine the detailed flow and concentration and reactivity patterns near the flamelets and to draw important conclusions about the flamelet breakup or bifurcation. Certain parts of flamelets have locally higher reactivity and these increases can be exaggerated under some conditions. Under suitable conditions, bifurcation occurs. When conditions are not suitable, the flamelet extinguishes or continues to spread. For (2) we have continued to examine a 2-D ignition and transition to steady flame spread. Here we have conducted an analytical analysis and supplemented that with numerical simulations for comparison. Of interest are comparisons to the results predicted for certain “macro” parameters that dictate overall results, and additional comparisons to various “micro” parameters that govern the details of the flame structure as it spreads. The 2-D basic physics simulation has enabled us to compare our results to theoretical predictions. We have written a paper that is in its final editing stage prior to being submitted to a journal.
The work of (1) was summarized in the PhD thesis of Mr. Y. Long, which was entitled “A Numerical Study of Flame Spread over Thin Cellulosic Fuels in Microgravity” and which was successfully defended in December, 2007.
Experimental Progress: A new test facility was designed by M.S. student K. Adkins during this research period. This facility is almost constructed and requires only a few finishing steps. We plan to use this facility both to examine simulated low-gravity flame spread and to examine flame spread in narrow gaps and spaces. We have given the facility the new name “The Narrow Channel Apparatus” or NCA. .
Experimental Analysis Progress: We have prepared a lengthy paper describing some of the results, which was accepted for publication subject to minor revisions in Combustion and Flame. The title of the paper is “Flame Spread Over Thin Fuels in Actual and Simulated Microgravity Conditions,” by S.L. Olson, F.J. Miller, S. Jahangirian, and I. S. Wichman. A second paper on this subject, focused more on flame spread testing and the details of the operation of the NCA facility and based almost entirely on the M.S. thesis of S. Tanaya is under preparation for a journal such as Fire and Materials. The tentative title of this paper is “On the Uses of the Narrow Channel Apparatus in Evaluations of Flame Spread and Material Flammability,” by I. S. Wichman, S. L Olson, F. J. Miller and S. A. Tanaya.

Task Progress:
Progress has occurred in four areas:
1) A new "Hele-Shaw" or "Turing" facility has been built and tested at NASA. It is capable of examining high oxygen concentration environments. Extensive tests have been performed at various gap spacings and flow velocities. Task Description:
This is a collaborative effort of NASA Glenn Research Center, the University of California, San Diego and Princeton University, to advance scientific knowledge of droplet combustion. Experiments are planned for space platforms, including the International Space Station. By reducing buoyancy effects, space-based experiments contribute to improved understanding of droplet combustion. In preparing for space experiments, ground-based microgravity experiments and theoretical and computational analyses are performed by the co-investigators, and relevant instrumentation is improved.
The objective of this collaboration is to provide scientific support for fundamental, single component, isolated (free and tethered) droplet burning experiments to be performed on board space platform. The specific objectives of these studies are to provide fundamental results which impact fire safety issues in low gravity environments and to advance the scientific understanding of droplet burning/flame/extinction dynamics over characteristic times which can not be studied in ground based configurations. Engineering and design support functions contribute to: developing and refining methods to perform isolated droplet combustion experiments in general; determining and testing methods to acquire appropriate experimental observations; developing and evaluating methods for presenting and analyzing the collected data. Experimental support functions include: theoretical analyses to define appropriate experimental conditions and to analyze the experimental results obtained; bench scale and drop tower e xperiments to test and verify methodologies to be applied in the space-based experiments.
The overall purpose of the research is to achieve fundamental advances in the science of droplet combustion, which is central to a number of energy-producing devices and systems. In particular, unsteady liquid and gas phenomenon, and extinction chemistry of normal alkanes and simple alcohol's are investigated.

Task Description:
The overall objective of the FLEX experiments (Flammability Limit Experiment) is to improve fundamental knowledge of droplet burning and other combustion processes relevant to fire safety in manned space environments. Specific objectives are to investigate influences of low-gravity environments on flammability conditions of different fuels in different oxidizing atmospheres representative of fire-suppression scenarios.
The first phase of FLEX was a focused set of science objectives designed to address spacecraft fire safety concerns. The primary objectives were the assessment of flammability limits in a range of habitable atmospheres and fire suppressant efficacies. The second phase is FLEX-2 with a more expansive set of science objectives designed to investigate fundamental phenomena associated with (i) fuel sooting, (ii) development of reference fuels for fuel surrogates, (iii) low flow convective effects on diffusion flames, (iv) spacecraft fire safety, (v) droplet interactions in spray combustion, and (vi) condensed phase effects on burning using bi-component fuel blends.
The research team for FLEX comprises externally funded Principal Investigators (PIs) and internally funded PIs. The lead researcher is Forman Williams for both FLEX and FLEX-2 and can be considered the de facto “PI” for FLEX (i.e., the combined experiments). The externally funded PIs are grantees affiliated with universities. The internally funded PIs are Michael C. Hicks (NASA-Glenn Research Center-GRC), Daniel L. Dietrich (NASA-GRC), and Vedha Nayagam (Case Western Reserve University).

Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2016
Task Progress:
The overall objective of the FLEX experiments (Flammability Limit Experiment) was to improve fundamental knowledge of droplet burning and other combustion processes relevant to fire safety in manned space environments. Specific objectives were to investigate influences of low-gravity environments on flammability conditions of different fuels in different oxidizing atmospheres representative of fire-suppression scenarios. Experiments with hepane as the fuel and with methanol as the fuel were performed aboard the ISS.
The project, in general, involved basic flammability-limit investigations relevant to fire-safety issues for manned space flight. In standard fire-suppression techniques, a suppressant jet is directed towards a fire or a smoldering region. In considering these techniques for space applications, it is necessary to analyze the effect of suppressant transport to both the near-field and far-field of the region of interest. Fire prevention can also be implemented by modifying the atmospheric composition of the environment so as to reduce the likelihood of a self-sustaining combustion event. Finally, the flammability properties of materials can also be modified by the addition of materials which suppress ignitability, enhance charring of surfaces, or chemically inhibit self-sustained burning. The research addressed these aspects of fire safety in space.
Some general directions of thrusts were as follows:
1. Map the flammability boundaries for liquid fuel combustion in reduced gravity.
2. Quantify the suppressant effectiveness of various gaseous suppressants over the range of candidate atmospheric pressures and O2 concentrations.
3. Develop predictive theoretical analyses and chemical-kinetic schemes to model flammability boundaries as a function effective gravitational acceleration on the unique ambient conditions encountered in space-exploration applications.
4. Devise improved and validated reduced (simplified) sub-models of important physical processes (chemical kinetics, etc.) that can be used in simulations of large scale, ‘realistic’ fires.
5. Determine combustion characteristics of liquid-fuel droplets of ethanol, decane, and liquid-fuel mixtures in varying atmospheres that can improve understanding of means for achieving clean and efficient power production.
6. Analyze cool-flame quasi-steady combustion of alkane droplets, especially heptane, but also decane and octane. The research at University of California, San Diego (UCSD) resulted in a number of publications, including:
1. J. Dzik, V. Nayagam, and F. A. Williams, “Ignition and Combustion of n-Heptane Droplets in Carbon Dioxide Enriched Environments,” International Communications in Heat and Mass Transfer 37, 221-225 (2010).
2. M. C. Hicks, V. Nayagam, and F. A. Williams, “Methanol Droplet Extinction in Carbon-Dioxide-Enriched Environments in Microgravity,” Combustion and Flame 157, 1439-1445 (2010).
3. J. Urzay, V. Nayagam and F. A. Williams, “Theory of the Propagation Dynamics of Spiral Edges of Diffusion Flames in von Karman Swirling Flows,” Combustion and Flame 158 255-272 (2011).
4. V. Nayagam and F. A. Williams, “Analysis of the Melt Phase of a Rotating Polymer Disc Supporting a Diffusion Flame,” Journal of Fluid Mechanics 687, 238-253 (2011).
5. V. Nayagam, D. L. Dietrich, P. V. Ferkul, M. C. Hicks, and F. A. Williams, “Can Cool Flames Support Quasi-Steady Alkane Droplet Burning?”, Combustion and Flame 159, 3583-3588 (2012).
6. G. Paczko, N. Peters, K. Seshadri, and F.A. Williams, “The role of cool-flame chemistry in quasi-steady combustion and extinction of n-heptane droplets”, Combustion Theory and Modelling 18, 515–531(2014).

In addition, preparation of other manuscripts is in progress.
The first two publications report analyses of experiments performed in ISS, while the next two report analyses of ground-based experiments, in all cases with the relationships to fire safety kept in mind. The fifth publication is the formal announcement of the discovery of quasi-steady droplet combustion supported solely by cool-flame chemistry in the ISS experiments, which was not expected in advance and which made news and resulted in the planned CFI (Cool Flame Investigation) experiments. The next entry is a computational study of how this phenomenon can occur, and the last citation reports corresponding analytical developments describing this phenomenon. The penultimate work listed is a theoretical investigation preparing for future analyses of the structures of these cool flames, while the one before that reports further experimental results concerning these cool flames, from measurements made in ISS, along with their interpretation. Finally, the seventh paper is a report from the entire FLEX team concerning the full range of results flowing from the program.
Citations to these publications and others from the project are listed in the Cumulative Bibliography.

Task Progress:
The overall objective of the FLEX experiments (Flammability Limit Experiment) is to improve fundamental knowledge of droplet burning and other combustion processes relevant to fire safety in manned space environments. Specific objectives are to investigate influences of low-gravity environments on flammability conditions of different fuels in different oxidizing atmospheres representative of fire-suppression scenarios. Experiments with hepane as the fuel and with methanol as the fuel are in progress aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
During the reporting period, there was extensive discussion about the specific tests that were performed on ISS. The chemistry of combustion of the fuel affects the combustion and extinction conditions. Research at University of California San Diego (UCSD) addressed problems of improving chemical-kinetic descriptions. In particular, extensive consideration of cool-flame chemistry in normal alkane droplet combustion was completed. This aspect of the research will be a major activity in future work.
The project, in general, involves basic flammability-limit investigations relevant to fire safety issues for manned space flight. In standard fire-suppression techniques, a suppressant jet is directed towards a fire or a smoldering region. In considering these techniques for space applications, it is necessary to analyze the effect of suppressant transport to both the near-field and far-field of the region of interest. Fire prevention can also be implemented by modifying the atmospheric composition of the environment so as to reduce the likelihood of a self-sustaining combustion event. Finally, the flammability properties of materials can also be modified by the addition of materials which suppress ignitability, enhance charring of surfaces, or chemically inhibit self-sustained burning. The research addressed these aspects of fire safety in space.
During the previous reporting period, special attention was paid to combustion in atmospheres enriched in carbon dioxide. Burning at both normal pressure and elevated pressures was studied, and detailed consideration was given to effects of radiation, which can be enhanced in such atmospheres. Atmospheres containing carbon dioxide are especially relevant to fire-safety issues of ISS because its fire-suppression system is based on the use of CO2 extinguishers. This research helped to improve our understanding of the physical and chemical mechanisms by which these extinguishers function under microgravity conditions.
During the present reporting period, the unexpected dual-mode phenomenon of alkane droplets combustion, observed for the first time in ISS, has been addressed intensively. Possible explanations have previously been developed and evaluated, and a written communication about this unexpected phenomenon has been prepared. This was published in Combustion and Flame Flame 159, 3583-3588 (2012) and continues to attract a lot of attention. Besides our Princeton group, we now have leading groups in Italy and in Germany studying this new discovery. A joint paper on this topic with the collaborators in Aachen, Germany has now appeared: G. Paczko, N. Peters, K . Seshadri, and FA Williams, The role of cool-flame chemistry in quasi-steady combustion and extinction of n-heptane droplets, Combustion Theory and Modelling 18 (2014) 515–531. By adding cool-flame chemistry to the descriptions of the chemical kinetics, we are beginning to be able to reproduce these previously unexpected results. In particular, at UCSD reduced chemistry has now begun to be derived for this new mode of droplet combustion.

Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2019
Task Progress:
This research reflects an added scope of the FLEX project. The overall objective of the FLEX experiments (Flammability Limit Experiment) was to improve fundamental knowledge of droplet burning and other combustion processes relevant to fire safety in manned space environments. Specific objectives were to investigate influences of low gravity environments on flammability conditions of different fuels in different oxidizing atmospheres representative of fire-suppression scenarios. Experiments with hepane as the fuel and with methanol as the fuel were performed aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
The project, in general, involved basic flammability-limit investigations relevant to fire safety issues for manned space flight. In standard fire-suppression techniques, a suppressant jet is directed towards a fire or a smoldering region. In considering these techniques for space applications, it is necessary to analyze the effect of suppressant transport to both the near-field and far-field of the region of interest. Fire prevention can also be implemented by modifying the atmospheric composition of the environment so as to reduce the likelihood of a self-sustaining combustion event. Finally, the flammability properties of materials can also be modified by the addition of materials which suppress ignitability, enhance charring of surfaces, or chemically inhibit self-sustained burning.
The research addressed these aspects of fire safety in space. Some general directions of thrusts were as follows:
1. Map the flammability boundaries for liquid fuel combustion in reduced gravity.
2. Quantify the suppressant effectiveness of various gaseous suppressants over the range of candidate atmospheric pressures and O2 concentrations.
3. Develop predictive theoretical analyses and chemical-kinetic schemes to model flammability boundaries as a function effective gravitational acceleration on the unique ambient conditions encountered in space-exploration applications.
4. Devise improved and validated reduced (simplified) sub-models of important physical processes (chemical kinetics, etc.) that can be used in simulations of large scale, ‘realistic’ fires.
5. Determine combustion characteristics of liquid-fuel droplets of ethanol, decane, and liquid-fuel mixtures in varying atmospheres that can improve understanding of means for achieving clean and efficient power production.
6. Analyze cool-flame quasi-steady combustion of alkane droplets, especially heptane, but also decane and octane.
7. Develop theoretical descriptions of combustion and flame extinction in droplet burning, with special emphasis on cool-flame phenomena.
8. Study the differences in cool-flame behavior for dodecane and lower alkanes, and offer possible explanations for the differences.
9. Complete asymptotic analyses of combustion of normal alkanes supported by cool-flame chemistry.

Task Description: This is a collaborative effort of NASA Glenn Research Center, the University of California, San Diego and Princeton University, to advance scientific knowledge of droplet combustion and to investigate flammability and suppression of combustion at reduced gravity. Experiments are planned for space platforms, including the Internationa l Space Station. By reducing buoyancy effects, space-based experiments contribute to improved understanding. In preparing for space experiments, ground-based microgravity experiments and theoretical and computational analyses are performed by the co-investigators, and relevant instrumentation is improved. The objective of this collaboration is to provide scientific support for droplet burning experiments to be performed on board space platforms. The specific objectives of these studies are to pro vide fundamental results which impact fire safety issues in low gravity environments and to advance the scientific understanding of droplet burning/flame/extinction dynamics over characteristic times which can not be studied in ground based configurations. Engineering and design support functions contribute to: developing and refining methods to perform isolated droplet combustion experiments in general; determining and testing methods to acquire appropriate experimental observations; developing and evaluating methods for presenting and analyzing the collected data. Experimental support functions include: theoretical analyses to define appropriate experimental conditions and to analyze the experimental results obtained; bench scale and drop tower experiments to test and verify methodologies to be applied in the space-based experiments. The overall purpose of the research is to achieve fundamental advances that will aid in improving fire safety in space environments. In particular, unsteady liquid and gas phenomenon, and extinction chemistry of normal alkanes and simple alcohols are investigated.
Research Impact/Earth Benefits: Task Progress & Bibliography Information FY2006
Task Progress: A scientific review was presented successfully. A new test matrix was completed, involving studies of droplet combustion in different atmospheres, directed towards evaluating fire-safety hazards and mechanisms of fire suppression. In particular, because of the fire-suppression systems on ISS, atmospheres containing carbon dioxide are to be studied. The results are intended to improve knowledge of combustion relevant to fire protection in space environments.

Program--Element:
COMBUSTION SCIENCE--Gaseous diffusion flames
Task Description:
The effects of electric fields on flame shape and size, combustion chemistry, soot formation, and emission are investigated in this project. A microgravity environment is utilized to create a spherically symmetric flame on which a concentric spherical electrical field is superimposed resulting in a one-dimensional configuration. This facilitates study of the interactions between the electric field and the flame. Fuel issues through a spherical burner assembly and burns in the surrounding air to form a spherical diffusion flame. The burner is surrounded by a spherical Faraday cage. The burner and the cage serve as the two electrodes between which the electric field is applied.
The overall objective of this project is to establish a fundamental understanding of the effects of imposed electric fields on flame region. These effects include impact on flame sheet location owing to the ionic wind effects and changing in flame chemistry, soot formation and emission, and combustion efficiency. Experimentally obtained data will be used to validate models of the flame processes.
Understanding the interaction between the electric field and flame processes is of theoretical, as well as practical, importance. Knowledge about the effects of electric field on flames can be used for flame control, soot reduction and combustion efficiency improvement in a wide variety of combustors.
